books.title: Peripheries
books.subtitle: A Journal of Word, Image, and Sound, No. 8
books.description: Peripheries: A Journal of Word, Image, and Sound is a literary and arts journal based at Harvard Divinity School. Established in 2017, Peripheries publishes an annual collection of artistic work, including poetry, fiction, creative non-fiction, visual art that is, broadly understood, “peripheral” exploring the interstices between discourses, traditions, languages, forms, and genres. Each edition includes guest-edited folios on specialized themes.
books.bio: Sherah Bloor is the co-editor and co-translator with Tayseer Abu Odeh of the anthology You Must Live: New Poetry from Palestine . Her poetry collection, The Gathering , an epic in cantos, is forthcoming and her poems have appeared in Chicago Review, Colorado Review, Conjunctions, Dialogist, Lana Turner, and Paperbark, among other magazines.

books.title: Philology in a Digital Age
books.subtitle: Selected Papers
books.description:
Philology in a Digital Age: Selected Papers brings together more than four decades of scholarship by Gregory Crane documenting the evolution of Classical Studies during the rise of digital technologies—including both published and previously unpublished essays ranging from early proposals in the 1980s to recent reflections on the role of AI, open data, and multilingual inclusion in the humanities. Together, these essays trace the transformation of Greco-Roman philology as it enters a new phase of engagement with digital media.

Drawing on his unique perspective as a traditionally trained classicist, an early architect of the Perseus Digital Library, and a professor working across the disciplines of Classics, Digital Humanities, and Computer Science, Crane explores the profound implications of transitioning from physical to digital infrastructure, not only in terms of access and scale, but in rethinking the very practice and goals of philology. Emphasizing lived understanding over static texts or tools, he argues for a field that must continuously adapt to new technologies while remaining committed to open, inclusive scholarship. Philology in a Digital Age is both a record of a scholarly transformation and a call to envision the future of humanistic inquiry in a world of ubiquitous digitization.
books.bio: Gregory Crane is Winnick Family Chair in Technology and Entrepreneurship in the Department of Classical Studies, and Professor of Classical Studies and Computer Science, at Tufts University. He is also the Editor-in-Chief of the Perseus Digital Library, the largest open-source digital library about Greco-Roman culture.

books.title: Philosophy of Correctability
books.tagline: A profound rethinking of the political categories of openness and closedness.
books.description:
In a new work building upon his Philosophy of the Tourist , Hiroki Azuma reconsiders the connection between the figure of the tourist and that of the family. Setting out from the reevaluation of the family as a figure of containment following the COVID-19 pandemic, in this exploration of the inside and outside of community, Azuma questions the shifting values of openness and security, challenging the distinction between the openness of civil society and the closedness of the family, which he deciphers as an artefact of a Western philosophical standpoint in which polis is opposed to oikos .

Via Wittgenstein’s notion of family resemblance and Kripke’s interpretation of language games, Azuma develops a new concept of the family as a closed unit that is paradoxically open to drastic transformations of its own rules of inclusion. The tourist, an anomaloous agent that escapes Carl Schmitt’s opposition between friend and enemy, can then be reinterpreted as a familial figure.

In this subtle rethinking of some of the most fundamental categories of modern political economy, the topology of the open society is reconfigured beyond the opposition between conservatism and liberalism: through close readings of Rorty and Arendt, Azuma sketches out a new vision of an open polis supported by the transformative sustainability of the oikos .
books.bio: Hiroki Azuma is the founder of Genron, a publisher and live forum for critical thought in Tokyo, Japan. A leading cultural critic in Japan, he is the author of seven books, including Ontological, Postal , which won the 2000 Suntory Literary Prize, Otaku: Japan’s Database Animals , General Will 2.0: Rousseau, Freud, Google , and Philosophy of the Tourist .

books.title: Photography's First Century
books.subtitle: Masterworks from the Bibliotheque nationale de France
books.tagline: Through more than 150 images, this book traces the history of photography in France from the 1840s to the 1940s
books.description:
Drawn from the holdings of the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, one of the world’s largest and most comprehensive collections of photographs, the more than 150 images showcased in this book tell the story of the first hundred years of photography in France, from the rise of the Daguerreotype and the calotype in the 1840s to the age of modernism in the interwar period. Among the major artists included are Henri Le Secq, Gustave le Gray, Félix Tournachon (Nadar), Édouard Baldus, Louis-Émile Durandelle, Eugène Atget, Sonia Delaunay, André Kertesz, Rogi André, Man Ray, and Brassaï. The beautifully reproduced prints were chosen by Sylvie Aubenas, director of the Department of Prints and Photography and one of the senior scholars in the field, and Flora Triebel, an expert in photographs of the nineteenth century; both contribute insightful essays and detailed entries to the book, which will also include a preface by Gilles Pécout, president of the Bibliothèque nationale de France, a foreword by Kimbell Art Museum director Eric M. Lee, a technical glossary, a chronology, and a selection of key texts from the history of the photograph in France.

Distributed for the Kimbell Art Museum

Exhibition Schedule:

Kimbell Art Museum, Fort Worth

(October 4, 2026–January 17, 2027)
books.bio: Sylvie Aubenas is director, Department of Prints and Photography, and Flora Triebel is curator in charge, nineteenth-century photographs, Department of Prints and Photography, both at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris. George T. M. Shackelford is deputy director of the Kimbell Art Museum, Fort Worth.

books.title: Reflections from a Cinematic Cesspool
books.tagline: A rollicking picaresque memoir on moviemaking from the titans of underground trash cinema.
books.description:
In the underbelly of underground cinema, the Kuchar brothers have long been the prophets of experimental filmmaking. Reflections from a Cinematic Cesspool is a raucous journey through the minds of these two transcendent artists.

The works of George and Mike Kuchar defy every convention of filmmaking. Reflections from a Cinematic Cesspool is their manifesto and their memoir, revealing the passionate madness behind films that challenge, shock, and inspire generations of underground artists and serve as a manual to all filmmaking freaks. John Waters sets the stage with his introduction celebrating the Kuchars' uncompromising vision. Here are the stories and secrets behind legendary works like Sins of the Fleshapoids , Hold Me While I'm Naked , and The Devil's Cleavage .

Irreverent, hilarious, and deeply personal, Reflections from a Cinematic Cesspool is a direct feed to the most gloriously deranged minds in independent film history.

Copublished with Varichon & Cie.
books.bio:
George Kuchar (Author)

George Kuchar was born in New York City in 1942 along with twin brother Mike. At an early age they made 8mm films and later attended the High School of Industrial Art in N.Y.C. (which is now the High School of Art and Design). Employed in the world of commercial art in Manhattan, George Kuchar was later laid off from work and never went back to that snake-pit; instead, he embarked on a fulltime movie career. Having been introduced to the avant-garde film scene in the early 1960s, he acquired an audience for his low-budget dramas and was hired by the San Francisco Art Institute to teach filmmaking. In 1985 he began making 8mm video diaries and has completed about 50 works in that medium. George died in 2011.

Mike Kuchar (Author)

Mike Kuchar has been a major influential figure in the underground film and comics scenes since the 1960s, first in his hometown of the Bronx and, from the 1970s on, in the creative hotbed of San Francisco. Together with his twin brother George, the Kuchars gained cult recognition for their over-the-top, no-budget films that sent up Hollywood epics, weepy romances, and sci-fi B movies, developing a distinctive style that jettisoned traditional narrative structure and acting professionalism in favor of extravagant, tender sagas that would have a significant impact on emerging theorizations and expressions of camp as an artistic sensibility.

books.title: Sculpture and the Making of the Human
books.tagline: A celebrated scholar’s profound examination of sculpture, making, and the nature of humanity
books.description:
What is sculpture? In this elegant volume, Anne Middleton Wagner delves into that essential question, juxtaposing carvings and ceramics from prehistory to contemporary works by Martin Puryear, Charles Ray, Rachel Whiteread, and others. In the process, Wagner argues that sculpture is a central means by which human beings have come to terms with the material world and their place within it.

The book is organized into chapters devoted to a single, foundational material—clay, wood, metal, stone, and plaster—tracing their use through millennia. Beautifully illustrated with works such as the Venus of Willendorf, Donatello’s Penitent Magdalene , and Michelangelo's David, it explores sculpture’s special blending of physical presence and imaginary perfection. Revealing the different ways in which sculpture embodies and transforms human beings, Sculpture and the Making of the Human will be essential reading in the history of art.
books.bio: Anne Middleton Wagner is professor emerita at the University of California, Berkeley.

praise.q: Unusually ambitious in scope and driven by Wagner’s ethical imperative, Sculpture and the Making of the Human is an exemplary articulation of a humanist understanding of sculpture.
praise.by: Alex Potts, author of The Sculptural Imagination: Figurative, Modernist, Minimalist
praise.cred: author of The Sculptural Imagination: Figurative, Modernist, Minimalist

praise.q: Wonderful—there is no book on sculpture like this. Teachers, artists, and devotees of art-guided thinking will devour, trade, and debate this book for years to come.
praise.by: Darby English, author of To Describe a Life: Notes from the Intersection of Art and Race Terror
praise.cred: author of To Describe a Life: Notes from the Intersection of Art and Race Terror

books.title: Sixty Miles Upriver
books.subtitle: Gentrification and Race in a Small American City
books.tagline: An unvarnished portrait of gentrification in an underprivileged, majority-minority small city
books.description:
Newburgh is a small postindustrial city of some twenty-eight thousand people located sixty miles north of New York City in the Hudson River Valley. Like many other similarly sized cities across America, it has been beset with poverty and crime after decades of decline, with few opportunities for its predominantly minority residents. Sixty Miles Upriver tells the story of how Newburgh started gentrifying, describing what happens when White creative professionals seek out racially diverse and working-class communities and revealing how gentrification is increasingly happening outside large city centers in places where it unfolds in new ways.

As New York City’s housing market becomes too expensive for even the middle class, many urbanites are bypassing the suburbs and moving to smaller cities like Newburgh, where housing is affordable and historic. Richard Ocejo takes readers into the lives of these newcomers, examining the different ways they navigate racial difference and inequality among Newburgh’s much less privileged local residents, and showing how stakeholders in the city’s revitalization reframe themselves and gentrification to cast the displacement they cause to minority groups in a positive light.

An intimate exploration of the moral dilemma at the heart of gentrification, Sixty Miles Upriver explains how progressive White gentrifiers justify controversial urban changes as morally good, and how their actions carry profound and lasting consequences for vulnerable residents of color.
books.bio: Richard E. Ocejo is professor of sociology at John Jay College and the Graduate Center, City University of New York. He is the author of Masters of Craft: Old Jobs in the New Urban Economy and Upscaling Downtown: From Bowery Saloons to Cocktail Bars in New York City (both Princeton).

praise.q: An engaging narrative that enhances our understanding of gentrification in smaller cities. As cities and the forces driving gentrification evolve continually, [ Sixty Miles Upriver ] provides a valuable addition to the field.
praise.by: Mario Hernandez, The Metropole

praise.q: Gentrification used to be a term associated with dense urban neighborhoods—but not anymore. Remote work and digitally enabled Zoom towns have put small communities in the Hudson Valley squarely in the crosshairs. In this engaging work, Richard Ocejo examines the economic contradictions and cultural challenges that this escalating process brings.
praise.by: Richard Florida, author of The Rise of the Creative Class
praise.cred: author of The Rise of the Creative Class

praise.q: Sixty Miles Upriver is a richly insightful account of how a small city experiencing new patterns of gentrification has become the center of complex negotiations over place, politics, discourse, and culture. This book will have a profound impact on the way we write and think about gentrification, race, and urbanism.
praise.by: Brandi Thompson Summers, author of Black in Place: The Spatial Aesthetics of Race in a Post-Chocolate City
praise.cred: author of Black in Place: The Spatial Aesthetics of Race in a Post-Chocolate City

praise.q: Ocejo illuminates the conflicts in a municipality grappling with issues of poverty and diversity, and a desire to stimulate neighborhood revitalization without advancing racial inequality. A nuanced account of a neglected American narrative, this is a must-read for anyone who wants to know what happens when a small city simultaneously pursues gentrification and equitable development.
praise.by: Derek S. Hyra, author of Race, Class, and Politics in the Cappuccino City
praise.cred: author of Race, Class, and Politics in the Cappuccino City

praise.q: A welcome addition to the literature on gentrification, Sixty Miles Upriver sheds light on the moral calculus that gentrifiers rely on as they transform the places they seek out and value. This engaging and timely book is a testament to the importance of studying smaller places, and, more specifically, of charting how gentrification unfolds across different scales, not just in the big metropolises on which most research focuses.
praise.by: Japonica Brown-Saracino, Boston University

books.title: The Death of Socrates
books.subtitle: Hero, Villain, Chatterbox, Saint
books.tagline: “An exceptionally lucid introduction to this famous trial and death . . . The history of the interpretation of Socrates’ death, it turns out, is in large part the history of philosophy itself.” —Thomas Meaney, Wall Street Journal
books.description:
There were heroic lives and deaths before and after, but none quite like that of Socrates. He died not by sword or spear, braving all to defend home and country, but as a condemned criminal, swallowing a painless dose of poison. And yet Socrates’ death in 399 BCE has figured large in our world ever since, shaping how we think about heroism and celebrity, religion and family life, state control and individual freedom, the life of the intellectual and of the ordinary citizen. In The Death of Socrates , best-selling translator and classicist Emily Wilson analyzes the enormous and enduring power that the trial and death of Socrates has exerted over the Western imagination.

Wilson offers a critical and comprehensive look at the death of Socrates as both a historical event and a controversial cultural ideal. She considers works by Plato, Cicero, Milton, Voltaire, Hegel, and Brecht, among others, that used the death of Socrates to discuss power, politics, religion, the life of the mind, and the good life. Wilson vividly shows how Socrates’ death—more than his character, actions, or philosophical beliefs—has mattered so much, for so long, to so many different people.
books.bio: Emily Wilson is a professor of classical studies at the University of Pennsylvania. She has been named a fellow of the American Academy in Rome, a Guggenheim Fellow, and a MacArthur Fellow. In addition to best-selling editions of Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey , she has published translations of Sophocles, Euripides, and Seneca.

praise.q: An exceptionally lucid introduction to this famous trial and death...The history of the interpretation of Socrates' death, it turns out, is in large part the history of philosophy itself.

Wilson has provided an invaluable resource for understanding the role of Socrates in western intellectual and artistic traditions. Moreover, she shows that Socrates’ presence in cultural history is not limited to texts and art of the highly educated but extends to various manifestations of the popular imagination.
Excellent…Wilson's work is primarily concerned with Socrates's posthumous career as (variously) martyr, hero, villain and saint.
Written with commendable clarity and punch. Professional philosophers and amateurs alike will find in it considerable food for thought.
This provocative and challenging work serves as a gadfly to enliven and deepen thought about the life of Socrates.

As imagined by Wilson, The Death of Socrates is therefore very much a story about a life of becoming that compels us, centuries later, to follow the example of Socrates, a philosopher who managed to be mythic and reflective and irritating in almost equal measure.

books.title: The Phenoumenodelic Ark
books.subtitle: Passages in the Wake of Pleromatica
books.authors: Edited by Jean-Christophe Goddard and Maya B. Kronic
books.tagline: Mapping out multiple paths through Gabriel Catren’s innovative psychedelic work of transcendental philosophy.
books.bio:
Jean-Christophe Goddard (Editor)

Jean-Christophe Goddard is a professor in philosophy at Université Toulouse-Jean Jaurès. He has published a number of works on post-Kantian German Idealism and twentieth-century French philosophy. For the last twelve years his work has focused on decolonial and feminist critical theory, contemporary African philosophy, and Amazonian counter-anthropology.

Maya B. Kronic (Editor)

Maya B. Kronic is a philosopher and Head of Research and Development at Urbanomic. The agent, patient, and product of ongoing research project on gender hyperstition and a recrypted philosopher, she is the co-author, with Amy Ireland, of Cute Accelerationism (Urbanomic, 2024).

books.title: The Philosophy of Biophysics
books.authors: Edited by Margarida Hermida and James Ladyman
books.tagline: A pioneering volume on the philosophy of interdisciplinary fields of biophysics, biochemistry, astrobiology, and origins of life research.
books.description:
The Philosophy of Biophysics brings together contributions from leading philosophers of biology across the globe to address the conceptual, foundational, and philosophical issues raised by biophysics. The contributions shed light on how physics and biology are integrated in scientific practice and contribute to a better understanding of the relationship between biology and other sciences. With chapters authored by experts in a number of fields, the book will inform debates on interdisciplinarity, causal explanation at different scales, the question of how biology relates to the physical sciences, and the unity of science.

The book:

— interweaves philosophical analysis and scientific details

— addresses causation, mechanisms, laws, reduction, and scientific methodology

— covers various areas of biophysics

— features collaborative work by philosophers and scientists
books.bio:
Margarida Hermida (Editor)

Margarida Hermida is a Postdoctoral Researcher at the University of Salzburg, and previously she held a Jacobsen Fellowship for her project The Physics of Life at King’s College London. Her work has been published in Philosophy of Science , Erkenntnis , and other journals.

James Ladyman (Editor)

James Ladyman is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Bristol and Past President of the British Society for the Philosophy of Science. He is an Associate Editor of Studies in History and Philosophy of Science . He founded the University of Bristol’s Centre for Science and Philosophy and is patron to the trustees of the philosophy in education charity Thoughtful.

books.title: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga
books.subtitle: C. G. Jung Seminars, 1932
books.tagline: Jung’s landmark seminar on Kundalini yoga and the symbolic transformations of inner experience
books.description: C. G. Jung’s seminar on Kundalini yoga, presented to the Psychological Club in Zurich in 1932, is widely regarded as a milestone in the psychological understanding of Eastern thought. Kundalini yoga presented Jung with a model for the developmental phases of higher consciousness, and he interpreted its symbols in terms of the process of individuation. The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga brings together these lectures and seminar discussions into a single illuminating volume. It gives today’s readers an appreciation of some of the questions that stirred the minds of analysts in the 1930s: What is the relation between Eastern schools of liberation and Western psychotherapy? What connection is there between esoteric religious traditions and spontaneous individual experience? What light do the symbols of Kundalini yoga shine on conditions diagnosed as psychotic? The book also includes a seminar by the Indologist Wilhelm Hauer, presented in conjunction with Jung’s own, and Sir John Woodroffe’s classic translation of the tantric text, the Sat-cakra Nirupana .
books.bio: C. G. Jung (1875–1961) was one of the most important psychologists of the twentieth century and the founder of analytical psychology. Sonu Shamdasani is Professor of Jung History and Co-Director of the Health Humanities Centre at University College London and the editor of Jung’s Red Book .

praise.q: The Psychology of Kundalini Yoga serves as an excellent introduction to the higher realms of consciousness. . . . I enthusiastically recommend this book as an introduction to realms of analytic thought generally outside the classical and mainstream views.
praise.by: David Nichol, Psychoanalytic Books: A Quarterly Journal of Reviews
praise.cred: Psychoanalytic Books: A Quarterly Journal of Reviews

praise.q: In these four lectures . . . Jung placed some very complex Indian concepts within the Western psychological understanding of his time, thereby helping us to grasp better both systems of thought and realization.
praise.by: Betsy Halpern, Quadrant

praise.q: Shamdasani has performed a valuable service by editing these seminar notes and making them available to a wider audience. In addition to Jung’s four lectures [he] provides an excellent introduction as well as informative footnotes. . . . A welcome addition.
praise.by: William E. Kotsch, Journal of Analytical Psychology

books.title: Threats to Power
books.subtitle: Methane Extraction on Lake Kivu, Rwanda
books.tagline: How a dangerous gas becomes a tool of national repair in post-genocide Rwanda.
books.description:
At the border of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo sits Lake Kivu, an infamous freshwater lake whose scenic beauty conceals vast stores of methane and carbon dioxide. On its shores, internationally financed companies, in partnership with the Rwandan state, have built the world’s only dissolved-methane-to-electricity project.

In Threats to Power , Kristin Conner Doughty situates these projects within the long shadow of Rwanda’s post-genocide reconstruction, asking how a lake came to be understood as an existential danger in a region shaped by devastating human violence. Drawing on ethnographic research conducted with engineers, government officials, and communities around Kivu, Doughty examines efforts to transform methane from threat to resource—and what these efforts reveal about the exercise of contemporary forms of power. Bringing energy into conversation with carceral geography and war ecologies, the book traces how a dangerous gas becomes a tool of national repair, uncovering the fraught relationships among technological promise, sovereign power, and the lived realities of those who dwell at the lake’s edge.
books.bio: Kristin Doughty is Associate Professor of Anthropology at the University of Rochester. Her research has been funded by grants from the National Science Foundation, Wenner-Gren, and the Fulbright Programs. She is the author of Remediation in Rwanda .

praise.q: Ethnographically rich and analytically incisive, Threats to Power fundamentally reframes how we understand renewable energy, showing that transitions are always also transformations of power, territory, and belonging.
praise.by: Omolade Adunbi, author of Enclaves of Exception: Special Economic Zones and Extractive Practices in Nigeria
praise.cred: author of Enclaves of Exception: Special Economic Zones and Extractive Practices in Nigeria

praise.q: Threats to Power is of value to those concerned with green energy, carceral projects, and the innovations that emerge from the alliance of states’ agendas and scientific expertise. Charting a path from critique to engaged scholarship linking Central Africa and the contemporary US, the book’s powerful postscript works to envision alternative ‘abolitionist’ energy ecologies.
praise.by: Brenda Chalfin, author of Waste Works: Vital Politics in Urban Ghana
praise.cred: author of Waste Works: Vital Politics in Urban Ghana

books.title: Two Women
books.tagline: The fictionalized, intertwining lives of two remarkable figures whose stories trace the contours of the twentieth century.
books.description:
In Two Women , Jacqueline Rose fictionalizes and intertwines the lives of two remarkable figures whose stories trace the contours of the twentieth century: Edith Stein, the German–Jewish philosopher, Catholic convert, and saint; and Gillian Rose, philosopher of German–Jewish thought, also a convert, and Jacqueline’s sister. Through a luminous weaving of fiction and history, Rose traces the parallels and distances between these women—their intellect, faith, suffering and courage—while also confronting the mysteries of love, loss, and belonging that shape every human life.

A deeply moving work, Two Women is at once an act of remembrance and a daring work of imagination by one of the most important feminist writers of our time.
books.bio: Jacqueline Rose is internationally recognized as one of the most important living feminist and cultural critics. She is the co-director of the Birkbeck Institute for the Humanities, a co-founder of Independent Jewish Voices, and a fellow of the British Academy and of the Royal Literary Society. Rose is a frequent contributor to the London Review of Books and the Guardian , among many other publications. Her books include Sexuality in the Field of Vision , The Haunting of Sylvia Plath , States of Fantasy , Women in Dark Times , Mothers: An Essay on Love and Cruelty , On Violence and On Violence Against Women , and The Plague .

books.title: Visions
books.subtitle: C. G. Jung Seminars, 1930–1934 (Volume 2)
books.tagline: Volume two of Jung’s legendary talks on the archetypal visions of one of analytical psychology’s most intriguing figures
books.description: For C. G. Jung, the beautiful and gifted twenty-eight-year-old Christiana Morgan was an inspirational force whose path in self-analysis paralleled his own quest for self-knowledge. Teaching Morgan the trance-like technique of active imagination, Jung launched her on a pilgrimage of archetypal encounters in a quest for psychological integration—encounters she recorded in the words and paintings that formed the basis of the seminar Jung would give to his circle in Zurich, presented here in the second of two volumes. Jung speaks candidly about Morgan’s visions even as he struggles with the feminine principle in his subject and his own psyche. The theories from his years of intellectual research—the anima and animus, the process of individuation, the mythopoetic archetypes of the collective unconscious—all spring to life in the fiery imagery of Morgan’s imaginal landscape. Recounting her journey, Jung employs his full range of scholarship and professional experience as he unravels the skein of archetypal parallels from Western myth and Eastern yoga.
books.bio: C. G. Jung (1875–1961) was one of the most important psychologists of the twentieth century and the founder of analytical psychology. Claire Douglas is a clinical psychologist and Jungian analyst and the author of Translate This Darkness: The Life of Christiana Morgan, the Veiled Woman in Jung’s Circle (Princeton).

praise.q: The Visions seminars constitute a brilliant and demanding masterpiece that was too long circulated in small circles and kept secret from the general public. The publisher and editor are to be congratulated for bringing this noteworthy historical work into the public domain.
praise.by: Polly Young-Eisendrath, coeditor of The Cambridge Companion to Jung
praise.cred: coeditor of The Cambridge Companion to Jung

books.title: Visions
books.subtitle: C. G. Jung Seminars, 1930–1934 (Volume 1)
books.tagline: Volume one of Jung’s legendary talks on the archetypal visions of one of analytical psychology’s most intriguing figures

Teaching Morgan the trance-like technique of active imagination, Jung launched her on a pilgrimage of archetypal encounters in a quest for psychological integration—encounters she recorded in the words and paintings that formed the basis of the seminar Jung would give to his circle in Zurich, presented here in the first of two volumes. books.title: Wagner
books.subtitle: Philosophy and Revolution
books.tagline: Wagner as revolutionary philosopher: a new reading of a trilogy of texts written by the composer in the aftermath of the failed Dresden Uprising
books.description:
Forced into exile to avoid arrest after taking part in the failed Dresden Uprising in 1849, Richard Wagner turned to philosophical writing, producing in rapid succession three theoretical works. In this compelling study, Brian O’Connor traces Wagner’s emergence in these texts as a radical political thinker with a distinctive revolutionary vision. O’Connor describes Wagner’s transformation from publicly engaged commentator to active insurrectionist, showing how revolution’s failure redirected Wagner’s energies toward systematic philosophical reflection. For a crucial period, this theoretical work took precedence over musical composition.

At the heart of O’Connor’s account is Wagner’s philosophical imagination. He explores Wagner’s conception of aesthetic spontaneity as a model of individual freedom and his belief in collective artistic creation as the foundation of a liberated society. By situating Wagner’s philosophy within the turbulent political and intellectual context of the time, O’Connor challenges its marginalization in previous accounts, restoring it to its proper place in nineteenth-century political thought. He shows how Wagner reworked ideas drawn from the German philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach into an original and provocative form of aesthetic materialism, and examines the interplay between these ideas and Wagner’s dramatic works. O’Connor also offers a straightforward treatment of the unavoidable subject of Wagner’s antisemitism, as expressed in an essay from 1850 about “Jewishness” in music.

O’Connor argues that Wagner’s philosophical writing is not only significant in its own right, but it also offers unique and invaluable insights into his music dramas—particularly the composer’s most celebrated work, the Ring cycle—illuminating their themes, characters, and revolutionary affinities.
books.bio: Brian O'Connor is professor of philosophy at University College Dublin. He is the author of Idleness: A Philosophical Essay (Princeton), Adorno , and Adorno’s Negative Dialectic .

praise.q: This contribution to the voluminous literature on Wagner amply justifies itself through genuine originality and careful argument, born in close study of the texts and their broader context. In its treatment of the trilogy of theoretical writings at its heart, it makes an excellent case both for their importance and for that of the author’s particular interpretation and synthesis.
praise.by: Mark Berry, author of Treacherous Bonds and Laughing Fire: Politics and Religion in Wagner’s “ Ring ”
praise.cred: author of Treacherous Bonds and Laughing Fire: Politics and Religion in Wagner’s “ Ring ”

praise.q: There is no other work with this level of conceptual sophistication that is specifically focused on the theoretical ideas underpinning Wagner’s work, as set out in a trio of important writings from the 1840s and early 1850s. This book will be a landmark in the literature considering Wagner’s philosophical significance.
praise.by: Andrew Huddleston, author of Nietzsche on the Decadence and Flourishing of Culture
praise.cred: author of Nietzsche on the Decadence and Flourishing of Culture

praise.q: Brian O’Connor’s new study of Wagner is a brilliant act of retrieval. Focusing on the neglected philosophical works, it illuminates Wagner’s sophisticated accounts of aesthetic value and revolution, inspired by the promise of 1848. At once probing and sympathetic, the book recovers fascinating dimensions of the creative life of an artistic genius.
praise.by: Richard Bourke, University of Cambridge

praise.q: Richard Wagner’s philosophical ideas are expressed in his music dramas, but also in several important, but not always well-structured, theoretical works. Brian O’Connor in his new book displays his characteristic erudition, acuity, hermeneutic skill and a scrupulous impartiality in uncovering, expounding and evaluating Wagner’s highly original philosophy, focusing on the prose treatises of the early period. This is the Wagner who is a philosopher of revolution, and O’Connor’s book is an indispensable key to understanding what is one of the major emancipatory projects of modern culture.
praise.by: Raymond Geuss, University of Cambridge

praise.q: Before Wagner came under the influence of Schopenhauer and morphed into the music master of Bismarck’s unified Germany, he was a fervent propagandist of revolution in politics, art and society. Brian O’Connor’s most welcome study presents Wagner’s revolutionary writings from 1848 through 1852 with an innovative focus on Wagner’s key philosophical concepts and their continued importance in his four-part music drama, The Ring of the Nibelung .
praise.by: Günter Zöller, University of Munich

praise.q: Brian O’Connor offers a riveting reappraisal of a trilogy of major prose works written by Richard Wagner soon after his frontline participation in the 1849 Dresden revolution and narrow escape to Switzerland under real threat of execution. No longer boring theoretical tracts, the texts in O’Connor’s hands are daring and philosophically original meditations on the dilemmas of revolutionary action. If you want to know why Wagner put his own life at such serious risk in 1849, you need to read this book.
praise.by: John Deathridge, King’s College London

books.title: Weaving
books.authors: Hector Manuel Meneses Lozano, Victoria Mitchell, Nilda Callanaupa Alvarez, Sophie Desrosiers, Ellen Harlizius-Kluck, Christine Giuntini, Lynda Pete, Caroline Fowler, Ittai Weinryb, Suzanne Lassalle, Annabel Vallard, Laurence Douny, Rodolphe Rougerie, Sophie Cersoy
books.tagline: A beautifully illustrated look at how weaving has influenced art, industry, and society worldwide
books.description:
Weaving is one of humanity’s oldest technologies and remains central to our global economies. Yet because of the fragility of textiles and their association with women’s labor and craft, they have often been marginalized in art history. From the early-modern Andes to the contemporary artist’s studio, weaving has shaped artistic practice and raised important questions for conservators and museums responsible for preserving these delicate materials.

At its core, weaving is an act of material transformation in which discrete threads are organized into coherent cloth. This book brings together some of today’s leading conservationists and art historians to examines this process, highlighting the structural principles that underlie an art often assumed to be intuitive. The contributors explore how weaving reshaped material production and social life across cultures and historical periods, creating networks of skilled makers and new forms of exchange and shared knowledge.

Taking readers from the human labor of the handloom to the mechanized production of the industrial age, Weaving demonstrates how a practice at the intersection of art, science, and community has shaped social, technological, and economic histories around the globe.
books.bio: Hector Manuel Meneses Lozano is director of the Museo Textil de Oaxaca in Mexico. Victoria Mitchell is a research fellow at Norwich University of the Arts in the United Kingdom. Her books include The Material Culture of Basketry .

books.title: What a Country Owes Its Soldiers
books.tagline: A clarion call to recognize soldiers’ rights, arguing that volunteering to fight and die for one’s country does not mean consenting to exploitation in the process.
books.description:
American leaders endlessly profess their admiration for military service members. But these effusive declarations hardly comport with reality. Soldiers receive shoddy equipment and inadequate medical care; they are ordered to commit crimes and deployed to illegal wars. Such treatment is rarely recognized for what it is: a violation of the duty owed to soldiers by their government. When American service members are injured or killed during training, for example, they and their families are barred from suing the military for negligence or malfeasance. And when the torture of detainees at Abu Ghraib came to light, the subsequent proceedings focused just on low-ranking perpetrators. The psychological harm done to the soldiers themselves by commanders who ordered them to commit torture in the first place went unacknowledged.

Examining statutes, treaties, court cases, and congressional hearings, Saira Mohamed shows how the law encourages the treatment of soldiers as mere instruments, to be used and abused however the government wishes. She also unearths overlooked laws that point in the other direction, suggesting the possibility of robust protections for service members. Paradoxically, these get ignored in part because of the popular adulation of the military—the vision of service members as heroes who selflessly endure unlimited sacrifice. The all-volunteer nature of the force also promotes the misguided notion that soldiers have willingly accepted whatever mistreatment they might experience.

What a Country Owes Its Soldiers shows how laws and mindsets can change, enabling genuine respect for soldiers’ humanity. Acknowledging their rights can transform our understanding of those who fight America’s wars, and of American warmaking itself.
books.bio: Saira Mohamed is Agnes Roddy Robb Chair in Jurisprudence, Ethics, and Social Responsibility and Professor of Law at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Law.

praise.q: What a Country Owes Its Soldiers is a deeply thoughtful and philosophically rich look not simply at how the state often fails to care for soldiers, but how those failures are built upon a dangerously flawed conception of the state’s relationship to violence and to the tools it uses to dole it out. A marvelous book.

This is a paradigm-shifting book for scholars, policymakers, and practitioners in the United States and around the world. We are used to seeing soldiers as perpetrators, not rights-holders. Saira Mohamed shows us irrefutably that they are both.

A bracing and deeply original book. At a moment when leaders openly treat the military as a tool of personal and political will, What a Country Owes Its Soldiers is not just a profound work of legal scholarship but an urgent moral reckoning—one that should change how lawyers, policymakers, and citizens alike think about war and the people we ask to fight in it.

Americans purport to hold their troops in the highest regard. In reality, as this compelling study shows, they routinely subject their fellow citizens in uniform to neglect, abuse, and casual mistreatment. An illuminating look at an important and overlooked subject.

Saira Mohamed persuasively argues that soldiers should be treated not as mere instruments of state power, but as people with rightful claims on the government they serve. What a Country Owes Its Soldiers is a bracing rethinking of war, law, and democratic responsibility—and a reminder that how a country treats its military personnel is the concern of every citizen.

A provocative and carefully documented case that US law actively sustains the treatment of military personnel as mere instruments of the state, ‘weapons’ rather than people—and that the law itself, examined more closely, already contains the tools to dismantle this legal architecture. Beautifully written, ambitious in scope, and humanistic in method, What a Country Owes Its Soldiers reads legal doctrine alongside the poetry of Wilfred Owen and the accounts of soldiers themselves to argue that recognizing service members as rights-holders, not just heroes or weapons, is both legally grounded and morally urgent.

books.title: A Historian's Handbook for Saving the World
books.subtitle: Responding to the Global Climate Emergency
books.tagline: A historian’s guide to the climate crisis: how research, teaching, and public engagement can help reshape the future of our environment.
books.description:
The work of historians is vital to this moment. As climate debates shift from “believing the science” to fighting for the massive changes needed to address cataclysmic environmental damage, historical work is a critical resource for tracing and challenging the deeply rooted structures of power that continue to drive climate change and for charting fair and livable futures. In A Historian's Handbook for Saving the World , Alexandra Hui and Emily Pawley assemble provocative thought-pieces and concrete resources to help historians mobilize and expand their skills, networks, public platforms, and research to respond to the unfolding polycrisis.

Organized into six sections, the book illuminates different possibilities for action. Three sections focus on research, exploring how historians have directly addressed the emergence of climate science and how historical work can help us imagine and shape the different futures that lie before us. The remaining sections move beyond the world of academic research, offering guidance on integrating climate stories into teaching, reshaping institutions, and communicating and collaborating with communities.
books.bio:
Alexandra Hui (Author)

Alexandra Hui is Associate Professor of History at Mississippi State University. She is the author of The Psychophysical Ear (MIT Press) and coeditor of Testing Hearing .

Emily Pawley (Author)

Emily Pawley is Walter E. Beach ’56 Professor of Sustainability Studies and Associate Professor of History at Dickinson College. She is the author of The Nature of the Future .

books.title: A Red Badge of Cotton
books.subtitle: The Treasonous Trade That Clothed the Union Army
books.tagline: How Confederate cotton journeyed from Texas plantation to New England mill to become a Union uniform on a Virginia battlefield
books.description:
The bloodstained shirt of the Union soldier has long been celebrated as a “red badge of courage.” Yet as a finished product it reveals a narrative not of heroism but of wartime profiteering. After North and South declared mutual trade to be treasonous, a new supply chain emerged to link the cotton plantations of Louisiana and Texas to the mills of the Northeast. In the neutral Mexican port of Matamoros, northern and European agents bought “Mexican cotton” from Confederate merchants for transshipment to New York and New England.

This treasonous cotton became woven into the entire outfit of the Union soldier—shirt, underwear, sleeping bag, tent, knapsack, even regimental flags. In a literal sense, the Confederacy was fighting a Union army it was clothing and sheltering.

David Montejano describes the entirety of this wartime trade, from cotton’s harvest on the plantation to its manufacture as uniform and flag, telling the stories of the countless human hands that touched cotton—the slaves, planters, merchants, teamsters, mariners, mill workers, nurses, and soldiers—as it journeyed from the western Confederacy to a Virginia battlefield.

David Montejano is Professor Emeritus of Ethnic Studies and History at the University of California, Berkeley. His prizewinning books include Anglos and Mexicans in the Making of Texas, 1836–1986 and Quixote’s Soldiers: A Local History of the Chicano Movement, 1966–1981. He lives in San Antonio, TX.
books.bio: David Montejano is Professor Emeritus of Ethnic Studies and History at the University of California, Berkeley. His prizewinning books include Anglos and Mexicans in the Making of Texas, 1836–1986 and Quixote’s Soldiers: A Local History of the Chicano Movement, 1966–1981 . He lives in San Antonio, TX.

praise.q: A tour de force. No one before David Montejano has ever traced the Civil War supply chain from southern plantations across Texas to Matamoros where the ‘Mexican’ cotton could be exported to northern mills and woven into flags, bandages, and uniforms.
praise.by: Alice Baumgartner, author of South to Freedom: Runaway Slaves to Mexico and the Road to Civil War
praise.cred: author of South to Freedom: Runaway Slaves to Mexico and the Road to Civil War

praise.q: A dazzling book. Through prodigious research, inspired analysis, and a host of richly-drawn laborers, schemers, and profiteers, David Montejano reconstructs cotton’s transnational sojourn from Confederate bale to Union bandage. One of our great borderlands scholars has given us an engrossing new perspective on the Civil War era.
praise.by: Brian DeLay, author of War of a Thousand Deserts
praise.cred: author of War of a Thousand Deserts

praise.q: The Civil War is an international commercial struggle in David Montejano’s capable hands. His account of covert cotton dealings ties southern planters, Mexican agents, and northern industrialists together in an uncommon transatlantic tale.
praise.by: Conrad Edick Wright, Massachusetts Historical Society

praise.q: A Red Badge of Cotton reframes the Civil War, detailing how southern cotton crossed into Mexico, then sailed to supply northern industries. While soldiers died, border merchants kept dueling economies alive—building capital that led to New York’s Citibank and Monterrey’s rise as Mexico’s industrial powerhouse.
praise.by: John Tutino, Georgetown University

books.title: Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management
books.tagline: A compelling account of the role of asset managers in driving consolidation across the American economy, offering a bold call to revive and reinforce US antitrust and antimonopoly policy.
books.description:
Recent decades have witnessed the rise of both finance and monopoly power in the United States. Although seemingly unrelated, these developments are in fact intimately linked. As Andrew McLean makes clear, asset managers—especially private equity houses and large index investors—are key contributors to the decline of competition in the American economy.

Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management explores two primary ways in which asset managers drive consolidation. First, there is the private equity practice of strategically acquiring numerous companies in a single industry. Such “roll-up” acquisitions are responsible for consolidation across many sectors, from local newspapers to ski resorts, and have been particularly prominent in healthcare, harming patients, workers, and the medical system at large. Second, a subtler form of consolidation is created by “horizontal shareholding,” in which asset managers hold shares in multiple companies operating in the same market. This phenomenon has grown alongside the increasing popularity of index funds from providers such as BlackRock, Fidelity, State Street, and Vanguard, and is associated with anticompetitive effects in a range of industries, from airlines to agriculture.

McLean proposes several ambitious reforms to contest finance-led consolidation, including banning acquisitions that would give a private equity house control of more than 30 percent of a market and imposing a maximum cap on the amount of equity capital that an asset manager may manage. Highlighting the close ties between monopoly and finance, Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management is a timely addition to debates about market power and the dangers of an excessively large and influential financial sector.
books.bio: Andrew P. McLean is Lecturer of Law and Political Economy at the University of Edinburgh.

praise.q: This is a bold book: bold in challenging the intellectual frameworks that shaped antitrust enforcement in the previous century but appear ineffective in the age of asset management, bold in proposing remedies for the resulting concentration of market and political power, and bold in examining how one particularly influential asset manager came to shape—and at times distort—the academic discourse surrounding it.

Antitrust ignores the gale force of financialization at its peril. Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management exposes how financial capitalism has fundamentally rewritten the rules of our economy and offers a definitive roadmap for structural reform.

Andrew McLean’s Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management is an engaging, sometimes riveting book: a kaleidoscope of the history and evolution of the control of markets by financiers and investors—led, in modern times, by asset managers who orchestrate roll-ups and overlapping top shareholding in rival companies. This is a wise, perceptive, and carefully researched work with a strong perspective on effective antitrust and corporate power.

Essential reading for anyone looking to understand how finance built monopoly capitalism. Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management reveals a path forward for meaningful restraint of finance-led corporate power.

Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management fills a major gap in the competition policy discourse by reconnecting financial power and corporate power—two issues that historically were intertwined and inspired populist politics in the United States. Breaking down the current separation between these topics, Andrew McLean explains how Wall Street’s relentless quest for easy and substantial profits has contributed to pervasive monopoly and oligopoly power in the American economy. He offers a sophisticated account of both how we got here and how we can start building a more just and democratic economy.

Andrew McLean has done a masterful job of explaining how the financialization of the US economy and the rise of asset managers have contributed to unhealthy economic concentration and collusion. More importantly, he has thoughtful recommendations for how to address the problems of private equity roll-ups and horizontal shareholding through increased antitrust enforcement, corporate governance reform, and legislation restructuring the financial sector. This is both first-rate research and a very good read.

Antitrust and the Age of Asset Management is destined to be a classic work of American business and financial history, as lucid and engaging as it is provocative and inspiring. This book is both a clarion call for change and a practical legal blueprint for achieving it.

A devastating and essential critique of how asset managers have conquered American industry. Through a thorough historical analysis, Andrew McLean reveals how asset managers have perfected what J. P. Morgan pioneered: the total subordination of competition to financial return. They own the portfolio companies, they dominate the shareholder base, they direct the boards. And nobody’s stopping them.

books.title: Artistic Labour Now
books.subtitle: Between Specificity and Generality, Materiality and Immateriality, Production and Reproduction
books.authors: Edited by Isabelle Graw and Daniel Birnbaum
books.tagline: On the specificity and generality, materiality and immateriality, production and reproduction of artistic labor.
books.description:
Based on a symposium initiated by Isabelle Graw and Daniel Birnbaum at Frankfurt’s Städelschule, Artistic Labour Now considers the relationship between the value-form of the unique artwork and the subject position of its maker in relationship to key artists and theorists.

In these collected essays, art historians, critics, artists, and writers approach modern and contemporary artistic labour from numerous angles, including Marxist theories of value, feminist theories of reproductive labour and contemporary theories of affective and immaterial labour.

Contributors also shed light on the specificity of artistic labour in view of an increasingly globalized and digitized art economy, considering emergent possibilities for producing and distributing art created by recent developments in virtual reality, blockchain technologies and cryptocurrencies within today’s immersive media landscape. In this expansive new sphere, notions of value, labour and economy in the broadest sense must be renegotiated, as the lines between specificity and generality, materiality and immateriality, production and reproduction are blurred.
books.bio:
Isabelle Graw is the publisher of the journal Texte zur Kunst , which she cofounded with Stefan Germer (1958–1998) in 1990, and professor of art history and art theory at the Hochschule für Bildende Künste–Städelschule, Frankfurt am Main. Her previous books include In Another World: Notes, 2014–2017 , The Love of Painting: Genealogy of a Success Medium , and High Price: Art Between the Market and Celebrity Culture .

Daniel Birnbaum is a Swedish art critic, theoretician, and curator. He was the director of the Museum of Modern Art (Moderna Museet) in Stockholm from 2010 to 2018, and currently directs the VR company, Acute Art.
subjects: Sternberg Press / Institut für Kunstkritik series

books.title: Atomic Disenchantment
books.subtitle: A Global History of Nuclear Energy
books.tagline: A global history of nuclear energy from 1945 to today—and why the atom has failed to become a dominant, cheap, and safe energy source.
books.description:
Nuclear energy is once again being promoted as the means to phase out fossil fuels and solve environmental problems. Yet nuclear energy has rarely delivered on its past promises. Instead, attempts to harness the atom have led to some of the most severe tensions and political struggles in modern history. In Atomic Disenchantment , Per Högselius argues that the failure of nuclear energy is best explained by the clashes and contradictions in the nuclear industry’s attempts to connect with older technological traditions and practices. He looks not only at the Western great powers and larger non-Western countries but also at smaller countries in Western and Eastern Europe and in the Global South.

Högselius examines the global history of nuclear energy from 1945 to today. Viewing nuclear power as a hybrid technology that combines new nuclear science discoveries with a range of older technological practices, he considers the history of nuclear power to be one of broken promises and unfulfilled visions and ambitions. Analyzing nuclear energy from a global historical perspective provides a necessary tool for understanding the ongoing nuclear debate.
books.bio: Per Högselius is Professor of History of Technology at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm. He is the author of Death on the Beach , Energy and Geopolitics , and Red Gas and the coeditor of The Nuclear-Water Nexus (MIT Press).

praise.q: A brilliant reversal of what we thought we knew about nuclear power. Högselius shows that the atomic age was, at heart, a new age of steam: Reactors succeeded or failed through their symbiosis with old technologies—boilers, turbines, dikes, and canals. Splitting the atom was the easy part; boiling water proved the hard one. A landmark in the history of energy.
praise.by: Jean-Baptiste Fressoz, author of More and More and More and Happy Apocalypse
praise.cred: author of More and More and More and Happy Apocalypse

praise.q: Per Högselius shows how the past failures of civilian nuclear energy had little to do with designing state-of-the-art nuclear reactors, but with failures to wed long-existing energy infrastructures—dams, turbines, plumbing—to nuclear energy. A truly international and innovative rendering of civilian nuclear history.
praise.by: Kate Brown, author of Tiny Gardens Everywhere and Manual for Survival
praise.cred: author of Tiny Gardens Everywhere and Manual for Survival

books.title: Banking on Groundwater
books.subtitle: The Quest to Replenish the World's Aquifers
books.tagline: The promise and challenges of managed aquifer recharge, a proven water-supply strategy that is benefitting communities around the globe
books.description:
Groundwater is essential for a healthy environment and thriving communities, but around the world, aquifers are drying up. Over-pumping, climate change, and pollution threaten to deplete this vital resource, with dire consequences for people and landscapes. One of the most promising solutions is to purposefully direct water back into the ground—a technique known as managed aquifer recharge, or MAR. Banking on Groundwater explores the global potential of this important strategy while helping water managers navigate political, social, and environmental pitfalls.

Though simple in concept, MAR raises thorny questions in practice. How does harvesting water upstream affect the places and people downstream? Will climate change alter the water sources available for MAR? Could recharge introduce contaminants into groundwater? How can those who recharge the water be assured of the ability to recover it? Through illuminating case studies, William Alley and Rosemarie Alley address these and other dilemmas while showing how MAR can help solve a host of problems, including water shortages, seawater intrusion, water-quality degradation, streamflow depletion, and the endangerment of ecosystems that depend on groundwater.

Examining various approaches to MAR in a wide variety of settings across the United States and around the world, Banking on Groundwater is essential reading for water managers, policymakers, educators, and other professionals engaged in water conservation.
books.bio: William M. Alley is director of science and technology at the National Ground Water Association and was chief of the Office of Groundwater at the US Geological Survey for nearly two decades. Rosemarie Alley is a freelance writer and public speaker whose books include The Water Recycling Revolution: Tapping into the Future ; The War on the EPA: America’s Endangered Environmental Protections ; and High and Dry: Meeting the Challenges of the World’s Growing Dependence on Groundwater , all coauthored with William M. Alley.

praise.q: Managed aquifer recharge is an important tool for conserving and restoring our groundwater resources. This book provides a very readable and comprehensive introduction to a process that should be included in every water management plan.
praise.by: Bruce Babbitt, former United States Secretary of the Interior
praise.cred: former United States Secretary of the Interior

praise.q: As groundwater depletion threatens water access, managed aquifer recharge offers a promising way to reverse these declining trends. This engaging book provides a comprehensive tour of recharge projects across the US and around the globe, illustrating how they actively help to refill depleted aquifers and improve long-term water security.
praise.by: Scott Jasechko, University of California, Santa Barbara

praise.q: This engaging collection of well-told stories of adaption to climate and environmental challenges will appeal to water managers, environmentalists, and educators. Managed aquifer recharge cases are brought to life within their historical context to demonstrate successful social and technical innovation. Accounts are balanced and include failures and problems that are essential reading for MAR developers and regulators.
praise.by: Peter Dillon, former cochair of the International Association of Hydrogeologists Commission on Managing Aquifer Recharge
praise.cred: former cochair of the International Association of Hydrogeologists Commission on Managing Aquifer Recharge

books.title: Basquiat, the Blue Ribbon Paintings, and the Art of Reproduction
books.tagline: A fascinating look at the role of printmaking in the art of Jean-Michel Basquiat
books.description:
The “Blue Ribbon paintings” represent a pivotal moment in Jean-Michel Basquiat’s career. Created in 1984 during a period of intense experimentation by the artist, the mixed-media compositions combine the vibrancy of acrylic paint and oil stick with the reproducibility of silkscreen, blurring the lines between painting and printmaking. Taking these richly textured canvases as a point of departure, this book sheds critical light on Basquiat’s radical engagements with replication and reproductive media, situating his work within postmodern concepts of the 1980s—authorship, appropriation, and the blurred boundaries between original and reproduction. Additionally, the volume places Basquiat in conversation with artists who profoundly influenced his visual practice, including Robert Rauschenberg and Andy Warhol, and with pioneering Black printmakers such as Robert Blackburn. Featuring nearly all of Basquiat’s known print projects, the book focuses a lens on Basquiat as a conceptual artist, exploring identity, reproduction, and visibility in an increasingly commercialized art world.

Distributed for the Princeton University Art Museum
books.bio: Jordana Moore Saggese is professor of modern and contemporary American art and director of the David C. Driskell Center for the Study of the Visual Arts and Culture of African Americans and the African Diaspora at the University of Maryland. AnnMarie Perl is a research scholar and lecturer at Princeton University. Rebecca VanDiver is associate professor of African American art at Vanderbilt University.

books.title: Camera Obscura
books.subtitle: A Novel
books.series: The Margellos World Republic of Letters
books.tagline: From Spain’s most celebrated author, an inventive, quietly radical novel that explores how books illuminate our lives
books.description:
In Camera Obscura , Enrique Vila-Matas returns with a novel-in-motion that turns the very act of looking into a literary method. Set in Barcelona, the novel follows widower Vidal Escabia as he undertakes a precise, time-bound task. Over the course of seventy-one days, he must construct an “untimely” counter-canon by entering his home library in darkness, reaching for a book at random, and, in the light of his picture window, selecting a single fragment. What begins as the fulfillment of his master's dying wish gradually gathers force, propelling the reader through a journey governed by luck yet shaped by necessity.

The fragments accumulate; so, too, do the stakes. As he moves through Barcelona among androids known as the Denver-7, Escabia is haunted by his estrangement from his only daughter, and by the absence of his beloved wife, lost to the cliffs of Tojinbo. In this unstable landscape, where human intention increasingly intersects with automation and chance, the novel builds a subtle but persistent tension: Is Escabia truly constructing the canon, or is another intelligence at work alongside him, in the dark?

Camera Obscura refracts Vila-Matas’s singular vision into a book about how we see, how we read, and how meaning assembles itself in the margins of our experience.
books.bio: Enrique Vila-Matas (b. 1948) is an acclaimed Spanish writer, critic, filmmaker, and journalist. He is the author of numerous novels, stories, and essay collections. Valerie Miles is an American writer, editor, and award-winning translator based in Spain.

praise.q: A splendid novel . . . A tribute to writing as a constant search for the ineffable or inexpressible . . . [by] a writer of the first order.
praise.by: La Voz

praise.q: Camera Obscura is an invitation to embrace literature not only as a way of life, but also as a refuge in dehumanizing times.
praise.by: La República

praise.q: A novel of thrilling complexity—a lightness of complexity, as Italo Calvino might put it—filled with humor and leaving us much like Beckett’s characters: in anticipation. For Camera Obscura demands to be re-read.
praise.by: El Periódico

praise.q: Revels in the space between the literal and the metaphorical; between laughter and profundity. . . A playful novel in which the magician Vila-Matas. . . masterfully shows his hand, which is no less delightful for its revelation.
praise.by: Letras Libres

praise.q: Arguably Spain’s most significant contemporary literary figure . . . By lifting the heavy weight of the past, by setting irony against dogmatism and rigidity, Vila-Matas allows his characters, and us, to contemplate the future.
praise.by: New Yorker

praise.q: A writer who has no equal in the contemporary landscape of the Spanish novel.
praise.by: Roberto Bolaño

praise.q: Enrique Vila-Matas has pioneered one of contemporary literature’s most interesting responses to the great Modernist writers.
praise.by: Paris Review

praise.q: Vila-Matas’s wildly original novels are all investigations of whether or not originality in fiction is still possible; every nook and cranny of literary history is explored and interrogated, the margin of every great novel frantically scribbled in.
praise.by: Dublin Review of Books
