praise.q: With its interviews of key policymakers, Simon Bowmaker’s book opens wide a door into the often-obscure world of Fed policymaking.
praise.by: Robert Hetzel, author of The Federal Reserve: A New History
praise.cred: author of The Federal Reserve: A New History

praise.q: A treasure trove of interviews of people who have played a notable role in shaping 21st century Federal Reserve policy.”—Kenneth Rogoff, author of Our Dollar, Your Problem: An Insider's View of Seven Turbulent Decades of Global Finance, and the Road Ahead

Fed Reckoning is a unique and indispensable resource for anyone who cares about central banking. The people who have done the most to shape the Federal Reserve—from the inside and outside—reflect candidly on the most important economic and institutional issues facing our economy today. The result ranges from the personal to the analytical and is essential reading for anyone trying to understand where the Fed has been and where it is headed.
praise.by: Jason Furman, Harvard University

subjects: Yale Program on Financial Stability Series

books.title: Feed the Soul
books.subtitle: Lessons from Aristotle on Living Well
books.tagline: A lively and personal guide to pursuing true happiness through a life grounded in empathy and shared purpose
books.description:
Of all the ancient thinkers, Aristotle is the humane, dynamic guide we need to navigate modern life. Unlike the Stoics, who advocated detachment and self-reliance, Aristotle knew that goodness grows through human connections. People flourish through friendship and community, and they wither when they retreat.

Distilling Aristotle’s core ideas, acclaimed scholar Nancy Sherman explores how connection, curiosity, and ethical character can help us make peace with the fragility of happiness, and how we can address the questions we struggle to answer:

• What is it to flourish?

• What is it to live a good life?

• How do we find joy in nature without exploiting it?

• How do we play without hurting, joke without mocking?

• How do we build strong friendships in an age of loneliness?

• What does it mean to have a good soul?

As Sherman walks beside the famous philosopher, she shows us why his vision speaks powerfully to our anxious and divided times—and how we can put that vision into practice.
books.bio: Nancy Sherman is Distinguished University Professor at Georgetown University. Her books include Stoic Wisdom: Ancient Lessons for Modern Resilience , Afterwar: Healing the Moral Wounds of Our Soldiers , The Untold War: Inside the Hearts, Minds, and Souls of Our Soldiers , and Stoic Warriors: The Ancient Philosophy Behind the Military Mind . She lives near Washington, D.C.

praise.q: A lovely, amazing book, packed with insights. Aristotle emerges not as the usual remote pedant but as a curious and gracious friend who accompanies the reader as he studies animals, reacts to tragic performances and athletic contests, and engages us throughout in pondering the difficulty and joy of living well.
praise.by: Martha C. Nussbaum, author of Justice for Animals

praise.q: Nancy Sherman is a master of ancient applied philosophy. Her exploration of Aristotle — his ethics, his biology, his vision of the good life — shows why he remains indispensable for anyone trying to live well in the twenty-first century.
praise.by: Massimo Pigliucci, author of How to Be a (Happy) Skeptic
praise.cred: author of How to Be a (Happy) Skeptic

praise.q: Erudite, engaging, and deeply relevant, Feed the Soul brings Aristotle into the modern world. From friendship and resilience to nature, sport, humor, and happiness, Nancy Sherman reveals how ancient Aristotelian philosophy can help us cultivate our character and strengthen our relationships.
praise.by: Donald Robertson, author of How to Think Like a Roman Emperor
praise.cred: author of How to Think Like a Roman Emperor

praise.q: Aristotle's insights into virtue and character make him one of humanity's greatest thinkers and guides on how to live a full and meaningful life. In Feed the Soul , Nancy Sherman confirms that she is one of the clearest and perceptive guides on how to understand Aristotle and his wisdom. Reading this book will enrich your life.
praise.by: Ezekiel J. Emanuel, author of Eat Your Ice Cream
praise.cred: author of Eat Your Ice Cream

praise.q: Feed the Soul is an introduction to Aristotle like no other. Nancy Sherman's vivid portrayal of this towering figure in Western thought reveals him as an extraordinary human being full of curiosity and ideas - sometimes erroneous, but often wise - that are surprisingly relevant to living well in our own times.
praise.by: Peter Singer, Princeton University, author and co-host of the podcast Lives Well Lived
praise.cred: Princeton University, author and co-host of the podcast Lives Well Lived

books.title: Financial Decision-Making
books.subtitle: Principles, Applications, and Cases
books.tagline: An introductory finance textbook that teaches personal, corporate, and investment decisions from one set of first principles.
books.description:
How much should I save for retirement? Should this company launch a new product? Is this stock worth its price? These questions look like they belong to three different subjects, and most introductory textbooks treat them that way. But this innovative introduction to finance shows that personal, corporate, and investment decisions come down to the same handful of principles. Drawing on more than two decades of teaching at Wharton, Michael Roberts develops each idea in context, working through real companies and live data, and returning to the core concepts often enough that they stick. Featuring hundreds of examples, frequent understanding checks, and extensive end-of-chapter problems, Financial Decision-Making is an essential learn-by-doing guide to practicing finance in our personal and professional lives.

Is organized by decision type rather than finance topic

Illustrates the thought process for tackling financial questions in varied contexts

Emphasizes relatable, practical applications throughout

Suits undergraduates, MBAs, executives, and general readers

Offers instructor resources including solutions, case studies, and slides
books.bio: Michael R. Roberts is the William H. Lawrence Professor and Professor of Finance at The Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania and a Research Associate of the National Bureau of Economic Research. He is a recipient of multiple Brattle Prizes ( Journal of Finance ) and the Jensen Prize ( Journal of Financial Economics ), and has won over a dozen teaching awards.

books.title: Gulbadan's Chronicle
books.subtitle: A Vagabond Princess in the Mughal Empire
books.tagline: A new edition of the only existing work of prose written by a woman of the magnificent Mughal Empire of India
books.description:
Ruby Lal’s Vagabond Princess unearths an extraordinary historical treasure—the only surviving history of the magnificent Mughal Empire written by a royal woman. Penned in the late sixteenth century by Princess Gulbadan Begum, this remarkable chronicle reveals a life defined by daring travel and migration, thrilling encounters with foreign cultures, and the exceptional influence she wielded with confidence and grace. Her groundbreaking account—which illuminates the unexpected freedoms enjoyed by both royal and common people—transforms our understanding of her era.

Now, as a companion to Vagabond Princess , Gulbadan’s Chronicle presents Victorian scholar Annette Susannah Beveridge’s masterful English translation of Gulbadan’s history. In a compelling introduction, Lal traces Beveridge’s intellectual journey and her deep connection to Gulbadan’s pivotal work. This edition brings a lost voice back to life, deepening our understanding not only of the Mughal world but of how two brilliant women—centuries apart—joined forces to preserve an irreplaceable piece of history.
books.bio:
Gulbadan Begum (1523–1603), the daughter of Mughal Emperor Babur, was a writer and adventurer.

Annette Susannah Beveridge (1842–1929) was a British scholar who translated The Babur Nama (the memoirs of Mughal Emperor Babur) and Gulbadan’s Humayun Nama into English.

Ruby Lal is professor of South Asian history at Emory University and the 2027 Kluge Chair in Countries and Cultures of the South at the Library of Congress. She is the author of Empress: The Astonishing Reign of Nur Jahan , a finalist for the Los Angeles Times Book Prize in History, and Vagabond Princess: The Great Adventures of Gulbadan , longlisted for the Cundill History Prize and finalist for the James Tait Black Prize.

praise.q: A rare window into the Mughal world, seen through the eyes of the fascinating Gulbadan Begum. Ruby Lal’s masterful introduction breathes fresh life into this royal memoir, revealing the Emperor Humayun not just as a ruler, but as a brother. This edition is bound to become a classic for scholars and casual readers alike.
praise.by: Sam Dalrymple, author of Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia
praise.cred: author of Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia

praise.q: A landmark achievement. Lal's Vagabond Princess was a sumptuous eye-opener; this companion to it tells the story behind Gulbadan's story by foregrounding the scholarship of a trinity of remarkable women. Gulbadan herself is the only woman to have written a personal account of the period; readable and highly revealing, it is here reproduced in full. And no one but Lal can claim to shed so much light on the first Mughals."--John Keay, author of India: A History

books.title: La Peregrina
books.subtitle: An Extraordinary Renaissance Pearl
books.tagline: Retraces the Peregrina Pearl’s many journeys and misinterpretations and revisits its famous and infamous owners
books.description:
No jewel has captured the imagination like the Peregrina Pearl, with its vivid history as a Spanish crown treasure and its dramatic disappearance from Madrid’s Royal Palace. Its last owner, Elizabeth Taylor, called it “the most perfect pearl in the world”.

The Peregrina was fished from the Gulf of Panama in 1577 by a young enslaved African and quickly became the most celebrated natural pearl of the Renaissance. Its extraordinary beauty, size and shape inspired the Milanese court jeweller Jacopo da Trezzo to christen it La Perla Peregrina – “ the rare one”. King Philip II of Spain secured it in 1586. For more than two centuries, successive Spanish queens, infantas and kings wore the Peregrina as a symbol of global rule and imperial power.

Drawing on decades of archival work in Austria, Italy, Portugal, Spain and France, Annemarie Jordan Gschwend assembles royal inventories, diaries, accounts and correspondence to publish, for the first time, the pearl ’ s full documentary history, which began in the New World in the late sixteenth century through to its place in the collection of Elizabeth Taylor.
books.bio: Annemarie Jordan Gschwend is a distinguished art historian, curator, scholar and author of many essays, articles and book. Her scholarly expertise encompasses court culture, patronage, and material culture in Renaissance Iberia, with particular emphasis on the global exchanges between Africa, Asia, the Americas, Portugal and the Habsburg courts.

books.title: Longstorming
books.subtitle: Beyond the Age of Haste
books.tagline: How temporal countercultures can ignite an ethos of patience—one that resists the techno-solutionism of the “longtermism” movement.
books.description:
To longstorm is to riff across horizons of time, creatively drawing together philosophies, histories, technologies, art, ancestral lineages, geophysical knowledge, even myths of spirits or lives after death—until the imagination is swept into a storm of new perspectives. In Longstorming, Vincent Ialenti explores how weaving together visions of future worlds can transform how we think, perceive, and live in the here and now. Through atmospheric nature writing and vivid ethnographic storytelling, the book invites readers to slow down, inhabit stillness, and cultivate wide-angle temporal imagination in an Age of Haste defined by digital overstimulation, information overload, and planetary crisis.

The book’s case studies reveal philosophical reflection, anthropological curiosity, and ecological wonder as counterforces to the Age of Haste’s distractionism: a 10,000-year monumental clock, an arboreal timepiece calibrated to bristlecone pines alive for millennia, an Indigenous knowledge keeper contemplating mortality and deep time in an imagined visit to Finland’s nuclear repository in 2121, and more. Longstorming invites readers not to control the future but to imagine it otherwise—plural, coauthored, and unfinished—and, in doing so, to reimagine themselves.
books.bio: Vincent Ialenti is a cultural anthropologist, former US Department of Energy official, and Senior Research Fellow at Tampere University. He is the author of Deep Time Reckoning. His research has been supported by the US National Science Foundation, the Mellon Foundation, the MacArthur Foundation, and the Berggruen Institute, and his writing has been featured by the BBC , NPR , Scientific American, Forbes, Physics Today, Psyche , and Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists .

praise.q: In this thrilling tempest of creative possibility, Vincent Ialenti shows how weathering the turbulence of our Age of Haste will take imagination, patience, and courage. Longstorming is an idea whose time has come.
praise.by: David Farrier, author of Nature’s Genius and Footprints
praise.cred: author of Nature’s Genius and Footprints

praise.q: Refreshingly original and deeply insightful, Longstorming is the first practical guide to time travel. Ialenti shares multiple escape routes from the claustrophobic Island of Now and provides guidance on how to be a responsible citizen of not only the present but also the future.
praise.by: Marcia Bjornerud, author of Timefulness and Turning to Stone
praise.cred: author of Timefulness and Turning to Stone

praise.q: Longstorming inspires individuals to dream solutions for the challenges of the deep future, providing essential knowledge we desperately need.
praise.by: William L. Fox, Director Emeritus, Institute for Art + Environment, Nevada Museum of Art
praise.cred: Director Emeritus, Institute for Art + Environment, Nevada Museum of Art

books.title: Magic and Mess
books.subtitle: The Artist’s Studio Revealed
books.authors: James Hall, Anita Sganzerla, Esner Rachel, Isabelle Sagraves, Daniel Robbins and Hannah Lund
books.tagline: Explores the theme of the artists’ studio, featuring previously unpublished works and essays
books.description:
Magic and Mess: The Artist ’ s Studio Revealed explores the myth and reality of the artists ’ studio in Europe through the long nineteenth century. Featuring works from the unrivalled Katrin Bellinger Collection and Leighton House, this richly illustrated catalogue features both famous and little-known artists and includes essays by leading scholars. Through essays and catalogue entries, the book explores the role of the studio, as both a practical space for artmaking and a constant source of inspiration to artists and writers.

Themes covered include the opulent and humble studio; the palette and pigment sets as symbols of the artist; the rise of the female model; the use of plaster casts, mannequins, prints, photographs and drawings; the contrast between the romantic fires of inspiration and the cold bohemian stove; innovations in window design and lighting; the emergence of the corner of the studio as a privileged zone, taking inspiration from Émile Zola ’ s cult of the corner, and from Lawrence Alma-Tadema ’ s In My Studio (1893), which belonged to Frederic Leighton and has recently been acquired by Leighton House.
books.bio:
James Hall has published extensively on related topics and is the author of the ground-breaking book The Artist’s Studio: a Cultural History (Thames & Hudson, 2022), already a standard work on the subject. (A Times Best Art Book of 2022)

Anita Viola Sganzerla is Curator of the Katrin Bellinger Collection and has published extensively on the theme of the artist at work. She is a specialist of Early Modern works on paper.

Rachel Esner is Associate Professor Modern and Contemporary Art at the University of Amsterdam and a specialist in French art and photography of the late nineteenth century.

Isabelle Sagraves is a PhD candidate at University College London and a Curatorial Assistant at the Katrin Bellinger Collection.

Daniel Robbins is Senior Curator at Leighton House and Sambourne House.

books.title: Making Beauty
books.subtitle: Hooks Brothers Studio, 1907–1984
books.tagline: This is the first book dedicated to the legendary Hook Brothers Studio in Memphis, featuring photographs from 1912 to 1983.
books.description:
Making Beauty introduces the prominent African American commercial photography studio founded by brothers Henry and Robert Hooks Sr. in Memphis, Tennessee. It accompanies a major exhibition at the Memphis Brooks Museum of Art, the first to survey their extensive archive. This catalogue positions the Hooks Brothers as activists who used photography to restore racial pride and cultural self-expression. Known for their technical proficiency and artistry, the Hooks Brothers were recognized for their precise and tender portrayals of Black Americans in the region.

The catalogue looks at the Hooks Brothers Studio collection, an archive developed by two generations of Black photographers, stored away and uncatalogued for almost thirty years. It places the Hooks Brothers’ practice in conversation with renowned Black photographers in the U.S. and abroad, such as James Van Der Zee, Addison Scurlock, Seydou Keita and James Barnor, among others, who documented their communities during the same period, to dispel racist imagery. The Hooks Brothers were the most prominent and longest-standing commercial photography enterprise of any race in the Mid-South region of the United States.

Exhibition Schedule:

Memphis Brooks Museum of Art

(6 December 2026–5 July 2027)
books.bio:
C. Rose Smith is a photographer and Assistant Curator of Photography at the Memphis Brooks Museum of Art.

Cheryl Finley is an art historian, author, curator, critic and the Inaugural Director of the Atlanta University Center Art History and Curatorial Studies Collective.

Earnestine Jenkins is an independent curator and scholar of art history and visual studies and Professor of Art History at the University of Memphis.

Mark Sealy is a British curator, cultural historian, and the director of Autograph ABP–Association of Black Photographers in London.

Rikki Byrd is a writer, scholar, educator, independent curator and consultant.

books.title: Nikolai Astrup
books.subtitle: Catalogue Raisonné of the Paintings
books.tagline: A milestone in Nordic art history, the forthcoming Catalogue Raisonné of Nikolai Astrup’s oil paintings presents the first comprehensive, critically annotated account of the artist’s oeuvre
books.description:
The result of fifteen years of research undertaken in collaboration with an international team of scholars, this catalogue raisonné by Dr. Tove Haugsbø presents

the entire body of paintings made by the Norwegian artist Nikolai Astrup (1880–1928).

Tracing Astrup’s visionary engagement with his rural home village, the garden and mystical folklore, the volume interweaves rigorous provenance, exhibition history and archival sources with indepth visual analysis. It documents 329 paintings, most reproduced in colour and accompanied by complete provenance, exhibition history,

and bibliography. Revealing previously overlooked works and refining attributions, the catalogue repositions Astrup as a pivotal figure in early twentieth-century art. Essential for collectors, historians and curators alike, it transforms our understanding of one of Scandinavia’s most original painters.

Distributed for the Kode Bergen Art Museum
books.bio: Tove Haugsbø is recognised as one of the leading authorities on Nikolai Astrup and the principal scholar behind the Catalogue Raisonné of Astrup’s oil paintings. A researcher and senior curator at Kode Art Museum and Composer Homes, Bergen, her work is grounded in the sustained first-hand study of the artist’s oeuvre. Astrup was the focus of her PhD in Art History at the University of Bergen (2015), which initiated a new critical reading of his work. For the past decade, Haugsbø has led the Astrup Research Centre at Kode, providing the scholarly foundation for this definitive catalogue.

books.title: Not a Disease
books.subtitle: Rethinking Addiction in the Heart of America's Overdose Crisis
books.tagline: A bracing—and compassionate—challenge to the idea of addiction as a disease. From a leading psychiatrist at the Yale School of Medicine and the medical director of a methadone clinic in Washington, DC.
books.description:
From a leading psychiatrist at the Yale School of Medicine and the medical director of a methadone clinic in Washington, DC.

Ask someone why they got a brain tumor. They won’t know. But ask someone why they developed an addiction and they’ll have a personal, meaningful explanation. Why? Because, Sally Satel argues, unlike a brain tumor, addiction is not a disease, and, in particular, not a brain disease. Dismantling the conventional framing of addiction, Not a Disease makes a compelling case for more refined—and useful—conceptual and clinical perspectives. Addiction, Satel suggests, is better understood as a symptom rather than a disease—a symptom of psychic pain that needs to be anesthetized. Only by recognizing this will we find a more effective approach to recovery.

A practicing physician who has worked with addicts for many years, Satel explores why people consume substances to excess, and why conflicting ideas—held by physicians, scientists, policymakers, and the public—complicate treatment and policy. Without dismissing biological factors, she looks at the drug epidemic in Ironton, Ohio, a small American town in decline, breaking down the conventional wisdom that ascribes too much power to the capacity of drugs to enslave users’ brains, and too little to the vulnerabilities of people and places that draw them to drugs in the first place. Her analysis of the misguided responses to the crisis of addiction to prescription opioids illuminates the plight of millions of patients plunged into needless and solitary agony.

Boldly recasting the nature of addiction, from painkillers to fentanyl, Not a Disease holds out hope for a more humane way to meet this deep and widespread societal challenge.
books.bio: Sally Satel, MD, is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and the medical director of a methadone clinic in Washington, DC. She is a lecturer at the Yale School of Medicine and the author of numerous books, including her most recent Brainwashed: The Seductive Appeal of Mindless Neuroscience, with Scott Lilienfeld, which was a finalist for the Los Angeles Times Book Prize in Science.

praise.q: The topic of addiction is vexing, complicated, highly important, and riveting.... Sally Satel’s point of view is useful, significant, and very much worth engaging with.
praise.by: Steven E. Hyman, Director, Program in Brain Health, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard
praise.cred: Director, Program in Brain Health, Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard

praise.q: This thought-provoking, often counterintuitive book proposes that addiction is the result of social and psychic decay rather than a biological disease. Mixing compelling anecdotes and peer-reviewed studies, Satel proposes that those who live desperate lives will turn to self-destruction to mitigate their pain, and that the disease model of addiction, though formulated with compassion, undermines self-determination: that its aura of forgiveness cloaks a fearful disenfranchisement.
praise.by: Andrew Solomon, author of Far From the Tree and The Noonday Demon
praise.cred: author of Far From the Tree and The Noonday Demon

praise.q: A fascinating, bracing, and humane reexamination of the opioid epidemic, and of the prevailing medical model of addiction. Satel writes with the authority of a psychiatrist who is not just deeply familiar with the scientific literature and with the history of drug policy and pain management but who also, more importantly, has worked for years with substance abusers, including at a methadone clinic in opioid-devastated Appalachia. This book will challenge your preconceptions about addiction—and it ought to provoke national debate about how we as a society manage it.
praise.by: Scott Stossel, National Editor, The Atlantic ; author of the international bestseller My Age of Anxiety
praise.cred: National Editor, The Atlantic ; author of the international bestseller My Age of Anxiety

praise.q: Nobody writes better than Sally Satel about the real and imaginary disorders that afflict the mind, and the public policies that compound our misconceptions in ways that harm the very people they are intended to help. In Not a Disease , she examines myths about addiction and recovery with the empirical mind of a scientist, the compassion of a practitioner, and the clarifying art of a writer.
praise.by: Jonathan Rosen, author of The Best Minds

books.title: Organizational Economics
books.subtitle: Foundations and Applications
books.authors: Daniel V. Barron, Robert S. Gibbons, Michael L. Powell
books.tagline: A wide-ranging introduction to the foundations and applications of organizational economics—essential for theorists and empiricists across a broad range of fields
books.description:
The rapidly expanding field of organizational economics studies the activities and interactions of organizations of all kinds, from the firms that are key participants in nearly all economic activity to nonprofits, schools, government agencies, hospitals, political parties, religious groups, labor unions, and more. Organizational Economics introduces students and practitioners to the governance mindset, an innovative, unified approach to understanding how organizations manage difficult transactions. It sheds light on the frictions that plague these difficult transactions as well as the wide variety of instruments that organizations use to manage these frictions. By analyzing foundational models and applying those models to some of the core problems that organizations must face, this comprehensive textbook demonstrates how governance works in the economy and identifies ways for managers, policymakers, and economists to help governance and the economy work better.

Introduces foundational theories in organizational economics and applies those theories to model important issues that real organizations face

Takes seriously the conditions under which parties actively manage their interactions rather than governing them by an arms-length transaction, either by choice or necessity

Covers foundational theories of incentives, control, influence, and relationships

Applies these models to important topics in organizational economics, including personnel economics, authority, organizational structure, firm boundaries, and interfirm relationships

Includes problems uniquely designed to help readers engage with the large and growing research literature

Identifies future directions for research
books.bio: Daniel V. Barron is associate professor of strategy at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management. Robert S. Gibbons is the Sloan Distinguished Professor of Management at MIT’s Sloan School of Management and professor in MIT’s Department of Economics. His books include (with John Roberts) The Handbook of Organizational Economics (Princeton). Michael L. Powell is professor of strategy at Northwestern University’s Kellogg School of Management.

praise.q: As organizational economics comes of age and attracts growing interest across economics and beyond, this is the book the field needs: comprehensive, lucid, and remarkably useful. An indispensable guide for specialists and newcomers alike.
praise.by: Andrea Prat, Columbia University

praise.q: Platforms, ecosystems, and AI are making organizational economics more relevant than ever. This lucidly written book provides the essential theoretical tools for interpreting the ongoing organizational transformations. An eye-opening read, enriched by recent empirical evidence.
praise.by: Bengt Holmstrom, Nobel Laureate in Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology
praise.cred: Nobel Laureate in Economics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

praise.q: Barron, Gibbons, and Powell’s book provides a masterful tour d’horizon of the large and expanding literature on organizational economics. Replete with interesting and useful models, it will be an invaluable resource and teaching tool for new initiates and seasoned researchers alike.
praise.by: Oliver Hart, Nobel Laureate in Economics, Harvard University
praise.cred: Nobel Laureate in Economics, Harvard University

praise.q: Nearly ninety years after Ronald Coase asked why firms exist at all, Barron, Gibbons, and Powell offer a detailed and engaging account of what we have learned since. Bringing together theory and evidence, this book shows why organizations matter and how organizational economics increasingly shapes work in other fields. This is an important book that deserves a wide readership among students, scholars, and practitioners.
praise.by: Oriana Bandiera, London School of Economics

praise.q: In doing my research with and within firms, I have long lacked guidelines for what to look for once I am there. This book delivers them. Barron, Gibbons, and Powell turn a sprawling literature into a single framework that is clear enough to teach and sharp enough to test.
praise.by: Guido Friebel, Goethe University Frankfurt

books.title: Polar Explorer
books.subtitle: A biography of Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld
books.tagline: Nils Uddenberg’s biography traces Nordenskiöld—scientist, explorer, and political rebel—who conquered the Northeast Passage and embodied restless nineteenth-century ambition and optimism.
books.description:
National hero. Scientist. Adventurer and explorer. Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld is the perfect image of these epithets. Yet he was also a liberal and rebellious agitator who was forced to leave his homeland of Finland after conflict with the Russian authorities.

Nordenskiöld achieved international fame when, aboard the ship Vega, he became the first to navigate the Northeast Passage, after a winter trapped in ice along Siberia's northeastern coast. Nils Uddenberg's book, the first major biography of Nordenskiöld, addresses all this and more. It recounts his numerous Arctic expeditions, his scientific work and political engagements, his achievements and missteps, his family and personal relationships.

The book also situates his life within the dynamic intellectual climate of the nineteenth century, marked by discoveries such as the theory of the Ice Age and Darwin's theory of evolution. Nordenskiöld emerges as a man in constant motion, the world before him—a restless optimist who accomplished what many considered impossible.
books.bio: Nils Uddenberg was a professor and writer. His research was, to a great extent, devoted to the interface between biology, medicine, philosophy, the humanities and theology. He was a political adviser to the Genetics Committee under the Swedish Department of Justice. He received several literary awards, including the Swedish literary award Augustpriset for his history of biology, Idéer om livet (‘Ideas About Life’), in 2003.

books.title: Portrait Diamonds of the Romanovs
books.tagline: A lavish, in-depth history of the portrait diamond in Russia
books.description:
Among all the precious historical jewels, few are as precious or rare as the portrait diamond—a miniature covered with a flat diamond, unique for its shape, perfection, and clarity. This publication examines the history of the portrait diamond in Russia, where this rare and unusual form achieved its greatest height under the patronage of the Romanovs. Of 55 recorded portrait diamonds, only 36 are extant today. This book focuses on an extraordinary private collection representing almost one-third of them.

The two-volume study is published as a complementary set which features new research, remarkable photographs, and diagnostic analysis of the genre of the portrait diamond. Volume I is illustrated with spectacular photographs of all the portrait diamonds, along with short descriptions of each and a summary introduction. Volume II includes a longer introduction that examines the portrait diamond within the history of the genre, with references to comparable examples made for members of the English and French courts, and that traces the history of the portrait diamond in Russia.
books.bio: Diana Scarisbrick (1928–2024) was an independent scholar based in London. A jewellery historian of exceptional renown, she published dozens of books on jewellery of all ages. Karen L. Kettering has held positions as curator of Russian art at Hillwood Museum & Gardens and senior specialist in the Department of Russian Art at Sotheby’s. She is the author of many studies on Russian decorative arts.

books.title: Saving the Wild Country
books.subtitle: Five Visionary Environmentalists and the Struggle for Nature in the American West
books.tagline: The gripping story of the trailblazing conservationists who shaped the wilderness of the American West into legend
books.description:
Driven by richly drawn characters and framed by cinematic showdowns in epic landscapes, Saving the Wild Country vividly combines narrative history, biography, cultural criticism, and outdoor writing to show how postwar wildland advocacy—and the Western myth—shaped American attitudes toward wilderness in a time of ferocious development and change.

In the boom years following World War II, a small but vital group of artists, writers, and advocates mobilized the visual and therapeutic power of the wilderness to combat the dizzying development of the American West.

With cinematic flair, Ben A. Minteer explores the motives and achievements of photographer Ansel Adams, conservationist David Brower, curator and writer Nancy Newhall, and authors Wallace Stegner and Edward Abbey, an ensemble united by a fierce commitment to preserving the American wildlands. Through a burst of creative projects, they struggled to control the narrative of development in the American West and offered an alternative vision to the culturally corrosive impacts of mid-twentieth-century industrialism and consumerism. But as the five visionaries fought the dams, bulldozers, and highways that slashed across the wild country, they also fought among themselves—and with their internal doubts and regrets—in a land where personality, myth, and activism collided.

In this volume, illustrated with compelling photographs, portraits, and iconic landscapes, Minteer

• investigates the intertwined truths and myths of the West that still permeate American culture

• provides nuance to the backgrounds and motivations of Adams, Stegner, Brower, Newhall, and Abbey

• sheds light on the perpetual battle against the negative cultural impacts of industrialism and consumerism

• engages with several influential western films, including The Searchers , Ride the High Country , Lonely Are the Brave , The Wild Bunch , and Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid

This long-overdue assessment by one of the top thinkers in environmental history and ethics shows why these postwar defenders of wilderness remain relevant for readers today.
books.bio: Ben A. Minteer is professor of environmental history, philosophy, and conservation at Arizona State University. He is author or editor of more than a dozen books, including Wild Visions: Wilderness as Image and Idea .

praise.q: Informative, entertaining, and inspiring, Ben Minteer's marvelous story of legendary conservationists will keep you turning pages. His imaginative portraits of Nancy Newhall and Robert Redford alone are worth the price of admission.
praise.by: Mark Fiege, author of The Republic of Nature: An Environmental History of the United States
praise.cred: author of The Republic of Nature: An Environmental History of the United States

praise.q: Minteer's compelling environmental history shows how the Western tapped our admiration for the untamed hero as an argument for saving wild places where you could still feel like one.”—Jordan Fisher Smith, author of Engineering Eden: A Violent Death, a Federal Trial, and the Struggle to Restore Nature in Our National Parks

Ben Minteer provides fresh portraits of five essential figures in the American wilderness movement. In tracing their complicated lives and meaningful legacies, he brings them back into our current conversations on the value of the wild.
praise.by: Curt Meine, author of Aldo Leopold: His Life and Work
praise.cred: author of Aldo Leopold: His Life and Work

praise.q: The West, the Wild, the Western in print and film—Ben Minteer deftly weaves them all with the lives of five people who notably shaped our appreciation of America’s wilderness.
praise.by: Stephen J. Pyne, author of The Pyrocene: How We Created an Age of Fire, and What Happens Next
praise.cred: author of The Pyrocene: How We Created an Age of Fire, and What Happens Next

praise.q: In 1967 Yale University Press published the first edition of my book, Wilderness and the American Mind . Six decades later, Ben Minteer extends and deepens the discussion. He skillfully roots his environmentalist ‘Wild Bunch’ in the popular culture that gave them prominence.
praise.by: Roderick Frazier Nash

books.title: Spencer House
books.subtitle: Chronicle of a London Mansion
books.tagline: Major study of Spencer House, one of London’s most important historic buildings and arguably its greatest surviving 18th-century town house.
books.description:
This major study of Spencer House, backed by extensive new research, builds on the author’s acclaimed history published in 1993 to produce a fascinating reappraisal of one of London’s most important historic buildings and arguably its greatest surviving 18th-century town house.

This handsomely illustrated volume includes specially commissioned photographs by architectural photographer Paul Highnam , which present Spencer House in a dramatic, fresh perspective. An extended introduction sets the survival and revival of Spencer House against the loss of many other great historic London houses, particularly in the period since the First World War, highlighting its unique importance in the cultural and social life of London.

The history of the house itself, enriched with a wealth of previously unpublished material, includes a new chapter which explores the background to its construction for the 1st Earl Spencer, looking at his forebears’ growing engagement with London and the increasing splendour of their previous houses in and around the capital, situating the building as the culmination of a process stretching back almost 200 years.
books.bio: Joseph Friedman is an independent art historian and consultant and has published and lectured widely on the history of the fine and decorative arts and collecting, including a previous edition of the present study marking the restoration of Spencer House, on which he advised.

books.title: Stunning Patterns
books.subtitle: Woven Textiles from Madagascar's Merina Kingdom
books.tagline: A history of Eastern African silk weaving and its contemporary significance
books.description:
Spanning the nineteenth-century Merina Kingdom, the French colonial state, and the contemporary republic, Stunning Patterns traces the rich history of Eastern African silk weaving in Madagascar, highlighting themes of royalty, resistance, reinvention, and resilience. As the first extensive publication on Malagasy textiles in more than 20 years and the only one to focus on Merina textiles, this richly illustrated book reflects new trends in studying Indian Ocean African arts and underscores the sustained relevance of Malagasy creative practices.

Drawing on international scholarship, the text examines the critical political, economic, and environmental factors affecting lamba —a pan-Malagasy textile used as a garment or shroud—and centers on the evolution of lamba akotifahana —a specific, intricately designed silk lamba —to analyze the impact of artists and stakeholder patrons on the art form’s transforming aesthetics, style, and materials. Showcasing previously unpublished works, this social art history sets revival lamba akotifahana in dialogue with ongoing tradition-based weaving and contemporary artworks, exploring pervasive concepts of authenticity, modernity, and identity.

Distributed for the Cleveland Museum of Art

Exhibition schedule:

Cleveland Museum of Art

(December 6, 2026–November 7, 2027)
books.bio: Kristen Windmuller is curator of African art at the Cleveland Museum of Art.

books.title: The Architecture of Stockholm
books.subtitle: From Baroque to Post-modernism
books.authors: Ann Katrin Pihl Atmer, Cathrine Mellander Backman, Mats Edström, Frank Salmon, Kerstin Barup, Stephan Fickler, Charlie Gullström, Jarl Kremeier, Christopher Landstedt, Lars Ljungström, Peter Lundevall, Johan Mårtelius, Magnus Olausson, Martin Olin, Frida Rosenberg and Martin Rörby

books.title: The Attack of the Science Populists
books.subtitle: In Defense of Fundamental Physics
books.tagline: A bracing rebuttal of the science populists who’ve built huge audiences on the basis of misleading critiques of fundamental physics, set against a sweeping tour of the deepest unanswered questions facing researchers today.
books.description:
A growing number of critics insist that fundamental physics is in crisis. In their view, our leading theories have produced only stagnation: Blinded by bias and intellectual error, diverted by misaligned incentives, physicists cling to outdated orthodoxies and unverifiable hypotheses. These salvos are not in the pages of scientific journals. Rather, detractors churn out popular books and find a huge reception on social media, podcasts, and YouTube.

The Attack of the Science Populists shows that this influencer-driven crisis narrative is mistaken and deliberately misleading. Theoretical physicist Dan Hooper scrutinizes the underlying claims and the polemical voices behind them, situating their story within the broader trend toward science populism. Subtler than purveyors of pseudoscience, science populists—including some climate-change deniers and anti-vaccine activists—appeal to the chimera of “common sense.” Their arguments are rarely obvious nonsense, which makes them all the more insidious.

Hooper invites readers to take seriously the puzzles of fundamental physics, including dark matter, dark energy, cosmic inflation, and quantum gravity. He explains why, contrary to the populists’ claims, multiple lines of evidence support the existence of dark matter, and why theories such as string theory are more than mere mathematical speculation, representing some of the most promising research avenues in theoretical physics. He also makes the case that the Large Hadron Collider has been a magnificent success and that it should ultimately be succeeded by even larger particle accelerators.

Both an incisive rebuttal and an approachable introduction to the mysteries facing researchers today, The Attack of the Science Populists celebrates the achievements of scientific inquiry, without shying away from the inevitable perplexities.
books.bio: Dan Hooper is Professor of Physics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and Director of the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center. A leading researcher in particle cosmology and astrophysics, he is the author of At the Edge of Time, Dark Cosmos, and Nature’s Blueprint, and cohost of the podcast Why This Universe?

praise.q: Modern physics is so bizarre and counterintuitive that it can seem downright arbitrary in places. Are physicists just making things up? In this important book, Dan Hooper explains not just where current physics is, but how we got there and why, and what it all means for where we go next. There are good reasons, it turns out, why physicists sound as crazy as they sometimes do.

A timely and much-needed book. Hooper offers a powerful, clear-headed response to movements that seek to undermine scientific institutions, pushing back against popular myths and exposing the incentives of those spreading misinformation.

In recent decades, there has been a growing mistrust of scientists and their institutions, sometimes viewed as driven by personal, financial, and political interests. Purveyors of such mistrust play on the public’s lack of understanding of the practice of science and the nature of critical thinking. Dan Hooper provides a thoughtful and well-written account of the scientific enterprise, the motivations of those who attack it, and, most importantly, what is at stake.

books.title: The Book Everyone Read
books.subtitle: The Sphere of Sacrobosco and the Origins of Modern Science
books.tagline: How an all-but-forgotten medieval astronomy book ushered in the modern age of science
books.description:
Few people today have heard of Johannes de Sacrobosco, yet his textbook was the most widely read astronomy book ever written. For five hundred years, from when it was first written in the Middle Ages to the dawn of the modern world, the Sphere introduced Europeans to the cosmos. The Book Everyone Read traces the unpredictable twists and turns of scientific knowledge and discovery through the stories of Sacrobosco’s readers—and in doing so, tells a new story of the emergence of modern science.

Kathleen Crowther shows how the secret to the Sphere ’s longevity lay with its readers themselves, who chose which aspects of Sacrobosco’s original thirteenth-century text to accept, which to modify, and which to reject. Far from unchanging, editions of the book were accompanied by commentary, corrections, and details that challenged and revised the book’s original worldview of a finite, Earth-centered cosmos. Crowther introduces us to the university professors who peppered their lectures on the Sphere with tales of the exciting new discoveries made with telescopes and musings on the new Sun-centered model proposed by Copernicus, the navigators who found their way across the Atlantic using information about the stars they found in the book, the missionaries who brought translations of it to the Americas and Asia, and many others.

Through the surprising life of a medieval book of astronomy, The Book Everyone Read charts a scientific conversation that extended far beyond what we understood before.
books.bio: Kathleen M. Crowther is professor in the Department of the History of Science, Technology, and Medicine at the University of Oklahoma. She is the author of Adam and Eve in the Protestant Reformation and Policing Pregnant Bodies: From Ancient Greece to Post-Roe America .

praise.q: Before social media, before bestseller lists, before book groups—even before the printing press—one slim volume managed to capture a wide, diverse audience that read it, recopied it, and repeatedly revised it in the light of new discoveries. Kathleen Crowther tells the fantastic tale of a breakthrough science book that held sway for four hundred years.
praise.by: Dava Sobel, author of Longitude and Galileo’s Daughter
praise.cred: author of Longitude and Galileo’s Daughter

praise.q: A compelling account of how one pithy, stunningly popular textbook shaped the way people saw the world for centuries. Wide-ranging and beautifully illustrated, Crowther’s book demonstrates why Sacrobosco’s accessible description of the medieval universe lasted well beyond its initial reception in the Middle Ages, to exert a vital influence on Copernicus and Columbus and reach readers from Mexico to China.
praise.by: Seb Falk, author of The Light Ages: The Surprising Story of Medieval Science
praise.cred: author of The Light Ages: The Surprising Story of Medieval Science

praise.q: Who knew that an introductory text for twelve-year-old boys would become one of the most-read books in the European corpus? Kathleen Crowther’s compelling account expertly makes a case for the continuing importance of De Sphaera over four hundred years of European colonization, religious upheaval, and scientific change. A superbly written introduction to the scientific revolution that provides new insights for experts as well.”—Pamela H. Smith, author of From Lived Experience to the Written Word: Reconstructing Practical Knowledge in the Early Modern World

This meticulously researched study traces the enduring influence of Sacrobosco’s De Sphaera through a rich body of archival evidence. Crowther’s work provides an accessible and valuable guide to the text’s reception and will be an indispensable resource for future scholarship.
praise.by: Matteo Valleriani, Max Planck Institute for the History of Science
praise.cred: Max Planck Institute for the History of Science

praise.q: For more than four centuries, from about 1230, one book contained everything that an educated European was expected to learn about the constitution and arrangement of the physical universe. Kathleen Crowther’s lucid and compelling presentation describes that picture of the world and deftly explains how it could have persisted for so long.
praise.by: Robert S. Westman, University of California, San Diego

praise.q: Kathleen Crowther’s brilliant work shows that a didactic text long considered evidence of scientific stagnation represented in fact a springboard for controversy and a vehicle for transformation. A history of medieval and early modern astronomy rather than just a study of Sacrobosco’s masterpiece, The Book Everyone Read will be enjoyed by scholars for its original and exhaustive approach, and by general readers for its accessible style. Indeed, a book everyone should read.
praise.by: Ivano Dal Prete, author of On the Edge of Eternity: The Antiquity of the Earth in Medieval and Early Modern Europe
praise.cred: author of On the Edge of Eternity: The Antiquity of the Earth in Medieval and Early Modern Europe

books.title: The Coming Surge
books.subtitle: Coping with a Climate Reckoning Through Energy
books.tagline: An expert compares renewables and nuclear power as sources of low-carbon energy for the electric grid
books.description:
As the earth warms and we hurtle toward a climate reckoning, many nations are seeking low-carbon, greener ways to generate electricity. Electrification promises to power our vehicles, devices, and infrastructure in a decarbonized future. But, as Peter Wynn Kirby reminds us in The Coming Surge , electricity is only as green as the means used to produce it. Kirby sets up a head-to-head comparison of the two top contenders in the race to produce low-carbon energy for the electric grid: renewables and nuclear. Along the way, he makes predictions about technological development, from AI to automated traffic systems and grid sensor expansion, and considers how political shifts could influence energy policy and environmental outcomes. Through it all, perhaps improbably, he remains optimistic about human resilience and the fate of the planet.

Drawing on extensive fieldwork and research conducted in France, Japan, China, Puerto Rico, Finland, the Netherlands, and Germany, Kirby explores the way different countries are grappling with such issues as global warming, energy-sucking data centers, unsteady grids, infrastructure gigantism, extractive ideology, and carbon culture deprogramming. He finds that, rhetoric aside, nuclear power has fared poorly in a number of countries, including the United States, because it has been unable to compete on the basis of cost. As solar and wind costs have plummeted in recent years, renewables now appeal to municipal governments and utility companies even in deep red states like Oklahoma, Kansas, and especially Texas—the country’s top wind producer. In the end, he suggests that the future of low-carbon power may hinge less on grand technological achievements than on which systems are quickly scalable and can survive the tumult of markets, politics, and time on a planet running out of leeway.
books.bio: Peter Wynn Kirby is a climate and energy specialist and ethnographer at the University of Oxford, where he is a Senior Member at St. Antony’s College. The author of Troubled Natures and Boundless Worlds , he has published op-eds and commentary in The New York Times , The Guardian , The South China Morning Post , The Daily Beast , and elsewhere.

praise.q: The Coming Surge is a compelling study of the energy challenges humanity faces amid global heating and the rapid rise of energy-hungry technologies like AI. Moving from the United States to Japan, and from Finland to Namibia, Peter Wynn Kirby offers a clear-eyed exploration of the alternatives before us, especially the difficult choices many nations face between nuclear power and renewables. Yet Kirby’s story is not one of inevitable global catastrophe or easy idealism. On the contrary, this timely and important book offers an optimistic but realistic path forward, grounded in scientific evidence, international cooperation, and courageous leadership.
praise.by: Simon Avenell, the Australian National University

praise.q: Kirby makes a compelling case for the superiority of renewables over nuclear as the electricity supply source of the future.
praise.by: Simon Dalby, author of Pyromania: Fire and Geopolitics in a Climate Disrupted World
praise.cred: author of Pyromania: Fire and Geopolitics in a Climate Disrupted World

praise.q: Resisting the default mode of emergency or insurgency, The Coming Surge takes us on a deeply intelligent and human excursion through our energy futures—in effect, the future for all of us. The very best of contemporary scholarship delivered in lucid prose.
praise.by: Bruce Grant, New York University

praise.q: Kirby is unmatched in distilling, into just a few punchy yet nuanced pages, the hidden interplay of technology and culture that defines the new geographies of power—electric and political—in our warming, energy-hungry world. He helps us understand that there is no Planet B, that time is running out, and that we must consider two options to decarbonize electricity production: nuclear and renewables. Smart, accessible, and empowering!
praise.by: Léonard Laborie, French National Center for Scientific Research
praise.cred: French National Center for Scientific Research

books.title: The Craving Mind
books.subtitle: Why We Get Hooked and How We Can Break Bad Habits
books.tagline: A leading neuroscientist’s internationally acclaimed account of how addiction works and can be overcome, now in a ten-year anniversary edition
books.bio: Judson Brewer , M.D., Ph.D., is director of research and innovation at Brown University’s Mindfulness Center and professor in behavioral and social sciences and psychiatry. He is the author of The Hunger Habit and the New York Times bestseller Unwinding Anxiety .

praise.q: Accessible and enjoyable, The Craving Mind brilliantly combines the latest science with universal real-life experiences—from falling in love to spending too much time with our phones.
praise.by: Arianna Huffington

praise.q: This masterful, personal, friendly, compelling, humorous, and erudite book offers us a radically new perspective on learning, on breaking habits of mind not by force or through the application of will power or the desire for a reward, but by truly inhabiting the domain of being.
praise.by: Jon Kabat-Zinn, from the Foreword

praise.q: The core perception that ‘something is missing’ drives us to addiction and deprives us of the chance to live fully. By bringing together cutting-edge Western science, the radical insights of Buddhist psychology, and mindfulness practices, Judson Brewer offers a direct pathway to freeing our minds from the domination of craving.
praise.by: Tara Brach, author of Radical Acceptance and True Refuge
praise.cred: author of Radical Acceptance and True Refuge

praise.q: The Craving Mind is a remarkable book, one that will help free us from the powerful habits of craving and addiction. Brewer lays out a practical and empirically based pathway to greater freedom and ease in our lives. For many readers, this book will be life-transforming.
praise.by: Joseph Goldstein, author of Mindfulness: A Practical Guide to Awakening
praise.cred: author of Mindfulness: A Practical Guide to Awakening

books.title: The Good Life and Other Fictions
books.tagline: How novels attune us to the broader role of fiction in our lives—our everyday yet remarkable ability to think and live “as if”
books.description:
Why do we weep at fictitious things? How do we act on the basis of them? How much of moral life revolves around make-believe? In The Good Life and Other Fictions , David Dwan shows how literary fictions confront us with the wider role of fictiveness in our lives—the storied character we give to experience, our reliance on ideation, idealization and metaphor, the ways we depend on ideas that we know to be untrue or are only true because we choose to believe in them. In an age of fake news and fake antifakery, Dwan argues that we need a more differentiated sense of the fictive. Fiction is not necessarily fraud, nor is it simply error and unreality. Indeed, it is often the source of what’s best about us—the space in which the good life is imagined and talked into being.

Drawing on over a century of literary fiction—and offering detailed studies of Charles Dickens, George Eliot, Henry James, Joseph Conrad, Virginia Woolf, Wyndham Lewis and Iris Murdoch—Dwan investigates different facets of fictional experience, from imaginative projection to wishful thinking to self-deception to lies. Novels, he contends, both express and expose the ways we see through illusion, spending much of our time in a twilight state between reality and unreality, credulity and doubt, assent and dissent. Interrogating the benefits and limits of a fictive attitude—our deep yet dangerous need to operate “as if”—Dwan makes a highly original contribution to the field of ethical criticism, and to our general understanding of how life is made livable through fiction.
books.bio: David Dwan is professor of English literature and intellectual history at the University of Oxford and a tutorial fellow at Hertford College. He is the author of Liberty, Equality and Humbug: Orwell’s Political Ideals .

praise.q: At a time when the relationship of fiction to reality has become so fraught in both our politics and our ways of seeing ourselves, David Dwan provides a subtle and penetrating exploration of the novel as a testing ground for values, emotions and ideas—including our ideas of reality itself. He shows how fictions are essential to our individual and collective lives and examines the different ways in which writers as diverse as George Eliot and Wyndham Lewis, Joseph Conrad and Virginia Woolf, Henry James and Iris Murdoch, weigh illusion and imagination against fact and necessity. This is a bracing reminder that, since we can never be free of fictions, we need novels to help us tell the good ones from the bad.
praise.by: Fintan O’Toole, author of We Don't Know Ourselves
praise.cred: author of We Don't Know Ourselves

praise.q: In the era of fake news, how we think about fiction becomes an urgent question. Dwan's astonishingly lucid and incisive book clarifies what has seemed unclarifiable—the ways in which our moral lives depend on the quality of our attention to each other as real and fictional characters. Dwan shows us, in a way that no longer seemed possible, how the close reading of literature can keep us arguing in the best possible way about what might matter most to us.
praise.by: Adam Phillips, author of The Life You Want
praise.cred: author of The Life You Want

praise.q: The Good Life and Other Fictions is a timely, beautifully written and wise book. An unfailingly judicious and thoughtful reader, David Dwan makes an important contribution to the study of literature’s relation to moral philosophy.
praise.by: Jennifer Fleissner, author of Maladies of the Will: The American Novel and the Modernity Problem
praise.cred: author of Maladies of the Will: The American Novel and the Modernity Problem

praise.q: David Dwan’s The Good Life and Other Fictions defies easy categorization in all the best ways. Exploring the moral dimensions of fictiveness, Dwan draws the reader’s attention to the novel’s persistent engagement with a specific set of epistemological and aesthetic stances—irony, doubleness, doubt, unknowingness—ultimately challenging the centrality of common notions of the moral to the larger question of the good. A book that is sure to promote wide conversations across the fields of literature and philosophy.
praise.by: Amanda Anderson, Brown University

praise.q: David Dwan writes with such keen sensitivity about the moral complications novels produce that you soon come to feel—and feel before you see—why a life without fiction is a deficient life. Every page is alive to the hazards that reading fiction holds for us, which is, as we learn, just the reason we read. If you have ever wondered whether you should be doing something more useful with your time than read a novel, this book is for you.
praise.by: Michel Chaouli, author of Thinking with Kant's Critique of Judgment
praise.cred: author of Thinking with Kant's Critique of Judgment

praise.q: David Dwan’s The Good Life and Other Fictions is a witty, patient and persuasive exploration of some of the ways readers and writers of fiction have worried about it—and failed to worry enough. What are we to make of the appearing and disappearing ironies of the form, how did we get so interested in disinterest, why do we linger among the bewilderments of the phrase ‘as if’? Dwan addresses a cluster of questions that have been endlessly discussed, hardly ever answered, and his book is a marvelous gift to inquisitive readers old and new.
praise.by: Michael G. Wood, Princeton University

praise.q: The Good Life and Other Fictions successfully makes the case for the essential role of literary thought in moral philosophical thinking. It is lucid, intelligent and extraordinarily wide-ranging. Dwan has managed to produce that rare thing: an inspiring but still strenuous work of critical scholarship in the humanities.
praise.by: David Russell, author of Tact: Aesthetic Liberalism and the Essay Form in Nineteenth-Century Britain
praise.cred: author of Tact: Aesthetic Liberalism and the Essay Form in Nineteenth-Century Britain

books.title: The King's Slaves
books.subtitle: The British Empire and the Origins of American Slavery
books.tagline: A provocative account of how empire and absolutism institutionalized slavery in America
books.description:
The original draft of the Declaration of Independence condemned British kings for supporting slavery in their empire. England’s two seventeenth-century revolutions were in part a reaction to the crown’s proslavery policies, with politicians such as John Locke arguing that all people were born equal and that government should be based on consent. But while these principles would underpin the American Revolution, the treaty that ended that war protected the legal foundations of the plantation system in the new republic. The King’s Slaves untangles this thorny history, arguing that American slavery was borne from authoritarian rule.

In this incisive and thought-provoking book, Holly Brewer challenges the notion that slavery arose naturally in the colonies through the interests of merchants and planters, showing how behind them lay a British crown that believed in absolute power over subjects and granted similar powers to proprietors and masters. British kings used their authority over navies and armies, judges and royal governors to create an elaborate plantation system that produced more crops for export and greater wealth from tariffs. Royal propaganda supported claims that some peoples had no rights while edicts and proclamations circumvented the legislative process. Brewer describes how African and Indigenous peoples resisted the king’s slavery, as did some colonists, English politicians, and reformers. Yet slavery persisted, becoming enshrined after independence as a dehumanizing legal foundation of American capitalism.

A bold work of scholarship by a historian at the height of her powers, The King’s Slaves shares new perspectives on America’s founding, exposing empire’s pervasive role in spreading and justifying slavery in the new world.
books.bio: Holly Brewer is the Burke Chair of American Cultural and Intellectual History and associate professor of history at the University of Maryland. She is the author of By Birth or Consent: Children, Law, and the Anglo-American Revolution in Authority .

praise.q: Once in a generation, if we are lucky, a book comes along that remaps the history of Atlantic slavery. The King’s Slaves is such a book. Drawing on an impressive array of new findings, Brewer reveals how the English empire of slavery was created, directed, and maintained by the crown.
praise.by: Lauren Benton, author of They Called It Peace: Worlds of Imperial Violence
praise.cred: author of They Called It Peace: Worlds of Imperial Violence

praise.q: In this brilliant book, Holly Brewer convincingly challenges decades of scholarship about the origins of enslavement in the English colonies in North America and the Caribbean. She demonstrates that Thomas Jefferson was correct when, in his initial draft of the Declaration of Independence, he blamed the British crown for establishing and perpetuating slavery in British America. The King’s Slaves is a remarkable achievement.
praise.by: Mary Beth Norton, author of 1774: The Long Year of Revolution
praise.cred: author of 1774: The Long Year of Revolution

praise.q: The King’s Slaves is a major contribution to historical scholarship that intervenes eloquently in the great contemporary debate over the past and future of the American republic’s experiment in self-government. Refreshingly original and persuasive, The King’s Slaves revolutionizes the way we think about slavery and freedom in the national narrative.
praise.by: Peter S. Onuf, coauthor of Thomas Jefferson Survives: American Independence in His Time and Ours
praise.cred: coauthor of Thomas Jefferson Survives: American Independence in His Time and Ours

praise.q: A stunning accomplishment. Most legal historians date the legal endorsement of American slavery to the Constitution. Brewer demonstrates why we must look back earlier to the crown’s interests in the financing difficulties of empire. Her masterful narrative carries the reader through financing schemes, bankruptcies, imperial grants, and political upsets, always keeping the eye on how they affected sovereignty and power in the legitimation of slavery.
praise.by: Lea VanderVelde, author of Mrs. Dred Scott: A Life on Slavery’s Frontier
praise.cred: author of Mrs. Dred Scott: A Life on Slavery’s Frontier

praise.q: The King’s Slaves is a stunning achievement, offering a thorough and persuasive reinterpretation of early American slavery. Emphasizing the royalist authoritarian character of human bondage in the British colonies, the book shatters conventional thinking about the most fundamental issues in our history. Abraham Lincoln repeatedly likened proslavery presumptions to the divine right of kings. Holly Brewer demonstrates, among many other things, the historical profundity of Lincoln’s judgement.
praise.by: Sean Wilentz, author of No Property in Man: Slavery and Antislavery at the Nation’s Founding
praise.cred: author of No Property in Man: Slavery and Antislavery at the Nation’s Founding

books.title: The Kuzari
books.subtitle: The Book of Refutation and Proof on Behalf of the Despised Faith
books.tagline: The definitive translation of a classic text of medieval Jewish thought
books.description:
Considered the crowning intellectual achievement of a renowned medieval Jewish poet, The Kuzari stages a fictional dialogue between a Jewish sage and the king of the central Asian Khazars. Comprising five treatises, it constructs a systematic defense of the truth of Judaism against the criticisms and attacks leveled from four different directions: proponents of Aristotelian philosophy, Christianity, Islam, and non-rabbinic Karaite Judaism. By focusing on axial moments in the Jewish narrative, considered empirically true because of the large number of witnesses to these events, Halevi innovates the concept of a Divine Order as the central principle of Judaism, which removes the Jewish people from the normal restraints of nature and history.

This translation, the first from the original Judaeo-Arabic in 120 years, features an introduction that traces the life, thought, and impact of this remarkable thinker; detailed notes that provide historical and linguistic context; and an exploration of the text’s enduring influence on Jewish thought and culture.
books.bio: Judah ben Samuel Halevi (ca. 1075–1141) was a poet of the golden age of Spanish Jewry and one of the most important medieval Jewish figures. Barry S. Kogan is the Clarence and Robert Efroymson Professor Emeritus of Philosophy and Jewish Religious Thought at Hebrew Union College–Jewish Institute of Religion.

books.title: The Language of Fiction
books.subtitle: The Craft of Writing and the Pleasures of Reading
books.tagline: A master class in the language of fiction and a vivid reminder of how great novels can enrich our lives.
books.description:
What distinguishes the prose of great novels? How have celebrated novelists shaped language into a lasting source of insight and aesthetic pleasure? In The Language of Fiction , Robert Alter—one of our most distinguished literary critics—explores the literary devices and techniques novelists have used to write fiction that is illuminating, surprising, and a delight to read.

Drawing on a lifetime of close reading, Alter guides readers through the writing of Jane Austen, Herman Melville, Charles Dickens, George Eliot, Edith Wharton, Willa Cather, James Joyce, Virginia Woolf, William Faulkner, Zora Neale Hurston, Vladimir Nabokov, Saul Bellow, and more. With his characteristic clarity and sensitivity, Alter shows how these writers make use of word choice, metaphor, rhythm, perspective, and syntax in crafting the language of their novels. He carefully explains, for example, how James Joyce introduces invented words in Ulysses to represent the mind of a husband tormented by the thought of his wife’s unfaithfulness, how Willa Cather uses figuration in her otherwise austere O Pioneers! to establish the felt world in which her story will unfold, and how Ann Patchett uses shifting perspectives in Bel Canto to explore the layered nature of language.

The Language of Fiction shows what true mastery of literary style looks like, something AI may imitate but cannot create. It offers not only a path to more attentive reading but a guide to writing itself, revealing how the prose of great writers can deepen our understanding, expand our inner lives, and inspire us to write with greater precision and power.
books.bio: Robert Alter is Professor in the Graduate School and Emeritus Professor of Hebrew and Comparative Literature at the University of California, Berkeley. He is the author of Nabokov and the Real World, Pen of Iron: American Prose and the King James Bible, and Necessary Angels: Tradition and Modernity in Kafka, Benjamin, and Scholem, among other books. Award-winning translator of the complete Hebrew Bible, Alter has received the National Jewish Book Award for Lifetime Achievement, the PEN Center Literary Award for Translation, and the Robert Kirsch Award from the Los Angeles Times for lifetime contribution to American letters.

praise.q: A feast both for the language-starved and for connoisseurs, The Language of Fiction instructs us how to read complex texts by doing it, by presenting and unpacking amazing feats of linguistic skill in an effort at once to allow their authors to dazzle us and to produce in us a hunger for more. It’s a very successful strategy presented in a succession of chapters of which the ones on rhythm and syntax are especially illuminating.

At a time when the art of reading feels increasingly endangered, The Language of Fiction makes a forceful argument for literature's incomparable joys. Beyond the depth and breadth of Alter’s erudition, what stands out is his infectious love of language. This book has helped teach me not only how to read, but how to write.

The Language of Fiction is a terrific entry point to the excitement of the close reading of literary fiction, alive to the 'artful distinctiveness' of what language and form can do. It is the culmination of a lifetime’s immersion in the written word and the pleasures of pedagogy.

Robert Alter has written a book for word junkies and story junkies, a guided tour through masterpieces of fiction in English. Readers well-versed in Sterne, Melville, James, Woolf, Joyce, and Faulkner will savor their distinctive styles again in Alter’s exuberant account, and readers eager to try these adventures for the first time could find no better teacher. Alter is a passionate, lucid, and generous reader.

In this exuberant meditation on the language of fiction, Robert Alter once again demonstrates that, as a sensitive reader of prose, he has no match. Considering figurative language and the intertwining of language, rhythm, and syntax, Alter shows how great novelists use the resources of language to convey a unique vision and for the sheer pleasure of inventiveness.

books.title: The Machine and the Microchip
books.subtitle: Inside the Secret War for Global High-Tech Supremacy
books.tagline: The story of the world’s most important machine and the global chip war to control the future of AI.
books.description:
On the island of Taiwan a company called TSMC produces 90 percent of the advanced microchips that power Elon Musk’s electric cars and space rockets, Apple’s iPhones and computers, ChatGPT’s AI systems, and NVIDIA’s stock price. TSMC can do so only with the extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography system manufactured by a Dutch company, ASML. How a little-known Dutch company and a vulnerable island in East Asia became central to the global balance of power is the story Cagan Koc and Diederik Baazil tell in The Machine and the Microchip . It is a thrilling narrative that takes readers from the White House Situation Room and government offices in Europe and Asia to the multi-billion-dollar cleanrooms where the world's most advanced technology is created—to explain why the struggle for control of advanced semiconductors may well determine the course of this century.

Drawing on original reporting, exclusive interviews, and previously undisclosed details, Koc and Baazil examine the technological breakthroughs, export controls, corporate rivalries, political decisions, and espionage campaigns that have transformed semiconductors into the strategic geopolitical battleground of the twenty-first century. Their book also connects the AI revolution to the semiconductor supply chain, revealing the hidden technologies, companies, and people that make AI possible. At once accessible and deeply informed, spanning the worlds of engineering, business, national security, and international politics, their work tells what could be the defining story of our time.
books.bio:
Cagan Koc (Author)

Cagan Koc has spent more than nine years with Bloomberg News , where he served as the Netherlands Bureau Chief from 2021 to 2025. Previously, he reported for The Wall Street Journal , covering a range of economic and corporate topics.

Diederik Baazil (Author)

Diederik Baazil served as Bloomberg’s political correspondent in The Hague and as Japan correspondent for the Dutch media outlets De Groene Amsterdammer and Het Financieele Dagblad . He currently resides in Brussels.

books.title: The Princeton History of American Political Thought
books.authors: Susan McWilliams Barndt, Roosevelt Montás, Nicholas Buccola, Tunde Adeleke, Eric Arnesen, Jeremy D. Bailey, Teresa Bejan, Jason Edward Black, David S. Brown, Katherine Elizabeth Brown, Jane E. Calvert, Joshua L. Cherniss, Soyica Diggs Colbert, Sue Davis, Andrew Delbanco, Kathy Ferguson, Marilyn Fischer, Jack Fruchtman, Alan Gibson, Simon Gilhooley, Samuel Goldman, Annette Gordon-Reed, Van Gosse, Burke Hendrix, Desmond Jagmohan, Carolyn Karcher, Harvey J. Kaye, Michael Kazin, Jared Anthony Loggins, Daniel Mandell, Shannon L. Mariotti, Luke Mayville, Sidney Milkis, Charles E. Morris III, José-Antonio Orosco, Rebecca Jo Plant, James Read, Julie L. Reed, Michael Sawyer, David J. Siemers, Nikhil Pal Singh, Rose Stremlau, Joshua Tait, Bob Pepperman Taylor, Natalie Fuehrer Taylor, Trygve Throntveit, Jack Turner, Carol W. White, Deva Woodly, Matthew H. Young, Michael Zuckert
books.tagline: The ultimate guide to the thinkers and ideas that have shaped the United States, featuring essential primary sources introduced by leading scholars
books.description:
The Princeton History of American Political Thought showcases the defining voices and debates in U.S. political history, spanning from the 1600s to the present. Each set of primary sources is accompanied by a short, accessible essay by a leading scholar, situating the writings in a broader American conversation about what the nation is, has been, and could be. Without shying away from the disagreements that have shaped the nation, the book shows how these controversies have played out within a broadly consistent set of questions, commitments, and concerns. The result captures the diversity, depth, and power of the American political tradition.

An essential reference, The Princeton History of American Political Thought is not just for scholars and students but for anyone who seeks to understand the United States: its past, its present, and its future possibilities.

Features short primary sources that range from the 1600s to the present

Includes accessible introductions and essays about each set of sources, written by leading experts

Showcases the wide variety of perspectives that characterize the American political tradition
books.bio: Susan McWilliams Barndt is professor of politics at Pomona College. Her books include The American Road Trip and American Political Thought and A Political Companion to James Baldwin . Nicholas Buccola is professor of government and the Dr. Jules L. Whitehill Professor of Humanism and Ethics at Claremont McKenna College. His books include One Man’s Freedom: Goldwater, King, and the Struggle over an American Ideal (Princeton). Roosevelt Montás is the John and Margaret Bard Professor in Liberal Education and Civic Life at Bard College and the author of Rescuing Socrates: How the Great Books Changed My Life and Why They Matter for a New Generation (Princeton).

praise.q: This capacious and essential volume presents American political thought not as a shared set of political commitments but as a shared resource that allows us to better understand rival commitments. It shows how the tradition privileges questions, not conclusions. To peruse this extraordinary anthology is to rediscover possibilities for shaping our collective political life.
praise.by: Russell Muirhead, Dartmouth College
