books.bio: Julie Crooks is curator of Arts of Global Africa and the Diaspora at the Art Gallery of Ontario. Jason Cyrus is an associate lecturer in cultural and historical studies at the London College of Fashion. Suzanne Boyd is editor-in-chief and publisher of Zoomer .

books.title: The Future of Freedom
books.subtitle: The Birth of Independence in the Puritan Revolution
books.tagline: A re-founding of the history of independence and future of freedom through the eyes of ordinary men and women in the Puritan Revolution
books.description:
Does human freedom stand a chance in the future? Drawing on fresh sources, Polly Ha shows how ordinary men and women in Independent congregations in early modern England and New England introduced new foundational layers for liberty. They informed prominent spokesmen such as John Milton and Roger Williams. In doing so, they expanded the moral, political, and temporal conditions for securing the future of freedom before Enlightenment assumptions reconfigured those terms. Such sources include:

• Hidden manuscripts documenting the earliest debates over independence

• Self-narratives by women, youths, and other unfamiliar authors

• Popular print, sermons, and commentaries

Challenging a series of myths surrounding the origins of the liberal West, Ha offers an alternative account of this pivotal moment in the history of liberty. In contrast to elites, these Independents began to apply freedom more universally, conscripting a broader range of participants across gender, age, race, and social hierarchies. They developed a deep historical consciousness and drew from sources that extended beyond the Latinate world. Spelling out exactly what was at stake in these debates, they shed further light on basic questions about what it meant to be human in the face of an uncertain future.
books.bio: Polly Ha is associate professor of early modern history in the Divinity School and History Department at Duke University, director of Transformative Ideas at Duke, and a McDonald Distinguished Senior Fellow at the Emory Center for Law and Religion.

books.title: The Princeton Field Guide to the Jurassic
books.authors: Nan Crystal Arens, Paul M. Barrett
books.tagline: A dazzling illustrated guide to the animals and plants of the Jurassic
books.description:
Spanning more than fifty million years, the Jurassic witnessed a proliferation of new life. As the supercontinent Pangaea broke up, sea levels rose and water flooded newly opened regions, creating shallows and sheltered lagoons where all manner of species flourished. Oceans teemed with life, while a once-arid climate on land became humid and subtropical. This book offers an unparalleled look at the period’s amazing animals and plants, from Stegosaurus and Diplodocus to conifers, ginkgos, ferns, and some truly weird seed plants. The Princeton Field Guide to the Jurassic is the ultimate illustrated guide to the awe-inspiring beasts and botanical wonders of the Jurassic.

Features more than two hundred illustrations, from full-color life studies and landscapes to detailed drawings of representative species

Profiles the breathtaking diversity of Jurassic fauna and flora

Discusses dinosaurs, marine reptiles, early birds, pterosaurs, mammals, amphibians, insects, and marine invertebrates

Offers an in-depth look at the trees and vibrant plant life of the Jurassic forests

A must-have reference book for anyone interested in the prehistoric world of dinosaurs
books.bio: Nan Crystal Arens is professor of geoscience at Hobart and William Smith Colleges. She is the author of The Princeton Field Guide to Mesozoic Plants (Princeton). Paul M. Barrett is individual merit researcher and head of science engagement at the Natural History Museum, London. The armored dinosaur Vectipelta barretti is named in his honor.

books.title: The Right Way
books.subtitle: The Conservative Worldview from the New Deal to Trumpism
books.authors: Marc J. Hetherington, Andrew M. Engelhardt, Jonathan Weiler
books.tagline: Why supporting big government, trade barriers, and unchecked executive power is still conservative—and why MAGA’s worldview is far more coherent than its critics think
books.description:
When Donald Trump surged to the lead in the 2015 fight for the GOP presidential nomination, bewildered political watchers struggled to understand why, because his policy positions were often at odds with what had been Republican orthodoxy since the days of Ronald Reagan. The Right Way reveals what these political observers missed, presenting a multidimensional understanding of the conservative worldview that explains why Trump has succeeded in both building up and tearing down what conservatives have traditionally embraced.

Marc Hetherington, Andrew Engelhardt, and Jonathan Weiler argue for a reimagining of conservatism that lends clarity to partisan paradoxes that otherwise seem inconsistent with the brand of conservatism most of us grew up with. Drawing on in-depth surveys from across America, they show how conservative voters rely on their general view of the world and human nature more broadly to understand the political world around them. Rather than preferences for limited government, conservative outlooks and dispositions explain why ordinary people who identify as conservatives vote the way they do on issues ranging from racial and gender equality to LGBTQ rights, immigration, redistribution, and foreign policy. They also tackle puzzles such as the willingness of today’s conservatives to support politicians who bend or even break norms and rules that have been central to democratic functioning throughout American history.

Essential reading for polarized times, The Right Way demonstrates that while the politics of the moment may be in flux, worldviews about authority, tradition, community, and personal responsibility consistently shape how conservative voters evaluate public policies and choose their leaders.
books.bio: Marc J. Hetherington is the Raymond Dawson Distinguished Bicentennial Professor of Political Science at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill. Andrew M. Engelhardt is assistant professor of political science at Stony Brook University, State University of New York. Jonathan Weiler is a teaching professor in the Curriculum in Global Studies at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

praise.q: Two of the most urgent questions for students of American politics are: Why has partisan polarization become so extreme and how has Donald Trump, despite all, managed to retain the support of most ordinary Republicans? The Right Way , by showing how prepolitical worldviews have powerfully shaped today’s partisan beliefs and attitudes, makes a major contribution to answering these questions as well as many others. It is essential reading for anyone looking for a deeper understanding of American political opinion and behavior.
praise.by: Gary C. Jacobson, University of California, San Diego

praise.q: Bringing to fruition a decades-long research program, this work brings into the open for the first time the complex of concerns and values—allied but distinct all the same—that propel the hyperaggressive worldview of the political right in today’s politics. It is a masterwork.
praise.by: Paul M. Sniderman, Stanford University

praise.q: The Right Way has the right stuff for understanding today’s conservative politics.
praise.by: John H. Aldrich, author of Why Parties? The Origin and Transformation of Political Parties in America
praise.cred: author of Why Parties? The Origin and Transformation of Political Parties in America

books.title: Think Again
books.subtitle: A New Introduction to Philosophy
books.tagline: An accessible, comprehensive, and innovative introduction to philosophy that connects timeless questions to the lives of students
books.description:
Think Again is a personal and cutting-edge introduction to philosophy by award-winning teacher and renowned public philosopher John Kaag. The book encourages students to relate to their own lives the important questions raised by philosophy over the millennia. Motivated by the belief that teaching is fundamental to philosophy, the book has been carefully designed and written to be accessible to a wide range of undergraduates at a broad array of schools.

Think Again proceeds historically, guiding students from the ancients through to 1900 and the birth of contemporary philosophy. From there, it proceeds thematically, covering topics as diverse as metaphysics and epistemology, philosophy of mind, moral and political philosophy, and philosophical approaches to oppression. It features skillfully selected excerpts of primary texts from philosophy to encourage students’ direct engagement with and close reading of foundational texts.

Personal and conversational style

Historical and thematic coverage

Primary text excerpts

Learning objectives

Chapter reviews that include a summary, key terms, review questions, and additional readings

Three types of boxed features: Historical Context, Writing Philosophically, and Thinking Critically
books.bio: John Kaag is professor of philosophy at the University of Massachusetts, Lowell, and external professor at the Santa Fe Institute. He is the author of two memoirs, Hiking with Nietzsche and American Philosophy . His other books include Thinking Through Writing ; Sick Souls, Healthy Minds: How William James Can Save Your Life ; and Henry at Work: Thoreau on Making a Living (all Princeton).

praise.q: Incredibly impressive. I felt smarter after reading this book, and think students will as well.
praise.by: Mariana Alessandri, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
praise.cred: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

praise.q: Kaag treats complex ideas in a patient way, leading students to understand larger questions and problems in philosophy. One of the book’s strengths is the attention it gives to teaching how to think and write philosophically. It not only explains how ideas emerged historically but how these ideas are used in everyday life. Moreover, the approach of thinking of philosophy as a way of being human anchors the practice of philosophy in the realm of action.
praise.by: Celia T. Bardwell-Jones, University of Hawaiʻi at Hilo

praise.q: Kaag is a gifted storyteller, and there is richer storytelling in this book than in many other philosophy textbooks I’ve read or used. The vivid imagery throughout the book and the interesting tidbits about philosophers and their stories make the material come alive. Think Again is exceedingly accessible to a wide range of readers.
praise.by: Tess Varner, Concordia College

praise.q: An excellent book. The writing is superior. Kaag masterfully weaves philosophical content, everyday experience, personal anecdotes, and current events. The substantial inclusion of primary texts allows instructors to enjoy the benefits of a textbook without sacrificing a commitment to the original text. And Kaag’s explanations and applications make the primary texts more accessible.
praise.by: Michael Ventimiglia, Sacred Heart University

books.title: Understanding the Digital World
books.subtitle: What You Need to Know about Computers, the Internet, Privacy, and Security, Third Edition
books.tagline: The popular introductory textbook that explains how computer hardware, software, and networks work—now fully updated for today’s fast-changing digital age
books.description:
Understanding the Digital World has established itself as the essential computer science textbook for nonmajors and a must-read for anyone who wants to know more about computers and communications. It explains how computers are built and how they compute, what programming is, how the Internet and the web work, Python programming, AI and machine learning, the inherent limitations of computers, and much more. Now completely updated, this informative and accessible book covers all facets of the digital world, revealing how computers affect security, privacy, property, and many other vital social, political, and economic issues.

Now covers large language models and chatbots like ChatGPT

Features timely new discussions of how LLMs are changing how we live and work, including how the use of AI is transforming programming itself

Gives updated examples of new technologies like self-driving cars and how they affect us

Provides added coverage of data breaches, facial recognition and biometrics, tracking, and other privacy issues

Offers expanded coverage of hardware like multiple cores and GPUs

Additional historical discussions cover topics such as Leibniz’s work on binary numbers

Includes suggestions for further reading and a glossary of technical terms and buzzwords
books.bio: Brian W. Kernighan is professor of computer science at Princeton University. His many books include Millions, Billions, Zillions: Defending Yourself in a World of Too Many Numbers (Princeton) and The C Programming Language .

praise.q: [Kernighan's] credentials as a computer scientist are stellar but what comes through in this book is a humanitarian concern about the place of technology in the modern world. . . . The grounding [the book] provides in the fundamentals of computing and how the technology interacts with our lives will remain relevant for a very long time.
praise.by: Steve Mansfield-Devine, Network Security "

praise.q: This is the clearest and simplest explanation of the world we now all depend on—how it works and why it does what it does—from one of our best-known inventors. Everyone on Earth needs to read it.
praise.by: Eric Schmidt, former executive chairman of Alphabet Inc. and Google
praise.cred: former executive chairman of Alphabet Inc. and Google

praise.q: This book takes the mystery out of computers and the Internet, and everyone can learn from it. With a friendly and accessible style, Kernighan connects what is happening inside machines to the news of the day and developments about the digital world.
praise.by: Harry Lewis, coauthor of Blown to Bits: Your Life, Liberty, and Happiness after the Digital Explosion
praise.cred: coauthor of Blown to Bits: Your Life, Liberty, and Happiness after the Digital Explosion

praise.q: Kernighan tells us exactly what we need to know about computers and computer science, focusing on ideas that are useful and interesting for everyday computer users. He covers a fascinating range of topics, including fundamentals such as computer hardware, programming, algorithms, and networks, as well as politically charged issues related to government surveillance, privacy, and Internet neutrality.
praise.by: John MacCormick, author of Thinking AI: How Artificial Intelligence Emulates Human Understanding
praise.cred: author of Thinking AI: How Artificial Intelligence Emulates Human Understanding

praise.q: Understanding the Digital World provides a broad overview of computers and electronic communications for a general audience. The book flows smoothly from topic to topic, and readers from diverse backgrounds will find it accessible.
praise.by: Bryan Respass, Bergen County Academies

books.title: Unipotent Ideals and Harish-Chandra Bimodules
books.authors: Ivan Loseu, Dmytro Matvieievskyi, Lucas Mason-Brown
books.tagline: A groundbreaking book that applies new geometric tools to one of the oldest problems in representation theory, expanding the field and paving the way for further progress
books.description:
In the 1920s, Hermann Weyl gave a complete classification of the irreducible unitary representations of a compact Lie group G. Around the same time, Fritz Peter and Weyl showed that these irreducible unitary representations are fundamental objects for harmonic analysis on G. If G is instead a noncompact Lie group, such as GL_n(R), the classification of the irreducible unitary G-representations is a much more diﬃcult problem, one that remains open in general. An idea, with its origins in the work of Kostant, Kirillov, and Vogan, is that the set of irreducible unitary G-representations should contain a finite set of “building blocks,” called unipotent representations, related to the set of nilpotent co-adjoint G-orbits. This book proposes a definition and theory of unipotent representations in the case of when G is a complex reductive Lie group, such as GL_n(C).

This definition is based on the theory of quantizations of symplectic singularities, especially the geometry of nilpotent co-adjoint orbits and their equivariant covers. The main theorems include a geometric classification of unipotent representations, a calculation of their infinitesimal characters, and a proof of their unitarity in the case of classical groups. Although further obstacles remain, this work paves the way for a general theory of unipotent representations of reductive Lie groups, which should in turn form the basis of the classification of irreducible unitary representations.
books.bio: Ivan Losev is professor of mathematics at Yale University. Lucas Mason-Brown is assistant professor of mathematics at Columbia University. Dmytro Matvieievskyi is visiting assistant professor of mathematics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

books.title: Volcanoes, People, and Teleconnection
books.subtitle: Local Spirits and Distant Monsters
books.tagline: A unique comparison of how people living in the shadow of volcanoes and those residing continents away experience and live with their effects
books.description:
In 1815, when the volcano Tambora in what was then the East Indies erupted, it precipitated global cooling that lasted for several years and led to one of the great subsistence crises in the western world. In the vicinity of the volcano itself, the eruption had equally devastating but differently interpreted effects. Surviving local accounts in the form of syair , epic Malay poetry, interpreted the cataclysm as divine punishment for everyday violations of traditional social orders.

Through the histories of three Indonesian volcanoes—Tambora, on the island of Sumbawa; Krakatau, with its catastrophic 1883 eruption, off the west coast of Java; and Merapi, which is in a state of near-continuous eruption in Central Java—Michael R. Dove compares the global perception of massive eruptions as an incomprehensible break in normality with local villagers’ practice of “domesticating” and thereby adapting to and wresting a livelihood from volcanic activity. Given the historic role of volcanoes as climate-forcing agents, this comparison offers a lesson in how local communities can understand and respond to a global phenomenon like environmental change.
books.bio: Michael R. Dove is the Margaret K. Musser Professor of Social Ecology, professor of anthropology, and curator of anthropology at the Peabody Museum, Yale University. He is the author of Hearsay Is Not Excluded: A History of Natural History and Bitter Shade: The Ecological Challenge of Human Consciousness .

books.title: Wild Indigo
books.subtitle: Poems
books.tagline: A stunning poetic narrative about a painter and his lover living on a former Southern slave plantation
books.description:
Wild Indigo is a remarkable poetic debut—a lyric narrative set on a former slave plantation in rural Louisiana, where love, art, and history exert competing claims. The speaker, a Black painter, has inherited the house from his white grandmother—a bequest that offers solitude and space for his creative work but also forces him to confront the trauma of slavery. His male lover, troubled by the morality of inhabiting such a place, believes the property is deepening his own depression. As the couple reckons with the lover’s mental state, Korey Williams’s poems trace a mounting tension between legacy and refusal, creation and complicity. As the story unfolds, Wild Indigo moves through a variety of poetic forms, from the sonnet to haibun, maintaining at once a powerful narrative momentum and the compression and musicality of lyric.

Mixing elements of Southern Gothic and the genre of the artist’s novel, Wild Indigo is written in the tradition of verse narratives such as Anne Carson’s Autobiography of Red , Natasha Trethewey’s Bellocq’s Ophelia , and Ciaran Carson’s For All We Know . Dreamy and uneasy, somber and erotic, Wild Indigo asks what it means to make art—and to make a life—on contested ground, where beauty and violence are bound together.
books.bio: Korey Williams is a poet and teacher in Chicago. His work has appeared in many publications, including Assaracus , The Offing , and Spoon River Poetry Review . He holds an MFA from Cornell University and a PhD from the University of Chicago.

praise.q: Reading Wild Indigo was joyous and enriching. I marveled at the prismatic storytelling. Each memory, each glimpse into the interiority of the speaker and his partner, cast its own exquisite light, but also dovetailed into an emotionally and intellectually dazzling arc. And what language! It’s rare to encounter a debut that’s thrilling and instructive at the level of language and craft. Korey Williams charges his poems with astonishing verbs, with lush and sweat-rich phrasing, and with a deft torquing of syntax. This is an astonishing debut.”—Eduardo C. Corral, Lambda Literary Award
praise.by: winning author of Guillotine: Poems

praise.q: Attention—that is, the poet’s patience, presence, and care—meets devotion with such passion in these poems that reader and beloved alike are absorbed, wafer and wine, and sanctified. Korey Williams’s discerning debut collection, Wild Indigo , is suffused with sorrow song and fever dream. Radiant from within like some ancient sculpture, each line begs to be touched.”—Gregory Pardlo, Pulitzer Prize
praise.by: winning poet and author of Spectral Evidence
praise.who: winning poet and author of Spectral Evidence

outlets: winning poet and author of Spectral Evidence

books.title: American Contradiction
books.subtitle: Revolution and Revenge from the 1950s to Now
books.tagline: How did Americans come to elect Barack Obama—and then Donald Trump? Those choices capture what Paul Starr calls the American contradiction.
books.description:
The whole truth about America, Starr argues in this new history of the United States since the 1950s, has never been contained in one consistent set of values or interests. The nation was born in the contradiction between freedom and slavery. Today it is beset by a contradiction between a changing people and a resisting nation, a nation with entrenched institutions that have empowered those who fear the changes and look to restore an old America of their imagining.

Starr tells this history from the dual standpoints of the progressive movements that changed the American people and of the movements that emerged in response. Black Americans, he argues, served as a model minority, setting in motion America’s twentieth-century revolutions in gender as well as race and rights. With industry’s decline and the rise of economic inequality, millions of Americans have felt dispossessed and want the old America back. Trump is their revenge. American Contradiction tells the story of how 1950s America became the almost unrecognizable America of the 2020s.
books.bio: Paul Starr is professor of sociology and public affairs at Princeton University and founding coeditor of the American Prospect magazine. He received the Pulitzer Prize for Nonfiction and Bancroft Prize in American History for The Social Transformation of American Medicine . Over a half-century he has written essays and op‑eds for newspapers and magazines as well as books on America’s institutions, history, and politics.

praise.q: This is the best book I’ve read that takes on and explicates that seemingly unanswerable question [how to make sense of recent American history]. On almost every page, I learned something new, or saw something in a novel way that helped my understanding of [everything].
praise.by: Greg Olear, Prevail (podcast)

praise.q: [A] thoughtful study of the push and pull from right to left and back again in the past 75 years. . . . A useful key to understanding how American politics and the American polity have become so intractably polarized.
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews

praise.q: A perceptive history of the past eight decades of U.S. partisan politics [and] a persuasive call for unity.
praise.by: Publishers Weekly

praise.q: I highly recommend American Contradiction to anyone seeking to understand how we arrived at our present political moment. . . . An ambitious act of synthesis by one of our most accomplished sociologists of institutions.
praise.by: Glenn Loury, “The Glenn Show” (Substack)

praise.q: Paul Starr, one of the great chroniclers of American institutions, provides a brilliant reinterpretation of the modern political era. His book unpacks the fundamental contradictions that have haunted the body politic since the 1960s. A country born in contraction between slavery and freedom has remained at odds with itself even as the issues changed. The bold attack by the progressive project on hierarchical institutions produced an equally fierce counterattack by those who wanted to restore an imagined earlier era. American Contradiction teaches us how, far from being an anomaly, the election of Donald Trump twice to the presidency was a result of deeply-rooted political forces that had been steadily gaining strength within the Republican Party for decades. This is a must-read book for sociologists, historians, political scientists, and any reader interested in our nation’s political history.
praise.by: Julian E. Zelizer, Princeton University, and author of In Defense of Partisanship
praise.cred: Princeton University, and author of In Defense of Partisanship

praise.q: American Contradiction is an extraordinarily instructive analysis of the perplexing character of the United States. Starr’s commentary on the journey from Eisenhower to Trump bristles with insight. As I read, I found myself constantly underlining his informative and accessible text.”—Randall Kennedy, Michael R. Klein Professor of Law, Harvard Law School, and author of Say It Loud! On Race, Law, History, and Culture

A fascinating examination of the clash between changing family, gender, and sexual norms, racial justice struggles, rightwing political campaigns, and accelerating economic inequality that underlies our current political crises. Eye-opening.
praise.by: Stephanie Coontz, author of The Way We Never Were: American Families and the Nostalgia Trap
praise.cred: author of The Way We Never Were: American Families and the Nostalgia Trap

praise.q: Anything Paul Starr writes is important to read, and this book is no exception. American Contradiction is a highly sophisticated history of the United States since the 1950s emphasizing the interplay between social movements, politics, culture, law, and social policy.
praise.by: Nelson Lichtenstein, coauthor of A Fabulous Failure: The Clinton Presidency and the Transformation of American Capitalism
praise.cred: coauthor of A Fabulous Failure: The Clinton Presidency and the Transformation of American Capitalism

books.title: Animals Matter
books.subtitle: The Case for a Kinder World
books.tagline: “Extraordinary and powerful.”—Peter Singer, author of Animal Liberation From the New York Times bestselling author, a bold new account of animal rights, why they may be on the verge of mass popularity, and why animals need a Bill of Rights
books.description:
In Animals Matter , Cass Sunstein offers a pathbreaking new argument for why we must change our practices to reduce the unjustified suffering of animals. This surprisingly personal book offers a simple proposition: The interests of animals count, and we should work to promote their well-being, just as we should work to promote the well-being of humans. Drawing on psychology, behavioral economics, and his White House experiences, Sunstein reveals why people are likely, in time, to increase their support for the legal protection of animals and why, ultimately, we should adopt a Bill of Rights for animals that affirms their right to live free from cruelty and deprivation.

Applying his research on “social cascades,” Sunstein compares the animal rights movement to previous causes such as civil rights that exploded in size once they passed a threshold moment. But this change won’t happen on its own. Sunstein demonstrates that we need to overcome deliberate ignorance about the mistreatment of animals, to make their suffering conspicuous and visible, and to create animal welfare cascades. Our governments need to recognize benefits and harms to animals in their policymaking. We need to give political and legal representation to animals who are being mistreated, and we need to use “nudges” to increase their well-being.

Animal rights are not radical or utopian; they are rooted in widespread moral judgments. Sunstein shows how we can eventually create a world in which most people will come to embrace rights for animals.
books.bio: Cass R. Sunstein is the Robert Walmsley University Professor at Harvard University, founder and director of the Program on Behavioral Economics and Public Policy at Harvard Law School, former head of the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, and recipient of the Holberg Prize. His many books include the New York Times bestseller Nudge (with Richard H. Thaler).

praise.q: In this extraordinary and powerful book, Cass Sunstein explains not only why animals matter but also how we can change public policy and individual behavior to make life better for animals and for ourselves. Read and learn!
praise.by: Peter Singer, author of Animal Liberation

praise.q: Brilliant, exhilarating, and heartfelt, this book by a preeminent legal theorist confronts willful ignorance and challenges us to stop torturing our fellow creatures and even to improve their lives.
praise.by: Martha C. Nussbaum, author of Justice for Animals

praise.q: Animals Matter is a seminal work that brings to bear Sunstein’s philosophical acumen, exceptional legal mind, extensive White House experience, and groundbreaking work in behavioral economics. The result is a stunningly original exploration of what we owe to animals, a trenchant defense of a welfarist approach to animal ethics, and a passionate and persuasive rallying cry for a Bill of Rights for animals.
praise.by: Mark Rowlands, author of The Word of Dog: What Our Canine Companions Can Teach Us About Living a Good Life
praise.cred: author of The Word of Dog: What Our Canine Companions Can Teach Us About Living a Good Life

praise.q: Cass Sunstein understands how social change happens, and in this wise, warm, and deeply personal book, he shows why we should build a better world for animals and how we can start. A landmark in practical moral leadership.
praise.by: Jeff Sebo, author of The Moral Circle and Saving Animals, Saving Ourselves
praise.cred: author of The Moral Circle and Saving Animals, Saving Ourselves

books.title: Astrosemiosis
books.subtitle: Grounds for Intelligent Life beyond Earth
books.tagline: A voyage into the mysterious world of alien intelligence
books.description:
Do advanced life forms exist beyond Earth? Is there intelligent life elsewhere in the cosmos? Ask an astrobiologist and you will usually get back a qualified “yes," but further investigation is stymied by the slipperiness of concepts like “advanced” and “intelligent.” Most astrobiologists then turn their attention to more tractable scientific issues, examining geological and biological conditions for life on Earth in order to propose how it might have arisen elsewhere. Their ambition is to understand life wherever it occurs as part of the processes of planetary formation and change.

Gary Tomlinson extends this scientific project as only a humanist can. Starting from the foundation of earthly meaning, sign making or semiosis , he opens a new path toward the alluring question of alien intelligence. He joins evolutionary science, information theory, and a theory of the constraints under which signs occur to delimit the grounds for the emergence of meaning-making life forms anywhere. Astrosemiosis identifies evolved features on earth plausibly required to meet semiotic constraints and gauges the likelihood that analogous features would evolve in extraterrestrial biospheres. Rethinking sign making as a planetary process, it narrows the gap between speculation on smart aliens and empirical astrobiological science.
books.bio: Gary Tomlinson is Sterling Professor of Music and Humanities at Yale University and the recipient of a MacArthur “genius” award. His recent research sits at the intersection of music, evolutionary theory, and philosophies of signs and meaning. In his earlier Zone books he set new terms for the question of how humans come to be musical creatures ( A Million Years of Music , 2015) and explored the reach of meaning-making beyond humans in our world ( The Machines of Evolution and the Scope of Meaning , 2023).

praise.q: Gary Tomlinson is our most important living semiotician. Astrosemiosis uses the expanse of the cosmos and the range of science fiction to create a universal doctrine of signs for any possible world. It is academic appointment reading.
praise.by: Leif Weatherby, Professor of German, New York University
praise.cred: Professor of German, New York University

praise.q: Gary Tomlinson has long been one of the most inventive interpreters of the dialogue between the natural sciences and the humanities, and in Astrosemiosis he takes up one of the most pressing questions: how life becomes capable of meaning. At a moment when intelligence is increasingly attributed to everything from microbes to machines, Tomlinson offers a rigorous and timely account of what meaning-making actually entails. Combining philosophical depth with environmental history and semiotics, Astrosemiosis rethinks life, signs, and intelligence as planetary processes, making it essential reading for anyone interested in what it means to be alive.”—Alfredo Thiermann, Professor of History and Theories of Architecture, Technology, and Media, Swiss Federal Technology Institute of Lausanne

This book is a bold and stimulating attempt to connect astrobiology and semiotics, two fields much concerned with signs, signals and signatures. Tomlinson offers astrobiologists a new conception of what makes some forms of life special: the capacity to make and use meaningful signs. Was the evolution of this capacity one of the ‘major transitions’ that profoundly altered the course of Earth’s evolutionary history? Can the study of sign-making in non-human animals (birds, whales, and apes for example) helpfully reframe the search for extraterrestrial intelligence? How widespread and various might ‘signworlds’ be among alien biospheres? In how many different ways might the cognitive circuitry necessary for sign-making be realized? Such are the compelling interdisciplinary questions at the heart of this book. Although highly original, Tomlinson’s book can be seen as a contribution to two broad movements in contemporary scholarship: first, the rise of planetary and indeed interplanetary thinking in the arts, humanities, and social sciences, and, second, the increasing role and stature of philosophical and conceptual work in astrobiology, the science of life in the universe.
praise.by: Sean McMahon, Professor of Astrobiology, University of Edinburgh
praise.cred: Professor of Astrobiology, University of Edinburgh

books.title: Boost
books.subtitle: How to Make Decisions in a World Designed to Manipulate You
books.tagline: A call to rethink behavioral science that empowers people to steer themselves toward good choices. From an internationally acclaimed, multiple award-winning expert on decision making and a leading philosophical voice in behavioral public policy.
books.description:
From an internationally acclaimed, multiple award-winning expert on decision making and a leading philosophical voice in behavioral public policy.

We all struggle to make good choices—what to eat, where to invest, when to get angry, whom to trust. For some time now, these struggles have been attributed to flaws in human reasoning: People are just not rational enough to do what’s in their own best interest. Policymakers, buying into this view, have focused on nudging citizens in the “right” direction rather than empowering them to figure things out for themselves.

In Boost, Ralph Hertwig and Till Grüne-Yanoff offer a fresh alternative: boosting . Instead of subtly steering people’s behavior, boosts enhance people’s competences to help them make the right call in all areas of life.

How can we eat more healthily? Manage our money? Save energy? Navigate the traps of the digital world? This book provides practical solutions for these everyday challenges and more, covering boosts from temptation bundling to psychological inoculation to disinformation detection trees. It shows how policymakers can use boosts—and why they should.

Boosts matter because lifelong learning matters, especially in the face of powerful industries—from Big Tech to Big Food—that seek to exploit our weak spots for profit. This book empowers us to unmask their tricks and fight back against manipulation, and enables policymakers to help us make wise choices in wicked times.
books.bio:
Ralph Hertwig (Author)

Ralph Hertwig is Director of the Center for Adaptive Rationality at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin.

Till Grüne-Yanoff (Author)

Till Grüne-Yanoff is a professor of philosophy at the Royal Institute of Technology (KTH) in Stockholm.

books.title: First Among Equals
books.subtitle: U.S. Foreign Policy in a Multipolar World
books.tagline: A fresh, concise roadmap for U.S. grand strategy in a multipolar world
books.description:
For the past thirty years, post–Cold War triumphalism and a desire to reshape the world have defined U.S. foreign policy. But the failures of the global war on terror, the return of conflict to Europe, and growing tensions with China all suggest that this approach to the world is flawed. For the United States—the country that has ruled the international system largely alone since 1991—this moment is particularly perilous. Can policymakers adapt American foreign policy to better fit the twenty-first century, and in doing so avoid the pitfalls and excesses of the past three decades?

In this book, Emma Ashford proposes a return to a more pragmatic, realist set of strategic principles, ones better suited for the emerging multipolar world, that would pursue narrower U.S. interests, cultivate the capabilities of friendly states, and emphasize room for maneuver over rigid alliances. In this she provides a valuable counterpoint to today’s liberal internationalist consensus, as well as a road map for policymakers who seek to change the course of U.S. foreign policy.
books.bio: Emma Ashford is a senior fellow at the Stimson Center, where she is part of the Reimagining U.S. Grand Strategy Program. She is also an adjunct professor at the Georgetown University School of Foreign Service and a columnist at Foreign Policy .

praise.q: Impressive. . . . Ashford’s taxonomy is an important contribution. By contrasting foreign policy positions in terms of a few core assumptions, she suggests paths for constructive dialogue among competing factions.
praise.by: Stacie E. Goddard, Foreign Affairs

praise.q: Thought-provoking.”—Sumantra Maitra, Engelsberg Ideas

[A] valuable new book. . . . Ashford has done an excellent job in mapping out what a better, more restrained strategy would look like in practice. U.S. policymakers would do well to read this book and follow her recommendations.
praise.by: Daniel Larison, Responsible Statecraft

praise.q: Every so often a book comes along that slices through comforting illusions and forces readers to face the world as it is. Emma Ashford’s First Among Equals is one of those books.
praise.by: Andrew Latham, Real Clear Defense

praise.q: Ashford’s First Among Equals dismantles the myth of unchallenged U.S. primacy with incisive clarity. To navigate a more multipolar and leaderless world, she challenges policymakers to ditch the liberal hegemony playbook and radically rethink America’s global role before it’s too late. Essential reading.
praise.by: Ian Bremmer, Eurasia Group and GZERO Media

praise.q: In First Among Equals , Ashford affirms her voice as important and her ideas as insightful for scholarly and policy debates about the twenty-first-century world and optimal American foreign policy strategy.
praise.by: Bruce W. Jentleson, Duke University

praise.q: In First Among Equals , Ashford delivers a bold reassessment of America’s role in a shifting world. Through sharp analysis and pragmatic solutions, she charts a path beyond unipolar overreach and toward a balanced, interest-driven foreign policy for the United States.
praise.by: Mark Leonard, director, European Council on Foreign Relations
praise.cred: director, European Council on Foreign Relations

books.title: Healthcare in the Age of Finance Capital
books.subtitle: Public Funds for Private Gain
books.tagline: How the financialization of healthcare has eroded the quality of care, driven up prices, and worsened health inequalities
books.description:
Financial actors and healthcare leaders increasingly view healthcare organizations as financial assets to be bought, sold, and managed for maximum profit, regardless of the effects on patient care. Healthcare in the Age of Finance Capital reveals how the federal government enables financial opportunism in healthcare and offers bold ideas for overhauling a failed system.

Rosemary Batt and Eileen Appelbaum provide a unique analysis of the financialization of healthcare, a process in which a growing proportion of the healthcare economy is owned and controlled by the financial sector. Healthcare organizations increasingly depend on financial machinations and the earnings derived from them rather than revenue generated from patient care.

The extent to which financial calculations overshadow the healthcare mission depends importantly on institutional legacies, reimbursement rules, and the failure of regulatory oversight. Batt and Appelbaum show how differences in regulations and financing rules shape whether financial actors can penetrate distinct healthcare segments—from hospitals, nursing homes, and ambulatory care to physician specialties, home health, hospice, and autism services. Nonprofit healthcare is not immune from this financial logic.

Evidence-based, accessible, and informed by real-world examples, Healthcare in the Age of Finance Capital sheds critical light on how financial deregulation coupled with the relaxation of health, tax, antitrust, and labor laws have allowed financially driven actors to exploit public funds for private gain at the expense of healthcare organizations, patients, communities, labor, and taxpayers.
books.bio: Rosemary Batt is the Alice Hanson Cook Professor of Women and Work, Emeritus, at Cornell University. Eileen Appelbaum is codirector of the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR). They are the authors, among other books, of Private Equity at Work: When Wall Street Manages Main Street and The New American Workplace: Transforming Work Systems in the United States .

praise.q: Healthcare in the Age of Finance Capital is a tour de force describing the many ways in which the healthcare sector has become financialized. Batt and Appelbaum trace the regulatory history that facilitated the transformation of healthcare from a productive economy to a financial one. The account is both concrete and sweeping, compelling and immensely readable, while situating policy and political choices at the heart of the tale and revealing potential policy roads to a different future. Ultimately, this book tells a story of power, profit extraction, and the struggle for the soul of the US healthcare system.
praise.by: Erin Fuse Brown, Brown University

praise.q: This incisive study pierces the veil surrounding private equity’s ownership of healthcare institutions, revealing its harmful effects on the availability, quality, and cost of care. A must-read for anyone committed to understanding—and improving—America’s healthcare system. There is simply nothing else like it.
praise.by: Sanford M. Jacoby, author of Labor in the Age of Finance
praise.cred: author of Labor in the Age of Finance

praise.q: Do you want to understand why your hospital stays cost so much? Where the hidden charges come from? Who is pocketing the profits? Then read Batt and Appelbaum’s masterful book, Healthcare in the Age of Finance Capital . Batt and Appelbaum brilliantly utilize the theoretical concept of ‘financialization’ to reveal a practical and important truth: our healthcare system is being undermined by a profit-oriented culture turbocharged by finance-focused owners from top to bottom.
praise.by: Gerald Epstein, author of Busting the Bankers’ Club: Finance for the Rest of Us
praise.cred: author of Busting the Bankers’ Club: Finance for the Rest of Us

books.title: How to Be Citizens of Empires
books.subtitle: Modern Lessons in Democracy from Ancient Athens and Rome
books.tagline: At a time when personal identity and private interests rule public life, a new political history of ancient Athens and Rome, where collective commitments of citizenship stood at the heart of self-government, is urgent.
books.description:
In ancient Athens and republican Rome, citizenship was not a mere right of abode or grant of access to a minimal and often self-interested form of democracy, as in present-day America. Citizenship was, rather, a demanding public responsibility. The claim civis Romanus sum could secure the state’s protection and command authority. In Athens, the citizenry exercised formidable powers, including even the ability to exile those deemed dangerous to the people’s sovereignty.

A deep historical inquiry that confronts political dilemmas of the twenty-first century, How to Be Citizens of Empires invites serious consideration of cultures in which public obligation was the heart of political life. Craige B. Champion shows how Athens and Rome managed pressures of expansion and rule. Athens limited access to citizenship while channeling imperial revenues into civic participation. Rome steadily extended citizenship across Italy and beyond, cultivating loyalty while diluting the influence of individual citizens as the empire grew.

Without overlooking well-documented Athenian and Roman slavery, militarism, and exclusion of women, How to Be Citizens of Empires highlights institutional resilience, thoughtful policies of incorporation, and rigorous standards of public accountability. By recovering these dimensions of the ancient world, Champion illuminates present debates over immigration, civic education, and national purpose and reminds us that Athens and Rome can still serve as magistri vitae —teachers for life—to Americans.
books.bio: Craige B. Champion is Professor of Ancient History and Classics at Syracuse University and the author of Cultural Politics in Polybius’s Histories and The Peace of the Gods: Elite Religious Practices in the Middle Roman Republic . A founding editor of The Encyclopedia of Ancient History, he has edited Roman Imperialism: Readings and Sources and The Landmark Polybius .

praise.q: What can we learn from two ancient societies, Athens and Rome, that will sustain American politics and heal the nation? In his trenchant and provocative new book, the ancient historian Craige Champion offers timely answers to this urgent question. This is powerful and serious scholarship, as well as an uplifting read.

A powerfully argued book that offers a fresh understanding of ancient Athenian and Roman empires on every page. Champion reminds us that contemporary American debates over citizenship are not exceptional, but a continuation of ancient problems under modern conditions.

"A clear-eyed evaluation of how citizenship was exercised in two very different imperial democracies—classical Athens and republican Rome—with profound philosophical and feet-on-the ground practical implications for America’s future.

Craige Champion, an expert in historiography, both Greek and Roman, and especially that of Polybius, is brilliantly equipped to write on Athenian and Roman imperial ideologies, citizenship myths, and legal disputes. He does so with verve, elegance, and insight in this fresh, original, comparativist tour de force .

Champion draws on his deep knowledge of the Athenian and Roman empires to explore America’s contemporary moment of national discord and proposes an inclusive and empowering definition of citizenship based on historical examples. How to Be Citizens of Empires is a stunning achievement that demands to be widely read and debated.

books.title: Play to Profit
books.subtitle: A Cultural History of Corporate Business Games
books.tagline: The little-known history of business games and simulations from 1955 onward—and how they influenced modern economic theory and rationality.
books.description:
The business simulation emerged around 1955, after the Second World War, in the context of social change. Companies in the post-war economy were confronted with globalization, increasingly complex management tasks, and changing concepts of control and planning. At the intersection of corporate management, human resource management, and scientific economic logics and rationalities, a training tool materialized in the form of business simulations—partly played on early mainframe computers—that was to give rise to a new type of manager: the professional manager.

In Play to Profit , Rolf Nohr reconstructs the popularity of those management games in the United States from the 1950s to the 1970s and its spread around the world. He traces, for example, the role of IBM in the development and distribution of these games, examines the influence of think tanks (such as the Rand Corporation), and questions the use of these games in educational institutions such as the American Management Association and business schools such as Harvard Business School.

As management simulations evolved from serious games to teaching machines to the logics of operations research and mathematical game theory, Nohr argues that we can observe the economic rationality that characterizes our current reality.
books.bio: Rolf F. Nohr is Professor for Media Aesthetics and Media Culture at the University of Arts, Braunschweig and an External Affiliate at the College of Humanities, University of Arizona.

books.title: Protecting the Internet's Core
books.subtitle: Critical Internet Protocols and Infrastructure in the Crosshairs of Geopolitics
books.authors: Edited by Dennis Broeders and Arun Sukumar
books.tagline: Why and how the foundational infrastructure and protocols that guarantee the functioning of the Internet are under threat—and what states can do to protect it.
books.description:
Protecting the Internet’s Core brings together an international group of renowned scholars to advance discussions on the public core of the Internet. They tackle questions such as: What is “public” about the public core, if most critical Internet resources are governed or managed by private actors? What does protection of the core actually entail from states? Should they commit simply to refrain from cyber operations targeting core infrastructure, or do they also have certain positive obligations to monitor and stop threats that impact the Internet beyond their borders? Why have some major powers embraced the concept, while others remain reluctant to adopt it?

The world has built its digital existence on top of core logical standards and protocols, like the TCP/IP suite, the Domain Name System and routing protocols, and core physical infrastructure like subsea cables and their landing stations, DNS servers, and Internet exchange points (IXPs). It is vital that the stability and integrity of these core protocols and infrastructure are safeguarded. This is no longer a hypothetical concern, as the war in Ukraine has powerfully demonstrated. While threats to core protocols have long existed, they have acquired a heightened degree of sophistication and severity in recent years.
books.bio:
Dennis Broeders (Editor)

Dennis Broeders is Full Professor of Global Security and Technology at the Institute of Security and Global Affairs (ISGA) of Leiden University, the Netherlands. He is the Senior Fellow of The Hague Program on International Cyber Security. He is the author of the book The Public Core of the Internet (2015) and served as a member of the Dutch delegation to the UN Group of Governmental Experts on International Information Security and the Open-Ended Working Group as an academic advisor (2019–2021).

Arun Mohan Sukumar (Editor)

Arun Sukumar is Assistant Professor of International Relations at Ashoka University. He is the author of Midnight’s Machines and the coeditor of Building an International Cybersecurity Regime and Responsible Behaviour in Cyberspace . His research has been published in Contemporary Security Policy, Policy & Internet, IEEE-CyCon proceedings, Journal of Cyber Policy, and other journals.

books.title: Rituals of War
books.subtitle: The Body and Violence in Mesopotamia
books.tagline: A groundbreaking analysis of the arts of war in ancient Mesopotamia
books.description: Rituals of War is an investigation into the earliest historical records of violence and biopolitics. In ancient Iraq (ca.3000-500 BC) rituals of war and images of violence constituted part of the magical technologies of warfare that formed the underlying irrational processes of war. Building on Michel Foucault’s argument in Discipline and Punish that the art of punishing must rest on a technology of representation, Zainab Bahrani investigates the ancient Mesopotamian record to reveal how that culture relied on the portrayal of violence and control as part of the mechanics of warfare. Moreover, she takes up the more recent arguments of Giorgio Agamben on sovereign power and biopolitics to focus on the relationship of power, the body and violence in Assyro-Babylonian texts and monuments of war. Bahrani brings together and analyzes facets of war and sovereign power that fall under the categories of representation and display, the aesthetic, the ritualistic, and the supernatural. The author describes these as the magical technologies of war, the realm of the irrational that enables the ideologies of just war in the distant past as well as today.
books.bio: Zainab Bahrani is the Edith Porada Professor of Ancient Near Eastern Art History and Archaeology at Columbia and she is also a native Iraqi who has been deeply involved in chronicling the destructive consequences of present imperial war and violence in a region she knows well. Although this book, which appeared in 2008, only indirectly addresses the then ongoing US sponsored war and occupation, its larger concerns are very much shaped by her experience of contemporary circumstances.

praise.q: Rituals of War is an ambitious attempt to find new ways of viewing the ancient past, and for that Zainab Bahrani should be applauded. What makes Bahrani’s examination of the Battle of Til-Tuba so fresh and exciting is that she is the first to combine the art-historical and narrative evidence.
praise.by: Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: Bahrani’s groundbreaking study of the arts of war in ancient Mesopotamia may seem at first glance to have only a distant connection to the current war on terror and the war in Iraq. But her investigation of the ‘magical technologies’ of ancient imperial warfare could not be timelier. Beheadings, mutilations, images of torture and triumph, displacement of populations, and ethnic cleansings justified as sacred missions are just as common today as they were in 1500 BC. Instead of the divination of animal entrails, we have ‘actionable intelligence’ to provide the rationale for war and a set of dubious predictions of its outcome. This brilliant book is a must read for anyone who wants to understand the role of images in war, and the way that media, symbolic representations, and ritualistic spectacles of iconoclasm play a role just as important as weapons and the movement of armies.
praise.by: W.J.T. Mitchell, author of Image Science

praise.q: Rituals of War applies as much to the U.S. war machine and the arts of war today as to ancient Mesopotamia. Even more so, given the blindness to magic and myth in the technological language of power that would shape destiny in the Middle East and the future of the world. With verve and enviable clarity, Bahrani gives us new ways to think the magic of the state, from torture to its reading of omens. How poignant that this superb work of theory and scholarship, while speaking of ancient Iraq, can be read allegorically in this way.
praise.by: Michael Taussig, author of Palma Africana

books.title: Shifts
books.subtitle: Nine Big Ideas That Revolutionized Computing
books.tagline: An engaging account of some of the most important shifts in computing and how they have changed how we design, build, program, analyze, connect, and use computers. From a pioneer in computing and programming languages, and a bestselling author.
books.description:
From a pioneer in computing and programming languages, and a bestselling author.

We live in a world with far more computers than people. Those computers affect every aspect of our lives, sometimes for better and often for worse. In Shifts, Brian Kernighan tells the story of how we got here, by describing nine shifts that dramatically changed computing—from the stored-program computer to high-level programming languages to billions of computers on the Internet to AI and LLMs. Most of these shifts weren't noticed while they were happening, but they are crystal clear in retrospect. For each shift, the author describes the historical context, explains the technology at an accessible level, and presents some of the people who made it happen.

Although one could slice and dice the “shifts” in different ways, or add or subtract a few, they share the common theme of looking at major changes that have affected how people build, program, and use computers. How did we get to where we are now? What can we learn from that? Can we predict where we might be going? Shifts answers all these questions and more.
books.bio:
Brian Kernighan is the William O. Baker *39 Professor in Computer Science at Princeton University. He is a co-creator of several programming languages, including AWK and AMPL, and a number of tools for document preparation, and the author of more than a dozen books. He is also a member the National Academy of Engineering and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

Author of The C Programming Language, The AWK Programming Language, UNIX: A History

books.title: Submersion
books.subtitle: Reconsidering John C. Lilly
books.authors: Edited by Hannah Zeavin and Jeffrey Mathias
books.tagline: An illuminating and wide-ranging edited collection on the life and career of John C. Lilly across disciplines, from animal studies to the history of architecture.
books.description:
John C. Lilly (1915–2001) was a neurophysiologist who had one of the most unusual careers in twentieth-century science: he theorized extra-terrestrial language and intelligence, wrote quasi-philosophical treatises about computer science and consciousness, self-experimented with LSD and ketamine, and developed the first sensory deprivation tank (which he later used for scientific tripping). Most famously, he worked with dolphins, trying to understand their forms of communication and to teach them to speak English, later aiming to mediate human and dolphin communication via computers.

Submersion, edited by Hannah Zeavin and Jeffrey Mathias, brings together scholars from a wide variety of disciplines—from animal studies to the history of the human sciences, from the history of architecture to feminist science and technology studies—to reevaluate Lilly’s life and career within his own moment and from our vantage point in ours. Ever relevant, Lilly’s work illuminates twentieth-century cultural and scientific phenomena ranging from cybernetics to the human potential movement. And his mid-century prominence as a neurophysiologist further makes him crucial to, albeit understudied within, the history of Cold War science and technology.
books.bio:
Hannah Zeavin (Editor)

Hannah Zeavin is Associate Professor of the History of Science in the Department of History and the Berkeley Center for New Media at UC Berkeley. She is the author of The Distance Cure and Mother Media (MIT Press) and Founding Editor of Parapraxis . In 2021, she cofounded The Psychosocial Foundation.

Jeffrey Mathias (Editor)

Jeffrey Mathias is a writer, psychoanalyst, and historian of science. His writing has appeared in journals such as Isis and Parapraxis.

books.title: The East Asian–Australasian Flyway
books.subtitle: A Field Guide
books.authors: Sayam U. Chowdhury, Yong Ding Li
books.tagline: A beautiful photographic field guide to the birds and habitats of the world’s largest migratory flyway
books.description:
Nearly 600 migratory bird species undertake long and daunting journeys in the East Asian–Australasian Flyway. This guide brings together a team of leading experts to describe the natural history of these incredible travellers, the threats they face, what is being done to protect them and the best places to see them. Blending stunning photos and graphics with engaging and informative text, The East Asian–Australasian Flyway provides a fascinating look at some of the world’s most intrepid migratory species.

Covers habitats across northeast Asia, from the boreal forests and steppe of Russia and Mongolia and Japan’s temperate forests to the rainforests of Thailand and Malaysia and the tidal flats of Australia

Describes the ecology of numerous Asian migratory species in detail, from sandpipers and plovers to terns and gulls, shorebirds and raptors, cuckoos and nightjars and owls and flycatchers

Features hundreds of color photos depicting diverse species and terrains

Describes the key conservation issues facing migratory birds in Asia

Reveals the hot spots for viewing spectacular congregations of migratory birds
books.bio: Sayam U. Chowdhury is a conservation biologist focused on the preservation of endangered species in Asia. He coordinates the Spoon-billed Sandpiper Task Force of the East Asian–Australasian Flyway Partnership. Yong Ding Li coordinates BirdLife International’s work on migratory bird conservation in Asia. His books include Birds of Malaysia and Singapore (Princeton).

books.title: The Life-Scale Revolution in European Painting
books.tagline: A study of the radical transformation of scale in European painting 1300-1600
books.description:
This brief book brings to light an unchronicled revolution in art — the “life-scale revolution,” which was launched at the end of the fifteenth century, quickly took hold in the sixteenth century, and changed European painting forever. In place of the medieval and early Renaissance systems of scalable images, around 1500 European pictures began to present figures and settings at a scale congruent with the body and world of the viewer. A non-arbitrary scale—life scale—became a new foundation for painting. All over Europe, painting of all kinds, from portraits and biblical and mythological subjects to genre scenes and still lifes, learned to engage viewers in a common language of life scale. This is not to say that from 1500 all paintings were made according to the new convention, but that life scale became a new standard with organizing force for painting generally, all the way through the nineteenth century.

Pictures at life scale are a generative paradox — self-proclaimed fictions in framed pictures, they nonetheless claim a continuity with the conditions of our perception of the world. Analyses of individual works by artists as diverse as Leonardo da Vinci, Dürer, Raphael, Titian, Rubens, Reni, and Velázquez explore the profound philosophical, anthropological, and social-political implications of the turn to life-scale painting. “As-if” pictorial extensions and warpings of our perceptual ecology, life-scale pictures offer parallel worlds. They model our interaction with the world, but they do so strangely, slowing us down, turning perception into performance and self-reflection, prompting intuitions about how inhabiting the world in and through our bodies shapes our relation to each other and to our environment. Life-scale pictures addressed individual viewers, but in generalized form, now as representative members of what would eventually be called a “public.”
books.bio: Alexander Nagel is Craig Hugh Smyth Professor at the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University. His teaching and writing explores visual art as a form of spatial and temporal intelligence. Publications include Anachronic Renaissance (2010), Medieval Modern (2012), and Amerasia (2023).

praise.q: Alexander Nagel's unprecedented book now finally brings our full attention to the elemental issue of life scale in art–its meaning and implications. Life scale is the objective point where a picture comes into an immediate, open, and unpredictable relation with the world in front of it. Nagel tells the history of its emergence and defines the phenomenon anthropologically, technically, culturally, and in terms of its resonance with elemental religious meanings that he notices still circulating in our society. I'm putting this book on a special shelf next to my copies of Kodak's Photography with Large-Format Cameras O-18H and Jacques Maroger's The Secret Formulas and Techniques of the Masters .
praise.by: Jeff Wall, artist

praise.q: It’s been there for all of us to see, and yet Alexander Nagel is the first scholar to see it: A radical transformation in European art, circa 1500, that found artists designing the figures in their paintings to match the size of the people looking at them. An art lover could reach out toward a portrait, and find that her hand was the same size as the hand of its painted sitter; the painted Christ, in an altarpiece, was calibrated to seem the same human height as the live priest at the altar before Him. Nagel calls this the 'life-scale revolution,' and shows how its effects—pictorial, but also philosophical—were felt for centuries, right across Europe and beyond. Nagel's discovery of this 'revolution' looks set to cause a revolution in our thoughts about art.
praise.by: Blake Gopnik, contributing critic, The New York Times
praise.cred: contributing critic, The New York Times

books.title: Thinking Historically
books.subtitle: A Guide to Statecraft and Strategy
books.tagline: A compelling and insightful argument for historical study as a way to understand and navigate the complex, often confusing world of decision-making
books.description:
Winner, 2026 Lionel Gelber Prize

“Gavin’s writing is nuanced and compelling. It’s also fun. . . . Churchill would have loved Gavin’s book and would have encouraged aspiring statespeople to study it carefully.”—John T. Shaw, Chicago Tribune

It seems obvious that we should use history to improve policy. If we have a good understanding of the past, it should enable better decisions in the present, especially in the extraordinarily consequential worlds of statecraft and strategy. But how do we gain that knowledge? How should history be used? Sadly, it is rarely done well, and historians and decision-makers seldom interact. But in this remarkable book, Francis J. Gavin explains the many ways historical knowledge can help us understand and navigate the complex, often confusing world around us.

Good historical work convincingly captures the challenges and complexities the decision-maker faces. At its most useful, history is less a narrowly defined field of study than a practice, a mental awareness, a discernment, and a responsiveness to the past and how it unfolded into our present world—a discipline in the best sense of the word. Gavin demonstrates how a historical sensibility helps us to appreciate the unexpected; complicates our assumptions; makes the unfamiliar familiar and the familiar unfamiliar; and requires us, without entirely suspending moral judgment, to try to understand others on their own terms. This book is a powerful argument for thinking historically as a way for readers to apply wisdom in encountering what is foreign to them.
books.bio: Francis J. Gavin is the Giovanni Agnelli Distinguished Professor and the director of the Henry A. Kissinger Center for Global Affairs at Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies. His previous books include Gold, Dollars, and Power ; Nuclear Weapons and American Grand Strategy ; and The Taming of Scarcity and the Problems of Plenty .

praise.q: Gavin’s writing is nuanced and compelling. It’s also fun. . . . Churchill would have loved Gavin’s book and would have encouraged aspiring statespeople to study it carefully.
praise.by: John T. Shaw, Chicago Tribune

praise.q: Francis Gavin has written a profound work of philosophy of history that is at the same time eminently readable. He writes not about history but rather about historical sensibility, a way of understanding and thinking about the world with all its complexities and uncertainties. Historical sensibility creates discomfort with linear reasoning and single causes. It embraces complexity, multiple chains that intersect and connect, and a story that changes with the perspective of time. In one elegant chapter after another, Gavin walks the reader through these complexities and leaves us less sure, more empathic, and wiser. Thinking Historically is a more important book than E. H. Carr’s Twenty Years’ Crisis in helping us understand the crises of our times.
praise.by: Jury statement, Lionel Gelber Prize

praise.q: Makes clear just how far surface-level historical fluency is from genuine historical thinking. . . . Gavin [offers] something distinctive: a clear articulation of what ‘historical sensibility’ actually means, and a practical twelve-question checklist that translates that sensibility into disciplined inquiry.
praise.by: Whitney D. Zimmerman, Substack

praise.q: Educational and thought-provoking. . . . A landmark study of applied history. . . . There is no more impressive defense of the past’s usefulness in print.
praise.by: Michael Paul Ferguson, H-War

praise.q: Winner, 2026 Lionel Gelber Prize, sponsored by the Munk Centre for International Studies
I devoured this book, and consider it essential reading for every policymaker on the front lines of statecraft and strategy, and for every student who aspires to a career in national security.
praise.by: Jake Sullivan, former National Security Advisor

praise.q: This is a remarkable and illuminating exploration of the value of an historical sensibility for policymakers, providing perspective and context, encouraging thoughts about causality and trends, and showing why it’s important to address the challenges of complexity, evidence, and bias.
praise.by: Lawrence Freedman, author of Strategy: A History

praise.q: A superb book on a question of great and enduring importance: what is a ‘historical sensibility,’ and how can political leaders—and the rest of us—go about acquiring it? Frank Gavin is one of our leading authorities on the subject, and he shows it on every page of this essential study.”—Fredrik Logevall, author of JFK: Coming of Age in the American Century, 1917

In today’s world, history is the daily weapon of national and international contests for power and authority. Frank Gavin shows how thinking historically can make a difference to statecraft and strategic decision-making. How do we not repeat the mistakes of the past? Here Gavin proves himself the best of allies for both IR and historical practitioners alike.
praise.by: Glenda Sluga, author of The Invention of International Order: Remaking Europe after Napoleon
praise.cred: author of The Invention of International Order: Remaking Europe after Napoleon

books.title: A Life Lived like a Storm
books.subtitle: Enver Pasha and the End of the Ottoman World
books.tagline: The definitive biography of Enver Pasha, the larger-than-life Young Turk revolutionary who bent the arc of history and reshaped the modern Middle East and Eurasia
books.description:
Enver Pasha (1881–1922) is a hotly contested figure whose career spanned the Young Turk Revolution, the First World War, the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, and the rise of global anti-colonialism. To millions he was an icon of hope and a folk hero. Others reviled him as a ruthless conspirator and a merciless sower of death. But all, from Kaiser Wilhelm II through Churchill to Stalin, found him a man of consequence. A Life Lived like a Storm tells the story of the man whom even a jealous rival, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, likened to the splendor of a setting sun.

The first biography of Enver to make use of an abundance of archival sources in multiple languages, this book radically transforms our understanding of Enver and his era. A reserved, pious boy from the Balkans schooled to become an elite officer in the Ottoman army, he vaulted to global fame in 1908 when he risked all to topple a repressive sultan’s regime. Bloodied on Balkan and North African battlefields, Enver later seized power, imposed one-party rule, married a princess. He plunged his empire into a world war—and ultimately into defeat—but also laid the foundation for the Turkish Republic. Hunted for war crimes, he fled the empire to make common cause against colonialism with the Bolsheviks, only to take up the banner of Islam and die battling the Red Army in Central Asia as the son-in-law of the Caliph.

An epic account of a consequential life by one of our foremost historians, A Life Lived like a Storm paints a riveting, multifaceted portrait of a man whose boundless ambition and lust for peril put him at the center of the collapse of one world and the birth of another.
books.bio: Michael A. Reynolds is associate professor of Near Eastern studies and codirector of the Program in the History and Practice of Diplomacy at Princeton University. He is the author of Shattering Empires: The Clash and Collapse of the Ottoman and Russian Empires, 1908–1918 , winner of the American Historical Association’s George Louis Beer Prize.

praise.q: A remarkable work of scholarship and storytelling, A Life Lived like a Storm transforms our understanding of one of the twentieth century’s most consequential and controversial figures. Michael Reynolds strips away a century of myth to recover Enver Pasha as a historical actor whose ambitions, ideas, and contradictions illuminate not only the collapse of the Ottoman Empire but also the emergence of the modern Middle East and new forms of Muslim internationalism. Elegantly written, deeply researched, this is the definitive biography of Enver Pasha, making us better understand why he was not simply a protagonist in the collapse of the Ottoman Empire but also one of the architects of a modern Muslim political imagination whose legacies extended far beyond his own lifetime.
praise.by: Cemil Aydin, author of The Idea of the Muslim World: A Global Intellectual History
praise.cred: author of The Idea of the Muslim World: A Global Intellectual History

praise.q: Enver Pasha was a complicated figure who lived through complex times. Michael Reynolds has produced a magisterial biography that finally does justice to his life and times. Based on deep research across many languages and numerous archives and informed by a deep human sensitivity, A Life Lived like a Storm is unlikely to be surpassed anytime soon!
praise.by: Adeeb Khalid, author of Central Asia: A New History from the Imperial Conquests to the Present
praise.cred: author of Central Asia: A New History from the Imperial Conquests to the Present

books.title: Art in a State of Siege
books.tagline: An art historical epic for dangerous times
books.description:
What do artworks look like in extreme cases of collective experience? What signals do artists send when enemies are at the city walls and the rule of law breaks down, or when a tyrant suspends the law to attack from inside? Art in a State of Siege tells the story of three compelling images created in dangerous moments and the people who experienced them—from Philip II of Spain to Carl Schmitt—whose panicked gaze turned artworks into omens.

Acclaimed art historian Joseph Koerner reaches back to the eve of iconoclasm and religious warfare to explore the most elusive painting ever painted. In Hieronymus Bosch’s Garden of Delights , enemies are everywhere: Jews and Ottomans at the gates, witches and heretics at home, sins overtaking the mind. Following a paper trail leading from Bosch’s time to World War II, Koerner considers a monumental self-portrait painted by Max Beckmann in 1927. Created when Germany was often governed by emergency decree, this image brazenly claimed to decide Europe’s future—until the Nazis deemed it to be a threat to the German people. For South African artist William Kentridge, Beckmann exemplified “art in a state of siege.” Koerner shows how his work served as beacon during South Africa’s racialist apartheid rule and inspired Kentridge’s breakthrough animations of drawings being made, erased, and remade.

Spanning half a millennium but urgent today, Art in a State of Siege reveals how, in dire straits, art becomes the currency of last resort.
books.bio: Joseph Leo Koerner is the Victor S. Thomas Professor of History of Art and Architecture and Professor of Germanic Languages and Literatures, Harvard University, and Senior Fellow of Harvard’s Society of Fellows. The author of Bosch and Bruegel: From Enemy Painting to Everyday Life (Princeton) and Caspar David Friedrich and the Subject of Landscape , he has written and presented documentaries for the BBC and wrote, produced, and directed The Burning Child , a feature film on Viennese homemaking in the shadow of the Holocaust.

praise.q: [A] brilliant book. . . . [with] ekphrastic tours de force. . . . [Koerner’s] investment delivers great insight.
praise.by: Hal Foster, London Review of Books

praise.q: Wise and inform­ative, it is indeed a book for and about our times.
praise.by: Gabriel Josipovici, Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: Captivating . . . Art in a State of Siege [is] leisurely, expansive and stunningly erudite.
praise.by: Christoph Irmscher, The Art Newspaper

praise.q: Art in a State of Siege is a compulsive expression of unease, delivered magisterially and at an opportune moment. . . . Ever-stimulating and often provoking.
praise.by: Julian Bell, New York Review of Books

praise.q: [A] rich and enigmatic book. . . . Each separate part [of the book] is a satisfying study of the given artist and the relation of their works to states of emergency, exhibiting Koerner’s characteristic erudition and brilliance of formulation. . . . Fascinating discussions.
praise.by: Kathryn Murphy, Apollo Magazine

praise.q: Deeply rewarding...[ Art in a State of Siege ] takes three artworks made in a time of social distress and political crisis—Hieronymus Bosch’s Garden of Delights (1500), Max Beckmann’s Self-Portrait in Tuxedo (1927) and William Kentridge’s Art in a State of Siege (1986)—to examine how artistic dissent is fomented under such conditions...With lively prose and rich references to aid his exegesis, Koerner shows how artists working in turbulent times often produce remarkable visual “omens.
praise.by: Observer

praise.q: Art in a State of Siege is destined to become one of the great classics of art history.
