Combining deep insights into the way artists work, patrons patronize, viewers respond, critics evaluate, and art historians investigate and theorize their own methods, it will be a model for generations to come.... One of the many wonders in this book is the sense that we are in the presence of a master teacher for whom all this is personal
praise.by: W.J.T. Mitchell, Berlin Journal

praise.q: [A] gripping new book."—Nancy Princenthal, Artforum

An exceptional study that is as much intellectual history as it is art history. . . . erudite and imaginative. . . . [ Art in a State of Siege includes] one of the most poignant passages by an art historian this reviewer has read. . . . Commentary such as Koerner’s is an ethical necessity.
praise.by: Christopher J. Nygren, Burlington Magazine

books.title: Art’s Properties
books.tagline: A revisionist reading of modern art that examines how artworks are captured as property to legitimize power
books.description:
In this provocative new account, David Joselit shows how art from the nineteenth to the twenty-first centuries began to function as a commodity, while the qualities of the artist, nation, or period themselves became valuable properties. Joselit explores repatriation, explaining that this is not just a contemporary conflict between the Global South and Euro-American museums, noting that the Louvre, the first modern museum, was built on looted works and faced demands for restitution and repatriation early in its history. Joselit argues that the property values of white supremacy underlie the ideology of possessive individualism animating modern art, and he considers issues of identity and proprietary authorship.

Joselit redefines art’s politics, arguing that these pertain not to an artwork’s content or form but to the way it is “captured,” made to represent powerful interests—whether a nation, a government, or a celebrity artist collected by oligarchs. Artworks themselves are not political but occupy at once the here and now and an “elsewhere”—an alterity—that can’t ever be fully appropriated. The history of modern art, Joselit asserts, is the history of transforming this alterity into private property.

Narrating scenes from the emergence and capture of modern art—touching on a range of topics that include the Byzantine church, French copyright law, the 1900 Paris Exposition, W.E.B. Du Bois, the conceptual artist Adrian Piper, and the controversy over Dana Schutz’s painting Open Casket —Joselit argues that the meaning of art is its infinite capacity to generate experience over time.
books.bio: David Joselit is Arthur Kingsley Porter Professor and Chair of Art, Film, and Visual Studies at Harvard University. He is the author of After Art (Princeton); Heritage and Debt: Art in Globalization , winner of the 2021 Robert Motherwell Book Award from the Dedalus Foundation; and other books.

praise.q: A fascinating history of art and representation debates . . . [from] the founding of the Louvre . . . to modern controversies over repatriation and representation.
praise.by: Shanti Escalante-De Mattei, ARTnews

praise.q: [In Art’s Properties ], David Joselit moves beyond the proprietary tendencies of the modern artist to advocate for an ethos of freedom and commonality. . . . Provocative.
praise.by: Alex Kitnick, 4Columns

praise.q: Joselit takes on often-debated topics like artistic cultural appropriation and the repatriation of artworks, grounding them in current understanding ofthe legacy of colonialism, slavery, and white supremacy. Art’s Properties is an excellentfollow-up to the author’s After Art.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: Art’s Properties offers a highly original argument that makes a far-reaching contribution to art historical scholarship. Simultaneously erudite and urgent, it is exhilarating to read, authored by a scholar at the very top of his game. An intellectual tour de force.
praise.by: Kobena Mercer, author of Travel and See: Black Diaspora Art Practices since the 1980s
praise.cred: author of Travel and See: Black Diaspora Art Practices since the 1980s

praise.q: Arts’s Properties links art, the history of capitalism, and decolonial criticism in startling and provocative ways. David Joselit has written an accomplished, incisive, jaggedly witty little bomb of a book.
praise.by: Andrei Pop, author of A Forest of Symbols: Art, Science, and Truth in the Long Nineteenth Century
praise.cred: author of A Forest of Symbols: Art, Science, and Truth in the Long Nineteenth Century

books.title: Cosmic Cycles of Life
books.subtitle: New Perspectives on Mawangdui Tombs
books.authors: Edited by Eugene Y. Wang, Xiaoming Duan, and Chenchen Lu
books.description: Cosmic Cycles of Life offers a groundbreaking look at the Mawangdui Han tombs in China—one of the twentieth century’s most important archaeological finds—through the lens of cutting-edge digital technology and interdisciplinary scholarship. Emerging from a collaboration between Harvard CAMLab and the Hunan Museum, it features sixteen essays that examine Mawangdui through intersecting lenses, such as ancient philosophy, medicine, musicology, and taxonomy. With 3D visualization and annotated line drawings, this volume vividly reconstructs the tomb artifacts with unparalleled precision. Together, these contributions reframe Mawangdui not as a static burial site but as a dynamic, cosmological model reflecting ancient Chinese understandings of life, death, and the universe.
books.bio:
Eugene Y. Wang is the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Professor of Asian Art at Harvard University, the founding director of Harvard FAS CAMLab, and a Guggenheim Fellow. He is the art history editor of the Encyclopedia of Buddhism, and his extensive publications range from early Chinese art and archaeology to modern and contemporary Chinese art and cinema.

Xiaoming Duan is Director of the Hunan Museum, where he presented the acclaimed exhibition, The Art of Life: Multimedia Exhibition of Mawangdui Han Culture, jointly organized with the Digital Library of China and Harvard FAS CAMLab.

Chenchen Lu, Co-Founder and Associate Director of Harvard FAS CAMLab,is an architect, art historian, media artist, filmmaker, and musician.

books.title: Courage Takes Many Forms
books.subtitle: The Untold Story of British Conscientious Objectors in the Second World War
books.tagline: A hugely original and engaging history of conscientious objectors in the Second World War
books.description:
One percent of all men conscripted in Britain during the Second World War conscientiously objected. However, the stories of the 60,000 men, four times as many as in WWI, who chose to say “no” to armed combat remain largely unknown.

Linsey Robb uncovers the experiences of the individuals who, driven by their convictions, chose the path of conscientious objection during one of the most tumultuous periods in modern history. Robb reveals how objectors made vital contributions to the war effort: working the land, tending the sick and serving as non-combatants in the army.

This compelling account captures the internal struggles faced by objectors as the scale of the war’s destruction and Nazi atrocities became apparent. Many objectors grappled with the consequences of their convictions, often channelling that reflection into humanitarian work to help mend the damage the conflict had caused. This is a gripping, surprising story of how thousands of men objected and contributed to their country at war.
books.bio: Linsey Robb is associate professor at Northumbria University. A specialist in the civilian experience of modern warfare, she is the author and editor of Men, Masculinities and Male Culture in the Second World War , Men at Work , and Women and War .

praise.q: This book examines a figure that has long been missing from our stories of Britain’s Second World War: the male Conscientious Objector. Drawing on a wide range of sources, Robb’s important history of these men, their beliefs and experiences enriches and expands our knowledge of the society that fought the Second World War.
praise.by: Lucy Noakes, author of The People’s Victory

praise.q: This is a powerful contribution to Second World War social history. Robb illuminates the experiences of Britain’s conscientious objectors with clarity, empathy, and scholarly depth. This book is essential reading for scholars of the Second World War.
praise.by: Alison Chand, author of Masculinities on Clydeside

praise.q: Drawing on an impressive range of source material, this fascinating study sheds new light on a long-overlooked topic. Robb demonstrates with clarity and conviction how courage did indeed take many forms.
praise.by: Juliette Pattinson, author of Women of War

praise.q: Robb combines meticulous research and nuanced analysis to tremendous effect. She convincingly demonstrates that the experiences of conscientious objectors were an important and revealing part of Britain’s war effort.
praise.by: David Littlewood, author of Military Service Tribunals and Boards in the Great War
praise.cred: author of Military Service Tribunals and Boards in the Great War

books.title: Empire of Violence
books.subtitle: A New History of the Armenian Genocide
books.tagline: A landmark history that redefines our understanding of the Armenian Genocide and the causes of ethnic violence
books.description:
During the First World War, the Ottoman Turks carried out the systematic destruction of the Armenians and their culture, with around one million people killed through starvation, death marches, and mob violence. Empire of Violence goes beyond conventional accounts of the Armenian Genocide as a single event, reconceptualizing it as a decades-long process within a broader pattern of anti-Christian violence against Armenians, Assyrians, and Greeks in the late Ottoman Empire.

Drawing on newly uncovered sources, Taner Akçam traces the interconnectedness of earlier episodes of violence with the genocide carried out during the war, locating this continuity not in fixed actors or enduring identities but in a structural dynamic shaped by the long crisis of imperial reform, in which different agents emerge, recede, and replace one another over time. From massacres in the 1890s to the Adana massacre of 1909, in which Ottoman Muslims killed and tortured thousands of Armenians, he shows how radicalization and annihilation practices at the peripheries of empire culminated in centrally coordinated decisions. Yet the genocidal process was not purely top-down. While central directives were crucial, mass participation by ordinary Muslims—including Turks, Kurds, and Circassians—played a decisive role. Akçam demonstrates how the weakness of the Ottoman state and the accumulated experience of the nineteenth century produced a political culture that normalized large-scale violence, and in doing so expands the conceptual boundaries of genocide studies more broadly.

By examining the culture of denial surrounding this tragedy, Empire of Violence also offers new perspectives on the political realities of contemporary Turkey while reframing critical debates about memory, justice, and recognition in the aftermath of genocide.
books.bio: Taner Akçam is a Turkish historian and director of the Armenian Genocide Research Program at UCLA’s Promise Armenian Institute. His many books include the award-winning A Shameful Act , The Young Turks’ Crime against Humanity (Princeton), and Killing Orders .

praise.q: Taner Akçam is without question one of the most important and creative scholars on the Armenian Genocide. This book is an exemplary achievement of a lifetime of diligent work to find and understand why the Young Turk government of the Ottoman Empire would turn on one of its subject peoples and attempt to eliminate them from their realm.
praise.by: Ronald Grigor Suny, author of “They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else”: A History of the Armenian Genocide
praise.cred: author of “They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else”: A History of the Armenian Genocide

praise.q: Taner Akçam’s Empire of Violence is a superb concise history of the Armenian Genocide, encompassing not only a detailed documentation of how the central and local Ottoman authorities implemented the eradication of Armenian civilization in Anatolia, but also outlining both the crucial long-term origins of this crime and examining its decades-long denial. A must-read for anyone seeking a better understanding of the nature of modern genocide and the price of impunity.
praise.by: Omer Bartov, author of Anatomy of a Genocide: The Life and Death of a Town Called Buczacz
praise.cred: author of Anatomy of a Genocide: The Life and Death of a Town Called Buczacz

praise.q: Akçam’s new book is without doubt the best concise introduction to the study of the Armenian Genocide available. It represents the state of the art in the field, carefully balancing the role of the central government with that of local actors, as well as giving a dispassionate account of the heated (and often politicized) debates on the issue of the last half century.
praise.by: Erik-Jan Zürcher, author of Turkey: A Modern History
praise.cred: author of Turkey: A Modern History

books.title: Fatal Monsters
books.subtitle: Cleopatra, Her Sister Queens, and the Downfall of a Dynasty
books.tagline: A reexamination of the rivalry between Cleopatra and her two sisters, Berenike and Arsinoe—three queens who shaped the tumultuous final years of the Ptolemaic dynasty
books.description:
In this dramatic political, cultural, and historical narrative of the period 60 to 40 BCE in Egypt and Rome, three sister queens are each seeking power for themselves: Cleopatra, who would become the most famous woman of the ancient world; Berenike, executed by their father, Ptolemy XII; and Arsinoe, murdered at Cleopatra’s request.

Jane Draycott profiles each queen in her historical and archaeological context—not just through Roman eyes but also through Greek and Egyptian ones. The overlooked story of the sister queens and the sibling rivalry that brought down a 300-year-old dynasty is now being told.
books.bio: Jane Draycott is a historian and archaeologist, and the author of Fulvia: The Woman Who Broke All the Rules in Ancient Rome and Cleopatra’s Daughter: From Roman Prisoner to African Queen . She is senior lecturer at the University of Glasgow and co-director of the university’s Games and Gaming Lab.

praise.q: Jane Draycott delves into the history of that most famous ruler of Egypt—Cleopatra VII—this time within the context of her contentious Ptolemaic family, painting a vivid picture of competition, betrayal, and assassination.
praise.by: Kara Cooney, author of When Women Ruled the World: Six Queens of Egypt
praise.cred: author of When Women Ruled the World: Six Queens of Egypt

praise.q: Draycott tells how Cleopatra, Berenike, and Arsinoe reigned—and wrangled with Rome—during two decades of political upheavals that demolished the Republic and the last Egyptian dynasty. Bringing Cleopatra’s sisters out of the shadows makes Fatal Monsters a compelling new history of a tumultuous time.
praise.by: Adrienne Mayor, author of Gods and Robots: Myths, Machines, and Ancient Dreams of Technology
praise.cred: author of Gods and Robots: Myths, Machines, and Ancient Dreams of Technology

praise.q: Fascinating, brilliantly researched, this sweeping, wonderful book brings Cleopatra and her sister queens to vibrant life. Gripping."—Kate Williams, author of Becoming Queen Victoria: Becoming Queen Victoria: The Unexpected Rise of Britain's Greatest Monarch
An utterly compulsive (ancient) family saga. The narrative is at once brilliantly researched and insightful, and novelistic in scope.
praise.by: Natasha Solomons, author of I Am Cleopatra

praise.q: Jane Draycott shines a refreshing light on this infamous period of Roman and Egyptian history, putting Cleopatra AND her sisters into the spotlight. The result is a gripping human story of familial love and conflict, set in the context of seismic political, military and social change. You won’t look at this fascinating era of the past in the same way again!
praise.by: Michael Scott, author of Themistocles: The Rise and Fall of Athens’s Naval Mastermind
praise.cred: author of Themistocles: The Rise and Fall of Athens’s Naval Mastermind

books.title: Harnessing Divinity
books.subtitle: Generative Design and the Buddhist Architecture of Early Medieval China
books.description:
In traditional studies of Chinese architecture, Buddhist halls are often seen as mere variations of imperial palaces and understood primarily as shelters. Harnessing Divinity challenges this view, arguing that ritual buildings in Early Medieval China were designed with active spiritual technologies that could harness natural energies and facilitate communication with higher realms.

Focusing on the Yellow River Valley during the beginning of state-sponsored Buddhism in China, this book reveals how a specific design strategy—the “floral diagram” or “daisy wheel”—was used to encode buildings with intrinsic, generative power. Tracy Miller demonstrates that this geometric method allowed structures to function as “mesocosms,” bridging terrestrial and celestial forces to support both state-building by the ruling elite and spiritual transformation of devotees.

Through detailed case studies of sixth-century monuments, Miller argues that creators integrated empirically verifiable design principles with ideologies from West, Central, and South Asia to construct ritually potent spaces. The mathematical precision, critical for structural integrity, allowed for the building of taller, grander structures that projected divine support for the state. By tracing the use of a particular “generative design,” this book offers a compelling new perspective on the intersection of science, religion, and material culture in pre-modern China, showing how architecture was scaled to aid both imperial and common patrons.
books.bio: Tracy Miller is Associate Professor of History of Art and Architecture and Asian Studies at Vanderbilt University.

books.title: Luísa Correia Pereira
books.subtitle: World Child
books.tagline: The wild and wonderful world of Luísa Correia Pereira, an obscure jewel of late modernism and 'énfant terrible' of the Portuguese art scene.
books.description:
“Portugal is not a place for women.”

These words propelled the artist Paula Rego to pursue an English education, which informed her future career and subsequent legacy. How would life have looked for Luísa Correia Pereira had someone told her something similar in view of being a queer woman in the 1970s and 1980s? Born into one of Portugal’s aristocratic dynasties, Pereira shunned her family, propelled instead by a singular pursuit of her art. At seventeen, in 1962, she volunteered to work on the World Expo in Brazil where she became aware of poetry, cosmology, and biodiversity—all major influences on her work.

Pereira then spent some time living with nuns at the Catholic Institute of Paris during the peak of the second-wave feminist movement, and studied library science, a field common to several women artists of the time. While working at the Foundation Nationale des Sciences Politiques in Paris she developed her painting practice after receiving a grant from the Gulbenkian Foundation. Here she was aided by the tutelage of the famed Portuguese artist Julio Pomar.

Following the Carnation Revolution in 1974, Pereira returned to Portugal, where she experienced spells of recognition before falling into obscurity, partly due to episodes of manic depression. The press dubbed her an enfant terrible. She was renowned for being able to draw people into her orbit, then alienate them just as quicky—a habit that few realized was a consequence of her complex post-traumatic stress. The emotional topography of her life transpires in her early works on paper including watercolors, frottage, and collage, often depicting surrealist landscapes with distended bodies blanketed under thick washes of color. Her later canvases portrayed amorphous limbs strung together by ladders that would become a recurring motif for the rest of her working life.

In this volume, author and cultural historian Dr. Omar Kholeif narrates a five-year journey through a collection of Correia Pereira’s works that variously speak, sing, and cry, returning us to a child of nature. Compiled from hundreds of hours of interviews during time spent in Portugal, France, and Brazil, this first monograph in English on the artist’s work and life is at once searing and heartwarming.

Includes a foreword and essay by Maria Filomena Molder, an interlude by Sarah Perks, and an afterword by Sofia Victorino.

Co-published by artPost21.
books.bio: Professor Omar Kholeif, PhD is an award-winning author, artist, curator, and cultural historian. Their research explores aesthetic culture in the age of the internet, with a focus on gender, critical race politics, and social justice. Kholeif is Professor of Global Art Theory and Practice at the Glasgow School of Art, and Head of Postgraduate Taught Programs in Curatorial Practice with the University of Glasgow. Recent authored volumes include Nil Yalter , recipient of the Golden Lion at the Venice Biennale, Otobong Nkanga , and Internet_Art . In 2012, they co-founded artPost21 as a platform for artists and their “dreamwork.”

books.title: Makers of Modern Strategy from Machiavelli to the Nuclear Age
books.authors: Peter Paret, Gordon A. Craig, Felix Gilbert, Russell F. Weigley
books.tagline: "Authoritative and convincing." —New York Times Book Review The classic, indispensable reference to the theory and practice of war, in the first new edition in forty years
books.description: The essays in this landmark book analyze the strategic characteristics of war and its political and social functions over the past five centuries, covering everything from key theorists and political and military leaders to the strategies used in major conflicts. Machiavelli, Clausewitz, and Marx and Engels are discussed, as are Napoleon, Churchill, and Mao. Contributors trace the interplay of theory and experience across generations, analyze the complex relationship between war, technology, and policy, and much more—all while placing military thought and action in their historical context. Now with a new foreword by Lawrence Freedman, Makers of Modern Strategy from Machiavelli to the Nuclear Age reinterprets and illuminates war, one of the most powerful forces in history and one that cannot be controlled in the future without an understanding of its past.
books.bio: Peter Paret (1924–2020) was the Raymond A. Spruance Professor of International History at Stanford University. His books include Clausewitz and the State: The Man, His Theories, and His Times (Princeton). Gordon A. Craig (1913–2005) was the J. E. Wallace Sterling Professor of Humanities Emeritus at Stanford University. Felix Gilbert (1905–1991) was professor emeritus in the School of Historical Studies at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. Lawrence Freedman is emeritus professor of war studies at King’s College London.

praise.q: [These essays] are authoritative and convincing. Taken together, they demonstrate the complexity of strategy and the importance of it being closely integrated with politics.
praise.by: New York Times Book Review

books.title: Must the Sun Set in the West?
books.subtitle: Japan’s Stunted Democracy and the American Liberal Hegemony
books.tagline: How an elitist concept of democracy promoted by the American political and academic establishments constrained Japan’s political development
books.description:
Japan’s historic pursuit of a full membership in “the West” may finally be close to fruition—even as the value of such membership seems greatly diminished. In Must the Sun Set in the West? , Koichi Nakano argues that, despite the common understanding that postwar Japan became a democracy thanks to the benevolent patronage of the United States, American interference actually stunted Japanese democracy. Tracing the interplay between American liberal hegemonic projection in East Asia and Japan’s efforts to achieve full-fledged Western status, Nakano examines the racist (and sexist) roots of the elitist theory of democracy propagated by the American political and academic establishments and its impact on postwar Japan.

Nakano traces the evolution of the elitist project through its various stages—liberal-internationalist “race development,” anticommunist/liberal “modernization theory,” and neoliberal-globalist “democracy assistance.” He argues that Japan, by virtue of its ambiguous position as almost Western (but not really Western), offers a unique vantage point for analyzing the Western hegemonic strategy. He first examines the encounter between American hegemonic projection and Japan’s imperialist modernization before World War II, when the American elite granted Japan an “honorary white” status. He then turns to the postwar period, examining the ways that democracy in Japan collided with the American hegemonic agenda. By revisiting the white supremacist roots of the elitist theory that equates democracy with an elite-pluralist procedure to create strong leadership—which, he points out, is still dominant in political science today—Nakano sheds light on the hidden liberal provenance of contemporary democratic backsliding.
books.bio: Koichi Nakano is professor of political science at Sophia University in Japan. In 2024–2025, he was visiting scholar at the program on U.S.–Japan Relations at Harvard University’s Weatherhead Institute for International Affairs. He is the author of Party Politics and Decentralization in Japan and France: When the Opposition Governs .

praise.q: This book is a tour de force, providing an incomparable insider’s analysis of Japanese politics and giving a voice to progressive views that are often overlooked or marginalized. There is no other similar work that takes on such an ambitious agenda, dissecting US-Japan ties and efforts to nurture a bilateral academic industrial complex supportive of those ties. It will be essential reading for Japanologists and specialists in American studies across a range of disciplines.”—Jeff Kingston, author of Japan in Transformation, 1945

Nakano’s brilliant account interrogates nothing less than the racist foundations of American political science and how its structure translates outside its loci of origin, particularly in Japan. Written with sheer command of the most relevant and contemporary arguments, it is at once a pithy history of modern political change in Japan and a searing critique of ‘white’ supremacies.
praise.by: Alexis Dudden, author of Troubled Apologies Among Japan, Korea, and the United States
praise.cred: author of Troubled Apologies Among Japan, Korea, and the United States

praise.q: In this dazzling broadside, political scientist Koichi Nakano reveals that U.S. Japan experts have been rediscovering the wheel for over a century. They invent new terminology, declare victory over the last (racist, paternalistic) generation, resurrect the old ideas, and reward themselves for advancing knowledge. What has gone unrecognized in all the theorizing until now is the role that the Japanese left has played in preserving the country’s democracy after continuous overt and covert interventions by successive U.S. administrations and their academic auxiliaries.
praise.by: Robert Vitalis, University of Pennsylvania

books.title: New War Machines
books.subtitle: The Nuclear Age and Its Dangerous Successors
books.tagline: How new military technologies require radically new thinking about peace, war, national security, and international order
books.description:
Dangerous military technologies are spreading to great powers, secondary, and even tertiary powers. Many more countries have access to nuclear weapons, hypersonic missiles, killer drones, cyber war, laser death rays, quantum radar, and designer bioweapons. AI’s role is to coordinate this ecosystem of new war machines.

Yale professor Paul Bracken presents a guide, in clear non-technical language, to the military and political realities to the days ahead. He argues that the arms race the world now faces require a big picture strategic view—one that focuses not on individual technologies but on how interconnected weapons make the coming years far more dangerous than are realized. Bracken adopts “possible worlds” theory, used in AI, technology management, and business to analyze the wars and arms races ahead. In an era when disruptive technologies are rapidly increasing, Bracken shows us new ways of thinking about survival and arms control in an all too multipolar world.
books.bio: Paul Bracken is professor emeritus of management and political science at Yale University. He is the author of The Second Nuclear Age: Strategy, Danger, and the New Power Politics .

books.title: Sacred Capital
books.subtitle: States, Religions, and Power in Global Politics
books.tagline: How the entanglements of states, religions, and power are reshaping global politics and order in the twenty-first century
books.description:
Can religion become a source of power for states in global politics? In Sacred Capital Gregorio Bettiza argues that just as certain states can be considered military great powers, some states can be thought of as religious great powers. Existing scholarship largely ignores the mutually reinforcing entanglements between states and religions, failing to take into account the ways that state power and influence can be fueled by religious forces and dynamics. Bettiza presents a novel theoretical framework that fills this gap, exploring why and how states can gain and exercise influence globally through faith. He shows that religious great powers are endowed with considerable forms of sacred capital by hosting geographical, cultural, and organizational centers of faith traditions and networks with transnational reach and appeal.

Bettiza identifies three kinds of sacred capital—symbolic, cultural, and social. He demonstrates how contemporary religious great powers indirectly benefit from or explicitly mobilize these different forms of sacred capital in pursuit of their international objectives. Using the cases of India, Iran, Israel, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and the United States—among the most prominent religious great powers today—to develop his theory, Bettiza’s account reveals how world affairs are shaped not just by secularly-oriented power politics or ideologies such as liberalism, but by religious faith as well.
books.bio: Gregorio Bettiza is associate professor of international relations at the Alma Mater Studiorum–University of Bologna. He is the author of Finding Faith in Foreign Policy: Religion and American Diplomacy in a Postsecular World .

praise.q: In Sacred Capital, Gregorio Bettiza advances a powerful new conceptual framework for analyzing the complex relationship between religions and states in international politics. A must-read for scholars of religion and politics.
praise.by: Philip Gorski, Geneva Graduate Institute

praise.q: The theoretical grounding that the author gives his work and the empirical narratives he builds on that grounding are innovative, provocative, and convincing. The book offers a truly new way of approaching the ways that states and religions interact.
praise.by: Timothy Byrnes, author of Reverse Mission: Transnational Religious Communities and the Making of US Foreign Policy
praise.cred: author of Reverse Mission: Transnational Religious Communities and the Making of US Foreign Policy

praise.q: That the sacred never belonged to religion alone is by now an established insight. Bettiza builds on it to show how states remain entangled with the ideas, institutions, and narratives of religions, and how the sacred becomes a political power in its own right rather than a resource borrowed from religion. Sacred Capital is a very important and welcome contribution to a growing literature that steps away from simplistic dichotomies such as secular/religious, sacred/profane, and politics/religion. Essential reading for anyone trying to understand how religion works in world politics today.
praise.by: Jocelyne Cesari, University of Birmingham and Georgetown University
praise.cred: University of Birmingham and Georgetown University

books.title: Serving the Wealthy
books.subtitle: The Exploitation of Domestic Workers in France
books.tagline: The invisible relationship between the ultra-rich and their domestic workers
books.description:
Behind the facades of luxurious Parisian buildings, the immense gates of châteaux, and the bay windows of vast villas on the Côte d'Azur, live the invisible workers who serve the ultra-wealthy of France. Housekeepers, butlers, maids and cleaners, laundresses, nannies, cooks, and chauffeurs work from morning to night—and often through the night—to satisfy the needs of the rich families who employ them. In Serving the Wealthy , Alizée Delpierre offers an inside view of this unlikely cohabitation.

Drawing on extensive immersive research, Delpierre calls the relationship between ultra-rich French employers and their domestic help “golden exploitation”: workers see the potential for social advancement, and the wealthy will do anything to preserve their class privilege, enjoying the fruits of their capital while outsourcing daily drudgery to others. The need for round-the-clock serving, however, does not compel the rich to pay their domestic workers a fair wage; some earn less than minimum wage—and off-the-books gifts of designer handbags don’t necessarily fill the gap. Most of these domestic workers are women, many of whom are immigrants, and Delpierre notes that it is considered perfectly normal for a wealthy employer to hire on the basis of ethnicity—to state explicitly a preference for Black and Arab maids, for example, or a distaste for Muslim workers.

The world inhabited by servants and their ultra-rich employers might seem archaic and absurd; but Delpierre’s account sheds light not only on these particular power relations but also on the extreme inequality of our current era.
books.bio: Alizée Delpierre is a sociologist and research fellow at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and the author of Les Domesticités . Her work has appeared in L'Observateur , Libération , Le Monde , and other publications.

books.title: Surviving Genocide in the American West
books.subtitle: Native Nations and the United States from the Fur Trade through the Civil War
books.tagline: A sweeping history of U.S. expansion west of the Mississippi through the end of the Civil War showing that American empire was built on systemic violence and genocide against Native nations
books.description:
Reframing the United States’ westward expansion as a continental empire-building project, historian Jeffrey Ostler shows how the country orchestrated a genocidal campaign against Indigenous populations across the Trans-Mississippi West through treaty coercion, massacres, forced removals, starvation, and the destruction of land and lifeways. As he debunks many long-standing myths, Ostler

• Describes how genocide unfolded across diverse geographies and colonial histories in the Pacific Northwest, California, Texas, the Great Plans, the Southwest, and elsewhere

• Documents the many forms of colonial violence beyond warfare that decimated populations in ways not always visible in traditional histories

• Highlights Indigenous agency and resilience, from voices that illuminate the lived experience and consciousness of genocide to Native nations’ diplomacy, resistance, and adaptation

• Breaks new ground on the Civil War’s western dimension and the ways that it intensified genocidal violence in the West, reshaping the region and Indigenous nations

This gripping history challenges myths of the “winning of the West” and illuminates Indigenous survival against overwhelming odds, making it essential reading for understanding America’s past and its enduring legacies.
books.bio: Jeffrey Ostler is professor emeritus of history at the University of Oregon. He is the author of Surviving Genocide: Native Nations and the United States from the American Revolution to Bleeding Kansas . He lives in Eugene, OR.

books.title: The Land Without Music
books.subtitle: English Identity and the Idea of Unmusicality
books.series: The Lewis Walpole Series in Eighteenth-Century Culture and History
books.tagline: Why the idea of English unmusicality arose and how the English sought to uphold national honor in the face of it
books.description:
Why, while touting their superiority in other spheres, did the English develop an idea of themselves as musically inferior to their neighbors? Historian Amy Dunagin shows that as the English musical marketplace expanded after 1660, evolving beliefs about the effects of climate on national character led the English to identify musicality—along with excess, passion, and effeminacy—as characteristic of a “southern” temperament from which they were eager to distance themselves.

Once established, the idea proved difficult to excise, and the ascendancy of foreign music, especially Italian opera, seemed to confirm it. Eighteenth-century English commentators disagreed about how best to present the state of their national music and developed competing narratives that resonated with Tory, Establishment Whig, and Patriot political ideologies, with profound implications for English cultural identity.

Dunagin traces the idea of English unmusicality as it emerged in the late Stuart period and shows how it became a contested national narrative—one that reflected broader anxieties about identity, virtue, and cultural engagement with Europe.
books.bio: Amy Dunagin is associate professor of history at Kennesaw State University. She lives in Atlanta, GA.

praise.q: In a bravura performance, Amy Dunagin takes English ‘unmusicality’ after 1660 as her theme, blending the commodification of music, the supposed effeminacy of Italian opera, and the politics of writing a history of the musical arts into a compelling ensemble.
praise.by: Paul Kléber Monod, author of Think of England: Nation, People, and Race in the English Imagination
praise.cred: author of Think of England: Nation, People, and Race in the English Imagination

praise.q: An original study that centers the role of music in creating hierarchies and identities. Dunagin takes us on a fascinating journey through party ideology, secularization, commerce, and gender politics over the long eighteenth century.
praise.by: Rachel Weil, Cornell University

praise.q: In this dramatic book, Dunagin brilliantly historicizes the debates about Britain’s lack of musicality and how it was entangled with the nation’s cultural identity, foreign relations, party politics, aesthetics, and the English language.
praise.by: Carl Wennerlind, co-author of Scarcity: A History from the Origins of Capitalism to the Climate Crisis
praise.cred: co-author of Scarcity: A History from the Origins of Capitalism to the Climate Crisis

praise.q: In this compelling book, Amy Dunagin shows how various political groupings promoted the notion of English ‘unmusicality’ in different ways, reflecting competing social, cultural, and imperial agendas and anxieties.
praise.by: Abigail L. Swingen, author of Competing Visions of Empire: Labor, Slavery, and the Origins of the British Atlantic Empire
praise.cred: author of Competing Visions of Empire: Labor, Slavery, and the Origins of the British Atlantic Empire

praise.q: In prose of elegant clarity, Dunagin crafts an argument of admirable complexity, demonstrating that the myth of English ‘unmusicality’ was not imposed from without but developed from within. A model of interdisciplinary synthesis, this monograph will prove essential reading for historians and musicologists alike.
praise.by: Julia Doe, Columbia University

books.title: The Model Company
books.subtitle: The Economics of Making Business Do the Greatest Good
books.tagline: What works—and what doesn’t—when companies try to do good
books.description:
Can companies really be “socially responsible”—and should they try? This debate is newly urgent as consumers, employees, and investors push companies to take a stand on everything from climate change to inequality. In this lively and clear-eyed book, economist Ray Fisman cuts through the rhetoric around “doing well by doing good” to show what actually changes corporate behavior and what doesn’t—and what corporations should really do if they have society’s interests at heart. He will answer questions many of us may be asking:

• Will consumers pay more for eco-friendly products?

• Will employees work harder if they’re paid a living wage?

• Do ESG (environmental, social, and governance) funds make a difference?

• Should you pay more for fair-trade coffee at your local café? (Yes, you should.)

Drawing on decades of evidence, Fisman examines which approaches to corporate responsibility make a genuine difference—and which are cheap talk, or worse. The result is a practical framework for understanding the tradeoffs between profit and purpose, recognizing which efforts to do good are likely to succeed, and how your choices can push companies to do better.
books.bio: Ray Fisman is the Slater Family Professor in Behavioral Economics at Boston University. His most recent book (with Liran Einav and Amy Finkelstein) is Risky Business: Why Insurance Markets Fail and What to Do About It . He lives in Brookline, MA.

books.title: The New Makers of Modern Strategy
books.subtitle: From the Ancient World to the Digital Age
books.authors: Hal Brands, John Bew, Lawrence Freedman, Walter Russell Mead, Toshi Yoshihara, Matthew Kroenig, Hew Strachan, Antulio Echevarria, John H. Maurer, Michael Cotey Morgan, James Lacey, Eric Helleiner, Jonathan Kirshner, Iskander Rehman, Matt J. Schumann, Michael V. Leggiere, Charles Edel, Kori Schake, Wayne Wei-Siang Hsieh, Sarah C. M. Stearns, Joshua Rovner, Thomas Rid, John Lewis Gaddis, Eric Edelman, Andrew Ehrhardt, Mark Moyar
books.tagline: The essential resource on military and political strategy and the making of the modern world—now with a new preface
books.description:
The New Makers of Modern Strategy is the next generation of the definitive work on strategy and the key figures who have shaped the theory and practice of war and statecraft throughout the centuries. Featuring entirely new entries by a who’s who of world-class scholars, this new edition provides global, comparative perspectives on strategic thought from antiquity to today, surveying both classical and current themes of strategy while devoting greater attention to the Cold War and post-9/11 eras. The contributors evaluate the timeless requirements of effective strategy while tracing the revolutionary changes that challenge the makers of strategy in the contemporary world. Amid intensifying global disorder, the study of strategy and its history has never been more relevant. The New Makers of Modern Strategy draws vital lessons from history’s most influential strategists, from Thucydides and Sun Zi to Clausewitz, Napoleon, Churchill, Mao, Ben-Gurion, Andrew Marshall, Xi Jinping, and Qassem Soleimani.

With contributions by Dmitry Adamsky, John Bew, Tami Davis Biddle, Hal Brands, Antulio J. Echevarria II, Elizabeth Economy, Charles Edel, Eric S. Edelman, Andrew Ehrhardt, Lawrence Freedman, John Lewis Gaddis, Francis J. Gavin, Christopher J. Griffin, Ahmed S. Hashim, Eric Helleiner, Wayne Wei-siang Hsieh, Seth G. Jones, Robert Kagan, Jonathan Kirshner, Matthew Kroenig, James Lacey, Guy Laron, Michael V. Leggiere, Margaret MacMillan, Tanvi Madan, Thomas G. Mahnken, Carter Malkasian, Daniel Marston, John H. Maurer, Walter Russell Mead, Michael Cotey Morgan, Mark Moyar, Williamson Murray, S.C.M. Paine, Sergey Radchenko, Iskander Rehman, Thomas Rid, Joshua Rovner, Priya Satia, Kori Schake, Matt J. Schumann, Brendan Simms, Jason K. Stearns, Hew Strachan, Sue Mi Terry, and Toshi Yoshihara.
books.bio: Hal Brands is the Henry A. Kissinger Distinguished Professor of Global Affairs at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies and senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. His books include The Eurasian Century: Hot Wars, Cold Wars, and the Making of the Modern World .

praise.q: [Brands] gathers a college of 45 such experts. All are wise after the facts of their field, and each attempts the historian’s equivalent of the owl’s neck rotation—a sweep that, taking in past and present, looks to the future . . . the scholarship on strategy has become internationalized, and Mr. Brands broadens his sights beyond the familiar theorists and practitioners—and beyond the battlefield.
praise.by: Dominic Green, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: The book is a great scholarly achievement that has set a new and probably long-lasting benchmark in strategic studies.
praise.by: Marco Wyss, International Journal of Military History and Historiography
praise.cred: International Journal of Military History and Historiography

praise.q: It is hard to overstate the importance of this book. The essays provide excellent starting points for research on almost any topic relevant to practitioners, and many of them will endure as the best summaries of thinking on their respective subjects. . . . Reading the book cover to cover would be terrific preparation for a year at any American professional military education institution—or for service in Congress or the executive branch at a time when American strategy appears to be faltering."—John C. Erickson and John A. Nagl, Parameters

Hal Brands has rounded up over 40 authors for his new edition of The New Makers of Modern Strategy: from the Ancient World to the Digital Age . . . .The third great volume of Makers of Modern Strategy that will feature on every pertinent university or staff college reading list.
praise.by: Beatrice Heuser, Journal of Strategic Studies

praise.q: Makers of Modern Strategy has long been a valuable resource for understanding the relationship between military strategy and political outcomes. This newest volume combines strategies from the past with insights gleaned from an impressive group of contemporary scholars and will undoubtedly remain an important read for decades to come.
praise.by: Condoleezza Rice, director of the Hoover Institution and former US secretary of state
praise.cred: director of the Hoover Institution and former US secretary of state

praise.q: A splendid endeavor, ambitious and wide-ranging. Broadly conceived, authoritative, and masterfully edited, this new volume retains and regains the pertinence and power of the original classic editions.
praise.by: Paul Kennedy, author of Victory at Sea and The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers
praise.cred: author of Victory at Sea and The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers

praise.q: This superb collection arrives just in time to help restore strategic competence. As geopolitical competitions intensify globally, we must not let the valuable lessons in Makers of Modern Strategy lie inert within these covers. These are essays to be read, discussed, and applied to the challenges we are facing today.”—H. R. McMaster, former national security advisor and author of Battlegrounds and Dereliction of Duty

Mining history’s cruel lessons, highlighting the enduring wisdom of great strategic thinkers, and delivering new insights about how democracies can thrive in an era of profound technological change and political uncertainty, The New Makers of Modern Strategy is an indispensable guide to the geopolitical challenges of the twenty-first century.”—Amy B. Zegart, professor and senior fellow at Stanford University and author of Spies, Lies, and Algorithms: The History and Future of American Intelligence

You may not be interested in war, but war has always been interested in you. It is hard to imagine a better introduction to our conflict-ridden era than this brilliant assortment of case studies of strategic thought and action. The work’s coverage from the ancient world to the digital age, its focus on the relationships between theory and practice, and its imaginative selection of topics and authors are truly admirable.
praise.by: MacGregor Knox, London School of Economics and Political Science
praise.cred: London School of Economics and Political Science

praise.q: It isn’t easy to improve upon a classic, but the contributors have done a remarkable job of updating Makers of Modern Strategy for the twenty-first century. This volume honors the spirit of the original while posing new questions that will keep both volumes relevant for decades to come.
praise.by: Michael S. Neiberg, author of When France Fell: The Vichy Crisis and the Fate of the Anglo-American Alliance
praise.cred: author of When France Fell: The Vichy Crisis and the Fate of the Anglo-American Alliance

books.title: The Second Great Awakening
books.subtitle: The Transformation of American Evangelicalism
books.tagline: From a leading historian, a sweeping account of the Second Great Awakening, one of the most significant eras of religious change in American history
books.description:
The Second Great Awakening, spanning from roughly 1790 to 1840, was the greatest period of Protestant growth in U.S. history. Marked by spectacular revivals, it dramatically changed the denominational landscape, elevating Baptists and Methodists from minor sects to America’s leading denominations. It also witnessed a mass conversion of African Americans to Christianity, spurred advancements in education and benevolent societies, fostered the burgeoning print trade, and helped to organize the frontier. Moreover, this period saw significant schisms within Protestant denominations over the issue of slavery.

In this first-ever comprehensive history of the Second Great Awakening, celebrated historian Thomas S. Kidd tells the dramatic story of this epochal period. Ranging from the United States to still-monarchical Canada and the British Caribbean, Kidd

• challenges the conventional view that the Second Great Awakening was a monolithic wave of democratization and

• portrays a period riddled with divisions, both regional and doctrinal, that prefigured the fissures leading to the Civil War.

A follow-up to Kidd’s influential book The Great Awakening: The Roots of Evangelical Religion in Colonial America , this meticulously researched account provides invaluable insights into this pivotal period in American religious history.
books.bio: Thomas S. Kidd is research professor of church history at Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary and senior research scholar at Baylor University’s Institute for Studies of Religion. He is the author of many books, including Thomas Jefferson: A Biography of Spirit and Flesh .

books.title: The World of a Wasp
books.subtitle: The Quest to Understand a Remarkable Insect Society
books.tagline: A world-renowned entomologist takes readers inside the world of social wasps to explore how these amazing insects organize a successful society
books.description:
Raghavendra Gadagkar was a teenager when he first encountered the Indian paper wasp and has since spent decades unraveling the secrets of this remarkable species. The World of a Wasp takes readers along on his research journey, exploring how these insects form a highly evolved society with a sophisticated division of labor, efficient communication, and elaborate mechanisms for balancing cooperation and conflict to survive in a harsh tropical environment.

Although all the wasps in a colony look alike, only one is the fertile reproductive queen. The rest function as sterile workers laboring for the welfare of the colony, with duties ranging from building the nest and bringing food to feeding the larvae and guarding and cleaning the nest. Each chapter of this engaging book centers on a question, explaining the reasons behind it and the avenues Gadagkar and his students followed to arrive at an answer. How does a wasp become a queen? Why do the workers accept a subordinate role? How does a worker know what work to do? Through these and many other questions, Gadagkar invites readers to form their own conclusions and join in the discovery.

Drawing on careful observations and elegant experiments, The World of a Wasp offers a rare glimpse into the workings of a fascinating insect society and shares perspectives from a leading researcher on the practice and pleasures of science.
books.bio: Raghavendra Gadagkar is professor and national science chair at the Centre for Ecological Sciences at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, India. He is the author of Survival Strategies: Cooperation and Conflict in Animal Societies ; The Social Biology of Ropalidia marginata: Toward Understanding the Evolution of Eusociality ; and Experiments in Animal Behaviour: Cutting-Edge Research at Trifling Cost .

praise.q: As Gadagkar notes, ‘The more we look, the more we are puzzled.’ How those puzzles led him to fall in love with his wasp study subjects is a wonderful story in itself, a meditation on where passions come from. He conveys the thrill of discovery along with the explanation for complex social behaviors such as dominance. The drama of who will become queen, and how he and his group disentangled the story, is as compelling as any soap opera.
praise.by: Marlene Zuk, author of Outsider Animals

praise.q: Gadagkar has two passions, learning everything he can about the social life of the Indian paper wasp and democratizing science. In this book, he uses a series of simple experiments to demonstrate how anyone armed only with curiosity, persistence, and humility can engage in cutting-edge research and make valuable contributions to knowledge.
praise.by: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy, author of Mother Nature , Mothers and Others , and Father Time
praise.cred: author of Mother Nature , Mothers and Others , and Father Time

praise.q: From one of the world’s leading animal behaviorists, The World of a Wasp is a delightful and enlightening journey into the complex world of insect society. The joys, trials, and tribulations of studying animals shine through, and the fundamental breakthroughs that have come from Gadagkar and his team’s work jump off the pages.
praise.by: Lee Alan Dugatkin, coauthor of How to Tame a Fox (and Build a Dog)
praise.cred: coauthor of How to Tame a Fox (and Build a Dog)

books.title: Tragedy
books.subtitle: The Dawn of Drama in Ancient Athens
books.tagline: A major new history of the revolutionary invention of tragedy that sheds fresh and surprising light on both ancient and modern drama
books.description:
Why did tragedy come into being—and why is it still so important 2,500 years after it first arose in fifth-century Athens? Does it serve a deeper purpose beyond entertainment? And was the birth of tragedy at the same time and place as the birth of democracy more than a coincidence? In this book, Oliver Taplin, one of the world’s leading authorities on ancient Greek drama, confronts these fascinating questions by offering a lively, personal and radical new account of how and why this transformative art form happened. By illuminating the foundations of Greek theatre, he offers surprising new insights into both ancient performance and the persistent power of drama.

Tragedy reveals the collaborations that were needed for the new theatrical events to be staged at the Festival of Dionysus each spring—turning storytelling into “story-doing.” It explores the bold theatricality of the earliest plays, especially those of Aeschylus. And it maps the profound impact dramatic performances must have had on their first audiences. Most of all, the book argues that drama, although enabled by democracy, did not reassuringly endorse the standard attitudes of its audience of male Athenian citizens. To the contrary, plays encouraged them to empathise with others, especially women and the disempowered.

As Tragedy persuasively argues, the combination of highly crafted performance and deep engagement with the sufferings of others in Greek drama helped to strengthen its audiences, like an inoculation, to face up to the pains of being fallible and mortal. And in doing so, Greek tragedy planted the seeds of drama’s rich flowerings down to today.
books.bio: Oliver Taplin taught for thirty-five years at the University of Oxford, specializing in Greek poetry and drama and their performance in both ancient and modern times. He has published books on Homer, tragedy and comedy, and on their reflections in vase-painting. He has also made verse translations of epic and tragedy, and has collaborated with creative practitioners including Tony Harrison, Lydia Koniordou and Katie Mitchell.

praise.q: The Ancient Greeks brought democracy and tragedy into the world at the same moment, creating theatre as a maintenance system for a new form of shared governance. In this summit of his immense and distinguished life’s work, Oliver Taplin takes us deftly into the heart of tragedy with light, air, grace and the possibility that the lessons of tragedy might actually deepen our fragile, endangered democratic practice.
praise.by: Peter Sellars, theatre director

praise.q: Tragedy is a thrilling provocation for classicists and theatre-makers alike, an invitation to revisit our most basic assumptions and to reanimate our current practices by understanding the radical ‘revolution’ that was Greek tragedy. As I followed Taplin’s lively and compelling argument, I found myself engaging with these ancient plays as if for the first time. I’m sure I will never direct a Greek tragedy the same way again!
praise.by: Carey Perloff, theatre director, playwright, and book author
praise.cred: theatre director, playwright, and book author

praise.q: To this day, Greek tragedy remains fascinating to readers and theatregoers throughout the world. No other living scholar has done more than Oliver Taplin to deepen our understanding of these plays. His new book draws on a lifetime of experience to answer the most fundamental questions they pose for readers and audiences who are interested in the life of tragedies and the tragedies of life.
praise.by: Glenn W. Most, University of Chicago

praise.q: Taplin expertly combines an introduction to early tragedy with a profound meditation on tragedy’s purposes and effects. Above all, he overturns the established view that tragedy served male Athenian citizens as a vehicle of self-definition and self-celebration at the expense of the ‘other.’ On the contrary, he shows that tragedy nurtured fellow feeling for others, helping instill the moral breadth that made democratic coexistence possible.
praise.by: Eric Csapo, University of Warwick

praise.q: After a long career of interpreting, translating and analyzing Greek tragedy, Oliver Taplin turns in this new book to provocatively reexamining for a general audience the controversial evidence for its early performance and its developing relation to Athenian democracy.
praise.by: Helene P. Foley, Columbia University

books.title: Weird
books.subtitle: A Life of Arthur Machen in Six Unearthly Books
books.tagline: A new life of Arthur Machen: decadent, bohemian, mystic, journalist, Welsh wizard and author of
books.description:
Arthur Machen is an all but forgotten master of the weird tale, and his circle included mystics and occultists as well as Oscar Wilde and Aubrey Beardsley. His work has profoundly influenced some of our most mysterious creative minds—including such masters of the modern gothic as H.P. Lovecraft, Stephen King and Guillermo del Toro—but he never achieved commercial success. Today his work has found a new generation of readers, buoyed up on the resurgence of weird fiction and folk horror.

Felix John Taylor’s bold new biography brings together Machen’s enigmatic life and shocking books for the first time. Inspired by occultism, decadence and Celtic folklore, Machen’s eerie tales encompassed ghostly apparitions, demonic possession, fairies, angels and the Holy Grail. By turns a jobbing actor, self-mythologiser, war correspondent and recluse, his life reveals a hidden weird Edwardian literary world, and the demands and compromises of creative life in London of the early twentieth century.

This is a powerful reappraisal of a writer whose work haunted his contemporaries—and has enchanted us ever since.
books.bio: Felix John Taylor is a librarian at the Queen’s College, Oxford, and an expert on the influence of Welsh mythology and folklore on modern British fiction. He is the author of The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn .

books.title: A Police State
books.subtitle: Politics and Public Safety in Minneapolis, 1945–2020
books.tagline: How the police in Minneapolis used electoral politics to accrue power and avoid accountability.
books.description:
The 2020 murder of George Floyd made Minneapolis synonymous with unjust policing and the pain and outrage left in its wake. The city became ground zero for police reform in the United States—even though liberal politicians in Minnesota had promised, and delivered, police reforms for decades. Centered on professionalization, these changes inadvertently exacerbated injustice. Better training and higher standards broadened the influence of the police, who then claimed expertise in public safety. They deployed it to bargain for governmental support, even when they treated residents unfairly. Though Black, Indigenous, and gay residents resisted, the political power amassed by the police rendered real change almost impossible.

In A Police State , historian and fourth-generation Minneapolis resident Michael J. Lansing chronicles how the police became a political force in one of the nation’s most liberal cities. Lansing shows how, in the years after World War II, public safety policies that appealed to voters in the overwhelmingly white city protected and expanded police discretion. As union members, administrators, and citizens, officers shaped these policies to shield themselves and their violent actions from scrutiny. They campaigned for better wages, secured legal safeguards, resisted race-neutral policing, and elected one of their own to the mayor’s office. Ultimately, they used democratic institutions to cultivate and sustain a police state that protected white people and harmed people of color. Lansing uncovers this dysfunctional relationship between a city and its cops while illuminating a larger American story about reform, resistance, and democracy.

A significant exploration of policing politics, this book helps us understand the history that led to George Floyd’s murder—and insists that the future of community safety depends on reenvisioning the role of police in our society.

praise.q: When Minneapolis exploded in 2020 as the epicenter of a global rebellion against police violence and the birthplace of the largest protest movement in United States history, many Americans asked, ‘Why Minneapolis?’ A Police State shows why. Dating back to the mid-twentieth century, Minneapolis police and their union began to establish themselves as uniquely powerful political actors on the local scene. Manipulating weaknesses in the city’s political and electoral systems, they pursued a set of politics that changed over time but that was always feverishly chasing greater power for themselves and less accountability for the things they did. In so doing and without remorse, they eventually emerged as a wildly reactionary force in the city’s politics, mangled relationships with communities of color, and sowed the seeds for the murder of George Floyd and the summer that shook the world.
praise.by: Simon Balto, author of “Occupied Territory: Policing Black Chicago from Red Summer to Black Power”
praise.cred: author of “Occupied Territory: Policing Black Chicago from Red Summer to Black Power”

praise.q: How did a famously liberal city become the national exemplar for police power? In A Police State , Lansing delivers the definitive history of ‘policing politics’ in Minneapolis from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Though the form of these struggles varied across the decades—from historic moments of collaboration between labor organizers, department leaders, and the mayor to outright political warfare between cops and communities—police continually built political power, often leveraging the reforms designed to rein them in. Grounded in the voices of marginalized communities fighting back, Lansing documents how ‘liberal law and order’ threatens both public safety and our democracy.
praise.by: Michelle S. Phelps, author of “The Minneapolis Reckoning: Race, Violence, and the Politics of Policing in America”
praise.cred: author of “The Minneapolis Reckoning: Race, Violence, and the Politics of Policing in America”

praise.q: Lansing has produced a magisterial and deeply illuminating work of urban history that challenges conventional narratives about policing and reform. Through meticulous research and absorbing prose, A Police State demonstrates how repeated efforts to reform policing in Minneapolis often strengthened, rather than constrained, police power, creating historical echoes that continue to reverberate through the city’s present. By centering the voices of those who challenged injustice while exposing the institutions that resisted meaningful change, Lansing offers an indispensable account of the fraught relationship between democracy, public safety, and accountability. At once a history of Minneapolis and a cautionary tale for the nation, A Police State is essential reading for anyone seeking to understand the enduring paradox of police reform in the United States.
praise.by: Yohuru Williams, coauthor of “More Than a Dream: The Radical March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom”
praise.cred: coauthor of “More Than a Dream: The Radical March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom”

praise.q: Lansing demonstrates that the political power exercised by the Minneapolis police, particularly by the police union, is at the root of conflicts over policing in the city. He unearths enough detailed evidence that, if this were a court of law and not a book, the verdict would surely be ‘guilty as charged.’ A Police State will have a significant impact on how Minneapolis’ history is understood, how its present will be understood, and how its future will be envisioned and shaped. This book presents an opportunity to disrupt the deeply ingrained and misrepresented history of this city and carve a new path.
praise.by: Peter Rachleff, author of “Hard-Pressed in the Heartland: The Hormel Strike and the Future of the Labor Movement”
praise.cred: author of “Hard-Pressed in the Heartland: The Hormel Strike and the Future of the Labor Movement”

books.title: Abstract Expressionism—and Beyond
books.subtitle: American Painting in the Collection Reinhard Ernst
books.authors: Edited by The Reinhard & Sonja Ernst Stiftung Foundation
books.tagline: Draws from a new museum collection to trace seventy years of abstract painting in the United States.
books.description:
From the color field paintings of Helen Frankenthaler to the plate-paintings of Julian Schnabel, this catalog showcases an outstanding variety of postwar art in the United States. Featuring pieces from the Museum Reinhard Ernst in Wiesbaden, a new institution devoted to abstract art, the book charts the evolution of postwar abstraction, offering insight into influential figures as well as groups like the New York School and the Washington Color School. More than one hundred color illustrations reproduce work by forty-five influential artists, including Josef Albers, Adolph Gottlieb, Franz Kline, Willem de Kooning, Lee Krasner, Robert Motherwell, Jackson Pollock, Frank Stella, and Andy Warhol. Together, their works demonstrate the variety of aesthetics and approaches within abstraction—improvisational forms confront rigorous geometric compositions, pictures enter into dialogue with sculptural objects, and paint and color conjure the sublime.

books.title: Deberlinization
books.subtitle: Refabulating the World, a Theory of Praxis
books.authors: Edited by Bonaventure Soh Bejeng Ndikung, Ibou Coulibaly Diop, and Franck Hermann Ekra
books.tagline: A multidisciplinary volume reflecting on the epistemological legacy of the colonial partitioning of Africa.
books.description:
In 1884, the Chancellor of the German Empire, Otto von Bismarck, convened a conference in Berlin to organize the division of the African continent among the industrial and military powers of the time. The result was a profound dismemberment of Africa’s original political structures, which, driven by nationalism and a barbaric ethos of rule, had a lasting impact on the continent’s political, socioeconomic, cultural, and spiritual development. One hundred and forty years after the Berlin Conference, it seems more than urgent to disentangle this complex of colonial appropriation, identify its after-effects, and question its epistemological legacy—all the more so as Europe searches for a new positioning in the changing geopolitical balance of power.

This multidisciplinary anthology takes up the idea of a transnational performative utopia to explore the possibilities of refabulating the world order and its future. Between creative action and resistance, memory and foresight, Deberlinization opens up perspectives on trans-African cohesion and outlines a new poetics of sovereignty.

books.title: Democracy in the Headwinds
books.subtitle: The Rise, Erosion, and Defence of Liberal Democracy
books.tagline: In Democracy in the Headwinds , Andreas Busch examines the growing threats to democracy worldwide and outlines the principles needed to safeguard it.
books.description:
A mob storms the United States Capitol. A Hungarian strongman hollows out courts, media, and civil society for sixteen years, then is voted out in a landslide. Brexit exposes the fragility of a constitution built on unwritten conventions. In Germany, one in five voters chooses a party classified by the state’s own security apparatus as a suspected threat to the democratic order. What is going on—and should it concern us?

Drawing on evidence from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Hungary, Poland, and the wider democratic world, Andreas Busch tells the story of liberal democracy’s rise, its erosion by elected leaders who dismantle institutions from within, and the defenses that hold. He traces how economic dislocation, digital disruption, and the polarization of political life have converged to put mature democracies under pressure they were assumed to have outgrown.

At the heart of the book lies a deceptively simple argument: the procedural core of democracy—free and fair elections and the peaceful transfer of power—is the foundation on which everything else rests. Protect the mechanics, and everything else can be rebuilt. Lose them, and nothing can.
subjects: Diplomacy, Foreign Policy, and International Relations

books.title: Diego Marcon
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.tagline: Both an artist’s book and a retrospective, Diego Marcon brings together images, drawings, and other behind-the-scenes material that mark twenty years of the artist’s film and animation practice.
books.description:
Diego Marcon’s practice primarily focuses on moving image and centers on the investigation of cinematic archetypes through a process that combines theoretical and structural approaches to filmmaking, with the sentimental attitudes of popular movie genres. His works––spanning film, video, and installation––often utilize a looped structure to articulate an emotional display that flirts with the pathetic aspects of popular entertainment and simultaneously draws attention to the media itself. Throughout Marcon’s work, empathy and vulnerability are deployed with intentional ambiguity, such that the instrumental use of their forms and figures constitutes a blurred morality. This ambiguity is viewed by Marcon first and foremost as a political weapon of defiance.

This book is published in conjunction with the exhibition Prom , presented at Lafayette Anticipations, Paris, from April 1 to July 19, 2026, and Krapfen at the Renaissance Society of the University of Chicago from September 13 to November 23, 2025.

books.title: Eating the Mountain, Eating the Sea
books.subtitle: A History of Food in China
books.tagline: A tantalizing guide to the diversity of regional foods in China.
books.description: Chinese cuisine is one of the world’s most celebrated and complex culinary traditions, yet much about it remains misunderstood. Beyond the stereotypes of exotic ingredients or the familiar dishes served in Chinese restaurants in Western countries, the reality of Chinese food is deeply regional, historical, and culturally significant. This book demystifies Chinese cuisine by examining five foundational ingredients that underpin its foodways, tracing how they are employed across eight major regions—from Sichuan’s fiery flavors to Guangdong’s delicate dim sum. Eating the Mountain, Eating the Sea shows that understanding what Chinese people really eat offers insights into China’s culture, identity, and influence. A fascinating guide for food lovers, students, and anyone interested in China’s culinary heritage.

praise.q: I had a fascinating time reading Gibas’s book. Eating the Mountain, Eating the Sea is filled with extraordinary insight about one of the great cuisines of the world. If you love Chinese food, you’ll devour this book!
praise.by: Ken Hom CBE, author, chef, and TV presenter

praise.q: What is Chinese cuisine? And how can it be defined? What common traits emerge from the interactions among a great variety of practices, techniques, and ingredients? In his comprehensive exploration of Chinese history and regional traditions, Gibas offers an expansive portrait of the complexity and diversity of Chinese food in its contemporary manifestations. ‘Native harvests’—unique crops and animal breeds that in the past were the result of poverty and ingenuity and have since become gourmet items—come to the foreground as the symbol of a culinary culture that takes full advantage of local conditions, allowing for innovation and endless creativity.
praise.by: Fabio Parasecoli, professor of food studies, New York University, and author of "Al Dente: A History of Food in Italy"
praise.cred: professor of food studies, New York University, and author of "Al Dente: A History of Food in Italy"

books.title: Eiffel Tower Confidential
books.subtitle: What It Meant and What It Stands For
books.tagline: A revelatory behind-the-scenes look at a universally recognized landmark: the Eiffel Tower.
books.description:
The Eiffel Tower is widely photographed, visited, and written about, but it holds a wealth of stories that are rarely told. When it was built, the three-hundred-meter structure was the tallest on earth, but it bore little resemblance to the stripped-down, modernized monument that is known and loved today. With Eiffel Tower Confidential , art historian Hollis Clayson makes this familiar landmark strange again, offering expert insight into the life of the Tower.

Here she traces the creative financing of the Tower before its construction began, shares images made in its early years, and illuminates the role the Tower played in celebrating French Imperialism. She tells the fascinating story of iron ornamentation that helped the Tower win approval as the centerpiece of the 1889 Universal Exposition but was ripped off and discarded in 1937, and she investigates the sinister backstory behind how the dazzling illumination of the Tower—which combined 10,000 gas lights in glass globes, two kinds of electric spotlights placed at the summit, and Bengal flames on the platforms—was designed to function as an instrument of surveillance.

This extraordinary account takes us into the long shadow of the Eiffel Tower, inviting readers to get to know this acclaimed landmark on an unprecedented level.

books.title: Fierce Unworking
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.authors: Ko Murobushi With a Preface by Stefan Barber
books.tagline: A collection of writings by one of the most important performers and choreographers in the contemporary Japanese performance scene.
books.description:
Ko Murobushi was one of the most important performers and choreographers in the Japanese performance scene of the twenty-first century and a key figure in the mediation between the experimental Butoh tradition of Hijikata Tatsumi and anti-logocentric French avant-gardes such as Antonin Artaud and Gilles Deleuze. Radically positioned at the intersection of the two movements, Murobushi reveals himself as an extraordinary and poetic author in his “thinking of the body.”

Fierce Unworking highlights his role as an unparalleled pioneer of contemporary paradigms such as body language, the third space, and embodied knowledge. Published ten years after his death, this volume brings together writings, poems, and diary fragments—many of which are available in English for the first time—in collaboration with the Ko Murobushi Archive in Tokyo.
