books.title: Fishel Rabinowicz
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.authors: Edited by Anita Winter and the Gamaraal Foundation
books.tagline: A collection of forty works by Holocaust survivor and artist Fishel Rabinowicz.
books.description:
Fishel Rabinowicz (1924–2024) was born in Sosnowiec, Poland. Growing up in an Orthodox Jewish family, he showed a talent for painting even as a child. In 1941, he was captured, and his ordeal with forced labor in nine different camps of the Nazi death machine began. In February 1945, he was sent along with 1,220 other prisoners on a two-hundred-mile death march to the Buchenwald concentration camp near Weimar, Germany, where he just escaped death when the camp was liberated in April 1945.

Following his four-year recovery in sanatoriums in Germany and Switzerland, Rabinowicz was offered the chance to study graphic design at the Zurich School of Art and Craft. Upon graduation, he settled in the Swiss canton of Ticino, where he married and started a family, and made his living as a graphic designer. Only after retirement did Rabinowicz turn to fine art, translating the story of his life, his experiences, and Jewish culture into abstract paper works that gained him international fame.

Fishel Rabinowicz features for the first time forty of his paper works in full-page plates, supplemented with brief explanatory texts by the artist himself and editor Anita Winter, and an essay by art historian and curator Dorothea Strauss.

books.title: Hans Pieler
books.subtitle: Architectures of Time
books.authors: Edited by Hubertus von Amelunxen and Ali Ghandtschi With Photography by Hans Pieler Contributions by Hermann Kern
books.tagline: Lavishly illustrated and featuring illuminating essays, the first-ever book on Hans Pieler’s photographs of calendar buildings.
books.description:
For thousands of years, people have built so-called calendar buildings: buildings that served as sundials for measuring time or were used for astronomical calculations. The most famous examples include the Pyramids of Giza, the Megalithic Temples of Malta, the Solarium Augusti on Rome’s Campus Martius, and the ancient observatories in Korea, Baghdad, Cairo, and Samarkand. The oldest known archaeo-astronomical device dates back to around 6000 BCE and was discovered only some twenty years ago at Nabta Playa in Egypt.

The German photographer Hans Pieler (1951–2012) dedicated himself comprehensively to these calendar buildings. In a wide-ranging photographic project spanning fifteen years, Pieler traveled the world in the search for such sites, studied them, and recorded many of them in striking photographs. His interest was focused both on the architecture and its particular coding through the respective culture as well as on the theory of photography, the allegorical image of the time. Due to Pieler’s premature death in 2012, the fascinating project remained unfinished and unpublished. This book for the first time features a selection of some one hundred of the best shots from the artist’s estate. Complemented by illuminating essays, they form a unique photographic study of these architectures and their meaning and purpose as a reflection of time in stone.

books.title: How the New Deal Was Run
books.subtitle: Reviews
books.authors: Edited by Sarah E. Igo and Ganesh Sitaraman
books.tagline: Notable historians delve into the brass tacks of launching and sustaining federal agencies.
books.description:
Critics regularly complain that the United States government can’t do big things. While their explanations differ, there is now a growing sense that American institutions are not delivering solutions to the problems of our time. The New Deal offers a striking contrast. During the 1930s, the United States created a wealth of new agencies, departments, offices, and programs—and in very short order.

This illuminating collection brings together leading American historians to offer fifteen detailed accounts of how this remarkable expansion of state capacity actually happened. From the Civilian Conservation Corps to the Rural Electrification Administration to the Securities and Exchange Commission, the authors dig into the nuts and bolts of how exactly the New Dealers did so much all at once. They detail the choices before state builders who, operating under the pressure and immediacy of the era, made decisions that held even greater consequences in the longer term.

In a time when federal agencies are under stress like never before, the contributors offer critical insights about what future administrations can learn from the New Deal’s extraordinary achievements and how they can build state capacity and deliver for Americans once again.

Features contributions by W. Tanner Allread, Mary Bridges, Brent Cebul, Sarah E. Igo, Meg Jacobs, Richard R. John, Neil M. Maher, Sharon Ann Musher, Sarah T. Phillips, Kathryn Olmsted and Eric Rauchway, Alex Platt, Jason Scott Smith, Ganesh Sitaraman, Abby Spinak, Chloe Thurston, and Mason B. Williams.

praise.q: This original book wonderfully elevates public administration and bureaucratic history to generate inventive accounts by a first-rate group of scholars. Together with the incisive framing by the editors, these essays reveal what the New Deal did, how it worked across policy subjects and agencies, and which features of state building fundamentally transformed American politics and society. In all, a fundamental contribution and a must-read for students of twentieth-century American history.
praise.by: Ira Katznelson, author of “Fear Itself”

books.title: Imaging the Universe
books.subtitle: Photography and Astronomy
books.tagline: An examination of how photographers shaped astronomy and how astronomers shaped photography, featuring both historical and contemporary images.
books.description: What does the universe look like? From daguerreotypes of the moon to colorful vistas of nebulae from space telescopes, photography and astronomy have developed hand in hand, transforming how our skies have been observed, understood, and viewed over the past two centuries. Charlotte Bigg reveals how astronomers, chemists, photographers, electronic experts, and other often forgotten individuals from different walks of life came together to develop new methods to record the light of the moon, the sun, and the stars, and to share their images with a broad audience. Featuring a wide variety of compelling images, Imaging the Universe explores the visual cultures of astrophotography and how they have shaped our visions of the cosmos.

praise.q: Since its earliest use two centuries ago, photography has had the most intimate relation with astronomy. Photos of the Moon or Mars, of remote nebulae or nearby stars, have long provided astronomers with their best means for careful observation and winning wide public fascination. This remarkably intelligent and beautifully illustrated book charts key moments in that relation, the ingenious manipulations and demanding labor that drove astronomical photography. Bigg’s compelling work demonstrates with wit and acuity how skilled judgment and cunning instruments played key roles in these vital histories of arts and sciences.
praise.by: Simon Schaffer, Darwin College, Cambridge

books.title: Instruments of Music Theory
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.tagline: Shows how musical instruments and the sounds they produce are not incidental, but an integral part of music theory.
books.description:
Many musicians dread music theory: its rules and diagrams can feel stern and lifeless, far removed from the sounds that make music so thrilling. In this book, Alexander Rehding looks at music theory from a different angle. He argues that the sound of the instruments on which music theory is demonstrated—starting with the piano in the music classroom—plays a much more active role than we usually notice. They are “instruments” in a double sense: musical noisemakers, but also tools in a kind of scientific experiment. Rehding strips these devices down to their sound-generating mechanisms to show us how to read musical instruments for their theoretical content.

Instruments of Music Theory turns our attention to instruments such as multiphonic sirens, tuning forks, Chladni plates, Aeolian harps, and Wheatstone concertinas—these devices generated sounds that called for new ways of listening, measuring, and thinking about music. Bringing together music theory, critical organology, and media theory, this book can be read as a user’s manual for how to put sound back into music theory. Rehding shows us how instruments do not only produce sound—they produce knowledge about music. Through the lens of these new instruments, Instruments of Music Theory recasts fundamental musical ideas such as pitch, harmony, form, and scale from the ground up to give new meaning to the stuff we call music.

books.title: Living with Machines | Consonance Computational Histories of the Age of Industry 1 12 Nov 2026
books.subtitle: Computational Histories of the Age of Industry
books.authors: The Living with Machines Team Edited by Ruth Ahnert, Emma Griffin, and Jon Lawrence
books.tagline: A data-driven history of the coming of the machine age in the long nineteenth century, arising from one of the largest interdisciplinary projects undertaken in the humanities.
books.description:
The world’s first industrial revolution in Britain resulted in an explosion in the creation and collection of documentary sources. Living with Machines harnesses the combined power of massive digitized historical collections, from maps to census returns, newspapers, and computational analytical tools, to examine how technology altered the very fabric of human existence on a hitherto unprecedented scale.

Collaboratively written and developed through open community review, this book features an innovative open-access edition enhanced with interactive maps, datasets, visualizations, digital notebooks, and multimedia content, including video, audio, and images. Its experimental approach uses easily reproducible methods based on open-source code and linked to publicly available datasets.

Historians will find in this book a wealth of accessible material illuminating the human, social, and cultural consequences of this historical moment. For digital humanists, cultural heritage professionals, librarians, and archivists, it is a rich example of the potential and methods of making collections available for digital scholarship. At once an exploration of the extraordinary impact of technology on humanity in the age of industry and a powerful digital artifact itself, Living with Machines is an essential text at the cutting edge of digital history.

books.title: Malady of Monoculture
books.subtitle: Pellagra, Public Health, and the Pathologies of Cotton’s Capitalism
books.tagline: How the cotton industry restricted sharecroppers’ access to nutritious food, a public health crisis that spurred a wave of influential and inspiring activism.
books.description:
Pellagra, a nutritional deficiency disease, was once widespread in the southern United States, where it was concentrated in areas of high-yield cotton production. This wasn’t a coincidence. In the early twentieth century, pellagra was ubiquitous in regions where monocultural cotton production foreclosed cotton workers’ access to nutritious foods. Planters paid sharecroppers and millworkers in their own currency—tokens, coins, and other substitutes for money—and sold them unhealthy and overpriced food in company-owned stores. Employers kept workers poor through wage theft, predatory credit systems, and labor coercion, all of which maintained a system of food scarcity.

In Malady of Monoculture , Dana Landress reveals how the unrelenting demands of the cotton economy during the Jim Crow South created a public health crisis in the form of pellagra. She carefully details a “closed food system” that restricted workers’ diets through employer-generated currency; the use of food as an instrument of labor compulsion; manufactured debt structures; alliances between government and private industry; and restrictions on foraging, gardening, and land use. Though official public health programs framed pellagra in personal and behavioral terms, those afflicted with the illness actively challenged the closed food system through union organizing, community health care, freedom farms, and collective action lawsuits. Excavating the landmark contributions of Black nutritionists to the field of public health, Landress spotlights the many constituencies that worked tirelessly to combat hunger and foregrounds their creativity, resilience, and determination.

praise.q: Malady of Monoculture is the story of cotton planters’ unmitigated greed and their unapologetic disdain for the sharecroppers who worked for them and lived in abject poverty bordering on peonage. Landress provides a new perspective on the medical condition of the sharecroppers based on the capitalist commitments of the planters and their corruption of the federal relief system designed to aid the sharecroppers following a 1927 flood. A must-read for anyone interested in twentieth-century Southern history.
praise.by: R. Douglas Hurt, author of "Agriculture in the Midwest, 1815–1900"

praise.q: Landress has written a remarkable book resurrecting pellagra from the dustbin of medical history and providing fresh insights into the workings of racial capitalism, cotton production, labor, nutrition, and civil rights. Food was a disciplinary tool used to create hunger and dependency among Black sharecroppers in the cotton economy. Malady of Monoculture uses an interdisciplinary lens to elevate the importance of Black nutritionists, dieticians, and a groundswell of local activism to combat one of the greatest public health crises of the twentieth century. This will be a rich addition to the history of medicine, southern labor history, Black politics, and food studies.
praise.by: Richard M. Mizelle Jr., author of “Backwater Blues: The Mississippi Flood of 1927 in the African American Imagination”
praise.cred: author of “Backwater Blues: The Mississippi Flood of 1927 in the African American Imagination”

books.title: Mapping the Megatext in Global Science Fiction
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.authors: Edited by Dale Knickerbocker and Bodhisattva Chattopadhyay
books.tagline: A voyage into the ever-expanding global space of science fiction ideas and works.
books.description: Science-fictional (SF) narratives help humanity to make sense of its reality and place in the universe. The twin phenomena of globalization and the emergence of new science fiction and futurism from outside the Anglophone world, and in minority languages or Indigenous societies, present a challenging yet exciting new frontier for criticism in the field. Critics can explore the relationship between such SF narratives and the different cultural realities they mediate, as well as their relationship to that storehouse of tropes, plots, themes, and images known as the SF megatext. The introduction and nine essays contained in Mapping the Megatext in Global Science Fiction take up that challenge, addressing texts by important authors from Bangladesh, the Afro-Caribbean, Syria, Hungary, Israel, Wales, Norway, Sweden, and the native Noongar peoples of Australia.

books.title: Matters of Life and Death
books.subtitle: Moral Responsibility, Care, and Dignity in Dying
books.tagline: A thoughtful examination of dignity at the end of life and the ethical limits of choice in modern medicine.
books.description:
For most of human history, death was shaped by circumstance, custom, and human presence. Today, it is increasingly mediated by medicine, law, and the language of choice. Our expanding capacity to prolong life and manage dying has outstripped the moral habits that once helped us make sense of such moments. What confronts us now is not only the question of what may be done, or what is permitted, but also how moral responsibility is borne when knowledge is partial and responsibility is dispersed.

Resisting moral certainty and procedural comfort, Stephanie O’Connor considers what is revealed and obscured when complex situations are reduced to questions of choice or rights alone. Considering dignity as a guiding moral concern at the limits of life, and drawing on healthcare ethics, case law, and contemporary debates—including those surrounding assisted dying and artificial intelligence—this book examines how decisions made under conditions of vulnerability are shaped not only by autonomy and consent, but also by dependence, unequal power, and institutional practice. Acutely attentive to the tensions that exist between compassion and restraint, as well as personal agency and shared responsibility, O’Connor does not propose solutions or offer moral closure. Instead, she asks what is owed: to those whose lives are ending, to those who care for them, and to the fragile shared moral life that binds personal decisions to their public consequences.

books.title: Medicine’s Labyrinth
books.subtitle: The Challenges of Our Treatment-Saturated Lives
books.tagline: A physician diagnoses why doctors and patients face so many uncertainties as they navigate a dizzying array of medical treatments and technologies—and lays out a treatment plan for better health care.
books.description:
Americans now depend on ever more potent drugs, devices, and procedures. While many of these interventions can improve our health and extend our lives, their widespread availability has created a medical landscape where patients make increasingly complex choices about their care.

In Medicine’s Labyrinth , physician historian Robert Aronowitz examines the challenging decisions posed by the widespread use of so many medical interventions. Drawing on medical literature, patient accounts, and historical case studies, he shows how medical progress can erode certainty, transform the illness experience, and deepen dependence on technology. To understand how these challenges have played out over the past century, Aronowitz explores medicine’s attempts to safely resuscitate premature infants, treat prostate cancer, and deal with too many disease diagnoses. He concludes with a call for physicians to pay renewed attention to patients’ lived experiences and to offer clinical judgments grounded in observations rather than algorithms.

Medicine’s Labyrinth is a clear-eyed exploration of how the very successes of modern medicine have made care harder, and why the fragile trust that sustains its institutions, policies, and practices must be rebuilt.

praise.q: Important, insightful, and provocative, Medicine’s Labyrinth recasts our understanding of sickness as situated, dynamic, and time-bound, not an unchanging entity, or a number in a disease classification. An enlightening read for anyone who thinks seriously about the practice of clinical medicine.
praise.by: Charles Rosenberg, author of “Our Present Complaint: American Medicine, Then and Now”
praise.cred: author of “Our Present Complaint: American Medicine, Then and Now”

praise.q: In Medicine’s Labyrinth , Aronowitz offers a brilliant and original assessment of the paradox of contemporary medical care: the widespread use of breakthrough technologies and medications often makes medical diagnosis and treatment more complex and uncertain, not less. Using an impressive array of historical case studies, he demonstrates that just as undertreatment leads to poor outcomes, so too can overtreatment. He argues that the intensification and complexity of contemporary medicine have the capacity to extend life, but at the same time to produce secondary effects that cause illness, suffering, and harm; in some instances, he shows how difficult it can be to determine whether symptoms are the result of the disease or the treatment. Aronowitz ultimately advocates for new and humane strategies to reduce the widening gap between cure and care.
praise.by: Allan M. Brandt, author of “The Cigarette Century: The Rise, Fall, and Deadly Persistence of the Product that Defined America”
praise.cred: author of “The Cigarette Century: The Rise, Fall, and Deadly Persistence of the Product that Defined America”

books.title: Milton Friedman and Economic Debate in the United States, 1973–1976, Vol. 3
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.tagline: The third installment in the definitive account of the famed economist’s role in economic debate—and his lasting influence on economic policy.
books.description:
Milton Friedman is widely recognized as one of the most significant contributors to economics in the modern age. Yet no previous study has distilled Friedman’s vast body of writings into an authoritative account of his research, his policy views, and his interventions in public debate. Through his sweeping series on the most influential economist of the second half of the twentieth century, Edward Nelson closes this gap: Milton Friedman and Economic Debate in the United States is the defining narrative on the famed public intellectual—the first to grapple comprehensively with Friedman’s research output, economic framework, and legacy.

Volume 3 chronicles Friedman’s activities from 1973 to 1976, encompassing his final years at the University of Chicago and a period that saw his further ascension in national prominence. In the mid-1970s, economic news dominated American political discourse as the nation endured double-digit inflation and recession. It was during this time that Friedman’s views became a center of economic debate in both the research world and public debate, while his explanation for “stagflation” formed part of the critique of stabilization policy that would lead to his 1976 Nobel Prize. Nelson details the controversies that Friedman faced in the media—including his contrarian stances on inflation’s cure, the economic implications of oil price shocks, and the social responsibility of business—and how Friedman concluded that the world needed a “new Adam Smith” to press the case for free markets. Drawing upon a large body of documentary sources, interviews with dozens of the people closest to Friedman, and his own expertise in Friedman’s research area of monetary analysis, Nelson provides the definitive account of the formative (and uneven) events in Friedman’s foray into life as a public intellectual and how his research permanently shifted economic thinking.
books.series: Milton Friedman and Economic Debate in the United States

books.title: Monochrome Multitudes
books.subtitle: Art of One Color from Albers to Zeisler
books.authors: Edited by Orianna Cacchione and Christine Mehring
books.tagline: A vividly illustrated volume tracing the monochrome as a fundamental yet expansive strategy in twentieth- and twenty-first-century art.
books.description:
Exploring a fantastic range of monochromatic artworks, Monochrome Multitudes upends traditional accounts of abstraction, revisits modernist ideas, and reveals the creative possibilities and global resonance of a seemingly reductive art form.

Bringing together examples spanning five continents, the book considers how artists such as El Anatsui, Mark Bradford, Lygia Clark, Lucio Fontana, Ellsworth Kelly, Yayoi Kusama, Kasimir Malevich, Gerhard Richter, Betye Saar, Amanda Williams, Haegue Yang, as well as little-known early cartoonists have experimented with monochrome compositions. Scholars of art history, film, music, law, disability studies, astrophysics, neurobiology, mathematics, and more reflect on monochrome artworks that build on foundational components of modernism. Together, they illuminate often overlooked cultural, political, racial, and gendered meanings of artworks; reveal the significance of materials ranging from fiber, wall paint, and videotape, to footballs, pantyhose, and candy; and engage North American art in a global dialog extending into Europe, Asia, Latin America, and Africa. Artworks are presented in monochromatic groupings—yellow, blue, white, red, gray, and black—and thematic sections trace connections across topics such as the body, the environment, urban space, sound, and media.

praise.q: Monochrome Multitudes is an exhilarating read that brings with it a groundbreaking approach to art history. A spirit of adventure suffuses every page and provides a visual and intellectual feast for any curious reader.
praise.by: Ann Temkin, Marie-Josée and Henry Kravis Chief Curator of Painting and Sculpture, MoMA
praise.cred: Marie-Josée and Henry Kravis Chief Curator of Painting and Sculpture, MoMA

praise.q: For a volume on single-color artworks, Monochrome Multitudes is quite colorful: it examines the cultural and art-historical significance of works whose artists intentionally applied limits and limitations but aims far beyond the singularity and individuality of doing so. Instead, it goes rogue, championing the cause of art-as-interdisciplinarity and inviting a collective response to modernism, offering it as a jointly global and local discourse.
praise.by: Jenni Sorkin, University of California, Santa Barbara

praise.q: Monochrome Multitudes is sure to become a prized reference for those within the fields of art history and visual studies. Readers with a more casual interest in the arts will also find it a wellspring—and revisit it again and again.
praise.by: Lynne Cooke, curator and editor of "Woven Histories: Textiles and Modern Abstraction"
praise.cred: curator and editor of "Woven Histories: Textiles and Modern Abstraction"

books.title: Of Interest to the General Public
books.subtitle: About a Coronation Cloak from Ethiopia
books.tagline: A multimedia narration inspired by the journey of an Ethiopian royal mantle to Berlin.
books.description:
The work of Maaza Mengiste draws from voices and stories that have been excluded, from gaps that seem inexplicable, from images, objects, and places that pulse with pasts unresolved. While exploring the African collections at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin, she was struck by an elaborate coronation cloak from Ethiopia on display. Inspired by the history of the 1868 British Expedition to Abyssinia (now Ethiopia) and the burning of the palace fortress at Magdala, Of Interest to the General Public uses photography and words to reimagine the journey of the royal mantle—out of battle, through fire, over mountains, to cross the waters into Berlin.

books.title: On Following
books.subtitle: Straight Lines and Infrastructural Sensibilities
books.tagline: A cross-disciplinary examination of the relation between straight lines and sensory capacities in modern art, architecture, and music.
books.description:
The human hand cannot draw a straight line, claimed nineteenth-century polymath John Ruskin. Straight lines are typically seen as incompatible with human bodies, and this is one of the reasons why their proliferation in modern art and architecture has been associated with the rational, universalist perspectives of a new industrial culture. With On Following , art historian Ina Blom traces a different genealogy of straight lines through modern and contemporary art, offering a perspective on straight-line works that addresses the close connections between the sensory capacities and experiences of human bodies and new media infrastructures. She considers what happens to aesthetic expression when bodies are surrounded by technologies that are themselves sensing systems.

Taking an expansive look at visual art, architecture, film, and music from the late nineteenth century to the present day, Blom considers practitioners including Walter De Maria, Marcel Duchamp, August Endell, Liam Gillick, Raoul Hausmann, Florian Hecker, Jenny Holzer, Ryoji Ikeda, Piero Manzoni, László Moholy-Nagy, Krzysztof Penderecki, Superstudio, Mies van der Rohe, and La Monte Young.

books.authors: Alexander von Humboldt Edited and with an Introduction by Stephen T. Jackson Translated by Philip Holt
books.tagline: The first English translation of an essay that is among Alexander von Humboldt’s least known but most important scientific works.
books.description:
In the nineteenth century, Alexander von Humboldt was arguably the world’s most famous celebrity after Napoleon. What started in 1799 as a serendipitous trip to the New World tropics with his friend Aimé Bonpland to collect plants and minerals expanded into a five-year exploration of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Mexico, and Cuba. The discoveries the two amassed were nothing short of staggering, and much of our knowledge of tropical botany, zoology, geography, and geology can be traced back to these journeys. The voyage, and the publication of Humboldt’s travel narratives and scientific studies from these expeditions, which totaled dozens of books, elevated Humboldt to cult status.

In the last two decades, Humboldt’s writings have been rediscovered in multiple fields, including biogeography; Earth and environmental sciences; American and Latin American studies; nineteenth-century art, poetry, and literature; and transatlantic cultural history. His ideas are profoundly relevant to twenty-first-century thought on the relationship between humans and nature, and the ecological framework in which he viewed the world remains essential two centuries after his travels.

Among his many interests and explorations, Humboldt invested considerable effort in explaining the underlying causes of the uneven distribution of plant species across the globe. His extended essay, On the Geographical Distribution of Plants, is among his least known but most important works, laying the foundations for the development of ecology, climatology, and evolutionary biology in the following decades. It was published originally in 1815 as an introduction to a seven-volume Latin botanical monograph, Nova Genera et Species Plantarum . The essay, republished in 1817 as a standalone volume, held great influence over nineteenth-century naturalists. It is his most comprehensive and detailed treatment of plant geography. In the essay, Humboldt applies botanical arithmetic to reveal ecological and biogeographic patterns of plants, applications that still ground modern macroecology, and provides frameworks to link vegetation patterns and climate, essential in modern Earth system science. Introduced and organized by ecologist Stephen T. Jackson and translated from Latin to English by Philip Holt, this book is essential for the libraries of scientists, historians, and all Humboldt admirers.

books.title: Paradigms and Opacity
books.subtitle: Volume One
books.description:
Stratal Optimality Theory (SOT) is a comprehensive theory of sound structure and its relation to word structure that integrates the complementary theoretical insights of lexical phonology and classical optimality theory. Paradigms and Opacity explores the many facets of SOT. Volume One focuses on constraint interaction and provides a principled solution to the problem of opacity: how, why, and when do constraints systematically apply where they apparently shouldn’t, or fail to apply where they apparently should? Analyzing evidence from a variety of languages—including English, Finnish, Arabic, Yowlumne Yokuts, Kashaya, Maltese, Dutch, Basque, Tigrinya, Spanish, and Catalan—Paul Kiparsky compares SOT with alternative theories, arguing that it is formally cleaner and makes better sense of a range of empirical phenomena.

books.title: Patchwork Ethnography
books.subtitle: A Methodological Guide
books.tagline: Offers an accessible new way to think critically and transparently about how researchers, especially those doing ethnographic work, can balance their personal commitments with long-term research.
books.description:
For ethnographers, spending a year or longer in a faraway place conducting fieldwork is becoming increasingly untenable due to competing life responsibilities and rising workloads, as well as disability, precarity, and geopolitical factors. If ethnographic methods are to remain relevant and viable for a diverse group of people in anthropology and beyond, Gökçe Günel and Chika Watanabe argue, we need to examine how our personal and professional lives intersect and shape one another.

In Patchwork Ethnography , Günel and Watanabe take seriously the conditions that render long-term fieldwork difficult for so many. Without being prescriptive, the book offers concrete ways for scholars to unpack the competing commitments in their lives and make those challenges feel more manageable. Blending theoretical analysis with practical exercises, the authors guide readers to rethink the relationship between their personal lives and their scholarship. Ultimately, they point to ways for transforming limitations into catalysts for fresh insights. By highlighting how shifting labor and living conditions profoundly alter knowledge production, Patchwork Ethnography calls for a paradigm shift in ethnographic research.
books.series: Chicago Guides to Writing, Editing, and Publishing

books.title: Playing Time
books.subtitle: Boys, Coaches, and Parents in the Battle for Minutes in Youth Basketball
books.tagline: An in-depth look at the timeless quandary of how average high school basketball players navigate their dreams of greatness with the adults who coach and support them.
books.description:
We all admire the stories of famous athletes with humble origins who rose to the top through hard work and dedication. Michael Jordan and Steph Curry, after all, both started as second-string players. But their climbs to athletic dominance call to us because they seem to prove a message we all want to believe: Anything is possible with hard work and determination. But for most people, it simply isn’t. Most of us will end up being more or less average rather than extraordinary.

In Playing Time , sociologist and sports scholar Scott N. Brooks introduces readers to young athletes who are middle-status players on their basketball teams—not the best, but not the worst—who often find themselves at odds with their coaches and teammates as they compete for playing time to show off their skills. Drawing on his extensive experience as a coach of middle and high school-age boys, Brooks invites us into the inner lives and daily experiences of kids, parents, and coaches, as players try to make sense of who they are and differentiate themselves on the court. These boys have been told by coaches, their parents, and society that hard work, effort, and attitude determine effectiveness, and Brooks reveals how that message affects them when it’s clear that their best efforts are not always enough. Middle-status boys often feel alone, alienated, socially stigmatized, and powerless to improve their fate.

By focusing on the boys stuck in the middle, Brooks uncovers essential aspects of the formative years of adolescence when kids dream of and plan for a future. As many of us will recognize our own dreams of greatness in these kids, we can all learn to support them as they build their sense of self, both on and off the court.

books.title: Reading Galileo’s Letters
books.subtitle: Experiments in Friendship, Knowledge, and Community
books.authors: Edited by Paula Findlen and Hannah Marcus
books.tagline: Essays by many of the foremost experts on Galileo offer an interdisciplinary approach to the legendary scientist’s correspondence.
books.description:
The Tuscan mathematician, physicist, and astronomer Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) is one of history’s most iconic and controversial figures. Letters form the backbone of what one early Galileo scholar called the “private Galileo,” and his correspondence is indeed a record of his family and friendships; his intellectual evolution; his professional interactions with other scientific figures; and his relations with patrons, brokers, and publishers. Last, but hardly least, his letters are a unique cultural artifact of Galileo the writer and master of vernacular prose.

Galileo’s correspondence crossed Europe in public mail pouches, through diplomatic messengers, and was written in code. Today, there are 3,272 surviving letters to or from Galileo and his many friends, family members, disciples, and rivals across Europe. This volume examines these letters as an essential aspect of Galileo’s personal and scientific career. They are what the editors call his “experiments in friendship,” which enabled, abetted, and often served as early drafts of the theories in his published works. This collaborative volume brings together different approaches, case studies, and forms of expertise—historical and literary, intellectual and material, archival and digital. It is a must-read for all Galileo enthusiasts and anyone interested in how to make the most of a rich record of correspondence.

praise.q: Reading Galileo’s Letters is a highly original volume based on the soundest scholarship. The contributors treat these famous letters not simply as sources, but as a historical question. In asking how Galileo used his correspondence, they highlight the influence of rhetorical and epistolary models, the ways scribal and material aspects of the manuscripts inform our understanding of the social realities that shaped Galileo’s research, his strategies in publishing and curating the letters and his other works, and successive interventions to this archive after his death. It is not easy to write an original book on such a well-researched subject as Galileo, but the editors and authors have succeeded.
praise.by: Filippo de Vivo, author of “Information and Communication in Venice”
praise.cred: author of “Information and Communication in Venice”

books.title: Scenes of the Avant-Garde
books.subtitle: Networks, Temporalities and Transformational Power
books.authors: Edited by Katharina Tchelidze, Julian Volz, and Beate Söntgen
books.tagline: The history of the avant-garde, told in a series of non-linear tableaus.
books.description:
This volume understands “avant-garde” as a constellation of moments, emphasizing its plural developments and its crucial interventionist role in culture and politics. Challenging the narrative of a linear avant-garde, the book sheds light on local scenes shaped by their distance from artistic practices and sociocultural conditions of their time. Scenes of the Avant-Garde brings together papers from a conference held in Tbilisi on the occasion of the centenary of the Futurist and Dadaist group H2SO4 (1924).

The contributions explore networks, relationships, and collaborations in artistic interventions. What transformational power lies in these practices? What are the gendered, social, and spatial structures, within which artistic groups test and create forms of community? And what can we learn from these overlooked or differently read stories?

The book offers new insights into avant-garde histories, drawing on case studies from countries such as Georgia, Algeria, India, Poland, Czechoslovakia, France, and the United Kingdom.

books.title: Sensitive, Problematic, Contested?
books.subtitle: Challenges and Opportunities in Dealing with Cultural Heritage in Museums
books.authors: Edited by Kunsthaus Zürich, Museum Rietberg Zürich, and Swiss National Museum
books.tagline: A necessary reckoning with the purpose and responsibility of the contemporary museum.
books.description:
The way in which museums deal with the cultural heritage they hold has increasingly become the focus of public debate. At the core is the critical examination of the histories and origins of the artifacts, as well as the reflection on traditional institutional and museum practices.

This volume brings together contributions on the topics of curating, collecting, researching, provenance, and presentation by museum practitioners, scholars from various disciplines, and artists. They explore new approaches to collecting, exhibiting, educating, and rethinking cultural heritage. Through case studies and topical essays, the book offers contemporary perspectives, pointing museums to new ways in which to deal with pressing issues such as restitution, representation, and cultural dialogue.

books.title: St Fagans Castle
books.subtitle: The Architectural and Social History of a Welsh Country House
books.tagline: The first comprehensive study of St Fagans Castle, an Elizabethan country house in Cardiff, Wales.
books.description: St Fagans Castle is significant as a grade I-listed building and has been home to St Fagans National Museum of History since 1948. The house was built by a local lawyer named Dr. John Gibbon in about 1580, and broke new ground as one of the first symmetrical country houses in Wales, influenced by the Italian Renaissance. This study takes a multi-period and cross-disciplinary approach to telling the story of St Fagans, with chapters spanning the twelfth to the twentieth century and interrelated sections on architectural history, garden history, and ownership. Key themes explored in the work include the impact of the Italian Renaissance on country houses in Wales; whether there is anything architecturally distinctive about country houses in Wales, especially compared with English country houses; the contribution of women to architectural and garden developments at St Fagans; and the colonial connection at St Fagans.

books.title: Subversive Affirmation
books.subtitle: Critique of Critique Revisited
books.authors: Sylvia Sasse Translated by Brian Alkire
books.tagline: An analysis of the concept of subversive affirmation, a radical alternative to saying “no” as a form of resistance.
books.description:
Since the 1960s, theory, the arts, and political activism have increasingly rejected the notion of resistance through negation, raising such arguments as: Doesn’t a critique based on negation make itself dependent on the very system it wants to overcome? Does it not remain trapped in a thinking of oppositions? Although coming from radically different angles, the formulation of concepts like subversive affirmation, hyperaffirmation, overidentification, paradoxical intervention, revolution of the yes, and affirmative sabotage all reflect the emergence of an affirmative critique that overcomes this negation while also making us aware of the difference between conscious consent and conformity, capitulation, indifference, or pragmatism. In her new book, Sylvia Sasse explores and analyzes subversive affirmation as a critical practice in different political systems. She examines the effectiveness of such criticism and its relevance at a time when various political actors have begun appropriating subversive affirmation and are no longer using it as a method of criticism.

books.title: Surviving Istanbul
books.subtitle: Struggles, Feasts and Calamities in the Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries
books.tagline: A fascinating exploration of everyday life in premodern Istanbul.
books.description:
In Surviving Istanbul , Suraiya Faroqhi takes the reader to seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Istanbul, with occasional forays into earlier and later periods, focusing in particular on the city’s ordinary inhabitants. From the foods eaten and the streets traversed, to the miseries endured because of recurring fires, Surviving Istanbul illustrates a city of immigrants, slaves, artisans, and rural dwellers supplying the urban markets, with all the struggles that living in (and around) the city entailed. At the same time, Faroqhi shows, the city’s relatively young population also found ways to have fun, such as celebrating at public festivals or taking a swim in a river emptying into the Bosporus. Drawing on archival and narrative sources, with particular reliance on the impressions of Evliya Çelebi (1611–about 1685), this book offers a mosaic of daily life in premodern Istanbul.

books.title: Taking Drugs in the Sun King’s Reign
books.subtitle: Reviews
books.tagline: The first full-length history of drugs during the first French Empire.
books.description:
Taking Drugs in the Sun King’s Reign is the story of how the French came to know and consume new non-European plants between 1660 and 1730, a period during which many exotic substances—like coffee, tea, cinchona bark, chocolate, and ipecacuanha—became everyday commodities. E. C. Spary treats the trajectories of these drugs as fragile complexes, made and remade by every exchange. Her book addresses well-known cases, but also drugs that never became popular in France, such as betel.

Taking Drugs is divided into three parts. The first offers a rich depiction of the world of drug-taking and drug-selling in Paris and Versailles at the outset of Louis XIV’s personal reign. The second explores features of monarchical power which explain the “drugs rush” of this period. Finally, the third offers an in-depth look at how priorities for the capture of exotic plant drugs changed within the royal naval administration. It asks how, under the conditions of early modern empires, information about drugs could be made or made trustworthy, who made it, and how it traveled. Spary shows how, over time, drugs transitioned from being natural bodies imbued with mysterious virtues to becoming calculable, replicable sources of profit. Her approach allows for new insights into how political and economic power transformed between the reigns of Louis XIV and his successor, Louis XV.

praise.q: Spary is one of the most exciting and original historians of science currently writing. Her new book, Taking Drugs in the Sun King’s Reign , focuses on the ‘drug culture’ present in France from the late seventeenth to the early eighteenth century as the country came to ingest a wide array of exotic substances of medicinal, cosmetic, dietary, recreational, and other uses. Written with flair, cogently argued and methodologically innovative, her study throws fascinating new light on the place of drugs in early modern France and on France’s place in a precociously globalizing world.
praise.by: Colin Jones, author of “The Great Nation”

books.title: The Bourbons
books.subtitle: The Sons of Saint Louis in France, Spain and Italy
books.tagline: A wide-ranging introduction to the history and legacy of one of Europe’s most influential royal families, past and present.
books.description: The Bourbon dynasty is one of Europe’s most enduring and influential royal families. This comprehensive history traces the Bourbons from their medieval origins to the twenty-first century, weaving together the lives of famous figures such as Louis XIV and Marie Antoinette with lesser-known princes, princesses, and even illegitimate offspring. Stretching across France, Spain, and Italy, the narrative highlights how Louis IX forged a dynastic identity that would shape European politics for centuries. Beyond individual biographies, Jonathan Spangler situates the dynasty within the broader political culture of early modern and modern Europe—from the War of the Spanish Succession to the French Revolution and the Italian Risorgimento—offering a richly textured account of power, family, and legacy across generations.

praise.q: A brilliant, detailed guide to over four centuries of the complex Bourbon dynasty, which ruled in Spain and Italy as well as France. Jonathan Spangler’s history, ranging from St Louis to his descendant Felipe VI, the current king of Spain, is particularly valuable for its use of international sources and accounts of impoverished cadet branches, as well as powerful monarchs.
praise.by: Philip Mansel, author of "King of the World: The Life of Louis XIV"
praise.cred: author of "King of the World: The Life of Louis XIV"

praise.q: In this highly readable and well-informed dynastic history, Spangler illuminates the ongoing importance of the Bourbon family, from its medieval origins to the court of Louis XIV and from its grounding in France to the thrones of Spain, Naples, and Parma, and eventually Brazil and Luxembourg. Spangler fruitfully integrates the concerns of cadet branches and other family members into his narrative, illuminating both continuity and change within this important dynasty.
praise.by: Hilary J. Bernstein, professor of history, University of California, Santa Barbara
praise.cred: professor of history, University of California, Santa Barbara

praise.q: Spangler’s engaging narrative of pre-modern governance on the Western flank of Europe brings into focus the complex history of the Bourbon dynasties. It invites readers to reconceptualize political history as an evolution of dynastic configurations, rather than as (more simply) one princely reign after another or a succession of the wars that consolidated realms.
praise.by: Carolyn Chappell Lougee, Stanford University

books.title: The Great Enrichment
books.subtitle: A New History of American Growth and Inequality, 1865–1945
books.tagline: A revelatory economic history of America’s Gilded Age—and how it wasn’t just the Robber Barons who benefited.
books.description:
The Gilded Age, spanning the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, was when Americans got rich. Or, rather, some Americans got rich. Because as much as the era is synonymous with staggering economic growth, it also doubles as America’s cautionary tale for the perils of leaving rich people and institutions unregulated. It was the time of extractive industrialists, worker exploitation, stifled economic mobility, and racial exclusion—lessons that the United States learned the hard way.

Vincent Geloso contests this traditional narrative by revisiting the math in this new empirical account of the Gilded Age. The Great Enrichment is an economic history of America’s rise to affluence, a period that doubled as a remarkable rise of the country’s economic floor. The conventional contrast of Robber Barons against huddled masses is, in Geloso’s analysis, unsubstantiated by economic data. The Gilded Age was the first egalitarian enrichment that humanity witnessed—a time when both rich and poor benefited in ways that were seismic, albeit unequal. Yet the net result was a great leap forward, not the lamentable birth of modern inequality.

Geloso marshals an expanded set of economic measures to account for factors not typically included in the Gilded Age economic story. The Great Enrichment sets a new standard for empirical history in one of America’s most consequential—and perhaps misunderstood—periods.
books.series: Markets and Governments in Economic History

books.title: The Logic of Rain
books.subtitle: A Unique Collection of Japanese Katagami Stencils for Dyeing Kimono Fabrics
books.tagline: A unique collection of rare Japanese katagami stencils from Dresden’s Museum of Decorative Arts.
books.description:
For 125 years, the Museum of Decorative Arts at Dresden’s Pillnitz Palace has been home to a treasure trove of Japanese craftsmanship that has remained largely unknown. It consists of ninety-two cassettes holding more than 15,000 dyeing stencils for textile printing. These katagami were used primarily for fabrics from which the kimonos of samurais were tailored. They depict geometric ornaments as well as patterns and motifs in nature handmade from mulberry bark in a lengthy process and engraved using the finest cutting techniques. Fabrics decorated with katagami prints came to Europe in the nineteenth century and soon had a strong influence on fine and applied art as well as emerging industrial design. This ancient technique remains influential today in graffiti and street art, such as in the works of celebrated street artist Banksy.

The Logic of Rain features for the first time around 140 katagami from the unique Dresden collection. This opulent book is dedicated to the representation of rain and water, which have been of major spiritual and cultural significance throughout Japan’s history. Two hundred and twenty illustrations, most presented in full color, are supplemented with essays by international scholars who explore in detail all aspects of these fascinating works of Japanese applied art.

books.title: The New Metropolis
books.subtitle: Power, Place, and Inequality in Twenty-First-Century America
books.tagline: A path-breaking investigation of changing patterns of inequality and contestation in America’s metropolises.
books.description:
Since 1990, a new political geography of winners and losers has emerged in metros across America. This new metropolis looks nothing like the old. In many exurbs, suburban mansions abut declining towns and distressed communities. In historic central cities, African American communities reel from institutional stripping, even as gentrification and immigration revitalize once forgotten neighborhoods. The New Metropolis considers why, despite all the changes over the past four decades, we have recreated a metropolis that makes it harder for low-income Americans—especially low-income Americans of color—to thrive and why some efforts to promote equitable opportunity succeed against the odds.

With a focus on Chicago, Atlanta, and Houston, The New Metropolis shows how multi-level political actors and translocal networks build power across political boundaries to determine the pool of local public resources and the scope of local powers. Weir demonstrates how the timing of urbanization set up distinct conflicts over the public sector in Frostbelt versus Sunbelt metropolises, explaining how partisan divisions now supercharge these conflicts.

The New Metropolis shows why the battle over the metropolis sits at the center of American politics. It determines the shape of the public arenas where we make decisions and, ultimately, the kinds of connections Americans have with one another.

books.title: The Universe in Thirteen Graphs
books.subtitle: Charting Cosmic Discoveries Across Space and Time
books.authors: Chris Lintott, Jeffrey Grube, and Daina Bouquin
books.tagline: See the Universe as astronomers do: These thirteen graphs distill the cutting-edge discoveries of the cosmos—from planets and stars to galaxies, to ripples in spacetime itself.
books.description:
From the front page of newspapers to your favorite t-shirt, the visual language of the cosmos is pervasive. Yet while you may have seen stunning images of planets, nebulae, and even the shadow of a black hole, pretty pictures alone cannot reveal the universe. Whether you’re looking for planets outside our solar system, searching for dark matter, listening for ripples in spacetime, or looking back to very early times, to truly understand the cosmos you need graphs.

In this fully illustrated and engaging book, astronomers Chris Lintott and Jeffrey Grube and data scientist Daina Bouquin focus on thirteen graphs to offer a tour of the major astronomical discoveries of the last century. Meet the HR diagram, which tells us about stellar lives; marvel at the Hubble diagram’s evidence for the expansion of the Universe; understand special relativity through Minkowski spacetime; and turn back time to the earliest visible light of the cosmic microwave background. With fascinating stories of discovery and accessible science for understanding ongoing debates, this book proves that while a picture may be worth a thousand words, a graph can show you the universe.

praise.q: More than just a collection of cool graphs, this is a chronicle of cosmological research, a document of how earthbound apes grasped the nature of the universe. Also, it’s a collection of really cool graphs.
praise.by: Ben Orlin, best-selling author of "Math with Bad Drawings"
praise.cred: best-selling author of "Math with Bad Drawings"

praise.q: Serious but accessible, broad-ranging but not oversimplified, and nicely weaving in the personal stories of its principal characters, The Universe in Thirteen Graphs walks a very confident narrative path through both the history and modern practice of astronomy.
praise.by: Jon Willis, author of "The Pale Blue Data Point"
praise.cred: author of "The Pale Blue Data Point"

praise.q: Lintott conducts this breezy tour with an engaging voice, a diverting sense of humor and a humble awe for the wonders of the universe.
praise.by: Marcia Bartusiak | The Wall Street Journal, on Lintott's “Accidental Astronomy”
praise.who: Marcia Bartusiak | The Wall Street Journal

praise.q: A riveting real-life Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy .
praise.by: The Telegraph, on Lintott's “Accidental Astronomy”

books.title: Uprising
books.subtitle: Brixton 1981
books.tagline: A powerful, engaged account of a pivotal moment in Black British history and antiracist struggle.
books.description: This book presents a radical, in-depth survey of the Brixton uprising of 1981 and the social inequalities and institutional racism of British politics and policing that led to it. Matt Clement situates the events of April 1981 within the long history of urban oppression and revolt in London, as well as the contemporary Caribbean struggles that shaped the consciousness of the local community. He examines how policing practices, economic marginalization, and the enduring legacy of empire produced the alienation that fueled resistance, and how Rastafarian thought articulated a powerful cultural challenge to Babylon, the name given for the evil values of society that must be resisted for justice to prevail. Bringing together historical analysis and social critique, Uprising reveals how and why Brixton fought back—and how its defiant energy helped reshape British culture, politics, and antiracist activism.

praise.q: Uprising is a gripping account that places Brixton at the center of Britain’s long history of crowd politics and resistance to racist state violence. Clement shows how this South London neighborhood illuminates the conditions that produced urban rebellions across late twentieth-century England. The result is a powerful, historically grounded narrative that connects local struggle to wider traditions of popular protest and Black-led, multiracial grassroots radical politics.
praise.by: Adam Elliott-Cooper, senior lecturer in social and public policy, Queen Mary University of London
praise.cred: senior lecturer in social and public policy, Queen Mary University of London

praise.q: This brings to life the uprisings of Black communities, placing them in the wider history of working-class resistance without diminishing their impact. For activists like me who were involved at the time, it helps us revisit and understand our own history in a new way. Detailed, accessible, and free of academic jargon, Uprising is a valuable resource for activists, social historians, and anyone wanting to understand this important part of Britain’s history and its impact.
praise.by: Leila Hassan Howe, editor, writer, antiracism activist and a founding member of Race Today Collective
praise.cred: editor, writer, antiracism activist and a founding member of Race Today Collective

subjects: Social Change, Social Movements, Political Sociology

books.title: WOJR—House of Horns
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.authors: Edited by William O'Brien Jr. and John David Todd
books.tagline: Studies WOJR’s “House of Horns,” a unique private residence outside of San Francisco.
books.description:
WOJR is an organization of designers based in Cambridge, MA who are committed to the idea of architecture as a form of cultural production, engaging the intersections of art, architecture, and urbanism. The House of Horns, a private residence located in the foothills of the Santa Cruz Mountains outside San Francisco, is the first major realized work of WOJR and represents the synthesis of core themes and ideas from the firm’s first decade of collaboration.

WOJR—House of Horns documents the built home in the form of a photographic narrative examining the central thesis of the house as a spatial and temporal instrument. Created in collaboration with architectural photographer Nick Dearden, this montage explores the house’s spaces with their characteristic horn-like forms, as they bring to life the changing light, shadow, and surrounding hillside meadow over the course of a day from dawn to dusk. In addition, a text by WOJR further reflects on the project, their process, and the discipline of architecture as a whole. Drawings, plans, sections, and elevations, as well as detailed information on the building, round off the beautiful, large-format volume.
