Despite facing near eradication in many places, gray wolves have evolved into an incredibly successful species, exhibiting wide variation in their personalities and physical features and sharing complex ties with humans. Wild Wolves takes readers inside the lives of these versatile creatures, blending stunning photography and the latest science with engaging stories about encounters with individual wolves. Written by a scientist with the groundbreaking Yellowstone Wolf Project, this is the essential illustrated natural history of wild wolves, covering everything from their inner lives and rich family ties to their hunting and feeding strategies, their parallel evolution with humankind, and their links to the domestic dog.

Provides invaluable global perspective on wild wolves, from the American Northwest and Canada to Italy, Scandinavia, and China

Illustrated throughout with superb color photos, many of them taken by the author

Sheds light on the evolution of wolves, their behavior, the social structure of wolf packs, and the conservation and future of the species

Features frequent “Wolf Stories” drawn from the author’s personal observations in the field
books.bio: Kira Cassidy is a research associate with the Yellowstone Wolf Project at Yellowstone National Park. Specializing in wolf territoriality, sociality, and behavior, she has been studying Yellowstone’s wolves for two decades.

books.title: the voice of the artist(s)
books.subtitle: another vocabulary
books.tagline: What do artists do that is different, where do they speak from, and what impact do they have beyond the exhibition wall?
books.description:
the voice of the artist(s) sets out from the premise that the artist’s voice is a primary source of knowledge. Moving beyond biography or critique, it explores artistic creation through the words, reflections, and insights of artists themselves. Based on an ongoing web-based, multimedia project (www.thevoiceoftheartist.net), this accompanying book takes the alphabet and weaves it into a polyphonic record in which artists articulate the beauty and tensions of contemporary life. It invites readers not only to look but also listen to the joy, doubt, conflict, and clarity that accompany the creative process. The core of the book comprises contributions from artists working in photography, film, dance, and performance. Each contributor was invited to responded visually to a chosen concept or word—from “Attention,” “Burden,” and “Collection,” to “Witch,” “You,” and “Zifzafa.” The outcomes reveal that artistic creation is not only a poetic or aesthetic art, but one that also produces a mode of inquiry and new knowledge. They are a gentle reminder that listening to artists can offer new ways of seeing, new sources of inspiration, and new reinterpretations from which we can all learn to imagine different possible futures.

Contributors

Noor Abed, Daniel G. Andújar, Aleksandra Aroshvili, Tekla Aslanishvili, Cecilia Bengolea, Pablo Bronstein, Ana María Caballero, Musquiqui Chihying, Marcus Coates, Lúa Coderch, Hannah Collins, Elyla, Tim Etchells, Arash Fayez, Esther Ferrer, Regina José Galindo, Lawrence Abu Hamdan, Gary Hill, Lynn Hershman Leeson, Nicole L’Huillier, Nástio Mosquito, Muntadas, Ingo Niermann, Yiannis Pappas, Olivia Plender, Ana Prvački, Ben Rivers, Ilê Sartuzi, Marta Skoczeń, Cally Spooner, Jonas Staal, Pedro Torres, Oriol Vilanova, and Abbas Zahedi.
books.bio: Gabriela Galcerán is a cultural producer working internationally with artists and platforms. In 2021 she founded The Voice of the Artist, a digital platform that invites artists to reflect on universal concerns and propose new perspectives on the world. From 2013 to 2016 she led Talking Galleries, an international platform that produces conferences and publications for the art sector. In 2017 she co-founded art\collisions, producing artist-led sessions for corporate leaders where creative problem solving, team building, and innovation are explored through artistic thinking. She has also collaborated closely with LOOP Fair and Festival, serving as Director of LOOP Fair from 2023 to 2024.

books.title: Lichens of the World
books.subtitle: A Guide to Every Family
books.tagline: A magnificently illustrated guide to the world’s extraordinary diversity of lichens
books.description:
Lichens are not autonomous organisms but a symbiotic partnership between fungi and photosynthetic algae or cyanobacteria. With more than 20,000 species found across the globe, they are an enormously successful life-form, capable of surviving in some of the harshest environments on the planet. This book provides a wide-ranging look at the 117 currently accepted families of lichen-forming fungi. The introductory section covers topics ranging from the biological structure of lichens to their lifecycle and symbiotic relationships with other organisms. This is followed by a fact-filled directory profiling at least one exemplar genus of each family and highlighting its unique characteristics. Lichens of the World is a self-contained reference for scientists, naturalists, and anyone interested in lichens.

Features hundreds of stunning full-color photos and distribution maps showcasing the variety, exquisite beauty, and diverse habitats of the world’s lichens

Sheds light on the significant ecological roles of lichens and their function as bioindicators of environmental health

Discusses the evolution, morphology, and classification of lichens, their role in ecosystems, and the conservation of lichens in the Anthropocene

Written by two leading experts

An essential guide for nature lovers everywhere
books.bio: Bibiana Moncada is professor at the Universidad Distrital in Bogotá, Colombia, and curator at the Botanical Garden and Botanical Museum of Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, where she presides over four hundred thousand lichen specimens. Robert Lücking is Head of the Department of Evolution and Biodiversity at the Botanical Garden and Botanical Museum of Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and the author (with Toby Spribille) of The Lives of Lichens (Princeton).

books.title: Lives of the Artists
books.tagline: A richly illustrated new translation of essential selections from Vasari’s masterpiece about the artists of the Italian Renaissance
books.description:
Giorgio Vasari’s seminal Lives of the Artists (1550/1568) set the foundation for art history. It established biography as a way to study artists and their work, while offering a sweeping narrative of creativity, rivalry, and genius. In this entirely new abridged and illustrated translation made for today’s readers, art historian and novelist Laura Morelli presents twenty-four of Vasari’s most important biographical portraits, including those of Giotto, Brunelleschi, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, Michelangelo, and Titian.

This beautiful edition of Vasari’s Lives features introductions, annotations, a glossary of key terms, and an index. Each biography includes the engraved portrait of the artist found in Vasari’s original text, as well as beautiful color reproductions of some of the artist’s most iconic works of painting, sculpture, and architecture—more than 80 illustrations in all.

Part history, part storytelling, and part personal reflection, Vasari’s Lives offers an intimate look at the birth of modern art and the extraordinary individuals who made it happen. With its vibrant modern translation, colorful illustrations, and insightful commentary, this edition brings Vasari’s masterpiece to life like no other edition, allowing readers to step into the world of the Italian Renaissance.
books.bio: Laura Morelli holds a PhD in art history from Yale University, where she was awarded a Mellon Doctoral Fellowship in art history and a Bass Fellowship for writing in the humanities. She has been a visiting scholar at the American Academy in Rome and an art history commentator for the History Channel. She is also a bestselling historical novelist, whose books include The Keeper of Lost Art , The Last Masterpiece , The Night Portrait , and The Gondola Maker .

books.title: Master Plan
books.subtitle: Architecture, Politics, and Power
books.tagline: How postwar architects asserted American soft power, development, and diplomacy through master planning
books.description:
After the Second World War, American architects were frequently called upon to design master plans at many scales for public and private clients. Functions ranged from sprawling campuses and resorts to airports, embassies, office complexes, factories, and even entire neighborhoods. This book provides the first in-depth history of this seemingly routine project type, exploring how these proposals were leveraged for social, political, and economic gain during a critical period of rising Cold War tensions at home and abroad.

Drawing on original archival research into dozens of familiar and newly recovered projects across the United States and around the world, Michael Abrahamson and Joss Kiely offer an unprecedented look at the era of the master plan. Spanning the years 1945 to 1975, when the practice flourished, they highlight unpublished materials and lesser-known projects by some of the biggest names in modern architecture, including Skidmore, Owings, and Merrill; Minoru Yamasaki; Gunnar Birkerts; Harrison and Abramovitz; and Edward Larrabee Barnes. They examine designs by women and minority architects who have long been marginalized, such as J. Max Bond Jr., Chloethiel Woodard Smith, and Blanche Lemco van Ginkel.

Beautifully illustrated, Master Plan shares new perspectives on famous—and infamous—works of large-scale architecture and planning, revealing how America’s postwar architects concealed political and economic agendas within the seductive visual language of concrete, glass, and steel.
books.bio: Michael Abrahamson is assistant professor of architecture at the University of Utah. His work has appeared in publications such as The Architectural Review , The Sunday Times , and the Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians . Joss Kiely is associate professor in the School of Architecture and Interior Design at the University of Cincinnati. His work has appeared in publications such as Fabrications , Arris , and the Journal of Architectural Education .

praise.q: An ambitious, sweeping examination of the master plan, a document so common in the postwar United States that it has eluded full investigation until now. This book convincingly illustrates the power of these visions of the future, revealing them as perpetually incomplete and thus profoundly influential from the home to the beach to the factory to the city.
praise.by: Brian D. Goldstein, author of Max Bond: The Life and Work of the People’s Architect
praise.cred: author of Max Bond: The Life and Work of the People’s Architect

praise.q: Master Plan is a timely reminder of architecture’s ability to imagine the world anew. Focusing on the decades after World War II, Abrahamson and Kiely highlight the efforts by architects to design for democracy even as citizens, activists, politicians, and power brokers hotly debated how a democratic society should function and whom it should serve.
praise.by: Gabrielle Esperdy, author of Modernizing Main Street: Architecture and Consumer Culture in the New Deal
praise.cred: author of Modernizing Main Street: Architecture and Consumer Culture in the New Deal

praise.q: Master Plan takes a synthetic view—as any master plan should—and introduces a vivid new perspective on architecture and planning in the twentieth century. This rigorous historical interpretation will be a critical reference that will influence future studies of the built and unbuilt legacies of the period.
praise.by: Timothy Hyde, author of Ugliness and Judgment: On Architecture in the Public Eye
praise.cred: author of Ugliness and Judgment: On Architecture in the Public Eye

books.title: Mathematics Is Not a Spectator Sport
books.subtitle: 10 Topics to Challenge and Engage
books.tagline: An exploration of ten intriguing areas of mathematics, from prime numbers and graph theory to fractals and knots
books.description:
This engaging book invites readers to dive into ten intriguing topics often left out of the standard curriculum yet essential to the mathematical enterprise. It guides the mathematically curious—undergraduates emerging from their comfort zones, high school students bored by what they are taught in math classes, general readers hungry for a challenge—through concepts and problems that encourage the active, hands-on learning that leads to real understanding. In ten chapters, readers meet prime numbers, graph theory, Pick’s Theorem, continued fractions, curves of constant diameter, computer logic, projective geometry and perspective, fractals, knots and links, and catastrophe theory, including the broader mathematical and historical setting. Along the way, they build their cognitive toolkit, encountering such ideas as theorem, proof, and algorithm organically and in context. Each chapter includes two problem sets, with answers provided in a final chapter.

The authors, both prominent educators and mathematicians, invite readers to think deeply about the problems they investigate and to enjoy the process of searching for solutions.
books.bio: Ian Stewart is emeritus professor of mathematics at the University of Warwick and a Fellow of the Royal Society. Author of more than 140 books and 230 research papers, he wrote Scientific American ’s “Mathematical Recreations” column for twelve years. David Wood is reader at the University of Warwick’s Mathematics Institute, where he was director of undergraduate studies for more than twenty years. During that time he was both a practitioner and consultant with Warwick’s National Academy for Gifted and Talented Youth (NAGTY) and the International Gateway for Gifted Youth (IGGY).

praise.q: Stewart and Wood prove how mathematics can be for everyone. In ten well-chosen topics, their clear and engaging writing will take eager readers of any age to an understanding of some of the riches of mathematics.
praise.by: John McCleary, Vassar College

books.title: Megalodon and Other Prehistoric Sharks
books.tagline: A state-of-the-art look at prehistoric sharks—bringing together the latest discoveries with stunning, full-color reconstructions of diverse species
books.description:
Sharks have ruled the oceans for more than four hundred million years, with an evolutionary tree that includes an astonishing variety of creatures, from the streamlined Devonian Cladoselache and the bizarre spiral-toothed Helicoprion to the awe-inspiring Megalodon . This book blends cutting-edge science with striking visuals to show how new scanning and imaging techniques reveal hidden details of soft tissues and body structures previously lost to time. Marvelously illustrated with fossil photographs alongside dramatic paleoart reconstructions by acclaimed illustrator Gabriel Ugueto, Megalodon and Other Prehistoric Sharks brings to life the diversity and strangeness of these ancient hunters.

Covers dozens of representative species and groups

Features newly commissioned paleoart that showcases the incredible variety of body shapes and behaviors in shark evolutionary history

Reveals how innovative CT scanning techniques and 3D modeling provide an entirely new understanding of prehistoric sharks

Discusses shark diversity, sharks in the fossil record, paleoecology, behavior, and more

Takes readers from the Devonian to the present day
books.bio: Jack Cooper is an internationally recognized expert on shark biology and paleobiology who is regularly consulted by museums and for books and documentaries. His work has been featured widely in the media, including on TV and in publications such as The Guardian . Gabriel Ugueto is a versatile graphic artist and illustrator whose paleoart has appeared in numerous books and publications, including National Geographic and BBC Science Focus .

books.title: Performance and Contradiction
books.tagline: A transformative history of the explosion of performance in both art and theory in 1970s America
books.description:
In the 1970s, something called “performance” was everywhere, cast as an innovative form of artistic practice and a burgeoning field of scholarly analysis. Yet it was impossible to define and subject to vociferous debate. Why was the decade a watershed era for performance and why were its discourses so roiled with conflict? In this richly illustrated new history, Catherine Quan Damman argues that the answer lies in the powerful ways artists used performance to theorize the emerging social contradictions of their time.

Though it has often been claimed that performance eludes commodification, Performance and Contradiction offers a major rethinking of the ways performance is enmeshed in historically specific capitalist logics. As the growing service sector’s sharp rise in waged affective labor collided with longstanding expectations of gendered naturalness and racialized authenticity, artists mobilized performance as a singular means to explore the socially compelled management of pretense.

Drawing on original archival research, Performance and Contradiction highlights the work of important but understudied figures, including Rosemary Mayer, Sheryl Sutton, Julia Heyward, Anthony Ramos, and the collective The Waitresses, placing them in dialogue with Laurie Anderson, Vito Acconci, Dan Graham, Allan Kaprow, Adrian Piper, Yvonne Rainer, Robert Wilson, and others. Treating performance as a pliable, capacious register, the book locates its subject in a range of formats. Indeed, as the book reveals, performance’s refusal of easy definition or tidy categorization is precisely what makes it a generative form for the critique of authenticity, authorship, and political economy.
books.bio: Catherine Quan Damman is an art historian and critic. She holds the Valeria Napoleone Linda Nochlin Professorship at the Institute of Fine Arts at New York University, where she is assistant professor of modern and contemporary art.

books.title: Perilous Passages
books.subtitle: Black Infant Death in America
books.tagline: From the final decades of US slavery to the present, a powerful and illuminating history of a profound inequity: the special burden of infant care and loss experienced by Black women.
books.description:
In the United States, Black infants are far less likely than white infants to survive their first year of life. Underlying this predicament is a history of profound loss and persistent striving, which has durably shaped Black life in America. Following generations of mothers, caregivers, laborers, and activists from the final decades of slavery to the present, Perilous Passages chronicles the intimate practices and collective strategies Black communities created and relied upon to sustain early life threatened by disease, inadequate medical care, and racialized harm.

Perilous Passages examines nineteenth-century domestic care practices that carried families through the violence of slavery and war, and traces Black eugenic ideas, the efforts of various grassroots movements, and myths and realities surrounding the 1980s panic over “crack babies.” Health professionals, legal officials, and scientific experts exerted pressure, sometimes directly—as in antimidwifery campaigns—and sometimes more subtly, through life insurance practices that devalued Black life. Wangui Muigai shows that at every turn, authorities recast infant deaths as the fault of Black women, with ongoing impact on birthing experiences and outcomes. Still, Black women and their communities have always done more than bear loss. They have produced vital knowledge about its causes, trained in specialized care, developed networks of cradle-to-grave support, and organized to reform society in ways that safeguard children.

Centering Black women’s experiences, Perilous Passages insists on visceral confrontation with the deadliness of American racism while also offering a powerful account of what makes life possible.
books.bio: Wangui Muigai is Assistant Professor of African and African American Studies and History at Brandeis University. An Andrew Carnegie Fellow, she has been awarded the Pressman-Burroughs Wellcome Fund Award and the Shryock Medal from the American Association for the History of Medicine for her work on race and health.

praise.q: An essential work of American history. Muigai beautifully traces the tenderness of Black mothers and their communities as they faced the pain of infant death, showing how progressive public health reforms, time and again, led to new modes of policing while also fueling Black women’s health activism.

In this imaginatively researched and beautifully written book, Wangui Muigai provides an indispensable revision of existing histories of infant mortality in the United States. She offers a bottom-up history of the structural inequality that has contributed to racial disparities in infant mortality rates and the dogged efforts of Black communities, and especially women, to safeguard infants’ health and give them dignity in death. This is an emotionally fraught history written with care and grace. A must-read for anyone interested in the intersecting histories of African American women, the Black family, medicine, and public health.

Wangui Muigai has written a haunting tribute to Black mothers who have experienced infant loss, offering a compelling human story that is more than just tragic or triumphant. Perilous Passages describes the human toll that medical racism wrought on Black people and the loving resistance Black people created to save their children's lives.

books.title: The Impeachment Power
books.subtitle: The Law, Politics, and Purpose of an Extraordinary Constitutional Tool
books.tagline: An essential primer on impeachment for today’s divided public square
books.description:
We are witnessing an unprecedented moment in American politics in which impeachments are increasingly common. In today’s partisan environment, it is more vital than ever that government officials, scholars, and ordinary citizens understand what an impeachment can reasonably be expected to accomplish. In this incisive and accessible book, Keith Whittington provides needed clarity on the constitutional power of impeachment, explaining why it exists and how it should be used to preserve American democracy.

Drawing insights from American and British history, congressional practice, and the language of the Constitution itself, Whittington shows how impeachment is a tool for checking abuses of elective office and defending constitutional norms. While we have come to associate impeachment with the presidency, it can be used to remedy gross misconduct by an array of officers of the federal government. Whittington cautions against abusing this immense and consequential power to settle political scores, demonstrating how it undermines the independence of the branches and makes Congress the seat of political power.

Required reading for the informed citizen, The Impeachment Power argues that impeachment is ultimately a political instrument and gives us the perspective we need to recognize when an impeachment might be useful and when we are better served by looking for alternative ways to solve our political problems.
books.bio: Keith E. Whittington is the David Boies Professor of Law at Yale Law School and a visiting fellow at the Hoover Institution. His books include Speak Freely: Why Universities Must Defend Free Speech and Political Foundations of Judicial Supremacy: The Presidency, the Supreme Court, and Constitutional Leadership in U.S. History (both Princeton).

praise.q: Timely. . . . Written with a commendably cool head, Whittington’s book will be a key guide for legal experts as well as lay readers.
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews

praise.q: [A] very engaging work. . . . Highly recommended for any reader interested in American government and politics.
praise.by: Library Journal

praise.q: [ The Impeachment Power ] is a balanced examination of a sensitive topic written in nontechnical language for the general reader.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: A truly exceptional contribution to the literature on impeachment. Whittington shows how impeachment is indeed about politics, but it must be a high constitutional politics that calls on elected officials to exercise the responsible judgment on which the health of democratic institutions ultimately depends. There is no doubt that this indispensable treatment of the subject will, as it should, find a wide audience in the nation’s capital and beyond.
praise.by: Bob Bauer, author of The Unraveling: Reflections on Politics without Ethics and Democracy in Crisis
praise.cred: author of The Unraveling: Reflections on Politics without Ethics and Democracy in Crisis

praise.q: As presidential impeachments descend to the realm of normal politics, many Americans are asking what impeachments are really for and how they work. This is the perfect book to answer those questions: nonpartisan, historically informed, reliable, and readable. Keith Whittington has done the country a favor.
praise.by: Michael W. McConnell, author of The President Who Would Not Be King: Executive Power under the Constitution
praise.cred: author of The President Who Would Not Be King: Executive Power under the Constitution

praise.q: A timely and penetrating treatment of the impeachment power in the United States from one of the nation’s foremost legal minds. Keith Whittington synthesizes the long history and rivaling rationales into a comprehensive new look at this extraordinary power. Essential reading for anyone interested in impeachment theory and practice.
praise.by: Jonathan Turley, The George Washington University Law School
praise.cred: The George Washington University Law School

books.title: The Qur’an, Surahs 1–2
books.subtitle: A Historical and Literary Commentary
books.tagline: A detailed commentary with a new translation that integrates intertextual, theological, literary, and historical perspectives
books.description:
This historical and literary commentary on the Qur’an’s first two surahs provides a structural analysis of the two texts, advances a novel theory of Surah 2’s intricate redactional history, contextualizes the Qur’an among writings from the Biblical tradition, and considers a variety of other textual, linguistic, and theological issues. It offers the first comprehensive historical and literary commentary in English on Surah 2, the longest and most complex Qur’anic text. Both surahs have been newly translated by the author.

Surahs 1 (Sūrat al-Fātiḥah, “The Opening”) and 2 (Sūrat al-Baqarah, “The Cow”) discuss such important theological notions as divine testing and divine foreknowledge; offer narratives about Adam, Abraham, Saul, and other figures; include polemics against Jews and Christians; and issue legislative commandments, with an emphasis on those relating to marriage and divorce. Building on his previous work, Key Terms of the Qur’an , Nicolai Sinai begins each surah commentary with an introductory overview, and then proceeds to a verse-by-verse exegesis. He pays particular attention to inner-Qur’anic parallels and doublets and to the resulting questions of textual chronology. Sinai’s commentaries make selective use of interpretive resources found in premodern Islamic Qur’an scholarship. Short summaries follow the detailed exegetical treatment of each surah.

The Qur’an, like the Bible, is a sophisticated work of literature that employs artful compositional techniques. This volume offers an original exploration of what the Qur’an might have meant to its first readers and how the Qur’an draws on, engages with, and diverges from ideas, narratives, and literary forms that may have informed it. The book will be an indispensable resource for scholars of Islam and Qur’anic studies.
books.bio: Nicolai Sinai is professor of Islamic studies at the University of Oxford and holder of the Sheikh Zayed Lecturership in Islamic Studies. He is the author of Key Terms of the Qur’an: A Critical Dictionary (Princeton) and The Qur’an: A Historical-Critical Introduction .

praise.q: This is a truly impressive piece of original scholarship. The author synthesizes and builds on his own extensive scholarly oeuvre as well as drawing on a rich selection of other work. The choice to structure the book as a verse-by-verse (or sometimes phrase-by-phrase) commentary is a bold and generative one. Throughout, the systematic attention to contextual meaning and to the interrelationships between parallel or echoing passages is beautifully clear and illuminating.
praise.by: Marion Katz, New York University

praise.q: This commentary provides a wealth of significant scholarship with careful and insightful judgments throughout. It engages modern Western scholarship and pays significant attention to premodern Muslim exegesis. I think all serious readers of the Qur’an will find it instructive and helpful. I learned a great deal from it.
praise.by: Michael Graves, Wheaton College (Illinois)

books.title: The Underground Atlas of Fungi
books.subtitle: Exploring the Hidden World of Mycelia and Mushrooms
books.tagline: A stunningly illustrated look at the tangled fungal web at the heart of our planet’s habitats
books.description:
Mushrooms are a familiar sight in nature, but they are just the temporary outgrowths of a hidden, weblike network of microscopic threads called mycelia. These underground fungal networks connect plants and fungi in a mutually beneficial partnership that helps sustain diverse ecosystems across the globe. Whether as mutuals, saprobes, or parasites, fungi are critical to global ecosystem function. The Underground Atlas of Fungi brings together a world-class team of experts to explore a wide range of environments—from forests and deserts to the poles and under the sea—to reveal how these crucially important systems work. Showcasing the latest findings in this exciting and fast-evolving area of research, backed with fascinating maps and infographics, The Underground Atlas of Fungi is the ultimate guide to the vast and mysterious fungal world beneath our feet and across the landscape.

Features a wealth of state-of-the-art maps and infographics

Spans ecosystems and biomes around the world

Looks at fungi in boreal and tropical forests, in the tundra, under the sea, and in coastal and fresh waters

Sheds needed light on the future of these fungal communities in the Anthropocene

An essential resource for mycologists and anyone interested in fungi
books.bio: Donald H. Pfister is the Asa Gray Professor of Systematic Botany Emeritus at Harvard University, where he is curator emeritus of the Farlow Library and Herbarium and a former director of the Harvard University Herbaria.

books.title: African Objects and the Fetish at Work in Early Modern Art History
books.series: Clark Studies in the Visual Arts
books.tagline: A study of how African objects shaped Western concepts of art, aesthetics, and value, and informed the foundations of art history
books.description:
While the central role of African art, objects, and rituals in shaping twentieth-century art history has been widely recognized, the longer genealogy of this influence remains an ongoing area of inquiry. This collection of essays examines how European encounters with African objects from the sixteenth century onward reshaped concepts of art, aesthetics, economics, and value during the age of colonial expansion. Drawing on archival, literary, and material sources—from travel literature and judicial proceedings to sales catalogues and museum collections—these essays reveal how African objects, often described as “fetishes,” were central to the emergence of art history as a discipline.

Distributed for the Clark Art Institute
books.bio: Anne Lafont is an art historian and professor at the École des hautes études en sciences sociales in Paris.
subjects: Clark Studies in the Visual Arts

books.title: C. G. Jung: The Critical Edition, Volume 1 (1896–1900)
books.subtitle: Student Years in Basel: Philosophy, Medicine, Science, and Spiritualism
books.authors: C. G. Jung, Caitlin Stephens, Gaia Domenici, Sonu Shamdasani
books.tagline: An authoritative new translation of Jung’s writings from his student years Featuring extensive original commentary as well as diary excerpts and other rare materials published here for the first time
books.description:
As a medical student at the University of Basel, C. G. Jung was a member of the Zofingia Society, a student fraternity, becoming president of the Basel section in the winter semester 1897–1898. Between 1896 and 1899, he delivered four lectures there, addressing empirical psychology, natural science, philosophy, spiritualism, metaphysics, and religion—topics that anticipate and illuminate his later work. In these early writings, Jung wrestles with the tension between scientific materialism and his religious-metaphysical interests, criticizing reductionist views in the sciences while still insisting on scientific method. He argues for a life principle irreducible to matter that would enable the possibility of the postmortem existence of the soul.

This volume presents Jung’s lectures together with the discussions that followed. It also includes transcripts of several of his sittings with his cousin Helene Preiswerk, material he later used for his medical dissertation. Beginning in 1898, Jung kept a personal diary; the volume offers excerpts in which he continues to reflect on philosophical, literary, and religious issues—including the aesthetics of music—together with an unpublished piece on Tolstoy’s Resurrection . Also included are philosophical notes he began compiling around 1897, portions of which continued in his diary, as well as a reading list with comments prepared for his Zofingia lectures. Two papers he wrote for his medical curriculum—on wound infection and pellagra—are likewise reproduced.

The Critical Edition of the Works of C. G. Jung is a monumental, multiyear publishing initiative that introduces Jung’s writings to a new generation of readers in a vibrant new English translation. Each volume features an in-depth historical introduction, informative annotations that draw on Jung’s unpublished correspondence, a detailed chronology, and variorum presentations of works that went through multiple editions.
books.bio: C. G. Jung (1875–1961) was one of the most important psychologists of the twentieth century and the founder of analytical psychology. Gaia Domenici is the author of Jung’s Nietzsche: Zarathustra, The Red Book, and “Visionary” Works and managing editor of Phanês: Journal for Jung History . Caitlin Stephens is a Jungian analyst-in-training and the translator of Jung on Ignatius of Loyola’s “Spiritual Exercises” (Princeton). Astrid Freuler is an independent professional translator.
books.series: The Critical Edition of the Works of C. G. Jung

books.title: Dear Reddit, Am I the Asshole?
books.subtitle: Our New Era of Advice
books.tagline: A lively and often hilarious exploration of Reddit—and how it is transforming the advice genre, usurping traditional columnists, and training our future AI advisors.
books.description:
From the Athenian Mercury of 1691 to “Dear Beatrice Fairfax” in 1898 to present-day subreddits, the history of the advice genre is a vast and varied chronicle. The genre is a public spectacle of personal conundrums aired for entertainment and the practice of folk ethics. In Dear Reddit, Am I the Asshole? , Joseph Reagle offers a delightful and deeply researched exploration of Reddit’s advice subreddits within the long history of the advice genre.

Once constrained by the newspaper’s narrow, vertical column, the advice genre now sprawls across the internet, where no such boundaries exist. And while both print and online advice venues support disclosure, suggestion, judgment, and their continued discussion, only online forums can specialize in function and topic.

This book discusses Reddit’s unique aspects and contributions to the genre, including historical reversals, such as users hacking Reddit so they could ask questions of one another, as well as its novelty: whereas traditional advice columnists kept their lives private, anonymous commenters online will have faced the same issue as the querist, have professional expertise, or both. Finally, the author speculates about how AI will change the landscape of the advice to come, as Reddit’s user-generated content is being used to train the AI advisors of our future.
books.bio: Joseph M. Reagle, Jr. is Associate Professor of Communication Studies at Northeastern University. His books include Wikipedia @ 20 , Hacking Life, Reading the Comments, and Good Faith Collaboration, all published by the MIT Press. A former resident fellow at the Berkman Klein Center at Harvard (in 1998 and 2010), he was also a Research Engineer at MIT’s Lab for Computer Science, where he served as an author and working group chair within the IETF and W3C on digital security, privacy, and Internet policy.

books.title: Digital Paradoxes
books.subtitle: Technological Promises and Educational Realities in Egypt
books.tagline: An exploration of the contradictions between technological promises and educational realities in Egyptian education.
books.description:
Digital Paradoxes is an inquiry into the realities of digital technologies in Egyptian education. Hany Zayed explores what actually happens when a constellation of digital technologies is inserted deep into an educational system with a long historical lineage, in a complex social milieu, amid a disruptive global pandemic, with the promise of transforming education. Using the case of the “digital transformation” of secondary education in Egypt, the book shows how digital technologies produce paradoxes in education—contradictions between technological promises and educational realities—on the levels of institutions like public schooling and private tutoring, processes like learning and assessment, and practices like resistance and refusal.

The author argues that the digital transformation of Egyptian education resulted in five key paradoxes. First, as opposed to fortifying public schooling and stemming private tutoring, digitalization weakened public schooling and created novel forms of private tutoring. Second, against an individualized ethos of self-directed learning, digitalization gave rise to learning communities encased in a social identity and imbued with a collaborative ethic. Third, instead of eliminating examination cheating, digital technologies afforded a new modality of collective cheating with an unprecedented scale and speed. Fourth, in contrast to ensuring educational control, technologies facilitated bottom-up resistance practices against the top-down educational change. Finally, rather than leveling the playing field, digitalization exacerbated inequalities based on class, geography, gender, and citizenship status.
books.bio: Hany Zayed is Assistant Professor of Sociology at Marquette University. Born and raised in Cairo, Egypt, he holds a PhD in Sociology from the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign.

books.title: Gainsborough and Reynolds
books.subtitle: The Art of Rivalry in Georgian London
books.tagline: When two ambitious young Englishmen arrive in the metropolis, their rivalry changes the course of Western Art
books.description:
Thomas Gainsborough (1727-88) and Joshua Reynolds (1723-92) were viewed as bitter rivals throughout their lifetimes and beyond. Despite similar upbringings in English counties far from the capital, they had completely different characters, opposing attitudes to life and art, and distinct career paths. Even when neighbours in London they were rarely seen in the same room at the same time, to the bewilderment of mutual friends and professional colleagues. Their common ground was the Royal Academy of Arts, of which Reynolds was founding president, with its annual showcase of contemporary art as the crucible of their shared competitiveness and personal animosity.

For the first time, three hundred years since they were born and with the Gainsborough tercentenary imminent, Jacqueline Riding explores the lives, loves and loathing of these two formidable artists side-by-side and in the round: venturing behind the closed doors of home and studio, alongside the hallowed halls of the Royal Academy and the civic and public realms. Structured around significant episodes and themes, she paints a vibrant double portrait that is fresh, captivating and surprising.
books.bio: Dr Jacqueline Riding specialises in eighteenth- and nineteenth century British history and art. She is author of Jacobites: A New History of the ’45 Rebellion (Bloomsbury, 2016), Peterloo: The Story of the Manchester Massacre (Head of Zeus, 2018), Hogarth: Life in Progress (Profile, 2021) the Sunday Times Art Book of the Year, and Hard Streets: Working-Class Lives in Charlie Chaplin’s London (Profile, 2026).

books.title: Good and Evil
books.subtitle: A Dialectical Ethics
books.tagline: An agenda-setting account of the foundation of ethics that brings together Aristotle, Kant, Hegel, analytic metaethics, and existential thought.
books.description:
The meaning of the good is the oldest problem in moral philosophy. A pathbreaking work, Good and Evil: A Dialectical Ethics bridges analytic and continental traditions to provide a novel, systematic account of the good that is the formal object of practical knowledge: that which we aim for when we consider the question of how it is good to live.

To elucidate his notion of the good—and its opposite, evil—Sebastian Rödl criticizes some of the most prominent metaethical theories of the last half century. He argues that the answer to the question of how we should live cannot be found in nature, as Aristotelean ethical naturalists such as G. E. M. Anscombe, Philippa Foot, and Michael Thompson would have it. Thus, any attempt to naturalize ethics will fail. He argues that the principle of living well is not to be found in the mutual recognition of individuals or communities as free and equal, as suggested by Stephen Darwall and Axel Honneth. And finally, Rödl argues that the foundation of ethics is not to be found in the Kantian claim that each of us is conscious of an unconditional law that is not externally imposed but that instead inheres in ourselves, as Christine Korsgaard has argued.

Rather, in what amounts to a new fundamental theory that he names dialectical ethics, Rödl somewhat unexpectedly turns to the existential thought of figures such as Martin Buber, Emmanual Levinas, and Simone Weil to argue that the foundation of ethics lies in the unilateral and absolute demand that others place upon us. And, he explains, we relate to the good of practical knowledge as we relate to a gift. Ambitious and compelling, Good and Evil is a landmark work of post-Kantian metaethics.
books.bio: Sebastian Rödl, University Professor of Philosophy at Leipzig University, is the author of Self-Consciousness and Objectivity, Categories of the Temporal, and Self-Consciousness .

praise.q: Extraordinary. A radical redescription of practical philosophy that imaginatively deploys concepts from a rich tradition, especially Aristotle and German Idealism, to articulate anew the nature of evil and the significance of forgiveness.

This remarkable book by Sebastian Rödl about good and evil is, in the deepest sense, thought-provoking. The thinking that it provokes is, however, not moral theorizing but rather a logical investigation of the knowledge of good and evil that each of us already has. Indeed, it is an investigation that exposes moral theorizing as, at best, nonsense and, at worst, a guise of evil. Here the reader will find absolute idealist philosophy at its finest: rigorous, transformative, and utterly fearless.

Sebastian Rödl’s new book concerns practical knowledge, knowledge of good and evil. Strikingly, it offers no theory but translates this knowledge into practical philosophy in a highly illuminating revival of old ideas. It steps beyond naturalistic and Kantian accounts but not to any opposing supernaturalism or particularism. Transcending such oppositions, it expounds the good as the absolute, at once individual and universal, and human life as spiritual life, unfolding in three moments: right, conscience, and the gift of life.

In Good and Evil , Sebastian Rödl attempts to rethink the very foundations of ethics using the methods of classical German Idealism. The result is a genuinely systematic picture of practical philosophy that demonstrates the often profound ways the German Idealist tradition continues to be relevant to contemporary ethical thought.

Good and Evil is an epoch-making work of philosophy: accessible, profound, and ambitious in scope. Its central provocation—that ethical life does not unfold within the natural order—poses a bold challenge both to philosophy and to a culture increasingly inclined to seek ethical guidance from the natural sciences. It also constitutes a break with the Aristotelian-inspired naturalism of so much recent ‘analytic German Idealism,’ and toward figures rarely heard from in this movement: for example, Weil and Løgstrop. It would be difficult to overstate the importance and originality of this book.

books.title: Hosea
books.subtitle: A New Translation with Introduction and Commentary
books.tagline: A new translation and commentary on the book of Hosea that invites readers into its rich literary universe
books.description:
The book of Hosea has traditionally been interpreted through the lens of its first three chapters, which employ the metaphor of marriage to describe the relationship between God and Israel. But the book’s symbolic landscape is replete with metaphors: lions and lambs, doves and vultures, spouses and children, ovens and cakes, dew and rain, vines and olive trees, and many more. Hosea features visions of reconciliation and restoration, but also unsettling depictions of cruelty and devastation, including recurring images of God as a fierce enemy of his own people.

In this new translation and commentary, Göran Eidevall invites readers to approach Hosea as a fascinating collection of diverse prophetic poetry. Paying particular attention to themes and metaphors in chapters 4–14, which have traditionally been underemphasized, Eidevall argues that unlike other prophetic books, Hosea is focused on the destiny of Ephraim, rather than Zion. With an extensive introduction that explores Hosea’s composition, major themes, reception history, and more, including new insights offered by trauma theory, this commentary is an indispensable guide to this key prophetic text.
books.bio: Göran Eidevall is Professor Emeritus of Old Testament in the Department of Theology at Uppsala University. He is the author of numerous books on prophetic literature, including the Anchor commentary on the book of Amos.

books.title: Intraterrestrials
books.subtitle: Discovering the Strangest Life on Earth
books.tagline: A biologist’s firsthand account of encounters with the planet’s most bizarre organisms—and how these discoveries are challenging our most basic assumptions about life on Earth
books.description:
Life thrives in the deepest, darkest recesses of Earth’s crust—from methane seeps in the ocean floor to the highest reaches of Arctic permafrost—and it is unlike anything seen on the surface. Intraterrestrials shares what scientists are learning about these strange types of microbial life—and how research expeditions to some of the most extreme locales on the planet are broadening our understanding of what life is and how its earliest forms may have evolved.

Drawing on her experiences and those of her fellow scientists working in challenging and often dangerous conditions, Karen Lloyd takes readers on an adventure from the bottom of the ocean through the jungles of Central America to the high-altitude volcanoes of the Andes. Only discovered in recent decades, “intraterrestrials”—subsurface beings that are truly alien—are demonstrating how life can exist in boiling water, pure acid, and bleach. They enable us to peer back to the very dawn of life on Earth, disclosing deep branches on the tree of life that push the limits of what we thought possible. Some can “breathe” rocks or even electrons. Others may live for hundreds of thousands of years or longer. All of them are living in ways that are totally foreign to us surface dwellers.

Blending captivating storytelling with the latest science, Intraterrestrials reveals what microbes in Earth’s deep subsurface biosphere can tell us about the prospects for finding life on other planets—and the future of life on our own.
books.bio: Karen G. Lloyd is the Wrigley Chair in Environmental Studies and Professor of Earth Sciences at the University of Southern California. Her work has appeared in leading publications such as Nature and Science .

praise.q: Lloyd is one of those rare gifted writers who can be as broadly profound as she is precise, able to make science both come raucously alive and resonate with meaning. She does this via perfect metaphors, an effortless wit, and a massively infectious enthusiasm for the outsize significance of her very small subjects. This science book is, furthermore, part adventure story, as she travels to the ends of the earth to pursue her small subjects, and generally bears witness to 'the shocking enormity of what we have been missing about life on Earth.’
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews (starred review)

praise.q: Lloyd, an environmental studies professor at the University of Southern California, debuts with an astonishing study of the remarkable microorganisms that thrive in the 'subsurface biosphere.' . . . Filled with mind-blowing trivia that will change how readers think about life on Earth, this captivates.
praise.by: Publishers Weekly (starred review)

praise.q: At a beach-bag-friendly 200 pages or so, this lively and compulsively engaging book is an unusual page-turner. Lloyd, a geomicrobiologist, expertly guides readers who have a taste for biological adventures to ‘intraterrestrial’ life: microorganisms that survive under the most extreme environmental conditions, such as in Earth’s deep sediments, deep ocean crust, volcanoes and permafrost soil. . . . Thanks to Intraterrestrials , the general reader can now peek into the work of this network of experts and hopefully leave with a changed perspective as regards microbial life on and within this planet, and of its antiquity, evolutionary pace, adaptability and extraordinary tenacity.
praise.by: Andreas Teske, Nature

praise.q: Intraterrestrials: Discovering the Strangest Life on Earth by Karen G. Lloyd is a much-needed field guide to Earth’s subterranean life. . . . Through witty prose, she brings us along on some of her own adventures chasing microbes from the high desert of the Andes to the perilous summit of a Costa Rican volcano. These are scenes out of an action movie: careful not to slip on the shards of volcanic glass, lest you fall into the lake of acid! . . . All this makes for fun and evocative reading about biogeochemistry—no easy feat.
praise.by: James Dinneen, New Scientist

praise.q: The author gives us a completely new appreciation of how deep life is embedded in our own planet.
praise.by: Bruce Dorminey, Forbes

praise.q: [This] book is so fascinating."—Mia Funk, One Planet Podcast
[Lloyd] manages to weave an interesting narrative that is provocative and compelling."—M. S. Field, Choice Reviews

The central question Lloyd poses in her fascinating exploration of underground microbial ecology—are there life-forms hiding inside Earth that are so strange that they change our conception of life itself?—is easily answered. Yes!
praise.by: Tony Miksanek, Booklist

books.title: Italian Paintings at the Yale University Art Gallery
books.subtitle: Volume 2: 1420-1490
books.tagline: Volume 2 of the comprehensive catalogue of the Yale University Art Gallery’s renowned collection of Italian paintings
books.description:
The Yale University Art Gallery is home to one of the largest and most distinguished collections of Italian paintings in the world. The second of four volumes covering this vast collection, this beautifully illustrated and expertly researched publication features more than seventy-five works dating from 1420 to 1490 by artists such as Gentile da Fabriano, Fra Angelico, Sassetta, Botticelli, and Neroccio de’ Landi. The book is particularly rich in Sienese and Florentine paintings, including one of the best-known Renaissance paintings in America: Antonio Pollaiuolo’s Hercules and Deianira . Also featured are an exceptional group of stucco reliefs that pair the efforts of major Florentine sculptors, including Donatello, with contemporary painters, and a rare, intact painted cassone by Paolo Uccello. Complete with detailed entries on each work—including technical notes, provenance, conservation history, questions of date and attribution, and wider cultural importance—this volume offers a nuanced picture of a fascinating period of Italian art and points to areas of future research in the field.

Distributed for the Yale University Art Gallery
books.bio: Laurence Kanter is chief curator and the Lionel Goldfrank III Curator of European Art at the Yale University Art Gallery. Pia Palladino is an authority on Italian manuscript illumination and panel painting of the thirteenth through the fifteenth century.

books.title: John Banting
books.subtitle: Britain’s Original Surrealist
books.tagline: This book recognises British artist John Banting as an important figure in Surrealism, from Paris to London and New York.
books.description:
This exciting book explores how British Surrealist John Banting (1902-1972) became an important figure from Paris in the 1920s, where he was championed by Marcel Duchamp. It follows his life to London in 1930s, where he was taken up by The Bloomsbury Group as a portrait painter, muralist and designer of book covers for Virginia Woolf. In the 1940s, he made films with Dylan Thomas.

The story follows Surrealism from its genesis in Paris to London and New York through John Banting, artist, designer, film maker and political activist. Fellow artist Julian Trevelyan remarked that Surrealism for John Banting was ‘not just a way of painting but a way of living.’ Art critic Richard Shone described Banting as ‘a dancer, demonstrator and designer who refused to clip the wings of his imagination.’

John Banting: Britian’s Original Surrealist features letters and diaries from the Tate Archive. It is fully illustrated with images of Banting’s wide-ranging works.
books.bio: Hugh St Clair is an experienced arts and design journalist with reviews and features published in numerous British and international magazines and newspapers, including House and Garden , Country Life , The Art Newspaper and auction house magazines.

books.title: Lovelight
books.subtitle: The Art of Beauford Delaney
books.tagline: The art and life of one of American modernism’s most important painters
books.description:
“Since love of life people and painting are to me the same as long as I can lift a brush my heart and mind remain dedicated and my faith steadfast,” Beauford Delaney (1901–1979) wrote of his existence as an artist. He lived up to these words. For more than fifty years, Delaney devoted himself to painting, moving from his birthplace in Knoxville, Tennessee, to Boston, New York, and eventually Paris in pursuit of artistic mastery. Along the way, he exhibited in the same galleries and museums as Jackson Pollock, Romare Bearden, and Sam Francis and amassed a circle of admirers that included James Baldwin, Henry Miller, Georgia O’Keeffe, and Ornette Coleman. Delaney faced tremendous obstacles on his artistic journeys. As a queer Black Southern man who suffered from auditory hallucinations and extreme poverty, Delaney struggled throughout his life. Nonetheless, his luminous paintings suggest hope and even transcendence. Building on his family’s teachings that art constitutes “the immortal sons and daughters of the soul,” Delaney painted a vision of artistic union and posterity that celebrates love in all its forms.

Lovelight explores the development of Delaney’s art from his early days in Appalachia through his final years in France. Drawing on extensive archival research, rarely seen images, interviews with Delaney’s friends, and the painter’s own writings, Mary Campbell gives a moving account of an artist whose work ranks among the great achievements of twentieth-century modernism.
books.bio: Mary Campbell is an associate professor of American art history at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. She is the author of Charles Ellis Johnson and the Erotic Mormon Image .

praise.q: In this beautifully written and expertly illustrated book, Mary Campbell gives us a new and extraordinary portrait of a great painter.
praise.by: David Leeming, author of Amazing Grace: A Life of Beauford Delaney
praise.cred: author of Amazing Grace: A Life of Beauford Delaney

praise.q: Mary Campbell’s deep dive into Beauford Delaney’s assorted spheres of influence—from post-Reconstruction era Knoxville to his final years in post–World War II café society Paris—offers compelling explanations for the artist’s idiosyncratic yet radiant modernism. Rather than creating analogies between biography and art, Lovelight makes the works themselves—portraits, landscapes, invented subjects, and abstractions—the celestial actors from where Delaney’s chronicles can be intercepted and absorbed.
praise.by: Richard J. Powell, author of Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect
praise.cred: author of Colorstruck! Painting, Pigment, Affect

praise.q: In Lovelight , Mary Campbell approaches Delaney with an insightful and expansive interpretive brush. She fleshes out the contours of the Black Knoxville of his childhood and deftly explores the kaleidoscopic turn of his New York and Paris years, illuminating his journey through abundant and revelatory archival research.
praise.by: Adrienne L. Childs, editor of Beauford Delaney: So Much Love and Beauty
praise.cred: editor of Beauford Delaney: So Much Love and Beauty

books.title: Magnetic
books.subtitle: Erebus and Terror and The Last Great Voyage of the Age of Sail
books.tagline: The compelling story of the James Clark Ross expedition to the Antarctic
books.description:
In 1839 James Clark Ross set out to unravel the mysteries of the Earth’s magnetic field and disclose the secrets of the Antarctic. In command of two former warships, HMS Erebus and HMS Terror , he traversed the south polar regions for four years. By the expedition’s end, he and his crews had seen for the first time some of the most astounding sights this world has to offer.

Stewart Weaver traces the story of the last long voyage of discovery under sail. He shows how Ross and other nineteenth century thinkers strove to understand why compass needles pointed north, why the magnetic poles were constantly moving and what lay at the southernmost latitudes of the earth. Weaver shows how efforts to answer longstanding scientific questions led to an unexpected encounter with a whole new continent: Antarctica.

This is the fascinating story of explorer-scientists striving to make their mark at the end of the Age of Sail, at the very moment of transition between the old world and the new.
books.bio: Stewart Weaver is professor of history at the University of Rochester in Rochester, New York, and the author of several books including Fallen Giants: A History of Himalayan Mountaineering from the Age of Empire to the Age of Extremes (with Maurice Isserman) and Exploration: A Very Short Introduction .

praise.q: Writing with characteristic grace, clarity, and insight, Stewart Weaver explores “the call of the magnetic south.” Weaver combines masterful research and lucid storytelling in this definitive account of exemplary seamanship, imperial ambition, and scientific accomplishment.
praise.by: Maurice Isserman, author of Continental Divide

praise.q: James Clark Ross is all but forgotten today, but in the nineteenth century, he was a superstar, and Stewart Weaver’s lively and engaging book reminds us why. Weaver restores Ross to his rightful place at the forefront of British polar explorers.
praise.by: Stephanie L. Barczewski, author of Titanic

praise.q: Stewart Weaver is remarkable among historians for flair and insight as well as scholarship. Magnetic helps us understand the mix of wisdom and wonder that drove explorers to the deadliest extremes of Earth, despite records of failure and deficient means. A gripping yarn and an impressive contribution to the history of science.
praise.by: Felipe Fernández-Armesto, author of How the Spanish Empire Was Built
praise.cred: author of How the Spanish Empire Was Built

praise.q: Magnetic , like the sea route to the South Magnetic Pole itself, is a magnificent and complicated journey. Far more than a tale of scientists and sea dogs, it is a story that unfolds in the halls of the Admiralty and the Royal Society, involving a cast of characters—James Ross, John Franklin, and John Herschel—who became the luminaries of British science and exploration. Weaver’s gifts, both as historian and storyteller, are on full display. It’s a fantastic read.
praise.by: Michael F. Robinson, author of T he Lost White Tribe
praise.cred: author of T he Lost White Tribe

books.title: Seeing Like an Official
books.subtitle: Huang Zhen, the Southern Song State, and the Limits of Governance in Thirteenth-Century China
books.description:
Seeing Like an Official offers a new perspective on the Southern Song state through the eyes of one of its most dedicated local officials, Huang Zhen (1213–1281). Drawing on Huang’s Daily Notes, an extraordinary compilation of administrative writings, Sukhee Lee reconstructs the daily practice of governance in thirteenth-century China from the ground up. Through close readings and analyses of Huang’s reports, petitions, and public notices, Lee reveals the complex negotiations that shaped law enforcement, famine relief, salt administration, and bureaucratic communication in an era of crisis and constraint.

Challenging the conventional view of the late Southern Song as a period of state retrenchment, Lee demonstrates that the state did not retreat so much as reorient. Its officials exhibited a distinct flexibility as they prioritized local experimentation and pragmatic coordination over uniform administrative imposition. The result is an illuminating portrayal of governance as an evolving process of adaptation—one driven by officials who enacted state ideals through locally grounded practice. By guiding readers to “see like an official,” this book offers a fresh perspective on how state capacity, local agency, and the limits of bureaucratic rule were negotiated in practice in premodern China.
books.bio: Sukhee Lee is an Associate Professor of History at Rutgers University–New Brunswick.

books.title: Sofonisba, Lavinia, Artemisia
books.subtitle: Their Radical Late Work
books.tagline: A groundbreaking account of the fascinating late paintings of three women Renaissance artists by one of the field’s pioneers
books.description:
Sofonisba Anguissola, Lavinia Fontana, and Artemisia Gentileschi—the most important women artists of Renaissance Italy—all deviated radically from their earlier work in their last years. Because their late paintings are anomalous and puzzling, they have been virtually ignored, and treated as peripheral to the artists’ core identities and oeuvres. In this book, Mary Garrard, a founding pioneer in feminist art history, presents a major reevaluation of the late works of Anguissola, Fontana, and Gentileschi, showing how in their final years they deliberately changed direction to produce bold, transgressive, and surprising paintings that upended gendered expectations.

While great male artists have been praised for their “heroic” or “tragic” late works, historians have largely overlooked the creative imaginations of older women artists. In this important book, Garrard questions that bias as she explores the adventurous late-life art of Anguissola, Fontana, and Gentileschi. What emerges is a compelling account of how each artist met the universal experience of ageing with an idiosyncratic response—Anguissola through influential formal innovation, Fontana through quirky yet deadly serious humor, and Gentileschi through satirical dialogue with her own early work.

Adding new chapters to the stories of these artists, Sofonisba, Lavinia, Artemisia challenges art historians and critics to consider what is missed when late-life creativity goes unnoticed.
books.bio: Mary D. Garrard is professor emerita of art history at American University and a pioneering authority on Artemisia Gentileschi and other women artists of the Renaissance and on feminist art history. Garrard’s books include Artemisia Gentileschi: The Image of the Female Hero in Italian Baroque Art (Princeton), which launched modern studies of the artist. With her colleague Norma Broude, Garrard created and coedited four volumes of essays in feminist art history that have become foundational texts in art history and women’s studies courses.

praise.q: Sofonisba, Lavinia, Artemisia provides fascinating new interpretations of the later paintings of these artists, and it’s so refreshing to see rightful attention being given to creative women in their elder years. These late periods have been long overlooked or misunderstood and, as Mary Garrard effectively argues, were influential on artists who followed.”—Julia Dabbs, author of Life Stories of Women Artists, 1550

Mary Garrard, a pioneer in the study of women artists in the early modern period, is universally acclaimed for the first serious study of Artemisia Gentileschi. Sofonisba, Lavinia, Artemisia goes beyond Garrard’s substantial corpus to consider the late careers of the three artists, suggesting new ways of framing the discussion. Garrard is in full command of her sources, and her interpretations will form the basis for future scholarly discussions of these important artists.
praise.by: Bette Talvacchia, editor of A Cultural History of Sexuality in the Renaissance
praise.cred: editor of A Cultural History of Sexuality in the Renaissance

books.title: The Conqueror's Gift
books.subtitle: Roman Ethnography and the End of Antiquity
books.tagline: The essential role of ethnographic thought in the Roman empire and how it evolved in Late Antiquity
books.description:
Ethnography is indispensable for every empire, as important as armies, tax collectors, or ambassadors. It helps rulers articulate cultural differences, and it lets the inhabitants of the empire, especially those who guide its course, understand themselves in the midst of enemies, allies, and friends. In The Conqueror’s Gift , Michael Maas examines the ethnographic infrastructure of the Roman Empire and the transformation of Rome’s ethnographic vision during Late Antiquity. Drawing on a wide range of texts, Maas shows how the Romans’ ethnographic thought evolved as they attended to the business of ruling an empire on three continents.

Ethnography, the “conqueror’s gift,” gave Romans structured ways of finding a place for foreigners in the imperial worldview and helped justify imperial action affecting them. In Late Antiquity, Christianity revolutionized the imperial ethnographic infrastructure by altering old concepts and introducing credal models of community. The Bible became a source for organizing the Roman world. At the same time, many previously unseen collective identities emerged across Western Eurasia in reaction to the diminution of Roman power. These changes deeply affected the Empire’s ethnographic infrastructure and vision of the world. Maas argues that a major consequence of these developments was the beginning of a sectarian age, as individuals and political communities came to identify themselves primarily in terms of religion as well as ethnicity. As they adjusted to changing ethnographic realities, Romans understood their place among the peoples of the world in new ways. Willingly or not, we continue to be recipients of the conqueror’s gift today.
books.bio: Michael Maas is the William Gaines Twyman Professor of History at Rice University. His most recent book, Empires and Exchanges in Eurasian Late Antiquity: Rome, China, Iran, and the Steppe, ca. 250–750 , edited with Nicola Di Cosmo, won a CHOICE Academic Book of the Year Award.

praise.q: A landmark study that synthesizes a vast array of data, this study reveals clearly for the first time details of how the Roman Empire (both East and West) engaged with foreign peoples. The processes of assimilation, exclusion, war and peace, astral and environmental determinism all have resonance with how our world of the 21 century is being shaped. This is a book for their time, for our time, for all time.
praise.by: Cliff Cunningham, Sun News Austin

praise.q: Michael Maas’s thought-provoking study The Conqueror’s Gift surveys the different structures by which the human population of the world was conceptualized and ordered in late antiquity. . . . [It] does an excellent job of highlighting the very different sections of ‘the ethnographic dossier,’ and in showing how contrasting models of conceptualizing the world became operative throughout late antiquity.
praise.by: Andy Merrills, Bryn Mawr Classical Review

praise.q: An important contribution to scholarship on late antiquity.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: Ambitious and elegantly written. . . . Maas works masterfully across scholarly siloes that have so often distorted understandings of the history of ethnicity: Greek and Latin, East and West, ‘pagan’ and Christian, ‘ancient’ and ‘medieval.’ In this respect, his book deserves to be placed alongside some of the best works that have emerged from the late antique historiographic project.
praise.by: John Merrington, Journal of Ecclesiastical History

praise.q: A wise and deeply learned book, The Conqueror’s Gift describes how the Roman Empire—an immense community of diverse peoples—saw itself, its neighbors, and the strangers in its midst. The story of how a once-unrivaled superpower came to face, in times of headlong political and religious change, an ever more recalcitrant reality is not without relevance to our own times.
praise.by: Peter Brown, author of Journeys of the Mind: A Life in History
praise.cred: author of Journeys of the Mind: A Life in History

praise.q: The Conqueror’s Gift is a fascinating and rich study of the complex history of Roman ethnography as a product of the dynamic interplay between strategies of exclusion and of inclusion. With great care and impressive command, Michael Maas reconstructs the evolution of the empire’s ethnographic infrastructure by exploring ethnography not as a genre, but as a complex amalgam of cultural, political, and religious practices, all constantly in reproduction. In doing so, he also provides a radical explanation for the enduring appeal of this discourse to later societies and cultures, including our own today.”—Helmut Reimitz, author of History, Frankish Identity and the Framing of Western Ethnicity, 550

This book makes a significant and original scholarly contribution to a vibrant and relatively new field of ancient history. I know of no other work that systematically brings classical Greek texts into dialogue with late antique sources in order to explore how ethnographic discourse was constructed and how it was used in practice, across multiple different spheres.
praise.by: Caroline Humfress, University of St Andrews

praise.q: Michael Maas’s The Conqueror’s Gift is a very important contribution to the history and historiography of Late Antiquity. Although there are some aspects to it that are familiar in their broad outlines, the combination of this material in a single volume is both unexpected and revelatory.
praise.by: Michael Kulikowski, Pennsylvania State University

books.title: The Enchanting Lives of Others
books.subtitle: A Novel
books.series: The Margellos World Republic of Letters
books.tagline: A celebration of the beguiling power of literature, from one of the world’s greatest storytellers
books.description:
At the Pigeon Book Club, a circle of readers gathers for exhilarating meetings to discuss literature. The only requirements for entry are an all-encompassing love of books and the intuition that to read is to love and to love is to read. Xiao Sang, a department store clerk, wonders if life can ever be as captivating as a novel. Newlyweds Fei and Han Ma struggle to build a marriage as Han Ma discovers a surprising gift for storytelling. Xiao Ma, a hopeful dreamer, explores the possibility of romance with an older man. Bound by a shared passion for fiction, each book club member seeks to understand the relationship between the stories they read and the lives they lead, reveling in both the quotidian details and the ecstasy of aesthetics.

This is the most accessible work yet from the celebrated writer Can Xue: a utopian comedy and a work of profound joy, a love song to literary inspiration and the remarkable beauty of the ordinary. The Enchanting Lives of Others explores what it means to know and be known to others through the transformative power of reading.
books.bio: Can Xue is the pseudonym of the Chinese writer Deng Xiaohua (b. 1953). Formerly a tailor, she began writing fiction in 1983. Her works include Barefoot Doctor , I Live in the Slums , Love in the New Millennium , Five Spice Street , and The Last Lover . Annelise Finegan is academic director and clinical associate professor of translation at New York University.

praise.q: A giant of avant-garde literature”—Fred Lunzer, Times Literary Supplement
Irish Times , Best Fiction of 2026 to Look Forward To
Can Xue has captured a peculiar conundrum of intimacy that all book lovers know well: that blurring of the lines between fiction and real life.
praise.by: Eva Dunsky, Asymptote

praise.q: Visionary, uncanny, yet down-to-earth, Can Xue’s voice is unique in Chinese, and global, fiction. This moving, magical novel celebrates the transformative power of literature itself—and shows why great readers make great lovers.
praise.by: Boyd Tonkin, author of The 100 Best Novels in Translation
praise.cred: author of The 100 Best Novels in Translation

praise.q: Are there differences between perceiving, remembering, imagining, and dreaming? And which do we use while reading? Can Xue writes as if the boundaries between these activities barely exist. In The Enchanting Lives of Others , her characters glide between mind-states: as fictional constructs of a writer’s psyche; as readers of invented novels; as dreamers of the author’s imagination. This novel places its readers in an almost surreal space within Can Xue’s fictional gymnastics—and submitting to her method reveals astonishing insights into the elasticity of the mind.
praise.by: Nick Barley, director, National Poetry Centre, United Kingdom
praise.cred: director, National Poetry Centre, United Kingdom

praise.q: Can Xue’s novelscape transforms how readers and writers are rearranged through passages and passageways of living, though who are the readers? Who are the writers?—you and I, the novel’s characters, or both? This book is a singular gem.
praise.by: Martine Bellen, author of An Anatomy of Curiosity
praise.cred: author of An Anatomy of Curiosity

praise.q: In this masterful novel, Can Xue invites readers on a journey through layers of meaning. As this book unfolds its wilder, more fantastical elements, the reader is invited to reassess their understanding of the very core of what it means to be human. The Enchanting Lives of Others is both an excellent starting point for anyone interested in Can Xue’s work, and a wonderful addition to her English-language oeuvre.
praise.by: Chad W. Post, Open Letter Books

books.title: The Girth Ramsey Theorem
books.tagline: An introduction to structural Ramsey theory that builds to a resolution of one of its long-standing conjectures
books.description:
Structural Ramsey theory is an area of combinatorics about Ramsey-type statements dealing with hypergraphs as well as other combinatorial structures. Rather than mainly focusing on numerical aspects such as Ramsey numbers, structural Ramsey theory focuses on the existence of Ramsey-type statements and their connection with some other fields of mathematics. In this book, Christian Reiher and Vojtěch Rödl introduce structural Ramsey theory and solve a long-standing problem regarding locally sparse Ramsey graphs.

The book has two parts. The first part, which is suitable for a topics course, introduces tools used in the construction of locally sparse Ramsey graphs and hypergraphs, and covers several well-known results, such as Ramsey’s theorem and the Hales-Jewett theorem. The focus is on structural Ramsey theory of hypergraphs and on the introduction of partite construction, which is illustrated by several of its applications yielding the proof of some older results in the area. The second part establishes the girth Ramsey theorem, resolving a decades’ old conjecture in structural Ramsey theory implying that for every graph G and every number of colors, there exists a Ramsey graph H with girth(H) = girth(G).
books.bio: Christian Reiher is a lecturer in mathematics at the University of Hamburg. Vojtěch Rödl is Samuel Candler Dobbs Professor at Emory University.

books.title: The Northern Grand Tour
books.subtitle: A History
books.tagline: "Truly a revelation.”—Simon Jenkins, author of A Short History of England The untold story of the British who travelled to Northern Europe to encounter the men and manners of the modern world
books.description:
Conventional understanding of the Grand Tour of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries is personified by the figure of a languid young British aristocrat sent to Italy to see the classical ruins, acquire some social polish, and return home with a crate of Roman busts and a copy of Piranesi’s Views . But Celina Fox’s groundbreaking book reveals an entirely different Grand Tour—one focused not on the ancient past but on the modern world of contemporary Northern Europe. The young men whom we meet were travelling to study in the great European universities, learn international law and languages, find innovative science and medicine, cut their diplomatic teeth at foreign courts, make commercial contacts in powerful trade centres, and understand new technologies.

Through their journals and letters, we share the excitement and indignities of travel for young men often at liberty for the first time in their lives and encountering new customs and societies. Letters from their parents—sometimes cajoling, sometimes coercive—attest to frustrated efforts to retain control, mediated by mentors who assisted them along the way. The travellers’ vivid accounts of what they saw and learned are skilfully woven into the complex historical narrative of their times.

Fox shows that the Northern Grand Tour arose out of the inability of the English education system, centred on the classics, to equip young men with the modern practical knowledge needed for their future careers. It was formative for many who later became influential in British society—and the benefits they derived from their travels were recognised and adopted on a wider scale back in Britain.
