books.bio: Celina Fox trained as a historian at Cambridge, Harvard, and Oxford, and has worked internationally as a museum curator, exhibitions organiser, arts administrator, art historian, and journalist. Her books include the award-winning The Arts of Industry in the Age of Enlightenment .

praise.q: At last a description of the ‘other’ Grand Tour, that of Northern Europe in the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries. Long ignored by history, it challenged France and Italy in its appeal and cultural richness. Fox brings her story alive through the letters and journals of its many participants in what is truly a revelation.
praise.by: Simon Jenkins, bestselling author of A Short History of Europe
praise.cred: bestselling author of A Short History of Europe

praise.q: The Northern Grand Tour is a magnificent exercise in cultural and intellectual recovery that adds considerably to our knowledge of social and diplomatic history. But just as authoritatively it provides superbly nuanced insights about many other subjects—including the history of education, science and medicine, the family, sex, politics, religion, trade, and the arts. It is a breathtakingly original achievement.
praise.by: Brian Young, University of Oxford

praise.q: Celina Fox takes readers on a marvellous journey. Retracing pathfinders’ steps across Europe’s north as travel became more organised and commercialised, as it filtered down through the middle classes, and as it became a rite of passage, especially for young men, Fox tells a story about new practices of making new identities for the modern age. This book is brilliant and beautiful.
praise.by: Jeremy Adelman, University of Cambridge

books.title: The Organization of Human Experience
books.subtitle: An Evolutionary Analysis
books.tagline: How an evolutionary psychology of agency explains dimensions of human behavior and experience overlooked by the computational model of mind.
books.description:
Modern cognitive science is dominated by a mind-as-computer model that pays scant attention to the evolutionary history via which human psychological processes came into existence. It thus struggles to explain why human psychology and experience are the way they are. In The Organization of Human Experience , Michael Tomasello seeks to fill this explanatory gap by proposing a complementary organism-as-agent model. Integrating findings from comparative research on ancestral species (using extant species as models) with concepts from modern philosophical theories of action and agency, he unearths the evolutionary foundations of human psychology and experience.

The specific claim is that all human psychological processes—and the forms of experience that they engender—evolved across species over evolutionary time for a common function: to empower individuals to make agentive decisions about how best to act in novel circumstances. Questions about why humans attend to and represent certain kinds of information and not others, why they learn certain kinds of things and draw certain kinds of inferences and not others, and why they understand events in terms of causal, intentional, and normative relations can only be answered via an evolutionary history of the ways in which humans’ ancestors made and executed agentive decisions.
books.bio: Michael Tomasello is Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience at Duke University, and Emeritus Director at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Leipzig, Germany. His previous MIT Press books are Origins of Human Communication , Why We Cooperate , and The Evolution of Agency .

books.title: The Power of Pi
books.subtitle: The Beauty and Obsession Behind the World's Favorite Number
books.tagline: A delightfully engaging, fact-filled account of the irrational number that has inspired revolutionary changes in mathematical thinking
books.description:
More than two thousand years ago, the Greek mathematician Archimedes showed how a single number—we now call it pi—transformed geometry. Since then, pi has revealed itself as a universal constant, turning up in unexpected places like Fibonacci numbers, the design of walled cities, and chaos theory. The Power of Pi ventures across centuries and continents with this singular number, exploring how it has stormed the mathematical world and inspired us to think deeply.

Marc Chamberland takes you behind the scenes, where pi travels the cosmos to answer questions about exoplanets. He discusses how understanding pi’s algebraic structure settled mysteries posed centuries earlier by the ancient Greeks. You’ll learn about pi’s present-day role in experimental mathematics and computation and why using many digits of pi helps find new, exotic equations. Chamberland introduces colorful personalities and their stories behind new discoveries about pi, including students who proved their world-class professors wrong and the brothers who built their own supercomputer. Along the way, he serves up “Slices of Pi” that offer a fun look at the number’s starring role in pop culture—from movies and TV to the craze for memorizing and reciting the digits of pi—as well as simple experiments that readers can try themselves.

Revealing how this mysterious constant extends far beyond the circle, The Power of Pi is an informative and entertaining tour of mathematics with the most beguiling irrational number as your guide.
books.bio: Marc Chamberland is the Myra Steele Professor of Natural Sciences and Mathematics at Grinnell College and the author of Single Digits: In Praise of Small Numbers (Princeton). He is the creator of the YouTube channel Tipping Point Math .

books.title: Trading Truth
books.subtitle: How Financial Markets Shape Reality
books.tagline: How financial markets fuel conspiracy culture and our crisis of truth—and why rethinking finance is democracy’s most urgent need. “An important book showing that ‘post-truth politics’ cannot be understood without studying the broader socioeconomic transformation of our times, especially the rise of finance. A must-read.” –Thomas Piketty
books.description:
“An important book showing that ‘post-truth politics’ cannot be understood without studying the broader socioeconomic transformation of our times, especially the rise of finance. A must-read.” –Thomas Piketty

Current debates treat disinformation as if it were a cultural failure, suggesting that our remedies should focus on restoring expertise, fact checking, or media literacy. But what if we are missing the crux of the issue? In Trading Truth , Aris Komporozos-Athanasiou argues that we are—that, in fact, distortion is not a glitch of political reality but a systemic feature of finance capitalism. Far from merely corrupting truth, financial markets—from machine-learning trading and cryptocurrencies to ETFs and prediction markets—reshape what counts as real and what gets dismissed as fake.

This book traces this distortion and its role in the making of a new kind of financial populism, one that binds Trump’s MAGA movement and tech lords to finance’s rising titans: asset managers and quant traders. This alliance—political as much as epistemic—takes shape around warped valuations, spurious correlations, and the systematic leveraging of volatility. And yet it draws in vast publics, offering a form of belonging and participation that mainstream politics has failed to provide.

The author shows how today’s conspiratorial culture is inseparable from the operations of finance in ways not recognized before . More than disinformation, fraud, or manipulation, distortion becomes a means of managing the vast complexity of our time, and even of finding community within it. The book offers readers a way forward: a theory of truth that meets finance head on and reimagines how it could be turned toward shared prosperity.
books.bio: Aris Komporozos-Athanasiou is Professor of Economy and Society at University College London, where he is Founder and Director of the UCL Centre for Capitalism Studies. His first book Speculative Communities was published in 2022 to international acclaim. His work has been featured in The New Yorker, El País, London Review of Books Podcast, and venues such as the Locarno Film Festival and the Deichtorhallen Gallery. He has written for The Guardian, Die Zeit, Aeon, Los Angeles Review of Books, and other publications.

books.title: Yale French Studies, Number 149/150
books.subtitle: Strange Landscapes
books.authors: Edited by Hannah Freed-Thall and Jill Jarvis
books.tagline: Number 149/150 of Yale French Studies investigates landscape relationally, as a way of being, vernacular improvisation, gathering of textures, terrain of extraction and resistance
books.description: Double issue Number 149/150 of Yale French Studies examines the vistas that emerge when we set aside familiar aesthetic conceptions of “nature” (forests, mountains, gardens) and consider instead a variety of stranger landscapes—spaces forgotten or unexplored, deserts, littoral edges, industrial and postindustrial terrain, matter made radiant by nuclear toxicity, and wastes. Contributors to this collection engage landscape as something other than a mere view, backdrop, or container for a person. Their contributions reflect the strange uses to which lands, waters, and skies have been put throughout and beyond the former French empire. Temporally, geographically, and methodologically, the issue is wide-ranging and diverse: it spans topics as varied as the poetics of medieval tree grafting, the desolation and resistance of sixteenth-century New World mines, the ghostly “elephant-landscapes” of French modernist fiction, and the “broiling favelas” of a Caribbean post-humanist near-future. Likewise, the articles gathered here consider richly divergent genres and objects, including travel narratives, novels, multimedia installations, sculpture, photography, architectural ruins, postapocalyptic cinema, and documentary film.
books.bio: Hannah Freed-Thall is professor of French literature, thought, and culture at New York University. She is the author of Spoiled Distinctions: Aesthetics and the Ordinary in French Modernism and Modernism at the Beach: Queer Ecologies and the Coastal Commons . She lives in New York, NY. Jill Jarvis is associate professor of French at Yale University. She is the author of Decolonizing Memory: Algeria and the Politics of Testimony and The Desert Is Alive: Aesthetic Cartographies of the Sahara . She lives in New Haven, CT.

books.title: Breathing with God
books.subtitle: The Teachings of a Sufi Mystic
books.tagline: The first translated collection of the thousand-year-old aphorisms of Kharaqani, one of the most original and important mystics in the Sufi tradition of Islam
books.description:
In this beautiful book, Omid Safi provides the first-ever English collection of the verses of Kharaqani (d. 1033 CE), a shepherd whose vivid and powerful conversations with God led to his being remembered as a Sufi master and the highest-ranking saint of his age in this Persian Islamic tradition.

Kharaqani was not concerned with mere salvation or getting to heaven. Instead, he sought to link the love of God with the love of humanity through his bold, fresh, and original teachings. He said:

A single breath taken with God

is better

than all there is

in heaven

or on Earth

Safi’s deeply researched translations and commentary bring Kharaqani’s original voice alive for modern audiences and show how Kharaqani has shaped the Sufi tradition—and how this simple man has captivated religious seekers for centuries in Iran, South Asia, and Turkey.
books.bio: Omid Safi is professor in the Department of Asian and Middle Eastern Studies at Duke University. His books include Radical Love: Teachings from the Islamic Mystical Tradition and Memories of Muhammad . He lives in Durham, NC.

books.title: Climate Apocalypse
books.subtitle: Catastrophic Global Warming Is More Likely Than Ever—but It’s Still Not Too Late to Save Ourselves
books.tagline: How we can beat the odds and avoid making Earth uninhabitable.
books.description:
Climate Apocalypse is a sobering account of the increasingly catastrophic risk and urgent measures we can take to save ourselves. Cautioning against unworkable approaches, climate scientist and geophysicist Wolfgang Bauer unravels what we know (and don’t) about the odds of climate change making our planet uninhabitable and transforming it into another Venus. Examining the past, present, and future of carbon in our atmosphere, oceans, biosphere, and Earth’s crust, he explains why existing computer climate models might miss exponentially rising, and potentially annihilating, surface temperatures before it is too late.

The author dives into fossil fuel alternatives, including renewable power sources, and how they can be deployed safely, efficiently, and even profitably. By eliminating the combustion of fossil fuels and replacing them with renewables, the book provides estimates of how large an investment the necessary transition would take, and how fast it would pay for itself, asking the big question: Are we prepared to put a price on an inhabitable planet? The choice is still ours.
books.bio: Wolfgang Bauer is University Distinguished Professor of Physics and Astronomy at Michigan State University.

books.title: Colors Play Tricks
books.subtitle: Adventures with Josef Albers's Interaction of Color
books.tagline: A playful introduction to concepts from Josef Albers’s theories of color interaction, written for young readers, ages 5–8
books.description:
Join Wilder, a curious child with an eye for color, on an adventure into the astonishing world of color interaction! You will learn that colors aren’t always what they seem. Follow along with interactive experiments, and be amazed as your eyes deceive you.

Based on the teachings of the acclaimed artist and educator Josef Albers, this story follows a delightfully inquisitive child named Wilder and his grandfather as they experience together five of Josef Albers’s most mind-bending color experiments. These experiments help children explore the ways our perception of color can shift and astonish us. Author and illustrator Zebedee Helm’s adaptations of the experiments are perfectly suited to a child’s sense of puzzlement and play.

Learn about:

• Seeing color in CONTEXT by experiencing how the colors we see can change relative to their surroundingss

• The AFTER IMAGE of colors by staring at one color and then looking away and “seeing” its complementary color
books.bio:
Zebedee Helm is a BAFTA-nominated illustrator, cartoonist, and author.

Josef Albers (1888–1976), one of the most influential artist-educators of the twentieth century, was a professor at the Bauhaus in Germany until it was closed in 1933. He then came to the United States, where he taught at Black Mountain College and at Yale University. He was renowned worldwide for his book Interaction of Color (Yale), which has helped generations of artists and students to understand and experiment with color and its properties.

books.title: Dark Virtues
books.subtitle: The Tragic Realism of Booker T. Washington
books.tagline: A landmark reevaluation that uncovers how a maligned African American leader hid his radicalism beneath a mask of moderation
books.description:
One of the most important but reviled figures in American history, Booker T. Washington (1856–1915) has long been accused of trading the rights of African Americans for menial gains and personal power. Dark Virtues offers a fundamental reinterpretation of Washington’s life and thought by drawing on a massive archive of his writings and other documents. Desmond Jagmohan argues that Washington practiced a deliberate politics of deception, wearing a compliant mask to conceal and enable his radical projects to uproot Jim Crow and improve the condition of black southerners.

In the Jim Crow South, Washington confronted a racial tyranny maintained through disenfranchisement, segregation, economic subjugation, and terrorism. Judging that open confrontation would be fatal for black southerners, he saw strategic equivocation, concealment, and deception as political virtues for the oppressed. Reexamining his rhetoric, writings, and actions, Dark Virtues reveals this unseen and subversive Washington, a leader who clandestinely fought for racial justice and economic empowerment, used his Tuskegee Institute to build black civic capacity under the cover of vocational training, and willingly bore the stain of treachery to protect black southerners from racial terror. This radical Washington stands in stark contrast to W.E.B. Du Bois’s damning and influential depiction of him as a mere accommodationist.

But Dark Virtues doesn’t rehabilitate Washington uncritically. It shows that his realism was tragic: politically necessary and morally regrettable. It also asks hard questions about politics and ethics in dark times: Does anyone survive oppression morally unscathed? What does resistance look like when protest can cost people their jobs—or even their lives?
books.bio: Desmond Jagmohan is assistant professor of political science at the University of California, Berkeley, where he received the university-wide Distinguished Teaching Award.

books.title: Days in the Clouds
books.tagline: The never-before-published last essays of the late Duncan Smith, at once heartbreakingly personal and bracingly intellectual.
books.description:
Following the appearance of his theoretical tour-de-force The Age of Oil and his AIDS diagnosis, Duncan Smith (1954–1991) produced Days in the Clouds , a collection of thirty-eight essays sparkling with his characteristic linguistic brilliance. Now published for the first time, Days in the Clouds chronicles Smith’s response to the disease that would kill him as well as its severe impact on downtown NYC culture. At once heartbreakingly personal and bracingly intellectual, these essays examine in exacting detail a range of subjects, from the semiotics of gay life and the visionary potential of nature to the shortcomings of Susan Sontag’s writings on illness, the literary criticism of Paul de Man, and, as always with Smith, the meanings hidden within proper names.

Alongside Days in the Clouds , Semiotext(e) is bringing out the much-awaited republication of Age of Oil , Smith’s brilliant and long out-of-print collection of essays from 1987.
books.bio: Duncan Smith (1953–1991) is known for his innovative writings that reflect his extensive research in psychoanalysis, semiotics, Marxist ideology, and literature. In 1976, Smith left undergraduate studies at the University of Washington to move to New York City, where he became a beloved friend for many in downtown avant-garde circles. In 1987, Slate Press published Smith’s first collection of cultural criticism, The Age of Oil . That same year, in the midst of earning his PhD at Cornell University, Smith learned of his HIV-positive status and embarked on a series of essays centered on his experiences with AIDS. These would become Days in the Clouds , completed in Portland, OR, some months before his death in February 1991.

books.title: Diego Velázquez
books.subtitle: The Portrait of Cardinal Gaspar de Borja
books.authors: Ximo Company Climent, Miquel Àngel Herrero-Cortell, Isidro Puig, María Antonia Argelich, Viviana Farina, Patricia Manzano and Eva Martínez
books.tagline: Brings to light the long-lost original version of Velázquez’s portrait of Cardinal Gaspar de Borja, which enhances our understanding of the artist’s work and legacy
books.description:
This book delves into the study of the portrait of Cardenal Gaspar de Borja , painted by Diego Velázquez around 1645. It reveals the true and original version of this portrait, a masterpiece that had long been assumed to exist but was only known through versions by Velázquez’s followers. It focuses on the rich historical and technical aspects of the portrait, examining its attribution and the various versions of the work that have existed throughout history. The book provides a comprehensive analysis of the portrait's journey, its rediscovery, and the technical methods employed in Velázquez's execution of the piece.

It presents a scholarly investigation that combines art history, technical analysis, and restoration studies, shedding new light on the portrait of Cardenal Gaspar de Borja and confirming its place as a true masterpiece by Velázquez. It represents a groundbreaking contribution to the history of art, as it brings to light the long-lost original version by Velázquez, a discovery that significantly enhances our understanding of his work and legacy.
books.bio:
Ximo Company Climent is Emeritus Professor of Early Modern Art at Universitat de Lleida, founder of the Centre d’Art d’Època Moderna (CAEM), member of the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Carlos in Valencia, and ICREA Academia researcher.

Miquel Àngel Herrero-Cortell is Professor at the Faculty of Fine Arts of Universitat Politécnica de Valencia, with a dual background in Fine Arts and Art History.

Isidro Puig is Professor at the Faculty of Fine Arts of Universitat Politécnica de Valencia.

María Antonia Argelich : Directora del Centre d’Art d’Època Moderna (CAEM) de la Universitat de Lleida.

Viviana Farina is Professor at the Accademia di Belle Arti di Napoli.

books.title: Elusive Cures
books.subtitle: Why Neuroscience Hasn’t Solved Brain Disorders—and How We Can Change That
books.tagline: A neuroscientist’s bold proposal for tackling one of the greatest challenges of our time—brain and mental illnesses
books.description:
Brain research has been accelerating rapidly in recent decades, but the translation of our many discoveries into treatments and cures for brain disorders has not happened as many expected. We do not have cures for the vast majority of brain illnesses, from Alzheimer’s to depression, and many medications we do have to treat the brain are derived from drugs produced in the 1950s—before we knew much about the brain at all. Tackling brain disorders is clearly one of the biggest challenges facing humanity today. What will it take to overcome it? Nicole Rust takes readers along on her personal journey to answer this question.

Drawing on her decades of experience on the front lines of neuroscience research, Rust reflects on how far we have come in our quest to unlock the secrets of the brain and what remains to be discovered. She shows us that treating a brain disorder is more like redirecting a hurricane than fixing a domino chain of cause and effect, arguing that only once we embrace the idea of the brain as a complex system do we have any hope of finding cures. Rust profiles the pioneering ideas about the brain that are driving research at the cutting edge to illuminate exactly how much we know about disorders such as Parkinson’s, epilepsy, addiction, schizophrenia, and anxiety—and what it will take to eradicate these scourges.

Elusive Cures sheds light on one of the most daunting challenges ever confronted by science while offering hope for revolutionary new treatments and cures for the brain.
books.bio: Nicole C. Rust is the Rose Family Endowed Term Professor of Psychology at the University of Pennsylvania. Recipient of the Troland Award from the National Academy of Sciences, she is a contributing editor at The Transmitter , a leading brain research news magazine.

praise.q: A compelling case that understanding the brain as a complex and constantly changing system instead of a ‘thing’ improves the chances of understanding the relationship between ‘mental disorders’ and ‘brain disorders,’ the role of neural networks, and finding cures. Accessible to lay readers, informed by the latest research, and filled with concrete examples, Elusive Cures is immensely useful to a subject that is relevant to all of us.
praise.by: Glenn C. Altschuler, Psychology Today

praise.q: An insider’s account of how contemporary neuroscience is tackling the failures of the bench-to-bed pipeline and how neuroscience is moving away from the molecular-genetic framework to a new grand plan that understands the brain as a complex, dynamic, computational system. Rust is a brilliant, accomplished, thoughtful, and philosophically and clinically informed neuroscientist. . . . the end result is an accessible book that is deeply intelligent and informative.
praise.by: Awais Aftab, Psychiatry at the Margins

praise.q: Written at an accessible level, this thorough summation explains neuroscience research and possible pathways forward to students, patients, caregivers, and educators.
praise.by: Library Journal

praise.q: An ambitious study of the search for cures to Huntington’s, Parkinson’s, schizophrenia, depression, Alzheimer’s, and ALS. . . . pepper[ed] with fascinating anecdotes . . . . The result is a cogent and impassioned account.
praise.by: Publishers Weekly

praise.q: Elusive Cures should be required reading for all neuroscience students. . . . Essential.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: What I most enjoyed and admired about the book was Rust’s willingness to get dirty in the intellectual trenches. It’s easy for a reader to say, as I have, that some of the proposed solutions don’t quite bite, but the author is dealing with overwhelmingly difficult questions that most of us spend a lot of time sidestepping. There is no sidestepping here.
praise.by: Vincent Walsh, Current Biology

praise.q: In Elusive Cures , neuroscientist Nicole Rust takes us along on her quest to understand one of the most ambitious scientific projects of our time. A gifted writer, Rust eases us into the complexity of psychiatric and neurological disorders with brilliant examples that help any reader understand what we know about how the brain works in health and disease. She is the perfect guide to the wonder and promise of modern neuroscience.
praise.by: Thomas Insel, MD, author of Healing: Our Path from Mental Illness to Mental Health
praise.cred: MD, author of Healing: Our Path from Mental Illness to Mental Health

praise.q: A number of scientists, me included, have been ranting about the sad state of affairs in the treatment of mental disorders for some time. In Elusive Cures , Nicole Rust offers a fresh and very useful perspective on the problem. If you are suffering, this is an excellent way for you to see that you are not alone, and that some scientists are working hard to make things better.
praise.by: Joseph LeDoux, author of The Four Realms of Existence: A New Theory of Being Human
praise.cred: author of The Four Realms of Existence: A New Theory of Being Human

praise.q: Elusive Cures is a remarkably compelling and enlightening deep dive into the state of brain research as relevant to disease. Combining the authority of a great teacher and the personal touch of a helpful guide, Rust offers a thought-provoking perspective on scientific thinking, progress, and discovery.
praise.by: Daphna Shohamy, director and CEO of the Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute, Columbia University
praise.cred: director and CEO of the Mortimer B. Zuckerman Mind Brain Behavior Institute, Columbia University

books.title: Energetics of the Otherwise
books.subtitle: A Laboratory of the Possible
books.tagline: A bold and revelatory exploration of Walter Benjamin’s theory of history alongside experiments in quantum physics, giving us flashes of possibility in this dark moment of danger
books.description:
Walter Benjamin’s concept of messianic materialism, developed as fascism overtook Europe, has held out hope to thinkers, artists, and activists for nearly a century. Benjamin’s key insight is that the potential for justice exists in the “thick-now” of the present moment, and not in pinning political hope on some future era. In this invigorating and audacious new book, philosopher and physicist Karen River Barad proposes a method to think time anew, one that brings Benjamin’s ideas into conversation with the discoveries of quantum physics and the mystical-materialist insights of Jewish Kabbalah.

Arguing that Benjamin was himself a kind of “bench scientist,” Barad demonstrates how Benjamin’s conception of messianic time and the thick-now of the present (flashing through with bolts of eternal time), are material matters to be literally grasped (if you dare!). Diffractively reading each of Benjamin’s key concepts together with natural phenomena (crystals, constellations, lightning), Barad transduces the tangible existence of Benjamin’s revelatory theories. The memory-encrusted world all around us, Barad argues, holds energetic possibilities for remembering past injustices, reckoning with historic violence, and reconfiguring the world in ways that move us toward more just material conditions.
books.bio: Karen River Barad is Distinguished Professor of History of Consciousness at the University of California, Santa Cruz, and author of the influential work Meeting the Universe Halfway: Quantum Physics and the Entanglement of Matter and Meaning .

books.title: Henry Highland Garnet
books.subtitle: A Passion for the Freedom-Idea
books.tagline: The story of a fiery Black abolitionist and how his radical ideology, unstinting commitment, and inspiring life remain relevant in the twenty-first century
books.description:
Born enslaved in Maryland, Henry Highland Garnet (1815–1882) escaped with his family via the Underground Railroad to New York City and went on to become a major voice in the Black abolitionist movement. He led community-based organizations that physically confronted kidnappers and slave traders preying on Black New Yorkers. Garnet caused a sensation in 1843 by publicly advocating for armed Black resistance to slavery.

Despite a painful disability—one leg was amputated—Garnet became renowned as a masterful orator, pastored several important Black churches, and was a fixture at Black political conventions. He and his rival and fellow former fugitive Frederick Douglass were frequently cited as the most famous Black men in the United States. Garnet crystallized the role of an activist clergy, anticipating Martin Luther King Jr.’s social gospel. Laying the groundwork for the Black nationalist politics of Marcus Garvey and Malcolm X, Garnet became an advocate of African emigration and was eventually appointed an ambassador to Liberia, where he died.

In this book, the first biography of Garnet in fifty years, Graham Russell Gao Hodges’s exhaustive research and innovative interpretations reveal Garnet’s unflinching defense of Black civil rights and his influential thinking about building Black communities, ideas that continue to reverberate in our debates around race and society.
books.bio: Graham Russell Gao Hodges is the George Dorland Langdon Jr. Professor of History and Africana Studies at Colgate University. He is the author of David Ruggles: A Radical Black Abolitionist and the Underground Railroad in New York City .

books.title: How to Be Persuasive
books.subtitle: An Ancient Guide to the Art of Rhetoric
books.tagline: A new translation of essential selections from Aristotle’s Rhetoric , which teaches how to recognize—and resist—persuasive techniques that can be used to mislead and manipulate
books.description:
Today, the word “rhetoric” is typically used to criticize language that is empty or misleading. But the study of rhetoric was originally designed to drain false speech of its power. Rhetoric grew up in ancient Athens alongside the first democracy because the arguments of citizens were needed to replace the diktats of kings and the demagoguery of tyrants. In How to Be Persuasive , Robin Reames presents a vivid new translation of essential passages from Aristotle’s Rhetoric —a work filled with insights about how words move our hearts and minds. Featuring illuminating commentary and the original Greek on facing pages, How to Be Persuasive offers a concise and accessible introduction to Aristotle’s timeless classic.

How to Be Persuasive includes at least one selection from nearly every chapter of Aristotle’s Rhetoric , covering the importance of a speaker’s character and an audience’s emotions; common topics that can be used in every kind of argument; style and delivery; and more. Aristotle instills a keen awareness of what makes words compelling—precisely what Athenians needed to defend themselves against the linguistic distortions that led to their devastating war with Sparta two generations before. Indeed, he may have been the first to argue that the less we know about rhetoric—including how to spot the difference between good and bad arguments—the more vulnerable we are to tyranny.

The result is an enlightening introduction to how persuasion works—and how we can resist its abuse.
books.bio: Aristotle (384–322 BCE) is one of the most important and influential figures in Western philosophy. Nearly every academic discipline—from physics to poetics—owes its first method, if not its very existence, to him. Robin Reames is professor of English and the Culbertson Chair of Writing at Indiana University. She is the author of The Ancient Art of Thinking for Yourself: The Power of Rhetoric in Polarized Times and the coeditor of The Rhetorical Tradition , among other books.

books.title: Immersive Worlds
books.subtitle: Japanese Folding Screens and Sliding Doors at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum
books.tagline: The beautiful and scholarly book looks at the Japanese screens of the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum.
books.description:
The first publication in over ten years focusing on Asian art at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, this book explores how Japanese folding screens and sliding doors in the Museum’s collection visually, socially, and conceptually create immersive and transportive experiences. It will accompany a major exhibition at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, which includes Scenes from the Tale of Genji , a pair of the Gardner Museum’s most celebrated Japanese artworks.

Gabrielle Niu introduces the place of Japanese folding screens in Isabella Stewart Gardner’s collecting and curatorial practices. Focusing on the Gardner Museum’s Scenes from the Tale of Genji screens , Melissa McCormick expands upon and redefines the immersive viewing experience of the folding screen. Talia Andrei relates the Museum’s Rice Cultivation in the Four Seasons screens to social-political histories and artistic exchanges between China and Japan. Kyoko Kinoshita presents the first survey of the Gardner Museum’s sugido and fusuma , one of the rarest and most important collections of Japanese sliding doors in North America.
books.bio:
Gabrielle Niu is Associate Curator of the Collection, Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Boston. She has curated several exhibitions.

Melissa McCormick is Andrew W. Mellon Professor of Japanese Art and Culture at Harvard University and the author of several books.

Talia J. Andrei is Assistant Professor of Art History and Assistant Professor of East Asian Studies at Wesleyan University and the author of several articles and books.

Kyoko Kinoshita is Professor of Japanese art history at Tama Art University in Tokyo and Project Associate Curator of Japanese art at the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

books.title: In Community, We Can
books.subtitle: Why Latine Students Succeed Together and How Academia Needs to Change
books.authors: Marybeth Gasman, Andrés Castro Samayoa, Andrew Martinez
books.tagline: How Latine students rely on relationships with peers, mentors, families, and communities to succeed in college and graduate school
books.description:
Contrary to conventional narratives, successful transitions from college to graduate school to a university professorship emerge not from isolated instances of knowledge, skill, determination, and grit but from networks of mutual support, shared vulnerability, and communal resilience. In Community, We Can draws on the stories of nearly one hundred undergraduates to explore how Latine students depend on relationships with peers, mentors, families, and communities to navigate college and prepare for graduate school. The authors provide evidence-based data and analysis to show that a focus on individual effort ignores not only how inequities shape opportunity but also how much students lean on one another. It also places the burden of success entirely on the individual rather than asking institutions to share responsibility for students’ academic futures.

In Community, We Can shows that shared resources, mutual accountability, and collaborative problem-solving, as practiced by these students, can transform higher education, benefiting academia as a whole rather than just exceptional individuals.
books.bio: Marybeth Gasman is the Samuel DeWitt Proctor Endowed Chair and a distinguished professor in the Graduate School of Education at Rutgers University. She is the author of Doing the Right Thing: How Colleges and Universities Can Undo Systemic Racism in Faculty Hiring (Princeton), HBCU: The Power of Historically Black Colleges and Universities , and many other books. Andrés Castro Samayoa is an associate professor in the Lynch School of Education at Boston College and the author of For the Love of Teaching: How Minority Serving Institutions are Diversifying and Transforming the Profession . Andrew Martinez is the director of college success for KIPPNYC and an adjunct instructor in the Graduate School of Education at Rutgers University.

praise.q: This book makes significant contributions to the field. The focus on community rather than individual student achievements is innovative. As a new department chair, I read this with care, and it has forced me to think about ways to improve the graduate school experience for all my students.
praise.by: Sylvia Martinez, coauthor of Understanding the Latinx Experience: Developmental and Contextual Influences
praise.cred: coauthor of Understanding the Latinx Experience: Developmental and Contextual Influences

praise.q: A compelling and urgently needed reimagining of Latine students’ pathways, from undergrad through graduate education and into the professoriate, at a moment when the commitment to diversifying academia appears increasingly fragile. This timely and necessary book reminds colleges and universities of their responsibility to build more equitable, humane, and sustainable academic pathways.
praise.by: Victor B. Saenz, coediitor of Ensuring the Success of Latino Males in Higher Education
praise.cred: coediitor of Ensuring the Success of Latino Males in Higher Education

praise.q: A timely and important volume to help faculty, staff, and administrators better support Latine undergraduate students on their journeys to and through graduate school while advancing systemic reforms that foster collective community success. This book is an essential read for higher education practitioners and leaders to honor their obligation to meet students where they are and uphold community and cultural ties.”—Richard J. Reddick, author of Restorative Resistance in Higher Education: Leading in an Era of Racial Awakening and Reckoning

Navigating the path to a PhD often feels like traveling without a map—especially for Latine students, who rarely receive one. This book is that map, grounded in real student voices: it argues that institutions must be transformed to make success relational, that community drives outcomes, not just morale, and that support is a responsibility, not a favor. It's essential reading for students charting the path and the institutions responsible for building it in the first place.
praise.by: Catherine Millett, coauthor of Three Magic Letters: Getting to Ph.D
praise.cred: coauthor of Three Magic Letters: Getting to Ph.D

books.title: Islamic Thought in Early Modern India
books.subtitle: History and Legacy
books.tagline: A wide-ranging new history of Islamic thought and practice in India from the early eighteenth century to the present
books.description:
Focusing on one of the most influential families in Indian Islam, this history provides a broad yet intimate view of Islamic thought and practice in India from the early eighteenth century to the present. As Muhammad Qasim Zaman shows, the imprint of Shah Wali Allah of Delhi (1703–1762) and his descendants on Islam in South Asia extends from political and social thought to law, theories of ritual practice, sectarian polemics, Qur’anic hermeneutics, historiography, and mysticism. The sheer breadth of the family’s intellectual engagements and their afterlives provide an unparalleled perspective on changing visions of Islam and their interconnections over the past three centuries.

Based on new manuscript research, Islamic Thought in Early Modern India describes the tumultuous events through which the Wali Allah family and their associates lived, and to which they responded, including the decline of the Mughal empire, invasions and famines, the rise of the British East India Company, and the establishment of British colonial rule. It was an age that saw great debates within the Muslim community about questions of religious authority and proper Islamic belief and practice. The book also tells the story of numerous people, many now forgotten, who curated the legacy of the Wali Allah family from the mid-nineteenth century onward.

Chronicling how Muslims in India and beyond have understood their past and present, India, and the world, Islamic Thought in Early Modern India helps explain how Islam has become what it is today.
books.bio: Muhammad Qasim Zaman is the Robert H. Niehaus ’77 Professor of Near Eastern Studies and Religion at Princeton University. His books include Islam in Pakistan and The Ulama in Contemporary Islam (both Princeton).

praise.q: A truly impressive work. This will surely become a classic study of Islamic intellectual history and be read by generations to come.
praise.by: A. Azfar Moin, author of The Millennial Sovereign: Sacred Kingship and Sainthood in Islam
praise.cred: author of The Millennial Sovereign: Sacred Kingship and Sainthood in Islam

praise.q: A definitive masterpiece. Muhammad Qasim Zaman’s eloquently written account of Shah Wali Allah is one of the most complete and rich intellectual biographies of any Muslim scholar. It will likely become and remain the benchmark in studies on Wali Allah. Zaman’s fresh analysis of Wali Allah’s works and those of his descendants, and his synthesis of previous scholarship, is comprehensive, unparalleled, and masterful.
praise.by: Marcia K. Hermansen, translator of The Conclusive Argument from God: Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi’s Ḥujjat Allāh al-Bāligha
praise.cred: translator of The Conclusive Argument from God: Shāh Walī Allāh of Delhi’s Ḥujjat Allāh al-Bāligha

books.title: Jermayne MacAgy
books.subtitle: Lessons from a Curator
books.tagline: A celebration of preeminent American, curator, art historian, and museum director Jermayne MacAgy’s life and work.
books.description:
On its fortieth anniversary, the Menil Collection honors Jermayne MacAgy (1914–1964), “one of the most brilliant exhibition directors of our time,” as described by the first director of the Museum of Modern Art, Alfred Barr. Revered for her innovative techniques and her facility for exhibition conception, design, and installation, MacAgy left behind an immense legacy in her roles at the California Palace of the Legion of Honor, Contemporary Arts Museum Houston, and Houston’s University of St. Thomas, where she promoted contemporary artists and modernism, as well as historical Euro-American traditions and Indigenous art of several continents—often in dazzling theme shows.

At the heart of this in-depth survey is an illustrated compendium of MacAgy’s groundbreaking, yet underrecognized, exhibitions in San Francisco and Houston. This highly illustrated “portfolio of exhibitions” brings together original research and archival materials to highlight MacAgy’s immersive installation techniques and her sustained focus on enchanting and educating through the art object. Essays by leading scholars reflect on MacAgy’s entire career—from her intellectual background and training to her pioneering installations at midcentury, including her landmark exhibition Totems Not Taboo (1959)—and consider her vital role within twentieth-century curating and the development of the modern American art museum.

Distributed for the Menil Collection
books.bio: Michelle White is senior curator at the Menil Collection.

books.title: Listening, Sound, and the Battle for an Educated Democracy in 20th-Century America
books.tagline: Why listening and sound were once important instructional modes in schools, and why they failed to live up to their promise for American democratic education.
books.description:
A hallmark of modern liberalism is the belief that most political problems can be solved by listening. Before our current distrust and lack of reciprocal communication, teachers and researchers in English and Speech believed that listening was on its way to becoming established as a respected field. Their work—the culmination of more than fifty years of efforts in different disciplines—was motivated by the goal to establish listening and sound in education for democratic change.

In Listening, Sound, and the Battle for an Educated Democracy in 20 th -Century America , Brian Gregory draws from music education, advertising, commercial and local radio, English, and Speech to detail the evolution of listening and sound as tools to foster educated democratic citizens. With the dawn of radio broadcasting, a battle ensued over the auditory effects of educational programming that demonstrated competing discourses: the power of entertainment culture on commercial radio versus critical listening and discussion to combat the effects of emotional stimulation with local radio and teachers. This book argues that assumptions and ideologies about listening and sound have continued to impede its effectiveness up to the present.
books.bio: Brian C. Gregory is Assistant Professor of Mass Communication and Director of the WVYC Radio Station at York College of Pennsylvania.

books.title: Losing the Law
books.subtitle: How Legal Polarization Threatens American Democracy
books.tagline: A gripping account of how the distinction between law and politics is collapsing in the United States and imperiling democracy itself
books.description:
The norms that have separated law from politics in America are eroding, making government by constitutional democracy increasingly hard to sustain. Losing the Law tells the story of how we came to this precarious moment. This powerful, persuasively argued book describes how a decades-long revolution in professional culture and legal thought is fueling the nation’s authoritarian slide. It also offers essential guidance on what we can do to change course, not just by crafting institutional reforms but by resetting professional incentives and popular beliefs about the power and limits of the rule of law in constitutional governance.

Looking behind the well-recognized politics of red and blue, Deborah Pearlstein charts the independent rise of “legal polarization”—a growing divide between lawyers and judges who believe there should be a difference between law and politics and those who no longer do. Drawing on original interviews and archival research, a close reading of American law and legal thought, and a sobering accounting of recent events, she unearths the conservative legal movement’s foundation-shifting secondary effects as it established a new career pipeline from law school to judgeship, promoted partisan loyalty above professional responsibility, and popularized legal theories in irreconcilable conflict with long-settled understandings of how law worked. From the early role of unitary executive theory in kneecapping major post-Watergate reforms to originalism’s inevitable rejection of precedent, Pearlstein traces how legal polarization has supercharged democratic backsliding under Trump 2.0.

An urgent call to action by one of today’s foremost legal minds, Losing the Law lays out the complex task ahead for those committed both to understanding the depth of the current crisis and to reestablishing sustainable constitutional governance in the years ahead.
books.bio: Deborah Pearlstein is director of the Program in Law and Public Policy and the Charles and Marie Robertson Visiting Professor of Law and Public Affairs at Princeton University. Her work has appeared in leading publications such as The New York Times , The Atlantic , and The Washington Post . A practicing lawyer before entering academia, she began her legal career as a clerk to Supreme Court Justice John Paul Stevens.

books.title: Markets, State, and People
books.subtitle: Economics for Public Policy
books.tagline: A textbook that examines how societies reach decisions about the use and allocation of economic resources
books.description:
While economic research emphasizes the importance of governmental institutions for growth and progress, conventional public policy textbooks tend to focus on macroeconomic policies and on tax-and-spend decisions. Markets, State, and People stresses the basics of welfare economics and the interplay between individual and collective choices. It fills a gap by showing how economic theory relates to current policy questions, with a look at incentives, institutions, and efficiency. How should resources in society be allocated for the most economically efficient outcomes, and how does this sit with society’s sense of fairness?

Diane Coyle illustrates the ways economic ideas are the product of their historical context, and how events in turn shape economic thought. She includes many real-world examples of policies, both good and bad. Readers will learn that there are no panaceas for policy problems, but there is a practical set of theories and empirical findings that can help policymakers navigate dilemmas and trade-offs. The decisions faced by officials or politicians are never easy, but economic insights can clarify the choices to be made and the evidence that informs those choices. Coyle covers issues such as digital markets and competition policy, environmental policy, regulatory assessments, public-private partnerships, nudge policies, universal basic income, and much more.

Markets, State, and People offers a new way of approaching public economics.

A focus on markets and institutions

Policy ideas in historical context

Real-world examples

How economic theory helps policymakers tackle dilemmas and choices
books.bio: Diane Coyle is the inaugural Bennett Professor of Public Policy at the University of Cambridge. She is a member of the UK Council of Economic Advisers and the Natural Capital Committee, as well as a Fellow of the Office for National Statistics. Her books include GDP: A Brief but Affectionate History and The Economics of Enough (both Princeton). Twitter @DianeCoyle1859

praise.q: US president Harry Truman longed for a one-handed economist, because 'All my economists say ‘on one hand’ then ‘but on the other’.' He was wrong to. Equivocal books do not usually do well in a polarised world. This one deserves to buck the trend.
praise.by: Giles Wilkes, Financial Times

praise.q: Integrating economic theory into social and political contexts, this is the textbook on public policy that students need. A pleasure to use.
praise.by: Paul Collier, University of Oxford

praise.q: This book is both wise and far-ranging. If I was teaching an introductory public policy course, this would be the economics that I would adopt.
praise.by: Edward Glaeser, Harvard University

praise.q: This is a great book for teaching because, unlike standard textbooks, it situates public policy in the wider context of the values that societies hold and the ways that markets are structured.
praise.by: Rachel Griffith, University of Manchester

praise.q: This masterful book is exemplary in its resistance to sweeping panaceas promoted by socialists, free-market worshippers, and fomenters of academic paranoia about established institutions. Our students and the public need sensible writing about policy choices and governance. This book is devotedly and insistently sensible.
praise.by: Don Ross, author of Philosophy of Economics

books.title: Nowhere Left to Go
books.subtitle: Jews and the Rise of the Global Right
books.tagline: A history of one of the most controversial and consequential geopolitical developments of the last fifty years: how Jews became allied with the global Right
books.description:
Nowhere Left to Go is a book about the upending of Western political life. It tells the story of how Jews, once the icons of liberal and progressive causes, emerged as avatars for illiberal political parties across the world over the last half-century. At one time identified with the Left, Jews became associated with the Right. Drawing from previously unexamined archives, dozens of new interviews with leading economists, politicians, and religious figures, and his own vast knowledge of Jewish history, Eliyahu Stern offers an unprecedented account of how and why this shift happened. For the first time, he reveals the pivotal role Jewish encounters with American Christian nationalists, European identitarians, and Russian Eurasians have played in the Middle East, the United States, and Europe from the 1970s through October 7, 2023.

Urging a return to a realist politics and a more diverse set of alliances, Stern confronts the failures of right-wing Jewish alliances to ultimately answer the Jewish question. What political wilderness will Jews find themselves in, he asks, if both the Right and Left turn on them? And what steps might Jews take to ensure their well-being and security? Impeccably researched and judiciously observed, this book is an eye-opening account of Jewish life in an increasingly polarized political landscape.
books.bio: Eliyahu Stern is professor of modern Jewish intellectual and cultural history at Yale University. He is the author of The Genius: Elijah of Vilna and the Making of Modern Judaism and Jewish Materialism: The Intellectual Revolution of the 1870s . He lives in Brooklyn, NY.

praise.q: Drawing on deeply sourced interviews and wide-ranging archival research, Stern challenges the conventional wisdom, corrects the historical record, and delivers a clear-eyed and ‘realist’ assessment of the causes and consequences of the alliance for Jews and non-Jews alike. This seminal study makes a vital contribution to the burgeoning literature on religion and the Right.
praise.by: Philip Gorski, The Geneva Graduate Institute

praise.q: Throughout the 20th century, the Jews were the natural allies of socialism and universalism . . . How then did they become key actors in the politics of the Right? This engaging and magnificently researched book offers a definitive answer, without excuses or vituperations. Its unflinching sobriety will leave you more intelligent.
praise.by: Eva Illouz, author of The Emotional Life of Populism
praise.cred: author of The Emotional Life of Populism

praise.q: Nowhere Left to Go is a massive yet mercifully readable study of national, religious, racial, and ethnic rift and drift, swing and sobriety, in which Jews as ever embody the zeitgeist, define its extremes, and redefine reality. Eliyahu Stern’s passion and rectitude shine from every page, in his accounts of backstage Washington and front-page Gaza. This landmark work demonstrates how rigorous intellectual history founded in personal experience can attain to a sort of prophecy.
praise.by: Joshua Cohen, author of Dead Herzls

praise.q: This book blew my mind. Once you’ve read what Stern has to say about the evolving relationship between Jews and the global right, you will never see the history or praxis of modern Jewish politics the same way again. Transformative.
praise.by: Abigail Green, University of Oxford

books.title: Rare Tongues
books.subtitle: The Secret Stories of Hidden Languages
books.tagline: An enthralling tour of the world’s rarest and most endangered languages
books.description:
Languages and cultures are becoming increasingly homogenous, with the resulting loss of a rich linguistic tapestry reflecting unique perspectives and ways of life. Rare Tongues tells the stories of the world’s rare and vanishing languages, revealing how each is a living testament to human resilience, adaptability, and the perennial quest for identity.

Taking readers on a captivating journey of discovery, Lorna Gibb explores the histories of languages under threat or already extinct as well as those in resurgence, shedding light on their origins, development, and distinctive voices. She travels the globe—from Australia and Finland to India, the Canary Islands, Namibia, Scotland, and Paraguay—showing how these languages are not mere words and syntax but keepers of diverse worldviews, sites of ethnic conflict, and a means for finding surprising commonalities. Readers learn the basics of how various language systems work—with vowels and consonants, whistles and clicks, tonal inflections, or hand signs—and how this kaleidoscope of self-expression carries vital information about our planet, indigenous cultures and tradition, and the history and evolution of humankind.

Rare Tongues is essential reading for anyone concerned about the preservation of endangered languages and an eloquent and disarmingly personal meditation on why the world’s linguistic heritage is so fundamental to our shared experience—and why its loss should worry us all.
books.bio: Lorna Gibb is associate professor of creative writing and linguistics at the University of Stirling. Her books include The Extraordinary Life of Rebecca West , Lady Hester: Queen of the East , and the novel A Ghost’s Story . Her writing has appeared in leading publications such as Granta and the Telegraph .

praise.q: A thought-provoking tour of the diversity within the world’s languages—and a strong case for their preservation.
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews

praise.q: Rare Tongues is at heart a personal journey. Drawing on her experience in dictionary-making and her childhood in a working-class Glasgow suburb, Gibb illustrates the perils of ‘creeping linguistic homogeneity’ and argues for the necessity of a linguistically diverse world. We are apt to label some languages ‘useful’ because of their large speaker base; that narrow definition is firmly challenged here. Gibb navigates complex and sensitive terrain—technical and politically charged—with both scholarly rigor and warmth.
praise.by: Henry Hitchings, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: A defiant manifesto for linguistic pluralism. . . . Gibb’s Rare Tongues is more than a book; it is a clarion call to recognize linguistic diversity as a cornerstone of human heritage. . . . This is essential reading for linguists, anthropologists, and activists alike. It earns its place in academic discourse by challenging disciplinary boundaries and advocating for a more inclusive, compassionate linguistics—one that hears, respects, and fights for every voice in humanity’s polyphonic chorus.
praise.by: Shuzhen Jiang and Junwei Zhu, Language in Society

praise.q: Lorna Gibb’s Rare Tongues offers a fresh and personal perspective and lots of interesting facts for people who love languages, giving a kaleidoscopic tour of linguistic curiosities and principles.
praise.by: K. David Harrison, author of The Last Speakers: The Quest to Save the World’s Most Endangered Languages
praise.cred: author of The Last Speakers: The Quest to Save the World’s Most Endangered Languages

books.title: Resource Rationality
books.subtitle: Foundations of Cognitive Economy
books.authors: Clarence Irving Lewis Professor of Philosophy and Professor of Computer Science (by courtesy) Thomas Icard
books.tagline: An exploration of central topics in the foundations of cognitive science through the lens of reasoning and decision-making with limited cognitive resources.
books.description:
The approach to rational decision-making known as resource rationality has recently seen rapid development in the cognitive sciences. In Resource Rationality , Thomas Icard explores central topics in the foundations of cognitive science through the lens of reasoning and decision-making with cognitive resource constraints. He utilizes resource rationality both as a framework for normative assessment and as a source of scientific hypotheses about how mental processes work. He also discusses resource rationality in the context of large language models and contemporary topics in deep learning and neural network interpretability (a method for explaining the behavior of AI neural networks).

Icard begins with background on traditional decision theory, basic learning theory, information theory, and elementary theory of computation, then presents empirical studies of human perception, reasoning, and decision-making. Finally, he turns to core theoretical questions in cognitive science on the nature of cognitive costs, human “rational faculties,” and algorithms and algorithmic implementation. He offers a novel account of cognitive costs: what they are and how they can be measured. Throughout, he grounds his discussion in the productive tension between the normative and the descriptive in the computational, philosophical, psychological, economic, and mathematical foundations of resource rationality.
books.bio: Thomas Icard is the Clarence Irving Lewis Professor of Philosophy and Professor of Computer Science (by courtesy) at Stanford University.

books.title: Roads Not Taken
books.subtitle: Lessons for Building a New Social Contract at Work
books.tagline: For American workers, the social contract is broken. This book gives a firsthand view of where the breaks occurred, and a prescription for rebuilding it to give workers their due.
books.description:
With AI making the decisions and CEOs and moguls making the money, sometimes it seems that most workers today might as well be drones. If not for a long string of missed opportunities over the last 50 years, it might have been different. In Roads Not Taken, Thomas Kochan reviews the turning points where the social contract fractured and broke, reducing workers’ voices as well as their compensation, benefits, and status. And in the lessons learned from these historical examples, he identifies the foundation for building a new labor relations system that ensures workers will share in the benefits from AI and puts America on course for an innovative and durable social contract at work.

As a longtime advisor to government, labor, and management leaders, Kochan offers an eyewitness perspective on the mounting mistakes made in America’s labor relations system beginning, roughly, with Ronald Reagan’s firing of striking air traffic controllers in 1981. His book makes a strong case for new strategies on the part of labor unions and other worker advocacy groups, business, and government—strategies not wedded to the legacy labor law and practice that have failed American workers for so long. Recasting the social contract on this basis, Kochan insists, is key to rebuilding our democracy and its institutions after the damage wrought in recent years.
books.bio:
Thomas A. Kochan (Author)

Thomas A. Kochan is the George M. Bunker Emeritus Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management and the MIT Institute for Work and Employment Research. He is coauthor (with Paul Osterman, Richard M. Locke, and Michael J. Piore) of Working in America (MIT Press).

books.title: Simeon Solomon
books.subtitle: Queer and Jewish in Victorian London
books.authors: Roberto C. Ferrari and Sophie Lynford
books.tagline: A landmark study of Simeon Solomon, a queer Jewish artist who reimagined faith, beauty, and desire in Victorian Britain
books.description:
Radiant biblical subjects. Haunting mythological visions. Intimate scenes of same-sex love. Few artists worked with such breadth, originality, and conviction as Simeon Solomon. Born into a middle-class Jewish family in Victorian London, he became one of the most daring and distinctive figures of the Pre-Raphaelite movement, hailed by fellow artist Edward Burne-Jones as “the greatest of us all.”

After Solomon’s arrest for attempted sodomy, his career faltered. Rejected by the art establishment in which he had once thrived, he lived for decades under precarious circumstances marked by alcoholism, homelessness, and repeated stays in workhouses. Yet Solomon did not disappear. He continued to produce an extensive body of work that found a new generation of champions, even as later histories of British art minimized his achievements or omitted him entirely.

This book restores Solomon to the ranks of the nineteenth century’s major artists by recognizing his Judaism and sexuality as essential to the power of his work. Drawing on Pre-Raphaelitism, Jewish tradition, and classical antiquity, Solomon forged an artistic vision that transcended the conventions of the Victorian era.

Exhibition Schedule:

Delaware Art Museum

(March 13 – June 27, 2027)
books.bio:
Sophie Lynford is the Annette Woolard-Provine Curator of the Bancroft Collection of Pre-Raphaelite Art at the Delaware Art Museum. She is the author of Painting Dissent: Art, Ethics, and the American Pre-Raphaelites and coauthor of Picturesque and Sublime: Thomas Cole’s Trans-Atlantic Inheritance.

Roberto C. Ferrari is the Curator of Art Properties at Columbia University. He has published extensively on the life and art of Simeon Solomon and is a specialist in British art of the long nineteenth century.

books.title: The Age of Oil
books.tagline: A long out-of-print lost classic, from a pivotal figure of New York’s art and No Wave film scenes.
books.description:
Originally published in 1987 and long impossible to find, The Age of Oil collects fifteen essays by Duncan Smith (1954–1991), a pivotal figure of the downtown New York art and No Wave film scenes. Drawing on Freud, Lacan, and Derrida, Smith developed a unique style that pushed the strategies of poststructuralism into the realm of experimental writing. Smith’s obsessive pursuit of “cryptograms” in essays such as the linguistic tour de force “Calling All Cars” paralleled and almost certainly influenced his friend Jean-Michel Basquiat’s use of text in his paintings. A candid chronicler of New York City gay life and a sharp-eyed observer of American pop culture, Smith also theorized, most notably in his text “On the Current Symbolic Status of Oil,” that the ubiquity of petroleum products has inescapably structured our language and society.

Simultaneously with this new edition of The Age of Oil , Semiotext(e) is bringing out Days in the Clouds , the never-before-published book Smith completed before his death from AIDS.
books.bio: Duncan Smith (1953–1991) is known for his innovative writings that reflect his extensive research in psychoanalysis, semiotics, Marxist ideology, and literature. In 1976, Smith left undergraduate studies at the University of Washington to move to New York City, where he became a beloved friend for many in downtown avant-garde circles. In 1987, Slate Press published Smith’s first collection of cultural criticism, The Age of Oil . That same year, in the midst of earning his PhD at Cornell University, Smith learned of his HIV-positive status and embarked on a series of essays centered on his experiences with AIDS. These would become Days in the Clouds , completed in Portland, OR, some months before his death in February 1991.

books.title: The Goldsmiths’ Company
books.subtitle: 700 years of craft and community
books.tagline: This lavishly illustrated publication is the first exploration of the
books.description:
The Goldsmiths’ Company today supports gold and silversmiths, jewellers, charities and consumers through a contemporary approach rooted in a remarkable history. For more than seven centuries it has played a pivotal role in Britain’s relationship with precious metal. Its work has found its way into the lives of ordinary people, guaranteeing the purity of coins and wedding rings and inspiring everyday turns of phrase such as ‘hallmark’ and ‘acid test’. Yet despite this cultural and economic significance, its history has not always been well-understood.

The Goldsmiths' Company: 700 years of craft and community provides an authoritative account of one of our oldest and most influential institutions, which has, unusually, maintained its foundational duties into the present. Helen Clifford ’ s approachable narrative tells this story for the first time in a single volume, beginning with a brotherhood of craftsmen in the political chaos of the 12th century and ending as their successors engage with the challenges of the 21st.
books.bio: Helen Clifford holds a Ph.D. in the eighteenth-century London silver trade. She is an academic, curator and independent author. She is a Freeman of the Goldsmiths’ Company and is currently the Archivist of the Worshipful Company of Grocers, for whom she recently wrote its history

books.title: The Iraq Wars
books.tagline: From the foremost scholar of the subject, a groundbreaking history of American involvement in Iraq to the present day
books.description: Since 1979, the United States has waged at least five wars with or against Iraq. Yet the history of American involvement there has not been told in full, and what has been told is often misconstrued. The Iraq Wars offers a comprehensive history of the United States and Iraq, explaining the events and factors that drove the political, diplomatic, and military choices the United States made with regard to the region. More than just a comprehensive history, The Iraq Wars also assesses alternative paths that we might reasonably have taken instead. What if the United States had not given Iraq a free hand in the 1980s to develop weapons of mass destruction? What if George H. W. Bush had extended Operation Desert Storm for another 48 hours—or marched on Baghdad—to bring down Saddam Husayn’s regime? Was the 2003 invasion of Iraq necessary? How should the United States have managed the aftermath? Even decades after the events took place, many aspects of the United States’ changing, vexing entanglement with Iraq remain controversial to the point of provoking partisan anger. This book offers indispensable guidance for citizens and leaders who wish to avoid repeating the same mistakes.
books.bio: Kenneth M. Pollack is vice president for policy at the Middle East Institute. He has served as a Persian Gulf military analyst at the CIA and as director for Persian Gulf Affairs at the National Security Council. His many books include The Threatening Storm , Arabs at War , and The Persian Puzzle .

praise.q: Kenneth Pollack emerges, with this book, as a Thucydides for our time. Like his ancient predecessor, he chronicles a great power’s involvement in a decades-long war that it didn’t know how to leave or win. He does so with extraordinary precision, but without losing sight of how regional cultures can subvert global strategies. The Iraq Wars , like The Peloponnesian War , should be required reading for anyone seeking to avoid the slippery slopes that so often accompany good intentions.
praise.by: John Lewis Gaddis, Yale University

praise.q: The most exceptional historical analysis of the trajectory of the U.S.–Iraq relationship yet written. The Iraq Wars is incisive, exhaustively researched, superbly detailed, and offers profound insights and thoughtful reflections on more than four decades of war, reconstruction, and political evolution. Drawing on firsthand observations, innumerable interviews with participants, and deep immersion in Iraq’s complexities, Pollack delivers a masterwork that will stand as the definitive account of the conflict and its enduring consequences.”—General David Petraeus, US Army (Ret.); former Commander of the Surge in Iraq, US Central Command, and Coalition Forces in Afghanistan; former director of the CIA; coauthor of Conflict: The Evolution of Warfare from 1945 to Gaza

For decades to come this will be the definitive study of a series of wars that have shaped the Middle East, American foreign policy, and international politics for well over a generation. Ken Pollack is the rare observer-participant who can care deeply but judge fairly, who can describe complexity and confess error, research deeply and write wonderfully. In The Iraq Wars he has produced a masterpiece of narrative, analysis, and policy reflection of enduring and profound value.
praise.by: Eliot A. Cohen, Arleigh Burke Chair in Strategy, CSIS
praise.cred: Arleigh Burke Chair in Strategy, CSIS

praise.q: Kenneth Pollack brings his formidable analytical abilities to bear in this well-researched and compelling history. The Iraq Wars sheds fresh light and understanding on America’s searing experience in a troubled and divided country. The lessons Pollack reveals across the experience of the past half century are crucial for U.S. policy and strategy today and tomorrow.”—H. R. McMaster, former National Security Advisor, author of Dereliction of Duty , Battlegrounds , and At War with Ourselves

Ken Pollack combines unmatched credentials as a historian and a policy practitioner to offer the definitive work on the tangled relationship between the U.S. and Iraq. He avoids easy answers, conveying the reality of the hard choices that confront political leaders. Equally important, he illuminates the domestic forces that inevitably shape foreign policy. The Iraq Wars is essential reading for anyone concerned about America’s place in the world. It is a magnificent book.”—Ryan Crocker, former U.S. Ambassador to Iraq“ The Iraq Wars is a detailed, illuminating, refreshingly measured history of U.S.–Iraq relations. Drawing on his vast experience in government, the academy, and think tanks, Kenneth Pollack cuts through the noise to expose the real reasons—and hard lessons—of America’s involvement in Iraq. As the Middle East’s opportunities and challenges continue to shape U.S. foreign policy, this indispensable book will serve as a vital resource for the next generation of policymakers, analysts, and students.
praise.by: Walter Russell Mead, author of The Arc of a Covenant: The United States, Israel, and the Fate of the Jewish People
praise.cred: author of The Arc of a Covenant: The United States, Israel, and the Fate of the Jewish People

books.title: The Medieval Moon
books.subtitle: A History of Haunting and Blessing
books.tagline: A vivid new history of how medieval people around the world perceived the moon
books.description:
When they gazed at the moon, medieval people around the globe saw an object that was at once powerful and fragile, distant and intimate—and sometimes all this at once. The moon could convey love, beauty, and gentleness; but it could also be about pain, hatred, and violence. In its circularity the moon was associated with fullness and fertility. Yet in its crescent and other shifting forms, the moon could seem broken, even wounded.

In this beautifully illustrated history, Ayoush Lazikani reveals the many ways medieval people felt and wrote about the moon. Ranging across the world, from China to South America, Korea to Wales, Lazikani explores how different cultures interacted with the moon. From the idea that the Black Death was caused by a lunar eclipse to the wealth of Persian love poetry inspired by the moon’s beauty, this is a truly global account of our closest celestial neighbour.
books.bio: Ayoush Lazikani is a lecturer at the University of Oxford. A specialist in medieval literature, she is the author of Cultivating the Heart and Emotion in Christian and Islamic Contemplative Texts, 1100–1250, and an associate editor for the Palgrave Encyclopedia of Medieval Women’s Writing in the Global Middle Ages .

praise.q: Offers a thoughtful step away from viewing the Moon as solely the domain of the astronomer. We learn the Moon—as fact, as metaphor, as symbol—is for everyone.
praise.by: Emily Winterburn, BBC Sky at Night

praise.q: We might not consider the moon a planet anymore, but we still feel the pull of its tender gaze and a sense of kinship with its magic, the many forms of which illuminate Lazikani’s book.
praise.by: Mathew Lyons, Literary Review

praise.q: Reading this sensitive study, it is hard not to feel a deep sense of connection with those long-ago skygazers. This celestial sphere has lost none of its mystery and allure.
praise.by: Katherine Harvey, Engelsberg Ideas

praise.q: Lazikani has committed to creating a work that is beautiful as well as informative, drawing us back through the ages to feel the moon observing and changing us, as medieval people did.
praise.by: Mary Hitchman, Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: Lazikani . . . offers a genuinely global vision of the period, taking in Japanese, Polynesian, and Mayan culture. [This] book powerfully reminds us that the moon was once, and can still be, the enchanted orb of poets.
praise.by: Francis Young, History Today

praise.q: The Medieval Moon opens up for us the mysterious world of our nearest celestial neighbour in a rich, vibrant fashion that will appeal to curious minds who want to understand the medieval world better.
praise.by: Holly A. Brown, Medieval Musings

praise.q: This book tells the extraordinary global story of the imaginative power of the medieval moon, via Sufi poetry and Zodiac men, Old English riddles and Inca statues, Andalusian medicine and Old Norse theology. The Medieval Moon is a beautiful and innovative book, accessibly written, rigorously researched, and touched by the transformative potential of its subject.
praise.by: Marion Turner, author of The Wife of Bath
praise.cred: author of The Wife of Bath

praise.q: Ayoush Lazikani triumphs again—this time with a deeply thoughtful and lyrically sublime book. This sensitive, dreamscape of a study offers alluring new insights and confirms Lazikani’s position at the very forefront of her field.
praise.by: Liz Herbert McAvoy, author of The Enclosed Garden and the Medieval Religious Imaginary
praise.cred: author of The Enclosed Garden and the Medieval Religious Imaginary

praise.q: The Medieval Moon presents not a moon, but the moons of poets and natural philosophers, astrologers and travellers from areas as far apart from one another as Japan, China, the Abbasid Caliphate, and the kingdoms of Christendom. Lazikani’s approach is as cross-cultural as it is interdisciplinary, written in a style that is both entertaining and erudite, filled with wonderful stories from a broad array of traditions.
praise.by: Scott E. Hendrix, Carroll University

praise.q: Ayoush Lazikani’s wonderful and beautifully-written book of the moon surveys the nights and enchantments of the middle ages, ranging widely in place, time and culture. Seldom has so much learning, and so much magic, been contained in one elegant and readable volume.
praise.by: Peter Davidson, author of The Last of the Light
praise.cred: author of The Last of the Light

books.title: The Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization, Volume 4
books.subtitle: Late Medieval Era, 1200–1500
books.series: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization
books.tagline: Volume 4 of The Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization, covering the later Middle Ages and highlighting the religious and cultural shifts of Jewish life at that time
books.description:
At the start of the late medieval period, the center of Jewish intellectual productivity had shifted from Muslim lands to Christian Europe. By its end, Jews had been expelled from most of western Europe. In the intervening three hundred years, Jews in western and central Europe, the Middle East, and beyond produced a wealth of literary, legal, philosophical, and scientific writings, primarily but not exclusively written in Hebrew.
