Adding to this rich abundance, Jewish migration fostered increased contact and intellectual exchange among far-flung Jewish communities, each of which possessed a distinct regional culture.

This volume gathers over a thousand primary sources—texts, translated from more than a dozen languages, as well as a stunning array of visual images—that represent the breadth and diversity of late medieval Jewish cultures. The birth of kabbalah, a major development in the field of Jewish mysticism, represents a highlight of these years. Alongside religious, literary, and scholarly writings, the volume presents personal letters, chronicles, communal records, account ledgers, tombstone inscriptions, legal contracts, court testimonies, and much more, giving expression to the full sweep of Jewish civilization. The texts and artifacts in this volume offer an exciting window into the social, political, economic, and religious life of Jews in the late Middle Ages.
books.bio: Jonathan S. Ray is the Sam Eig Professor of Jewish Studies at Georgetown University. He is the author of Jewish Life in Medieval Spain: A New History and After Expulsion: 1492 and the Making of Sephardic Jewry , among other books. Deborah Dash Moore is Jonathan Freedman Distinguished University Professor of History and Professor of Judaic Studies at the University of Michigan. She is editor in chief of The Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization.
subjects: Posen Library of Jewish Culture and Civilization

books.title: The Secret Life and Death of Ornament in Berlin
books.tagline: A riveting and deftly rendered meditation on the removal of ornament from the built environment in Berlin. An illustrated urban history guaranteed to make you see your city anew, from an award-winning contemporary poet.
books.description:
An illustrated urban history guaranteed to make you see your city anew, from an award-winning contemporary poet.

When the poet Donna Stonecipher first moved to Berlin in 2004, she noticed something strange: street after street was lined with blank façades. Where once ornament had gamboled across those surfaces, now rows of scraped-clean apartment buildings greeted the passerby. As she began to dig deeper into the question, she discovered that over half of Berlin’s pre–World War I buildings had had their ornament removed. There was a dramatic story behind this removal—a story containing a pocket history of ideas about class, taste, excess, deceit, art, aesthetics, meaning, authenticity, and more—and how they are reflected through our built environment.

A personal, propulsive, and insightful meditation, The Secret Life and Death of Ornament in Berlin tells the story of this intriguing quest. Taking the reader along on her long revelatory walks and bike rides around Berlin, Stonecipher delves into the surprising, uncanny, enchanting, and sometimes haunting stories that figured in the banishing of ornament. We learn about everything from an obsession with hygiene to a mania for crystals, from a housing structure called “rent barracks” to the humiliation of losing a world war—and ultimately, why the erasing of ornament had such a profound effect on Berlin’s visual landscape, and in turn, the world’s.
books.bio: Donna Stonecipher is the author of six books of poetry, most recently The Ruins of Nostalgia , which was named a best book of 2023 by NPR, and Transaction Histories , which was listed by The New York Times as one of the 10 best poetry books of 2018. She has also published one book of criticism, Prose Poetry and the City . Her poems have been translated into seven languages, and her translation of Austrian poet Friederike Mayröcker received a National Endowment for the Arts fellowship.

books.title: The Story of Drawing
books.subtitle: An Alternative History of Art
books.tagline: Winner of the Apollo Book of the Year Award 2024
books.description:
Drawing is at the heart of human creativity. The most democratic form of art-making, it requires nothing more than a plain surface and a stub of pencil, a piece of chalk or an inky brush. Our prehistoric ancestors drew with natural pigments on the walls of caves, and every subsequent culture has practised drawing—whether on papyrus, parchment, or paper. Artists throughout history have used drawing as part of the creative process.

While painting and sculpture have been shaped heavily by money and influence, drawing has always offered extraordinary creative latitude. Here we see the artist at his or her most unguarded. Susan Owens offers a glimpse over artists’ shoulders—from Michelangelo, Rembrandt, and Hokusai to Van Gogh, Käthe Kollwitz, and Yayoi Kusama—as they work, think, and innovate, as they scrutinise the world around them or escape into imagination.

The Story of Drawing loops around the established history of art, sometimes staying close, at other times diving into exhilarating and altogether less familiar territory.
books.bio: Dr Susan Owens is a writer, art historian and former V&A curator. Her previous books include The Art of Drawing , Spirit of Place and Imagining England’s Past .

praise.q: [A] compelling and enlightening book.”—Michael Prodger, Apollo
Owens’s selection of artworks is superb. Each provides a plot point in her history of drawing. . . . Its scope is enormous, but the book feels suitably intimate.
praise.by: Daisy Dunn, Literary Review

praise.q: Owens’s book matters because drawing continues to be marginalized in public understanding of what art is. . . . The Story of Drawing makes the case for drawing as uniquely able to convey aspects of human experience that no other medium can.
praise.by: Ben Street, Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: It is a history of materials as well as of style, taking in developments in paper-making and implements.
praise.by: Apollo

praise.q: Susan Owens shows not just the centrality of graphic art from prehistory onwards, but how artists from Dürer to Seurat used pen and pencil as a way to investigate their most private thoughts.
praise.by: Michael Prodger, New Statesman

praise.q: With Owens’s expertise as a curator and art historian, it is detailed and precise—the history of paper, the qualities of pen-nibs and the properties of chalk all feature—but most of all, it reads as a story of delight in its objects.
praise.by: Apollo

praise.q: With accuracy and passion, [Owens] carefully dissects everything from the history of paper through to the properties of chalk.
praise.by: Wedlake Bell

praise.q: [Owens] has a clear sense that there is simply something about drawings: something personal and contingent; something that makes them exciting.
praise.by: Keith Miller, Art Newspaper

praise.q: It is fascinating to follow Susan Owens as she dissects the sketches of artists ranging from Michelangelo to Käthe Kollwitz. [This book] offers a way of understanding artists at their most unguarded.
praise.by: Phoebe Frangoul, Elle Decoration , “Best Books to Give (or Keep),” Christmas 2024
praise.cred: Elle Decoration , “Best Books to Give (or Keep),” Christmas 2024

praise.q: [This book is] comprehensive and tantalises enough about each of her subjects to encourage us to look for more.
praise.by: Nicholas Cranfield, Church Times

books.title: The Structure of Intellectual Evolution
books.subtitle: A New History of Knowledge from the Bronze Age to Isaac Newton
books.tagline: A monumental history of human knowledge from the ancient world to the Enlightenment
books.description:
The Structure of Intellectual Evolution challenges the widely held belief that humanity’s most transformative intellectual advances resulted from dramatic ruptures with tradition, revealing instead how our greatest breakthroughs emerged from established systems of learning. It tells the stories of the people and institutions behind these changes, from the scribes of ancient Mesopotamia and the philologists of Alexandria to the astronomers of the Islamic world and the logicians of the medieval university. This sweeping, multifaceted history culminates in the Europe of Erasmus, Galileo, and Newton, offering bold new perspectives on the intellectual transformations of the Renaissance, the Scientific Revolution, and the Enlightenment.

Dmitri Levitin takes us into temples, madrasas, universities, and other institutions of learning to show how new knowledge was anchored in educational practices and how those practices structured intellectual change. Spanning both the sciences and the humanities—from alchemy to anatomy, grammar to geology—he sheds light on the social and ideological forces that stimulated inquiry and gave rise to new ways of thinking that took on a life of their own.

A dazzling tour de force from one of the world’s leading historians of ideas, The Structure of Intellectual Evolution reframes our understanding of human knowledge, showing how its gradual advance was rooted in established educational institutions and scholarly traditions.
books.bio: Dmitri Levitin is a fellow of All Souls College, University of Oxford, and a regular contributor to Literary Review , The Times Literary Supplement , and the London Review of Books . His books include The Kingdom of Darkness and Ancient Wisdom in the Age of the New Science .

books.title: The Two-Leviathan Problem
books.subtitle: Why Rival Hegemons Cannot Coexist
books.authors: Joshua Byun and John J. Mearsheimer
books.tagline: A major theoretical statement on why a world with two hegemons is dangerous and unstable
books.description:
Should the United States—the dominant power in the Western Hemisphere since the late nineteenth century—fear another great power rising to a similar position elsewhere in the world? This is a vital question on which there is little agreement, yet until now no one has analyzed in a rigorous way what a world of rival hegemons would look like. In this book, Joshua Byun and John J. Mearsheimer argue that such a world would be far more dangerous than our current world. Being the world’s only regional hegemon is so advantageous that, in a world with two, each side would have an overwhelming incentive to erode the other’s dominance in its neighborhood. Intense security competition would compromise each state’s ability to defend its security interests and accumulate wealth.

This book is for anyone seeking to understand what would happen if China were to dominate East Asia, and how the balance of power in distant regions affects U.S. national security.
books.bio: Joshua Byun is assistant professor of security studies in the Edmund A. Walsh School of Foreign Service, Georgetown University, and author of The Adversary’s Veto: Rival Powers, Alliance Politics, and the Limits of Grand Strategy . John J. Mearsheimer is the R. Wendell Harrison Distinguished Service Professor of Political Science at the University of Chicago. He is author of The Tragedy of Great Power Politics and The Great Delusion: Liberal Dreams and International Realities , and coauthor of How States Think: The Rationality of Foreign Policy .

books.title: The West
books.subtitle: The History of an Idea
books.tagline: A comprehensive intellectual history of the idea of the West
books.description:
How did “the West” come to be used as a collective self-designation signaling political and cultural commonality? When did “Westerners” begin to refer to themselves in this way? Was the idea handed down from the ancient Greeks, or coined by nineteenth-century imperialists? Neither, writes Georgios Varouxakis in The West, his ambitious and fascinating genealogy of the idea. “The West” was not used by Plato, Cicero, Locke, Mill, or other canonized figures of what we today call the Western tradition. It was not first wielded by empire-builders. It gradually emerged as of the 1820s and was then, Varouxakis shows, decisively promoted in the 1840s by the French philosopher Auguste Comte (whose political project, incidentally, was passionately anti-imperialist). The need for the use of the term “the West” emerged to avoid the confusing or unwanted consequences of the use of “Europe.” The two overlapped, but were not identical, with the West used to differentiate from certain “others” within Europe as well as to include the Americas.

After examining the origins, Varouxakis traces the many and often astonishingly surprising changes in the ways in which the West has been understood, and the different intentions and consequences related to a series of these contested definitions. While other theories of the West consider only particular aspects of the concept and its history (if only in order to take aim at its reputation), Varouxakis’s analysis offers a comprehensive account that reaches to the present day, exploring the multiplicity of current, and not least, prospective future meanings. He concludes with an examination of how, since 2022, definitions and membership of the West have been reworked to consider Ukraine, as the evolution and redefinitions continue.
books.bio: Georgios Varouxakis is professor of the history of political thought at Queen Mary University of London and Codirector of the Centre for the Study of the History of Political Thought. He is the author of Mill on Nationality , Victorian Political Thought on France and the French , and Liberty Abroad: J. S. Mill on International Relations and the coauthor of Contemporary France .

praise.q: In The West: The History of an Idea , Georgios Varouxakis tells this story with wit, insight, and erudition. It is our great fortune that the first comprehensive history of the idea of the West is also, for the foreseeable future, the best. Anyone with ideas on the subject will be well advised to read it closely and keep it within reach.
praise.by: Yuri Slezkine, New York Review of Books

praise.q: Illuminating. . . . As talk of the West is once again resurgent, Varouxakis’s book offers the best guide to understanding the meaning of this deeply elusive idea.
praise.by: Jacobin

praise.q: Georgios Varouxakis’s history of the idea of the West. . . is enormously illuminating.
praise.by: Hans Kundnani, Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: The West is a monumental achievement of scholarship. Its chief contribution is its decentering of imperial and racial paradigms, which have become politicized and turned into stale orthodoxies that have led to distortions in historical understanding.
praise.by: Max Skjönsberg, Law & Liberty

praise.q: A seriously impressive piece of intellectual history.
praise.by: Nick Spencer, The Spectator

praise.q: This book will serve as a salutary reminder of how recent our ideas about the ancient past can really be and how deceptively complex are the ties that bind us with it.
praise.by: Mark Mazower, Financial Times

praise.q: [A] masterful study."—G. John Ikenberry, Foreign Affairs
Georgios Varouxakis has written a much-needed book: The West: The History of an Idea . . . . The kaleidoscope of quotations in his book testifies to a Herculean scholarly effort.
praise.by: Jaroslaw Kuisz, Foreign Policy

praise.q: A deeply erudite yet highly readable work that lays many myths to rest. Varouxakis may have written the most original history book of the year.
praise.by: Daniel Johnson, The Critic

praise.q: [ The West ] is a model of intellectual history, tracing the idea of the West from its surprising origins, through two centuries of shifting sands, to the current (but hardly unique) crisis, without ever unduly praising or burying the phenomenon. A cool intellectual breeze for an overheated debate.
praise.by: Nick Spencer, The Tablet

books.title: The World Atlas of Language
books.subtitle: Mapping the Story of Speech and Writing
books.tagline: A fascinating visual exploration of all things linguistic, tracing how words, sounds, scripts, norms, and borders are in constant flux
books.description:
Did you know that more than 7,000 languages are spoken today, but that fifty percent of the world’s people use only fifteen of them? Or that there are hundreds of separate sign languages? Or that a dog’s bark is represented with wildly different sounds in English, Czech, and Thai? In The World Atlas of Language , Gaston Dorren, the international bestselling author of Lingo , Babel , and other books about languages, invites readers on a captivating journey that charts the geographical spread of languages and dialects around the world through the ages—and tells the incredible stories behind them in his unmistakable style. The result is an essential reference for anyone who loves how humans speak, write—and vary.

Organized by theme and richly illustrated throughout with full-color maps, timelines, and other graphics, this book traces the origins and evolutions of the world’s languages and of the communities that nurture and live in them. From Old, Middle, and Modern English and the great linguistic variety of the Americas to the lingua francas of Africa and the many unique tongues that are about to fall silent, the atlas reveals an astonishing linguistic diversity.

Features 100 full-color maps, timelines, and other graphics

Tells engaging stories about the origins and evolutions of languages and how they have been carried around the world by nations, religions, and empires

Includes sections on:

Where—Where languages are spoken and where they have moved over time

What—Words, scripts, sounds, and grammar

When—Language diversity and the way languages grow, decline, and change across history

What Else—Language and nationalism, books and readers, names, and related topics

An essential reference for readers interested in languages, words, and their histories
books.bio: Gaston Dorren is the author of the international bestsellers Lingo and Babel , which have been published in more than a dozen languages each, and the Global Edition of League of the Lexicon, the popular game about words and language. Ross Perlin is a lecturer in Slavic languages at Columbia University, codirector of the Endangered Language Alliance, and author of the acclaimed Language City.

books.title: Tinderbox
books.subtitle: The Unpredictable Rise and Uncertain Future of Modern India
books.tagline: An eloquent portrait of contemporary India that reveals how the Hindu nationalist movement threatens the country’s political and economic future
books.description:
This fascinating account of India’s remarkable political and economic transformation over the past quarter century braids together background, reportage, and analysis to chronicle how the world’s most populous nation, once a pluralistic parliamentary democracy synonymous with poverty, evolved into a Hindu majoritarian polity and an aspiring economic superpower.

While acknowledging the vast gains for the Indian economy in this century, Sadanand Dhume raises concerns about the rise of an extreme brand of Hindu nationalism that now controls governmental power and dominates society in much of the country. Dhume delves into the roots of Hindu nationalism and explains how this once-fringe ideology came to eclipse its rivals.

Shedding light on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s disturbing clampdown on the freedoms of association and expression and minority rights, Dhume not only questions the conventional Western view of India as a liberal democracy that will act as a counterweight to autocratic China, but also argues that the decline of democratic ideals imperils India’s prospects for enduring peace and continued economic advancement, with vast repercussions for the United States and the rest of the world.
books.bio: Sadanand Dhume is a columnist for the Wall Street Journal and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. He lives in Washington, DC.

books.title: Unlicensed
books.subtitle: The Literary Underground of Enlightenment England
books.tagline: A major reinterpretation of the English Enlightenment that reveals how its radical ideas were shaped by a thriving literary underground
books.description:
In early eighteenth-century England, books could be deadly, and dangerous ideas had to circulate in secret. Even though pre-publication licensing had ended in 1695, the book trade remained subject to government surveillance and harassment. Those caught producing seditious, blasphemous, or treasonous works risked beatings, prison, fines, and even death. Yet, despite such intense censorship, clandestine networks of daring and ingenious authors, printers, and booksellers enabled political debates, religious controversies, and literary experiments to flourish. In Unlicensed , Joseph Hone takes readers behind the scenes of this remarkable literary underground, following texts from manuscript to sale—through false imprints, hidden presses, and cross-border smuggling routes—and showing how censorship shaped the culture of enlightenment England.

Drawing on extraordinary evidence, including informant reports, interrogation transcripts, and forensic bibliographical analysis, Unlicensed offers a vivid panoramic account of the early eighteenth-century underground book trade, and uncovers how illicit books were produced, disguised, distributed, and read. Printers emerge as active agents shaping which works reached the reading public, while back-alley distributors, booksellers, and even criminal gangs ensured that forbidden books circulated widely. At the same time, anonymous and illicit texts cultivated a discerning, skeptical readership attuned to questions of attribution and authority.

By mapping the interactions between authors, printers, publishers, booksellers, readers, spies, and government enforcers, Unlicensed demonstrates that censorship was not merely a constraint but a formative force in the early eighteenth-century English literary world. The result is a fresh perspective on enlightenment England, revealing how law, commerce, and society together shaped the circulation of ideas and the cultures of writing and reading.
books.bio: Joseph Hone is Reader in Literature and Book History at Newcastle University. His books include The Book Forger , Alexander Pope in the Making , and The Paper Chase . He is a recipient of the Philip Leverhulme Prize for his work in bibliography and literary studies.

praise.q: A new milestone of book history, Unlicensed provides extraordinary insight into the intricate and often dangerous trade of underground publishing in eighteenth-century England. This is a thoughtful, well-researched and beautifully constructed book.
praise.by: Andrew Pettegree, author of The Bookshop: A History of Bookselling from the Dawn of Print to the Twenty-First Century
praise.cred: author of The Bookshop: A History of Bookselling from the Dawn of Print to the Twenty-First Century

praise.q: A rich and illuminating exploration of the murky worlds of government censorship and clandestine print in early eighteenth-century England, written by a consummate literary sleuth.
praise.by: Fara Dabhoiwala, author of What Is Free Speech? The History of a Dangerous Idea
praise.cred: author of What Is Free Speech? The History of a Dangerous Idea

praise.q: Written with fizzing vivacity, powerful scholarly acuity and forensic virtuosity, this book turns upside down what we thought we knew. The end of press licensing in 1695 did not end press censorship. Yet, despite the efforts of a surveillance state, a resourceful clandestine press sustained a vibrant culture of disruptive ideas. Joseph Hone does for the English Enlightenment what Robert Darnton did for the French.
praise.by: Mark Goldie, University of Cambridge

praise.q: Joseph Hone tells a rigorous, intriguing story about how eighteenth-century print was risky, dangerous, and precarious even as the period celebrated transparency and reason. Unlicensed reveals a literary underground that is all but indistinguishable from the literary establishment. A salient reminder of how print culture holds a mirror to other fissures and tensions in society.
praise.by: Sophie Gee, author of The Barbarous Feast: Eating and Writing in the Eighteenth-Century World
praise.cred: author of The Barbarous Feast: Eating and Writing in the Eighteenth-Century World

praise.q: Through meticulous archival research, world-leading book historian Joseph Hone has recovered the literary underground of eighteenth-century England in glorious detail. Unlicensed is not only a scholarly triumph; it is also a compelling read.
praise.by: Max Skjönsberg, author of The Spirit of the British Constitution
praise.cred: author of The Spirit of the British Constitution

praise.q: An enticing, compelling, and original contribution to book history, Unlicensed confirms Joseph Hone’s standing as one of the leading literary and cultural historians of his generation. He convincingly undermines the Whig history of the first half of the eighteenth century, from Voltaire’s founding myth of complete freedom of expression to Habermas’s influential portrayal of a peaceable public sphere. Offering a granular counternarrative, Hone skilfully details the often-violent realities of Grub Street, as nervous statesmen sought to control its subversive activities. Augustan England will never look the same again.
praise.by: Brian Young, University of Oxford

books.title: Van Eyck
books.subtitle: The Portraits
books.tagline: The first book in English devoted to Jan van Eyck’s pioneering contribution to the birth of modern portraiture.
books.description:
Some stories do not have a beginning. Portraiture is one of them. It seems to burst onto the scene fully formed in the 1430s under the brush of Flemish artist Jan van Eyck. Pushing the possibilities of oil painting to convey a convincing illusion of reality, his portraits present us with individuals pulsating with life, every detail of their appearance captured.

Van Eyck not only transformed the style of contemporary portraiture but also challenged the definition of who should be portrayed. The men and women in his paintings are not royalty or aristocrats but the artist’s relatives, affluent merchants and successful craftsmen. Rendering their likeness in meticulous detail, van Eyck immortalised these figures through vivid depictions and allowed them to speak to us through enigmatic inscriptions.

This book will be the first ever published in English on the artist’s powerful portraits, accompanying a groundbreaking exhibition at London’s National Gallery.

books.title: War Is Interested in You
books.subtitle: The Breakdown of International Order and the Threat of World War Three
books.tagline: A leading foreign affairs commentator’s exploration of the growing number of conflicts around the world—how they developed, and where they might lead
books.description:
A long period of peace and stable relations between the world’s most powerful nations is coming to an end.

Major wars have broken out in Europe and the Middle East, tensions are rising in East Asia, and world leaders have spoken publicly about the possibility of a third world war. Intelligence agencies have never seen the world in a more dangerous and precarious state.

Making use of his extensive access to leaders in political and intelligence spheres around the globe and offering insightful analysis, Gideon Rachman explores how we got to this point and, crucially, what lies ahead—in this case, the increasing risk of global conflict.

As Leon Trotsky once put it, “You may not be interested in war. But war is interested in you.”
books.bio: Gideon Rachman is chief foreign affairs columnist for the Financial Times . He hosts the weekly podcast The Rachman Review and is the author of Easternisation: War and Peace in the Asian Century and The Age of the Strongman: How the Cult of the Leader Threatens Democracy around the World , among other titles.

praise.q: Simply brilliant. A masterful blend of contemporary history, incisive analysis, and insightful conceptualization. War indeed is interested in us all, and it is high time we understand why--and what the world can do to stop it. This book helps us do both.
praise.by: Serhii Plokhy, author of The Russo-Ukrainian War: The Return of History
praise.cred: author of The Russo-Ukrainian War: The Return of History

praise.q: In this brilliant book, Gideon Rachman explains how strongmen leaders like Putin and Trump, in their zeal to use force to press their advantage, have taken the world over the brink into war. Rachman's deep historical knowledge, flair for instructive analysis, and keen eye for detail, as well as his first-hand encounters with key players at critical moments, create an absorbing narrative. This book could not be more important or timely for highlighting the perils of this dangerous moment.
praise.by: Fiona Hill, author of There Is Nothing for You Here and Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin
praise.cred: author of There Is Nothing for You Here and Mr. Putin: Operative in the Kremlin

praise.q: A fast-paced, readable reminder that peace is not the natural condition of mankind.
praise.by: Graham Allison, Harvard University

praise.q: Few have better access to the people who start wars—and the people who try to stop them—than Gideon Rachman. War is Interested in You is a must-read field report on the G-Zero world’s violent turn, and a convincing case that we haven't seen the worst of it yet.”—Ian Bremmer, author of The Power of Crisis: How Three Threats—and Our Response
praise.by: Will Change the World

praise.q: War is Interested in You is both a geopolitical masterclass and a warning: the decline of Western power, the rise of strongman leaders, and the breakdown of international order are converging to make a third world war frighteningly thinkable. At the centre of the story is an America in the throes of an identity crisis, wavering in its commitment to an alliance system that remains essential to keeping the peace. Drawing on decades of reporting and extraordinary access, Gideon Rachman delivers a trenchant, clear-eyed guide to a world edging ever closer to the brink.
praise.by: Edward Fishman, author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare
praise.cred: author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare

books.title: Water and Wall Street
books.subtitle: Infrastructure, Finance, and Affordability in America's Cities
books.authors: Martin Doyle, Lauren Patterson and Erika Smull
books.tagline: How water infrastructure finance drives the size of our water bills, who can afford them, and the geography of urban landscapes.
books.description:
“Water crises” have emerged in the US with increasing regularity, from Flint, MI to Jackson, MS. Simultaneously, the rise in water bills for the past decade has far outpaced the rising cost of groceries, gas, or electricity, leading more Americans to add water to the growing list of their unaffordable basic necessities. Water and Wall Street by Martin Doyle, Lauren Patterson, and Erika Smull uncovers how the seemingly arcane world of infrastructure finance underlies these and other water trends in US cities, and how water infrastructure shapes the most basic landscape of cities and suburbs.

The authors begin by describing the basics of how water infrastructure works, and more importantly, how it is financed by municipal bonds, the backbone of urban finance. They then trace the history of municipal bonds for water from the founding of Philadelphia in the eighteenth century to the bankruptcy of Detroit in the twenty-first. Along the way, they also explore financial geography : how water bills, water affordability, and the peculiarities of infrastructure finance create distinct geographies of water capital. Finally, they take a speculative look at alternative future states for our cities, our infrastructure, and our water.
books.bio:
Martin Doyle (Author)

Martin Doyle is a water scientist at Duke University. He is the author of The Source and Streams of Revenue, with Rebecca Lave (MIT Press).

Lauren Patterson (Author)

Lauren Patterson is a water data scientist and researcher. Her work specializes in integrating and analyzing complex datasets that inform water, climate, and environmental policy and decision-making.

books.title: William Demby
books.subtitle: Goth Before It Was Cool
books.tagline: A critical biography of the legendary Afro-Gothic novelist, actor, and screenwriter in mid-century Italy.
books.description:
The latest from the legendary author of Mumbo Jumbo and The Haunting of Lin-Manuel Miranda , William Demby: Goth Before It Was Cool is Ishmael Reed's first book-length work of non-fiction in over a decade, and a unique and urgent document. Combining memoir, biography, oral history, and criticism, Reed has concocted something only he could write—at once scathing and eye-opening, a loving tribute to a great writer and a personal appraisal of why he never got his due in life. A novelist, screenwriter, journalist, actor, and all-around renaissance man whose pioneering works of gothic atmosphere and metafictional depth continue to reverberate today, Demby is an enduring figure of intrigue in whom Reed also sees the embodiment of cultural currents both personal and political.

Careening from 1950s Italy to Sag Harbor of the 1980s, and touching on third rails of race, gender, and class, Reed evokes debates and milieus crossing continents and eras, with cameos from Roberto Rossellini to Betty Friedan, resurrecting the story of a great mid-century Black artist (who is only now receiving the reissue treatment from Vintage), as well as Reed's own parallel journey as publisher, raconteur, and of course as one of our greatest living writers.

Featuring never-before-seen photographs from Demby's archives and a foreword from Demby scholar Melanie Masterton Sherazi, this unclassifiable book is a late-career milestone from Ishmael Reed, and a perfect introduction to his peerless non-fiction. Post-war Italy, Black Arts, and American literati collide in a revelatory work setting the record straight about a significant author and the times in which he lived.
books.bio: Ishmael Reed is the author of over twenty-five books including Mumbo Jumbo , Yellow Back Radio Broke-Down , Conjugating Hindi and The Haunting of Lin-Manuel Miranda . He is also a publisher, television producer, songwriter, radio and television commentator, lecturer, and has long been devoted to exploring an alternative black aesthetic: the trickster tradition, or Neo-Hoodooism. A regular contributor to CounterPunch and founder of the Before Columbus Foundation, he taught at the University of California, Berkeley for over thirty years, retiring in 2005. Reed is the only person to be nominated for the National Book Award in two categories in the same year.

books.title: Aeroesthetics
books.subtitle: The Art of Streamlining
books.authors: Gautam Sen Illustrated by Alain Bouldouyre Photographs by Xavier de Nombel
books.tagline: A history of aerodynamic thinking in automotive design from the end of World War I to the brink of World War II.
books.description:
Following World War I, car design in many European automobile companies underwent significant changes as they gained increased exposure to aviation expertise. Engineers and manufacturers, whose skills had been sharpened by wartime demands, began applying their knowledge to car design. In doing so, they redefined notions of shape and form, aiming to create vehicles that could slice through the air more efficiently. However, while many designs appeared aerodynamic, they often fell short in performance, while some of the most aerodynamically advanced vehicles featured unconventional or visually challenging aesthetics. Aeroesthetics: The Art of Streamlining explores the science of aerodynamics in depth and examines its influence on vehicle design up to the outbreak of World War II.

books.title: American Cosmos
books.subtitle: Globes and the Global Imagination in Early America
books.tagline: The first book to explore the forgotten terrestrial and celestial globes of early America—and the global imagination they shaped.
books.description:
Ranging from early modern Europe to the modern United States, American Cosmos introduces the objects, people, practices, and ideas that constituted the long-forgotten world of globes. As Tamara Plakins Thornton shows, paired terrestrial and celestial globes were important components of early American social, cultural, and intellectual life. They served as markers of learnedness and social status, provided a material vision of a human-centered cosmos, and as 3-D problem-solving devices, offered distinctive imaginative perspectives on global connections and human difference. Only some had access to these globes—including genteel families, men of science, navigators, and students in colleges, academies, and missionary schools—but in the nineteenth century, many more encountered mass-produced, stripped-down globes in common school classrooms and parlors. Yet with new cultural concerns taking root, these modern globes assumed a much-diminished role in American life and thought, and an older world of globes, rich with meaning and possibility, disappeared.

As we increasingly encounter global-scale experience—climate change, pandemics, human migrations, the economy—and as American historians strive to look beyond national borders, we can learn about the origins of American global thinking by looking at globes themselves and the people who used them.

books.title: Anxiety as a Weapon
books.subtitle: From Public Secret to Collective Solidarity
books.tagline: Challenges the idea of anxiety as an individual flaw and highlights its roots in social, economic, and political structures.
books.description:
Anxiety as a Weapon reframes anxiety not as a personal failing but as a response to the deep social, economic, and political instabilities of our time. Challenging a culture that promotes self-blame and individual solutions to stress—from therapy apps to mindfulness courses—this book exposes how systemic forces like precarious labor, austerity, and social disconnection fuel widespread psychological and emotional distress. Rather than diagnosing individuals as defective, it exposes how dominant narratives, technologies, and institutions isolate and shame people, pushing them to internalize suffering and acquiesce in the commodification of self-care. Drawing on historical and empirical research, it introduces the concept of “anxious solidarity”: a powerful, collective response to the atomizing pressures of neoliberal capitalism. By tracing the structural roots of anxiety and critiquing the mainstream mental health solutions on offer, the book provides a framework for transforming anxiousness into a means for connection, resistance, and widespread social change. It is both a critique and a call to action.

books.title: Art, Intellect and the State
books.subtitle: Cultural Histories of Late Pahlavi Iran
books.authors: Edited by Bianca Devos and Robert Steele
books.tagline: A cross-disciplinary volume on the intersections of—and tensions between—culture and government in Iran’s late Pahlavi period.
books.description:
In recent years, scholarly interest in Iran’s late Pahlavi period (1941–1979) has grown significantly and historians are increasingly approaching the era not merely as a prelude to the Iranian Revolution, but as a period worthy of study in its own right. New generations of scholars have uncovered fresh sources and offered original perspectives on the cultural and social life of this era. Yet opportunities for cross-disciplinary engagement among scholars from different fields who are exploring similar questions remain limited. This volume, the product of two international workshops at the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna and the University of Marburg, respectively, is a collection of the work of scholars at various stages of their careers from various disciplines investigating the cultural history of late Pahlavi Iran from a multiplicity of perspectives, including: archaeology, architecture, scholarship, media, art, film, literature, politics, religion, museums, music, philosophy, education, and theater.

Chapters explore the interactions between state ideology and the sociocultural sphere, exploring ideas such as: the influence of the press and literature on social discourses; the culturally strategic and identity-forming role of the performing arts; the relationship between state education policy and culture; the employment of foreign artists, architects, scholars, and musicians in the context of Iran’s cultural diplomacy; and the dynamics of (state) religion, spirituality, nationalism, and psychology in modern media or through their dissemination in the media. The volume explores not only the Pahlavi state’s direct participation in facilitating cultural activity or scholarly endeavors, but also how artists, writers, historians, and other cultural actors flourished independent of (sometimes in spite of) the state apparatus.

The volume does not seek to provide an encyclopaedic collection detailing every aspect of culture in the Pahlavi period, but the case studies explored demonstrate the breadth and complexities of this field in the historiography. Moreover, by shedding light on the various features of culture in the late Pahlavi era and encouraging multidisciplinary discussions, the volume aims to contribute to a greater understanding of the vibrant cultural life in Iran during this period.

books.title: Baroque Architecture in Bohemia
books.subtitle: Reviews
books.authors: Edited by Petr Macek, Jakub Bachtík, and Richard Biegel Translated by Anna Bryson Gustová, Lea Bennis, and Branislava Kuburovic
books.tagline: A complete history of Bohemian architecture during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.
books.description:
The art of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries forms one of the most important chapters in the cultural history of Bohemia. In this period, art attained a remarkably high level, with Bohemia emerging as a rival to the other cultural centers of Europe. This was especially true in terms of architecture, which not only transformed the appearance of towns and villages in Bohemia but also played a part in the creation of the phenomenon known as the Baroque, which to this day remains an essential part of Czech cultural identity.

The monumental Baroque Architecture in Bohemia brings together multiple generations of art historians from Charles University and the Czech Academy of Sciences to offer the single most comprehensive examination and exploration of Bohemian architecture during this extraordinary period. The book begins with the Renaissance roots of Baroque Bohemia: it introduces readers to the influence of the cultured and eccentric Rudolf II, who moved the seat of the Holy Roman Empire back to Prague, inviting foreign artists, architects, and alchemists with him; it shows the importance of Albrecht von Wallenstein, whose military success in the Thirty Years’ War heralded a massive building campaign that helped usher in the Baroque age. When the book moves to the period commonly understood as the Baroque, it discusses leading Czech architects, such as Jan Blažej Santini-Aichel and Kilian Ignaz Dientzenhofer, but also focuses on lesser-known regional architects and the important Italian architects and artists who left their mark on Bohemia. The architectural and artistic developments are all set among the broader cultural and social context of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

The book contains extensive pictorial documentation—most impressively Vladimír Uher and Martin Micka’s gorgeous architectural photographs.

praise.q: Baroque Architecture in Bohemia is a magnificent book.

books.title: Cultivating the City
books.subtitle: The Long Struggle to Put Land to Use
books.tagline: A story of law and social policy in a place you might not expect: community gardens and urban farms.
books.description:
Though Chicago is a city of legendary skyscrapers and dense apartment blocks, it is also a city of wide-open tracts of land. This surprising juxtaposition can be viewed as an opportunity, in that available land can become a food source for urban dwellers, especially those experiencing poverty or limited access to grocery stores. But most empty land in Chicago remains empty — why? In Cultivating the City , sociologist and legal scholar Nate Ela examines the history of Chicago’s urban farms and gardens, their promotion as a tool to support the poor and unemployed, and their repeated failure to take root as a permanent part of Chicago’s landscape.

Ela’s fresh take on contemporary urban agriculture features a new perspective on social policy and urban governance. For hundreds of years, social reformers have worked to address poverty and unemployment by letting people use land to grow food. Reformers experimented with the possibilities of property use, including deals to match gardeners with public or private land, proposals to let growers use land without owners’ permission, and the transformation of private land into municipal gardens. By exposing the dynamics of this longstanding but long-overlooked form of social policy in Chicago, Ela offers a new strategy for cultivating cities that are productive, resilient, and just.

praise.q: That idle land is to be put to productive use is a longstanding property mantra. While this has too often been put to violent and exclusionary ends, Nate Ela’s Cultivating the City uncovers a different path, revealing a long history of attempts by social reformers to let people in need use idle urban land to grow food. In that property is fundamental to social possibility and constraint, urban agriculture offers vital lessons regarding the potential for cultivating new forms of urban life.

books.title: Deviant Art Histories
books.subtitle: From Radical Psychiatry to Cultural Citizenship
books.tagline: A groundbreaking examination of the entanglement between psychiatry, art, and art history.
books.description:
Looking beyond the white walls of art galleries and museums, Kaira M. Cabañas explores art history through the psychiatric wards of the twentieth century, offering a reevaluation of the relationship between madness, making, and the art world and considering the deeply intertwined fields of psychiatry and art.

Putting aside romanticized myths about “outsider art,” Cabañas argues for a radical revisioning that centers artists in psychiatric settings not as deviants and curiosities but rather as skilled, sophisticated innovators and active participants in shared culture. Beginning with the story of legendary art historian Aby Warburg, whose own psychiatric internment and subsequent recovery serve as a point of departure, the narrative then covers the globe, following visionary reformers such as Nise da Silveira in Brazil and Franco and Franca Basaglia in Italy. The book tracks how psychiatrists collaborated with professional artists and patients to turn clinical spaces into laboratories of liberation. By documenting how patient-artists moved from being subjects of clinical study to recognized cultural producers, Deviant Art Histories demonstrates how art was a primary vehicle for reclaiming their agency. Featuring a diverse cast of figures—including Lygia Clark, Ornette Coleman, and Antonin Artaud—the book offers a powerful testament to art’s ability to break the clinical frame and transform the definition of what it means to be a creative citizen in the modern world.

books.title: Everyday Sciences
books.subtitle: Practical Knowledge and Knowledgeable Practice in Medieval South Asia
books.tagline: How people across society in medieval South Asia—including coppersmiths, merchants, bureaucrats, philosophers, and physicians—pioneered new vernacular sciences.
books.description:
Starting in the eleventh century, South Asian scholars and artisans began to investigate and shape the world in a novel manner. Intellectuals translated Sanskrit texts into regional languages such as Kannada, situating knowledge in particular places. At the same time, architects and artisans began to assert their intellectual and literary presence, often claiming the title of “scholar” as they negotiated a space between classical textual erudition, professional expertise, and personal experience. Working within the perilous world of court politics, a new class of scholar-administrators began collecting recipes and composing texts about weather prediction, horticulture, mathematics, astrology, sexual life, and medicine.

Everyday Sciences traces this emergence of vernacular sciences by engaging with untapped archives and an array of sources in multiple languages. By exploring how historical actors resolved disputes about the physiology of vision, the use of meat and alcohol in medicine, and the management of information in elephant stables, Eric Moses Gurevitch unveils the complex textual and social orders that structured medieval society in India. He argues that a focus on everyday sciences in the non-modern non-West allows historians to reassess how places outside—and even inside—Europe are brought into narratives of a global history of science. Gurevitch articulates a “big-enough” history of science in South Asia, one open to little voices and unexpected connections that might not make their way through the fray in other histories.

Everyday Sciences demonstrates how practical, everyday activities were engines of profound intellectual innovation—and it shows the promise of revisiting the past without colonial hang-ups, and with fresh eyes.

books.title: Ex Ante
books.subtitle: Power and Prediction in the Real-Time Future
books.tagline: An incisive framework for understanding how predictive AI has reshaped our relationship with time.
books.description:
Ex Ante argues that AI systems draw us into a new experience of time, a continuous stream of machine-generated futures that reshapes our relationship to ourselves, to capitalism, and to infrastructure. Unlike other predictive tools that help us prepare for what might come, these projections—produced by algorithms and sourced by massive flows of data—calibrate our actions moment by moment, second by second.

In this book, John Cheney-Lippold offers a framework he calls the ex ante , Latin for “before the event,” as a way to consider how the future has become capitalism’s latest resource for exploitation. Through case studies spanning TikTok beauty filters that have fueled a surge in plastic surgery consultations, chess engines that redefine how the game is played, online sports betting platforms that commodify probability itself, hospital sepsis algorithms that transform the labor of nursing, and coordinated vehicle networks that collectively anticipate their surroundings to function, Ex Ante offers an exploration and powerful critique of our algorithmic present and the powers behind it.

books.title: Gastrodiplomacy
books.subtitle: Chinese Exclusion and the Ascent of Chinese Restaurants in New York City, 1870–1943
books.tagline: Traces how Chinese migrants challenged racialization and disenfranchisement by establishing Chinese restaurants during the Gilded Age.
books.description:
In Gastrodiplomacy, Heather Ruth Lee dives deep into not just the history of Chinese restaurants in early twentieth-century New York City but the delicate, inchoate, and constantly evolving dynamics among their owners, workers, and their predominantly white clientele. Lee argues that the stylistic and capitalist choices made by restaurateurs (“gastrodiplomats”) had outsized political effects on paternalistic white diners (“gastroliberals”) who patronized their establishments, particularly when it came to racial relations in cities that were growing and diversifying. Lee is not starry-eyed—satisfying white tongues and stomachs didn’t lead to an urban utopia of peace, harmony, and brotherhood—but she shows the great and subtle influences of Chinese migrants on American urban space, culture, and metropolitan identity in a defining time.

In Lee’s capable and compelling telling, the Chinese restaurant becomes a distinctive locus for the negotiation of political power, cultural influence, urban identity, and more. Gastrodiplomacy reveals much about burgeoning and increasingly cosmopolitan American cities, as well as about their dynamic relationships with the fluidities of the American character.

praise.q: The history of Chinese restaurants is an integral part of the American story. Heather Lee’s work helps to shed light on the subject from a new angle.
praise.by: Curtis Chin, author of 'Everything I Learned, I Learned in a Chinese Restaurant'

books.title: In the Company of Artists
books.subtitle: A History of Skowhegan School of Painting & Sculpture
books.authors: Edited by Faye Hirsch, Ingrid Schaffner, Skowhegan, and Dancing Foxes Press With Essays by Faye Hirsch and Ingrid Schaffner
books.tagline: A first glimpse into a celebrated art school that explores its artistic contributions and history.
books.description:
In the Company of Artists is the first major study of the Skowhegan School of Painting & Sculpture, founded in 1946. It explores the institution's history, philosophy, and impact, by uncovering narratives on Skowhegan and providing an institutional record. Drawing from primary source material, including new and unpublished interviews and roundtable discussions with faculty and alumni artists, photographs and film stills, ephemera, and artworks produced over seventy years, it expands our understanding of American art production and alternative art schools in the post–World War II era. Through firsthand accounts from artists, the book is a window into this intensely private institution that was ahead of its time concerning representation, equity, and inclusion. With a commissioned portfolio of photographs by celebrated artist Elle Pérez evocatively rendering Skowhegan’s sylvan campus, the book vividly asserts the significance of the school’s rural Maine setting to its pedagogy while demonstrating its impact and influence on the art world at large.

books.title: Inventory
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.tagline: A book-length poem serving as a son’s elegy for his late father, an artist and forest steward.
books.description:
Rob Schlegel’s long poem Inventory emerges from three discrete inventories the poet must catalog in the aftermath of a sudden loss: a selection of his father’s art to be organized for a posthumous exhibition, two hundred acres of trees in a forest stewarded by his father in western Oregon, and his own emotional landscape in the aftermath of his father’s death. As Schlegel moves through these collections of objects and emotions, he learns how to navigate grief. His father’s paintings act as an inventory of the poet’s own life, with each landscape recalling a moment in time, each sketch holding a story. Celebrating a close relationship while mourning its loss, Schlegel reflects on the ties between art and grief, parents and children, people and trees.

At the time of his father’s death, an extreme heatwave was moving across the region, broadening the scope of grief from the personal and familial to encompass tragedies on a larger scale. Social disintegration and climate disaster weave through the lives of a family in mourning as they navigate the complexity of how to sit with loss, change, love, and art. Through quiet, measured verse and arresting simplicity, Inventory extends the ekphrastic tradition into a contemporary elegy rich in both profound sadness and optimism for the future.

books.title: Iran
books.subtitle: Beauty and Tyranny
books.tagline: Ramin Jahanbegloo turns to ancient philosophy as an antidote to contemporary authoritarianism in Iran.
books.description:
From the rule of Cyrus the Great to the present day, Iran has been plagued by a recurrent syndrome of tyranny. For Ramin Jahanbegloo, the cure for this persistent cycle lies in a reengagement with the idea of a beautiful society. He presents beauty as an antidote to authoritarianism and as a methodology of freedom: one first taught by the philosophers of ancient Greece, who bound beauty and goodness together in the principle of kalokagathia , and later revived by the German Enlightenment.

A work of hope and faith in the people of Iran, this provocative and timely intervention from the author of The Idea of Persia turns to the past in order to imagine a way forward. Drawing on Hegel, Schiller, Arendt, Camus, and more, Jahanbegloo lays out a vision of how Iran and Iranians might come to live in beautiful freedom.

books.title: Mammal Pit
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.tagline: A strange, cacophonous, and contemplative long poem following a posthumous narrator making meaning of life and death.
books.description:
Lloyd Wallace’s book-length poem Mammal Pit uses the imaginative technologies of literature to try to say something true about being alive. Conceived as though spoken in a single, long breath by an ostensibly posthumous narrator, this soliloquy accrues fragments, images, impressions, jokes, and regrets as it progresses. The narrator recalls moments from his past life, running through the American South, crossing the long Ohio River into Pittsburgh, and zigzagging over to the oiled, silent hallways of the US Capitol, all while calling up and attempting to make sense of what it was to be alive in a human body surrounded by the heavy liquid of time. Studded with strange, exacting images—“Men dreaming of knives / In such excruciating detail / They wake up with paper cuts / Saliva wife”—Wallace’s debut collection attempts to ask the questions poetry is made to answer: What do you do with death? What do you do when it’s standing beside you? What can you do but hold its hand?

Wallace’s humorous and morbid romp across America and across the boundaries of life and death whirls language away from expected patterns and forms. Committed to the question of what it means to die, Wallace faces its inevitability and the fact that we are all doing it as we speak.

Mammal Pit is the winner of the 2027 Phoenix Emerging Poet Book Prize.

books.title: Mobilized
books.subtitle: How Bipartisan Interest Groups Advance Democracy and Reduce Polarization
books.tagline: A fresh look at how interest groups mobilize their members and the effects that follow.
books.description:
Most contemporary accounts of interest group politics emphasize how contemporary interest groups mirror and exacerbate partisan polarization, and understandably so: many of the largest and most visible coalitions do just this. But the term “interest groups” masks considerable variety. Despite what many seem to believe, the majority of interest groups are bipartisan, and, as Amy D. Meli shows, even when groups have a clear affinity with one party over the other, many still choose to pursue a bipartisan strategy.

In Mobilized , Meli develops a method for identifying the partisanship of interest groups and explores how different types of groups communicate with their members. She finds that groups adopting bipartisan policy strategies lobby and mobilize their members differently than those who choose partisan strategies. This, in turn, influences how their members perceive government and politics, leading people involved with these groups to have higher efficacy and lower levels of affective polarization. For decades, we have understood that higher levels of political involvement result in higher levels of polarization, but Meli shows that when involvement is mediated by bipartisan interest groups, affective polarization levels actually go down. Bipartisan groups advocate on issues they care about, and, most of the time, they do so with some support from both parties.

books.title: Modern Autocracy
books.subtitle: The Rise of Authoritarian Economies—and Why Only Some Can Succeed
books.tagline: Strongman governments are back. What becomes of their economies?
books.description:
Autocracy has once again become a rising force. Today, two thirds of the world’s population live under regimes where electoral democracy is either absent or debased. Moreover, even many functioning democracies are now facing a significant share of their citizens who favor switching to authoritarian rule. But as states return to their old authoritarian ways, what happens to their still-modernized economies?

Simon Commander and Saul Estrin examine the scale of this change—and the unevenly distributed economic consequences that will soon accompany it. Modern Autocracy reveals how authoritarian economies generally perform worse than economies in democratic states, in part because many authoritarian states are centralized around a leader whose economic stewardship facilitates political favor and cronyism. In all, these features, combined with the likelihood of repression, sap economic vitality and stymie competition, innovation, and, ultimately, growth.

The exception, the authors reveal, is that autocracies can perform better when they’re built around an institutional framework rather than simply a leader. That is because they can pursue strategic goals, including innovation; even so, their autocratic foundations open up major vulnerabilities and tensions. Brimming with political relevance, Modern Autocracy is a defining taxonomy of economies and their natures in this century.

books.title: Music Metropolis Berlin
books.subtitle: Three Centuries of Musical Culture in the Capital City
books.tagline: Tracing the development of Berlin as a center of music from the eighteenth century to the present, examining how its music survived despite its turbulent history.
books.description:
Berlin is a music-lover’s paradise, offering up everything from operas to raves. Yet unlike Vienna, Leipzig, or even Nashville, Berlin does not immediately come to mind as a city of music. Instead, its turbulent history evokes images of industry, commerce, militarism, destruction, division, and resurrection. Over the past three centuries, Berlin was the capital of a kingdom, an empire, a republic, and a dictatorship; it was ravaged by war and occupied by foreign powers; and its division and reunification made it a powerful symbol of the Cold War. Through all these highs and lows, the music played on. Music Metropolis Berlin is the first full-length exploration of how Berlin became a city of music against all odds.

Unlike the other European music centers that stake their reputations on the fame of composers like Bach or Beethoven, Berlin is known for its ensembles, artists, theaters, organizers, intellectuals, and media stars. This is because Berlin took a very different, and almost accidental, route to becoming a city of music. Hampered for centuries by rulers who were more focused on military and industrial expansion than on cultural prestige, Berlin’s musical life prospered thanks to the ambitions of entrepreneurs and politicians who saw the value in serving the ever-changing music public in an expanding urban landscape. By focusing on Berlin as a rapidly developing global capital, Music Metropolis Berlin looks beyond the music, its creators, and its institutions to reveal how political, economic, and social forces fueled the creation of the Berlin metropolis and continue to nurture a vibrant and diverse musical life.

books.title: Policing the Project
books.subtitle: State Violence and the Dismantling of Chicago Public Housing
books.authors: Madeleine Hamlin With a Foreword by Jamie Kalven
books.tagline: Shows how policing shaped the trajectory of public housing in Chicago and paved the way for its eradication and privatization.
books.description:
Public housing should be a great public good, providing an essential basic need for people with lower incomes. Unfortunately, in the United States, policymakers turned their backs on public housing early on. Intended to be a utopia for the working poor, public housing in many cities became characterized by racial isolation, extreme poverty, and infrastructural breakdown, all of which left residents vulnerable to crime. State abandonment had one major exception, however: policing. In Policing the Project , geographer Madeleine Hamlin details how police played an important role in Chicago’s public housing from its origins in 1937 to the eve of its demolition at the turn of the millennium.

Based on archival data as well as extensive interviews with former residents and police officers, Hamlin describes the progressive institutional entanglement of public housing and policing as it unfurled over the course of the twentieth century. Policing the Project transcends mere description of how policing impacted everyday life for public housing residents, instead considering how policing shaped the institution of public housing as a whole. Hamlin argues that policing conditioned public housing’s downfall: draining housing budgets while exacerbating rather than mitigating crime and violence. Thus, policing played an important role in shaping the dramatic transformation of Chicago’s housing landscape, which entailed widespread privatization and the displacement of tens of thousands of Black Chicagoans.

books.title: Racing in the Shadows
books.subtitle: An Illustrated Retrospective
books.authors: John Nikas With Contributions by Jackie Oliver and Rodger Attaway
books.tagline: Racing in the Shadows tells the story of Don Nichols, one of the most intriguing designers in professional car racing, and his company, Shadow Racing.
books.description:
Written with unprecedented access to company records as well as private letters and notes, renderings, drawings, and photos from Nichols’ life, Racing in the Shadows provides a compelling account of the true story behind Shadow Racing’s remarkable racing cars and the individuals who created them. Beginning with his difficult childhood and service as a WWII paratrooper, this book provides a comprehensive overview of Don Nichols’ motorsports and manufacturing career, with a special focus on his innovative work with Shadow Racing in the 1960s and ’70s. Shadow Racing’s entire lifespan is detailed—from the company’s early setbacks to their eventual Formula One victory in 1974—along with exploits from Nichols’ later career, which included military work and efforts to create an early hybrid vehicle. Illustrated with almost 1000 photographs, most of them never before seen by the public, Racing in the Shadows is a lavish and loving look at a singular racecar designer.

books.title: Representation in America
books.subtitle: Majority Rule in a Divided Political System
books.tagline: A landmark appraisal of how Congress represents public opinion.
books.description:
Drawing on nearly two decades of the Cooperative Congressional Election Study of American public opinion and more than one hundred key legislative proposals, Representation in America presents the most comprehensive, data-driven look at how Congress has represented the American public, spanning the presidencies of George W. Bush through Joe Biden. The result is a sweeping account of how electoral and legislative institutions channel and amplify majority preferences while tempering the most divisive proposals.

Stephen Ansolabehere and Shiro Kuriwaki trace each stage of the representation process, from constituents to their representatives to Congress’s collective decisions. Contrary to conceptions of democratic dysfunction, Ansolabehere and Kuriwaki find a strong majoritarian tendency: most proposals on the legislative agenda enjoy the support of the majority of Americans; voters tend to choose legislators whose positions they agree with; most legislators vote in line with the majority of their constituencies most of the time; and legislative districts magnify rather than mute majority opinion. When majority rule falls short, it usually takes the form of popular legislation stalling rather than Congress passing laws the public opposes.

books.title: Rover: Design and Engineering
books.subtitle: The Inside Story 1945-1976
books.tagline: The first in-depth account of the car manufacturing company Rover’s postwar design and engineering journey, from independent auto maker to technological pioneer.
books.description:
Lost in the collapse of the automotive conglomerate British Leyland, it is easy to forget that Rover was once a proudly independent maker of high-quality vehicles. The company managed to be both orthodox and innovative, respecting traditions but prepared to push boundaries, not least in its pioneering and successful work with gas-turbine cars. Some of its models remain design landmarks; others showed huge promise but never made it to production, snuffed out by British Leyland’s dog-eat-dog internal politics. The thread running through all these cars is a sparkling creativity: a willingness, born out of painstaking research and experimentation, to do things differently if that meant doing them better.

Based on a treasure trove of detailed interviews from the late 1990s and backed up by recent interviews, this is the first book to tell the true inside story of post-war Rover design and engineering. Full of fascinating firsthand testimony, it shows how a relatively small and essentially family-run concern could lift itself up to be a technological leader.

books.title: Spirit and Folk
books.subtitle: Jewish Mysticism and the Struggle for German Nationhood
books.tagline: A study of the twentieth-century construction of a Jewish mystical tradition by German Jewish intellectuals.
books.description:
For most of European history, the notion of Jewish spirituality was unthinkable—buried beneath a pervasive desire to understand Judaism as uniquely material and Christianity as uniquely spiritual. In Spirit and Folk , Amir Engel tells the story of how a group of Jewish intellectuals, seeking greater involvement in political life, worked to invent a mystical tradition for Judaism amid the existential crises of twentieth-century Germany.

Beginning with Martin Buber in 1900 and ending with Gershom Scholem in 1942, Engel traces the rich debate among thinkers both well-known and forgotten about the need to imagine and construct a uniquely Jewish mystical tradition from historical religious sources. This quest and the tradition that emerged, Engel argues, developed in response to one of the most volatile questions of the last century: can Jews be Germans? The invention of Jewish spirituality, Engel shows, was not only a religious innovation but also a political gambit—a demand to be accepted as equal contributors to the German national project.

books.title: Star Day
books.subtitle: A Story of 24 Hours and 24 Stellar Lives
books.authors: Marcia Bartusiak and Stephen Lowe Illustrated by Matthew Green
books.tagline: An hourly guide that tracks twenty-four stars, stellar clusters, and constellations across the sky to reveal their luminous lives and lore.
books.description:
Over the course of a day, the constellations slowly shift, rising in the east and setting in the west, all due to the Earth’s rotation. A full turn of the celestial sphere, that bowl above us where the stars seemingly appear fixed to the surface, is completed once every twenty-four hours. In fact, the stars first defined the twenty-four-hour day, and one star, our sun, rules the circadian rhythms of all life on our planet. This short book sweeps through the celestial sphere hour by hour, introducing a remarkable cast of stellar characters with each chapter. Celebrated science writer Marcia Bartusiak and mathematician Stephen Lowe blend practical astronomy with fascinating history to share unique cosmological stories.

This husband and wife team explain that observers have long split the sky into twenty-four hours of “right ascension”—a celestial equivalent of longitude and a universal scheme for locating cosmological objects. Each chapter of Star Day presents a single right ascension hour, from the stellar death of Supernova 1885A (0th Hour)—an explosion that helped reveal the size of the universe—to Scheat (23rd Hour), an aging red giant. Twice the mass of the Sun and some 1,500 times as bright, Scheat sometimes guides amateur astronomers to distant galaxies . In between, we learn about humans’ pole star, Polaris (2nd hour), and meet the supermassive black hole at the center of our Milky Way galaxy (17th hour). By the end of our star day, we will appreciate both our own stellar origins and the fragile and deep connections between human civilizations and the ever-changing heavens. Star Day reminds us that wonder and discovery are easily available, all for the simple price of looking up.

For each chapter, artist Matthew Green has depicted these stellar scenes with entrancing pen-and-ink drawings. Working together to narrate and illustrate these stars, Bartusiak, Lowe, and Green have created an engaging read that is a perfect way to spend an hour or two—and a true gift to both seasoned skywatchers and curious beginners.
