books.title: The Black Model Minority Student
books.subtitle: African Immigrants and the Contradictions of Race in America
books.tagline: Explores the contradictory perceptions of African immigrant students in New York City and reveals how anti-Blackness persists even within predominantly Black and Brown schools.
books.description:
African immigrant students are often celebrated in the United States as academically successful and culturally disciplined. But what happens when praise itself becomes part of a racial hierarchy? In The Black Model Minority Student , sociologist of education Mercy Agyepong traces the complex experiences of West African immigrant students attending public high schools in New York City.

Using ethnographic and interview data from predominantly Black and Brown schools in the Bronx, Agyepong shows that African immigrant students are often viewed through two competing yet coexisting narratives: as intellectually capable and hardworking, yet also as uncivilized or socially inferior. These perceptions are not incidental, but central to how anti-Blackness operates and how racial hierarchies are sustained in the United States. While the model minority stereotype shaped their experiences in Black and Brown high schools, West African immigrant students found that this seemingly favorable stereotype mattered less once they graduated and entered the white spaces of higher education and other social settings. At every step, African students—regardless of their national origins—were disadvantaged by racial stereotypes.

Theoretically grounded yet deeply human, The Black Model Minority Student offers an important new perspective on race, immigration, and education in contemporary America.

books.title: The Book of Cunning and Treachery
books.subtitle: Writing, Slavery, and Sovereignty in a Qing Indigenous Domain
books.tagline: An ethnographic history of one of the dozens of indigenous domains that occupied China’s border regions during the Qing dynasty and before.
books.description:
Erik Mueggler’s The Book of Cunning and Treachery is an ethnographic history of a chiefly household that ruled one of the many indigenous domains scattered through upland southwest China during the late Ming and Qing dynasties. The imperial colonization of this region proceeded by way of defeating indigenous polities and absorbing them into a system of indirect governance. In this system, indigenous chieftains inherited power over multiethnic domains, subject to ratification by the imperial court. Mueggler tracks the history of two crucial yet unexamined archives pertaining to this household—a trove of Chinese-language legal, military, and administrative documents, and hundreds of ritual manuals, histories, and morality books written in the indigenous Né script—to show how the chiefly house reproduced itself through these languages, each with its own forms of ritual, recitation, and inscription.

As Mueggler demonstrates, through different forms of access to writing in Chinese and Né, male and female chieftains, domestic slaves, enslaved bondsmen, bonded tenants, chiefly concubines, and more existed in a complex ecology of relations. House and domain were governed through a dynamic process in which residents continuously worked out the status hierarchies that animated their relations with one another as well as the relations between the chiefly house and the local administrative system. This groundbreaking book provides a compelling account of the intertwined problems of writing, slavery, and sovereignty, as well as a vivid portrait of the unique form that indigenous jurisdiction took in this era.

books.title: The Liberal Arts Advantage
books.subtitle: Measuring the Deeper Value of a College Education
books.authors: Edited by Richard Arum, Paul Courant, and Allyson Flaster
books.tagline: Showcases new measurement strategies for assessing the impact of a liberal arts education on students and society.
books.description:
More than ever before, our society is questioning the meaning and value of higher education, and liberal arts education, in particular, has come under substantial scrutiny. Economic detractors characterize liberal arts education as impractical, claiming that college should prepare students for the workforce. Others object to the curriculum, portraying it as broken or misdirected. According to these critics, the liberal arts education being offered in the United States is marked by its rejection of core intellectual and ideological commitments.

In The Liberal Arts Advantage, a wide range of scholars argue for how and why a liberal arts education uniquely develops skill sets and expertise needed for individuals and society to thrive in the twenty-first century. The contributors address foundational questions about what liberal arts education is, how it has been conceptualized in the past, and what we can learn from its societal and professional impacts. They present compelling, unique research and new methodological tools for assessing the outcomes of liberal arts graduates. Offering grounded and well-founded arguments in favor of our education system, The Liberal Arts Advantage persuasively explains why educational leaders should reinvest in liberal arts education.

praise.q: At a time when liberalarts education is notoriously hard to define and its efficacy hard to measure, this book is a welcome response to the rash assessments that often pass for reasoned debate about its value. Anyone concerned with the future of our imperiled democracy should read it with care and appreciation.
praise.by: Andrew Delbanco, author of College: What it Was, Is, and Should Be
praise.cred: author of College: What it Was, Is, and Should Be

books.title: The Politics of Decency
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.description:
A thoughtful examination of how to recenter decency in politics and public life, told through conversations between a long-time historian and public servant and new voices at the helm. After surveying eighty years of the UK’s political and constitutional journey, Peter Hennessy prepares to bid farewell to public life. And he’s left with one thought: that the essential quality of decency needs to be placed—once again—back at the heart of public life and public discourse. But what does decency look like today, where does it spring from, and how might we all play a role in recentering it in public life? In this book, Hennessy considers such issues alongside a group of people who might pick up his baton. He has been inviting old friends, colleagues, and those he has long admired, along with younger voices from politics and public life, into his home for conversations about what decency means to them. And he will be reflecting on what they have shared with him. Hennessy’s interest in this question springs from a concern about constitutional proprieties, but these conversations range much further afield—from the constitution to service delivery, from schooling to social media. What he hears is both worrying and uplifting: a real sense that there is a problem, a real commitment to tackle it, and ideas for how that might be done, and what role all of us can play.

books.title: The Rage of John Dos Passos
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.tagline: A close look at the emotional and intellectual world of writer John Dos Passos, who was at one time America’s leading modernist, that reveals the political and cultural rhythms of the twentieth century.
books.description:
John Dos Passos (1896–1970) was a prolific writer—at once compulsive and enigmatic—who became famous in the 1930s as America’s leading literary modernist, only to be eclipsed in the second half of his life because of his own political and aesthetic choices. The Rage of John Dos Passos adopts a psychoanalytic perspective to comprehend the curious career of a man whom Jean-Paul Sartre described in 1938 as “the greatest writer of our time.”

As a young man after World War I, Dos Passos wrote books that won him notoriety as an intemperate critic of American society. His Three Soldiers (1921) was called an insult to the army in which he had been enlisted. His impressionistic novel of New York City, Manhattan Transfer (1925), was dismissed as “spattered filth.” Then in the 1930s, three wildly creative and politically engaged novels written under the collective title U.S.A. truly made his name. Yet Dos Passos then abandoned his youthful radicalism to embrace strident anticommunism and the second Red Scare.

The Rage of John Dos Passos examines the central strands of the author’s life, from infancy until death, and the full range of his writing, including his often-scorned late novels. Christopher Tomlins aims to fuse history, biography, and literary analysis in understanding Dos Passos and his times—and our own.

books.title: The Rise and Fall of “The Bridge”
books.subtitle: Bridgehampton Race Circuit 1955–1997
books.tagline: This book offers the first truly comprehensive history of Bridgehampton Race Circuit, tracing its rise, its struggles, and its ultimate demise.
books.description:
Bridgehampton Race Circuit, affectionately known as The Bridge, was one of America’s most beloved yet beleaguered road courses. From its opening in 1955 to its final laps in 1997, it stood alongside Thompson Raceway and Lime Rock Park as one of the three pillars of northeastern motorsport, shaping the region’s sports car and single-seater culture for more than four decades. While major events occasionally drew national attention, Bridgehampton’s survival was perpetually threatened by financial instability, shifting ownership, restrictive “Blue Laws,” and persistent noise complaints from the surrounding communities of Bridgehampton and Sagaponack. Despite these challenges, generations of racers—from local amateurs to future stars—considered The Bridge one of America’s most demanding and exhilarating circuits.

Drawing on an extensive trove of surviving records, archives, newsletters, and local press coverage, Terry O’Neil reconstructs the track’s story in unprecedented detail. This volume also highlights race results often overlooked in previous histories, particularly from the 1970s through the 1990s, when reporting was inconsistent, and many events were held without spectators. The meticulous assembly of these fragmented records records the circuit’s full competitive history.

Bridgehampton’s legacy is one of passion, perseverance, and place: a world-class track fighting for survival amid shifting political, social, and economic pressures. Whether remembered for its traditional clockwise configuration or the later counter-clockwise Laguna Bay layout, the circuit forever influenced American motorsport. This book is the definitive chronicle of a lost racing treasure—an essential volume for enthusiasts, historians, and anyone drawn to the drama and romance of America’s great road courses.

books.title: The Rothmans Porsche Turbo Cup
books.subtitle: Origins of Porsche Cup Racing
books.authors: Gregory Coe and Dr. Ronald Tiejtan Photographs by Paul Strak
books.tagline: The definitive account of the evolution of the Porsche 944.
books.description:
What began as showroom-stock racing in the late 1970s evolved by the spring of 1985 into a global phenomenon: a single-marque racing series known as Porsche Cup, using a bespoke, factory-built race car. This book documents the development of that car—the 944—which was initially dismissed by some as a “Volkswagen with a Porsche badge” but soon proved itself a serial race winner. Porsche Cup began as a humble grassroots effort to boost sales of an entry-level vehicle, yet it ultimately changed the landscape of motorsport forever.

The Rothmans Porsche Turbo Cup explores the evolution of the front-engine Porsche concept, the races that forged its reputation, and the formal factory-supported series established around the 944. Extensive archival research reveals the inner workings of the Cup, while interviews with the series’ architects and drivers paint a vibrant picture of the era. Illustrated with previously unpublished images that capture both the facts and the ambiance of the time, this volume brings a history that has lain dormant for over thirty years back to life.

books.title: Thinking in Cases
books.subtitle: Fiction, Law, and the Case History
books.tagline: How the form of the case history became an important way of studying the individual as an exemplary case in medicine, psychoanalysis, law, and the novel.
books.description:
What does it mean when we address ourselves to a specific problem and treat it as a “case” that needs resolution, a resolution that may in turn offer us more general lessons? The “case history” has become a central form of thought and analysis in our culture, but rarely has it been studied on its own. In Thinking in Cases , the distinguished critic Peter Brooks zeroes in on a kind of thinking that we all know—and often use—without understanding its dimensions and its history.

This book ponders what we do and mean when we think in cases—when we take up specific instances with a view to making them exemplary. Brooks brings to this study decades of reflection on the psychoanalytic case history, the rhetoric of the legal case, and novels that unfold as cases seeking solutions. Brooks focuses on the case-history’s emergence in the late nineteenth century: first, he examines how Henry James’s uses of narrative parallel case-study methods in law, medicine, and psychoanalysis. Elsewhere, he traces the case history from Hippocratic medicine through Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s detective fiction to a startling legal case from Victorian England involving shipwreck and cannibalism. Other chapters discuss a tale of madness by Balzac and Freud’s most speculative works, especially Moses and Monotheism . A final chapter examines recent novels—Duras’s The Ravishing of Lol Stein , Coetzee’s Disgrace , Modiano’s Dora Bruder , and Erpenbeck’s Kairos —as case studies.

books.title: Thirteen Sisters
books.subtitle: The 1979 Boston Murders and the Resistance They Inspired
books.tagline: The murder of thirteen women and girls in 1979 and the social movement they launched.
books.description:
In four terrifying months in 1979, thirteen women and girls—twelve Black, one white—were murdered in Boston. All were found in or near Roxbury, a predominantly Black neighborhood in a city famously beset by racial strife and division. Fears of a serial killer spread within Black communities. But the authorities wouldn’t hear of it: these were just ordinary, everyday murders of unimportant people, killed by men they knew. The police said Black residents had nothing to fear—and the media implied that white people could safely ignore the carnage.

Yet Black feminists refused to accept the murders of Black women and girls. The real serial killers, they argued, were chronic racism, sexism, poverty, and domestic violence, including violence committed by Black men. Something had to be done.

Thirteen Sisters tells the gripping stories of the women who died—their lives, their brutal deaths, the attempts to solve them—and the renowned Combahee River Collective, whose activism in the wake of the murders brought national attention to the overlapping oppressions that made Black women and girls so vulnerable to violence. Historian Andrew S. Baer interviews family members and activists to introduce readers to the victims as complete people and investigate the events surrounding their deaths, unspooling a fast-paced and urgent narrative about crime, race, and marginalization. Baer also pays tribute to the Black feminists who saw the social roots of this violence and called for radical change, demands that remain all too relevant today.

Riveting, enraging, and humane, Thirteen Sisters is an indictment of the neglectful institutions that have failed Black women and a testament to the activists who transformed how we understand systemic oppression.

praise.q: Thirteen Sisters is a terrific and thoroughly engaging book on an important topic. Baer explores how a series of seemingly unrelated murders in the Roxbury section of Boston in 1979 mobilized African American residents, particularly feminists, to become activists. Their grassroots, neighborhood-based response to the violence spawned a dynamic, resilient social movement. Elegantly written, passionate, and well researched, Thirteen Sisters offers a powerful analysis of the connection among murder, race, and second-wave feminism. It deserves a wide audience.
praise.by: Jeffrey S. Adler, author of “Bluecoated Terror”

books.title: Till the Light Leaps
books.subtitle: Essays on Playing Attention
books.tagline: A ranging, erudite, and intimate examination of the nature of knowledge, by a thinker and creator who defies categorization.
books.description:
Attention is in short supply and high demand. But when we bring our minds and time and senses to something—an idea, an object, another person—we tap into a human capacity for observation, patience, candor, and presence. Look long enough, and we can reliably catch a bright flash, a shift in the light, even a dawning.

In Till the Light Leaps , historian of science D. Graham Burnett explores the questions that have been major drivers of his intellectual life: How do we know what we know? And how are we changed by that effort? Written during a period of radical, collective, and creative experimentation with attention, the twenty-six essays collected here span topics like technology, science, art, and religion. Together, they comprise a sustained reflection on the relationship between empirical matters and the shiver-work of the human spirit. A brief history of spectroscopy offers an occasion to consider the solemn power of fire, as well as the righteous lessons of a childhood science experiment gone wrong. Skywriting invokes military might, but also the expressionistic bravura of a solo aeronaut, Art Smith. The Greek ritual of throwing plant matter in celebration is a thread connecting animal sacrifice, confetti production, and capitalist excess. In the final, previously unpublished essay, Galway Kinnell’s 1980 poem “Saint Francis and the Sow” becomes a heroic call to love and an allegory of attention in its richest sense.

Till the Light Leaps , a reference to the writings of Simone Weil, advises us to look at something “until the light leaps,” whether it yields a wink or an illumination. Burnett models the work—and the pleasure—of staying present with the world, and his essays test what science can offer, even as they feel for what it cannot.

praise.q: Burnett can make anything interesting. These dazzling essays cover an extraordinary range of subjects, from contrails to the Greenwich Meridian to financialized capitalism. Burnett writes about attention, and this book is a masterclass in observational acuity, full of tiny details that open up whole worlds. The sentences are supremely entertaining, but it is not just a fun read, it is a profound, existential, elegiac meditation on what it means to be human in a techno-scientific society.
praise.by: Cathy Gere, author of “Finding the Beautiful Commons”

books.title: Tyrannies of Freedom
books.subtitle: African Exceptionalism and the Neocolonial Assemblage in the Millennial Age
books.tagline: Examines the enduring myth of Ghanaian exceptionalism and neoliberal freedom.
books.description:
What is the legacy of the African Revolution today? Black Studies scholar and anthropologist Bayo Holsey addresses this question by examining the twenty-first-century relationship between the United States and Ghana, a nation that was once associated with a powerful vision of Black freedom. In Tyrannies of Freedom , she demonstrates that the period that saw the expansion of the US counterterror state also witnessed attempts to discredit this vision of freedom and replace it with another—one that centers the agency of US politicians, media pundits, and development experts.

Analyzing international development discourses, the anti-trafficking regime’s representational economy, and the expansion of Ghana’s branding as a homeland of the African diaspora, Holsey interrogates the operation of a millennial neocolonial assemblage that asserts, in various ways, that the United States is the guarantor of Ghanaian freedom while simultaneously implementing policies of surveillance, endangerment, and exploitation. At the same time, Holsey shows how Ghanaians and other Black subjects have contested these projects. Tracking the transformation of the Ghanaian nation from a beacon of Black freedom and Pan-African possibility to a battleground over the meanings of African sovereignty in a post-9/11 world, this important book addresses pressing questions concerning the operation of US power in Africa and the production and legitimation of a racialized global hierarchy.

books.title: Argonautica
books.subtitle: Edited and translated by Mark Heerink
books.tagline: The Roman retelling of the quest for the Golden Fleece.
books.description:
The Flavian epic poet Valerius Flaccus is the author of the most extensive surviving narrative of the Argonautic myth in Latin. His poem tells the story of how the Argonauts under Jason’s leadership travel over the open sea in the Argo, the first ship, to obtain the Golden Fleece. After arriving in Colchis, Jason is supported in this task by the local princess Medea, who has fallen in love with him through divine intervention. After successfully winning the Golden Fleece, Jason and Medea depart from Colchis, at which point, in the middle of its eighth book, the poem breaks off. Within Valerius’ epic program, the narrated action is presented as part of Jupiter’s plan for ruling the world, which includes the transfer of power from one nation to another.

This Latin version of the Argonautica , written under the Flavian emperors in the late first century AD, resonates with contemporary issues of hegemony, expansion, and domestic conflicts even as it provides a gripping narrative.

The Hellenistic epic Argonautica by the Greek poet Apollonius Rhodius provides the starting point for the key elements of the story. In addition to Apollonius Rhodius, Valerius engages with the entire literary tradition before him, particularly the works of Homer and Virgil. Among other details, his refashioning of standard epic motifs and episodes demonstrates his literary sophistication.

This edition provides a revised Latin text and a new English translation, as well as ample explanatory and illustrative material.
books.bio: Mark Heerink is Associate Professor of Latin Literature at the University of Amsterdam.

books.title: Dr. Bot
books.subtitle: Why Doctors Can Fail Us—and How AI Could Save Lives
books.tagline: How does AI compare to a doctor when it comes to saving lives?
books.description:
Doctors are under-resourced and face unprecedented levels of stress, with rising patient numbers and ever developing medical knowledge. But at the same time, they are all too human, prone to racial, class and social biases that affect the care patients receive.

Can we improve patient experience and alleviate the burdens of doctors at the same time?

In this groundbreaking study, Charlotte Blease reveals how AI, if handled with care, could emerge as the most reliable physician in history. Drawing on interviews with authorities in AI, doctors and patients, Blease shows how technology – despite some resistance – is already making a difference. From diagnosis and second opinions to treatment and aftercare, AI has the potential to revolutionise our healthcare.
books.bio: Charlotte Blease is a health researcher exploring how AI can transform patient care by changing how healthcare works, making it more effective, ethical and responsive in ways humans alone cannot achieve. She focuses on what technology can do for patients, not just how AI works. She is currently Associate Professor at Uppsala University and Researcher at Harvard Medical School.

praise.q: Blease’s arguments have reframed how I think about AI’s role in medicine.
praise.by: Dr Leana Wen, The Washington Post

praise.q: Change is inevitable and, as Blease’s thought-provoking book shows, necessary.

praise.q: A strong case that doctors should be open to using AI to be fully effective.

praise.q: This book asks the challenging question: could AI perform better than doctors?… From the outset, the author is careful not to antagonise doctors: she empathises with their plight…. But at the same time, she points out that they are all too human…
praise.by: Dr Muiris Houston, The Irish Times

praise.q: This is very, very interesting... and a stylish book
praise.by: Pat Kenny, Newstalk

praise.q: A bold, brilliant diagnosis of medicine’s blind spots, Dr Bot is the second opinion that medicine didn’t ask for, but desperately needs. It is sharp, savvy and impossible to ignore.

praise.q: [Blease’s] evidence-driven sceptical approach is part of what makes this such a good book.

books.title: Fungi of the World
books.subtitle: A Guide to Every Phylum
books.tagline: A beautifully illustrated guide to the world’s fungi—the essential one-stop reference for scientists, naturalists, and fungi enthusiasts
books.description:
From lowly molds in our refrigerators and pantries to the delicate networks of mycorrhizae supporting entire ecosystems, fungi are everywhere—and they are doing far more than we realize. This book takes readers on an extraordinary journey through one of Earth’s most enigmatic and essential realms, explaining what fungi are and how they live while offering a panoramic survey of their remarkable diversity. Whether you’re a seasoned mycophile or a curious newcomer, Fungi of the World opens a window into fungi’s ecological brilliance, evolutionary surprises, and taxonomic splendor.

Provides a comprehensive introduction to fungi, their ecology, and importance and how they differ from other kingdoms of life

Features a wealth of color photos, figures, and maps

Covers all 11 known phyla, from the familiar Basidiomycota and Ascomycota to the lesser-known Zoopagomycota and the microsporidian fungi

Profiles some 100 fungal families, describing key features such as distribution, habitat, and representative species, with notes on morphology and field identification

Explores fungi’s expanding role across medicine, food, industry, conservation, and art

Discusses how readers can help to preserve these often overlooked yet vital organisms
books.bio: Britt A. Bunyard is the author of The Little Book of Fungi and The Lives of Fungi (both Princeton) and (with Tavis Lynch) The Beginner’s Guide to Mushrooms , among other books. He is the founder, publisher, and editor in chief of Fungi , the widest-circulating mycology magazine in North America, and serves as executive director of the Telluride Mushroom Festival.

books.title: History and Halakhah, Intellect and Spirit
books.subtitle: Essays by Isadore Twersky
books.description:
History and Halakhah, Intellect and Spirit gathers the major scholarly essays, including many newly translated from Hebrew, of a master of medieval and early modern Jewish intellectual history. Isadore Twersky (1930–1997) was one of the outstanding Maimonidean scholars of his time, whose work spanned Jewish historical creativity from Geonic times through the seventeenth century, and also touched on contemporary issues and figures. He was the Littauer Professor of Hebrew Literature and Philosophy at Harvard University and founder of its Center for Jewish Studies.

This volume presents Twersky’s works on Maimonidean studies, halakhic scholars and literature, Halakhah and meta-halakhah, Jewish intellectual history and contemporary themes. The introduction surveys Twersky’s life and presents the major themes and ideas in his scholarship to a new readership.
books.bio:
Isadore Twersky (1930–1997) was the Littauer Professor of Hebrew Literature and Philosophy at Harvard University and founder of its Center for Jewish Studies.

Carmi Horowitz taught at Ben Gurion University of the Negev and Bar Ilan University, served as Dean of the Touro Graduate School of Jewish Studies in Jerusalem, Rector of the Lander Institute in Jerusalem, President of the Givat Washington Teachers College, and chair of the graduate program in Jewish Thought at Michlalah Jerusalem College.

Michael A. Shmidman is Dean Emeritus and Victor J. Selmanowitz Professor of Jewish History at Touro Graduate School of Jewish Studies and editor at Touro University Press. He is co-author with Isadore Twersky of Law and Philosophy: Perspectives on Maimonides’ Teaching . He also served as editor of Tradition: A Journal of Orthodox Jewish Thought .

books.title: Incentives
books.subtitle: A Critical History of a Powerful Idea
books.tagline: A challenge to incentivization as a dominant framework for understanding and governing people
books.description:
From corporate management and consumer behavior to public health and climate policy, incentives are widely treated as a neutral and effective way to shape how people act. In this book, Guus Dix shows that incentives are not simple policy nudges; they lull us into a passive understanding of ourselves as being merely responsive to changes others make to our environment. They foster a politics of incremental tweaks to a socially and ecologically destructive economic system that we are expected to accept without question. Dix argues that it is time to challenge the reign of incentives in contemporary science and public life.

Dix traces the evolution of the incentive, from the engineering of performance charts and rewards for factory workers to combating gridlock at Britain’s National Health Service. He describes the function of incentives under socialism, theories of adjustment incentives developed at the Harvard Business School to manage employees, and incentivizing whole economies—both socialist and capitalist. He shows that incentivization is a distinct way of wielding power. Incentives have become part of a quasi-universal governing philosophy that keeps us from addressing such major issues as poverty and the climate crisis. Finally, Dix analyzes the limits of incentivization, arguing that being governed by incentives keeps us from considering government policies that have the potential to bring about meaningful and transformative change.
books.bio: Guus Dix is assistant professor in sociology of science and technology at the University of Twente, the Netherlands.

praise.q: The arguments are coherent and compelling, presented in a way that is both accessible and engaging. This book will occupy an important niche in the intellectual history tradition as well as introduce a more practice-oriented perspective that it is often lacking in such work.
praise.by: Simone Polillo, author of The Ascent of Market Efficiency: Finance That Cannot Be Proven
praise.cred: author of The Ascent of Market Efficiency: Finance That Cannot Be Proven

books.title: Infinite Coal
books.subtitle: How Britain Became the First Fossil Fuel Economy
books.tagline: Why Britain's energy path gave rise to an ideology of endless growth
books.description:
Despite the warnings of climate scientists, the world remains dangerously addicted to fossil fuel. Why has it been so difficult to break this habit? In a major new account, Fredrik Albritton Jonsson suggests that the planetary emergency has profound historical roots reaching back to the making of the first fossil fuel economy in eighteenth century Britain. Rather than look for a single dramatic rupture centered on the steam powered factory system, in Infinite Coal Albritton Jonsson shows that there was a much more gradual and multidimensional development of the first coal economy, stretching from the deep mine and ironworks to the household and the global food system.

Albritton Jonsson explores not only the material forces behind the British energy path but also how ideas about fossil fuel energy reoriented politics and society towards a new ideal of growth. At the same time an environmental and political history of Britain’s energy transformation, Infinite Coal explains why and how coal became so deeply embedded in our way of life. Albritton Jonsson argues that the most important legacy of Britain’s early fossil fuel economy is fossil cornucopianism—the idea of a bountiful, never-ending energy source—which still haunts modern politics and economics.
books.bio: Fredrik Albritton Jonsson is associate professor of British history and history of science at the University of Chicago. He is the author of Enlightenment’s Frontier: The Scottish Highlands and the Origins of Environmentalism and the coauthor of Scarcity: A History from the Origins of Capitalism to the Climate Crisis .

books.title: Let's Take It All!
books.subtitle: Autonomia and the Italian 1970s
books.tagline: For a decade in Italy, communism wasn't a future to wait for—it was all around them, ready to be cracked open.
books.description:
"We want everything" was the slogan of Italian activists in the late 1960s. But by the 1970s, movements stopped demanding things of politicians and bosses and instead turned to each other and said, "Let's take it all!" For a while, it looked like they might.

Across Italy, a communist movement known as Autonomia exploded. For the autonomists, communism did not mean a distant future utopia planned by a central state. Instead, it was all around them, ready to be cracked open by people who turned their revolutionary energy toward the remaking of daily life and the defense of their ability to do so.

First published in French in 2011, Marcello Tarì's history of Autonomia is a kinetic narrative through this movement, taking readers through its tactical innovations, its strategic debates, its internal conflicts, and the depth of its transformation of everyday life—which left a lasting mark on communist theory and practice. Appearing for the first time in English, this book and the movement it recounts deserve to be discussed, debated, and mined for inspiration by those who are finished waiting for anyone to come save us.

In an original introduction, Idris Robinson explains why this movement's experience half a century ago is not so distant from ours today, and why Autonomia is a crucial reference from which to begin any realistic strategy for revolution now.
books.bio: Marcello Tarì is a renowned participant-researcher of contemporary social movements. He is the author of There Is No Unhappy Revolution: The Communism of Destitution (2021) and is the Italian translator of the Invisible Committee's The Coming Insurrection , To Our Friends , and Now . He lives in Italy.

books.title: Obliquity
books.subtitle: Why Our Goals are Best Achieved Indirectly
books.tagline: An updated classic from the award-winning economist: how to achieve success by aiming sideways—and unlock new goals along the way
books.description:
“Provocative, profound and counterintuitive.”— Wall Street Journal

It may feel paradoxical, but in business and in life, our goals are often best achieved when approaching them indirectly. In a traffic jam, the quickest route home might involve going the long way round. Those who deliberately seek love rarely find it and the endless pursuit of happiness often leads to misery. For a corporation, focus on cutting-edge engineering, new technology or a unique product is what generates profit; making profit the sole purpose of a business usually leads to its collapse.

From the award-winning economist John Kay, Obliquity remains a manifesto for aiming slightly off-target: drawing on examples from football to forest fires, Kay shows that problems are best solved obliquely, through a gradual process of risk-taking and discovery. This new edition adds two entirely new chapters and substantial revisions throughout, extending Kay's argument to the age of artificial intelligence, Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Vladimir Putin.
books.bio: Sir John Kay , fellow of St John’s College, Oxford, has a distinguished career in academia, business, and finance. His writing includes The Corporation in the Twenty-First Century, the best-selling Other People’s Money, and a regular column for the Financial Times , has been recognized by numerous awards.

praise.q: Kay offers an intelligent, engaging analysis that shows how indirect paths can be better than more obvious, rational plans in a complex and uncertain world
praise.by: Harvard Business Review

praise.q: Persuasive, rigorous, creative and wise. Brilliant.
praise.by: Tim Harford, author of The Undercover Economist

praise.q: John Kay is an admirable debunker of myths and false beliefs—he can see substantial things others don't. Read this book.
praise.by: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, author of The Black Swan

books.title: Sex Strikes and Suffragettes
books.subtitle: The Power of a Political Idea
books.tagline: What suffragettes’ debates over sex and birth strikes reveal about the women’s suffrage movement and the cultural and intellectual world of the early twentieth century
books.description:
Women’s suffrage activists are remembered for their tactical ingenuity; they organized mass marches, broke windows and chained themselves to railings for the cause. Two tactics, not widely used but hotly debated, remain largely forgotten: sex strikes and birth strikes. In Sex Strikes and Suffragettes , Tania Shew pieces together for the first time the spirited and often tense discussions that took place at the turn of the twentieth century over whether suffrage campaigners in both Britain and the United States should refuse to have sex with men or bear their children as tactics to win the vote.

With Shew, readers listen in on suffrage meetings, stand in the crowd at suffrage talks and sit among the audiences at Edwardian cinemas and theatres. Shew finds suffrage campaigners staging adaptations of the Ancient Greek play Lysistrata and drawing broad inspiration from the sex strike depicted within it. She outlines the transatlantic connections of the movement, pointing to the impact of previously unknown feminist foot soldiers and revisiting well-known thinkers including Charlotte Despard and Emma Goldman. Suffrage campaigners, Shew explains, drew from a wide range of influences including trade union activism, emerging Freudian ideas about psychology and personality and Malthusian theories—which made for strange ideological bedfellows. She examines what the interest in sex and birth strikes reveals about suffragette thinking on the wider themes of democracy and militancy. Shew argues that these debates about women’s economic and social roles from a century ago shed light on ideas about women’s agency that resonate today.
books.bio: Tania Shew is research fellow and college lecturer at Corpus Christi College, University of Cambridge.

praise.q: Shew has identified a significant, yet underexplored, aspect of the decades-long campaigns for women’s political enfranchisement in both the United States and the United Kingdom, drawing on an intriguing array of sources not traditionally utilized in discussions of the campaign for women’s enfranchisement, or, for that matter, intellectual history. An innovative and original contribution to the field.”—Laura Mayhall, author of The Militant Suffrage Movement: Citizenship and Resistance in Britain, 1860

This is a lively history of the idea of the sex strike as a tool of feminist organizing in the early twentieth century. The writing is clear and engaging, and the characters that the book follows include some of the better-known activists of the time as well as others who are now mostly forgotten. A thought-provoking piece of scholarship that should be accessible to more than a specialist audience.
praise.by: Dawn Teele, author of Forging the Franchise: The Political Origins of the Women’s Vote
praise.cred: author of Forging the Franchise: The Political Origins of the Women’s Vote

books.title: Social Distancing
books.tagline: A candid exploration of the implosion of a friendship in the third year of the COVID pandemic.
books.description:
Ripping off the wig versus throwing off the wig. Hysterical laughter. The celebration of cruelty. The eroticism of brutality. The violence and camp, the violence in camp, the violence.

To flee in sequined dresses. To kiss the blood, to caress the decay, that sudden dance. The crossing and recrossing of the chest. Lip-synching toward and away from justice. Or do I mean feeling. I mean feeling injustice.

Social Distancing candidly explores the implosion of a friendship in the third year of the COVID pandemic, and the ramifications of this loss as it ruptures time.

Using the films of Derek Jarman as a gateway out of emotional overwhelm, Sycamore moves from current-day Seattle to the theaters of the imagination when she was coming of age in San Francisco in the early nineties. Here she explores the very meaning of friendship, and its centrality as a model for queer kinship.

Sycamore’s investigation leads her from the isolation of the COVID pandemic to the trauma of the AIDS crisis and an interrogation of personal and structural abandonment. This is a book that searches for its own form—from the cruising park to the films of Hal Hartley, Nan Goldin’s photos to the overwhelm of everyday survival.

Ultimately Social Distancing offers a searing, original examination of the possibilities of care in an uncaring society and the importance of friendship in queer lives.
books.bio: Mattilda Bernstein Sycamore is the Lambda Literary Award-winning author, most recently, of Terry Dactyl , described by the New York Times Book Review as “a remarkably grounded look at what it means to be fully alive.” She is the author of four novels and three nonfiction titles, and the editor of six nonfiction anthologies. The Freezer Door , her 2020 memoir, was a New York Times Editors’ Choice, and a finalist for the PEN/Jean Stein Book Award, and Touching the Art , her 2023 title, was a finalist for a Washington State Book Award and a Pacific Northwest Book Award. Her next anthology, ACT UP Beyond New York: Stories and Strategies from a Movement to End the AIDS Crisis , will be out in Fall 2027.

praise.q: I’ve hardly come across such a deep and candid work about friendship—and friendship ending—than Mattilda Bernstein Sycamore’s Social Distancing . A reflection on pain, aloneness, and the pandemic, but also touch, attachment, and community. While reading it, I felt close to this book.
praise.by: Amina Cain, author of Indelicacy

praise.q: Mattilda Bernstein Sycamore does what I have come to rely on her to do: she writes into contradiction and paradox not as problems to solve but places to live. Her books move by branching, doubling back, gossiping, picking up companions along the way, cruising for unexpected kinships. Social Distancing orbits a vital question: what forms of kinship remain possible in a world that repeatedly abandons us? No writer of our generation has mapped the textures of queer life with more wit, precision, or generosity. Sycamore reminds us that queer life is composed not only of identities or desires, but of conversations, arguments, loyalties, betrayals, and impossible acts of faith that keep us returning to one another. This is a book that knows friendship is where humanity rehearses itself.
praise.by: Johanna Hedva, author of How to Tell When We Will Die: On Pain, Disability, and Doom
praise.cred: author of How to Tell When We Will Die: On Pain, Disability, and Doom

praise.q: Say the quiet part loud. Mattilda has created a generous stream of memory COVID record like none other, where survival is critique and critique offers the intimacy that could allow us to admit that we want a world loving enough to save our lives.
praise.by: Alexis Pauline Gumbs, author of Survival Is a Promise: The Eternal Life of Audre Lorde
praise.cred: author of Survival Is a Promise: The Eternal Life of Audre Lorde

books.title: Tatiana Bilbao Estudio
books.subtitle: Stories, Practice, and Archive
books.tagline: The first major monograph about Mexico’s celebrated and award-winning architect Tatiana Bilbao and her acclaimed studio known for social values, collaboration, and sensitive design. A fully illustrated and beautifully produced book with over 300 photographs, drawings, and collage, offering insight into one of the twenty-first century's most exciting architects.
books.description:
A fully illustrated and beautifully produced book with over 300 photographs, drawings, and collage, offering insight into one of the twenty-first century's most exciting architects.

Tatiana Bilbao Estudio is the first comprehensive monograph to showcase Mexico’s celebrated and award-winning architect Tatiana Bilbao and her acclaimed studio. Known for its keen attention to social values, collaboration, and sensitive design, the Bilbao studio is celebrated internationally.

Unlike most architecture monographs that simply present the finished work, this volume centers process. Purposefully eschewing digital tools, Bilbao creates design concepts through a decades-long practice of precise drawing, collage, and model-making. This richly illustrated and beautifully produced full-color book captures the spirit of Bilbao’s work, uniting visually bold forms with intuitive understanding.

Over 18 projects—proof of successful concept—are showcased here, including houses, parks, chapels, public spaces, and institutional buildings. Revealing an uncommon site-sensitivity, these spaces—in France, Spain, Germany, the USA, and Mexico—epitomize spatial design made for lingering, enjoyment, and community.

Designed by Estudio Herrera, a woman-led studio, this book reveals the force and elegance of a woman-led firm, offering inspirational insight into one of the most exciting architecture practices in the world today.
books.bio: Tatiana Bilbao holds a recurring teaching position at Yale University School of Architecture and has taught at Harvard University GSD, Columbia University, and Rice University, among other institutions. Her work has been published in The New York Times, Architect’s Newspaper, Monocle, Domus , and others. Bilbao was recognized with the Kunstpreis Berlin, named an Emerging Voice by the Architecture League of New York, awarded the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture Prize by the LOCUS Foundation, the Marcus Prize Award, Tau Sigma Delta Gold Medal of 2020, the Richard Neutra Award, the AW Architect of the Year 2022, the J.Irwin and Xenia S. Miller Prize and ArpaFil Award, and in 2024, Boston Architectural College awarded Bilbao an Honorary Doctorate in recognition of her contributions to the field.

books.title: The Ancient Jerusalem Hymnal
books.subtitle: The Festal Hymns
books.description: The Ancient Jerusalem Hymnal, known in Georgian as Iadgari, presents the first complete English translation of the proper hymns for the major annual feasts celebrated in the city around the end of the sixth century. Preserving thousands of lines of theological poetry, the Hymnal is among the largest early Christian chant corpora, yet it has remained long overlooked because its Greek original is lost and the collection survives only in Old Georgian translations produced in early medieval Palestine. Stephen J. Shoemaker’s translation offers a continuous, readable rendering of the festal cycle based on its most important witness, Sinai geor. 18, which best preserves Jerusalem’s public worship with minimal later “monasticizing” revisions. The result is an unusually direct window onto early Christian devotion and theology in the Holy Land, introduced and annotated to illuminate its language, theology, and liturgical setting.
books.bio: Stephen J. Shoemaker is Professor and Ira E. Gaston Fellow in Christian Studies at the University of Oregon.

books.title: The Art of Making Dinosaurs
books.subtitle: How Science and Imagination Bring Them to Life
books.tagline: An illustrated history of dinosaur art—from the first fossil finds to the age of CGI
books.description:
In 1824, English naturalist William Buckland formally described Megalosaurus —the first dinosaur to be scientifically named—marking a pivotal moment in the emergence of modern paleontology. Since then, dinosaurs have become popular visual icons, from displays of skeletons and paintings in museums to hyperrealistic animations in films and documentaries. Images of dinosaurs are everywhere, yet tensions have long existed between paleontologists and the artists and designers who create them. The Art of Making Dinosaurs tells the story of how dinosaurs became stars of art, illustration, and media, from the first attempts to portray these strange leviathans to the revolutionary digital methods used today.

Victoria Coules and Michael Benton introduce readers to artists like John Martin, Alice B. Woodward, and Rudolph Zallinger, whose groundbreaking images shaped public perceptions of dinosaurs and paleontology more broadly. The visual reconstruction of dinosaurs from fossilized bones has always involved speculation, and while some scientists have embraced paleoart as a means of raising awareness about their field, others have argued that such images could be misleading. Coules and Benton shed light on these controversies while examining how the representation of dinosaurs has developed amid new discoveries and a changing visual culture.

The Art of Making Dinosaurs blends engaging storytelling with stunning fossil images and iconic depictions of dinosaurs over the past two centuries, revealing how art and illustration have played a central role in the rapidly evolving science of paleontology.
books.bio: Victoria Coules is an art historian at the University of Bristol who specializes in the representation of dinosaurs in visual culture. Michael J. Benton is professor of vertebrate paleontology at the University of Bristol and a fellow of the Royal Society. His many books include Dinosaur Behavior: An Illustrated Guide (Princeton) and Dinosaurs: New Visions of a Lost World .

praise.q: Two hundred years ago, the word ‘dinosaur’ didn’t exist. So how did these creatures become the pop culture icons they are today? This fascinating question is the focus of The Art of Making Dinosaurs . This engaging and thought-provoking book is brimming with surprises, and by the end of it, you’ll understand how our modern conception of dinosaurs emerged over time and be greatly entertained along the way.”—Steve Brusatte, University of Edinburgh paleontologist and New York Times / Sunday Times bestselling author of The Rise and Fall of the Dinosaurs

An insightful account of all the ways scientists, artists, and fans have imagined dinosaurs. Poring over some of the most influential, debated, controversial, and just plain fun depictions of dinosaurs going back more than a century and a half, Coules and Benton have taken a step back from arguments over accuracy to tell the story of our ever-changing relationship with dinosaurs.
praise.by: Riley Black, author of Tyrant Lizard Queen and The Last Days of the Dinosaurs
praise.cred: author of Tyrant Lizard Queen and The Last Days of the Dinosaurs

books.title: The Colors of Dinosaurs and the Prehistoric World
books.subtitle: Exploring the Prehistoric Palette
books.tagline: A marvelously illustrated look at the fossil evidence of color in extinct life, from dinosaurs and mammoths to ancient insects and plants—revealing the amazing technologies and fossils that allow us to visualize the prehistoric world in more detail than ever
books.description:
The colors of dinosaurs and other extinct organisms are typically considered as being lost to time. Rare fossils, however, contain remnants of ancient pigments or structures that manipulated light to create color, allowing scientists to make predictions about the hues and patterns of species extinct for millions of years. The study of such fossils, first collected centuries ago, has been revolutionized in recent decades as new technology has allowed for increasingly sophisticated assessments of colors in dinosaurs and other ancient reptiles, as well as fish, mammals, invertebrates, and even plants and microbes. This book explores the development of color across billions of years of evolution, explaining how extinct color palettes can be reconstructed as well as what details still elude us. Written and illustrated by one of the world’s leading paleoartists, The Colors of Dinosaurs and the Prehistoric World blends an artist’s eye for nature with a paleontologist’s expertise to present prehistoric life as you have never seen it before.

More than 150 illustrations, photographs, and graphics that showcase the amazing array of color and pattern data found in the fossil record

Reconstructs extinct species and environments with the hues and tones predicted by paleontological science, showing the appearance of feathered and scaly dinosaurs, flying and swimming reptiles, ancient reefs, Ice Age mammals, the early days of Earth, and more

Reveals the diverse means used to predict ancient coloration, from analyses of ancient pigments to mapping the distribution of biological color on evolutionary trees, and even using cave paintings to inform depictions of prehistoric mammals

Outlines the long history and modern science of paleocolor restoration and explores what reconstructing color in ancient organisms tells us about ancient ecology and behavior

Traces the brilliant diversity of color of the modern natural world to its evolutionary roots
books.bio: Mark P. Witton is a paleontologist, author, and artist based at the University of Portsmouth. He designs and advises on extinct creatures for films and documentaries, including the hit Apple TV+ series Prehistoric Planet and the Walking with Dinosaurs series, and his artwork is widely featured in books and museums around the world. His books include King Tyrant: A Natural History of Tyrannosaurus rex and Pterosaurs: Natural History, Evolution, Anatomy (both Princeton).

books.title: The Evolution of Imperfection
books.subtitle: The Science of Why We Aren’t and Can’t Be Perfect
books.tagline: How understanding our genetic imperfections can change our view of evolution and enrich what it means to be human
books.description:
If we start with the presumption that evolution is a constantly improving process, some aspects of our evolution just do not make sense. We have a high rate of genetic diseases, for example, and much of our DNA seems to be pointless. In The Evolution of Imperfection , Laurence Hurst explores our apparently rotten genetic luck.

Hurst, a leading authority on evolution and genetics, argues that our evolutionary imperfections proceed directly from two features: the difficulties of pregnancy and the fact that historically there are relatively few of us. In pregnancy, natural selection can favor chromosomes that kill embryos in species (including ours) that continuously receive resources from the mother. Most fertilized eggs don’t make it, and incompatibilities between the fetus and mother can lead to lethal disorders of pregnancy. The historically small population size enhances the role of chance, which in turn leads to both accumulation of unnecessary DNA and more mutation.

So what can save us? One answer may lie in genetic medicine, which has given us therapies that make killer conditions preventable and even curable.

Hurst suggests that our seeming imperfections could be the key to a new way to understand evolution itself. Looking at circumstances that seem to defy explanation, we might come to a richer understanding of how evolution really works, and what it means to be human.
books.bio: Laurence D. Hurst is professor of evolutionary genetics in the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath. His research on how genetic systems evolve, and the application of this knowledge to medicine, has been recognized with national and international prizes and fellowships.

praise.q: [Hurst] does a nearly perfect job of showing how and why, as his subtitle indicates, 'we aren't and can't be perfect.' . . . He is contagiously enthusiastic about the simple yet stunning reality of our very existence.
praise.by: David P. Barash, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: [The Evolution of Imperfection] is accessible for interested lay readers, offering a nice round-up of the history of and current scientific understandings of evolution.
praise.by: Library Journal

praise.q: Stimulating. . . . Hurst excels at teasing out the counterintuitive implications of natural selection.
praise.by: Publishers Weekly

praise.q: Anyone with a life science background will gain a superior understanding of evolution by reading this book.
praise.by: David Reznick, Quarterly Review of Biology

praise.q: Hurst, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of Bath, is a gifted story teller. . . . The Evolution of Imperfection comes close to perfection. I highly recommend it to those from medicine who are interested in a thoughtful and nuanced discussion of the relevance of evolutionary genetics to their practice. I also recommend it to biologists interested in evolutionary medicine. It will provide much background reading for evolutionary medicine courses.
praise.by: Norman A. Johnson, Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health

praise.q: A richly detailed exploration of the genetic mechanisms that influence everything from our individual chances of existence and subsequent health to the evolution of life on this planet, bursting with metaphors and examples that help to unpack the complexity of this fascinating topic.
praise.by: Kat Arney, author of Rebel Cell: Cancer, Evolution, and the New Science of Life’s Oldest Betrayal
praise.cred: author of Rebel Cell: Cancer, Evolution, and the New Science of Life’s Oldest Betrayal

praise.q: A profound yet accessible synthesis of evolutionary thinking in the molecular era. I unreservedly recommend this book!
praise.by: Joanna Masel, author of Bypass Wall Street: A Biologist's Guide to the Rat Race
praise.cred: author of Bypass Wall Street: A Biologist's Guide to the Rat Race

praise.q: A very interesting and useful book that covers many ideas and discoveries with clear and accessible writing.
praise.by: Russell Bonduriansky, coauthor of Extended Heredity: A New Understanding of Inheritance and Evolution
praise.cred: coauthor of Extended Heredity: A New Understanding of Inheritance and Evolution

books.title: The Latent Brain
books.subtitle: The New Science of How We Think, Feel, and Act
books.tagline: A neuroscientist argues we’ve misunderstood the brain by focusing on individual neurons and unveils a new theory of how the brain really works.
books.description:
In 2007, doctors in Marseille discovered that their patient had a gaping, fluid-filled hole in his brain. His neurons had disintegrated, severing the fragile connections that form the brain's communication system. And yet, the man’s only complaint was weakness in one leg. He could still read, remember, and reason. How was that possible?

The Latent Brain is the surprising answer. For decades, neuroscientists have insisted that our thoughts, feelings, and actions depend on the rapid electrical signals fired by each of the brain’s neurons. But they can’t explain why many neurons carry no useful information, or why, when neurons die, our behavior doesn’t necessarily change. Mark Humphries offers a radically new idea. Our mental lives, he argues, arise not from the activity of individual neurons but from collective signals formed by vast networks of neurons acting in concert. These signals guide our behavior; enable different brains to perform the same tasks; and even explain how we learn—why it's sometimes easy and sometimes devilishly hard. Humphries’s theory promises a revolution in neuroscience: a set of laws that map the activity of billions of neurons to the immense catalog of human behavior and experiences.

Bold, lucid, and ambitious, T he Latent Brain is a big-idea science book by every measure.
books.bio: Mark Humphries is Chair in Computational Neuroscience at the University of Nottingham, UK, and author of The Spike: An Epic Journey Through the Brain in 2.1 Seconds .

praise.q: The Latent Brain beautifully captures a ​recent change in how neuroscience thinks about brains. Humphries turns this perspective into an unusually clear way of thinking about how populations of neurons compute, why some things are easier to learn, how brains remain functional despite variability, and what it may mean to understand a brain.

books.title: The Song Dynasty
books.subtitle: A New History
books.authors: Patricia Buckley Ebrey, Charles Hartman, Christian Lamouroux
books.tagline: A definitive new history of China’s influential Song dynasty and its pivotal role in East Asia and beyond, by one of its leading historians
books.description:
Despite constant pressure from the powerful steppe empires on its borders, the Song dynasty lasted for more than three centuries, from 960 to 1279, becoming one of the longest-running and most consequential dynasties in Chinese history. In this sweeping history, Christian Lamouroux, one of the world’s leading authorities on the period, offers a masterful reinterpretation of the Song empire, focusing on its interactions with its neighbors and emphasizing its crucial role in the longer economic, social, and political history of China, East Asia, and the world.

Reevaluating a century of scholarship, including the most recent historical approaches, The Song Dynasty explains how the Song monarchy differed from earlier and later Chinese empires and describes the measures the Song adopted to resist the steppe empires. Among the most important of these were profound institutional changes that encouraged unprecedented urban growth and economic and financial development. Lamouroux also tells how the Song gave birth to a bureaucratic regime in which scholar-officials, promoted through civil-service examinations, held social and political sway—a system that dominated the governing of China until the early twentieth century. He places the successes and failures of this literary class within the context of their relations with other branches of Song government, especially its military, and describes how the literati’s reinterpretations of ancient Chinese culture continue to fuel scholarly debate even today.

Distilling a lifetime of research, The Song Dynasty offers a compelling new account of a transformative period in Chinese history whose legacy continues to be felt in China and beyond.
books.bio: Christian Lamouroux, professor emeritus at the School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences in Paris, has published widely on the Song dynasty. Charles Hartman is professor emeritus of Chinese studies at the University of Albany. His books include Structures of Governance in Song Dynasty China, 960–1279 CE. Patricia Buckley Ebrey is professor emerita of history at the University of Washington and the author of The Cambridge Illustrated History of China , among other books.

praise.q: Rich in detail and remarkably engaging, The Song Dynasty will appeal to anyone interested in Chinese, Asian, and comparative history. Combining meticulous primary research, a sophisticated synthesis of existing scholarship, and fresh, thought-provoking interpretations, Christian Lamouroux offers a compelling new understanding of Song dynasty China that will shape the field for years to come. Essential reading for historians of China, this book transforms our understanding of the Song while opening exciting new avenues for future research. It will undoubtedly inspire the next generation of scholars.
praise.by: Cong Ellen Zhang, author of Transformative Journeys: Travel and Culture in Song China
praise.cred: author of Transformative Journeys: Travel and Culture in Song China

praise.q: This elegant translation of Christian Lamouroux’s landmark study is the finest single-volume introduction to the Song dynasty available in English. In this book, which is greatly enhanced by its rich illustrations and beautifully rendered maps, Lamouroux realizes Deng Guangming’s vision of an ‘enlarged Song history,’ integrating the complexity of the Song’s domestic order with the inescapable influence of its enduring confrontation with the steppe. Lamouroux recounts the key events and principal figures of Song political history with uncommon zest, and offers a masterful synthesis of developments across Song society, economy, politics, and culture.
praise.by: Paul Jakov Smith, coeditor of The Cambridge History of China, Volume 5, Part One
praise.cred: coeditor of The Cambridge History of China, Volume 5, Part One

praise.q: A magnificent achievement. Invaluable to scholars and students alike, this volume stands as a trusted anchor for the field. Sweeping yet precise, it breaks new ground by bringing global scholarly lineages from Asia, Europe, and the Americas into a beautifully balanced framework. Through this unified lens, Lamouroux masterfully weaves a narrative that reaches deeply into the state, society, economy, religion, and intellectual world of Song China.
praise.by: Ya Zuo, author of Shen Gua’s Empiricism

books.title: The State of Housing Design 2027
books.authors: Edited by Aaron Smithson, Sam Naylor, Daniel D’Oca, and Chris Herbert
books.description: The State of Housing Design 2027 collects works on recently built housing projects notable for addressing issues of affordability, social cohesion, sustainability, aesthetics, density, and urbanism. Through critical essays, drawings and diagrams of featured buildings, data visualizations, and a crowdsourced survey, it provides both designers and the general public with a contemporary snapshot of the forces at play in the design of housing nationally. This is the second edition in the State of Housing Design book series, the first of which was published in 2023 by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, a research center that has produced analysis of housing markets and policy for over 60 years.
books.bio:
Aaron Smithson is the Housing Design Fellow at the Joint Center for Housing Studies and has worked with a range of architecture firms, planning consultancies, and public agencies in New York, Boston, and New Orleans. His writing on design, housing, and cities has been published by Architectural Record, Colorado Review, Dwell, Urban Omnibus, and MoMA, among others.

Sam Naylor is an architect, educator, and researcher. He is a founding partner of Nominal︎, an architecture and design firm based in Boston and Minneapolis, and an Adjunct Associate Professor in Practice at the University of Minnesota College of Design.

Daniel D’Oca is an urban planner and Associate Professor in Practice of Urban Planning at Harvard University’s Graduate School of Design and a principal and cofounder of the New York-based architecture, urban design, and planning firm Interboro Partners.

Chris Herbert is the managing director at Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies and a lecturer in the Department of Urban Planning and Design at Harvard’s Graduate School of Design.

books.title: The Vision of Hyman Minsky
books.subtitle: The Reconstruction of Macroeconomics
books.tagline: Hyman Minsky’s rebooting of macroeconomic theory
books.description:
Economist Hyman Minsky is known for his financial instability hypothesis, but his larger project was a complete reconstruction of macroeconomics. Minsky rejected the neoclassical synthesis, basing his ideas on an earlier institutionalist tradition but informed by Keynes’s General Theory and influenced by Joseph Schumpeter, Minsky’s dissertation supervisor. In The Vision of Hyman Minsky , L. Randall Wray traces the broad evolution of Minsky’s rethinking of macroeconomic theory over five decades of academic work, from the 1950s to the mid-1990s.

Wray explains that in Minsky’s view, capitalism is a financial system; whether economic development will promote enterprise or speculation depends on the financial structure. He disavowed the mainstream notion that markets seek equilibrium, insisting that the natural instability of capitalism must be constrained by institutional ceilings and floors. Wray shows that these themes run through Minsky’s earliest work—including even his undergraduate and graduate studies—as well as his later work envisioning a reconstituted financial structure that would promote the capital development of the economy. The continuing relevance of Minsky’s vision became clear during the global financial crisis of 2008, which The New Yorker called “the Minsky Moment.” Today, with the growing influence of crypto and private equity in financial markets and the unprecedented levels of debt created to finance artificial intelligence, Minsky’s warnings about the instability of what he called “Money Manager Capitalism” are more urgent than ever.
books.bio: L. Randall Wray is senior scholar and professor at the Levy Economics Institute of Bard College and the recipient of the 2022 Veblen-Commons Award for lifetime contributions to evolutionary institutionalist economics. He is the author of Why Minsky Matters (Princeton), Making Money Work for Us , Understanding Modern Money Theory: Money and Credit in Capitalist Economies , and A Great Leap Forward: Heterodox Economic Policy for the 21st Century .

praise.q: Although Minsky is best known for his financial instability hypothesis, this book shows that Minsky had interesting and useful things to say on a much wider scale of macroeconomic analysis. It offers a valuable contribution to the history of economic thought and expands our understanding and appreciation of a leader in the field.”—Charles Goodhart, coauthor of The Great Demographic Reversal: Ageing Societies, Waning Inequality, and an Inflation Revival

Wray has taken on the challenge of providing a guided tour of Minsky’s ideas in depth, from the 1950s through his last years—and then beyond. Other scholars who refer to Minsky’s work, who use it, pick up the Minsky they want or need—not the whole person. Wray doesn’t use Minsky for his own purposes, as so many do; he lets Minsky’s own intentions come through.
praise.by: Gary Dymski, author of The Bank Merger Wave: The Economic Causes and Social Consequences of Financial Consolidation
praise.cred: author of The Bank Merger Wave: The Economic Causes and Social Consequences of Financial Consolidation
