books.title: Hymns and Fragments
books.tagline: An annotated bilingual edition of Hölderlin’s radical and influential late poetry
books.description:
Despite his influence on such figures as Nietzsche, Rilke, Heidegger, and Celan, Friedrich Hölderlin (1770–1843) is only now being fully appreciated as perhaps the first great modern of European poetry. Drawing on the most recent scholarship, this annotated translation conveys the radical idiom and vision that continue to make him a contemporary. Richard Sieburth includes almost all Hölderlin’s late poems in free rhythms from the years between 1801 and 1806, the period just prior to his hospitalization for insanity.

Sieburth’s critical introduction discusses the poet’s career, assesses his role as the link between classicism and romanticism, and explores Hölderlin’s ongoing importance to modern poetics and philosophy. Annotations explicate the individual poems, a number of which are translated into English for the first time.
books.bio: Richard Sieburth teaches French and comparative literature at New York University.

praise.q: [Sieburth] has set out to represent the movement, the rush and swirl of Hölderlin's verse, his fast-spilling lines, and he seems to me to have succeeded remarkably well.
praise.by: New York Times Book Review

praise.q: This is an admirable work. It reads like poetry, which is not true of all translations. The introduction and notes are extremely valuable.
praise.by: Lisel Mueller, translator of Selected Later Poems of Marie Luise Kaschnitz
praise.cred: translator of Selected Later Poems of Marie Luise Kaschnitz

praise.q: This is a very exciting book. Sieburth’s translations are transparent; they let Hölderlin come through.”—D. S. Carne-Ross, Boston University

books.series: The Lockert Library of Poetry in Translation

books.title: I Sought a Dead Man and Found God
books.subtitle: The Notebooks of Anna Kamienska
books.series: The Margellos World Republic of Letters
books.tagline: A poet’s unexpected journey through devastation toward belief
books.description:
“An earnest quest for the Holy. . . . unusual, beautiful.”—Adam Zagajewski

“[Kamienska is] one of the great poet-mystics.”— Poetry

The author of over twenty books of verse, the poet, essayist, and translator Anna Kamieńska (1920–1986) belonged to the same generation of Polish poets as Nobel Prize winners Wisława Szymborska and Czesław Miłosz—a generation that, she writes, came of age “amidst the rat-tat-tat of firing squads and bomb explosions.” But despite her literary stature and professional success, much of Kamieńska's most moving writing is found in the pages of her Notebooks, which she never intended to publish.

The sudden death of her husband became the catalyst for one of the twentieth century’s most profound spiritual records, documented within these pages. &ldqup;A non-believer wrote the Notebook's early sections,” Kamieńska writes. “Then comes a mental and spiritual crisis, and the drama of a faith that is never fixed, never fully attained.” Composed over the course of several decades, this searching book fearlessly confronts the inevitability of death and the elusiveness of joy, situated at the crossroads of poetry and prayer.

In the tradition of Simone Weil’s Waiting for God and C. S. Lewis’s A Grief Observed , Kamieńska’s real-time record of conversion unfolds in a masterful translation by award-winning translator Clare Cavanagh.
books.bio: Anna Kamieńska (1920–1986) was a Polish poet, essayist, translator, and editor. Her work includes twenty collections of poetry, two volumes of Notebooks, and commentaries on the Bible. Clare Cavanagh , an award-winning translator of Polish literature, is Frances Hooper Professor in the Arts and Humanities and professor of Slavic languages and literatures at Northwestern University. She is the author of Lyric Poetry and Modern Politics: Russia, Poland, and the West , winner of the National Book Critics Circle Award. Christian Wiman is professor at the Yale Institute of Sacred Music and author of My Bright Abyss: Meditation of a Modern Believer .

praise.q: Reading [Kamienska] is like listening to someone who is intent on saying only the most important things.
praise.by: Booklist

praise.q: A major Polish writer, and equal to Nobel Prize winners Wislawa Szymborska and Czeslaw Milosz.
praise.by: Polish American Journal

praise.q: Reading her, I realized how rich she was and myself, how poor / Rich in love and suffering, in crying and dreams and prayer.
praise.by: Czeslaw Milosz, “Reading the Notebooks of Anna Kamienska”

praise.q: There is nothing pietistic about Kamienska’s brand of belief. Religion, for her, was a ‘luminosity’ that ‘does not negate reason.’ It simply exists as ‘a kind of poetic sensibility open to the world.’
praise.by: Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: A book of meditation in which a poet shares with the reader her experiences acquired on a road to a symbolic Santiago de Compostela.
praise.by: Adam Zagajewski

books.title: The Chicano Manual of Style
books.subtitle: Fashion in Paper and Print
books.tagline: A stylish celebration of a half century of Chicanx artists working at the intersection of fashion and printmaking
books.description:
In the 1970s, Chicanx artists began working in the plentiful and inexpensive medium of paper to blur the boundaries between printmaking and fashion design. Borrowing from Day of the Dead border craftworks as well as other cultural touchstones such as papeles picados , piñatas, and decorations, these artists experimented with paper-based fashion designs and screen printing, imbuing their work with a politics of style and socially transformative intent. In print workshops and underground fashion shows, practices leaped from the two-dimensional mesh screen to the three-dimensional dress form through the revival of a dormant trend from the 1960s—paper fashion.

Three thematic sections—fashionista icons and politics, maquillage and mirage, and text and textile—examine the dynamic confluence of paper and fashion in Chicanx cultural production and the ways it has evolved over the past fifty years. Featuring contributions from an interdisciplinary group of scholars, this exciting book considers the deep relationships among printmaking, the body, performance, and self-presentational embodiments to reveal new facets of Chicanx art.

Highlights the work of artists including

• Sean Carrillo

• Melanie Cervantes

• Alex Donis

• Richard Duardo

• Sandra C. Fernández

• Michael Menchaca

• Shizu Saldamando

• Joey Terrill

• Patssi Valdez

And workshops including

• Self Help Graphics, Los Angeles

• MeChicano Art Center, Los Angeles

• La Raza Silkscreen Center, San Francisco

• Mission Gráfica, San Francisco

Published in association with Print Center New York

Exhibition Schedule:

(January 21–May 2027)
books.bio: Robb Hernández is professor of English and director of Fashion Studies at Fordham University. He is the author of Transplanetary Americas: Art, Outer Space, and the Latinx Imagination and Archiving an Epidemic: Art, AIDS, and the Queer Chicanx Avant-Garde .

books.title: The Dirty Bicker
books.subtitle: Princeton, the Jews, and the Scandal of 1958
books.tagline: A riveting account of the 1958 Princeton antisemitism scandal, when dozens of Jews were rejected by the school’s exclusive eating clubs
books.description:
In February 1958, at the end of the annual “bicker” period—when Princeton sophomores seek admission to the university’s prestigious eating clubs—an unusually high number of students got no offers—and most of them were Jews. The “dirty bicker,” as it came to be known, was a troubling episode that laid bare the persistence of antisemitism in higher education. The Dirty Bicker tells the story of the affair that rocked the world of upper-class privilege, shedding light on the challenges that ambitious, upwardly mobile young Jewish men faced in postwar America.

Drawing on exclusive interviews with the men involved, both the rejected students and those who rejected them, Mark Oppenheimer transports readers to a time when status was tied to family heritage and even the ability to select the right blazer for the occasion. He addresses questions about what it means to belong—both in the Ivy League and in society more broadly. Were students blackballed because they were Jewish or because they were public schoolers in a pecking order presided over by preps? Were there quotas or just a gentleman’s agreement not to admit too many “undesirables”? And what was the role of the administration in perpetrating a system that treated some boys as more equal than others?

A must-read for anyone who wants to understand campus antisemitism today, The Dirty Bicker is an absorbing account of a national scandal that spoke to the barriers confronting minority and working-class students in their struggle to be accepted in the upper echelons of society.
books.bio: Mark Oppenheimer is professor of practice at Washington University in St. Louis and the author of many books, including Judy Blume: A Life and Squirrel Hill: The Tree of Life Synagogue Shooting and the Soul of a Neighborhood . He is the creator of the hit podcast series Gatecrashers , which traces the hidden history of Jews and the Ivy League.

praise.q: If you were Jewish at Princeton University in the 1950s, being passed over for another, more favored son wasn’t just a tale from Genesis. It was a daily terror, which came to a head in 1958 when a group of Jewish students were excluded from the campus’s exclusive eating clubs. With perfect prose and exquisite balance, Mark Oppenheimer turns a provincial scandal of postwar America into a national story of permanent, larger meaning. The Dirty Bicker is a brilliant portrait of how class is lived in America.
praise.by: Corey Robin, author of The Reactionary Mind

books.title: The Met Highlights
books.tagline: More than three hundred iconic works of art and stunning architectural photography bring The Met to you in this overview of one of the world’s largest and most comprehensive art museums
books.description:
Encompassing over five thousand years of worldwide art and cultural history, this compact volume is the perfect introduction to The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s most popular holdings. Organized chronologically, it illuminates unexpected connections between the hundreds of featured works of art, each accompanied by a concise description that provides helpful context. Among these world-renowned objects are the Egyptian Temple of Dendur; Roman wall paintings from outside Pompeii; a Byzantine mosaic; samurai armor; Incan textiles; drawings by Michelangelo and Leonardo da Vinci; illustrated manuscripts from the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp ; ritual objects from Africa and Oceania; fashion by Christian Dior; paintings by artists from Velázquez, Rembrandt, and Vermeer to Cézanne, Monet, Van Gogh, Picasso, Matisse, Georgia O’Keeffe, and Jackson Pollock; and so much more. The book also includes sweeping views of the Museum’s architecture and gallery spaces, offering a glimpse into the majesty of this National Historic Landmark that is a work of art in its own right. A must-have for art lovers and museum aficionados, this portable book encapsulates the breathtaking range of human creativity from prehistory to the present.

Published by The Metropolitan Museum of Art/Distributed by Yale University Press
books.bio: Max Hollein is the Marina Kellen French Director and CEO of The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

books.title: The Ministry of Truth
books.subtitle: Soviet Cybernetics and the Rise of the Information State
books.tagline: How an obsession with data collection brought down the Soviet Union and built our global information age.
books.description:
The Ministry of Truth provides an alternative history of our global information age, one that traces the modern obsession with digital data surveillance to Soviet cybernetic utopias of the 1960s. Aro Velmet argues that, faced with a stagnating economy, the Soviet Union empowered cyberneticians and social scientists with extraordinary freedoms to gather information about the empire’s industries and citizens, in the hopes that they would wrest from this data the key to the Union’s renewal. Instead, these data scientists, working in Tallinn, Tartu, Kyiv, and Novosibirsk, became critics of Soviet centralization, and leaders of Perestroika-era opposition movements, such as the Estonian Popular Front.

In the post-socialist period, engineers trained in Soviet Estonia reprofiled themselves as champions of the global information age. From Estonia and Ukraine, to Benin and Brazil, these experts promoted a unique vision of digitization, one that emphasized a strong state, decentralized networks, and economic efficiency over the right to privacy. The Ministry of Truth provides a new history of the information age told from the Second World, a new interpretation of the collapse of the Soviet Union, and a reframing of the post-socialist period, particularly in the Baltics.
books.bio: Aro Velmet is a historian of science, technology and modern imperialism. He is the author of Pasteur’s Empire and numerous articles on technological utopias and their unintended consequences in the French and Soviet empires in the modern age.

books.title: The Politics of Hell
books.subtitle: The Problem of Cooperation in Evil
books.tagline: A fascinating historical and philosophical exploration of the source of unity and cooperation among the wicked.
books.description:
Individuals motivated by immoral ends can work together to accomplish their joint plans—often more efficiently than other groups. But what accounts for the success of this cooperation? How can we explain that morally bad actors, who may be prideful, disloyal, disobedient, and lacking in empathy, can work together successfully toward some goal? In The Politics of Hell, Daniel Schwartz provides a history of philosophical efforts to solve this puzzle.

Schwartz shows that prominent medieval and early-modern thinkers such as Aquinas, Bonaventure, Francisco Suárez, and John Milton tackled the problem of cooperation in evil in their attempts to explain how the paradigmatic evil beings—demons—could efficiently cooperate to pursue their wicked ends. And he engages more recent discussions of the problem of cooperation in evil—more recent instantiations of these demonic political philosophies. For, as Schwartz argues, the disappearance of belief in demons in the modern and contemporary eras did not put the problem of cooperation in evil to rest; it merely resurfaced in other guises. Specifically, he shows that contemporary philosophers have grappled with the persistent problem of cooperation in evil, even if unwittingly, when trying to account for whether members of a criminal association, such as an idealized Mafia, have genuine obligations to one another.

From older sources, Schwartz draws lessons about the necessary and sufficient requirements of efficient social cooperation. Combining these with contemporary philosophical discussions of group agency of those in criminal or otherwise malevolent groups, The Politics of Hell is an original addition to the tradition of problem-based history of philosophy, guiding readers through possible understandings of unity among the wicked.
books.bio: Daniel Schwartz is Professor in the Departments of Political Science and International Relations at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and the author of Aquinas on Friendship and The Political Morality of the Late Scholastics .

praise.q: Daniel Schwartz’s exploration of what binds communities of vicious people together is both fascinating and groundbreaking. Moving masterfully and with great analytical rigor from the accounts provided by medieval and early modern philosophers and theologians and literary figures to those of contemporary theorists of human cooperation, The Politics of Hell exemplifies history of philosophy at its best. It is a must-read for political philosophers and historians of political thought alike.

In this fascinating book, Daniel Schwartz asks how to understand the possibility of cooperation among rational agents with evil ends. Versions of this question were a focus of medieval theological reflection on cooperation among demons and have arisen in contemporary philosophy of social action. Putting these traditions in conversation with each other, Schwartz avoids a problematic appeal to normatively substantive obligations to do what is evil and highlights the potential role of powerful emotions such as hate and despair in support of cooperation among rational but evil agents.

This superb book about the possibility and nature of political society among the supremely evil considers various medieval and early-modern accounts of this problem and concludes with John Milton that shared hatred might be sufficient to ground such an association. It is an excellent work of historical and philosophical analysis that has illuminating resonances with our contemporary situation.

The Politics of Hell shows that we have a lot to learn from demons about cooperation, rational motivation, and social hierarchy. By turning an illuminating spotlight into some dark places—hell, among others—Daniel Schwartz teaches us some striking things about our own associations, our own attitudes to virtue and vice, and our own best hopes for a just society.

Philosophers have long been divided on whether a society of devils, to use Kant’s famous formulation, could cooperate socially or establish a political state. In this truly remarkable book, Daniel Schwartz traces the history of this debate from Aristotle through the Middle Ages and into contemporary philosophy. The result is an original and thought-provoking contribution that sheds new light on both the nature of evil and the foundations of political life. It is essential reading for anyone interested in political philosophy, moral theory, or the enduring problem of evil.

books.title: The Power of Everyone
books.subtitle: Leading Together to Shape a Better World
books.tagline: A groundbreaking new model for leading that emphasizes relationships and collective intelligence over the individual. An HBR 10 Must Reads on Leadership contributor and a leadership, negotiation, and “crisis expert” heralded by the New York Times and Financial Times .
books.description:
An HBR 10 Must Reads on Leadership contributor and a leadership, negotiation, and “crisis expert” heralded by the New York Times and Financial Times .

What if most of what you know about leadership is wrong—or at least not useful in a world growing ever more complex and ever faster? In The Power of Everyone , Eric McNulty looks both to the past and the future to explore leading as a collective undertaking, not the preserve of singular superheroes.

Drawing on examples from ancient wisdom traditions and modern practices, McNulty shows how people have always led together and are doing so now to tackle some of our most vexing problems. The book explores changes in thinking and practice that can reawaken our inherent cooperative and collaborative abilities through communities of leading, an approach that balances shared needs, values, and goals with individuals’ ability to contribute. Throughout the book, leading is a verb—something you do to achieve change not tied to a position or title.

From the work of the late Jane Goodall in wildlife conservation to a nascent community bank in New Hampshire reshaping the food economy to a global nonprofit working with communities adjacent to protected rainforests and even in corporate settings, the book demonstrates the power and potential of working together. The stories are profound and inspiring, highlighting efforts to create thriving organizations and communities that live with respect for both humans and other-than-humans sharing planet Earth.
books.bio: Eric J. McNulty is the author of more than 200 bylined articles, case studies, and e-books, and is coauthor of You’re It: Crisis, Change, and Leading When It Matters Most and Renegotiating Healthcare: Resolving Conflict to Build Collaboration . He teaches leadership, negotiation, and conflict resolution at Harvard, MIT, and elsewhere.

books.title: What Might Be
books.subtitle: Confronting Racism to Transform Our Institutions
books.authors: Anurima Bhargava, Goodwin Liu, Susan Sturm, Freeman Hrabowski
books.tagline: How to turn the paradoxes built into anti-racism work into drivers of learning and change
books.description:
Even as anti-racism practices seemed to be gaining momentum, the nation shows signs of falling back into long-standing patterns of racial injustice and inequality. Leaders who introduce anti-racist approaches to their organizations often face backlash from white colleagues and skepticism from colleagues of color, leading to paralysis. In What Might Be , Susan Sturm explores how to navigate the contradictions built into our racialized history, relationships, and institutions. She offers strategies and stories for confronting racism within predominantly white institutions, describing how change agents can move beyond talk to build the architecture of full participation.

Sturm argues that although we cannot avoid the contradictions built into efforts to confront racism, we can make them into engines of cross-racial reflection, bridge building, and institutional reimagination, rather than falling into a Groundhog Day –like trap of repeated failures. Drawing on her decades of experience researching and working with institutions to help them become more equitable and inclusive, Sturm identifies three persistent paradoxes inherent in anti-racism work. These are the paradox of racialized power, whereby anti-racism requires white people to lean into and yet step back from exercising power; the paradox of racial salience, which means that effective efforts must explicitly name and address race while also framing their goals in universal terms other than race; and the paradox of racialized institutions, which must drive anti-racism work while simultaneously being the target of it. Sturm shows how people and institutions can cultivate the capacity to straddle these contradictions, enabling those in different racial positions to discover their linked fate and become the catalysts for long-term change.

The book includes thoughtful and critical responses from Goodwin Liu, Freeman Hrabowski, and Anurima Bhargava.
books.bio: Susan Sturm is the George M. Jaffin Professor of Law and Social Responsibility and the Founding Director of the Center for Institutional and Social Change at Columbia Law School. She is the coauthor (with Lani Guinier) of Who's Qualified? A New Democracy Forum on the Future of Affirmative Action .

praise.q: Sturm’s advice on bridge-building and reimagination can help leaders in their work.
praise.by: Library Journal

praise.q: Susan Sturm’s unflinching and poignant narrative urges white leaders and collaborators to think more critically about anti-racist praxis without coopting it. Crucial for our times, What Might Be is an orienting and intimate guide.
praise.by: Swethaa S. Ballakrishnen, University of California, Irvine, author of Accidental Feminism
praise.cred: University of California, Irvine, author of Accidental Feminism

praise.q: Susan Sturm works hard to convince folks to be their best, to use their power and privilege for good, to collaborate across racial lines, and to do the work to confront racism in the academy and elsewhere. The beauty of this book is how Sturm uses her own experiences, presenting an authentic perspective.
praise.by: Marybeth Gasman, Rutgers University, author of Doing the Right Thing
praise.cred: Rutgers University, author of Doing the Right Thing

praise.q: As a white man leading an institution whose origins epitomize white male privilege, I wish I had had this book years ago when embarking on an intentional and ongoing participatory process of institutional transformation towards anti-racism and antisexism. Susan Sturm has provided an inspiring and practical guide to the deep work of multiracial collaboration that fuses theory, reflection, and practice to powerfully advance equity and justice.
praise.by: Stephen Heintz, President and CEO, Rockefeller Brothers Fund
praise.cred: President and CEO, Rockefeller Brothers Fund

praise.q: During a time of division and conflict, Susan Sturm offers powerful stories linked to instructive analysis of bridge-building in pursuit of equality, excellence, and effective collaborations against racism. What makes this work so essential is its honesty and clarity about the dilemmas that arise when people use their power and privilege to try to alter the patterns affording them authority.
praise.by: Martha Minow, author of When Should Law Forgive?
praise.cred: author of When Should Law Forgive?

praise.q: What does antiracist institutional change work look like in real life? It’s messy, nonlinear, and requires sustained long-term commitments to persist in the face of predictable backlash. It helps to have both a scaffolding framework and inspiring real-life examples as a guide. Susan Sturm offers both in her thoughtful and wise book, a text especially useful for institutional leaders seeking to use their power to facilitate lasting change.”—Beverly Daniel Tatum, President Emerita, Spelman College, and author of Why Are All the Black Kids Sitting Together in the Cafeteria? And Other Conversations About Race

books.title: When Machines Act
books.subtitle: The Promise and Peril of Navigating Our Agentic AI Future
books.authors: Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, David Siegel and Stephen Henriques
books.tagline: Beyond the hype and above the panic: how autonomous AI reshapes work, competition, and power, and the judgments that decide where it leads.
books.description:
The agentic AI conversation has hardened into two camps—the champions who promise frictionless transformation and the cynics who forecast societal collapse. But neither can help the person who actually has to make tangible decisions on any given day: the business leader who must choose where to deploy an autonomous agent; the investor who wants to separate signal from circular financing; the policymaker who writes rules that will shape a decade; or the rest of us living through a world in flux.

When Machines Act is the compass for the disciplined middle. In this book, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, David Siegel, and Stephen Henriques offer readers a clear account of the defining shift of the decade: the arrival of autonomous AI. These are systems that no longer merely answer questions but take actions, make decisions, and execute work across an entire organization or an individual’s daily life.

The book draws on decades of collective experience across the authors—as either world-renowned advisors to Fortune 500 CEOs, pioneering technologists of the computing age, or investors in major public and private enterprises. Informed by dozens of expert interviews with leaders in technology and off-the-record dialogues with more than 300 chief executives at the Yale CEO forums, it distills essential principles you can carry into a boardroom, a statehouse, or a kitchen-table conversation.
books.bio:
Jeffrey Sonnenfeld (Author)

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld is the Lester Crown Professor in the Practice of Management at the Yale School of Management and founder and president of the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute, the world’s first school for incumbent CEOs. He has advised five U.S. presidents from both parties and is the author of multiple books, most recently the New York Times bestseller Trump’s Ten Commandments . His Yale CEO forums have hosted more than 1,500 of the world’s most influential business leaders, and his commentary appears regularly in Fortune, the Wall Street Journal, The New York Times , CNBC, MS NOW, CNN, and across national media.

David Siegel (Author)

David Siegel is a computer scientist, entrepreneur, and philanthropist. He co-founded Two Sigma, a leading investment management firm that leverages technology, AI, and data science. Guided by his focus on education and science, he founded Siegel Family Endowment to examine how technology shapes society, and Open Athena, a nonprofit organization that bridges the gap between academic research and the AI frontier. He also serves on several prominent boards, including MIT, Cornell Tech, and the DoE Science Advisory Committee.

Stephen Henriques (Author)

books.title: While We're Here
books.subtitle: On Belonging in This World
books.tagline: A thought-provoking reflection on finding our way through an imperfect world
books.description:
We all seek to belong in this world—to fit in with our family, friends, and wider communities. Many of us assume that we achieve this by sharing similar traits or beliefs with others. While We’re Here shows how belonging means to embrace not only our commonalities, interests, and delights but also our worries, doubts, and disagreements. It requires us to contemplate and interpret ourselves, our place in the world, and what we want to preserve or change. This book charts a path through this lifelong process.

Avram Alpert explains what belonging means and demonstrates how we can achieve it through personal and collective action. He explores how humans belong in a universe whose ultimate bounds are unknowable and reflects on why the act of writing is a necessary part of our search to understand belonging. Drawing on diverse ideas from philosophy, religion, psychology, politics, and personal experience, Alpert challenges us to think deeply about the complexities of belonging and to consider it an inherent, crucial aspect of human existence.

Offering a broader, more realistic conception of what it means to belong, While We’re Here enables readers to lead fuller, more enriching lives by coming to terms with the mistakes, mishaps, and moments of joy that give meaning to the brief time we share on this earth.
books.bio: Avram Alpert is a lecturer in the Writing Program and Department of Comparative Literature at Princeton University. His work has appeared in publications such as The Guardian , The New York Times , and Dissent . His books include The Good-Enough Life (Princeton).

books.title: Who Elected Big Tech?
books.subtitle: How Your Phone Hijacked the Constitution
books.tagline: How technology companies became de facto governors of public life—and how democracy can evolve to survive
books.description:
Across the globe, technology companies have risen from innovative disruptors to powerful actors that are shaping public discourse, the democratic process, and individual freedoms. With the help of advertising, data extraction, and algorithms, today’s platforms influence what billions of people see and believe, yet they bear no legal responsibility for it. They manipulate this distribution with an eye only to profit, and they are heedless of the political or social consequences of doing so. These companies are entities the framers of the Constitution never contemplated, making political interventions they never imagined.

In Who Elected Big Tech? , Allison Stanger combines technological expertise, First Amendment scholarship, and political theory to explain how this happened and what it means. She traces the legal origins of platform power, shows how algorithms structure attention and quietly normalize manipulation, examines the evolution of content moderation from simple rules to opaque systems of control, and reveals why these questions grow only more urgent in the age of artificial intelligence.

Preserving human agency and values requires more than regulatory tweaking, Stanger argues. It demands a fundamental reimagining of how democratic societies govern the digital world. Stanger provides essential context for understanding our predicament and guidance for finding a path forward—before unchecked technological power erodes freedom and equality beyond repair.
books.bio: Allison Stanger is Distinguished Endowed Professor at Middlebury College, an external professor at the Santa Fe Institute, and codirector of the GETTING-Plurality research network at Harvard University. Her books include Whistleblowers: Honesty in America from Washington to Trump and One Nation Under Contract: The Outsourcing of American Power and the Future of Foreign Policy .

praise.q: Stanger asks the question that should keep every policymaker awake: who governs the infrastructure of public discourse, and by what authority? Her answer— no one, and that’s the problem —is delivered with devastating precision. Who Elected Big Tech? is essential reading for anyone who believes that code should serve the law, not override it.
praise.by: Audrey Tang, CyberAmbassador.TW and first Digital Minister of Taiwan
praise.cred: CyberAmbassador.TW and first Digital Minister of Taiwan

books.title: Documentary Sources on the History of Rus’ Metropolitanate
books.subtitle: The Fourteenth to the Early Sixteenth Centuries
books.description:
Documentary Sources on the History of Rus’ Metropolitanate is an extensive collection of letters and documents relating to the late medieval Orthodox Church, edited and curated by the renowned medievalist Andrei Pliguzov. This book is a rich resource for any reader interested in the controversies and preoccupations of the Orthodox hierarchy and the clergy throughout the Rus´ metropolitanate up to the early modern period.

For the first time, the volume includes acts, edicts and decrees regarding the lands in the metropolitanate’s jurisdiction, reports prepared for the metropolitans by their secretariat, and the letters of the hierarchs themselves. The published documents pertain to all aspects of the metropolitanate’s activity and reflect the various concerns and debates that defined the life of the Church and its relations with other religious entities and the secular leaders.
books.bio: Andrei I. Pliguzov (1956–2011) was a historian of Kyivan Rus’ and an expert in church history, with a focus on sources from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. He was the author of numerous publications on a variety of topics, including the Battle of Kulikovo, the Union of Florence, the Time of Troubles, early modern Old Belief, and the place of ethnic minorities in the Russian imperial imagination.

books.title: Language in the Human-Machine Era
books.subtitle: New Technologies and the Coming Transformation of Language
books.authors: Edited by Dave Sayers, Maggie Glass, Helen Kelly-Holmes and Robert Fuchs
books.tagline: An interdisciplinary exploration of interaction and language use in the new human-machine era.
books.description:
New devices do more than simply transmit language: they can alter and augment it. This blurs our conventional understanding of language and gives rise to a number of challenges—theoretical, moral, legal, and pedagogical. Language in the Human-Machine Era, edited by Dave Sayers, Maggie Glass, Helen Kelly-Holmes, and Robert Fuchs, explores the emerging features of language in this human-machine era. The contributors discuss not only the benefits of the new technologies, but also the risks and inequalities, which are often of little concern to tech companies or their shareholders. They also suggest ways forward that are more equitable and inclusive.

Contributors examine two major trends of the new era: Speaking through technology, e.g., when AI translates our words into another language in real time, in our own voice; and speaking to technology, as when we have lifelike conversations with our smart devices. Both trends have enormous consequences for our understanding of interaction and language use. The chapters all follow the same format, facilitating comparisons, for example, between the current “digital era” and the coming “human-machine era.”

Contributors: Tope Adebiyi, Mohammad Alenezi, Dorka Balogh, Štefan Beňuš, Inge Birnie, Lynne Bowker, Vincent Briva-Iglesias, Eliot Bytyçi, Luis Mauricio Calvo Rubio, Henrique Lopes Cardoso, Parthena Charalampidou, Matt Coler, Alain Couillault, Adriana Dervishaj, Doris Dippold, Iker Erdocia, Robert Fuchs, Vicky Garnett, Balázs Szabolcs Gerencsér, Maggie Glass, Edlira Gugu, Tunga Güngör, Yaakov HaCohen-Kerner, Barbara Heinisch, Marcelo Yuji Himoro, Sviatlana Höhn, Maram Khamaiseh, Helen Kelly-Holmes, Blanka Klimova, Maarit Koponen, Petra Lea Láncos, Mandy Lau, Raquel Lázaro Gutiérrez, Didem Leblebici, Caroline Lehr, Eve Lejot, Márta Lesznyák, Chaya Liebeskind, Miriam Lind, Netaya Lotze, Belén Lozano Sanudo, Lieve Macken, Lina Mavrina, Hugues de Mazancourt, Philipp Meer, Fanny Meunier, Bettina Migge, Sharon O'Brien, Giedré Valūnaitė Oleškevičienė, Antonio Pareja-Lora, Nataša Pavlović, Maarija Pendevska, Marcel Pikhart, Martina Podboj, Fernando Prieto Ramos, Cynog Prys, Päivi Rainò, Edina Robin, Lucia Ruiz Rosendo, Melody Ann Ross, Rebekah Rousi, Mehmet Şahin, María del Mar Sánchez Ramos, Beatrice Savoldi, Burkhard Schafer, Britta Schneider, Olívia Seidl-Péch, Márta Seresi, Anna Setkowicz-Ryszka, Muhammad Shakir, Angela Soltan, Rui Sousa-Silva, Silvia Terribile, Rita Vallentin, Auli Viidalepp, and Miklós Zorkóczy.
books.bio:
Dave Sayers (Editor)

Dave Sayers is Senior Lecturer in language and communication studies at the University of Jyväskylä.

Helen Kelly-Holmes (Editor)

Helen Kelly-Holmes is Professor and Chair in Applied Languages at the University of Limerick, Ireland.

Robert Fuchs (Editor)

books.title: One Summer's Night, Under the Starry Sky
books.subtitle: Reflections on Anarchy and Revolution
books.tagline: "We hardly see the stars anymore. What revolution can be dreamed under an empty sky?"
books.description:
In this short essay, at once scholarly and accessible, philosopher Maria Kakogianni proposes to refresh our ideas about revolution and anarchy.

Starting from a simple yet terrible observation—that we hardly see any stars anymore—she draws out a metaphor for the world: we live in a dis-astrous age, an age devoid of stars.

The book is divided into twenty-two short sections, like beams extending in all directions. Along the way, we encounter Catherine Malabou and Margaret Thatcher, Kant and Blanqui, Vincent Bolloré and the Invisible Committee. Themes include everyday fascism, pirate pleasures, Plato, and even Tai Chi.

A book of politics, poetry, and philosophy, One Summer's Night, Under the Starry Sky is propelled at its heart by the need to invent a positive and durable anarchy, with its feet firm on the ground and its head nourished by the stars.
books.bio: Maria Kakogianni is a Greek philosopher who teaches at Université Paris 8 and 9. She has published numerous books, including Entretien platonicien with Alain Badiou, Le Printemps précaire des peuples , and Surgeons et autres pousses . One Summer's Night, Under the Starry Sky is her first book published in English.

books.title: Partisan Analysis of the Present
books.subtitle: Best of Ill Will 2012–2025
books.tagline: The most decisive essays from Ill Will's first eleven years as a journal of partisan research.
books.description:
Ill Will began in 2013 as an eclectic zine library on a thumb drive, assembled by expats who were grappling with the political limits of the radical scene in Europe. When it later relocated to North America, growing from a humble Tumblr page to an independent web platform, Ill Will maintained its international orientation, emphasizing the circulation of ideas and practices across a global terrain of struggle. It has since become one of the most influential online venues for radical thought, publishing works of engaged or "partisan" theory from an uncommonly wide range of writers, from rock-throwers to renowned philosophers.

This volume gathers twenty-five of the most decisive essays from Ill Will's first eleven years.

Contributors

Athena, Ian Alan Paul, Jerome Baschet, Research & Destroy, Franco “Bifo” Berardi, Kristin Ross, Invisible Committee, Idris Robinson, Hugh Farrell, Shemon, Michel Garau, Nicholas Smaligo, Jules Gleeson & Judith Butler, Kevin Suemnicht, Inhabit, Tiqqun, City Inhospitable, Wang Nangxian & Paul Torino, Jackson and Nevada, Mario Tronti, Kate Davis Jones, Mauvaise Troupe, Maria Kakogianni, Frank B. Wilderson, III, Phil Neel, Adrian Wohlleben, Ceci Nelson
books.bio: Adrian Wohlleben is a partisan researcher living in the Midwest, and founding editor of illwill.com. His essays include “Revolts without Revolution,” “Autonomy in Conflict,” and, with Paul Torino, “Memes with Force.”

books.title: The American Guitar
books.subtitle: A 20th-Century Icon
books.authors: Jayson Kerr Dobney and Daniel Wheeldon
books.tagline: A celebration of the instrument that helped define twentieth-century music and culture
books.description:
For most of the twentieth century, the history of American music—and of much American culture—was inseparable from the history of the guitar. This volume features 150 guitars that trace the evolution of the design and sound of the instrument made popular by musicians including Charlie Christian, Mother Maybelle Carter, Merle Travis, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Jimi Hendrix, and Keith Richards. The astounding selection of electric and acoustic guitars features pristine examples of classic instruments that shaped blues, country, jazz, and rock music. They detail the aesthetic and functional development of acoustic guitars, the invention and rise of the electric guitar, and the remarkable legacy of this uniquely influential and versatile instrument. The American Guitar also traces the underappreciated influence of Hawaiian music and reaffirms the central role of Black musicians, while emphasizing the guitar’s pivotal place in American culture and society. This fascinating exploration of a nation’s soundtrack through its most popular and iconic instrument will delight any music lover.

Published by The Metropolitan Museum of Art/Distributed by Yale University Press

Exhibition Schedule:

The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

(March 25, 2027–Ongoing)
books.bio: Jayson Kerr Dobney is Frederick P. Rose Curator in Charge and Daniel Wheeldon is collections manager, both in the Department of Musical Instruments, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

books.title: The Earth Is Ours, Not Mine
books.subtitle: A History of Environmental Justice
books.tagline: Tracing the roots of environmental justice through five centuries
books.description:
In The Earth Is Ours, Not Mine, Aaron Sachs shows that the idea of environmental justice goes back not decades but centuries—that it originated not in late twentieth-century campaigns against disproportionate environmental harm, but hundreds of years earlier, when English commoners attempted to reclaim the commons and Native Americans tried to protect their land against encroachment by European settlers. Sachs chronicles five hundred years of dissent and resistance against capitalism, colonialism, and environmental destruction, constructing a family tree for today’s environmental justice movement.

Sachs recovers the history of the Diggers, an anti-Enclosure organization in seventeenth-century Britain—whose leader declared, “the Earth is ours, not mine”—and describes the surprising overlap between their discourse and the practices of American Indigenous communities around communal land. From this unusual convergence, Sachs traces the evolution of ideas and principles underpinning a collectivist ethic in thinkers as varied as John Milton, Mary Shelley, Rachel Carson, and Murray Bookchin—a twentieth-century theorist of environmental justice and a Vermonter who positioned himself to the left of Bernie Sanders.

Environmentalists often focus on the future, dismissing modern history as inherently destructive and providing no models to build on. Sachs counters this by showing that the careful practice of history in fact offers hope and possibility, tempered by realism. If we want a future in which social justice and environmentalism converge, we must first rethink the past.
books.bio: Aaron Sachs is the Ernest I. White Professor of American Studies at Cornell University. He is the author, most recently, of Up from the Depths: Herman Melville, Lewis Mumford, and Rediscovery in Dark Times (Princeton), short-listed for the National Book Critics Circle Award, and Stay Cool: Why Dark Comedy Matters in the Fight Against Climate Change .

books.title: The Emotional Advantage
books.subtitle: Why Humans and Other Animals Evolved to Show Emotion
books.tagline: A leading neuropsychologist reveals what facial displays, body language, and vocal expressions tell us about the evolution and purpose of emotions in nature and society
books.description:
Since the time of Charles Darwin, emotions have come to be viewed as adaptive benefits shaped by distinct anatomies, abilities, and environments. The Emotional Advantage draws on groundbreaking research into human and nonhuman expressions to reveal what scientists are learning about the evolutionary origins of emotions, how they manifest across species, and how this knowledge can benefit humans and other animals alike.

Emotions are expressed in many ways—through the face, body, voice, even smell. Mariska Kret takes readers into the lab, out into the field, and under the skin to describe how she and her team are studying these expressions using various innovative methods to understand what emotions are good for and how they influence others. She explains why expressions of fear, joy, and sadness evolved as they did and explores the importance of mental states like curiosity and empathy in shaping behavior, strengthening social bonds, and adapting to environmental advantages. She introduces readers to key debates about emotions in psychology and weighs the societal implications of advancing technologies like social media, AI, and social robots.

Blending vivid storytelling with the latest technological developments, The Emotional Advantage invites us to rethink the emotional lives of animals and humans alike, demonstrating how emotions are a unifying thread across species and cultures in an interconnected natural world.
books.bio: Mariska Kret is professor of comparative psychology and affective neuroscience at Leiden University in the Netherlands and a member of the Royal Holland Society of Sciences and Humanities. She is the recipient of several prestigious prizes, including the Dr. Hendrik Muller Prize of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences and the European Research Council’s Public Engagement with Research Award. She is coeditor in chief of the journal Behaviour .

books.title: The Sphere and the Labyrinth
books.subtitle: Avant-Gardes and Architecture from Piranesi to the 1970s
books.tagline: The 40th anniversary updated edition of the highly influential foundational text that changed how we think about architecture, the limits of avant-garde movements, and the connection between design, power, and politics.
books.bio: Manfredo Tafuri (1935–1994) was an influential Italian Marxist architect, historian, theoretician, critic, and academic.

books.title: The Story of Junk
books.bio: Linda Yablonsky is an art critic, fiction writer, and journalist renowned for her commentary and reporting on exhibitions, artists, and the art world internationally. Over the last forty years, her byline has appeared in The New York Times and T Magazine , The Art Newspaper , Artforum , Bloomberg , ArtNews , W Magazine , Wallpaper , Family Style , and Palmer Palm Beach , among many other publications. She is the author of numerous critical essays as well a producer of live literary events in New York, where she lives. Currently, Ms. Yablonsky is writing the biography the artist Jeff Koons and completing a second novel.

praise.q: Dryly hilarious and scarily polite, the most sober-minded novel about drugs I’ve ever read.
praise.by: John Waters

praise.q: The most detailed, forceful, and eloquent account I’ve ever read of how drug addiction happens—how it can happen to you. It’s a swift read, thanks to Linda Yablonsky’s taut prose, and a vivid slice of social history as well.
praise.by: Lucy Sante

praise.q: When people talk about The Story of Junk , words like "shocking" and "harrowing" are bound to come up. Those terms certainly apply. I hope, though, that people who’ve read the book won’t be so overwhelmed by its power that they forget to use words like "penetrating," "relentless," and "brilliant" as well. I’ve never read anything like this. It’s an important piece of work.
praise.by: Michael Cunningham

praise.q: Yablonsky has written a bold, sometimes devastating, odyssey, a long night of the soul.
praise.by: Lynne Tillman

books.title: Transforming Education
books.subtitle: Lessons from Around the World
books.tagline: How countries across the globe have transformed schools, and how policymakers can turn resistance into momentum for change.
books.description:
Is it possible to transform something as vast, complex, and politically entrenched as education? In Transforming Education , Andreas Schleicher answers that question with evidence and hope. Lack of progress in education, he says, cannot be explained simply by a lack of resources or of promising policy initiatives. Drawing on his experience assessing reform efforts across Europe, the Americas, Asia, and Africa, he offers insights and practical guidance on how policymakers can transform their educational systems and turn resistance into momentum for change.

Schleicher explores why some education reforms ignite change, while others vanish without a trace. Real change, he shows, requires understanding the politics of change as deeply as the pedagogy. Looking at education systems in countries as different as Estonia and Viet Nam, he shows how policymakers can create transformative change in education systems wired for stability; manage the asymmetries between costs and benefits in educational reform; and secure success beyond electoral cycles.
books.bio: Andreas Schleicher is Director for Education and Skills at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

books.title: Translating Sex in the Hebrew Bible
books.subtitle: How Mistranslation Leads to Misinterpretation
books.tagline: How words related to gender, sex, and sexuality in the Hebrew Bible have been mistranslated—and what we gain by retranslating words we thought we knew
books.description:
Even those who have not read the Hebrew Bible know some of its phrases by heart: “Thou shalt not commit adultery.” “Do not lie with a male as with a woman.” “For I am a jealous god.” But are these translations reliable? In this groundbreaking book, Sara Milstein argues that words in the Hebrew Bible related to sex, gender, and sexuality have been consistently mistranslated, resulting in the misinterpretation of numerous passages. Peppering her analysis with tidbits from ancient and modern law, Greek literature, the study of emotions, and the history of sexuality, Milstein offers fresh interpretations of terms and texts that have been lost in translation for millennia.

In a series of illuminating case studies, Milstein reveals how the earliest translators introduced concepts that were foreign to the ancient Israelites. These concepts then spread to other translations and interpretations, religious and scholarly alike. Paradoxically, she argues, translation is both the obstacle and the cure. Rather than begin with the English (or German, or Chinese, or . . .) and work backwards, we must start with the Hebrew and move forward, approaching familiar texts from a new position of unfamiliarity. It’s time, Milstein suggests, to rethink our assumptions about sex in the Bible, one word at a time.
books.bio: Sara J. Milstein is professor of Hebrew Bible and ancient Near Eastern studies at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver. She is the author of Making a Case: The Practical Roots of Biblical Law and Tracking the Master Scribe: Revision through Introduction in Biblical and Mesopotamian Literature , winner of the Frank Moore Cross Award from the American Society of Overseas Research.

praise.q: Highly readable and enjoyable. The style is clear, the prose is elegant, and the argument is cogently construed. Milstein achieves her purpose brilliantly. This is one of the rare books that truly changes the way you read the Bible.
praise.by: Karel van der Toorn, author of Israelite Religion: From Tribal Beginnings to Scribal Legacy
praise.cred: author of Israelite Religion: From Tribal Beginnings to Scribal Legacy

praise.q: Milstein has broad expertise in the study of the Hebrew Bible in its ancient Near Eastern and Mediterranean context, and it shows. The book combines thorough textual analysis with substantive theoretical work on aspects of human sexuality. Milstein very successfully balances the competing demands of fully demonstrating her argument to a specialist audience and keeping the text engaging for nonspecialists.
praise.by: Molly Zahn, author of Genres of Rewriting in Second Temple Judaism: Scribal Composition and Transmission
praise.cred: author of Genres of Rewriting in Second Temple Judaism: Scribal Composition and Transmission

books.title: Why Reconstruction Matters
books.authors: Gregory P. Downs and Kate Masur
books.tagline: A sweeping, ground‑level reinterpretation arguing that Reconstruction both created the country we live in and sparked the battles that threaten to engulf it today
books.description:
Far from a brief epilogue to slavery’s end, Reconstruction was an era of epochal change. Emancipation transformed everyday life for nearly four million formerly enslaved Black southerners who became architects of freedom: creating independent institutions, organizing mass political movements, and, with white allies, driving the passage and implementation of the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments that established birthright citizenship, equal protection, and voting rights. This is the constitutional framework that structures American democracy today.

Taking readers on a site-seeing journey across the South’s commemorative landscape, Downs and Masur ground the narrative in nine distinct places that show Americans’ struggles to deliver on the most egalitarian promises of the Founding era, including

• Green-Meldrim House in Savannah, where Major General William T. Sherman was headquartered and met with local Black leaders

• First African Church in Richmond, a center for Black politics and community-building

• Grant Parish Courthouse in Colfax, Louisiana, site of the massacre of dozens of Black men

• Beaufort Naval Hospital in South Carolina, location of a January 1, 1863 meeting where formerly enslaved soldiers urged a large crowd to fight for complete freedom and equality.

This accessible narrative shows how Reconstruction both created the country we live in today and sparked the battles that threaten to engulf it.
books.bio: Gregory P. Downs is professor of history at the University of California, Davis. Kate Masur is the John D. MacArthur Professor at Northwestern University. Downs and Masur are coeditors of the Journal of the Civil War Era.

books.title: A Book of Consolation
books.subtitle: Seeing Our Quests for Love, Success, and Meaning in a New Light
books.authors: Andrew Stark Edited by Mark Reschke
books.tagline: An invitation to rest in the mystery that there is no single route to fulfillment, but many—often contradictory, unpredictable, endlessly available.
books.description:
Our lives are restless. Though we strive for meaning, we are often unfulfilled: our loves fail, our careers stall, and our purpose eludes us. We may temporarily ease our frustration by blaming our methods or embracing our limitations, and we may even embrace the self-defeating lie that we must discover the one, linear path for success in love, work, or life. In A Book of Consolation , Andrew Stark offers a liberating third way between self-abandonment and complacency, revealed through a simple mystery: for each road where someone found fulfillment, someone else walked the opposite path to the same end.

Drawing on literature, popular culture, philosophy, and more, A Book of Consolation invites us to appreciate, even marvel at, the possibility that the routes to love, success, and meaning are so various that even inverse lives can satisfy us. Stark holds up a series of opposing journeys for consideration—from the contradictory loves in modern romantic comedies, to the regrets of Dolly Parton and Ernest Hemingway, to the mindsets behind Tiger Woods and Richard Nixon’s success. In juxtaposing these lives, Stark expands our sense of what counts as fulfillment and what alternatives may be available when our own paths falter. Rich in possibility but without prescription, A Book of Consolation encourages us to navigate the frustrations of our finitude by cultivating a faith that the paths to fulfillment are far more pluralized—and often more contradictory—than we know.

books.title: A Quieter Illness
books.subtitle: Narratives, Selves, and Silences
books.tagline: In this sequel to The Wounded Storyteller , Arthur W. Frank reminds us of the power of narrative in the lives of ill people and those who care for them.
books.description:
The Wounded Storyteller became a classic by witnessing the voices of ill people, recognizing how they express themselves in three prevalent narratives: restitution stories, evocations of chaos, and quest stories. Thirty years later, Frank expands this framework. He proposes a fourth narrative: one that seeks no restitution, claims no quest, yet feels no chaos—the stillness narrative. This story allows us to see more clearly our interdependence as well as the wisdom of uncertainty; it also teaches the value of letting go and waiting.

In the stillness narrative, Frank finds new opportunities for dialogue with clinical professionals. They too need healing, and healing moments occur when everyone recognizes their mutual, if asymmetrical, dependence. As Frank tells the stories that won’t leave him, he guides readers toward understanding how the stories they tell and hear affect their capacity to heal both themselves and others.

books.title: A Short History of Bath
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.tagline: This highly readable guide to Bath details the entire history of the historic city, from the Roman period to the present day, as well as its historic architecture, thermal springs, and other attractions.
books.description: Any time spent in Bath is a pleasure. The historic city buzzes with vitality and its designation as one of UNESCO’s World Heritage Sites is confirmed by the annual arrival of some four million visitors from Britain and all over the world. Whereas most accounts of Bath’s history focus on the Roman and Georgian periods, skipping over much of the rest, this short history offers a chronological survey of the entire span of Bath’s existence, supplemented by lively accounts of its food, its fashions, its theatrical and artistic heritage, its music, and its memorials. Almost two-thirds of the city center is a conservation area, the largest in Britain. One in six of the city’s houses was built before 1850, almost half before the twentieth century. The city’s highlights include not only the Roman baths, the elegant Pump Room, the majestic abbey, and half a dozen museums, but also one of only four bridges in the world with shops on both sides and Britain’s last remaining Georgian pleasure gardens. With the opening of the striking new Thermae Spa complex, Bath entered the twenty-first century by reasserting its original identity as a uniquely therapeutic location.

books.title: Calculating Worth
books.subtitle: A History of Value in Nineteenth-Century North America
books.authors: Edited by Joanna Cohen Laura F. Edwards
books.tagline: Explores the history of value as a concept, one that we regularly use but tend to take for granted as the monetary expression of market mechanisms.
books.description:
Calculating Worth, a collection of essays edited by historians Joanna Cohen and Laura F. Edwards, reshapes our concept of what “value” meant in the past. Collectively, the essays reorient conventional narratives and reveal multiple methods of determining value, some traditional, some new, but all based in human agency. Calculating Worth brings together scholars of legal history, Native American history, women’s history, material culture, the history of slavery, and African American history, with topics that range widely over the nineteenth century, across North America and beyond.

Through studying subjects as varied as personal property, land, enslaved people, and intangibles such as prayer, reputation, and suffering, this portrait of value is diverse, humanistic, and far more capacious than what typically fits within the bounds of the concept of capitalism. Rather, value turns out to be a question of power—and how it is used.

books.title: Chicago Rebuilt
books.subtitle: Seeing Yesterday’s City Today
books.authors: Ryan Chester and Vincent L. Michael Illustrated by Ryan Chester
books.tagline: Reveals Chicago’s lost architecture and tells the remarkable stories of their creation and destruction.
books.description:
As you walk or drive down the street, do you ever wonder what it might have looked like in years gone by? What buildings used to be there, and how the surroundings have changed throughout time?

For the first time, through the skill and energy of Ryan Chester’s drawings, readers can see buildings throughout Chicago that were demolished decades before they ever lived. Chicago Rebuilt explores the myriad architectural styles that have been popular over the last two centuries and brings them to life in an entirely new way. Included are forty-four intricate, full-color architectural drawings of the city, juxtaposed with archival photographs and materials, as well as informative essays on each building. Together with Vincent L. Michael, Chester illuminates the fascinating histories of who made these structures, why they succeeded or failed, and why the buildings were each ultimately lost.

Enchanting and haunting, Chicago Rebuilt tells the story of a vanished city by conjuring it anew through energetic renderings from one of Chicago’s most masterful architectural and artistic talents.

books.title: Death by a Thousand Clicks
books.subtitle: How Search and Social Media Entangle Us with Engagement and How to Break That Cycle

books.title: Dividing Time
books.subtitle: The Invention of Historical Periods in Early Modern Europe
books.tagline: A bold reconstruction of the origins of the “ancient, medieval, modern” trope used to define historical eras and the transitions between them.
books.description:
We are used to dividing time, indicating the beginning or end of an era based on a year, a month, or even a specific day, after which (supposedly) “nothing was the same.” In this book, historian and classicist Frederic Clark looks at a particularly enduring form of dividing time—the tripartite distinction between antiquity, the Middle Ages, and modernity—in order to analyze the history of this division, how it has been constructed and deployed, and what its past and present implications are.

Clark argues that the study of the past has always depended on subdividing it into multiple parts, which tend to underpin any attempt to articulate a system of culture or value. After all, certain eras, ages, and epochs are celebrated as having ushered in a new, better time, whereas others are depicted as extended periods of decay and darkness. Clark provides an ingenious critique of the foundational assumptions underlying our narratives of periodization and the complex and messy process by which historical schemas develop, from the Renaissance through the early modern period to the Enlightenment and beyond. The result is an engaging and erudite tour through time and its many contested divisions, imagined and reimagined across history.

books.title: Dodging
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.tagline: A new, expansive collection by one of the most provocative and inventive poets of our time.
books.description:
In Dodging , Charles Bernstein pushes his poetics toward new kinds of formal and tonal attentions. This multifaceted work brings together comic velocity, pointed political critique, and passages of lyric intensity. Bernstein calls these poems “too late”: written late in life as irreversibility presses against reflection, regret, and renewed resistance—a situation in which dodging is not evasion but survival, a way of moving through political catastrophe and personal loss without being silenced by either.

The collection unfolds in three interrelated “fits”—a term suggesting bursts of composition, rhythmic surges, and formal groupings—titled “Dodging,” “Struggle,” and “Reflection.” These sections move from a series of flashes and fragments, then to assembled riffs and collaborations with poet Tracie Morris, and finally turn to refractions and aphorisms that embrace active contradiction. Together they trace a shifting field of contrasts: between satire and elegy, volatility and concentration, comedy and grief.

Both fundamentally true to Bernstein’s voice and radically radiant in its range, Dodging is a work that moves restlessly across forms and tones—by turns sly, searching, and unguarded, where humor and grief occupy the same ground.

books.title: Encrypted Propaganda
books.subtitle: The Democratic Promise and Despotic Peril of Chat Apps
books.authors: Inga Kristina Trauthig and Samuel Woolley
books.tagline: Essential reading on a hard-to-study but dominant communication tool, encrypted messaging apps—WhatsApp, Signal, and their kin—showing their promise and dangers.
books.description:
Pundits have long pointed to social media’s power to catalyze or end political movements—and to strengthen or weaken democracies. But this power is shifting from social media platforms (such as Facebook and YouTube) to lesser-studied encrypted messaging apps (such as WhatsApp and Signal). This urgent book explains how these technologies work and how they differ from their predecessors, outlining their strengths and vulnerabilities at a crucial stage in their evolution.

While many Facebook users have at least heard of propaganda and the algorithms used to filter and highlight content on that platform, they are more likely to trust messaging apps as sources of authentic and secure information. Paired with a growing distrust of traditional media, more people are joining large groups on these apps and using them as news sources, even when those groups include relative strangers. This makes these apps particularly vulnerable to political propaganda—and even government espionage.

Security studies scholar Inga Kristina Trauthig and propaganda scholar Samuel Woolley consider both the role of these apps in spreading disinformation and as tools for maintaining free speech and civic discourse in the face of censorship. The same closed nature that makes these apps seem trustworthy has made them particularly difficult to research. And so this qualitative study draws on some 180 interviews with propagandists, activists, influence campaigners, and other users in fourteen countries. The book’s findings and the authors’ recommendations are crucial for understanding the future of online communication and safeguarding democratic speech.

praise.q: Unsettling. . . . A rigorous, nuanced, and policy-relevant contribution. . . . Actors that undermine inclusive and accountable institutions—whatever their self-presentation—are part of the problem, not part of the solution. For analysts and decision-makers, this is precisely the uncomfortable lesson that makes the book worth reading and debating.
praise.by: Perspectives on Terrorism, on Trauthig’s "Ruining Revolution"

praise.q: Manipulation and deception has always been a part of politics. But it is particularly abundant and influential on the web. . . . Woolley believes society is unprepared and needs to fight back—a point he hammers home.
praise.by: The Economist, on Woolley’s "The Reality Game"

praise.q: A well-informed cautionary tale on alarming issues that show no signs of abating as disinformation continues to proliferate.
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews, on Woolley’s "The Reality Game"

books.title: Finding the Beautiful Commons
books.subtitle: Confessions of a Bourgeois Environmentalist
books.tagline: A call to pleasurable and sustainable action that centers our shared stewardship of shared spaces.
books.description:
Environmentally-conscious decision-making can seem like an exercise in self-denial: don’t fly, don’t drive, don’t eat meat. But bringing our tote bags to the grocery store will never be enough to solve the climate crisis, nor will dropping out of society. Many of us crave a collective movement that acknowledges the value of comfort, a framework for making choices that are inherently imperfect, but ones we can live with.

In Finding the Beautiful Commons , historian Cathy Gere offers a relatable and inspiring guide to environmental action in a consumerist culture. Recounting her experiences as a young activist at the Greenham Common Women’s Peace Camp in Berkshire, as an anarchist and guerrilla gardener in a New York City squat, and as an academic working to decarbonize the University of California system, Gere argues for initiatives grounded in common property—streets, libraries, parks, and other shared spaces—where our communal interests can drive sustainability. These are also sites where we can put bourgeois values like beauty and personal enjoyment to good use protecting local landscapes and resources.

Funny, wise, and honest about the contradictions of life during climate crisis, Gere shows us that the commons we already know—the everyday infrastructure of mass transit, natural reserves, and public beaches—is the very foundation for a livable future.

books.title: Fossil Lake and the Rise of Modern Birds
books.subtitle: Snapshots from Early Avian Evolution
books.authors: Lance Grande, Daniel T Ksepka, and Gerald Mayr
books.tagline: Lavishly produced with color fossil photographs throughout, the first comprehensive summary of findings at one of the world’s best fossil bird localities, offering profound insight into early avian evolution after the end-of-Cretaceous extinction event.
books.description:
What is today a high mountain desert in southwestern Wyoming was, 52 million years ago, a magnificent subtropical lake system. Part of the famed Green River Formation, the limestone layers of this region’s Fossil Lake provide an unparalleled record of life in the Early Eocene of North America. Evolutionary biologist Lance Grande has spent much of his career collecting and studying the beautiful and diverse assemblage of fossils from this locality. Since his 2013 book, The Lost World of Fossil Lake , researchers have uncovered many new fossil bird specimens—often stunningly preserved skeletons, sometimes even including feathers—and benefited from significant advances in our understanding of avian evolution. Their findings help to illuminate the early days of bird life on Earth.

In this volume, Grande and his collaborators—paleornithologists Daniel T. Ksepka and Gerald Mayr—explore these birds of Fossil Lake, where various researchers have formally named and described thirty avian species. The authors also present an additional twenty possible new species awaiting further study and formal review, birds that may soon be added to that list. Fossil Lake and the Rise of Modern Birds then places these avian ancestors within the global context of other fossil birds. Like Grande’s previous publications, this comprehensive work features stunning imagery, including nearly two hundred detailed fossil photographs—fifty that have never appeared elsewhere.

Whether you are an ornithologist, paleontologist, evolutionary biologist, or amateur fossil enthusiast interested in the early evolutionary diversification of modern birds, this book is a treasure.

praise.q: Lush. . . . An in-depth portrait of an aquatic community that thrived in a subtropical wonderland of jungles and volcanoes.
praise.by: Nature, on Grande’s "The Lost World of Fossil Lake"
praise.cred: on Grande’s "The Lost World of Fossil Lake"

praise.q: Enchanting. . . . A splendidly illustrated compendium . . . written with grace and authority.
praise.by: Times Higher Education, on Grande’s "The Lost World of Fossil Lake"
praise.cred: on Grande’s "The Lost World of Fossil Lake"

books.title: How Revolutions Happen
books.subtitle: Reviews
books.tagline: From the Russian intellectual-in-exile Konstantin Sonin, a grand theory of when and how rapid political change happens—or doesn’t.
books.description:
In 2015, economist Konstantin Sonin solidified his status as an enemy of the Russian state when he published an article predicting that Vladimir Putin’s presidency would produce the country’s third revolution by the middle of this century. Forced to flee the country, Sonin settled in Chicago. In the decade that followed, the Russian government continued to pursue him—placing him on their state wanted list, tracking his movements, and sentencing him in absentia to eight years in prison. Sonin’s research and political advocacy continued unabated. So did his writing.

Now, Sonin has completed his masterpiece: a revelatory and sweeping investigation of a timeless question—what makes a revolution? How Revolutions Happen pinpoints why they arise, why they don’t, and where they’re likely to occur next. Tracing examples of successful and failed examples from history—in China, France, Haiti, Ukraine—Sonin shows that revolutions don’t grow out of mere popular unrest; they happen when states cease to evolve. This argument extends well beyond why nations fail, considering also why nations almost fail and why other nations fail repeatedly. Drawing on both empirical evidence and his firsthand experience, he also argues that although revolutions are an important part of human societies, they are not inherently good or bad—or quick to end.

Wry, sweeping, and erudite, How Revolutions Happen recasts everything we think about political change. From one of the world’s foremost political economists, this book is a momentous cumulation of knowledge that allows us to fully understand what a revolution is, why they occurred in the past—and how to measure where they might be coming.

praise.q: A milestone—a parsimonious theory of revolutions written by the most prominent formal theorist of the phenomena. A rare combination of analytical clarity with historical depth and erudition.
praise.by: James A. Robinson, coauthor of Why Nations Fail and winner of the Nobel Prize in Economics
praise.cred: coauthor of Why Nations Fail and winner of the Nobel Prize in Economics

books.title: How to Find a Martian
books.subtitle: A Fossil Hunter’s Guide to the Red Planet
books.tagline: Join today’s search for signs of alien life in fossil remains from prehistoric Mars, an Earth-like world that glittered with rivers, lakes, and deep blue seas.
books.description:
Billions of years ago, there was another Earth in our solar system: the temperate and blue-streaked world of ancient Mars. Today, the rocky ruins of that lost world offer our best hope of finding signs of alien life. In How to Find a Martian , astrobiologist and paleontologist Sean McMahon argues that we may soon find fossils on Mars—perhaps even in our lifetime.

There are now thousands of astrobiologists around the world, using the tools of modern science to answer some of the most profound, intellectually exciting questions that have ever been asked: What is life? How does it evolve and proliferate across vast spans of space and time, and what forms might it take on alien worlds? The search for life on Mars is a mainstay of this research program, and it has never been more advanced, more sophisticated, or better funded than it is today. Although scientists have not yet found fossils on Mars, astrobiologist Sean McMahon says, we have at least learned how to find them. We now know which regions and landscapes on Mars could once have supported life and preserved its remains in rocks and minerals. We know how the remains of living organisms can end up woven into the texture of ancient rocks, transmuted into minerals or transcribed into the subtle language of fossil carbon molecules. But we have also learned to be cautious—and not to be fooled when non-living nature imitates the patterns of life.

Accessibly explaining trailblazing ideas and findings in astronomy, geology, microbiology, and paleontology, McMahon makes a persuasive and alluring case that we have the tools, ideas, methods, and missions to find past life on Mars.

books.title: I Contain Multitudes
books.subtitle: A New Life of Walt Whitman
books.tagline: Read More about I Contain Multitudes
books.description: Read Less about I Contain Multitudes

books.title: Leo Strauss on Hobbes
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.authors: Leo Strauss Edited by Karl Dahlquist
books.tagline: Leo Strauss’s final seminar on Thomas Hobbes, representing the culmination of more than four decades of close engagement.
books.description:
Leo Strauss spent more than four decades studying the work of Thomas Hobbes. In Strauss’s distinctive genealogy of political thought, Hobbes emerges as a decisive counterpoint, not only to the Ancients, but also to Strauss’s own project. Strauss saw Hobbes as both the founder of modern natural rights and the modern esoteric writer par excellence.

Strauss’s final seminar on Hobbes from 1964 is the culmination of his engagement with Hobbes’s corpus and contains the richest account of Strauss’s final insight into the nerve of Hobbes’s thought, linking human consciousness to power and passion. The seminar reflects on the tension between Hobbes’s scientific and political frameworks, Hobbes’s emphasis on rights over duties, Hobbes’s atheism, and Hobbes’s attention to causal thinking as the core capacity that sets humans apart from other animals. It also includes Strauss’s most sustained exchange with the Marxist political theorist, C. B. Macpherson . Their rival interpretations of why the state of nature takes the form of a war of all against all led Strauss to reconsider his earlier writings on Hobbes, including those parts that pertain to other thinkers, such as Aristotle, Locke, and Spinoza.

With an introductory essay by Karl Dahlquist that traces the evolution of Strauss’s thinking on Hobbes and frames Strauss’s dialogue with Macpherson, this 1964 seminar on Hobbes is a vital contribution to political thought and intellectual history.
