books.title: Pop Against Empire
books.subtitle: Art as Masked Critique in Japan, Okinawa, and the US Diaspora
books.tagline: How Pop artists confronted the legacies of modern Empire of Japan and post-1945 American imperialism from the 1960s to the present.
books.description:
Looking at a pivotal period spanning the 1960s to the present, Hiroko Ikegami explores how artists in Japan, Okinawa, and the United States have adopted Pop strategies to critique legacies of imperialism.

Ikegami focuses on locales—Tokyo, Okinawa, Minidoka, and New York—that were deeply impacted by the complex relationship between the Japanese and American empires and considers artists across different situations and generations. The book begins with Tokyo Pop artists and graphic designers, including Shinohara Ushio and Tanaami Keiichi, who critically parodied American Pop during the long 1960s. It then turns to Okinawa, where Tom Max probed Okinawans’ convoluted reality regarding the American Occupation and the Vietnam War. Artists in the second half of the volume confronted legacies of the Asia-Pacific War as a historical condition of the present. Roger Shimomura, the third-generation Japanese American who had been incarcerated in the Minidoka camp as a child, dealt with the subject by appropriating motifs of ukiyo-e woodblock prints. Takashi Murakami, now a global art star, created otaku-inspired art and capitalized on his country’s experience of the atomic bombs in promoting his “Superflat” enterprise. The book concludes with a new generation of artists protesting repercussions of empire in the twenty-first century. This is the first study to treat artists of post-1945 Japan, Okinawa, and the US diaspora in a single volume as mutually independent yet interrelated, using Pop’s criticality as a connecting thread.

books.title: Sailing Close to the Clouds
books.subtitle: Selected Worlds of Lucian of Samosata
books.authors: Lucian of Samosata Edited and Translated by Cynthia C. Polsley
books.tagline: Approachable translations and discussions of Lucian that reveal his world-building, world-bending, and multiversal thinking.
books.description:
Lucian of Samosata was ahead of his time. A rhetorician and writer active in the second century CE, he was one of the earliest known worldbuilders and science-fiction enthusiasts. Popular and prolific in antiquity—more than eighty texts attributed to him have come down to us today, including satires, dialogues, and part of a fictional work called True History —Lucian crafted astonishing tales that unfold on the surface of the moon or other planets, high above in Earth’s atmosphere, or through the eyes of underworld inhabitants or other entities who view mortal humans as otherworldly beings.

Ideal for readers interested in science fiction, fantasy, and mythology, this accessible collection offers a guided journey through Lucian’s many worlds. Bringing together fresh vernacular translations of eight works with substantial discussion, this selection showcases Lucian as a proto-multiversal thinker, presenting multiform narratives that herald developments in modern genres ranging from literature and film to gaming and fan fiction. Translator and editor Cynthia Polsley introduces each with a short excerpt from another piece of classical literature, showing how other ancient authors—including Homer, Ovid, and Vergil—influenced Lucian’s literary landscapes or were inspired by him in turn.

books.title: Scenes and Their Senses
books.subtitle: Close Reading as Theory and Method
books.tagline: Makes the case for close readings of small scenes appearing in works of literature, scholarship, film, and visual art, showing how close attention to details can reveal the meaningful sociological action that often occurs on the margins.
books.description:
Why do certain images, stories, and scenes impress upon us so strongly, inviting us to linger over the nuances of their meaning? In Scenes and Their Senses , sociologist Robin Wagner-Pacifici seeks to uncover the deeper meaning behind twenty “scenes” that have captured her theoretical imagination over her lifetime. Some of these come from classics of sociological theory or literature—Geertz, Habermas, Strauss, Zola—and some are more contemporary, including the films Good Will Hunting and Luis Buñuel’s The Phantom of Liberty. She seeks here to understand each scene less as examples of a given condition or conundrum and more as worlds in themselves.

As Wagner-Pacifici shows, close attention to the forms and flows of these minor, often quiet scenes reveals how meaningful action occurs in what might appear to be the margins or interstices of the bigger, noisier story being told. Providing an entry point to larger social conditions, relations, and change, the scenes analyzed here evoke sociological themes of belonging and exile, strength and weakness, cleanliness and pollution, reality and fantasy, courage and cowardice, and vision and obscurity, among others. As an ethnography of texts recalled from previous readings and revisited by the author, the scenes highlight the role of memory in sense-making. Furthermore, the activation of the scenes as a focused point of sustained contemplation functions as a remarkable bridge between method and theory.

books.title: Secrets of Responsibility
books.subtitle: Table of Contents
books.authors: Jacques Derrida Edited by Ginette Michaud and Nicholas Cotton Translated by E. S. Burt and Katie Chenoweth
books.tagline: Jacques Derrida on the problem of secrecy, the first in a ten-seminar series on questions of responsibility.
books.description:
Delivered at the École des hautes études en sciences sociales in Paris during the 1991–92 academic year, Secrets of Responsibility is the first of ten seminars given by Jacques Derrida under the umbrella “Questions of Responsibility,” a cycle that includes Hospitality , Perjury and Pardon , Death Penalty , and The Beast and the Sovereign —each also published by the University of Chicago Press.

In this seminar, Derrida asks a basic question—what is a secret?—which he then explores across scientific, technical, social, political, and religious domains. Over twelve sessions, we are treated to analyses of industrial, state, military, professional, and religious secrets as well as secret societies and secret police. Derrida also tackles secrecy in literary fiction (especially in Melville, James, Poe, and Baudelaire) and philosophical texts (including Freud, Kant, Heidegger, Kierkegaard, Patočka, Nietzsche, Levinas, and others). The result is a set of profound and surprising insights delivered as only Derrida can.

books.title: Steel Flowers
books.subtitle: The Women of the Vietnam War (1964–1975)
books.tagline: An estimated one million women fought in the Vietnam War (1964–1975) in the former South Vietnam. For the first time, we hear their stories in their own voices.
books.description:
This unique collection of oral histories fills a gap in the history of a war typically told by American and South Vietnamese veterans, mainly men. The Vietnamese women veterans, dehumanized in US war propaganda, deliver a collective condemnation of war in this compelling and balanced account compiled and edited by Sherry Buchanan.

They were known as the Long-Haired Army, part of the communist National Liberation Front or Viet Cong fighting for unification and liberation from US-occupying forces in the former South Vietnam. They lived clandestinely in the jungle, in tunnels, and in villages in the liberated zones ,under bombardments from the air, land, and sea. They served as snipers and artillery gunners, as logistics supply personnel, and as unarmed civil defense workers, spies and couriers, doctors and nurses, actors, singers, and poets.

The veterans share memories of their fighting exploits, of caring for children and family during war, and of the pain of lost loved ones. They remember wartime lovers killed in combat, and friends who died too young to have known love. A guerrilla fighter describes the trauma of abandoning her crying baby in the jungle to save her platoon, another about sparing the life of American soldiers, and another about rape when detained without charge.

Their stories of torture, sexual abuse, and rape in the US-administered prisons and interrogation centers of the former South Vietnam fill another gap in history. The torture of American POWs in North Vietnamese jails has been well documented. In contrast, the torture of women, NLF combatants and civilians, has not. Survivors describe the infamous tiger cages, the beatings, waterboarding, and electric shock. They also reveal the story of their organized prison rebellions against their criminal treatment by prison authorities.

They share their post-war memories, their gratitude of being able to have children in spite of injuries, Agent Orange, and torture. They talk of survivors' guilt and PTSD, of looking for the remains of lost loved ones after the war, and of caring for less fortunate sisters-in-arms. Their stories must be shared.

In a spirit of reconciliation, the collection includes testimonies from American and South Vietnamese women who served in Vietnam and their negative and positive interaction postwar with the other side in an effort to rebuild a new Vietnam.

Two million Vietnamese civilians were killed across North and South, a million to two million Vietnamese combatants, and over fifty-thousand American combatants. The International War Crimes Tribunal in 1967 unanimously found the United States “guilty on all charges, including genocide, the use of forbidden weapons, maltreatment and killing of prisoners, violence and forceful movement of prisoners.”

Read More about Steel Flowers

Read Less about Steel Flowers

praise.q: Sherry Buchanan’s mantra is “No More War!”—the phrase of the Vietnamese artist Tran Trung Tin who painted in Hanoi during the bombings of the city. More war only brings suffering to other human beings, especially to young women. As sisters, wives, mothers and grandmothers, women must be loved and respected. Women must be free, happy and healthy and be able to live in a peaceful environment. Only then can they bring up a better, kinder and more peaceful next generation.
praise.by: Le Ly Hayslip, author of When Heaven and Earth Changed Places
praise.cred: author of When Heaven and Earth Changed Places

praise.q: Finally, Sherry Buchanan challenges the female stereotypes of Vietnam War movies. . . . We need more books like Buchanan’s as a starting point to humanize Vietnamese women.

praise.q: Sherry Buchanan challenges American exceptionalism and innocence. . . . Despite the War’s moral implications, the mass death it wrought, the long aftermath of chemical weapon use, and the decades of physical and psychological trauma it caused Vietnamese civilians and fighters as well as American soldiers, Buchanan argues the U.S. has yet to truly grapple with what the invasion says about the country’s seemingly insatiable penchant for violent supremacy.

books.title: Street Dog
books.subtitle: On the Origins and Future of Our Best Friendship
books.authors: Lee Alan Dugatkin and Anindita Bhadra
books.tagline: A fascinating look at the lives of the world’s largest dog population—street dogs—offering essential insights into your dog’s behavior and the mysterious origins of human-dog cooperation.
books.description:
Today, there are close to a billion dogs on the planet. Some twenty thousand years ago, there were none. How did dogs originate from wolves? And how did we begin our best friendship? Although we can’t go back in time, we can study modern dogs for clues. Of today’s dogs, about eighty percent are street dogs, which don’t live in human homes, but near them, existing in a space between wild and domesticated.

This fascinating and eye-opening book offers us a chance to meet these street dogs and, through them, to imagine the earliest stages of human-canine companionship and collaboration. Award-winning author and animal behaviorist Lee Alan Dugatkin and world canine expert Anindita Bhadra take us from the hallways of Bhadra’s Dog Lab onto the bustling streets of Kolkata, India, where we encounter the intelligent, resourceful, and sometimes mischievous street dogs that have lived alongside humans for hundreds of dog generations. By observing these street dogs’ social structures, survival strategies, and personalities—and comparing them to foxes, wolves, and house dogs, among other species—we learn a lot about canine behavior. Take, for example, Bhadra’s discovery that, no matter how vital food is to a street dog, when given a choice between a meal and a gentle carress, dogs choose love over the food. We also learn that many dogs prefer yellow to other colors; that dog grandmoms may adopt unrelated puppies; and that dog genes harbor a mutation that, in humans, is associated with extreme friendliness. We even begin to understand why dogs pee on, well, everything—particularly on other dog pee.

Watching dogs live independent lives alongside humans, we also start to wonder, as Bhadra does, about the origins of human-dog cooperation. She persuades us that early dogs and humans likely protected each other, as many still do today, and that street dogs may help us to imagine our ancestors’ interactions with the earliest proto-dogs. In their engaging exploration, Dugatkin and Bhadra show that getting to know street dogs may help us understand the past, present, and future of our unique interspecies relationship.

praise.q: By the end of the book, the thesis that wolves may have been no less complicit in the process of their domestication than humans has come to seem entirely probable.
praise.by: Time Literary Supplement, on Dugatkin and Trut’s “How to Tame a Fox (and Build a Dog)”

books.title: The Business State
books.subtitle: Empire and Big Business in the Twentieth-Century British State
books.tagline: Narrates how big business guided policy and expanded the state in early twentieth-century Britain.
books.description:
During World War I, British businessmen streamed into government service. When Britain faced unprecedented economic challenges after the war’s end, civil servants turned to the same businessmen with whom they had worked. The result was a durable public-private network of both bureaucrats and executives: the business state.

In this book, Ian Kumekawa throws light on the previously obscured and hidden world of the business state and the economic thinking of its administrators. He breaks new methodological ground by treating the state and business together as a single entity. Twentieth-century states, he argues, were porous networks in which lines between business and governance were not clearly defined. In liberal democracies, the term “business-friendly” has long been understood as synonymous with laissez-faire. The Business State explores the historical limits of that assumption by focusing on Britain, the self-identified small, liberal state par excellence . In doing so, the book shows how a liberal democracy was effectively co-opted by private interests and explores how actively assisting big business became not just acceptable—but a political necessity.

books.title: Under the Rug
books.subtitle: The (Not So) Hidden History of Men and Their Hairpieces
books.tagline: False hair can reveal honest truths—about the past, gender, identity, and the stories men tell about themselves.
books.description:
History has seen its share of famous toupees. John Wayne’s. Frank Sinatra’s. Humphrey Bogart’s. Hairpieces can reveal a wearer’s inner motivations, reinforce gender norms, cause embarrassment, and even provoke disgust. Although false, they can create real meaning.

In Wendy A. Woloson’s hands, the toupee helps us see how men have understood themselves and fashioned their identities over time. Starting in the late eighteenth century, when men stopped wearing white powdered wigs, and moving to the 1920s, when toupees could be easily mass-produced, Woloson tells the story of the “Toupee Age.” She investigates why balding was considered such a problem in the first place, how hair became entangled with anxieties about aging, and the ways that looking old posed a threat to manhood. She details the bear’s grease pomades, brush-on dyes, elixirs, false whiskers, and hairpieces that were created to meet shifting notions of masculinity and style. Under the Rug also introduces readers to the people who styled and traded hair, made wigs, and hawked baldness cures. Drawing on business records, advertisements, graphic images, and a host of other primary sources, Woloson incisively explains how such trades seeded fears about thinning hair and sold men solutions. This vanity project continues today, as hair transplants, medications to stimulate hair growth, and Toupee TikTok encourage people to reinvent the way they’re seen—by others and themselves.

books.title: Writing the Land
books.subtitle: French Imperial and Colonial Mapping of West Africa, 1854–1892
books.tagline: Reveals the intertwined nature of imperial mapping and map history through the making of the colony of French Soudan in nineteenth-century West Africa.
books.description:
Thomas J. Bassett’s Writing the Land argues that mapping played a key role in France’s territorial conquest of Africa, and that the process of imperial expansion and colonization shaped map history by influencing how maps were constructed, circulated, and used. Analyzing military and surveying campaigns over half a century in an area that became the colony of French Soudan, Bassett focuses on the social and spatial problems that surveyors and mapmakers tried to solve in the process of territorial conquest, as well as the conflicts that arose as they pursued their goals.

In their efforts to obtain this territory, French military leaders, cartographers, and expedition members came into continual contact with local Africans, with whom they negotiated and clashed. Often, imperial officers relied on intermediaries to navigate West African geography, drawing on the knowledge of political authorities, interpreters, guides, and long-distance traders; the maps they produced are inextricable from these interactions. Ultimately, Bassett claims, examining the processes of mapping in the context of these encounters leads us to understand these maps anew as Euro-African constructions, ones that emerge from a complex process of exchange and domination.

books.title: A Field Guide to Accessible Birding in the United States
books.tagline: An essential guide to accessible birding in all lower 48 states—the first comprehensive resource of its kind for bird lovers with disabilities, illnesses, or injuries
books.description:
One of the biggest obstacles for disabled birders is knowing which locations will meet their access needs. A Field Guide to Accessible Birding in the United States provides details on more than 200 accessible trails, stationary birding locations, and car birding opportunities, enabling disabled birders to make informed decisions about visiting. Organized by state, each entry addresses a variety of access features, and every location was visited by the author to ensure accuracy and reliability. Whether you’re a wheelchair hiker, a birder living with an injury or chronic illness, or a parent who struggles to find sites where you can easily push a stroller, this guide is your passport to discovering amazing, accessible places to enjoy birds. Nondisabled birders, too, will appreciate this collection of awe-inspiring birding experiences from across the country.

In-depth entries share invaluable information on the accessibility of each site, from parking and trail surfaces to benches, bathrooms, guide ropes, blinds, observation platforms, audio tours and loaner equipment, and potential barriers such as steps or gates

Highlights spectacular migration experiences and the most accessible places to find specialty birds, from Tufted Puffins and Greater Prairie-Chickens to Bicknell’s Thrush and White-tailed Ptarmigan

Uses icons for at-a-glance reference, noting the best season to visit, opportunities for birding by ear, and the availability of car, boat, bike, indoor, and stationary birding

Provides a map for every state in the continental US along with stunning photos

Tips and suggestions help birders choose the locations that best suit their needs and offers encouragement to try different styles of birding

Draws on the author’s lived experience as a disabled birder, perspectives from a variety of birders with disabilities, and best practices from the research
books.bio: Freya McGregor is a disabled birder and an occupational therapist with a background in blindness and low vision services. She works with nature organizations to improve access and inclusion for birders with disabilities through her consulting business, Access Birding, and as a researcher in the Dayer Human Dimensions Lab at Virginia Tech.

books.title: A Political Theory of Academic Freedom
books.tagline: What academic freedom means—and why it matters—when liberal democracy itself is no longer a given.
books.description:
A Political Theory of Academic Freedom advances a bold thesis about academic freedom: it’s imperiled not simply by its authoritarian adversaries, Adam Sitze argues, but also by its advocates’ own diminished capacity to say what it’s for.

Recovering what he calls the “triadic principle”—the idea that the university has historically defined itself in relation to church and state—Sitze argues that the renewal of academic freedom today begins with a recognition of its kinship with its two counter-majoritarian constitutional cousins: judicial independence and religious liberty. The result is a novel theory of academic freedom: just as judicial independence safeguards the administration of justice and religious liberty safeguards the exercise of faith, academic freedom safeguards the pursuit of truth.

Through discussions of academic tenure, religious pluralism, and university autonomy, Sitze challenges the idea that academic freedom grants scholars special privileges. Instead, he contends, it’s a constitutional principle rooted in the same logic that guarantees judges their tenure and protects religious communities from state interference: the common good is best served when those who seek justice, faith, and truth remain free to follow those goods wherever they may lead.
books.bio: Adam Sitze is the John E. Kirkpatrick 1951 Professor in Law, Jurisprudence, and Social Thought at Amherst College. His writings on academic freedom have appeared in venues such as The Chronicle of Higher Education , The Massachusetts Review , and Yale Journal of Law and the Humanities . He has been awarded fellowships from the MacArthur Foundation, the ACLS/SSRC/NEH, the Mellon Foundation, the Leslie Humanities Center at Dartmouth College, and the Institute for Human Sciences in Vienna, Austria.

books.title: All Good People
books.subtitle: Difference, Diversity, and the Invention of Opportunity
books.tagline: A critical history of STEM DEI, the twenty-first century reforms of education and work that sustain very old systems of differing people, deserving different lives.
books.description:
In All Good People, Amy Slaton provides the first extended historical study of STEM DEI, a concerted effort by educational, corporate, governmental, and philanthropic sectors in recent decades to address the disproportionate participation of majority individuals in U.S. science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.

Unlike educational or workforce policy studies of minority experiences in STEM, this book follows the historical roots of American faith in technoscience as a scaffold for democratic values: the belief that the U.S. is at heart a meritocracy where anyone of talent can succeed. Despite the well-intentioned reforms of recent DEI initiatives, the outcome has been an extremely slow rate of change in participation by Black, Brown, female, LGBTQAI+ and disabled communities in STEM. The author traces what has counted as STEM talent, prevailing ideas about learning and productivity, and the epistemic features of technoscience to find not insincerity or even simply under-resourcing as the causes of this social stasis, but a national commitment to upholding the stratified and ultimately unjust character of the industrial polity—what scholars and activists have long described as a system of racial capitalism. The book aims to create possibilities for new forms of dialogue on the nature of fairness in the twenty-first century U.S.
books.bio: Amy E. Slaton is Professor Emerita of History at Drexel University. She is the author of Reinforced Concrete and the Modernization of American Building, 1900-1930 ; Race, Rigor, and Selectivity in US Engineering ; and editor of New Materials .

books.title: Animal Collateral
books.subtitle: The Silent Poisoning of Wildlife, Pets, and People
books.tagline: A groundbreaking exposé of the widespread use of rat poisons and their deadly toll on animals—and us
books.description:
Bald eagles are a conservation success story, rebounding after DDT and other harmful chemicals, which drove them to near extinction, were banned. But today, eagles and other wildlife face a new threat: rat poisons. Animal Collateral reveals the truth about these poisons the chemical companies and their lobbyists don’t want you to hear, describing how SGARS—an especially deadly class of poison used in bait boxes found around homes, businesses, and communities—are killing owls, hawks, eagles, foxes, coyotes, and other wildlife. SGARs and other lethal anticoagulants are also killing pets as well as people and have even sickened large numbers of children—all while proving ineffective at solving the rodent problem.

Laura Kiesel shares the tragic stories of Flaco, the owl who captured the hearts of New Yorkers after escaping from the Central Park Zoo; MK, a female bald eagle that became a local celebrity in Boston; and P-45, a pregnant California mountain lion. She investigates the industries that are prioritizing profits over public health, exposing the dubious tactics used by chemical companies to protect their bottom line despite mounting evidence of harm. Kiesel also interrogates our deep prejudices against rats, examining why we demonize some species while revering others.

Animal Collateral ultimately delivers a message of hope, describing the practical steps each of us can take to protect our families and communities and profiling the courageous individuals and grassroots organizers who are leading the charge against these poisons.
books.bio: Laura Kiesel is the founder and director of Save Arlington Wildlife and the nonprofit Save Mass Wildlife. She has an academic background in environmental science and wildlife biology and has been advocating and reporting on issues affecting our natural world for decades. She has written about the environment and public health for many outlets, including Salon , The Guardian , The Washington Post , Vice , and The Atlantic , and is the author of the poetry collection Swallowing the Stem of Adam’s Apple .

books.title: Antitrust Policy Design
books.tagline: A robust examination of the history and current state of US antitrust policy, including the growing role of internet commerce.
books.description:
Antitrust regulations are historical and political as much as legal or economic. In Antitrust Policy Design , Herbert Hovenkamp engages the central antitrust issue today: the growing role of internet commerce. Protection of consumers and labor interests, says Hovenkamp, have always been the paramount concern of antitrust legislation. He examines the structure of antitrust policy, underlining that current antitrust policy makes no distinctions between online and offline trade. We are best served, he says, by policies that favor consumers and suppliers, including suppliers of labor, and unrestrained innovation. He makes clear policy recommendations, especially in the area of remedies.

Hovenkamp begins with the original understandings of the antitrust statutes, followed by a brief account of the various “schools” of antitrust thought that reflect changing commitments to markets, free enterprise, and economic growth. He examines the most significant deviations from these ideas, then explores the metrics that antitrust policy makers use to evaluate particular practices, including its use of economics. Finally, he evaluates antitrust policy toward dominant firms, remedies, mergers involving complementary products, and anticompetitive agreements.
books.bio: Herbert Hovenkamp is the James G. Dinan University Professor, University of Pennsylvania Law School and the Wharton School. His books include Antitrust Law , 20 vols. (with Erik Hovenkamp, the late Phillip E. Areeda, and the late Donald F. Turner); Tech Monopoly (MIT Press); Federal Antitrust Policy; The Opening of American Law, 1870–1970 ; The Antitrust Enterprise ; and Enterprise and American Law, 1836–1937 .

books.title: Autonorama
books.subtitle: The Illusory Promise of High-Tech Driving
books.tagline: The danger of a driverless future built on false promises—now with a new preface and afterword and a revised introduction by the author
books.description:
“The foundation has been laid for fully autonomous,” Elon Musk announced in 2016, when he assured the world that Tesla would have a driverless fleet on the road in 2017. “It’s twice as safe as a human, maybe better.” Promises of technofuturistic driving utopias have been ubiquitous wherever tech companies and carmakers meet.

In Autonorama , technology historian Peter Norton argues that driverless cars cannot be the safe, sustainable, and inclusive “mobility solutions” that tech companies and automakers are promising us. The salesmanship behind the driverless future is distracting us from investing in better ways to get around that we can implement now. Unlike autonomous vehicles, these alternatives are inexpensive, safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Norton takes the reader on an engaging ride—from the GM Futurama exhibit to “smart” highways and vehicles—to show how we are once again being sold car dependency in the guise of mobility. He argues that we cannot see what tech companies are selling us except in the light of history. With driverless cars, we’re promised that new technology will solve the problems that car dependency gave us: Zero crashes! Zero emissions! Zero congestion! But these are the same promises that have kept us on a treadmill of car dependency for eighty years.

Now with a new preface and afterword and a revised introduction by the author, Autonorama is hopeful, advocating for wise, proven, humane mobility that we can invest in now, without waiting for technology that is forever just out of reach. Before intelligent systems, data, and technology can serve us, Norton suggests, we need wisdom. Rachel Carson warned us that when we seek technological solutions instead of ecological balance, we can make our problems worse. With this wisdom, Norton contends, we can meet our mobility needs with what we have right now.
books.bio: Peter Norton is associate professor of history in the Department of Engineering and Society at the University of Virginia. He is the author of Fighting Traffic: The Dawn of the Motor Age in the American City .

praise.q: This is a bracing challenge to the dogma of autonomous vehicle enthusiasts and a clarion call for more varied and humane mobility solutions.
praise.by: Booklist

praise.q: From my own experience with this text in the classroom, the book was very well-received by undergraduates interested in transportation planning and I am certain the book would make a fine addition to a graduate student’s reading list. The author’s broader message is necessary for transportation planning practitioners and our colleagues within motordom.

praise.who: Journal of Planning Education and Research

praise.q: Offering iconoclastic arguments that are well worth our attention, Autonorama: The Illusory Promise of High-Tech Driving by Professor Peter Norton is especially and unreservedly recommended for community, college, and university library Automotive History and Contemporary Social Issues collections.
praise.by: Midwest Book Review

praise.q: [Norton] concludes that the only way to end the vices caused by automobile dependency is to reduce automobile dependency itself—to rebuild public transit and facilitate walking and cycling, so that Americans have the same level of transportation choice as Europeans and Asians.
praise.by: Planetizen

praise.q: Two decades into the 21st-century, we should heed Norton’s warnings about Autonorama, turn our backs on car culture, and begin the rewarding task of reclaiming urban space for efficient public transit, safe cycling, and healthy and stress-free walking.
praise.by: Resilience

praise.q: [Norton’s] contention that the public is being sold a bill of goods that further reinforces car dependency and freedom against alternative options that are more environmentally and socially friendly creates a thought-provoking analysis of the underlying influences of car company business interests on future choices.
praise.by: Donovan's Literary Services

praise.q: Provocative, forcing AV proponents to explain why things will be different this time around after the failed promises of the past 80 years, and whether the answer to the urban transportation problem can actually be more, albeit smarter, automobiles.
praise.by: Journal of Urban Affairs

praise.q: Autonorama is a ‘road-switch’ for a human-powered age, showing that safer, more livable cities will be achieved not by the tech in our cars, but by our actions on our streets.
praise.by: Janette Sadik-Khan, Bloomberg Associates and former commissioner, New York City Department of Transportation
praise.cred: Bloomberg Associates and former commissioner, New York City Department of Transportation

praise.q: Autonorama is a timely reminder from a first-class mind that, like the cartoon dog catching the car, realizing the sixty-year-old dream of autonomous driving can only ever be a disappointment. Norton demonstrates that the snake-oil promises of zero crashes, zero emissions, and zero congestion hide the goal of perpetual and damaging car dependency. He also shows that the urban mobility modes too often degraded and therefore despised—public transit, walkability, bicycling—would bloom if only they were funded with a fraction of the financial love lavished for too long on automobility.
praise.by: Carlton Reid, Senior Sustainability Contributor, Forbes.com, author of Roads Were Not Built for Cars and Bike Boom
praise.cred: Senior Sustainability Contributor, Forbes.com, author of Roads Were Not Built for Cars and Bike Boom

praise.q: Autonorama is a thought-provoking, timely, and profoundly important book that will enable readers to avoid being taken in by false promises of high-speed, delay-free cities for drivers. Peter Norton reveals how the pursuit of self-driving cars is not only unrealistic; it’s a dangerous distraction from far cheaper, healthier, sustainable, and equitable transportation solutions.
praise.by: Sally Flocks, founder and former president, Pedestrians Educating Drivers on Safety (PEDS)
praise.cred: founder and former president, Pedestrians Educating Drivers on Safety (PEDS)

books.title: Being and Time
books.subtitle: An Annotated Translation
books.tagline: A new, more accessible translation of one of the most important philosophical works of the twentieth century
books.description: Martin Heidegger’s seminal work Sein und Zeit ( Being and Time ) is an exploration of the founding conditions of our being in any world, and of the varying revelations that allow for radically different experiences of things. But the very originality of the work, and the relentless stream of neologisms that Heidegger used to express concepts for which philosophy had no vocabulary, make the book a daunting read. This translation by Cyril Welch, classroom tested for more than twenty years, is far more readable than previous versions. It includes explanatory footnotes, as well as a translator’s preface that sets out Heidegger’s overall purpose and strategy in this complex and essential work.
books.bio: Martin Heidegger (1889–1976), one of the most original and important philosophers of the twentieth century, spent most of his career at the University of Freiburg. His work deeply influenced many of the schools of modern philosophy, including existentialism, phenomenology, deconstructionism, and postmodernism. Cyril Welch is professor emeritus of philosophy at Mount Allison University, New Brunswick, Canada.

praise.q: Cyril Welch’s accurate and elegantly written translation of Heidegger’s Being and Time provides the best available English translation of this difficult work. It makes a welcome contribution to the interpretation of Heidegger’s thought and of twentieth-century philosophy more generally.”—Jeffrey Andrew Barash, author of The Politics of Historical Interpretation: Reflections on Ideology and the Perplexities of Political Myth

Cyril Welch’s translation of Being and Time is a remarkable achievement. Welch has avoided the palimpsest of linguistic obfuscation that plagued earlier translations, while remaining true to the colloquial flavor of Heidegger’s German. At long last, English-speaking readers have at their disposal a lucid and readable translation of Heidegger’s 1927 masterpiece.
praise.by: Richard Wolin, author of Heidegger in Ruins

books.title: Buried
books.subtitle: The Toxic Truth About Our Soil and Groundwater
books.tagline: How the environmental disaster underground is taking place in our own backyards—and how we can fix it. From an award-winning science writer, geologist, and researcher.
books.description:
From an award-winning science writer, geologist, and researcher.

As everyday life goes on, fallout from what seem like distant crises—the floods, the wildfires, the toxic spills—is poisoning the soil and water underneath neighborhoods and farms and cities at home and around the world. This is the urgent message delivered in Buried , a book that is deeply informed, deeply personal, harrowing, but never without hope. Geologist, field researcher, and outdoor guru Ruby McConnell pursues the larger story of widespread hidden contamination through the experience of the places she knows best, in Oregon.

Drawing on her years working directly on cleanup sites, the author takes readers into the underground world where leaking infrastructure, toxic industrial sites, and abandoned facilities spread chemicals through soils and aquifers everywhere. These contaminants, in turn, are linked to unsafe drinking water, failing crops, cancer clusters, biodiversity decline, and deepening environmental injustice.

McConnell’s real-world experience and vivid storytelling bring this buried, ongoing disaster to the surface in a powerful, accessible way. As PFAS contamination, fracking byproducts, and dwindling clean-water reserves force public awareness, her book offers clarity and urgency, along with pathways toward realistic solutions. Part investigation, part narrative journey, and part call to action, Buried shows why understanding what lies beneath our feet is essential to building a healthier and more resilient future on a global scale.
books.bio: Ruby McConnell is a writer, geologist, and environmental advocate whose award-winning work has appeared in Ms. Magazine , the Wall Street Journal, Huffington Post , and High Country News . She is the author of Wilderness and the American Spirit and the outdoor series A Woman’s Guide to the Wild and A Girl’s Guide to the Wild , as well as the essay collection Ground Truth , which was a finalist for an Oregon Book Award.

books.title: Campus Speech and Academic Freedom
books.subtitle: A Guide for Difficult Times
books.tagline: Expert guidance for navigating the difficult new issues around free speech rights in higher education
books.description: In their earlier book, Free Speech on Campus , Erwin Chemerinsky and Howard Gillman argued that colleges and universities should permit the expression of the widest possible range of views. Nearly ten tumultuous years later, many issues have arisen that this simple principle does not adequately address. To what extent must an institution provide expensive security for extremely controversial speakers? Should colleges and universities defend faculty, students, or administrators who find themselves the victims of social media firestorms? How should they handle the expression of controversial views or the use of offensive language in classrooms? May academic departments or other administrative units—or an entire school—take positions on controversial political issues? What rules should exist around campus protests or disruptive activities? How should we assess government efforts to control faculty speech or curricular choices? In Campus Speech and Academic Freedom , two law professors and university administrators who have confronted these questions for years draw on their extensive real-world experience to help campus leaders, campus communities, government officials, and the public better understand and address the contentious issues surrounding campus speech.
books.bio: Erwin Chemerinsky is the dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law at Berkeley Law, University of California. His books include Worse Than Nothing and No Democracy Lasts Forever . Howard Gillman is the chancellor of the University of California, Irvine. His books include The Votes That Counted: How the Court Decided the 2000 Presidential Election . Chemerinsky and Gillman are the coauthors of Free Speech on Campus , and they cochair the national advisory board for the University of California’s Center for Free Speech and Civic Engagement.

praise.q: [Chemerinsky and Gillman] offer a clear and compelling framework for understanding what academic freedom protects and how it differs from free speech.
praise.by: Glenn C. Altschuler and David Wippman, The Hill
praise.who: Glenn C. Altschuler and David Wippman

praise.q: An excellent analysis of free speech on college campuses. . . . The book is correctly critical of administrators and activists who engage in censorship, and offers many good recommendations for colleges to improve their policies and practices.
praise.by: John K. Wilson, Inside Higher Education

praise.q: Timely . . . Much-needed . . . does an excellent job of educating readers on these complex conceptions, reflecting both authors’ backgrounds as scholars and teachers.
praise.by: Zach Greenberg, Journal of Urban Affairs

praise.q: This lucid, compelling book combines rigorous legal analysis with sound practical advice. Written by two of America’s most distinguished constitutional scholars and successful university leaders, Campus Speech and Academic Freedom is essential reading for anyone concerned about the state of free speech and higher education today.”—Christopher L. Eisgruber, president, Princeton University, and author of Terms of Respect: How Colleges Get Free Speech Right

Clarifying enduring legal and normative principles, the authors provide an unflinching analysis of current campus speech struggles, which neither courts controversy nor shies away from it. An essential book for scholars, administrators, and organizers.
praise.by: Sigal Ben-Porath, author of Cancel Wars: How Universities Can Foster Free Speech, Promote Inclusion, and Renew Democracy
praise.cred: author of Cancel Wars: How Universities Can Foster Free Speech, Promote Inclusion, and Renew Democracy

praise.q: Campus Speech and Academic Freedom belongs on the desk of every university leader. Chemerinsky and Gillman clearly and cogently explain the case law and provide many examples from campuses across the country. Most important of all, they offer practical advice that university leaders can use. This book will quickly become the go-to source for solutions to questions of freedom of expression and academic freedom on campus.
praise.by: Barbara R. Snyder, president, Association of American Universities

outlets: Glenn C. Altschuler and David Wippman

books.title: Contested Terms
books.subtitle: Critical Keywords in Library and Information Studies
books.authors: Edited by nicholae cline and Jorge R. López-McKnight
books.tagline: A provocative and disruptive collection of keyword essays that rethink key terms in library and information studies from critical orientations.
books.description:
Contested Terms offers a timely and critical examination of the core vocabulary shaping the field of Library and Information Studies (LIS). Edited by nicholae cline and Jorge López-McKnight, this collection arises from a crucial moment marked by ongoing global crises, persistent social domination, and questionable scholarly critiques. Contributors explore the evolving meanings and political implications of foundational and emerging LIS terms, tracing their historical lineage and situating them within the broader context of the field’s principles, frameworks, and practices. The forty essays delve into the tensions, conflicts, and complexities embedded within these concepts, fostering critical reflection, new understandings and action, and future possibilities for LIS.

This book distinguishes itself by its collective approach, bringing together voices from across the LIS profession, including early career scholars, practitioners (archivists, librarians, administrators), and established academics. This breadth of perspectives offers a rich, insightful, and nuanced exploration of the field’s intellectual terrain while also challenging readers (students and scholars alike) to think beyond given or preconceived definitions of each term and our notions of the field. The collection’s authorship, with a majority of contributors identifying as Black, Indigenous, Latinx/e; Asian and Pacific Islander; queer, trans, and/or disabled, further amplifies voices, methodologies, politics, and theoretical interventions that significantly attend to difference. While other keyword-style texts exist in related disciplines, such as the NYU Keywords series and MIT’s Uncertain Archives , this volume is the first to specifically address the LIS field.
books.bio:
nicholae cline (Editor)

nicholae cline is a knowledge worker at Indiana University.

Jorge R. López-McKnight (Editor)

Jorge R. López-McKnight is a community college library worker in Austin, Texas.

books.title: Crossroads Africa
books.subtitle: African Engagement in the Making of Early Modernity
books.authors: Edited by Cécile Fromont, Sarah M. Guérin, and Carlo Taviani
books.description: Crossroads Africa explores the role of Africa and Africans in shaping the early modern world (c. 1300–1700). These essays identify and analyze key spaces, objects, and ideas that emerged on the continent as it engaged with the early modern world and that continue to inform the circulation of people, goods, and ideas today. Focusing on a set of related geographies—West Africa, its Atlantic archipelagos, Ethiopia, and the Italian peninsula—this collection examines the exchange of materials, including ivory, coral, glass beads, textiles, and metalwork; the circulation of knowledge and technologies; enslavement and the formation of creolized communities and cultures; and representations and perceptions of power. Throughout the book, art historians, archaeologists, and historians innovatively and productively cross historiographical and geographical boundaries, building the emerging field of early modern African studies.
books.bio:
Cécile Fromont is Professor of the History of Art and Architecture at Harvard University and the author of The Art of Conversion: Christian Visual Culture in the Kingdom of Kongo and Images on a Mission in Early Modern Kongo and Angola .

Sarah M. Guérin is Associate Professor of Medieval Art at the University of Pennsylvania. Her first book, French Gothic Ivories: Material Theologies and the Sculptor’s Craft was awarded the John Nicholas Brown Prize, and she served on the steering committee for the award-winning exhibition Caravans of Gold, Fragments in Time: Art, Culture and Exchange across Medieval Saharan Africa .

Carlo Taviani is Associate Professor of Early Modern History at the Università degli Studi di Teramo and a fellow of the Royal Netherlands Institute in Rome. He is the author of The Making of the Modern Corporation: The Casa di San Giorgio and Its Legacy (1446–1720) .

books.title: Dream house (Dream city)
books.tagline: A dizzying, gripping journey through our world via appropriated and original text.
books.description:
There is a lion in a cage

I tell you to poke the lion through the cage

Dream house (Dream city) is the tour-de-force book-length poem and debut from rising star Elijah Jackson. A mosaic of original and appropriated texts, Dream house (Dream city) is urgent, riotous, and provoking, bringing a new and vital register to the poetic discourse. In relentless couplets, along with an afterword and index that deepen and complicate the text, Jackson careens in scope and tone: "The entire restaurant is surveilled/equally This mold will eat you." Taking its title from Walter Benjamin’s Arcades Project , and rooted in a close reading of it, the book’s roving eye pinballs from the quotidian to the philosophical, generating endless images and juxtapositions—a new way to look at the world.
books.bio: Elijah Jackson is a writer based in New York. Dream house (Dream city) is his debut collection. Previous work has been published by Second Factory , Fence , Flash Art , Annulet , and others.

books.title: I Tatti, the History of a House
books.subtitle: From Fortified Villa to locus amoenus
books.description: I Tatti, the History of a House traces the architectural evolution of Villa I Tatti in Florence from its early origins around the year 1000 through the 1930s, when Bernard and Mary Berenson redesigned the estate and transformed it into an epicenter for the promotion of Italian Renaissance art to the Anglophone world. This book captures a web of local and international intersecting stories that follow the villa’s medieval, Renaissance, and eighteenth-century life as a Florentine residence and explores its place in the ex-pat world of nineteenth-century Florence. The Berensons’ renovations are also documented, their creation of a rarefied environment of aesthetic debate and intellectual discovery not unlike those cultivated in Virginia and Leonard Woolf’s Bloomsbury circle or in the Steins’ rue de Fleurus. I Tatti is a history of a house, its life, and the people around it in the longue durée—a portrait of the city and Tuscan countryside that includes actors whose names are not celebrated in history, but whose lives recovered here offer a vivid image of changing habits and mores as well as attitudes to property and to the land that no history book records.
books.bio:
Francesca Carrara is an architect and architectural historian in Florence and Tuscany. She is the author and co-author of several books including Palazzo Peruzzi, Il Trebbio in Mugello (with R. Budini Gattai), and L’Abbazia di Vallombrosa .

Alina Payne is Paul E. Geier Director of Villa I Tatti, The Harvard Center for Italian Renaissance Studies and Alexander P. Misheff Professor of History of Art and Architecture at Harvard University. Most recently she published L’architecture parmi les arts and The Land Between Two Seas . She received the 2006 Max Planck and Alexander von Humboldt Prize in the Humanities and is a Fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a Fellow of the Society of Architectural Historians.

books.title: In Walking Distance
books.subtitle: How 5-Minute Neighborhoods Are Reinventing Downtown
books.tagline: How to prepare downtowns for a rapidly evolving future by designing them for people
books.description:
At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, America’s downtowns still envisioned a future for themselves embodied in ever-taller, ever-shinier, still more valuable office towers. That future is gone. The pandemic exposed a crisis two decades in the making, one marked by steadily rising office vacancy, creeping retail loss, and growing privilege. In Walking Distance reimagines what downtowns can and need to be, showing how some are already being transformed by introducing the vibrant mixed-use, walkable neighborhoods that are essential for downtowns to thrive as the hubs of the knowledge and innovation economies that our cities and regions need.

David Dixon begins by tracing the diminishing appeal of downtown to investors, workers, and visitors amid the plummeting demand for office and retail space and a growing need for housing that people can afford. He then describes how, by artfully tapping unprecedented housing demand, downtowns can lead their cities and regions into a new era of opportunity and inclusion through collaborative local leadership, zoning and regulatory frameworks grounded in community-based goals, public-private partnerships, and government policies that support rather than hinder local initiatives. Dixon explains why genuine efforts to prepare downtown for its future mean resisting the urge to pick up where the pre-pandemic downtown left off—and instead leveraging recovery to unleash reinvention.

Drawing on interviews with planning, downtown management, and design experts in cities across the United States and Canada, In Walking Distance presents a bold vision for the future in which downtown becomes a place where people can live, work, play, and find interactive community.
books.bio: David Dixon, FAIA, is the Urban Places Fellow at Stantec, a global, interdisciplinary firm focused on every aspect of community building. He is the coauthor of Urban Design for an Urban Century: Shaping More Livable, Equitable, and Resilient Cities and the coeditor of Suburban Remix: Creating the Next Generation of Urban Places (Island Press).

books.title: Journey to the East of France
books.tagline: On the limitations of literature to addressing the teenage experience of incest.
books.description:
“I had one last option: Make do. Which is to say: Abandon the person I was, accept becoming someone different. That was my last possibility. It lay at the bottom of my mind in case of failure. If the others didn’t work. And if there wasn’t any other escape. Accept not having a life, having a failed life, adapting to it. I would tell myself it’s not so serious. That was a final possibility. To continue to live if the other courses failed. It was not the solution I liked best. It was the solution of despair. But it wasn’t suicide. It wasn’t death. It implied a radical change of vision with respect to what I had imagined for my person and my future, but it wasn’t the end. It allowed me to wait.”

Since the 1990s, the French writer Christine Angot has written with provocative insistence about relationships surrounding, and disrupted by, incest. When she published her first book on the subject, Incest , in 1999, the audience was polarized and she quickly became the center of public controversy regarding discussions of sexual violence. In Journey to the East of France , the third of Angot’s books to be translated into English following Incest and then Impossible Love (2015), she returns to the place where her father imposed his first incestuous relationship on her. Angot writes about the site—a Strasbourg hotel—with haunting precision, recalling the rooms’ light sources, the color of the wallpaper, the hotel’s entrances and exits. The psychic suffocation and mental strain required to stay sane become apparent as she describes her experience at age thirteen. Angot writes, “To distort the reality—on one side, a total blackout, on the other, an excessive illumination—cost me a lot of effort. I had to ignore whole swaths of reality, cast a light on the positive points, pretend to have forgotten certain scenes, keep a level of pride afloat.” Journey to the East of France continues Angot’s project of encountering this disturbing subject again and again in writing. Each time she wrestles with limitations of literature as the form to address her experience. Beyond an account of trauma, her work meticulously describes the power structures that produce such sexual violence with an ever-frenzied rage.
books.bio: Christine Angot is one of the most provocative and controversial authors writing today in France. Born in 1958 in Châteauroux, Angot studied law at the University of Reims and began writing at the age of 25. Her literary works have received prizes including the Prix France Culture in 2005 (for Les Désaxés and Une partie du cœur ), the Prix Flore in 2006 (for Rendez-vous ) and the Prix Sade in 2012 (for Une semaine de vacances ), which she refused. In 2015 she won the Prix Décembre for her novel Un Amour impossible . Journey to the East of France won the Prix Médicis. In 2024, she directed her first film, Une famille .

praise.q: To read Journey to the East of France is to have an idea of what pain is, and what literature is.
praise.by: Elle

praise.q: An incredibly powerful text about silence, inaction, and tacit collaboration.
praise.by: Les Inrockuptibles

books.title: Make Your Home in This Luminous Dark
books.subtitle: Mysticism, Art, and the Path of Unknowing
books.tagline: A philosopher journeys back to the mystics to learn how to live with uncertainty in the twenty-first century
books.description:
How do we live when we don’t know what to believe, or who to believe, or how we could even know? In this deeply felt book, philosopher James K. A. Smith explores how radical uncertainty can be liberating, opening us to another way of being. The pain of his own profound uncertainty led Smith to a surprising source for modern consolation: the mystical experiences of St. Teresa of Ávila, St. John of the Cross, and the author of The Cloud of Unknowing . These mystics testify to a deeper truth beneath distraction, anxiety, and fear: love.

Drawing on ancient traditions of contemplation as well as on contemporary novels, poetry, film, and paintings, Smith speaks to the fundamental yearnings that persist in late modernity, including the philosophical quest for knowledge and certainty. He shows us how the gifts of the Christian contemplative tradition and the riches of creative works embody a liberating spirituality that recovers the fullness of being human.

In bringing a philosopher’s questions to the mystics, Smith brings a mystical heart back to philosophy.
books.bio: James K. A. Smith is professor of philosophy at Calvin University. He is the award-winning author of a numerous books, including You Are What You Love: The Spiritual Power of Habit and On the Road with Saint Augustine: A Real-World Spirituality for Restless Hearts . He lives in Grand Rapids, MI.

praise.q: Smith writes that, far from being spiritually vapid, [contemporary] art can lead viewers to a ‘contemplative posture that might make us open to the mystical.’ Abstract and experimental art, he argues, is innovative, meaningful, and conducive to the sort of habits that can bring people closer to God.
praise.by: Luis Parrales, The Atlantic

praise.q: Make Your Home speaks beautifully to the heart of what troubles us most today—fear, distraction, human suffering—and reminds us to embrace the luminous dark: an ancient, “generative” place of remembering where we can rest, be healed, and be guided by love.
praise.by: Sarah James, Sojourners

praise.q: Mines the lives of Christian mystics for wisdom on cultivating a spirituality rooted in love.
praise.by: Publishers Weekly

praise.q: A Most Anticipated Book of Spring 2026, Englewood Review of Books
A beautiful book of experience, the author’s own, written in such a way that many will be able to learn from what he has undergone.
praise.by: Jon M. Sweeney, Spirituality & Practice

praise.q: There’s something undeniably special happening in these pages. Smith’s book ultimately asks to be read in the spirit it praises: with the analytic mind quieted and our hearts attentive.
praise.by: Griffin Gooch, Front Porch Republic

praise.q: In this thoughtful and finely written book, James K. A. Smith brings together two fields that are rarely considered together: Christian mysticism and contemporary art, literature, and film. Make Your Home in This Luminous Dark articulates the author’s struggle to make sense of his life as a philosopher and practising Christian—though ultimately as a suffering, confused human being. Drawing on a wide range of source materials, Smith skillfully weaves these diverse threads into a passionate and engaging narrative.
praise.by: Stephen Batchelor, author of Buddha, Socrates and Us: Ethical Living in Uncertain Times
praise.cred: author of Buddha, Socrates and Us: Ethical Living in Uncertain Times

praise.q: As a philosopher whose business is to know, James K. A. Smith invites us into a different way of being—the experience of unknowing. In Make Your Home in This Luminous Dark , Smith shares his unknowable childhood experience of abandonment by his father, and his gentle book teaches liberation found in the down-to-earth contemplative wisdom of the medieval masterpiece The Cloud of Unknowing and of many other sages. May we join Smith in being vulnerable, open, beloved by God, and filled with wonder and loving.”—Carmen Acevedo Butcher, poet, core faculty member at Center for Action and Contemplation, and award-winning translator of The Cloud of Unknowing

We long for clarity and for comfort, and many books promise it to us. They cannot deliver. James K. A. Smith invites us to embrace mystery, darkness, solitude, and silence, and with all that the hope of true peace.
praise.by: Zena Hitz, author of Lost In Thought: The Hidden Pleasures of an Intellectual Life
praise.cred: author of Lost In Thought: The Hidden Pleasures of an Intellectual Life

praise.q: This is a deeply moving and invaluable book. Smith is known for his intellectual clarity and sound reasoning, but this book also exhibits heartfelt honesty, vulnerability, and courage. . . . It transforms and transfigures philosophy. Smith takes us into the realm of mysticism and darkness to be met with the Real. As an artist, I truly appreciated his path toward the ‘gift of the unknown.’
praise.by: Makoto Fujimura, author of Art Is: A Journey into the Light
praise.cred: author of Art Is: A Journey into the Light

books.title: Making the World Their Own
books.subtitle: A History of Americans Living Abroad
books.tagline: A panoramic, two-hundred-year history of the American overseas experience and how it redefined the United States and its place in the world
books.description:
American citizens have lived abroad for a host of reasons—to spread their religion, to flee persecution, to make money, or simply to seek new experiences. Making the World Their Own tells the stories of these individuals, describing what motivated them to go abroad, the risks they faced, and the complicated relationship they shared with their government back home.

Taking readers from the nineteenth century to today, Sarah Snyder reconstructs the richly varied worlds of Americans living abroad, from missionaries and educators to journalists, entrepreneurs, artists, and adventurers. She shows how the imperial footprint of American schools, businesses, and clubs predated the formal expansion of America’s influence beyond its borders and has endured as an element of the country’s soft power. Yet Snyder also documents how overseas citizens complicated U.S. diplomacy when they were taken hostage, murdered, imprisoned, or caused embarrassment to the government. We meet Black Americans who moved to Liberia as part of the American Colonization Society; citizens who went to Paris, Moscow, and Shanghai in search of utopia; dissidents who fled anticommunism and racial discrimination; and many others.

Drawing on original archival research in seven countries, Making the World Their Own casts the history of U.S. foreign relations in an entirely new light, revealing the outsized role of ordinary citizens in extending the influence of the United States around the globe.
books.bio: Sarah B. Snyder is a professor in the School of International Service at American University and president of the Society for Historians of American Foreign Relations. She is the author of From Selma to Moscow: How Human Rights Activists Transformed U.S. Foreign Policy and Human Rights Activism and the End of the Cold War: A Transnational History of the Helsinki Network .

books.title: Pairs 07
books.authors: Edited by Robin Albrecht, James Blue, Tyler White, and Cayden Zayne Abu-Arja
books.description:
Pairs is a journal of conversations edited by students at the Harvard Graduate School of Design. Each issue centers on a series of interviews that unfold around two pairings: first that of interviewer/interviewee and second, the pairing of an interviewee with an object. The journal does not have a theme, but instead organizes a diversity of threads and concerns relevant to our moment in the design disciplines: covering architecture, landscape architecture, and urban design and planning. The conversations are in turn not comprehensive accounts but open-ended exchanges, eliciting often candid and provisional ideas in progress.

Pairs 07 features conversations with Paola Antonelli, Iwan Baan, Hélène Binet, Petra Blaisse, Meriem Chabani, Michael Abel Deng and Nile Greenberg, Sonja Dümpelmann, Pezo von Ellrichshausen, Daisuke Hattori and Saori Hattori, Abidin Kusno, James Langdon, Jenelle Parker, Becky Webster, and Emmett Zeifman.
books.bio:
Robin Albrecht holds a Master of Architecture from the Harvard Graduate School of Design.

James Blue is a Masters student in Design Studies at the Harvard Graduate School of Design.

Tyler White holds a dual Master of Urban Planning and Master in Design Studies from the Harvard Graduate School of Design.

Cayden Zayne Abu-Arja is a dual Masters student in Architecture and Urban Planning at the Harvard Graduate School of Design.

books.title: Platforms
books.tagline: What lies underneath digital platforms—their invisible architecture and governance that determine everything visible.
books.description:
Every time you unlock your phone, stream a show, or start your car, you’re entering a world shaped by thousands of engineering decisions you’ll never see. Most platform conversations fixate on their visible canopy—business models, user experience, competitive strategy—the “leaves,” in a sense. Platforms by Amrit Tiwana excavates their roots.

The book begins with a simple DNA test that separates authentic from faux platforms, then traces the forces turning tractors, pacemakers, and elevators into platforms. Using the platform trinity, the author explores principles behind why platforms behave so differently, why superior technology doesn’t always win, and why—unlike products that reach a final form—platforms never stop evolving.

From there the book explains platforms’ two hidden root systems: The first system, architecture, shows how Lego-like “modular” design, frozen interfaces, and prefab building blocks let thousands of outsiders contribute pieces that snap into colossal systems. The second system, governance, describes where architecture confronts human behavior. Elegant architecture flails with poor governance, so both demand discipline.
books.bio: Amrit Tiwana is Fuqua Distinguished Professor of Internet Strategy at the University of Georgia.
subjects: The MIT Press Essential Knowledge series

books.title: Provincializing Europe
books.subtitle: Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference
books.tagline: A foundational work that puts Western understandings of history into conversation with postcolonial perspectives
books.description: Can European thought be dislodged from the center of the practice of history in a non-European place? What problems arise when we translate cultural practices into the categories of social science? In this landmark book, Dipesh Chakrabarty examines how postcolonial thinking impacts on the social sciences. Through a series of linked essays, he explores the problems of thought that present themselves when we think of a place such as India through the categories of modern European social science and history. Now with a new preface by the author, Provincializing Europe globalizes European thought by exploring how it may be renewed both for and from the margins.
books.bio: Dipesh Chakrabarty is the Lawrence A. Kimpton Distinguished Service Professor of History at the University of Chicago. His books include The Climate of History in a Planetary Age and Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (Princeton).

praise.q: Chakrabarty's work gives us a richer, more penetrating language to deal with modernity and the colonial encounter. . . . It is the ambiguity of Chakabarty's own position as both a critic and archivist of modernity that gives his study its poetic undertow and its intelligent irresponsibility.
praise.by: Amit Chaudhuri, London Review of Books

praise.q: The great value of this book lies in Chakrabarty's exceptional ability to bring to light what constantly gets glossed over and forgotten when we can only speak the standard languages of the academy. To do this requires the kind of bilingual consciousness which can bring into illuminating relation Adam Smith and Tagore. Chakrabarty makes you regret that so few are capable of doing this with a high degree of eloquence and insight.
praise.by: Charles Taylor, IWM Newsletter

praise.q: This masterful re-examination of rationality, universality, and difference in the postcolonial world should prove inspiring for serious historians of all lands.
praise.by: Alice Ballard, Theory and Society

praise.q: The idea of provincializing Europe has been around for some time, but mostly as an insight waiting for elaboration. In this book, Dipesh Chakrabarty develops the idea into a project informed massively by fact and brilliantly by theory. A work of exemplary scholarship, it is a call to raise the level of current debates about modernity and the colonial experience and reexamine our approach to histories and cultures on both sides of the colonial divide. A formidable challenge.
praise.by: Ranajit Guha

praise.q: Chakrabarty offers a fundamental rethinking of the most important and misunderstood of all historical categories—time itself. Never facile, always willing to confront the most intractable dilemmas, Chakrabarty forces us to reconsider our deepest historicizing impulses. His work is must reading for anyone with an interest in the future of historical studies.
praise.by: Lynn Hunt, University of California, Los Angeles

books.title: Republic and Empire
books.subtitle: Crisis, Revolution, and America's Early Independence
books.authors: Trevor Burnard and Andrew Jackson O'Shaughnessy
books.tagline: A fresh look at the American Revolution as a major global event
books.description:
At the time of the American Revolution (1765–83), the British Empire had colonies in India, Africa, the Caribbean, the Pacific, Canada, Ireland, and Gibraltar. The thirteen rebellious American colonies accounted for half of the total number of provinces in the British world in 1776. What of the loyal half? Why did some of Britain’s subjects feel so aggrieved that they wanted to establish a new system of government, while others did not rebel? In this authoritative history, Trevor Burnard and Andrew Jackson O’Shaughnessy show that understanding the long-term causes of the American Revolution requires a global view.

As much as it was an event in the history of the United States, the American Revolution was an imperial event produced by the upheavals of managing a far-flung set of imperial possessions during a turbulent period of reform. By looking beyond the familiar borders of the Revolution and considering colonies that did not rebel—Quebec, Nova Scotia, Bermuda, India, the British Caribbean, Senegal, and Ireland—Burnard and O’Shaughnessy go beyond the republican, liberal, and democratic aspects of the emerging American nation, providing a broader history that transcends what we think we know about the Revolution.
books.bio: Trevor Burnard (1960–2024) was Wilberforce Professor of Slavery and Emancipation at the University of Hull and director of the Wilberforce Institute. He was the author of numerous books on Caribbean plantation history and imperial history and served as editor of the Oxford Bibliography Online in Atlantic History. Andrew Jackson O’Shaughnessy is professor of history at the University of Virginia. His books include An Empire Divided: The American Revolution and the British Caribbean and the prizewinning The Men Who Lost America: British Leadership, the American Revolution, and the Fate of the Empire .

praise.q: Republic and Empire shows how a global perspective can yield fresh insight even on a topic as well-trodden as the American Revolution.
praise.by: New Criterion

praise.q: Here is proof of one undeniable good achieved by the revolution: when it came to ‘the greatest curse that ever has afflicted the human race,’ it reawakened not only the American but the world’s conscience. Republic and Empire , in its unflinching way, carries on that tradition.
praise.by: Edward Short, Literary Review

praise.q: An adroit shaping of a complex period.”—Jeremy Black, NYMAS Review
This book will bring general readers up to speed with current scholarship on the Age of Empires.
praise.by: David Armitage, HistoryExtra Magazine

praise.q: In this impressive distillation of a wide range of imperial scholarship, the authors present a compelling case for recognizing both the roots and the course of the American Revolution as profoundly influenced by events in the wider British Empire following its expansion in and immediately after the Seven Years’ War.
praise.by: Stephen Conway, University College London

praise.q: The American Revolution was at once a civil war, a war of colonial liberation, and an imperial crisis. Viewing the conflict through empire’s eyes, O’Shaughnessy and Burnard reveal hidden connections and overlooked legacies that shaped the world of 1776 and continue to ramify around the globe.
praise.by: Jane Kamensky, Monticello

praise.q: Timely, critically important contribution to our understanding of the American nation’s origins in a constitutional crisis and civil war that led half of Britain’s American colonies to declare independence. Balancing a welcome emphasis on the uncertain progress of the war with convincing accounts of why so many other colonies remained loyal, Burnard and O’Shaughnessy illuminate the contingent contexts that shaped individual and collective decisions in a revolutionary age.
praise.by: Peter S. Onuf, University of Virginia

praise.q: A masterful reappraisal of the American Revolution by two preeminent historians. Andrew O’Shaughnessy and the late Trevor Burnard brilliantly capture the duality at the heart of America’s founding: 1776 was both the beginning of a protracted imperial civil war and the birth of a democratic republic.”—Christa Dierksheide, author of Beyond Jefferson: The Hemingses, the Randolphs, and the Making of Nineteenth-Century America

books.title: Siegelands
books.subtitle: Early Modern Warfare and the Monumental Print
books.tagline: The first in-depth study of siege prints, a monumental form of art depicting the vast scale of early modern warfare
books.description:
In the first half of the sixteenth century, the technologies of artillery warfare and large-format printmaking converged to give rise to a new type of art. Siegelands examines an extraordinary series of enormous woodcuts created in the Holy Roman Empire at a time when political turmoil and religious strife tore apart northern Europe.

As the distance between enemies became the defining condition of war, artists confronted the challenge of representing a slow form of violence that was singularly unheroic. Sieges were vast gatherings of people, mobile camps on the scale of temporary cities that aimed to conquer an enemy through attrition rather than through combat. The makers of monumental siege prints confronted these realities by pushing the limits of their medium.

With superb illustrations, many published here for the first time, Siegelands recovers a neglected genre of art that arose at a pivotal moment in European history. Carolyn Yerkes describes the complicated narratives of strategy, attack, settlement, and stalemate embedded in the context of landscape and urban architecture. These works on paper—designed to rival the period’s grandest achievements in tapestry, fresco painting, and relief sculpture—were created from multiple sheets to form expansive wall-sized compositions, many of which survive only in single impressions. With the ambition of history painting, the prints brought sophisticated political arguments about the stakes of war to the society that war created.
books.bio: Carolyn Yerkes is associate professor of early modern architecture at Princeton University. Her books include Drawing after Architecture: Renaissance Architectural Drawings and Their Reception and, with Heather Hyde Minor, Piranesi Unbound (Princeton).

books.title: The Cornell Lab of Ornithology Handbook of Bird Biology
books.subtitle: Fourth Edition
books.authors: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Irby J. Lovette, Jennifer Walsh
books.tagline: A fully revised fourth edition of the acclaimed ornithology textbook from the Cornell Lab of Ornithology
books.description:
This highly anticipated fourth edition of The Cornell Lab of Ornithology Handbook of Bird Biology is an essential resource for anyone interested in learning more about birds, from backyard birders to students of ornithology. With contributions by a team of experts from around the world, it covers all aspects of avian diversity, evolution, behavior, ecology, physiology, and conservation. A tool for lifelong learning about birds, this comprehensive and accessible handbook is the companion volume to the Cornell Lab’s popular distance learning course in bird biology, a self-paced online offering that has enabled tens of thousands to broaden their knowledge about all things avian.

Features a new chapter on approaches and methods for birding and ornithological research

Stunningly illustrated with hundreds of full-color images

Discusses feathers and plumages, avian flight, anatomy, mating and breeding, vocalization, migration, and much more

Draws on examples from every corner of the globe, distilling the many fascinating scientific discoveries about birds and their biology

Ideal for birders and students as well as educators, ecologists, conservationists, and resource managers

Includes an extensive glossary and index, a list of all common and scientific names mentioned in the text, and a complete reference section
books.bio: Irby J. Lovette is the Fuller Professor of Ornithology at Cornell University. Jennifer Walsh is a Senior Research Associate at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology.

books.title: The Knowledge of the Game Master
books.subtitle: Imagination, Performance, and the Craft of Guiding Tabletop Role-Playing Games
books.tagline: A deep dive into the development of game mastering, or GMing, as a practice, and why it matters.
books.description:
In a tabletop role-playing game, the game master, or GM, is generally understood to be the person who organizes and manages the game, plays the role of all nonplayer characters, and is responsible for the overall experience of the players at the table.
