But how does one learn how to GM? And when one has mastered the art of the game master, what exactly does one know how to do?

In The Knowledge of the Game Master , William White answers these questions and more, connecting the worlds of game studies scholars, game designers, and players of tabletop role-playing games to explore GMing as a communication practice. He shows how it takes shape as an expression of ideas about imagination and performance, and he examines the circulation of those ideas among various communities of play.

Using a theoretical apparatus derived from Algirdas Greimas, Erving Goffman, and Marshall McLuhan, White offers a media-ecological microhistory of GMing in popular culture and fan discourse, provides a systematic overview of contemporary GM advice, and draws examples from actual play to show the GM’s communicative roles in action. The book provides a detailed description of the GM workshop facilitated by the author and concludes with a role-playing game that deconstructs the role of the GM by making use of the framework developed over the course of the book.
books.bio: William J. White is Professor of Communication Arts & Sciences at Penn State Altoona. He is the author of Tabletop RPG Design in Theory and Practice at the Forge, 2001–2012 and coeditor of Immersive Gameplay as well as a contributor to Analog Game Studies, International Journal of Role-Playing, and The Japanese Journal of Analog Role-Playing Game Studies.

books.title: The Migrant's Jail
books.subtitle: An American History of Mass Incarceration
books.tagline: A New Yorker Best Book We’ve Read This Year Winner of the Frederick Jackson Turner Award and the Ellis W. Hawley Prize, Organization of American Historians A century-long history of immigrant incarceration in the United States
books.description:
Today, U.S. Immigration & Customs Enforcement (ICE) detains an average of 37,000 migrants each night. To do so, they rely on, and pay for, the use of hundreds of local jails. But this is nothing new: the federal government has been detaining migrants in city and county jails for more than 100 years. In The Migrant's Jail , Brianna Nofil examines how a century of political, ideological, and economic exchange between the U.S. immigration bureaucracy and the criminal justice system gave rise to the world’s largest system of migrant incarceration. Migrant detention is not simply an outgrowth of mass incarceration; rather, it has propelled carceral state–building and fostered intergovernmental policing efforts since the turn of the twentieth century.

From the incarceration of Chinese migrants in New York in the 1900s and 1910s to the jailing of Caribbean refugees in Gulf South lockups of the 1980s and 1990s, federal immigration authorities provided communities with a cash windfall that they used to cut taxes, reward local officials, and build bigger jails—which they then had incentive to fill. Trapped in America’s patchwork detention networks, migrants turned to courts, embassies, and the media to challenge the cruel paradox of “administrative imprisonment.” Drawing on immigration records, affidavits, protest letters, and a variety of local sources, Nofil excavates the web of political negotiations, financial deals, and legal precedents that allows the United States to incarcerate migrants with little accountability and devastating consequences.
books.bio: Brianna Nofil is associate professor of history at William & Mary.

praise.q: Nofil’s book, dense with archival evidence, documents how the federal government has long warehoused immigrants in local jails, and, in so doing, evaded oversight and responsibility for horrific, even deadly, conditions.
praise.by: The New Yorker

praise.q: There is perhaps no better place to start in tracing the roots of this moment than The Migrant’s Jail , historian Brianna Nofil’s magisterial study of the mutual development of U.S. penal and immigration policy over more than a century. . . . In moving detail, Nofil brings to life the voices of hungry, sick, sweltering, and shivering migrants caught up in the immigration system through the decades, many of whom were driven to suicide or its brink while languishing in detention.
praise.by: Marie Gottschalk, Boston Review

praise.q: A revealing, potent history of mass incarceration and deportation, told through the stories of migrants in American jails.
praise.by: Martin Chilton, The Independent

praise.q: Compelling. . . . An insightful and alarming history of the nation’s failures in detaining and deporting migrants.
praise.by: Kirkus

praise.q: Essential reading. . . . This is history at its best: it aids our understanding. Brianna Nofil’s book offers original scholarship informed by deep and wide-ranging research. It is an engrossing read and essential to understanding our world today.
praise.by: Marilyn Lake, Australian Book Review

praise.q: Groundbreaking and deeply researched. . . . required reading.
praise.by: Stephane Hinnershitz, Journal of American History

praise.q: Illuminating and timely. . . . despite its expansiveness, the book is never superficial in its treatment. . . . An indispensable addition to scholarship on immigrant detention, providing a nuanced and poignantly rendered account of immigrant detention as a key component of the carceral boom in twentieth century America.
praise.by: Emily Pope-Obeda, American Historical Review

praise.q: In The Migrant’s Jail , Brianna Nofil offers a timely and detailed examination of the relationship between federal immigration officials and state and local law enforcement. Using immigration as a lens, she shows how the federal response to incoming migrants over the span of a century helped create the massive carceral system the United States has today.
praise.by: Elisabeth Marsh, Journal of American Ethnic History

praise.q: Part of what makes Nofil’s work so readable and compelling is her eye for individual stories. . . . Nofil has written a wide-ranging, important history of migrant detention that has much to contribute to our understanding of federal immigration policy and the carceral state. . . . As the next chapter in this history unfolds, Nofil’s clear-eyed picture of migrant detention’s local dimensions can be a guide, showing us where to look and reminding us that we can act and organize locally to resist this vast and powerful system.
praise.by: Carly Goodman, Diplomatic History

books.series: Politics and Society in Modern America

books.title: The Network of Life
books.subtitle: A New View of Evolution
books.tagline: Why evolution is like a network, not a family tree—and why it matters for understanding the health of all living things
books.description:
In The Network of Life , David Mindell explains why the conventional narrative of evolution needs to evolve. Ever since Darwin, evolution has largely been thought to work like a family tree in which species are related through a series of branching events. But, today, a growing knowledge of the ways species share genetic materials in a process known as horizontal evolution has revealed that evolution is actually a network of shared genealogy in which species are more interconnected than previously thought. In this book, Mindell presents this new narrative of life’s evolution and its profound implications for all life on Earth.

The Network of Life describes the drivers of horizontal evolution—interbreeding and genetic recombination, the merger of species, horizontal gene transfer, and coevolution. The network view of evolution that emerges supports a new symbiotic theory of health, which holds that the future health of humans, other species, and our shared environments depends on evolution and adaptation across life’s network.

Difficult times lie ahead for many of Earth’s species as climates and habitats transform. At the same time, new and altered life-forms are arising and spreading in association with human activities. We are also learning to reshape and create life by mimicking the mechanisms of horizontal evolution, and we are coevolving with technology as we enhance our bodies, brains, and life spans. The Network of Life shows why and how increasing our knowledge of horizontal evolution can provide critical lessons as we navigate our looming challenges.
books.bio: David P. Mindell is a senior researcher at the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology at the University of California, Berkeley. He is the author of The Evolving World: Evolution in Everyday Life , which won the Independent Publisher Book Awards Gold Medal in Science, and the coeditor of The Theory of Evolution . He is a former professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Michigan, director of the UM Museum of Zoology, and dean of science at the California Academy of Sciences.

praise.q: Mindell is an excellent guide to this complex picture. . . . [ The Network of Life ] offers good, solid science and a clear illustration of an emerging perspective that is beginning to pay dividends in our understanding of evolution.
praise.by: David P. Barash, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: Eye-opening analysis. . . . The heady ideas will change how readers understand some of biology’s most fundamental concepts.
praise.by: Publishers Weekly

praise.q: A perspective-shifting reconceptualization of evolution.
praise.by: Wade Lee-Smith, Library Journal

praise.q: There are many rewards to reading the book. . . . The Network of Life is engaging and contains exciting text.
praise.by: Arturo Becerra, Quarterly Review of Biology

praise.q: I am quite sure that Darwin, were he alive today, would embrace this added view of evolution and would be foremost in its supporters. . . . The book is beautifully written and thought-provoking in myriad ways.
praise.by: David Gascoigne, Travels with Birds

praise.q: There are a number of books on networks in the biological and computer sciences, but none that explore the horizontal connections that Mindell finds so important. A valuable book.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: An important book."—David Lorimer, Paradigm Explorer

Mindell’s wide-ranging inquiry into the network of life is as mind-expanding as it is bold. Mindell does nothing less than trace the outlines of a new view of life and the implications of humanity’s coexistence with nature, technology, and an ever-changing planet. From bacteria to birds, from Aristotle to Emily Dickinson (and of course Darwin), the breadth of scholarship and integration of emerging concepts is breathtaking.
praise.by: Scott V. Edwards, Harvard University

praise.q: In this excellent book, David Mindell presents a new picture of evolution. He compellingly argues that decentralization brought about by horizontal evolution is indispensable for biological innovation. Highly recommended for anyone interested in quickly grasping the recent paradigm shift in evolutionary biology.
praise.by: Eugene Koonin, National Institutes of Health

books.title: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson, Volume 50
books.subtitle: 11 July to 30 November 1806
books.tagline: A definitive scholarly edition of the correspondence and papers of Thomas Jefferson
books.description: This volume covers Jefferson’s residence in Virginia in the summer of 1806 and an intense period of work after he returns to the capital in the fall. The summer is marked by a prolonged lack of rainfall in Virginia and other parts of the country. Jefferson goes home to Monticello in July, and in August makes a brief trip to Bedford County to arrange for the shipment to market of tobacco from his Poplar Forest plantation. At Monticello, Edmund Bacon takes on the position of overseer. Jefferson’s detailed instructions for Bacon outline work to be completed and include information about the enslaved laborers. James and Dolley Madison and Henry and Dorcas Dearborn visit in September. Back in Washington in October, Jefferson argues with Benjamin Henry Latrobe about the installation of skylights in the roof of the Capitol and receives Meriwether Lewis’s letter announcing that his expedition safely reached the Pacific and has returned to St. Louis. Reports from the lower Mississippi Valley indicate that friction in the Orleans Territory boundary zone could tip Spain and the United States into war. Unverified intelligence warns that Aaron Burr may be planning to raise an armed force of several thousand volunteers for an unknown purpose. In addition, questions have been raised about the loyalty of General James Wilkinson. Jefferson consults with the cabinet five times in October and November. After a confidential dispatch from Wilkinson alleges that Burr’s objective is Vera Cruz, Jefferson issues a proclamation prohibiting expeditions “against the dominions of Spain.”
books.bio: Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826), one of America’s most important Founding Fathers, was the third president of the United States, the founder of the University of Virginia, the principal author of the Declaration of Independence, and the author of Notes on the State of Virginia . James P. McClure, a senior research historian at Princeton University, is general editor of The Papers of Thomas Jefferson.

books.title: Thinking Organizationally
books.subtitle: Seven Perspectives on How Organizations Work
books.tagline: An integrative guide to understanding how organizations succeed, fail, change, and endure.
books.description:
Thinking Organizationally provides an accessible guide to understanding the organizations we work in, encounter, and depend on in everyday life. Drawing on decades of scholarship across sociology, psychology, management, and organizational studies, Jose Eos Trinidad introduces a new framework to organize major theories into seven perspectives, captured by the acronym SCRIPTS: structure, culture, relations, institutions, professions, transformation, and social conflict.

Each chapter introduces key concepts, surprising findings, and practical examples to help readers understand why organizations succeed or fail, how they change, and why they produce unintended consequences. Whether you are a leader, professional, student, or researcher, the book provides needed tools to interpret the complexities of organizational life.

With examples ranging from Silicon Valley tech companies to the Italian mafia, from Chicago bankers to low-wage workers in developing countries, the book shows how different perspectives illuminate real-world organizational challenges. The result is a new way of seeing organizations and a deeper understanding of how they shape the world we live in.
books.bio: Jose Eos Trinidad teaches organizational theory at the University of California, Berkeley. His research has been published in various outlets like the American Sociological Review, Social Science & Medicine, and Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis.

books.title: Wildlife Photography Field Notes
books.subtitle: A Pocket Guide to Camera Settings and Tips
books.tagline: A compact, field-friendly guide to wildlife photography that slips easily into your pocket or camera bag
books.description:
Wildlife Photography Field Notes is a practical guide designed for photographers who want quick, clear answers while out in the field. Full of invaluable tips from one of today’s leading wildlife photographers, this easy-to-use reference can be consulted in seconds when faced with changing light, fast-moving subjects, or unfamiliar camera settings. Whether photographing birds in flight, mammals at dawn or insects at close range, users can quickly find the information they need without having to search through lengthy explanations. Practical, portable, and straightforward, this field manual is an indispensable companion for any outing with a camera.

Distils years of practical experience into concise, accessible guidance

Features high-quality photos that demonstrate key techniques and concepts along with clear diagrams and easy-to-read tables that summarise essential settings and recommendations

Covers camera setup, exposure, autofocus, shutter speeds, aperture choices, ISO settings, metering, composition, and fieldcraft

Organised for rapid access, with colour-coded page markers directing readers to key topics

The brand-neutral advice is applicable to all major camera systems, making it equally useful to users of Canon, Nikon, Sony, OM System, Fujifilm, Panasonic, and other camera brands

Designed for beginners and experienced photographers alike, providing a reliable source of information when it is needed most
books.bio: David Tipling is one of the world’s most widely published wildlife photographers, renowned for his breathtaking images and a career spanning more than three decades. A recipient of major international awards whose work has been exhibited in venues around the world, he is the author and photographer behind numerous acclaimed books, including Britain’s Birds (Princeton WILD Guides ), Birds & People , and Penguins: Close Encounters .

books.title: Windows into a World
books.subtitle: The Collection of the Yale Center for British Art
books.tagline: Extraordinary artworks from the most important collection of British art outside the United Kingdom.
books.description:
This remarkable book traces the development of British art from the fifteenth century to the present through the world-renowned collection of the Yale Center for British Art. The volume features over two hundred works that revolutionized British art and changed the course of creative practices around the globe. Key artists include William Blake, John Constable, Barbara Hepworth, Gwen John, Yinka Shonibare, and J. M. W. Turner. Richly illustrated and exquisitely produced, this publication will delight and inform anyone interested in British culture and history––and excite everyone who appreciates the power of great works of art.

Published by the Yale Center for British Art/Distributed by Yale University Press
books.bio: Martina Droth is the Paul Mellon Director of the Yale Center for British Art.

books.title: Women Who Dare
books.subtitle: A New History of Greenland Exploration
books.tagline: A riveting, multifaceted history of women’s exploration of Greenland and a stirring portrait of a nation contending with the climate crisis and the legacy of colonialism
books.description:
Arctic exploration is dominated by the myth of the valiant male hero, yet this mythmaking leaves us with a skewed sense of history and a limited understanding of the nature of exploration itself. Women Who Dare offers an entirely new perspective, recounting the experiences of women who have played vital roles in Greenland exploration, from guides and translators to ethnographers, botanists, photographers, artists, scientists, and activists.

Joanna Kafarowski introduces readers to the trailblazing Indigenous and non-Indigenous women who have been written out of polar history, tracing the connections between past women explorers and contemporary women who may not even think of themselves as explorers. We meet such figures as Tookoolito, who worked alongside Charles Francis Hall on the 1871 Polaris Expedition; Arnarulunnguaq, who was an active member of Knud Rasmussen’s Fifth Thule Expedition of the 1920s; filmmaker and botanist Isobel Wylie Hutchison; and geographer Louise Arner Boyd, who led four expeditions to Greenland in the 1930s. Today, Greenland is a harbinger of global climate change. Kafarowski tells the stories of women who are redefining exploration in the face of this crisis, such as paleoclimatologist Dorthe Dahl-Jensen, artist Pia Arke, activist-turned-politician Mariane Paviasen Jensen, and dog sledder Ane Sofie Lauritzen.

Women Who Dare reveals what can be learned about a land and its people by asking what constitutes exploration and who can be an explorer, showing how women are rewriting the past and helping us meet the formidable environmental challenges ahead.
books.bio: Joanna Kafarowski, PhD, is an independent scholar, geographer, and writer. She is the author of Antarctic Pioneer: The Trailblazing Life of Jackie Ronne and The Polar Adventures of a Rich American Dame: A Life of Louise Arner Boyd and the editor of Gender, Culture, and Northern Fisheries .

books.title: The Green and the Red
books.subtitle: The Early Years of the Loeb Classical Library (1911-1939)
books.description:
The Green and the Red provides a meticulously researched, captivating history of the formative years of the Loeb Classical Library (LCL), the landmark publishing series that revolutionized our engagement with antiquity. For over a century, these iconic green and red volumes have served as the bridge between modern readers and the ancient world. By presenting the original texts of Greek and Latin classics alongside facing-page English translations, the series democratized access to well-known and lesser-known voices of the past.

This volume traces the LCL’s complex evolution from its start to the dawn of the Second World War. Based on the examination of previously untapped archival materials, including private correspondence and unpublished documents, The Green and the Red uncovers the collective efforts of eminent scholars, enthusiasts, and publishers collaborated to make ancient literature available to academics and the general public alike.

The LCL’s early decades were far from a straightforward success story, defined by trans-Atlantic social tensions, negotiations with rival publishers, and logistical hurdles brought on by global crises such as the First World War and the Great Depression. However, bolstered by the philanthropic patronage of James Loeb and later secured by an institutional transfer to Harvard University in the 1930s, the pioneering project turned into a monumental achievement in the humanities. This book offers fascinating, behind-the-scenes insights into the project's editorial struggles—from defining the classical canon and navigating literary censorship, to balancing scholarly rigor with accessible translations.

The Green and the Red is an essential, enlightening read for classicists, bibliophiles, historians, and anyone fascinated by ancient studies.
books.bio: Mirte Liebregts is a classicist and cultural historian, as well as an author and editor committed to making the history of scholarship and ancient knowledge accessible to modern audiences.

books.title: A Field Guide to Social Media
books.subtitle: Exploring the Pluriverse
books.authors: Chand Rajendra-Nicolucci, Ethan Zuckerman, Gregory Asmolov, Elham Azad, Samuel Barros, Viktor Chagas, Casey Fiesler, Fiammetta Ghedini, Idayat Hassan, Dal Yong Jin, An Xiao Mina, Joyojeet Pal, Tim Raats, Michael Sugarman, Karin van Es and Xiaowei R. Wang
books.tagline: A lively and comprehensive deep dive into the diverse world of social media, going well beyond the usual platforms that dominate our online landscape. A beautiful volume with one-of-a-kind illustrations, inspired by field guides for birds.
books.description:
A beautiful volume with one-of-a-kind illustrations, inspired by field guides for birds.

A Field Guide to Social Media is an approachable introduction to social media written by leading scholars in the field. Chand Rajendra-Nicolucci and Ethan Zuckerman, along with several coauthors, argue that social media is, and should be seen as, a pluriverse—“a world where many worlds fit.” It encompasses everything from neighborhood forums to extremist message boards, from encrypted chat apps to professional networks, and from question-and-answer sites to algorithmically-driven video sharing platforms.

The authors go well beyond Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, and TikTok to show that social media can and does represent many different values and business models, offer many different affordances, and serve many different audiences, from Brazil to Nigeria to Russia and China and more.

This book looks across different platforms and issues—including algorithms, child abuse, free speech, content moderation, memes, surveillance, and more—to offer a comprehensive overview of the space that lends itself to repeated use in different contexts, from classrooms to startups to policymaking. And finally, it offers an international perspective rarely found in contemporary discussions of social media.
books.bio:
Chand Rajendra-Nicolucci (Author)

Chand Rajendra-Nicolucci is a law student at the University of Chicago Law School. He previously held fellowships with the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University and the Initiative for Digital Public Infrastructure at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

Ethan Zuckerman (Author)

Ethan Zuckerman is Associate Professor of Public Policy, Information, and Communication at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst and Director of the Initiative for Digital Public Infrastructure. He is the author of Mistrust and Rewire . Previously, he directed the Center for Civic Media at MIT and taught at the MIT Media Lab.

Dal Yong Jin (Author)

books.title: Arachne's Threads
books.subtitle: Why the Greeks Told Myths—and Why They Endure
books.tagline: From a leading expert, a fascinating introduction to ancient Greek myths and why we can’t stop retelling them in new ways
books.description:
Did the ancient Greeks really believe in their myths? Arachne’s Threads addresses this and other questions as it explores why the Greeks created myths and why we still love them more than two millennia later. Sarah Iles Johnston, one of the world’s leading experts on Greek mythology, offers an engrossing and provocative account of Greek myths and their capacity to convey ideas, in antiquity as well as now.

Although Greek myths may seem eternal and unchanging, Arachne’s Threads demonstrates that it is in fact their striking malleability that ensures their continuing relevance: the Persephone we meet in today’s novels and comics is decidedly different from the one the Greeks knew. Along the way, the book discusses the important cultural work that Greek myths did by considering how they helped to build belief in the gods’ existence, why those gods were so often portrayed as treating humans badly, and how the Greeks tweaked cross-cultural stories such as that of the Great Flood. It challenges some popular misunderstandings of myths, narrates surprising versions of familiar tales, traces the changing stories of Arachne and Icarus across the centuries, and considers contemporary reinterpretations of myths. The book ends with a close look at how the Odyssey works , arguing that Odysseus creates his own myth and emphasizing the enigmatic nature of his wife, Penelope, who has her own tales to tell.

Enlightening and entertaining, Arachne’s Threads will deepen your understanding and appreciation of the enchanting stories and characters of Greek mythology.
books.bio: Sarah Iles Johnston is the College of Arts and Sciences Distinguished Professor of Religion in the Departments of Classics and Comparative Studies at The Ohio State University, where she teaches courses on ancient Greek mythology and religion. Her books include Gods and Mortals: Ancient Greek Myths for Modern Readers (Princeton), which retells 140 myths.

books.title: Are We Well?
books.subtitle: The Untold Story of Psychiatry's Construction, Critiques, and Care
books.authors: Derek Bolton and Mohammed Abouelleil Rashed
books.tagline: How the new mental health aware world—puzzling, alarming, and exasperating—has been constructed.
books.description:
Are We Well? takes a bird’s-eye look at the rapidly rising public profile of mental health in recent decades. Clinical psychologist Derek Bolton and psychiatrist Mohammed Abouelleil Rashed explore not only individual, family, and social mental health perspectives, but also the expansion of the mental health world, the growing media attention to high levels of mental health difficulties, and the concerns that our current hyperawareness of the topic may be overreaching.

The book focuses on major changes in Western psychiatry and culture since the mid-twentieth century, highlighting the twin policy directions of deinstitutionalization—the closing of large mental hospitals to be replaced by care in the community—and the planned development of public mental health services for the population at large. The authors argue that both movements unsettled long-held ideas about mental disorder, normality, and how we distinguish between them, prompting a period of reconstruction that is still unfolding.

Drawing on a wide range of topics in psychiatry, including diagnostics, epidemiology, and causes and treatments, the book also discusses cultural and political dimensions such as mental health activism (from civil rights to Mad Pride), responses to stigma and social exclusion, emerging concepts like neurodiversity, and widespread social acceptance of diagnostics and treatments.
books.bio:
Derek Bolton (Author)

Derek Bolton is Emeritus Professor of Philosophy and Psychopathology at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at King’s College London, and Honorary Consultant Clinical Psychologist in the South London & Maudsley NHS Trust.

Mohammed Abouelleil Rashed (Author)

Mohammed Abouelleil Rashed is a researcher and lecturer in philosophy of psychiatry and mental health. He practices psychiatry at a community mental health team in the NHS and is Senior Editor for the journal Philosophy, Psychiatry, and Psychology.

books.title: Citizens of Tomorrow
books.subtitle: Using AI to Revive Local Democracy
books.authors: M. L. Bitton and Elizabeth Haas Edersheim
books.tagline: How we—and not Big Tech—can use AI to build stronger democracies and cities that are both smart and humane.
books.description:
When we think about our future with AI, we tend to imagine a dystopian future in which tech giants use ever more sophisticated algorithms to take control of our lives. A technocratic model of governance in which the people have no place. In Citizens of Tomorrow, Mathis Bitton and Elizabeth Haas Edersheim argue that an alternative is possible, that we can build a future in which AI can give us more ownership over decision-making. They argue that AI can:

• reflect us back to ourselves . AI can give communities access to high-level analytics that reflect the complexities of local preferences and situations.

• expand our political imagination . AI can work alongside our communities to show us possibilities that would otherwise remain inaccessible. It can help us imagine fairer futures, showing us novel solutions around which we can unite.

• build continuous and localized decision-making. AI agents can represent us in dynamic systems—services and policies—and can negotiate on our behalf, giving an equal voice to everyone.

Drawing on three years of work with cities and the U.S. Conference of Mayors, original survey data, and hundreds of interviews, the authors profile a coalition of civic technologists, community organizers, and forward-thinking officials working to turn AI from an instrument of top-down control into a platform for bottom-up engagement.

By showing that AI can help us revive local democracy, the authors show that our cities can be smart and humane at once—and it’s up to us to build them.
books.bio:
M. L. Bitton (Author)

Mathis Bitton is a PhD candidate in Government at Harvard University and a researcher at NYU’s Emerging Technologies Collaborative. His writings have been published in outlets such as the Harvard Business Review and The New Statesman .

Elizabeth Haas Edersheim (Author)

Elizabeth Haas Edersheim, a former partner at McKinsey & Company, studies and advises organizations and cities. She also teaches at NYU and co-leads its relationship with the U.S. Conference of Mayors Professional Sports Alliance.

books.title: Empires of the Silk Road (Revised and Updated)
books.subtitle: A History of Central Eurasia from the Bronze Age to the Present
books.tagline: A revised and updated new edition of the groundbreaking history of Central Eurasia
books.description:
A complete history of Central Eurasia from ancient times to the present day, Empires of the Silk Road presents a fundamental rethinking of the origins, history, and significance of this major world region. In this new edition, which draws on the most recent evidence, Christopher I. Beckwith describes the rise and fall of the great Central Eurasian empires, including those of the Scythians, Attila the Hun, the Turks and Tibetans, and Genghis Khan and the Mongols. He explains why Central Eurasia led the world economically, scientifically, and artistically for many centuries despite invasions by Persians, Greeks, Arabs, Chinese, and others.

Beckwith recounts the Indo-Europeans' migration out of Central Eurasia, their mixture with local peoples, and the resulting development of the Graeco-Roman, Persian, Indian, and Chinese civilizations; he details the basis for the thriving economy of premodern Central Eurasia, the economy's disintegration following the region's partition by the Chinese and Russians in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and the damaging of Central Eurasian culture by Modernism; and he discusses the significance for world history of the partial reemergence of Central Eurasian nations after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Placing the region within the framework of world history, Beckwith provides a new understanding of Central Eurasian states and shows how their people revolutionized Eurasian civilization.
books.bio: Christopher I. Beckwith is Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Central Eurasian Studies at Indiana University. His books include The Scythian Empire and Greek Buddha (both Princeton).

praise.q: [Beckwith] suggests in his recent book, Empires of the Silk Road , that 'the most crucial element' of societies all through Central Eurasia . . . was the 'sociopolitical-religious ideal of the heroic lord' and of a 'war band of his friends' that was attached to him and 'sworn to defend him to the death.' This idea, he suggests, affected the organization of early Islam as well as the structure of Tibetan Buddhist devotion. In fact, this 'shared political ideology across Eurasia,' Mr. Beckwith suggests, 'ensured nearly constant warfare.' The region's history is a history of competing empires; trade became part of what was later called the Great Game.
praise.by: Edward Rothstein, New York Times

praise.q: This is no mere survey. Beckwith systematically demolishes the almost universal presumption that the peoples and powers of Inner Asia were typically predatory raiders, and thus supplied themselves by extracting loot and tribute from more settled populations. . . . With his work, there is finally a fitting counterpart to Peter B. Golden's magnificently comprehensive An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples: Ethnogenesis and State Formation in Medieval and Early Modern Eurasia and the Middle East , based on Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Greek, Latin, and European medieval sources. By reading just two books anyone can now sort out Charlemagne's Avar Ring, the Golden Horde, modern Kazakhs and Uzbeks, ancient Scyths, Borodin's Polovtsian dances (they were Cumans), present-day Turks, Seljuks, Ottomans, early Turks, and Bulghars and Bulgarians, among many less familiar states or nations.
praise.by: Edward Luttwak, New Republic

praise.q: In the process of illuminating this essential piece of the human past, Beckwick constructs a scrupulously researched narrative that is wholly accessible, and demands close attention.
praise.by: Nicholas Basbanes, Fine Books & Collections

praise.q: Erudite and iconoclastic, [ Empires of the Silk Road ] provides a wealth of new ideas, perspectives, and information about the political and other formations that flourished in that large portion of the world known as Central Eurasia. . . . [A] major contribution to Central Eurasian and world history.
praise.by: Nicola Di Cosmo, Journal of Global History

praise.q: This volume is certain to provoke lively discussion across the field.
praise.by: Scott C. Levi, American Historical Review

praise.q: This book demands our attention and will stimulate interest and debate in many circles. The author is to be congratulated on a book that is both thoughtful and provocative in its call for a reassessment of Central Eurasia and its role in world history.
praise.by: Michael R. Drompp, Journal of Asian Studies

praise.q: Beckwith is the first to have carried off the feat of actually writing a history of this whole expanse of time and space in a way stimulating enough to make the reader think about it from start to finish."—T. H. Barrett, Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies
The result of a lifetime's work on Central Asia and a complete overturning of many of our preconceptions. . . . Essential.
praise.by: Hugh Andrew, Glasgow Herald

praise.q: Beckwith's arguments are persuasive, and backed by considerable empirical evidence. He is scrupulous about noting where the evidence is murky and noting where further research is needed. Beckwith provides an interesting Central Eurasian perspective on world history. . . . Empires of the Silk Road is work that any scholar who seeks to write about Central Eurasia will need to address closely. It is a benchmark—indeed a high one—for Central Eurasian, and indeed, world history.
praise.by: Thomas D. Hall, Cliodynamics

books.title: Equality Is a Struggle
books.subtitle: Bulletins from the Front Line, 2021-2025
books.tagline: An acclaimed economist’s observations on four years of events that have shaped the world
books.description: In this new volume drawn from his columns for the French newspaper Le Monde , renowned economist Thomas Piketty takes measure of the world since 2021: leaders grappling with the aftershocks of a global pandemic; politics shifting rightward in Europe and America; and wars breaking out and escalating, from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to the conflict in Israel and Gaza. Together with an extended introductory essay arguing that an ecological socialism remains the best hope for global equality, these articles present Piketty’s vivid first draft of history—on the rise of China, political upheaval, armed conflict, inequity within and between nations, discrimination, and beyond. Despite the gathering clouds, Piketty continues to find reasons for hope.
books.bio: Thomas Piketty is professor of economics and economic history at the School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences at the Paris School of Economics. His books include Capital in the Twenty-First Century , A Brief History of Equality , and Time for Socialism: Dispatches from a World on Fire, 2016–2021 . He lives in Paris, France.

praise.q: Piketty has made a distinguished career of explicating the whys and wherefores of inequality. . . . His outlook for a social democratic future is lucid and refreshingly optimistic.
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews

praise.q: Piketty gives us fresh eyes with which to look at politics and economics in the UK, Europe and the US. Essential reading.
praise.by: Sophie Charara, Shortlist

praise.q: In this compelling book, Piketty advocates for ecological socialism. His vision is ambitious but realistic, being based on a majestic understanding of the history of capitalism and detailed pragmatic knowledge of anti-inequality policies.
praise.by: Ha-Joon Chang, author of 23 Things They Don’t Tell You About Capitalism
praise.cred: author of 23 Things They Don’t Tell You About Capitalism

praise.q: A powerful case for rethinking capitalism through the lens of sustainability and inclusion. A valuable read for anyone—of all political viewpoints—interested in systemic solutions grounded in data and evidence.
praise.by: Alex Edmans, author of Grow the Pie: How Great Companies Deliver Both Purpose and Profit
praise.cred: author of Grow the Pie: How Great Companies Deliver Both Purpose and Profit

praise.q: Equality Is a Struggle captures the relationship between equity and the design of our political economic system. Nothing is inevitable.
praise.by: Mariana Mazzucato, author of Mission Economy: A Moonshot Guide to Changing Capitalism
praise.cred: author of Mission Economy: A Moonshot Guide to Changing Capitalism

books.title: Executive Function, Reflection, and the Developing Brain
books.subtitle: A Multilevel Account of the Development of Conscious Control
books.authors: Nancy M. and John E. Lindahl Leadership Chair Philip David Zelazo
books.tagline: A comprehensive theory of the development of conscious control skills by one of the leading researchers in the field of cognitive development.
books.description:
Conscious control of one’s thoughts, feelings, and actions, which depend on reflection and executive function (EF) skills, are essential for success in school and in life. In Executive Function, Reflection, and the Developing Brain , Philip David Zelazo draws on his more than 30 years of research to explain the development of conscious control. He presents evidence that reflection and EF skills can be improved through brief interventions during the preschool years—a period of relative plasticity in the underlying neural systems.

Spanning multiple levels of analysis, Zelazo addresses biology, culture, computational processing, behavior, real-world outcomes, and consciousness. Viewing conscious control in terms of the developing brain, he says, suggests a new approach to early childhood education that starts with the cultivation of reflection and EF skills. It also raises the prospect of better (and earlier) identification of potential difficulties and the creation of more effective therapeutic interventions for a variety of clinical conditions that emerge in childhood.
books.bio: Philip David Zelazo holds the Nancy M. and John E. Lindahl Leadership Chair at the Institute of Child Development, University of Minnesota.

books.title: Furious Minds
books.subtitle: The Making of the MAGA New Right
books.tagline: A Financial Times Best Book of the Year “The definitive account of the academic and philosophical origins of the American far-right.”—Anne Applebaum, Open Letters “Fascinating and important."— New York Times The story of the radical conservative intellectual movement shaping Donald Trump’s agenda—and how it threatens American freedoms, values, and democracy
books.description:
Donald Trump is not a big thinker, but his 2016 presidential victory presented a grand opportunity for people who are, and it set off a radicalization and reconfiguration of the American conservative intellectual world. In Furious Minds , Laura Field, who spent close to a decade in conservative academic circles, chronicles the rise of the New Right—the network of academics, public intellectuals, and influencers who provide ideological fuel to Trumpism. This movement includes figures such as Patrick Deneen, Christopher Rufo, Peter Thiel, and JD Vance. Their agenda is built to last, and it has dire long-term implications for liberal democracy.

The New Right has precedents in American history, but it is distinct for its youthfulness, misogyny, and extraordinary successes—most notably the elevation of Vance to the vice presidency. The movement—which draws together associates of the right-wing Claremont Institute, National Conservatives, Postliberals, and the Hard Right—advocates nationalist economics, tight borders, isolationism, and reactionary social values. It helped to strategize January 6th and created Project 2025. But above all, the New Right is engaged in a vast culture war against modern liberal pluralism. It is determined to harness state power and use it in new, illiberal ways, from college campuses to the international scene—all driven by the fantasy of restoring a pure America.

Incisive and urgent, Furious Minds tells the story of the thinkers of the New Right—and their powerful assault on American freedoms, values, and ideals.
books.bio: Laura K. Field is a scholar in residence at the Niskanen Center and an associate with the Illiberalism Studies Program at George Washington University. She has written about the New Right for The New Republic , Politico , The Bulwark , and other publications, and holds a PhD in government from the University of Texas at Austin.

praise.q: The definitive account of the academic and philosophical origins of the American far-right.
praise.by: Anne Applebaum, Open Letters

praise.q: Fascinating and important. . . . Field is an excellent and intellectually honest guide. . . . Furious Minds includes some surprisingly witty and playful moments, which stand in stark contrast to the turgid moralizing and hostility she examines in the book.
praise.by: Jennifer Szalai, New York Times

praise.q: [A] lively, devastating taxonomy and critique of MAGA’s ideologues.
praise.by: George Packer, The Atlantic

praise.q: Furious Minds is the most up-to-date introduction we have to the MAGA intellectual right reshaping America with astonishing speed today.
praise.by: Mark Lilla, New York Review of Books

praise.q: A great new book about the intellectual roots of MAGA.
praise.by: Greg Sargent, The New Republic

praise.q: [An] excellent new book."—Michelle Goldberg, New York Times
Furious Minds is the closest thing we have to a mole’s-eye view of the New Right, and it is revelatory.
praise.by: Alexandre Lefebvre, Los Angeles Review of Books

praise.q: In the ever-growing field of books aiming to explain the rise of the MAGA movement, Furious Minds , by a political theorist with longstanding experience in conservative academia, stands out for its emphasis on ideas. Field shows how the New Right, drawing on a loose network of academics and influencers, has coalesced around a vision of America that is socially reactionary, economically isolationist and deeply skeptical of pluralism as an inherent social good.
praise.by: New York Times

praise.q: A nuanced and sophisticated look at MAGA’s intellectual and institutional infrastructure.
praise.by: David Austin Walsh, Washington Monthly

praise.q: A fascinating taxonomy of the wild world of far-right thinking.
praise.by: Zack Beauchamp, Vox’s The Gray Area

books.title: Growing Up in Science
books.subtitle: The Untold Stories of Today’s Brain Scientists
books.authors: Weiji Ma, Alaa A. Ahmed, Mariam Aly, Sonia Bansal, Megan R. Carey, Clinton Cave, Anne Churchland, Daniel Colon-Ramos, Ishita Dasgupta, Gabrielle Gutierrez, Suzana Herculano Houzel, Clare Kelly, Rogier Kievit, Hakwan Lau, Elizabeth Claire Leininger, Teenie Matlock, Amanda Montoya, Fanuel Muindi, Vishnu (Deepu) Murty, Yael Niv, Rafael Polania, Rosanne Rademaker, Srikanth Ramaswamy, Annabell Segarra, Ivan Simpson-Kent, Heidi Vuletich, Bei Xiao
books.tagline: Leading brain scientists from around the globe talk about becoming and being a scientist in their in their own words
books.description:
Scientists often struggle to talk openly about the obstacles they face, particularly in the highly competitive brain sciences. On paper, science rewards the highly successful individuals whose landmark discoveries have helped us to understand how the brain works. But behind the awards, published papers, and media are people who have navigated difficulties, doubts, failures, and detours on the road to becoming a scientist. Growing Up in Science brings together twenty-eight short essays by brain scientists who write candidly about their personal and professional journeys, which make abundantly clear that a smooth and straight career path is rare. While broadly focused on the brain sciences, this collection will resonate with scientists of any field. It presents diverse perspectives from people in various stages of their careers and from very different backgrounds. Each scientist has their own way of telling their story yet many of them share similar struggles, from imposter syndrome and self-doubt to gender equality, mental health challenges, and difficult financial and family circumstances. They also speak of meaningful mentorships, rewarding academic accomplishments, and significant growth as both scientists and individuals.

Essential reading for aspiring and established scientists who want to learn from the experiences of their peers, these illuminating and disarmingly vulnerable essays offer an instructive and inspirational inside look at what it is really like to grow up in science.
books.bio: Weiji Ma is professor of neural science and psychology at New York University. He is the coauthor of Bayesian Models of Perception and Action: An Introduction . In 2014, he and fellow NYU neuroscientist Cristina Alberini founded Growing Up in Science, a mentorship series where brain scientists share their unofficial stories, which is now active worldwide.

books.title: Guesswork
books.subtitle: Accuracy for Uncertain Believers
books.tagline: A new approach to assessing the accuracy of beliefs.
books.description:
In Guesswork , Sophie Horowitz develops a new theory of accuracy for degrees of belief. She proposes that we can understand accuracy in terms of all-or-nothing guesses in response to forced-choice questions. Horowitz argues that your credences, or degrees of belief, are accurate insofar as they license true guesses. (If you are asked whether it will be rainy or sunny tomorrow, for example, and you are more confident of rain, you will be licensed to guess “rain.”) The book explores applications of this theory of accuracy, as well as perennial questions about the connection between rationality and truth.

Horowitz shows that guessing can be used in service of the “accuracy first” approach to formal epistemology and suggests connections between the degreed-belief framework and topics in traditional epistemology, such as reliability and (full) belief. Throughout, she contrasts the guessing approach with epistemic utility theory, the most dominant recent movement in formal epistemology. She shows that although guessing is less powerful than epistemic utility theory, it is simpler, requires fewer controversial commitments, and can often be discussed in accessible, nontechnical language. Therefore, she argues, many popular principles in formal epistemology can be justified on simpler grounds than has been assumed.
books.bio: Sophie Horowitz is professor of philosophy at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

praise.q: A terrific achievement. How often do we get a wholly new theory in epistemology? This is a major work, proposing a new theory and defending it in great detail. A very significant scholarly contribution.
praise.by: Richard Pettigrew, author of Epistemic Risk and the Demands of Rationality
praise.cred: author of Epistemic Risk and the Demands of Rationality

praise.q: This book is a pleasure to read. The author has set out to write formal philosophy in a way that doesn’t feel offputtingly technical, and she has succeeded. After reading it, I am convinced that the guessing paradigm is significantly different from other paradigms in formal epistemology. It’s extremely valuable to have a book that considers its implications in detail.
praise.by: Ray Briggs, University of Chicago

books.title: How to Change the Future
books.subtitle: Unleashing the Power of Collaborative Imagination
books.tagline: A playful field guide to imagination: humanity’s greatest superpower and our only hope for surviving the twenty-first century.
books.description:
Our relationship with the future is broken. Looming crises—from AI disruption and economic injustice to the collapse of democratic norms—can overwhelm us with feelings of apathy and hopelessness. The answer to these challenges is imagination, the overlooked human superpower that is the ignition system for empathy, anticipation, and resilience. In How to Change the Future , Ed Finn delivers an engaging field guide to imagination, revealing how we can practice and share this amazing capacity to see our world differently and envision a better tomorrow.

Drawing on fields ranging from creativity and futures studies to philosophy and cognitive science, Finn argues that imagination is the hidden architect of human experience. In conversation with legendary science fiction authors like Neal Stephenson, Kim Stanley Robinson, Margaret Atwood, and Ted Chiang, he moves from the individual to the collective, making the case that imagination is inherently collaborative: a team sport. Through the stories and projects of engineers and designers, activists and world leaders, writers and researchers, Finn illustrates how we can harness imagination to dream up better futures and transform reality—not just as individuals, but as the caretakers of Planet Earth, and ancestors of those who will inherit it from us. How to Change the Future offers up a playbook for navigating present challenges and reigniting imagination for a hopeful future.
books.bio: Ed Finn is Founding Director of the Center for Science and the Imagination at Arizona State University. He is the author of What Algorithms Want and coeditor of Future Tense Fiction, Frankenstein, and Hieroglyph , among other books, and he has written for The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal , and MIT Technology Review .

books.title: How to Retire
books.subtitle: A Guide for Academics
books.tagline: Thoughtful advice on how to leave academia gracefully and build your best life in retirement
books.description:
Retirement is one of the most challenging transitions in an academic’s career, and it’s natural to feel overwhelmed by the changes that lie ahead. This how-to guide explains how to structure your last few years of employment so that you retire well and feel good about it. Drawing on engaging personal stories from across academia, it shares concrete tips for letting go of one key phase of life and embracing the opportunity to reinvent yourself in the next. How to Retire makes the case that you have the ultimate say in charting your path through retirement, aging, and whatever comes next after academia—and provides the guidance you need to do so.

Susan Shaw describes the lessons she learned from her own retirement experience and those of her colleagues, highlighting what worked and what didn’t while paying special attention to the things that make the academic workplace unique. She outlines the four-year retirement plan she developed for herself and suggest some steps colleges and universities can take to honor the service of faculty members and help them to stay connected after retirement. Along the way, Shaw examines some of the downsides of aging in the academy and discusses relevant differences in academic experiences, covering topics such as gender, race, and sexuality.

Focusing on so much more than just financial planning, How to Retire empowers you with social, psychological, and philosophical tools to leave the academy on your own terms and thrive in retirement.
books.bio: Susan M. Shaw is professor emerita of women, gender, and sexuality studies at Oregon State University. Her many books include God Speaks to Us, Too: Southern Baptist Women on Church, Home, and Society ; Feminist Theologies: The Basics ; and Women and Religion: Global Lives in Focus .

books.title: Knowledge, Industry, and the Endogenous Growth of Nations
books.tagline: An analytically tractable and flexible model of economic growth that builds a bridge between short-run and long-run macroeconomics.
books.description:
The pursuit of economic growth requires an understanding of the mechanisms that drive it, the policies that support it, and the institutions that allow it to flourish. In Knowledge, Industry, and the Endogenous Growth of Nations , Pietro Peretto presents a theory of economic growth that builds a bridge between short-run and long-run macroeconomics. His industrial-organization-based theory of endogenous growth has at its core firms and the knowledge-accumulation activities they undertake in direct competition with the other firms active in their industry. Peretto’s framework is especially useful to researchers and policy practitioners tackling questions that thus far have resisted progress because they are inherently dynamic.

In many cases, Peretto’s dynamic macroeconomic models, with their industrial organization core, can be solved analytically. Though not alone in proposing models with firms at their core, Peretto is notable for his focus on tractability and transparent analytical results. Extensions include endogenous markups and a more general notion of market power, technological spillovers across firms, government interventions in the economy such as public R&D and fiscal policy, natural resources, and foreign trade.
books.bio: Pietro F. Peretto is Professor of Economics at Duke University and Associate Editor of The Journal of Economic Growth and of The European Economic Review .

books.title: Morality Within the State
books.subtitle: Decision-Making in the US Asylum System
books.tagline: How frontline bureaucrats respond when institutional mandates conflict with deeply held professional and moral commitments
books.description:
Many US asylum officers entered their profession because they wanted to provide safety for people in need. On the job, however, they find themselves constantly trying to reconcile competing demands arising from the law, professional norms, and moral convictions. In Morality Within the State , Talia Shiff explores how these frontline bureaucrats navigate moral dilemmas when implementing laws. Drawing on interviews with asylum officers, policy documents, legal decisions, and agency materials, Shiff develops a new framework for understanding moral conflict in organizational life. She identifies three forms of moral incongruence that shape decision-making: routinized work and the erosion of meaningful engagement; tensions between legal classifications and moral judgments of deservingness; and conflicts between institutional directives and moral commitments.

Shiff shows that asylum officers respond to these moral dilemmas by reinterpreting legal categories, redefining professional identities, and renegotiating their relationship to the institutions they serve. They do more than implement policy; they participate in the ongoing construction of organizational practices and institutional legitimacy. Although her research specifically examines US asylum officers and their work before the second Trump administration, Shiff’s account helps us understand how frontline workers with institutional mandates that conflict with moral obligations—including in healthcare, education, policing, and welfare administration—shape the state.
books.bio: Talia Shiff is assistant professor of sociology at Tel Aviv University, with appointments in the Department of Sociology and Anthropology and the Department of Labor Studies.

praise.q: Thought-provoking, well organized, and beautifully written. Shiff’s insights add theoretical depth and nuance to understandings of how individual and collective moral action occurs through experimentation, emotional labor, and improvisation.
praise.by: Jaime Lee Kucinskas, author of The Loyalty Trap: Conflicting Loyalties of Civil Servants Under Increasing Autocracy
praise.cred: author of The Loyalty Trap: Conflicting Loyalties of Civil Servants Under Increasing Autocracy

praise.q: Morality Within the State is exceptional, offering a compelling and fresh account of moral judgment, events, and turbulent times from the postwar era to the present. A remarkably timely book on an ever-crucial matter of collective concern.
praise.by: Ron Levi, University of Toronto

books.title: Proceedings of the Harvard Celtic Colloquium, 44
books.authors: Edited by Dolan Wells Gallagher, Rory Yarter, Katherine Scheidt, and Tony Vitt
books.description: Proceedings of the Harvard Celtic Colloquium Volume 44 includes several contributions touching upon the connection of language with ethnicity, leading off with Robert Dunbar’s J. V. Kelleher lecture that surveys the perception of other ethnic groups by the Gaelic diaspora in North America from the eighteenth to early twentieth century. Sarah Zeiser’s keynote examines the internal clues of a Latin manuscript and identifies its Welsh origins based on inferences of ecclesiastical culture. Articles on Welsh literary works examine stylistic crossover with Latin elegy, in one instance, and Arthurian romance, in another. The Irish language is examined in two presentations: one on constructions for expressing emotion, and another on the emergence of queer terminology. Irish popular music features in a case study on a song moving from Ireland to America as well as in a project to restore archived songs to current oral song tradition. Other articles examine poetic traditions and contemporary society in Irish literary works. This volume also features an article on the revival of Manx in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century and one on the importance of the Late Antique tin trade to Classical references to “Celts.”
books.bio:
Dolan Wells Gallagher is a graduate student in the Department of Celtic Languages and Literatures at Harvard University.

Rory Yarter is a graduate student in the Department of Celtic Languages and Literature at Harvard University.

Katherine Scheidt is a graduate student in the Department of Celtic Languages and Literatures at Harvard University.

Tony Vitt is a graduate student in the Department of Celtic Languages and Literatures at Harvard University.

books.title: Resonance & Radiance
books.subtitle: How Light Reveals the Chemistry of Our World
books.tagline: A narrative and illustrated exploration of the singular field of spectroscopy. How the interaction of light and molecules is not only a science of astonishing beauty, but also a powerful analytical tool, from assessing air quality to medical imaging.
books.description:
How the interaction of light and molecules is not only a science of astonishing beauty, but also a powerful analytical tool, from assessing air quality to medical imaging.

So much of what we know about our world—everything we can see, and much of what we can’t—is through spectroscopy. By shining different types of light through the air—infrared, visible, and ultraviolet—we can measure the pollutants in our air and determine an air quality index. Using radio frequency light and superconducting magnets, we can “see” into our bodies with magnetic resonance imaging. Spectrometers allow us to see what is happening on the molecular level, like a telescope to the atomic realm. In Resonance & Radiance , spectroscopist Debbie Gale Mitchell brings these discoveries to life through beautifully illustrated chapters that reveal how photons with different wavelengths of light serve as nature’s messenger.

Spectroscopy powers some of science’s most transformative applications—tools for measuring greenhouse gases, lasers for surgery, CT imaging, and genetic sequencing—yet few realize the breadth of its impact on our daily lives. The author traces these elegant connections between chemistry, physics, and engineering, inviting readers to discover the beauty and hidden complexity of our world. Light is the ultimate messenger—and this book teaches us how to see its message.
books.bio: Debbie Gale Mitchell is Teaching Professor at the University of Denver. As a magnetic resonance spectroscopist and chemistry professor, she has studied a variety of molecular systems over the last 20 years. Her work has appeared in journals such as the Journal of the American Chemical Society , the Journal of Magnetic Resonanc e, and the Journal of Physical Chemistry.

books.title: Rural Versus Urban
books.subtitle: The Growing Divide That Threatens Democracy
books.tagline: How the urban-rural divide drives partisan polarization
books.description:
Why have Americans living in different places come to experience politics as a battle between “us” and “them”? In Rural Versus Urban , Suzanne Mettler and Trevor Brown argue that political polarization is not just about red states and blue states, or coastal elites who alienate those in fly-over country. Instead, polarization permeates every region and every state—and has become organized through a pernicious rural-urban division. Mettler and Brown explain the evolution of this gulf across five decades, charting political trends in both places. Drawing on data on individuals, communities, and members of Congress, as well as interviews with local party leaders and former elected officials, they show how the divide emerged and why it poses a threat to democracy.

Until about thirty years ago, both political parties attracted support from rural and urban voters. But after place-based inequality grew due to deregulation and trade liberalization, white rural dwellers began to view urban people and Democrats as affluent elites out of touch with their needs. Politically active evangelical churches, antiabortion organizations, and gun groups helped deepen the divide, encouraging many of these rural residents to become staunch supporters of the GOP. Now, regional one-party rule in rural America gives Republicans a systematic edge for gaining control of crucial political institutions, including the Senate, House of Representatives, the Presidency, and even the Supreme Court. This is helping enable an extremist political party and pushing democracy to the brink. Mettler and Brown argue that the divide can be repaired—but only if the Democrats build their own robust local organizations and offer citizens a meaningful choice.
books.bio: Suzanne Mettler is the John L. Senior Professor of American Institutions in the Government Department at Cornell University. She is the author of The Submerged State and Degrees of Inequality: How The Politics of Higher Education Sabotaged the American Dream , among other books, and the coauthor of Four Threats: The Recurring Crises of American Democracy . Trevor E. Brown is assistant professor of political science at the University of Oregon.

praise.q: A massive rural-urban divide has opened in our country’s politics. Urban and rural voters used to vote pretty much in lock step. But then in the 1990s, that split. Urban voters became reliably Democratic, and rural voters became overwhelmingly Republican. We treat this as an inevitability in our politics, but it is only a few decades old, and our political future and stability might rest on reversing it. Certainly for the Democratic Party, any durable political power rests on reversing it. Reversing it isn’t going to be easy. But it begins with understanding it and taking seriously the resentments that fuel it. Rural Versus Urban , a new book by the political scientists Suzanne Mettler and Trevor Brown, is the best place I’ve found to start.
praise.by: Ezra Klein, New York Times

praise.q: I read a very good book this week by Suzanne Mettler and Trevor Brown called Rural Versus Urban . I think that you need to revisit organizing all the way down in the country, and you need to put pressure on Republicans. Because until some of the Republicans who clearly know better are willing to say so, it’s going to be very hard to break this power that Trump is amassing."—E. J. Dionne, New York Times
Essential for scholars of electoral politics and those seeking solutions to renew local party organization in the US. . . . Highly Recommended.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: The partisan divide between metropolitan and rural America has become a canyon. It makes governing our country far more difficult and reaching consensus, even on once-unifying issues, nearly impossible. In Rural Versus Urban, Suzanne Mettler and Trevor Brown offer a brilliant and genuinely innovative analysis of how this happened. They bring together methodological sophistication, moral seriousness, and lively writing. It’s an essential book for everyone, but Democrats especially need to take heed.”—E. J. Dionne Jr., author of Our Divided Political Heart

I will be keeping this carefully researched and beautifully written book close at hand and sharing it with students, researchers, and the many members of the public I encounter who express concern about the rural versus urban divide. This is just an invaluable resource for understanding the origins of rural resentment and the divide in the United States, and how it has mattered for our national politics.
praise.by: Katherine J. Cramer, author of The Politics of Resentment
praise.cred: author of The Politics of Resentment

praise.q: Political science’s blind spot in understanding the politics of rural Americans has undermined its ability to make sense of the urban-rural divide. In this beautifully written and reasoned book, Mettler and Brown answer questions that a disproportionately nonrural profession has mostly ignored. It is a must-read for every scholar of American politics.
praise.by: Marc Hetherington, University of North Carolina

books.title: Sacred Treasure
books.subtitle: Crusaders and the Hunt for Relics in the Holy Land
books.tagline: An insightful new history of crusading, revealing the vital role holy places and relics played in fuelling medieval religious violence
books.description:
The Crusades have long been understood as a conquest of the Holy Land directed by the papacy in order to expand Christian control over the medieval Mediterranean world. But what motivated individual crusaders? And why were specific sites targeted over others?

In this bold new account, William Purkis reveals how religious ideas fuelled generations of crusading violence in the Holy Land. Drawing on a wide range of medieval texts, images and objects, he uncovers how the prospect of losing sacred material culture played a more significant role in triggering crusade enthusiasm than the opportunities for worldly material gain. Purkis argues that these devotional concerns, which were integral to medieval Latin Christianity, were fundamental drivers for the practice of crusading.

This is a fascinating and original history that shows how this period was characterised by contradiction, triumphalism and ultimately dejection.
books.bio: William J. Purkis is professor of medieval history at the University of Birmingham. A specialist in medieval religious cultures, he is the author or editor of numerous books and articles, including A Companion to Medieval Pilgrimage .

books.title: She Sailed
books.subtitle: The Dangerous Voyages of Ordinary Women in World War II
books.tagline: The overlooked story of non-combatant women who risked and bizarrely relished dangerous seas during the Second World War
books.description:
In wartime, women and children are supposed to be kept out of danger zones. But during the Second World War, thousands of civilians voyaged in one of the most significant waterborne mobilisations in history. Military personnel and merchant seafarers were sailing to defeat the enemy and transport essential supplies; by contrast, women took to the seas, impelled by love, professional ambition, and adventurousness. They braved bombs and torpedoes with prams and swimsuits.

Jo Stanley reveals the other side of war at sea by unearthing the voyage stories of entertainers, refugees, escorts, military dependents, and missionaries. Sallying forth to new lands, or fleeing to safe havens, some were pregnant, faking courage, or having fun ashore when they could. Against the wishes of admirals and ship’s captains, unwelcome women negotiated realms of masculine bellicosity, as well as hyper-protective chivalry. Thousands created domestic niches on war vessels and explored a culture that had previously excluded civilian femininity.

Jo Stanley retells the story of wartime women at sea, and shows how they shaped the maritime world.
books.bio: Jo Stanley is a creative public historian whose work focuses on gender at sea, from women pirates to queer waiters. Part of a Liverpool seafaring family, her books include Seafaring Women Through History and Women and the Royal Navy .

books.title: Small Trades
books.subtitle: Real and Imagined
books.authors: Mark McDonald and Jeff L. Rosenheim
books.tagline: A fascinating look at how trades and occupations—and the people who perform them—have been popularized through prints and photographs
books.description:
Small Trades: Real and Imagined explores the social and cultural significance of everyday occupations, as portrayed in prints and photographs from the early sixteenth to the mid-twentieth century. This beautifully illustrated volume features nearly two hundred works on paper depicting tradespeople—from blacksmiths and bakers to chimney sweeps and grocers—as well as those in less savory professions, such as pickpockets and ratcatchers. Incisive essays uncover the multifaceted intents behind these images, be it laughter, disgust, or voyeuristic admiration. Beyond mere genre scenes or portraits, however, these compelling images by artists such as Abraham Bosse, Annibale Carracci, William Hogarth, Eugène Atget, and August Sander offer fascinating insights into the relationship between class and consumerism, as well as the transformation in social dynamics that followed the dawn of the industrial age. The book concludes with an in-depth look at Irving Penn’s arresting series Small Trades (1950–51) that reveals how these seemingly simple images of ordinary working people became landmarks in the history of twentieth-century photography and icons of modern art.

Published by the Metropolitan Museum of Art/Distributed by Yale University Press

Exhibition Schedule:

The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

(March 25–August 8, 2027)
books.bio: Mark McDonald is curator, Department of Drawings and Prints, and Jeff L. Rosenheim is Joyce Frank Menschel Curator in Charge, Department of Photographs, both at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

books.title: Telos
books.subtitle: Selected Poems
books.tagline: An exciting selection of work by the important contemporary Greek poet Stamatis Polenakis presented by acclaimed American poet and translator A. E. Stallings
books.description:
Telos offers a wide-ranging selection of poems by Stamatis Polenakis, one of the most distinctive Greek poets writing today. Polenakis is a poet rich in T. S. Eliot’s “historical sense”—aware of the “pastness of the past” but also its presence. Contemporary Greece, especially a Greece wracked by the economic crisis and austerity measures of 2009–2019, is glimpsed darkly in these poems through the glass of twentieth-century European history, literature, and film, as well as Homeric myth jolted awake by anachronism. Polenakis has said that his work involves “the idea of revolution, both continuous and glorious in its failure,” but his pessimism and irony are leavened with beauty and modulated by a faith in poetry.

The translator, A. E. Stallings, herself an accomplished poet, has worked closely with Polenakis to bring his work to life in English, accurately conveying his plainspoken but allusive vernacular in English poems that work on their own terms. The result is an ideal combination of poet and translator. The book also features an introduction by Stallings that provides important context about Polenakis and the historical events that have influenced him.
books.bio: Stamatis Polenakis (b. 1970) is an acclaimed Greek poet, playwright, and novelist who has received Greece’s highest award for poetry. Born in Athens, he studied Spanish literature in Madrid and has lived in Spain and Ireland. A. E. Stallings is the Oxford Professor of Poetry and an award-winning U.S.-born poet and translator who has lived in Athens since 1999. She has been a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry, and her translations include volumes of Hesiod and Lucretius for Penguin Classics.
books.series: The Lockert Library of Poetry in Translation

books.title: Tempting to Touch
books.subtitle: Surface and Substance in 20th-Century American Art
books.authors: Edited by Virginia M. G. Anderson
books.tagline: A groundbreaking reimagining of art history through the sense of touch. A beautiful, full-color die-cut gift book, perfect for art lovers.
books.description:
A beautiful, full-color die-cut gift book, perfect for art lovers.

What if we experienced art through our fingertips instead of our eyes alone? Disrupting the sight-dominated narrative of conventional art history, Tempting to Touch, edited by Virginia M. G. Anderson, offers an incisive exploration of art that foregrounds the sense of touch. This beautifully illustrated book features internationally acclaimed artists such as Ruth Asawa, Mary Cassatt, Nick Cave, Marcel Duchamp, Jasper Johns, and Yoko Ono, whose work centers tactility and connection.

Exploring themes of accessibility, tactility, preservation, and community, the book demonstrates how considering art in a multisensory way creates more inclusive experiences. The book features essays by leading artists and scholars Ellen Lupton, Georgina Kleege, DeafBlind author John Lee Clark, Angelik Vizcarrondo-Laboy, and editor Virginia Anderson, who offer wide-ranging perspectives on how texture, movable elements, and touch can reshape our understanding of 20th-century American art.

This volume accompanies the groundbreaking traveling exhibition Tempting to Touch: Surface and Substance in 20th-Century American Art . Both the exhibition and catalog spotlight tactile processes, textured materials, movable elements, and depictions of touch, honoring the growing movement of multisensory art.

Contributors: John Lee Clark, Christine Downie, Charlotte Gaillet, Georgina Kleege, Ellen Lupton, Eclair Morton, Linda Owen, Anne Schaffer, and Angelik Vizcarrondo-Laboy
books.bio: Virginia M. G. Anderson is the senior curator of American art and head of the department of American Painting & Sculpture and Decorative Arts at the Baltimore Museum of Art (BMA). She has organized numerous exhibitions, including Fratino and Matisse: To See This Light Again , Seeing the Essential: The Sigmund M. and Mary B. Hyman Collection of American Art , Art/Work: Women Printmakers of the WPA , Free Form: 20th-Century Studio Craft , and By Their Creative Force: American Women Modernists .

books.title: The African Revolution
books.subtitle: A History of the Long Nineteenth Century
books.tagline: A panoramic global history of Africa in the age of imperialism
books.description:
Africa’s long nineteenth century was a time of revolutionary ferment and cultural innovation for the continent’s states, societies, and economies. Yet the period preceding what became known as “the Scramble for Africa” by European powers in the decades leading up to World War I has long been neglected in favor of a Western narrative of colonial rule. The African Revolution demonstrates that "the Scramble” and the resulting imperial order were as much the culmination of African revolutionary dynamics as they were of European expansionism.

In this monumental work of history, Richard Reid paints a multifaceted portrait of a continent on the global stage. He describes how Africa witnessed the emergence of new economic and political dynamics that were underpinned by forms of violence and volatility not unlike those emanating from Europe. Reid uses a stretch of road in what is now Tanzania—one of the nineteenth century’s most vibrant commercial highways—as an entry point into this revolutionary epoch, weaving a broader story around characters and events on the road. He integrates the African experience with new insights into the deeper currents in European societies before and after conquest, and he shows how the Africans themselves created opportunities for European expansion.

Challenging the portrayal of Africa’s transformative nineteenth century as a mere prelude to European colonialism, The African Revolution reveals how this turbulent yet hugely creative era for Africans intersected with global intrusions to shape the modern age.
