books.bio: Richard Reid is professor of African history at the University of Oxford and a fellow of St Cross College. His many books include Shallow Graves: A Memoir of the Ethiopia-Eritrea War ; A History of Modern Uganda ; and Warfare in African History .

praise.q: An interactive history. . . . [and] a fresh perspective.
praise.by: Library Journal

praise.q: A well researched book about a much neglected period of African history. . . . An important contribution for allowing the history of Africa to stand in its own right rather than in relation to Europeans.
praise.by: Roger McKenzie, Morning Star

praise.q: This is a big book from a skillful writer: clever, full of ideas and insights and stimulating, as well as provocative.
praise.by: Justin Willis, Irish Times

praise.q: Richard Reid provides a wealth of scholarly evidence about an era often neglected in favour of a European narrative of colonial expansion.
praise.by: Martin Meredith, Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: Reid . . . revises readers' understanding of the traditional division of the African past, which typically presupposes that it moved from a precolonial, to a colonial, and then more recently to a postcolonial period, through a problematic understanding of the implementation of the colonial period via the Scramble.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: [A] tour de force. . . . Reid’s book is a critical intervention and brings much new and needed detail to the field of African Studies.
praise.by: Emma Christopher, Australian Book Review

praise.q: Richard Reid fills a gap with his book. Africa was never a continent excluded from history. . . He provides impressive evidence of this for the 18th century.
praise.by: Christoph Nick, Literatur Review

praise.q: [An] authoritative survey."—Zachariah Mampilly, Foreign Affairs

Impressive. . . . This book, [written] by a giant in the field of African History, should be widely read since it could inspire new case studies that can shed light on the history of the long nineteenth century of the African continent.
praise.by: Frank Gerits, The Journal of Development Studies

books.title: The Little Book of Bees
books.tagline: A charming, richly illustrated, pocket-size exploration of the world’s bees
books.description:
Packed with surprising facts, this delightful and gorgeously designed book will beguile any nature lover. Expertly written and beautifully illustrated throughout with color photographs and original color artwork, The Little Book of Bees is an accessible and enjoyable mini-reference about the world’s bees, with examples drawn from around the globe. It fits an astonishing amount of information in a small package, covering a wide range of topics—from evolution, the bee families, and habitats to reproduction, behavior, and threats and conservation. The result is an irresistible guide to the amazing lives of bees.

A beautifully designed pocket-size book with a foil-stamped cloth cover

Features more than 100 color illustrations and photos

Makes a perfect gift
books.bio: Stephen L. Buchmann, a pollination ecologist who specializes in bees, is an award-winning author or coauthor of many books, including The Forgotten Pollinators , which was a finalist for the Los Angeles Times Book Prize, and What a Bee Knows (both Island Press). An adjunct professor in the departments of Entomology and Ecology & Evolutionary Biology at the University of Arizona, he is a fellow of the Linnean Society of London and a frequent guest on public media, including NPR’s All Things Considered and Science Friday . Tugce Okay is a natural history illustrator who works primarily with watercolors. Her work has appeared in many books and magazines.

A beautifully designed pocket-size book with a foil-stamped cloth cover

Features more than 100 color illustrations and photos

Makes a perfect gift
books.bio: James Duncan, a conservation zoologist who has studied owls for more than four decades, is the author of The Complete Book of North American Owls and Owls of the World . He is the former director of the Wildlife and Fisheries Branch of the Government of Manitoba, Canada, and the founder of Discover Owls, which offers education, research, and conservation programs focused on owls and other birds of prey. Tugce Okay is a natural history illustrator who works primarily with watercolors. Her work has appeared in many books and magazines.

He is the author of Sharkpedia and the coauthor of Shark: The Illustrated Biography and The Lives of Sharks: A Natural History of Shark Life (all Princeton), among other books. Makes a perfect gift
books.bio: Emily N. Taylor is director of the Physiological Ecology of Reptiles Laboratory (PERL) at California Polytechnic State University and the author of California Snakes and How to Find Them , among other books. Her research focuses on the environmental physiology, behavior, and conservation biology of snakes and lizards. Tugce Okay is a natural history illustrator who works primarily with watercolors. Her work has appeared in many books and magazines.

books.title: The Quantitative Analysis of Stratigraphic Event Order
books.tagline: An introduction to the application of quantitative methods for inferring the historical order of deep-time stratigraphic events
books.description:
Many earth scientists today collect data using methods that would have been familiar to their nineteenth-century predecessors. Modern quantitative-analysis methods, designed to promote data integration and explore patterns in the data, are available but remain underutilized in stratigraphic analysis. Moreover, few university-level instructional programs provide training in the use of these powerful tools. To fill this gap, this book offers an introduction to quantitative methods by which stratigraphic data can be integrated and the historical order of stratigraphic events inferred. Its emphasis is on providing a deep understanding of the concepts, data, and assumptions that underpin each procedure while also viewing these approaches in practical earth-science contexts.

Features include:

• A stand-alone overview that covers the history of using quantitative methods to analyze stratigraphic event orders, a classification of mathematical techniques used, and practical challenges

• A background section for those not familiar with stratigraphic concepts and terms

• Detailed discussions of theory, methods, and applications of linear deterministic, probabilistic, and optimization search-based approaches along with hybrid procedures

• Dedicated discussion of two widely applied supplementary analyses: cyclostratigraphy and taxon richness analysis
books.bio: Norman MacLeod is professor in the School of Earth Sciences and Engineering at Nanjing University and was Keeper of Paleontology at the Natural History Museum, London, from 2000 to 2013. He is the author of The Great Extinctions: What Causes Them and How They Shape Life . Yukun Shi is professor at the School of Earth Sciences and Engineering, Nanjing University.

books.title: The Return of Martin Guerre
books.tagline: A classic account of stolen identity in a sixteenth-century village, by one of the world’s greatest modern historians—now in a new edition for the first time in over forty years.
books.description:
In 1548, a French peasant by the name of Martin Guerre abruptly left his village in the Pyrenees, abandoning his parents, his young wife, and their infant son. When he suddenly reappeared eight years later, he was welcomed home and quickly restored to his status as heir and householder. Yet this Martin Guerre had a secret: He was not Martin Guerre at all, but an imposter named Arnaud du Tilh.

In a now-classic work of historical reconstruction, Natalie Zemon Davis reveals the world of an ordinary family in extraordinary circumstances. What motivated the imposter du Tilh? Why did Bertrande, Martin Guerre’s wife, play along despite knowing the truth? As the rest of the Guerre family’s suspicions grew, the ruse boiled over into a criminal trial that captured imaginations across the continent. When the true Martin Guerre swaggered into the court and denounced the imposter, du Tilh’s fate was all but sealed. Guerre reclaimed his identity, his property, and his wife; du Tilh was sentenced to execution.

Yet the story of the two Martin Guerres continued to captivate, told and retold over the centuries. Presented in a new edition with a foreword from Jill Lepore, The Return of Martin Guerre is an enduring masterpiece that has inspired and influenced generations of historians.
books.bio:
Natalie Zemon Davis was a preeminent social and cultural historian of early modern Europe. Her many books include Women on the Margins, Fiction in the Archives, and Trickster Travels . The recipient of a National Humanities Medal, she taught at Brown University, the University of Toronto, the University of California, Berkeley, and Princeton University, where she was Henry Charles Lea Professor of History.

Jill Lepore is the David Woods Kemper ’41 Professor of American History at Harvard University and Professor of Law at Harvard Law School. A recipient of the Pulitzer Prize and the Bancroft Prize, she is a staff writer at the New Yorker and the author of numerous books, including the New York Times bestsellers We the People and These Truths .

praise.q: A fascinating reconstruction of a famous incident of impostorship and love in sixteenth-century rural France. Davis delicately deploys historical fact to suggest what is singular about the modern individual.

Natalie Zemon Davis…has scoured the legal and notarial records of south-western France to recreate for the reader not merely a highly entertaining story but a vivid picture of the world which fashioned its principal characters. Her observations on property rights, inheritance, customs, family relationships and the mechanisms of the law are welded together by a rare blend of historical craft and imagination.

In her intelligent and subtle analysis, the story gives an inside view of an otherwise little-known world, the private lives of peasants…One can only admire Natalie Davis for the major work of historical reconstruction she has performed without any kind of ideological bias…About Martin Guerre, I would say, without hesitation, the movie was great, but Natalie Davis’s book is even greater.

Written in a lively prose style that is accessible without ever being simplistic. The Return of Martin Guerre may be the most vivid, informative and entertaining history writing since Barbara Tuchman’s A Distant Mirror …a rich and colorful picture of life, love and justice in 16th-century France.

The fullest account to date of this extraordinary tale. Davis has constructed a fine piece of social history, a look into the lives of 16th-century peasants who left no records because they could neither read nor write.
A fascinating anecdote, with enough colorful background, psychological complexity, and unsolved mysteries to delight any intelligent audience.

books.title: The Unruly Universe
books.subtitle: The Struggle to Decipher Our Expanding Cosmos
books.tagline: How the quest to determine a single number—the expansion rate of the universe—is upending our understanding of the cosmos.
books.description:
For more than a century, ever since Edwin Hubble discovered that galaxies are receding from us, cosmologists equipped with powerful space telescopes have sought to pin down the Hubble constant, the rate at which the universe expands. By the start of the twenty-first century, a consensus seemed within reach. Then came a surprise. Measurements of the faint afterglow of the big bang pointed to a significantly slower expansion. The two approaches stubbornly refused to agree.

In The Unruly Universe, Nobel Prize–winning cosmologist Adam G. Riess and science writer Donald Goldsmith chronicle the high-stakes quest to describe the universe with a single number. What emerges is a sobering possibility. The standard model of cosmology—our best account of dark matter, dark energy and gravity, and even cosmic history—may be incomplete.

Abandoning a model that has explained so much would be no small step. But as Riess and Goldsmith show, the universe has no obligation to conform to our expectations. It may be more complex, more surprising, and more unruly than we imagined.
books.bio:
Adam G. Riess is Bloomberg Distinguished Professor of Physics and Astronomy and Thomas J. Barber Professor in Space Studies at Johns Hopkins University. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery that the universe’s expansion is accelerating.

Donald Goldsmith has written and edited more than twenty books on astronomy, including Origins with Neil deGrasse Tyson, The End of Astronauts with Martin Rees, and Exoplanets. He was the science editor and cowriter of the PBS television series The Astronomers and the cowriter of NOVA's Is Anybody Out There? with Lily Tomlin.

books.title: The Western Idea of Race
books.subtitle: From the Middle Ages to the Enlightenment
books.tagline: Two eminent historians offer a groundbreaking study of the origins of race in early modern Western Europe, tracing its development through Enlightenment justifications of global hierarchy and colonization.
books.description:
Race is often thought of as an invention of the eighteenth century. In this ambitious book, the first to provide a complete origin story of race, Jean-Frédéric Schaub and Silvia Sebastiani trouble that notion, tracing the concept of race back to the roots of the Renaissance and following its evolution in succeeding centuries. Crucially, they show how race, racialization, and antisemitism developed alongside—rather than despite—the political and scientific advances of the period. Major Enlightenment thinkers advanced universalism while also taking part in debates about human origins, miscegenation, and the genealogy of race, at once advocating for equality and dividing human beings into rigid hierarchies.

Beginning with early modern conceptions of “blood purity” among nobles, Schaub and Sebastiani reveal how supposed impurity developed into an elaborate system of classification that justified notions of racial superiority. Initially, impurity was exemplified by Jewish and Muslim conversos in Iberia; later, impurity became a trait associated with New World populations of mixed Spanish, African, and Indigenous ancestry. Examining the creation of racial markers, Schaub and Sebastiani demonstrate how emerging demarcations and structures of belonging were implemented across empires, often with ambiguity or contradictions.

Covering more than three hundred years of transatlantic history and drawing on diverse sources, including scientific papers, artworks, and philosophical treatises, The Western Idea of Race is a revelatory account. It lays bare one of the key foundations of modern social inequality.
books.bio:
Jean-Frédéric Schaub, Professor of History at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes en Sciences Sociales (EHESS) in Paris, is the author of Race Is About Politics: Lessons from History .

Silvia Sebastiani is Professor of History at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes en Sciences Sociales (EHESS) and the author of The Scottish Enlightenment: Race, Gender, and the Limits of Progress .

Henry Louis Gates, Jr., is the author of numerous books and has written extensively on the history of race and anti-Black racism in the Enlightenment. His most recent works include Stony the Road and The Black Church . He is the Alphonse Fletcher University Professor and Director of the Hutchins Center for African and African American Research at Harvard University.

praise.q: This is a book that will serve as both an indispensable reference and a key intervention in a critical historical debate. Schaub and Sebastiani, drawing on a vast source base, have written a clear and authoritative history of the origins of modern racial ideas. Casting these ideas as an instrument of domination rather than a coherent system, they take the story from late medieval Iberia to the Enlightenment and the height of the early modern slave trade, demonstrating the deep connections between the two.

Startling in its erudition, this is not a simple history of race and racism in the modern era. Schaub and Sebastiani set out to understand how Western Europe and its empires built differences between social groups upon a supposedly natural foundation, according to racial categories.

A galvanizing essay...Here the authors study the polysemic origins of race as a ‘political resource’ by showing how it became a power struggle from the end of the Middle Ages to the Enlightenment, well beyond simply the stigmatization of skin color and alterity.

The ambition of writing a complete history of race at the intersection of intellectual and social history, the rigor of its scholarship, and the innovative chronology make the work an essential contribution to French studies of race. Reading it can only shed light on the complexities of a problem that continues to haunt our societies today.

books.title: What’s on Her Mind
books.subtitle: The Mental Workload of Family Life
books.tagline: The mental labor that keeps families afloat—and why women do most of it
books.description:
Mothers and fathers use their time differently, with women spending roughly twice as many hours on family labor as men. But what about the gendered differences in the ways women and men think? What’s on Her Mind provides an illuminating look at the cognitive labor that families depend on and reveals why this essential aspect of family life is disproportionately handled by women—even in couples that aspire to practice equality.

While most accounts of household labor center on how people use their time, Allison Daminger focuses on a less visible and less easily quantifiable aspect of family life. She introduces readers to the concept of cognitive labor—anticipating, researching, deciding, and following up—and shows how women in different-gender couples do most of this critical work. She argues that cognitive labor has less to do with personality traits—for example, she’s type A while he’s laid-back—and more to do with learned skills that men and women deploy in distinct ways. Yet not all couples fall into the personality trap. Daminger looks at different-gender couples who achieve a more balanced cognitive allocation while also exploring how queer couples carve out unique relationships to the gender binary.

Drawing on original, in-depth interviews with members of different- and same-gender couples, What’s on Her Mind points to new ways of understanding the interplay between who we are as individuals and the cognitive work we do on behalf of our families.
books.bio: Allison Daminger is assistant professor of sociology at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Her work has been featured in leading publications such as The New York Times , The Guardian , Psychology Today , and The Atlantic .

praise.q: It is exactly [the] notion of how gender is embedded in our minds that Daminger’s What’s on Her Mind tackles, helping readers understand how couples negotiate the mental load of family life. . . . Daminger points us to the importance of centering the mental load in our discussions and not dismissing it as a ‘woman’s issue,’ carefully articulating why having women bogged down in worries about lost socks and dirty dishes is a problem for everyone.
praise.by: Leah Ruppanner, Science

praise.q: [ What’s On Her Mind ] makes a compelling, evidence-based case for recognising [mental load] imbalances and identifying where and how to correct them. Perfect family reading over the holidays.
praise.by: New Scientist

praise.q: Daminger’s work goes beyond the typical Fair Play conversation. She is most interested in the invisible work required to keep the family running, the cognitive labor that, for the most part, women are responsible for in heterosexual relationships. . . . Daminger does an incredible job of laying out the different components of cognitive labor and names that anticipating issues and monitoring results are some of the most laborious components (high burden, she calls it) but with less obvious benefits.
praise.by: Cindy DiTiberio, The Mother Lode

praise.q: An informative analysis. . . . Daminger demonstrates that although many Americans endorse gender equality, a substantial majority of women do most of the cognitive (and more than their fair share of the physical) work. She explains why and suggests how a more balanced allocation of responsibilities might be achieved.
praise.by: Glenn C. Altschuler, Psychology Today

praise.q: What’s on Her Mind is a succinct and enjoyable book. Daminger writes well and thoughtfully explains her research.
praise.by: Bonnie Kristian, Christianity Today

praise.q: A must-read."—Terri Schlichenmeyer, Nashville Ledger

The division of labor within families is typically examined through diaries or interviews that inquire about tasks such as lawn mowing, food preparation, and dishwashing. [What’s On Her Mind], however, shifts the focus to the cognitive and mental workload of family life, encompassing initiation, planning, worrying, directing resources, and remembering to follow through. . . . Recommended.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: What’s on Allison Daminger’s mind? It’s cognitive labor, her term for a vital form of housework we all do but hadn’t named until this pathbreaking work. Through captivating research with diverse couples, Daminger shows that gender equality will remain elusive until we attend to mind use in housework. Already it feels like a classic.
praise.by: Caitlyn Collins, author of Making Motherhood Work: How Women Manage Careers and Caregiving
praise.cred: author of Making Motherhood Work: How Women Manage Careers and Caregiving

praise.q: What’s on Her Mind is an essential contribution to our ongoing conversation about household work and gender norms. Daminger is remarkably successful in documenting cognitive labor through mind-use journals and, importantly, how it feels to be the cognitive laborer. By including queer and nontraditional couples, she brings important stories and perspectives to a typically heteronormative research space.
praise.by: Kate Mangino, author of Equal Partners: Improving Gender Equality at Home
praise.cred: author of Equal Partners: Improving Gender Equality at Home

praise.q: Allison Daminger breaks new ground in revealing the sources and consequences of gender inequality by introducing us to the invisible but essential work of cognitive labor. An indispensable guide through the uncharted territory where couples decide who should carry the mental load of identifying and addressing their families’ needs.
praise.by: Kathleen Gerson, author of The Unfinished Revolution: Coming of Age in a New Era of Gender, Work, and Family
praise.cred: author of The Unfinished Revolution: Coming of Age in a New Era of Gender, Work, and Family

books.title: Yellow Earth
books.subtitle: Regional Chinese Ink Painting and Global Postwar Modernism
books.description:
Yellow Earth reinterprets Maoist-era Chinese ink painting through the lens of the postwar geopolitical landscape by examining the Chang’an School, a collective of six Xi’an-based artists led by Shi Lu and Zhao Wangyun. Active during the “Seventeen Years” (1949–1966)—a foundational period for China’s socialist values—the school transformed ink painting from a traditional, studio-based practice into a dynamic, hybrid genre that infused the Chinese medium with Western realism. By producing lucid portrayals of peasants and the rugged Northwest landscape, these artists crafted a visual manifesto of national strength and artistic modernity, effectively anchoring China’s socialist aspirations in its ancient cultural heritage.

Positioning this regional movement within the context of global modernism, Yang Wang argues that ink painting served as a strategic tool for the Chinese state to assert itself as an emergent leader of the Third World. The Chang’an School articulated a distinct, indigenous modernity that challenged the Euro-American-centric discourse of postwar art. While standard narratives about Western modernism often focused on the tension between realism and abstraction, mid-twentieth-century Chinese art prioritized developing aesthetic forms—such as realism, nativism, and neo-traditionalism—specifically designed to bolster the nation-building efforts of the newly established People’s Republic of China.
books.bio: Yang Wang is an Associate Professor of Art History at the University of Colorado Denver.

books.title: A Circle of Friends
books.subtitle: Bloomsbury and the Art of Modernism
books.tagline: Reveals the intricate web of professional and intimate relationships and wider networks that helped a collection of extraordinary individuals form the hugely influential Bloomsbury Group
books.description:
Networks were fundamental to Bloomsbury’s contribution to twentieth-century culture and society. It achieved its ambitions and exerted influence through a wealth of connections. This book drills down into the detail of how the circle of friends supported one another and worked together to stand outside society and produce controversial, innovative new work. And it unravels the complex web of wider relationships that gave traction to Bloomsbury’s ideas.

Bloomsbury fascinates because, like a good television series, the lives and interests of its cast of characters interlock. They each have back-stories that inform the drama. Their published letters and diaries provide voyeuristic insights into their insecurities, the challenges of facing down conventional expectations, and their aspirations. A Circle of Friends offers new readings of Bloomsbury’s intimate correspondence, showing how spats and bitchy remarks among the friends sparked a creative rivalry. It offers new insights into Bloomsbury’s queer networks and shows how sex, sexuality and non-normative relationships were more than a side show. They were driving forces, binding and motivating Bloomsbury as the rebels of their day.
books.bio: Wendy Hitchmough is an Emeritus Senior Lecturer at the University of Sussex. She was previously Curator at the Bloomsbury artists’ home, Charleston and has an extensive knowledge of Bloomsbury art, literature and sources. Her previous books include The Bloomsbury Look (Yale, 2020) and Vanessa Bell (Yale, 2024).

books.title: (Berlin, Miami)
books.subtitle: A Novel
books.tagline: A hallucinatory near-future dystopia, cowritten with an AI, about language on the verge of collapse.
books.description:
“I was dead but also wasn’t. And with that, I had also understood what happened to my father.”

(Berlin, Miami) is an experimental novel written in collaboration with a language model, fed four German novels, and translated from the German by Noah Harley. In it, Hannes Bajohr presents, in Dadaistic fashion, a near-future Miami and Berlin populated by characters caught up in a world reshaped by an undefined catastrophe called THE DIFFERENCE. Real or hallucinatory objects and creatures—the jawling, Vapor Pools, co-yoga—appear and reappear. The prose, absurd and often hilarious, moves between social realism, bureaucratic report, and dream logic, deteriorating by the end into garbled tokens and multilingual fragments, closing on the literal string <|endoftext|>.

The novel continues the long tradition of experimental writing that has used formal disruption to challenge the limits of narrative: Burroughs’ cut-up, the Language poets, Ballard, Acker, and the generative fictions of electronic literature. But (Berlin, Miami) is and isn’t a book about AI; it’s a book made from what AI does to language. For experimental literature readers—fans of Dalkey Archive and Fitzcarraldo Editions—the novel is a rigorous formal achievement in a tradition they already value. For the broader cultural conversation about AI and authorship, it offers one of the first major examples of collaboration with a language model as a principle of literary form.
books.bio: Hannes Bajohr is a poet, essayist, and Associate Professor of German at the University of California, Berkeley. His scholarly work focuses on German intellectual history, theories of the digital, and the confluence of AI and literature; his literary work includes computational poetry and prose.

books.title: Accounting for Prosperity
books.subtitle: How Modern Accounting Informs Economic Decisions
books.authors: Mary E. Barth and Wayne R. Landsman
books.tagline: How accounting can help society achieve greater prosperity by enabling investors to make better investment decisions.
books.description:
Accounting for Prosperity reveals how modern financial accounting can help economic decision makers, such as business executives and policymakers, lead their organizations and society to greater prosperity by enabling investors to make more informed—and thus more efficient—investment decisions.

Challenging the conventional perception of accounting as “counting beans,” modern accounting transforms the economic activities of firms into decision-useful information. Mary Barth and Wayne Landsman trace the origins of modern financial accounting from the 1929 Stock Market Crash through the 2008–2009 global financial crisis and into the modern era. They present findings from cutting-edge accounting research from the past 50 years in a way that is engaging and accessible.

The book can help:

• investors interpret information in financial reports and use that knowledge to inform investment decisions;

• business executives improve communication with investors through financial reporting, thereby improving effectiveness at raising capital for their firms;

• standard setters and securities market regulators choose accounting alternatives that provide investors with more decision-useful information; and

• other policymakers understand how investor and business executive responses to public policies are likely to affect the economy.

Insights from the book also can enable finance and accounting professionals to offer better advice and assurance.
books.bio:
Mary E. Barth (Author)

Mary E. Barth is the Joan E. Horngren Professor of Accounting, Emerita , at Stanford University, Graduate School of Business. Barth is a prolific researcher whose award-winning research focuses on financial accounting and reporting. She has served as Vice Chair of the Financial Accounting Foundation Board of Trustees and as a member of the International Accounting Standards Board. Barth was inducted into the Accounting Hall of Fame in 2018.

Wayne R. Landsman (Author)

Wayne R. Landsman is the KPMG Distinguished Professor of Accounting at the Kenan-Flagler Business School, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He has published over seventy articles in academic and professional accounting journals, several of which have received prestigious awards. Landsman has served as a member of the Financial Accounting Standards Board Advisory Council and as a consultant to the US Securities and Exchange Commission.

books.title: Artist-Mother
books.subtitle: Reshaping the Self, the Studio, and the World
books.tagline: How the role of the artist-mother transforms how we think about being an artist and making art, and why this change matters now more than ever. A personal and candid journey through art history—the perfect gift book for any artist-mother.
books.description:
A personal and candid journey through art history—the perfect gift book for any artist-mother.

What does it mean to be an artist-mother, and why does it matter?

Art and motherhood have long been a taboo combination, if not a career-ender, but in recent years, a profound cultural shift has taken place. Many contemporary artists—as well as writers, poets, filmmakers, and other creative practitioners—now make mothering the subject of their work, as well as its condition. In Artist-Mother , Tara McDowell argues that the artist-mother reimagines what we understand an artist to be, while making the maternal experience visible. In doing so, these artists produce art, and an artistic subject, in which relationships are central.

The author posits that this model—the artist-mother as a form of relation rather than as a fixed identity—is one from which we can learn much in this moment of climate catastrophe, individual alienation, and the erosion of social and communal bonds.

Each chapter of the book—on Tala Madani, Camille Henrot, Moyra Davey, Simone Leigh, and d harding and Kate Harding—offers a close reading of a contemporary artist’s work, which becomes a lens onto a rich intersection of artmaking and mothering, illuminating new and long-needed models for art history. The author covers a range of artistic media, from painting to photography to video to sculpture, and a variety of topics around motherhood, including abortion, miscarriage, postpartum depression, maternal ambivalence, collective mothering, and Indigenous matriarchy. Building on a long overdue if growing canon of work, McDowell delivers not only the definitive study of contemporary artist-mothers, she models an unflinchingly fresh form of art history in the making.
books.bio: Tara McDowell is Professor and founding Director of Curatorial Practice at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia. Her books include The Artist As (Sternberg Press) and The Householders (MIT Press), which was recognized with the Millard Meiss Award. She currently leads the Australia Research Council project Care and Repair . In 2022, she co-founded the Climate Aware Creative Practice Network.

books.title: Cryptocurrency and Blockchain
books.tagline: A clear, nontechnical guide to why cryptocurrency exists, how it reshapes trust and money, and why it matters beyond speculation.
books.description:
How do we build trust in a digital world where institutions, platforms, and intermediaries increasingly mediate money, identity, and ownership? In Cryptocurrency and Blockchain , Marco Di Maggio offers an essential guide to cryptocurrencies and blockchains—two of the most misunderstood technological and economic transformations of the digital age. Rather than focusing on price charts, hype cycles, or programming details, Di Maggio explains why these technologies exist, what problems they attempt to solve, and why they matter for people who are not crypto insiders.

Using plain language, analogies, and real-world examples, the book explains how cryptocurrencies reshape core concepts of money, property, markets, and governance. The author explores topics such as how and why Bitcoin is used as a financial fallback, what stablecoins are and how they have become critical infrastructure for global payments, and how NFTs introduced a new notion of ownership and identity on the internet. Written for curious readers, journalists, students, policymakers, and professionals, Cryptocurrency provides a conceptual framework for understanding crypto as infrastructure, not ideology—helping readers see past the noise to grasp the deeper forces reshaping money, trust, and coordination in the digital economy.
books.bio: Marco Di Maggio is Professor of Finance at Imperial College Business School. Previously, he was Associate Professor at Harvard Business School, where he founded and directed the Fintech, Crypto, and Web3 Lab, connecting the academic world with the fast-paced world of fintech.
subjects: The MIT Press Essential Knowledge series

books.title: Freedom Itineraries
books.subtitle: Native and African American Journeys in Revolutionary New England
books.tagline: A pathbreaking study of intertwined Black, Indigenous, and Anglo-colonial communities in revolutionary New England
books.description:
In this interdisciplinary social and cultural history, historian Christine DeLucia recounts the intertwined lives of Native, African American, and Euro-colonial people in eighteenth-century New England. Offering a dynamic retelling of the familiar years of the American Revolution and its aftermath, DeLucia recovers routes of mobility, resistance, and opportunity from Narragansett Bay to the Piscataqua River, to the streetscapes of New Haven and Newport.

Told through the intersecting stories of the African American family of Newport, Violet, and their son Jacob Freeman, the Native American (Nehantic) family of Ruth and her son Aaron Waukeet, and Ezra Stiles, the prominent colonial minister and later President of Yale College whose own family enslaved, indentured, and dispossessed over many decades, Freedom Itineraries shows how Native and African American families fought to secure their independence, communities, cultures, and homes as they reckoned with the stressful shifts and the searing violence and displacement of the American Revolutionary War.

By refusing to take contemporary colonial writers like Ezra Stiles at their word about Black and Native people and politics of New England, DeLucia helps us imagine a far more complex and contested world, thus also giving an example of how to write inclusive and expansive history.
books.bio: Christine M. DeLucia is a historian at Williams College and the author of Memory Lands . She lives in Bennington, VT.

books.title: How Progress Ends
books.subtitle: Technology, Innovation, and the Fate of Nations
books.tagline: Shortlisted for the Financial Times and Schroders Business Book of the Year Award How 1,000 years of global history show why technological and economic progress is often followed by stagnation and even collapse
books.description:
In How Progress Ends , Carl Benedikt Frey challenges the conventional belief that economic and technological progress is inevitable. For most of human history, stagnation was the norm, and even today progress and prosperity in the world’s largest, most advanced economies—the United States and China—have fallen short of expectations. To appreciate why we cannot depend on any AI-fueled great leap forward, Frey offers a remarkable and fascinating journey across the globe, spanning the past 1,000 years, to explain why some societies flourish and others fail in the wake of rapid technological change.

By examining key historical moments—from the rise of the steam engine to the dawn of AI—Frey shows why technological shifts have shaped, and sometimes destabilized, entire civilizations. He explores why some leading technological powers of the past—such as Song China, the Dutch Republic, and Victorian Britain—ultimately lost their innovative edge, why some modern nations such as Japan had periods of rapid growth followed by stagnation, and why planned economies like the Soviet Union collapsed after brief surges of progress. Frey uncovers a recurring tension in history: while decentralization fosters the exploration of new technologies, bureaucracy is crucial for scaling them. When institutions fail to adapt to technological change, stagnation inevitably follows. Only by carefully balancing decentralization and bureaucracy can nations innovate and grow over the long term—findings that have worrying implications for the United States, Europe, China, and other economies today.

Through a rich narrative that weaves together history, economics, and technology, How Progress Ends reveals that managing the future requires us to draw the right lessons from the past.
books.bio: Carl Benedikt Frey is the Dieter Schwarz Associate Professor of AI and Work at the Oxford Internet Institute and Oxford Martin Citi Fellow at the Oxford Martin School, both at the University of Oxford. He is also a fellow at Mansfield College, the Institute for New Economic Thinking at Oxford, and Lund University’s Department of Economic History. His books include The Technology Trap: Capital, Labor, and Power in the Age of Automation (Princeton).

praise.q: In How Progress Ends , Carl Benedikt Frey offers a detailed and compelling account of how entrepreneurial, institutional and cultural forces have shaped periods of technological advance and stagnation across the world. In doing so, Frey, an economist and economic historian, draws timely lessons for today’s policymakers as the race for supremacy in artificial intelligence and green technology continues. . . . The present moment underscores the relevance of Frey’s writing. Business dynamism appears to be fading across much of the advanced world. . . . How Progress Ends is, therefore, an essential warning for the new era.
praise.by: Tej Parikh, Financial Times

praise.q: In How Progress Ends , Frey investigates the historical relationship between social structure and economic growth. His sweep is wide, stretching from the Western Zhou dynasty . . . to the European Union today. Both free marketeers and die-hard central planners may find that his conclusions challenge their view of the world. . . . [His] historical analysis has more than a little relevance to today.
praise.by: Marc Levinson, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: [Frey] is a world-leading expert on the sources and consequences of technological progress. In this important book, he analyses the . . . impact of artificial intelligence and, more broadly, the prospects for future economic growth.
praise.by: Martin Wolf, Financial Times

praise.q: Compelling. . . . A thoughtful, deeply informed study, How Progress Ends is both a historical journey and a warning. It challenges readers to recognize that progress is not self-sustaining and that the choices we make now will determine whether innovation continues or quietly fades away.
praise.by: Margaret Linak, Science

praise.q: Can we take for granted that AI will usher in a new era of growth and save us from stagnation? A little less than 40 years after Fukuyama (1992) declared the end of history, Frey steps into the breach on this question with a meaty tome reminding us that history is very much alive. . . . When the Berlin Wall fell, it seemed obvious to many that capitalism’s defeat of communism would usher in a new world order of technological progress in which peace and prosperity would prevail. Instead, that peace has proven fragile, that progress fleeting. Frey’s book offers a persuasive and well-written reminder that this is not an exception to history but rather the norm.
praise.by: David Robinson, Journal of Economic Literature

praise.q: It is tempting to assume that progress will always continue. How Progress Ends offers a sobering lesson: great leaps forward often grind to a halt when institutions fail to adapt.
praise.by: Bernard Marr, Forbes

praise.q: We are living in a golden age of big books on economic history. I would add Carl Benedikt Frey's, How Progress Ends: Technology, Innovation and the Fate of Nations , to the list of must reads.
praise.by: Adrian Wooldridge

praise.q: On a giant macroeconomic and historical scale . . . [ How Progress Ends ] has huge lessons . . . for both the US and China. . . . it’s a heavyweight book that gives you a grand historical perspective on the key question of how to guarantee growth and continued technological advance.
praise.by: Andrew Hill, Five Books

praise.q: Progress isn’t a straight line. Frey traces a millennium of innovation to show the tension between the decentralization that can spur new technologies and the bureaucracy crucial to scaling them. Countries and institutions — from Britain to China — can either stifle change or scale it, getting the balance right matters now.
praise.by: Tunde Olanrewaju CBE, Bloomberg

books.title: Lord Byron
books.subtitle: The Man and the Mask
books.tagline: A revelatory new biography of the poet that uncovers the vulnerable private man who self-consciously played the public role of the romantic hero
books.description:
He was “mad, bad, and dangerous to know”—or was he? Lord Byron (1788–1824) spent his career inventing a character, the Byronic hero. In public, he played the role to the hilt—but Byron’s method acting collapsed in his private life. For two centuries, Byron’s biographers have followed the poet’s lead by concealing the sides of his character that contradicted the world-historical figure he wished to be. In this groundbreaking new biography, Arden Hegele, who had rare access to personal letters and manuscripts, paints a thoroughly modern portrait of the man behind the mask.

Byron was a bestselling poet, a record-setting swimmer, and a martyr to Greek freedom. But his refusal to break his Byronic character came at a heavy personal price—especially when he lost control of his reputation. Covering the full span of Byron’s life and works, Hegele’s riveting account reconstructs the hidden Byron by restoring what was censored out of his story—from the verses he excised to the manuscripts his friends destroyed after his death. The book’s revelations include important new information about Byron’s marriage, his lovers of both sexes, and his medical history, as well as new perspectives from the women in his circle.

Authoritative and enthrallingly readable, Hegele’s book shows us how modern Byron was—not only as a bold, brilliant poet, but as an unrelenting curator of himself in an era when social media was print on paper. Byron said he was “born two hundred years too early.” This book puts to the test his prediction that he was living not for his age, but for ours.
books.bio: Arden Hegele is Lecturer in English and Comparative Literature at Columbia University and the author of Romantic Autopsy.

books.title: Miyazaki and the Mouse
books.subtitle: Ghibli, Disney, and the Pursuit of Enchantment
books.tagline: Disney and Ghibli: Two animation empires, two worldviews, and a century-long quest to imagine a better future
books.description:
This groundbreaking book tells the story of the creative dialogue—and creative rivalry—between the world’s two most influential animation studios: Walt Disney Studios and Studio Ghibli. Susan Napier reveals how the films of Walt Disney (1901–1966) and Hayao Miyazaki (b. 1941) offered radically different visions of hope and happiness—visions shaped by the contrasting histories of twentieth‑century America and postwar Japan.

Inspired by sometimes-harmonizing, sometimes-opposing philosophies, the studios complicate, echo, and haunt each other as they grapple with the aftermath of devastating world wars, shifting gender norms, seismic technological advancements, and encroaching ecological destruction. Author of the acclaimed Miyazakiworld , Napier blends cultural history with close readings of these beloved films to explore

• How Disney and Ghibli imagined utopia after war and trauma

• Why Ghibli’s worldview resonates powerfully in the twenty‑first century

• Evolving depictions of heroines, childhood, technology, and animism

• The global cultural impact of animation as a serious art form

• Ghibli’s growing influence on Disney itself

Drawing on deep knowledge of animated cinema and Japanese culture, Napier offers an essential guide to how animation has shaped—and continues to reshape—our collective imagination.
books.bio: Susan Napier is the Goldthwaite Professor of Rhetoric and Japanese Studies at Tufts University. She is the author of Miyazakiworld: A Life in Art and Anime from Akira to “Howl’s Moving Castle”: Experiencing Contemporary Japanese Animation , among other books.

books.title: Of an Ilk
books.tagline: The 121st winner of the Yale Series of Younger Poets prize offers a radiant meditation on grief and hope, queerness and mercy
books.description:
In this volume, JC Andrews tells a lesbian coming-of-age story from the foothills of the Arkansas Ozarks. Her poems—stories of the rural South and of mothers and grandmothers—hold questions as a form of caretaking. Andrews populates her work with kitchens, angels, chimes, horses, and moons, drawing us into a resonant landscape. She writes, “I dream about spinning / in this field until I dig a hole good / enough to lie in. I dream about / being stuck in it like a music box. / Play me, God. I want to know / what I sound like.”

“These poems slice effortlessly through the grim malignancies of our present moment,” writes judge Monica Youn, “carving out new forms and opening up new spaces for love and survival.”
books.bio: JC Andrews is a student and teacher at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln. She is the author of the chapbook Trillion Amber Trumpets , and her work has been published in Gulf Coast , Massachusetts Review , Waxwing , and elsewhere. Monica Youn is the author of four poetry collections, including the award-winning From From .

books.title: On Truth in Politics
books.subtitle: Why Democracy Demands It
books.tagline: The “philosopher of truth” (Jill Lepore, The New Yorker ) shows why truth is an essential democratic value—and how it can be strengthened
books.description:
Do any of us really care about truth when it comes to politics? Should we? In a world of big lies, denialism, and conspiracy theories, democracies are experiencing two interlocked crises: a loss of confidence in democracy itself and the growing sense among many that politics is only about power—not truth. In this book, Michael Patrick Lynch argues that truth not only can—but must—matter in politics. He shows why truth is an essential democratic value—a value we need to sustain our democratic way of life—and how it can be strengthened.

Despite evidence that people are rarely motivated by truth when it comes to politics, On Truth in Politics argues that this isn’t inevitable. Accessibly written and rigorously argued, it draws on the American pragmatist tradition to develop an original theory of the nature and value of truth in the messy world of politics. Contrary to the belief of many, political beliefs can be true or false. But if democracy is to continue to be a space of reason and not just an arena of power, we must build a better infrastructure of knowledge, including stronger schools and media, and renew our commitment to science and history.

A vital and timely book, On Truth in Politics makes an original case for why democracy cannot survive without truth.
books.bio: Michael Patrick Lynch is Provost Professor of the Humanities and Board of Trustees Distinguished Professor of Philosophy at the University of Connecticut. His books include The Internet of Us: Knowing More and Understanding Less in the Age of Big Data and Know-It-All Society: Truth and Arrogance in Political Culture , winner of the Orwell Award for Distinguished Contribution to Honesty and Clarity in Public Language.

praise.q: Lynch makes an eloquent case for the importance of truth as a core but increasingly tenuous democratic value. . . . If democracies are to survive, their citizens will need to regain their belief that they inhabit a common space in which facts, data, and evidence do exist.
praise.by: G. John Ikenberry, Foreign Affairs

praise.q: On Truth in Politics is about an important topic, arguably the most important topic facing us today: how do we foster both truth and responsible politics? How do we preserve both our democracy and our contact with reality, and how are these connected? For those concerned with these questions—which should be everyone—this book is essential reading.
praise.by: John Capps, Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews

praise.q: Lynch has provided a timely and thoughtful re-examination of the role of truth as a vital component in democratic practice.
praise.by: Jeff Roquen, LSE Review of Books

praise.q: Accessible. . . . Highly recommended for readers interested in current public affairs and the contemporary state of politics.
praise.by: Library Journal

praise.q: Stimulating and challenging. . . . Highly recommended.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: In this book, Michael Patrick Lynch makes a compelling, down-to-earth case for the necessity of truth. His argument is vitally important and timely, especially in our disturbing age of political regress, in which fair elections are declared stolen and bizarre conspiracy theories are held by a staggering number of people.
praise.by: Cheryl Misak, author of Frank Ramsey: A Sheer Excess of Powers
praise.cred: author of Frank Ramsey: A Sheer Excess of Powers

praise.q: On Truth in Politics is a provocative and compelling argument about what truth is and how we should go about understanding its role in our lives as democratic citizens.
praise.by: Robert B. Talisse, author of Civic Solitude: Why Democracy Needs Distance
praise.cred: author of Civic Solitude: Why Democracy Needs Distance

books.title: The Accidental Venture Capitalist
books.subtitle: Why Evidence Beats Instinct in Early-Stage Investing
books.tagline: How most investing decisions differ from what the data say works—and how replacing myth with measurement can improve outcomes.
books.description:
The Accidental Venture Capitalist examines how early-stage investment decisions are actually made—and why so many of them diverge from what the evidence says should work. Written by an academic-turned-venture capitalist Scott Shane, the book sits at the intersection of rigorous research and lived investing experience. Its central premise is simple but uncomfortable: in venture capital, folklore and intuition dominate practice, even though decades of empirical research offer more reliable guidance on selection, pricing, portfolio construction, and incentives.

The book follows the full arc of the venture process, from fund design and deal sourcing to valuation, syndication, follow-on investing, governance, and exits. Each chapter takes a familiar maxim—“bet on the jockey,” “do more diligence,” “double down on winners”—and tests it against large-sample academic evidence and real investment outcomes.

Shane’s analysis is grounded in power-law economics, behavioral decision-making, and incentive alignment. And he is transparent about mistakes as well as successes, treating his own funds as a living laboratory rather than a victory lap. The book also offers practical tools—checklists, heuristics, simple models—that translate evidence into decisions investors can actually implement.
books.bio: Scott Shane is the Mixon Professor of Entrepreneurial Studies at Case Western Reserve University and the 2009 winner of the Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research. He is also Managing Director of Comeback Capital, a pre-seed stage venture capital fund that invested outside the Bay Area and New York City.

books.title: The Age of Reconstruction
books.subtitle: How Lincoln’s New Birth of Freedom Remade the World
books.tagline: A sweeping history of how Union victory in the American Civil War inspired democratic reforms, revolutions, and emancipation movements in Europe and the Americas
books.description:
The Age of Reconstruction looks beyond post–Civil War America to tell the story of how Union victory and Lincoln’s assassination set off a dramatic international reaction that drove European empires out of the Americas, hastened the end of slavery in Latin America, and ignited a host of democratic reforms in Europe.

In this international history of Reconstruction, Don Doyle chronicles the world events inspired by the Civil War. Between 1865 and 1870, France withdrew from Mexico, Russia sold Alaska to the United States, and Britain proclaimed the new state of Canada. British workers demanded more voting rights, Spain toppled Queen Isabella II and ended slavery in its Caribbean colonies, Cubans rose against Spanish rule, France overthrew Napoleon III, and the kingdom of Pope Pius IX fell before the Italian Risorgimento. Some European liberals, including Victor Hugo and Giuseppe Mazzini, even called for a “United States of Europe.” Yet for all its achievements and optimism, this “new birth of freedom” was short-lived. By the 1890s, Reconstruction had been undone in the United States and abroad and America had become an exclusionary democracy based on white supremacy—and a very different kind of model to the world.

At home and abroad, America’s Reconstruction was, as W.E.B. Du Bois wrote, “the greatest and most important step toward world democracy of all men of all races ever taken in the modern world.” The Age of Reconstruction is a bracing history of a remarkable period when democracy, having survived the great test of the Civil War, was ascendant around the Atlantic world.
books.bio: Don H. Doyle is the author of The Cause of All Nations: An International History of the American Civil War and other books on America and the world in the Civil War and Reconstruction era. He is professor emeritus of history at the University of South Carolina and has had visiting appointments at universities in Britain, Italy, France, and Brazil.

praise.q: [Doyle] sets out to reveal a neglected aspect of Reconstruction—its revolutionary effects beyond America’s shores. . . . Reconstruction may have had a more lasting success abroad, as Mr. Doyle so vividly shows, by inspiring a generation of diverse and forward-looking leaders.
praise.by: Fergus Bordewich, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: A compelling new history of Reconstruction. . . . Highly recommended.
praise.by: Choice Reviews

praise.q: The Age of Reconstruction is ambitious and wide-ranging and the author skilfully combines the history of ideas with that of international relations.
praise.by: Leslie Jones, Quarterly Review

praise.q: Doyle has delivered a readable and enjoyable account of the influence that US Americans imagined they wielded—and sometimes really did wield. It also represents a useful stocktaking of a relatively young historiographical field and offers plenty of scope for future research.
praise.by: David Sim, H-Net Reviews

praise.q: If it is now advisable to assess the American Civil War in the context of contemporary global history, it is also revealing to see how that conflict and its aftermath shaped international events. Such is the task undertaken by Don H. Doyle. At a time when many historians are trying to redefine Reconstruction, he offers a long-overdue examination of its international dimensions. . . . [ The Age of Reconstruction ] mark[s] a transition in studies of the American Civil War and Reconstruction. . . . A substantial contribution.
praise.by: Brooks D. Simpson, Journal of Southern History

praise.q: [ The Age of Reconstruction ] not only presents readers with a fresh look at the global effects of the American Civil War, but assesses the remaking of a young nation in the wake of slavery’s destruction. . . . Doyle’s treatment of Reconstruction beyond the American border is therefore appropriate for any student or historian seeking to better understand the nuanced nature of international policy in a post-emancipation society.
praise.by: Rich Condon, Emerging Civil War

praise.q: Doyle’s broader perspective [on the Reconstruction period] allowed me to see the connections between the significance of the Union victory and an era usually treated separately—the pan-European turmoil over the rise of the mercantile and working classes, demands for democratic government, and the rise of nationalism. . . . Despite the diverse locations and peoples discussed in The Age of Reconstruction , Doyle keeps the momentum going through his engaging, nimble prose.
praise.by: Ron Slate, On the Seawall

praise.q: With this pathbreaking transnational history of Reconstruction and its impact on the Euro-American world, Don Doyle has provided us with a much-needed sequel to The Cause of All Nations , his acclaimed international history of the U.S. Civil War. By thoroughly investigating the myriad ideological and political links between the United States and a host of democratic movements, initiatives, and ideas in Europe and the Americas, The Age of Reconstruction demonstrates that it is now impossible to think about the United States after Lincoln in isolation from the Euro-American context.
praise.by: Enrico Dal Lago, University of Galway

praise.q: By tracing the reverberations of Union victory and Reconstruction beyond the borders of the United States, The Age of Reconstruction shows how the convoluted efforts to put a shattered Union back together turned the United States into an instigator of freedom and the precursor of a more democratic world, if for a brief moment.
praise.by: Erika Pani, El Colegio de México

praise.q: In this gem of a book, Don Doyle uncovers the largely untold international history of American Reconstruction. Significantly, he reveals the worldwide struggle for democracy inaugurated by Lincoln and Reconstruction, which was overthrown at home and abroad by racist reaction and the quest for empire. At this fraught moment in U.S. and global history, this revelatory book and its lessons could not be timelier.”—Manisha Sinha, author of The Rise and Fall of the Second American Republic: Reconstruction, 1860

books.title: The Divine Comedy
books.authors: Dante Alighieri, Charles S. Singleton, Simone Marchesi, Roberto Abbiati
books.tagline: For the first time in one volume, the most elegant and accessible translation of Dante’s enduring masterpiece
books.description:
Charles Singleton’s English-language translation of The Divine Comedy is widely considered to be one of the finest renderings of Dante’s masterpiece. Singleton’s prose is both faithful and scholarly, and sensitive to the subtle nuances of meaning and richness of reference in Dante’s epic poem. Here for the first time is the single-volume edition of Singleton’s celebrated translation.

This beautifully illustrated book brings together all three volumes of Dante’s poem, describing his travels down to the circles of Hell, up over the mountain of Purgatory, and his ultimate ascension through the celestial spheres of Paradise. Dante’s divine tour provides a timeless allegory for the journey of one’s soul toward union with God.

Featuring an incisive introduction by Simone Marchesi, a glossary, and stunning illustrations by acclaimed artist Roberto Abbiati, this handsome edition of The Divine Comedy introduces a new generation of readers to what is perhaps the preeminent achievement of Italian literature.
books.bio: Charles S. Singleton (1909–1985) was professor of humanistic studies at Johns Hopkins University and a world-renowned scholar of medieval literature. Simone Marchesi is professor of French and Italian at Princeton University. His books include Dante and Augustine: Linguistics, Poetics, Hermeneutics . Roberto Abbiati is an artist, actor, and book designer. His books include illustrated editions of Herman Melville’s Moby-Dick and Jules Verne’s Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Seas .

praise.q: A handsome volume. . . . A commemorative edition of a work by an important contributor to the afterlife of Dante’s poem in contemporary America.
praise.by: Andrew Frisardi, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: Impressive. . . .Beautifully produced."—Alan Price, London Grip
Princeton University Press. . .have produced a book that’s both easy to read and truly delightful to handle and enjoy.
praise.by: Terry Potter, The Letterpress Project

praise.q: Refreshing. . . . Above all, immensely readable. Add Roberto Abbiati’s wonderfully darksome illustrations, which manage to evoke medieval symbol while resisting kitsch, and you have the perfect edition for every new – or old – reader.
praise.by: Fiona Sampson, The Tablet

praise.q: Simone Marchesi’s introduction provides an excellent overview of what is at stake in the poem, doing justice both to Dante's world and to Singleton’s scholarly legacy.
praise.by: John Walsh, Irish Catholic

praise.q: Like Shakespeare’s Hamlet , Alighieri’s The Divine Comedy can be read and embraced, as well as devoured and misconstrued, time and again (and again). But one thing’s for crystal clear certain:one never ultimately reaches a pristine conclusion. Let alone an end. And that is why this particular publication of The Divine Comedy , along with its excellent Introduction by Simone Marchesi and its glorious Illustrations by Roberto Abbiati is so necessary. And so very implicit to its understanding.
praise.by: David Marx, David Marx Book Reviews

praise.q: One cannot but be grateful for Singleton’s great achievement.
praise.by: Speculum

praise.q: Singleton’s edition of the Divine Comedy will certainly be the edition for readers in English. The translation is much the most satisfactory one I know.
praise.by: Francis Fergusson

books.title: The Human Economists
books.subtitle: How Fin-de-Siecle Visionaries Imagined a Better World
books.tagline: How a forgotten generation of Central European thinkers rejected capitalism’s logic at the turn of the twentieth century—and offered solutions that remain urgent today
books.description:
Financial panic, widening inequality, environmental crisis, authoritarian politics—a remarkable generation of Central European thinkers faced all of it, and they had answers. In the aftermath of the Panic of 1873, German-speaking intellectuals refused to accept capitalism as a natural law or economics as a value-free science. Drawing on anthropology, evolutionary biology, and sociology, they proposed sweeping alternatives: universal basic provisions, wealth and land taxes, cooperative ownership, democratic planning, and even money-less economies. Vienna was the crucible, but the influence spread across Central Europe and eventually the world.

In making the case that the insights of this forgotten tradition are needed more urgently than ever, Janek Wasserman

• recovers a lost “third way” between industrial capitalism and communism, prioritizing human dignity, social welfare, and democratic decision-making;

• traces how forced exile under fascism carried these ideas into the development economics practiced at the UN, World Bank, and IMF; and

• connects the crises of the fin de siècle to our own, offering a “usable past” for today.

The Human Economists demonstrates that there is no reason to reinvent the wheel. These thinkers already imagined—and partly designed—the world we still need.
books.bio: Janek Wasserman is professor of history at the University of Alabama. He is the author of Black Vienna: The Radical Right in the Red City and The Marginal Revolutionaries: How Austrian Economists Fought the War of Ideas .

books.title: The Long Run
books.subtitle: A New History of the International Financial System
books.tagline: A bold new history of global finance over seven centuries—and what its long evolution reveals about the future of the world economy
books.description:
The twenty-first century has been marked by what many see as unusual instability in global finance—negative interest rates, geopolitical tensions, and unprecedented market interventions. What if these developments are not an aberration but rather a return to deeper historical patterns?

In this ambitious new history, Paul Schmelzing draws on thousands of archival sources to reconstruct the evolution of the international financial system from the Renaissance to today. He shows how long-run trends in interest rates and asset markets helped shape our modern system—and how those trends may now be reversing.

That system took form during the upheavals of the sixteenth century, when governments—starting with the Habsburg Empire—emerged as the world’s most trusted borrowers and their debt became the foundation of modern markets. Over time, this arrangement culminated in America anchoring the international financial order.

Now, that long-standing order is eroding. As debt rises, financial pressures mount, and China’s economic trajectory converges with the West's, the world could be entering a new era of instability—one that, in key respects, echoes the financial system that existed before 1550.
books.bio: Paul Schmelzing is assistant professor of finance at Boston College and a research fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University. He has advised central banks, the IMF, and global macro hedge funds. He lives in Boston, MA.

books.title: The Planner's Pledge
books.subtitle: An Oath to Reform a Wayward Profession
books.tagline: A manifesto and guidebook for refocusing planners on the task of building a more livable world. From the bestselling author of Walkable City and a prominent urban planning educator.
books.description:
From the bestselling author of Walkable City and a prominent urban planning educator.

“Cities are the future of the human race,” remarked New Yorker writer David Owen, “and Jeff Speck knows how to make them work.” With the renowned planning professor Emily Talen, Speck brings that knowledge to bear in The Planner’s Pledge— a manifesto and practical handbook that redirects city planning toward healthier, fairer, and more sustainable outcomes.

The growing call for walkable mixed-use communities is drowned out by the seemingly ceaseless construction of car-dependent single-use sprawl. The Planner’s Pledge aims to cut through the static and jumpstart the planning profession’s commitment to building more livable cities and a more workable world.

Speck and Talen organize their Pledge around 56 clear statements—each supported by evidence and examples—that form a coherent and practical framework for contemporary planning. The result is a compact, highly usable guide that connects big-picture goals—public health, equity, climate resilience, economic vitality, and social life—to everyday decisions about zoning, streets, housing, parking, transit, and historic buildings.

At once a critique, a teaching tool, and a call to action, The Planner’s Pledge gives practitioners, students, and engaged citizens a shared vocabulary and a set of priorities for creating walkable, mixed-use, transit-supportive, and socially diverse communities. Pairing moral clarity with practical guidance, the book equips the planning profession with the tools it needs to recover its public purpose and reclaim a leadership role in shaping better places.
books.bio:
Jeff Speck (Author)

Jeff Speck , former Director of Design at the National Endowment for the Arts and a founding principal of the firm Speck Dempsey, has worked on some of the most influential urban planning projects of the past thirty years. His book Walkable City is the bestselling city planning title written this century, and his TED talks have been viewed more than six million times.

Emily Talen (Author)

Emily Talen is Professor of Urbanism at the University of Chicago, where she teaches urban design and directs the Urbanism Lab, and the author of Neighborhood and What Cities Say , among many other books. She is a fellow of the American Institute of Certified Planners and the recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship.

books.title: The Power Revolution
books.subtitle: What the Judges Have Wrought
books.tagline: From a renowned legal scholar, a new vision of how the judiciary has reconfigured rights and power.
books.description:
Ambitious and erudite, The Power Revolution is a new challenge to conventional wisdom from one of our most prominent constitutional scholars. Philip Hamburger’s prior scholarship initiated the current judicial reconsideration of the administrative state. Here, he makes the broader point that the acclaimed rights revolution has been accompanied by a much more substantial power revolution—a vast judicial expansion of government power and a corresponding judicial erosion of rights.

The slant toward power goes much further than has been understood, and because it cuts across much of the Constitution, its effects are sobering. It threatens both our freedom and our government. It even undermines the nation’s stability. It’s therefore important to understand the contemporary realities of unconstitutional power, not just our old constitutional ideals.

In observing the judiciary’s responsibility for how we are governed now, The Power Revolution calls upon Americans to push back against unconstitutional power and urges the judges to reconsider what they have done. After so much damage to the Constitution, it is time for repair.
books.bio: Philip Hamburger is Maurice and Hilda Friedman Professor of Law at Columbia Law School and CEO of the New Civil Liberties Alliance. He is a Nonresident Senior Fellow of the American Enterprise Institute. A member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, he is the author of S eparation of Church and State, Law and Judicial Duty, Is Administrative Law Unlawful? and Purchasing Submission .

books.title: The Recovery of Loss
books.subtitle: American Afterlives of Ancient Greece
books.tagline: How American invocations of ancient Greece produced varieties of cultural and historical loss
books.description:
Ancient Greece has often been used as a part of a triumphalist story about American exceptionalism and invulnerability to loss. In The Recovery of Loss , Emily Greenwood shows how attempts to locate ancient Greece in modern America have produced different types of cultural and historical loss as well as ways of making loss intelligible. Across three chapters, Greenwood examines the interweaving of ancient Greece in accounts of Native American, African American, and Asian American histories,]. The nineteenth-century historian Horatio Bardwell Cushman (1820–1904), for example, superimposed ancient Greek history onto Indigenous history when he substituted passages from Thucydides for the words of the Shawnee leader Tecumseh and the Choctaw chief Pushmataha—making ancient Greece overshadow Native American history in the very act of representing that history.

Greenwood goes on to describe how Anna Julia Cooper (1858–1964) and Mary Church Terrel (1863–1954), used their knowledge of ancient Greece to articulate the losses sustained by Black women intellectual leaders. For these writers, the intellectual and moral purpose of turning to ancient Greece was to make past and present losses palpable. Finally, Greenwood draws from contemporary poetry and the work of Monica Youn and Ocean Vuong, which recycles the containers of Greek myths to replenish loss, giving tangible outlines to diverse Asian American immigrant and refugee experiences. These Greek-struck stories of loss, Greenwood shows, are an important source of new knowledge about North American histories.
books.bio: Emily Greenwood is the James F. Rothenberg Professor of Classics at Harvard University. She is the author of Thucydides and the Shaping of History and Afro-Greeks: Dialogues Between Anglophone Caribbean Literature and Classics in the Twentieth Century .

praise.q: Greenwood is one of the most exciting and insightful voices that the field of classics has ever produced. This book is an invaluable contribution to the growing body of scholarship on classical reception in American life. Greenwood’s case studies are all exceedingly rich and shed light on compelling forms of erasure conditioned by American interactions with the Greco-Roman past.
praise.by: Christopher Waldo, author of Classical Reception in Asian American Literature
praise.cred: author of Classical Reception in Asian American Literature

books.title: Threat Multiplier
books.subtitle: Climate, Military Leadership, and the Fight for Global Security
books.tagline: The inside story of the military’s fight for global security in the face of a changing climate—now with a new preface that examines the security threat posed by accelerating climate change and the politics of denial
books.description:
Threat Multiplier takes us onto the battlefield and inside the Pentagon to show how the US military is confronting the biggest security risk in global history: climate change. More than thirty years ago, when Sherri Goodman became the Pentagon’s first Chief Environmental Officer, no one would have imagined this role for our armed forces.

Indeed, for much of the twentieth century, the Department of Defense (DOD) was better known for containing the Soviet nuclear threat than protecting the environment. And yet, today, the military has moved from an environmental laggard to a clean energy and climate leader, recognizing that a warming world exacerbates every threat—from hurricanes and forest fires, to competition for increasingly scarce food and water, to terrorism and power plays by Russia and China. The Pentagon now considers climate in war games, disaster relief planning, international diplomacy, and even the design of its own bases.

What was the key to this dramatic change in military thinking? What keeps today’s generals and admirals up at night? How can we safeguard our national defense and our planet? No one is better poised to answer these questions than Sherri Goodman, who was at the vanguard of environmental leadership among our armed forces and civilian representatives. In Threat Multiplier , she tells the inside story of the military’s fight for global security, a tale that is as hopeful as it is harrowing.
books.bio: Sherri Goodman is Secretary General of the International Military Council on Climate and Security and a Distinguished Fellow at the Atlantic Council.

praise.q: A memoir by a fighter in a decades-long campaign to make U.S. defense policy take climate change and the environment seriously. . . . What is distinctive, even special, about Goodman’s book is her description of how she moved from academia to Senate staff work to a senior Pentagon position to a perch in the think tank universe. That is a successful career, even a highly successful one, but it is also the sort of trajectory that rarely gets documented. . . . Goodman’s perspective is valuable. It’s a reminder that progress can be made, however slowly it may go. More significantly, it’s a reminder that progress mostly has less to do with sudden revolutionary change than with the steady work of repeating oneself in nice conference rooms in the hopes of catching the ear of people who can change policy ever so slightly.
praise.by: Washington Post

praise.q: [Goodman] provides valuable insights on the role of science and technology in the ‘greening’ of the US military. . . . Her accessible writing style and the personal anecdotes she brings to the narrative provide a welcome humanization of the military’s work in the context of environmental policy. This book will be an important chronicle of a pivotal period in global environmental and military history.
praise.by: Science

praise.q: A thought-provoking and enjoyable read. . . . I challenge anyone to read Threat Multiplier and remain skeptical that militaries around the world need to think about climate change.
praise.by: Lawfare

praise.q: The climate crisis has enormous national security implications, and no one knows that better than Sherri Goodman, who long ago coined the phrase ‘threat multiplier’ to capture the ways this environmental wrecking ball would inform policymakers in situation rooms everywhere. There is no one better to take readers along on the Pentagon’s journey wrestling with this new and evolving reality implicating basing, training, peacekeeping, and much more. A must-read for everyone who wants to understand why climate imperatives aren’t just for environmentalists.
praise.by: John F. Kerry, former Secretary of State and Special Presidential Envoy for Climate
praise.cred: former Secretary of State and Special Presidential Envoy for Climate

praise.q: This is an immensely informative and very important book. The story of how climate change and global security are intertwined—and how the US Department of Defense grasped this reality to become the US government leader in embedding climate-change resilience into its core responsibilities—is told here by a woman whose deep insight and remarkable political skill helped her do more than anybody to achieve this stunning result.
praise.by: John P. Holdren, Harvard University, former Science Advisor to the President
praise.cred: Harvard University, former Science Advisor to the President

praise.q: Over the course of my naval career, I came to appreciate how climate change was affecting global politics—literally altering the geostrategic landscape.
