Sherri Goodman tells the untold story of how many of our nation’s military leaders came to appreciate this challenge and recognize climate change as one of the key global threats of our age.
praise.by: Admiral James Stavridis, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander and coauthor of 2054: A Novel
praise.cred: former NATO Supreme Allied Commander and coauthor of 2054: A Novel

praise.q: Climate change adds additional instability to a world already disrupted by strategic competition with China, Russia and Iran, two regional wars, and mounting challenges from new technologies such as AI and cyber. Sherri Goodman shows how the US military is managing these risks and why a bipartisan approach to building a more resilient future supports our national security.
praise.by: Stephen J. Hadley, former US National Security Advisor

praise.q: As Secretary of Defense, my job was to protect the nation from all manner of threats. Climate change was one of those threats. But it’s not just one among a list of many. It’s the threat that multiplies all others. Sherri Goodman gives us a first-hand account of how climate change affects the military and our national security—and the steps we must take to build a more secure future.
praise.by: Leon Panetta, former Secretary of Defense

praise.q: When I led US forces in Europe and Latin America, I witnessed how a changing climate creates instability, from weather extremes to environmental degradation. Threat Multiplier is a must-read for military, civilian, and humanitarian leaders who want to understand how a changing climate and the energy transition affect decision making on these critical global challenges.
praise.by: General Wesley Clark, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander

praise.q: When the scientific understanding of climate change and its impacts was just beginning to solidify, Sherri Goodman realized that climate change will be at the very heart of military security, for the United States and every other country. Her leadership on climate change as a threat multiplier has been the stimulus for a rich and dynamic body of scholarship and policy. This book connects the threads that link the science and the strategy. And it points the way to a safe world.
praise.by: Christopher Field, Director, Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment
praise.cred: Director, Stanford Woods Institute for the Environment

books.title: Unauthorized Welfare
books.subtitle: The Rise and Consequences of Immigrant Status Restrictions
books.tagline: The evolution of federal welfare policies between the 1930s and the 1970s, and the roots of today’s anti-immigrant politics
books.description:
Between 1935 and 1972, US federal welfare policy did not distinguish between citizens and noncitizens. Noncitizens, including unauthorized immigrants, were eligible for Social Security and unemployment insurance as well as other mean-tested programs. But that changed in the 1970s, when the federal government first barred unauthorized immigrants from virtually all federal welfare programs and loosened confidentiality provisions that prohibited health and welfare officials from sharing information with immigration authorities. In Unauthorized Welfare , Cybelle Fox examines the emergence of federal immigrant status restrictions in American social welfare policy and describes its wide-ranging effects. She shows that, contrary to previous accounts, the roots of today’s anti-immigrant politics are found not in the 1990s, when California’s Proposition 187 banned undocumented immigrants from almost all nonemergency services, but in the 1970s with the new federal constraints.

Fox explores the consequences of this restrictive turn in federal welfare policy for undocumented immigrants, their US-citizen family members, and anyone suspected of being in the country without authorization—especially Mexicans and Mexican Americans. She also considers the effects on state and local communities, which were no longer reimbursed for the costs of care they provided to unauthorized immigrants. Over time, federal restrictions increased intergovernmental tensions, contributed to popular nativism, and helped propel the passage of anti-immigrant state and federal initiatives two decades later. With Unauthorized Welfare , Fox sheds new light on the origins of anti-immigrant policies and politics.
books.bio: Cybelle Fox is Class of 1944 Professor of Sociology at the University of California, Berkeley. She is the author of Three Worlds of Relief: Race, Immigration, and the American Welfare State from the Progressive Era to the New Deal (Princeton).

praise.q: Unauthorized Welfare is bound to be a classic. Without question, this major contribution to the scholarship on welfare and immigration policy in the United States is simply masterful and full of new insights that will command attention from historians, sociologists, and political scientists in this area.
praise.by: Filiz Garip, author of On the Move: Changing Mechanisms of Mexico-US Migration
praise.cred: author of On the Move: Changing Mechanisms of Mexico-US Migration

books.series: Princeton Studies in American Politics: Historical, International, and Comparative Perspectives

books.title: Welcome to Analogville
books.subtitle: Low-Tech Solutions from the Front Lines of Urbanism
books.tagline: A provocative case for why we must rediscover and adapt proven human-scale solutions to meet the challenges of climate change and social upheaval
books.description:
Technological innovation is often presented as the answer to every challenge, but many of the solutions we need for the future are not new at all. Drawing on experiences from the COVID-19 pandemic, his years on the ground doing volunteer work in wartime Ukraine, and examples from cities around the globe, urban design expert Mikael Colville-Andersen explores how communities respond when modern systems fail and reveals what they can teach us about building resilient societies in challenging times.

Reporting from the front lines of war, climate change, and global pandemic, Colville-Andersen shows how crisis exposes what actually works—and how our future may depend on rediscovering what we already know. From low-tech urban practices that have been forgotten or overlooked to contemporary experiments in some of the world’s most innovative cities, he shares a rich catalogue of proven tactics that can help communities facing climate change, social fragmentation, resource constraints, and growing uncertainty.

Through stories of citizen-led initiatives, public-space transformation, and creative approaches to everything from mobility and food security to water management and climate adaptation, Welcome to Analogville offers a hopeful vision of how citizens and cities can become more resilient, adaptable, and human-centered in an increasingly unpredictable world.
books.bio: Mikael Colville-Andersen is a Danish urban designer and one of today’s leading voices on urbanism, championing human-scale design in cities around the world. He is the author of Copenhagenize: The Definitive Guide to Global Bicycle Urbanism (Island Press).

books.title: When You Listen to This Song
books.subtitle: On Memory, Loss, and Writing
books.tagline: A quietly powerful exploration of memory and forgetting, from one of France’s leading feminist public intellectuals
books.description:
“A labyrinth of looping, interlocked narratives which spiral out beyond the Annex as the night progresses. . . . The penultimate pages of this elegiac book are a sword-thrust to the heart.”—Laurel Berger, Irish Times

In 2021, the award‑winning French writer Lola Lafon was granted permission to stay overnight—alone for ten hours—in the Annex in Amsterdam where Anne Frank and her family had hidden from the Nazis between 1942 and 1944. Lafon’s visit to this space, where Anne Frank wrote her famous diary, evoked the confinement and constant danger suffered by the Franks, and the family’s ghostly presence as well. “The night was inhabited, lit by reflections,” Lafon writes. “Some urgency still dwelled at the heart of the Annex, crouched there, ready to be discovered.”

Exploring the many stories told about Anne Frank, Lafon tries to find the precocious girl at the heart of the venerated and exploited myth, a disciplined writer whose famous diary is in fact a wonderfully constructed literary work. Throughout, Lafon reflects on what it means to lose loved ones, both Lafon’s own family in the Holocaust and her childhood friend to the Khmer Rouge. A prizewinner and bestseller in France, this book asks us to consider the stories we tell ourselves about tragedy, how we grapple with loss, and why, in the face of danger and confinement, women write.
books.bio: Lola Lafon is a French writer who grew up in Eastern Europe and studied dance and music in Paris and New York. Her prizewinning books include The Little Communist Who Never Smiled and Reeling: A Novel . She lives in Paris, France. Lauren Elkin is a French and American writer and translator. She is the author of several books, including Flâneuse and Scaffolding , and lives in London, UK.

praise.q: More than Lafon’s elegant recapitulation of the facts, what’s interesting here is how she constructs a labyrinth of looping, interlocked narratives which spiral out beyond the Annex as the night progresses. . . . The penultimate pages of this elegiac book are a sword-thrust to the heart.
praise.by: Laurel Berger, Irish Times

praise.q: Lafon is unflinching in her observations . . . and in her questions. . . . The story of the Franks and the author’s quest to investigate her own experience intertwine to create a testament to the power of words. A poignant historiography of Anne Frank’s writing and the author’s response to it.
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews (starred review)

praise.q: This is a gor­geous book, and the trans­la­tion reads as flaw­less. It is hard to find a new approach to the Holo­caust, Anne Frank, and to those who died and those who sur­vived, but Lafon does so in this mov­ing and orig­i­nal book.
praise.by: Shara Kronmal, Jewish Book Council

praise.q: Named a Kirkus Reviews Best Nonfiction Book of 2025
An indispensable guide to the afterlife of the death of ‘that man’, a story which, fully 70 years after its belated confirmation, only seems likely to continue.
praise.by: Paul Moore, History Today

praise.q: Lola Lafon’s book is an unusually haunting meditation on history, memory, and what the living owe to the dead, via a uniquely personal immersion in the story of Anne Frank.
praise.by: Ruth Franklin, author of The Many Lives of Anne Frank
praise.cred: author of The Many Lives of Anne Frank

praise.q: This book brings Anne Frank to life not as a victim, but as a writer. In meditating on Frank’s genius, Lafon lets us into writing’s intent: ‘We write . . . to lay hold of reality.’
praise.by: Darcey Steinke, author of This Is the Door: The Body, Pain, and Faith
praise.cred: author of This Is the Door: The Body, Pain, and Faith

praise.q: Lola Lafon’s memoiristic meditation sneaks up on us with a quiet but distinct emotional and intellectual intensity. Rather than narrate in booming voiceover the familiar story of the very famous and doomed Anne Frank, Lafon slips in through a much more interesting writerly side entrance, as she prepares herself for an unlikely sort of sleepover with the dead.
praise.by: Adina Hoffman, author of Till We Have Built Jerusalem: Architects of a New City
praise.cred: author of Till We Have Built Jerusalem: Architects of a New City

praise.q: Grand prix des lectrices de Elle, Prix Décembre, and Prix Les Inrockuptibles

books.title: Zionism Before Israel
books.subtitle: Jewish Nationalism in the Age of Empire
books.tagline: A major revisionist history of the Zionist movement, showing that many early Zionists pursued imperial alliances rather than Jewish sovereignty.
books.description:
It is often said that the Zionist movement has always been devoted to the idea of Jewish nationhood and deeply hostile to foreign rule. Yet before the creation of Israel in 1948, many influential Zionists imagined a future defined not by independence but by limited self-governance under the British Empire. In parallel, British bureaucrats and politicians increasingly came to view the Zionist project as compatible with their own imperial aspirations. The result was an unlikely alliance built on the dream of imperial federalism, which would unite multiple self-governing polities in a Commonwealth of Nations.

Arie Dubnov traces the rise and fall of this fraught British-Jewish collaboration from the late Victorian era to the Suez Crisis in 1956. During the interwar years, especially, Zionist and British visions of Jewish autonomy under empire came to anchor debates about the future of Palestine. Some, for example, sought to turn Palestine into a British dominion. Others imagined dividing it along the Swiss model of confederation, with Jewish, Muslim, and Christian cantons. These now-forgotten proposals were regarded as realistic, even promising, options at the time. During the late 1930s, however, the British began to repackage such visions into the idea of partition. At the same time, a new generation of revolutionary Zionist activists began to pivot fully toward the pursuit of Jewish nationhood.

Reconstructing the diplomatic gambits, political alliances, and colonial violence that undergirded these forgotten debates, Zionism Before Israel invites us to reconsider the influence of both nationalism and imperialism on the Zionist road to statehood.
books.bio: Arie M. Dubnov is Associate Professor of History and International Affairs and Max Ticktin Chair of Israel Studies at George Washington University. He is the author of Isaiah Berlin: The Journey of a Jewish Liberal and coauthor of Zionism: A New History .

praise.q: Brilliant and exhilarating. Israeli independence has made the path that led to it difficult—indeed, impossible—to understand. That is, until this remarkable book followed it without presuming where it would lead. Along the way, Arie Dubnov reanimates what once was: the inseparability of the British empire and Zionist goals until surprisingly late in the day.

books.title: Art and Ecological Impact
books.subtitle: An Artist's Guide to Environmental Practice
books.authors: Edited by Mary Mattingly and Suzanne Watters
books.tagline: An expansive resource for how art can help us imagine and practice more regenerative ways of living on the planet
books.description:
With contributions by over sixty artists from around the globe—including Mark Dion, Olafur Eliasson, the Guerrilla Girls, and Maya Lin—this richly illustrated volume brings together diverse approaches to ecological art making across disciplines, cultures, and generations, with each artist offering insights into their materials, processes, and strategies for encouraging public engagement.

More than a survey, Art and Ecological Impact is a call to action. It emphasizes creative approaches that move beyond representation and highlights art’s impact not only on living systems but also on the social values that cultural change depends on. The book invites artists, students, and nonpractitioners alike to consider how materials are sourced, how communities are involved, and how artistic practice can contribute to cultural and ecological regeneration.

Primarily geared toward artists, art educators, and art students, it provides:

• A road map of socioecological practices rooted in care, interconnection, and responsibility.

• An indispensable reference for those seeking ways to align their practices with ecological values.

• A practical teaching tool with concrete methods, questions for reflection, prompts, and other resources.

• A global snapshot of environmental art in the twenty-first century that reveals art’s impact on ecosystems and society.
books.bio: Mary Mattingly is a Brooklyn-based visual artist whose work explores issues of sustainability, climate change, and displacement. Suzanne Watters is a Brooklyn-based textile artist focused on nature connectedness and sustainability.

praise.q: An inspiring kaleidoscope of idea and intentions for anyone invested in the future of the planet.
praise.by: Brianne Cohen, author of The Empathic Lens: Art, Animism, and Ecology in Contemporary Southeast Asia
praise.cred: author of The Empathic Lens: Art, Animism, and Ecology in Contemporary Southeast Asia

praise.q: An invitation to consider, even soul search, what it means to meaningfully make and consume works of art in our time of ecological and social predicaments.
praise.by: Cameron Davis, University of Vermont

books.title: Before West and East
books.subtitle: The Byzantine Empire in World History
books.tagline: A revelatory new history of Byzantium that shows it was a center of global power for a thousand years, dominating the medieval world and shaping the emergence of the Latin West and the Muslim East
books.description:
The seeds of contemporary Western culture are rightly identified with Greece, Rome, and Christianity. But this cultural combination was forged across the entire Mediterranean world by the “inner Greek fire” of Byzantium long before there was a self-conscious West and East. In Before West and East , acclaimed historian Judith Herrin sets out how the thousand-year civilization of Byzantium preserved and expanded Christian belief and then withstood the Islamic explosion that it inspired. In this brief, richly illustrated history, she shows that both the Latin West and the Muslim East were founded upon the existence of Byzantium at the center of the medieval world.

Herrin reveals how the “New Rome” of Constantinople (now Istanbul) became the leading metropolis of the Middle Ages thanks to the remarkable administrative machine that ran the empire from the vast palace complex of the Palation. Strikingly, she demonstrates how Byzantium’s capacity to survive through reinvention owes much to the role of the “imperial feminine” as the wives, mothers, and sisters of emperors acted to preserve their dynasty or restore orthodoxy. She also explains why the Byzantine Empire has long been ignored, abused, and treated as the “Other”—and how this hostility became a lasting prejudice after Constantinople, then the capital of Christianity, was sacked by the Venetians in the Christian crusade of 1204.

Written in a brilliant style and featuring close to 100 color illustrations, Before West and East restores one of history’s most important empires to its rightful place.
books.bio: Judith Herrin is an award-winning historian and the author of many books, including Byzantium , Ravenna, and The Formation of Christendom (all Princeton), which have been translated into many languages. She was the first Stanley J. Seeger Professor of Byzantine History at Princeton University and was awarded the Heineken Prize, the Dutch “Nobel,” for history. She is professor emeritus in the Department of Classics at King’s College London and an honorary citizen of Ravenna.

books.title: Cinderella Tales
books.subtitle: An Anthology of Translations
books.authors: Laura Nüffer, Newell Ann Van Auken
books.tagline: A captivating collection of Cinderella tales translated from more than fifteen languages and cultural traditions, revealing surprising new dimensions to an iconic story
books.description:
This anthology brings together fresh, contemporary translations of lesser-known Cinderella tales representing the story’s full geographic range. With an emphasis on Asia and the Middle East, it includes orally transmitted lore along with highly crafted literary tales. Many of these stories are presented here in English for the first time.

The tales in this volume challenge popular assumptions about what a Cinderella story ought to be. Though sharing familiar core elements—a dead mother, a cruel stepmother, a magical helper, a lost shoe—they diverge from the well-known storyline in startling ways. Fairy godmothers are vanishingly rare, and fish, cows, frogs, and even ogresses play the part of magical helper. While the heroine is often identified by a shoe, romance tends to remain on the margins. Instead, bitter rivalries between sisters and enduring bonds of affection between mothers and daughters drive the plots. Each tale is accompanied by a brief note introducing its source and cultural context. The book’s invaluable introduction explores the transformations that Cinderella tales have undergone in traveling across languages, cultures, and time, and the role of translation in these transformations.

The contributors to this volume, many of whom are award-winning literary translators and writers, have produced splendid new translations that inspire us to reexamine our assumptions about one of the most recognizable fairy tale heroines.

The languages from which the tales are translated include Chinese (modern and classical), Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, HMoob, Tibetan, Persian, Arabic (from Iraq, Oman, and Egypt), Hausa, Greek (modern and ancient), Yiddish, Brazilian Portuguese, French, German, and the Bolognese dialect of Italian.
books.bio: Newell Ann Van Auken teaches classical Chinese literature and a course on Cinderella at the University of Iowa. Her books include Spring and Autumn Historiography: Form and Hierarchy in Ancient Chinese Annals . Laura Nüffer is assistant professor of East Asian languages and cultures at Colby College. Her work has appeared in edited volumes such as A Cultural History of Fairy Tales in the Age of the Marvelous .

books.title: Digital Queers and High Tech Gays
books.subtitle: The History of LGBTQ+ Cyber Activism
books.tagline: How LGBTQ+ cyber activists in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom shaped the Internet and how the Internet shaped LGBTQ+ activism.
books.description:
Digital Queers and High Tech Gays tells the history of LGBTQ+ cyber activism in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom and how it ultimately shaped the Internet as we know it.

Beginning in 1980, queer cyber activists founded regional, national, and international organizations of engineers, scientists, and high-tech professionals. From advocating for tech workers’ rights to equipping LGBTQ+ organizations with the hardware and software needed to do their work to creating in-person and online spaces where they shared information, socialized, and preserved queer histories, LGBTQ+ cyber activists used analog and digital technologies to transform queer folks’ lives both on the Internet and away from the keyboard.

Queer cyber activists also built crucial Internet infrastructures and expanded the idea of who could be an Internet user. And, through their work with LGBTQ2S+ archives, they ultimately created the tools needed to preserve their own history. In this book, Alex Ketchum shares their untold, pathbreaking story.
books.bio: Alex Ketchum is Associate Professor at McGill University's Institute for Gender, Sexuality, and Feminist Studies and Director of the Just Feminist Tech and Scholarship Lab. She is an elected member of the Royal Society of Canada: College of New Scholars and author of several books including Engage in Public Scholarship , Ingredients for Revolution, and How to Organize Inclusive Events and Conferences . She is also the coeditor of Queers at the Table .

books.title: Empire of Destruction
books.subtitle: A History of Nazi Mass Killing
books.tagline: The first comparative, comprehensive history of Nazi mass killing—showing how genocidal policies were crucial to the regime’s strategy to win the war
books.description:
Nazi Germany killed approximately 13 million civilians and other noncombatants in deliberate policies of mass murder, mostly during the war years. Almost half the victims were Jewish, systematically destroyed in the Holocaust, the core of the Nazis’ pan-European racial purification programme.

Alex Kay argues that the genocide of European Jewry can be examined in the wider context of Nazi mass killing. For the first time, Empire of Destruction considers Europe’s Jews alongside all the other major victim groups: captive Red Army soldiers, the Soviet urban population, unarmed civilian victims of preventive terror and reprisals, the mentally and physically disabled, the European Roma and the Polish intelligentsia. Kay shows how each of these groups was regarded by the Nazi regime as a potential threat to Germany’s ability to successfully wage a war for hegemony in Europe.

Combining the full quantitative scale of the killings with the individual horror, this is a vital and groundbreaking work.

praise.q: In this meticulous, vivid, and grim accounting of the deliberate murder of civilians by Nazi Germany, Kay manages to keep a balance between careful analysis of the evidence and reminders of the horrors of the events he is describing, including individuals’ harrowing recollections of surviving by hiding among dead bodies—often those of their own relatives.
praise.by: Lawrence D. Freedman, Foreign Affairs

praise.q: The book’s great contribution is that it coherently brings together a range of findings, offering a single point of reference for innovative research from the past two decades and beyond. . . . A must-read for anyone teaching classes on the history of World War II, the Nazi period, or twentieth-century Germany more broadly, as well as graduate students studying the Holocaust, Germany, the USSR, or war in twentieth-century Europe.
praise.by: Maris Rowe-McCulloch, German History

praise.q: The book hits the mark due to the fact that it is not individual acts of murder but the entirety of the extermination of civilians by Germans and Austrians in the Second World War that is presented and analysed in an academically rigorous manner. Anyone who wants to understand German and Austrian history— and, beyond that, anyone who wants to understand the human condition—should read the book.
praise.by: Hans-Heinrich Nolte, Zeitschrift für Weltgeschichte (Journal of World History)
praise.cred: Zeitschrift für Weltgeschichte (Journal of World History)

praise.q: Kay has produced a truly exceptional book that will be of great interest to general readers and students as well as academics. He presents us with a compendium of Nazi mass killing that both illuminates understudied areas and places them in dialog.
praise.by: Waitman Wade Beorn, History: The Journal of the Historical Assocation
praise.cred: History: The Journal of the Historical Assocation

praise.q: Empire of Destruction by Alex J. Kay is an inclusive, compelling, and innovative history . . . comparative history at its best. . . . Kay masterfully overcomes the challenges involved in writing about a staggering number of victims.
praise.by: Jan Burzlaff, Holocaust and Genocide Studies

praise.q: Kay has written an impressive book in all respects. Despite the depressing topic, the book provides a fascinating read and is very accessible, the argumentation convincing and sound. By using many eyewitness accounts, diaries, and other personal documents, the author gives a face to all those killed, so that we do not forget that behind the statistics were individuals. It often makes the book a slap in the face. Kay does an excellent job in showing the multilayered explanations for the way the Third Reich acted in its ‘Empire of Destruction.’ This is a reference book that no one interested in the history of Nazi Germany and the process of mass murder and genocide can afford to miss.
praise.by: Martijn Lak, Journal of Slavic Military Studies

praise.q: Empire of Destruction offers students and scholars alike an up-to-date account of Nazi collective violence that pushes us to reconsider how parallel atrocities can help to explain each other.
praise.by: Chelsea Sambells, European History Quarterly

praise.q: This thought-provoking integrative history of Nazi mass killing sets up a new standard for books on Germany’s darkest period.
praise.by: Sönke Neitzel, coauthor of Soldaten: On Fighting, Killing and Dying
praise.cred: coauthor of Soldaten: On Fighting, Killing and Dying

praise.q: Alex Kay performs a great service by juxtaposing the fates of the different population groups who fell victim to Nazi persecution in a way that clarifies the Nazis’ uncompromising drive to domination. The monstrous brutality and vast scale of Nazi mass murder is laid bare here unequivocally, clearly, and unflinchingly.
praise.by: Dan Stone, author of The Liberation of the Camps
praise.cred: author of The Liberation of the Camps

praise.q: Building on his earlier insightful work about Nazi policies of destruction, Alex Kay now offers a powerful and empirically convincing account of German war crimes that, for the first time, brings together the history of the Holocaust and genocidal policies against other population groups in a single analytical frame. Lucid and innovative, Empire of Destruction is a major milestone.
praise.by: Robert Gerwarth, author of Hitler’s Hangman

books.title: How to Quit Writing Forever and Never Look Back
books.tagline: One gay boy’s weaponized self-loathing emerges as a growing fracture of psychedelic despair and deep psychic violence.
books.bio: R. Fay is a writer from bumfuck nowhere North Carolina. They now live in Philadelphia. This is their first book.

books.title: I Was Called
books.subtitle: The Activist Life of Coretta Scott King
books.authors: Edited by Jeanne Theoharis and Traci Parker
books.tagline: A groundbreaking portrait of Coretta Scott King, whose brilliant activism and extraordinary life has been obscured in popular memory—until now
books.description:
Coretta Scott King is one of the most memorialized yet misunderstood figures in the American civil rights movement pantheon, remembered as beautiful, respectable, and endlessly supportive of her famous husband. We don’t know her at all.

Scott King was a visionary activist in her own right. More of an activist than King when they met, Scott King led her husband to live his faith through social justice, fought throughout her life against the triple evils of poverty, racism, and militarism, and led the charge inside mainstream civil rights organizations for LGBTQ rights. The Kings’ marriage was a political partnership that directed the course of the civil rights struggle. After Dr. King’s death, her activism in support of global justice and racial-economic justice continued for decades.

Edited by the New York Times –bestselling author Jeanne Theoharis and accomplished historian Traci Parker, and featuring contributions from leading civil rights movement historians, this collective biography shows that it is high time we know the real Coretta Scott King, lifelong freedom fighter and powerful force in American history.
books.bio: Jeanne Theoharis is distinguished professor of political science and history at Brooklyn College and the author of many books, including the New York Times-bestselling The Rebellious Life of Mrs. Rosa Parks . Traci Parker is an associate professor of history at the University of California, Davis, and the author of Department Stores and the Black Freedom Movement.

books.title: In Praise of Purple Prose
books.subtitle: A Guide to Writing with Elegance, Opulence, and Indulgence
books.tagline: A playful and irreverent argument for—and practical guide to—writing in a rich and extraordinary style
books.description:
When it comes to literary style, the commonplace wisdom of composition classrooms, newsrooms, and editorial offices has long been that less is more. Students are taught that the best prose is that which eschews ornamentation and rhetorical flourish. But what if sometimes more is more? In Praise of Purple Prose playfully and cheekily contests a century worth of convention that rejects the baroque and byzantine as “purple prose,” making the case that fun and joy in language can be as important as concision and comprehension. Part style guide and part manifesto, the book rewrites the rules on writing.

Ed Simon encourages writers to embrace the extraordinary, to call upon the classical rhetorical devices, and to relish in the richness of description and the erudition of allusion. He demonstrates that serpentine syntax, eccentric diction, and idiosyncratic punctuation, when used judiciously, can express the complexity of experience, bring out the pleasures of language, and help readers develop a unique voice in a world where AI threatens to make everyone sound alike. To illustrate its arguments, the book features examples of extraordinary prose from dozens of writers, including John Donne, Virginia Woolf, Joan Didion, Salman Rushdie, Marilynne Robison, and Zadie Smith.

Playful and provocative, In Praise of Purple Prose will leave readers with a new appreciation for fancy prose and inspire writers to draw on all of the liveliest and most powerful resources of English in their work.
books.bio: Ed Simon is Public Humanities Lecturer in English at Carnegie Mellon University and the editor in chief and founder of The Pittsburgh Review of Books. A monthly columnist at Literary Hub , he is the author of several books, including Devil’s Contract: The History of the Faustian Bargain , which was named a New Yorker Best Book of the Year .

books.title: Inequality and Globalization
books.subtitle: Improving Measurement through Integrated Financial Accounts
books.tagline: A remedy for the gap between micro and macro data, making measures of inequality and national income consistent with each other
books.description:
Increasing inequality, the impact of globalization, and the disparate effects of financial regulation and innovation are extraordinarily important topics that fuel spirited policy debates. And yet the facts underlying these debates are of doubtful accuracy. In reality, as Archawa Paweenawat and Robert Townsend show in Inequality and Globalization , there is a large gap between micro household surveys, which measure key outcomes such as inequality, and aggregated financial accounts, which measure macroeconomic totals and growth. Paweenawat and Townsend propose a remedy: integrated financial accounts, in which the flows in income statements, including saving and investment, are consistent with the changes in financial assets and liabilities in the balance sheet at micro and macro levels. None of the leading US micro household surveys or macro accounts meets this criterion.

Drawing on extensive data from fieldwork in Thailand, Paweenawat and Townsend show how consistent integrated financial accounts at the individual household and small enterprise level can be created using household and firm survey data. Aggregated to the village level, these accounts can link anecdotal stories of individual households to their financial accounts, document the real impact on them from growth, and assess what would have happened to them if trade and financial liberalization had not been allowed. Paweenawat and Townsend then describe the next logical step: creating integrated financial accounts for the United States, working from the ground up and the top down. Only with these integrated accounts will policy debates on inequality and globalization have a solid factual basis.
books.bio: Archawa Paweenawat , a development economist, is Head of Business Research of the Puey Ungphakorn Institute for Economic Research at the Bank of Thailand. Robert M. Townsend is the Elizabeth and James Killian Professor of Economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. He is the author of Distributed Ledgers: Design and Regulation of Financial Infrastructure and Payment Systems , Chronicles from the Field: The Townsend Thai Project , Households as Corporate Firms: An Analysis of Household Finance Using Integrated Household Surveys and Corporate Financial Accounting.

praise.q: The book is a significant scholarly contribution. The authors, both leading experts on the topic, present new methods and concepts for integrating financial data from multiple sources to provide consistent, integrated financial accounts.
praise.by: Nirvikar Singh, University of California, Santa Cruz

praise.q: Everyone has an opinion on inequality. Few realize how hard it is to appropriately conceptualize and measure, in particular if one wishes to make suggestions as to how policy might reduce inequality. This book represents the absolute frontier in measurement and brings the double entry method of bookkeeping to bear on household finances.
praise.by: Andrew Caplin, New York University

books.title: Isn’t It Ironic.
books.subtitle: The Amazing Saga of a Not-Bad Figure of Speech
books.tagline: From the ancient Greeks to the “irony-poisoned” Generation Z, an enlightening, entertaining, and surprising history of an essential idea and rhetorical tool that people love, hate, and love to debate
books.description:
For 2,500 years, irony has been a subject of fascination—and vexation. In Isn’t It Ironic , acclaimed author Ben Yagoda presents a compelling tour of irony’s complicated history in literature, philosophy, the arts, and popular culture—from Plato and Jane Austen to Ralph Ellison and David Letterman, and from the post-9/11 “end of irony” to today’s debates about being “irony-pilled” or “irony-poisoned.”

Beginning in ancient Greek comedy and adopted by Plato to describe Socrates, irony was viewed for two millennia as a potent rhetorical tool: making a point by saying something different (and sometimes opposite) from what you really meant. But the word took a turn in the nineteenth century, when a clergyman named Connop Thirlwell first to used “ironic” in the now familiar, but still controversial, sense of a striking incongruity between expected and actual outcomes. At the same time, philosophers like Kierkegaard proposed irony as nothing less than a core principle of life. The last century has seen ever-faster pendulum swings: irony outbreaks followed by backlashes against it.

As it traces the changing meanings and fortunes of irony, Isn’t It Ironic explores masters of the trope such as Swift, Flaubert, Twain, and Hemingway, and anti-ironists like David Foster Wallace. It also argues that the most ironic century was the eighteenth, but the most ironic decade was the 1970s.

A witty yet authoritative literary and cultural history, Isn’t It Ironic is a captivating demonstration of why irony has intrigued writers, artists, and their audiences for so many centuries.
books.bio: Ben Yagoda is the author or editor of fifteen books, including Gobsmacked! The British Invasion of American English (Princeton), About Town: The New Yorker and the World It Made , and Will Rogers: A Biography . His writing has appeared in The New York Times , The New Yorker , The Atlantic , and many other publications. He has been a Guggenheim and MacDowell fellow and is professor emeritus of English at the University of Delaware.

books.title: Mathopoly
books.subtitle: A Play About Elitism, Inequality, and Friendship in Academia
books.authors: Indira Chatterji, Christian Gorski, Annette Karrer and Giulio Tiozzo
books.tagline: A darkly humorous play about three mathematicians navigating academic life amidst privilege, elitism, and inequality in academia.
books.description:
Mathopoly is an artistically illustrated theatrical play following the early academic lives of three mathematicians as they navigate ambition, friendship, privilege, elitism, and inequality within academia. Philosophical in tone yet shaped by irony and dark humor, the play, written by Indira Chatterji, Christian Gorski, Annette Karrer, and Giulio Tiozzo, explores the tensions of academic life through fictional scenes inspired by real experiences.

The project originated in the spring of 2024 during the thematic program on Randomness and Geometry at the Fields Institute, where mathematicians from around the world exchanged stories about their academic lives. Despite their different backgrounds, many realized their experiences shared similar themes: competition and collaboration, hierarchy and belonging, and uncertainty and pressure. From these conversations, a collection of scenes emerged that the authors wove into the play.

Mathopoly is part of the Academic Scenes initiative, which employs theater as a tool for dialogue within academia.
books.bio:
Indira Chatterji (Author)

Indira Chatterji is Professor of Mathematics at University of Côte d'Azur. She specializes in geometric group theory, with interests in societal and applied problems.

Christian Gorski (Author)

Christian Gorski is Postdoctoral Scholar at University of Washington. His research lies at the intersection of probability and metric geometry and sometimes includes forays into group theory and ergodic theory.

Annette Karrer (Author)

books.title: Nations Ascendant
books.subtitle: The Global Campaign Against Imperialism and the Making of Our World
books.tagline: How an international community of anticolonial activists, thinkers, and campaigners came together during the interwar period to demand the end of formal imperialism across the world
books.description:
This book chronicles the formation of a global community of anticolonial activists and thinkers and how they developed ideas about universal decolonization and the end of empires. At the turn of the twentieth century, the global imperial order was imperiled. In cities across the world, revolutionary factions emerged where nationalists deliberated radical, even violent paths to a post-imperial world.

Vladimir Ilyich Lenin belonged to and wrote about this world, one primarily defined by the crisis of imperial order and the looming question of the future of national communities. As he and his compatriots seized power in Moscow in October 1917, he announced the dawn of a new era in which the empires of the world would eventually fall in the throes of the impending world revolution. Zaib un Nisa Aziz shows how Lenin’s call resonated with imperial decriers, who saw in his victory the possibility of a new world. Anticolonialists from all over the world turned to Moscow to help realize their own political visions. In so doing, they forged an international revolutionary movement that sought universal liberation and social revolution.
books.bio: Zaib un Nisa Aziz is assistant professor of modern South Asian history in the Faculty of History at the University of Cambridge and a fellow at Corpus Christi College.

books.title: Objects of Inquiry
books.subtitle: A Field Guide to Interdisciplinary Learning in Art Museums
books.tagline: A detailed and practical guide to creating and implementing transformative object-based learning experiences across a range of academic fields
books.description:
With visits from more than one hundred Harvard courses each semester, the Harvard Art Museums are a leader in object-based learning. From single-class visits exploring themes through selected works to semester-long seminars based in the museums, these partnerships take many forms, fostering critical thinking and museum literacy for students in disciplines from art history to environmental science to gender studies to law. Building on these experiences as well as a rich body of theoretical scholarship, Objects of Inquiry shares the Harvard Art Museums’ evidence-based pedagogy with educators across disciplines and levels of experience with object-based learning.

In engaging chapters that build on one another, Jen Thum and Laura Muir—key architects of the Harvard Art Museums’ pedagogical approach—share their thoughts about how to design unique learning experiences aligned with course-specific goals. A roundtable discussion of student and faculty perspectives highlights the lasting impact of museum visits and critical engagement with diverse artworks across time and place.

As a practical resource for museum professionals and educators, Objects of Inquiry features scripts for forming partnerships and examples of how to conduct outreach to faculty across campus; a detailed guide to visit planning; a dozen active learning strategies with thorough descriptions; an exploration of the importance of teaching data; and case studies from actual Harvard courses.

Distributed for Harvard Art Museums
books.bio: Jen Thum is the associate director of Academic and Campus Partnerships and research curator and Laura Muir is the director of academic and public programs, division head, and Louis Miller Thayer Research Curator, both at the Harvard Art Museums, Cambridge, MA.

books.title: Our Mental Health, Their Mental Illness
books.subtitle: Blurry Boundaries in the Twenty-First Century
books.tagline: How mental health and illness have transformed from medical concepts into widely shared cultural ideas
books.description:
Discussions about mental health are ubiquitous, and individuals’ “challenges,” “struggles,” and “crises” are frequent fodder for media coverage and online content. Mental illness, however, is strikingly absent from these conversations. Why are we comfortable talking about mental health but not about mental illness? In Our Mental Health , Their Mental Illness , Amy Johnson argues that as these two terms became widely shared cultural ideas, their meanings diverged. People can struggle with their mental health and still be considered “normal”; meanwhile, the language of mental illness is deployed to describe those who are perceived as abnormal—or even dangerous. Drawing on articles from major US newspapers published between 1980 and 2020 and Reddit posts from 2019 to 2023, Johnson explores how the public came to understand mental health and mental illness as two sides of a social—and not simply medical—boundary.

Employing methods of computational text analysis as well as qualitative close reading, Johnson shows that despite open discussions of mental health, mental illness remains a stigmatized category, broadly used to denigrate certain groups and often deployed as an explanation for violent acts. The boundary between mental health and mental illness, drawn by actors other than medical professionals, clearly delineates who is normal and who is not, creating an axis of inequality that intersects with other axes such as race and gender. The twenty-first century focus on mental health has not created universal acceptance but has instead contributed to social division.
books.bio: Amy L. Johnson is assistant professor of sociology at Indiana University Bloomington.

praise.q: The book is a significant contribution. The cultural toolkit behind ‘mental illness’ and ‘mental health’ has not been explored before, and the idea that mental health, as constituted today, is a new and significant concept rings absolutely true.
praise.by: Jason Schnittker, author of Unnerved: Anxiety, Social Change, and the Transformation of Modern Mental Health
praise.cred: author of Unnerved: Anxiety, Social Change, and the Transformation of Modern Mental Health

praise.q: There are many contemporary books about the ubiquity of medicalization, the spread of diagnostic categories, or the rise of wellness paradigms. However, this book is unique in that it grounds these claims in systematic textual data and shows the flip side of the normalization of mental health in the ongoing stigmatization of mental illness.
praise.by: Alex V. Barnard, author of Conservatorship: Inside California’s System of Coercion and Care for Mental Illness
praise.cred: author of Conservatorship: Inside California’s System of Coercion and Care for Mental Illness

books.title: Out of the Shadows
books.subtitle: Native American International Activism, 1975-1981
books.series: The Henry Roe Cloud Series on American Indians and Modernity
books.tagline: A revelatory history of the Native American activists who reshaped international politics—building international alliances, redefining sovereignty, and laying the foundation for today’s global Indigenous rights movement
books.description:
This book uncovers the pivotal yet long‑overlooked story of how Native American activists reshaped international conversations on sovereignty, human rights, and Indigenous self‑determination during the transformative decade of the 1970s. Drawing on extensive archival research and new oral histories, Jennifer R. O’Neal reveals how Native leaders built powerful alliances across borders, international organizations, and Indigenous nations to confront centuries of erasure and reclaim their place on the world stage.

Set against the backdrop of the Red Power movement, evolving federal Indian policy, and the rise of Cold War human rights politics, this groundbreaking study traces the work of key organizations—including the International Indian Treaty Council, the National Congress of American Indians, the National Indian Brotherhood, and the World Council of Indigenous Peoples—as they navigated shifting political landscapes to influence both domestic and global policy.

Through a lens of Indigenous relationality and resurgence, O’Neal demonstrates how activists

• reframed sovereignty as a living practice rooted in land, culture, and community, and

• resisted settler‑colonial political constraints while forging new pathways toward justice.

Illuminating a defining era of Indigenous political innovation, O’Neal brings this history out of the shadows—honoring the activists who envisioned a different future and built the foundations of today’s global Indigenous rights movement.
books.bio: Jennifer R. O'Neal is assistant professor in the Department of Indigenous, Race, and Ethnic Studies at the University of Oregon. She is an enrolled member of the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde.
subjects: The Henry Roe Cloud Series on American Indians and Modernity

books.title: The Age of Plunder
books.subtitle: Winners and Losers in the Low Growth Era
books.tagline: Why the consequences of a prolonged period of weaker economic growth will be more profound than anyone dares to predict
books.description:
In the heady progress of the post-war era, our lifestyles changed, our political systems adapted, and rapid economic growth became the model of every developed economy. But this prevailing consensus is falling apart around us. Growth is now, at best, no more than anaemic. Policymakers dream about an AI revolution and tweak their fiscal rules to accommodate a newly-austere economic reality but, all the while, government debt soars, financial markets become increasingly jittery, and voters lose trust in their politicians.

Celebrated economist Stephen D. King asks how our politics will adapt to such persistently low growth. While leaders make fiscal promises based on a future that is unlikely to materialise, nationalism thrives, battlelines are drawn between perceived winners and losers, and the rules-based international order crumbles. The absence of growth triggers invidious political wrangling over tax, welfare, defence and infrastructure, intensifies competition for resources, and leads to social instability.

King shows how our new world is governed by them-and-us divisions over limited economic spoils. This is the political economy of plunder.
books.bio: Stephen D. King is senior economic adviser at HSBC, and fellow of the Academy of Social Sciences and the Society of Professional Economists. He is the author of four previous books, including Financial Times book of the year We Need to Talk About Inflation .

books.title: The Divided Totality
books.subtitle: War and Revolution in the 21st Century
books.tagline: Democracy is a façade stretched over a deepening authoritarian core.
books.description:
Traversing the wreckage of financial crises, imperial wars, and ecological collapse, Maurizio Lazzarato maps the inner logic of a capitalism that has fused the powers of the state, the military, and finance into a single machine of domination. From the trenches of 1914 to today's techno-military experimentation, he shows how capital's "creative destruction" has become a permanent strategy of rule—one in which production and devastation are indistinguishable, and in which democracy survives only as a façade stretched over a deepening authoritarian core.

Gathering Lazzarato's most urgent recent essays, this volume offers a devastating critique of neoliberal fantasies, Western innocence, and the naive liberal belief that capitalism can be governed into civility. Against the West's new imperial wars and the financial aristocracies that command them, Lazzarato insists on the centrality of class struggle, global revolt, and the strategic alliances emerging across the South and the banlieues alike. A book for the crises we are already living through, it calls for nothing less than a total rupture with the state–capital machine and a political imagination adequate to the coming century of struggle.
books.bio: Maurizio Lazzarato is an Italian sociologist and philosopher whose work spans political theory, labor studies, and the critique of contemporary capitalism. Now based in Paris, he first became active in the Autonomia movement in Italy before going into exile in France. Lazzarato's studies of immaterial labor, debt, neoliberalism, war, and global class struggle have been translated into numerous languages. A researcher at the National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University, he is the co-author, with Éric Alliez, of Wars and Capital , and the author of The Intolerable Present: the Urgency of Revolution , among many others.

books.title: The Last Persian Empire
books.subtitle: A History of the Sasanians
books.tagline: A major new history of the Sasanian Persians
books.description:
The Sasanian Empire was the largest state in late antiquity. Its frontiers reached north into the Caucasus, south to the Persian Gulf, and from the Oxus River to the Euphrates. Over four centuries, belief systems were codified, new allegiances forged, and immense fortifications erected. The Sasanians built great cities, like Nishapur, and created beautiful artefacts that were shipped to far-flung places—their glassware even reached as far as Japan.

In this engaging, insightful new history, Eve MacDonald traces the story of the Sasanian Empire from the second century CE to its collapse in the seventh. Moving through key individuals, MacDonald explores the importance of Zoroastrianism, the remarkable power of its queens, and the increasing influence of Christianity. This is an unforgettable account of an extraordinary dynasty and the indelible mark it left on the legends, folklore, and cultures of the world, from the Mediterranean to China.
books.bio: Eve MacDonald is an archaeologist, lecturer, and travel guide. She has taught at several universities in the UK and Canada and is currently a senior lecturer in ancient history at Cardiff University. She is author of Hannibal and Carthage .

books.title: The Market for Skill
books.subtitle: Apprenticeship and Economic Growth in Early Modern England
books.tagline: How apprenticeship shaped the English economy
books.description:
Apprenticeship dominated training and skill formation in early modern Europe. Years spent learning from a skilled master were a nearly universal experience for young workers in crafts and trade. In England, when apprenticeship reached its peak, as many as a third of all teenage males would serve and learn as apprentices. In The Market for Skill , Patrick Wallis shows how apprenticeship helped reshape the English economy.

Some historians see apprenticeship as a key ingredient in the industrial revolution; others agree with Adam Smith in seeing it as wasteful and conservative. Wallis shows that neither of these perspectives is entirely accurate. He offers a new account of apprenticeship and the market for skill in England, analyzing the records of hundreds of thousands of individual apprentices to tell the story of how apprenticeship worked and how it contributed to the transformation of England. Wallis details the activities of apprentices and masters, the strategies of ambitious parents, the interventions of guilds and the decisions of town officials. He shows how the system of early modern apprenticeship contributed to the growth of cities, the movement of workers from farms to manufacturing and the spread of new technologies and productive knowledge.

In this groundbreaking study, Wallis argues that apprenticeship succeeded precisely because it was a flexible institution which allowed apprentices to change their minds and exit contracts early. Apprenticeship provided a vital channel for training that families could trust and that was accessible to most young people, whatever their background.
books.bio: Patrick Wallis is professor of economic history at the London School of Economics and Political Science and the coeditor of Apprenticeship in Early Modern Europe .

praise.q: Authoritative. . . .This thoroughly researched and well-argued book reminds us, if it had slipped our minds, that the development of future human capabilities remains vital, no matter what wonders the tech bros continue to promise us.
praise.by: Stefan Stern, Financial Times

praise.q: Economists now consider human capital to be one of the most significant sources of growth. This book, the product of extensive research and unique data, revisits the Industrial Revolution from the point of view of apprenticeship and paints an exciting picture of its contribution to the transformation of the English economy.
praise.by: Maarten Prak, Utrecht University

praise.q: An excellent study that explores very important aspects of human capital formation through apprenticeship in England, in a period of great economic change. It brings together a large body of original evidence and uses it skillfully to solve many key controversies, offering the reader an overall understanding of the main features that made apprenticeship in early modern England so unique. A significant scholarly contribution.
praise.by: Karine van der Beek, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev

praise.q: Conjoining quantitative rigor with acute cultural sensibility and theoretical elegance, Wallis’s brilliant study contributes mightily to the rehabilitation of apprenticeship as a crucial economic and social lever in early modern England.
praise.by: Steven Laurence Kaplan, Cornell University

books.title: The Prophet's Daughter
books.subtitle: The Life of Fatima Zahra
books.tagline: A groundbreaking biography of Fatima Zahra, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad
books.description:
Fatima Zahra was the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad and wife of his spiritual heir Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth caliph of Islam and the first imam for Shia Muslims. Today, she is more than a revered historical figure: she is a symbol of resistance, knowledge, and divine light. Her famous Khutbat al-Fadakiyya (Sermon of Fadak)—a powerful protest against the confiscation of her inheritance—remains a cornerstone of Islamic discourse on women’s rights, legal justice, and political resistance.

Hassan Abbas and Benish Zahra explore the life of the Prophet’s daughter. Charting her experiences and influences, Abbas and Zahra examine Fatima’s roles as a mystic, theologian and reformer in early Islam. They reveal the theological, legal, and political dimensions of Fatima’s teachings, and position her as a foundational thinker for contemporary discussions on gender and justice in Islam.

This fascinating biography illuminates Fatima Zahra’s devotion to the Prophet and his mission, her partnership with Ali in faith and moral courage, and her enduring significance as a source of spiritual guidance and inspiration.
books.bio: Hassan Abbas is Distinguished Professor of International Relations at National Defense University in Washington D.C., and author of The Prophet’s Heir and The Return of the Taliban . Benish Zahra is a human rights activist based in Maryland, and co-author of Ali ibn Abi Talib on Leadership and Good Governance .

books.title: The Singing Lives of Warblers
books.subtitle: Understanding the Songs of All 50 Species across the USA and Canada
books.authors: Donald Kroodsma, Bruce Byers, Scott Weidensaul
books.tagline: An immersive journey into the hidden world of warbler song
books.description:
The Singing Lives of Warblers explores the singing minds of the tiny, winged jewels that visit from the tropics all too briefly each spring and summer. Through fifty you-are-there narratives, two scientists with nearly a century of combined field experience take readers into the field on listening adventures filled with discovery. In the first account, prowl through the night with the Ovenbird, discovering that its complex nocturnal song is likely intended for females. In the fiftieth, stand at dawn with Painted Redstarts, marveling at their astonishing rapid-fire exchanges as rival males duel in song across a territorial boundary. And for all 48 species in between, readers accompany the authors to hear these warblers as few people have ever heard them. Comprehensive and authoritative yet deeply inviting and engaging, this accessible book is an invitation to listen mindfully and attentively to one of the world’s most beloved groups of birds.

Covers all 50 regularly occurring species in the United States and Canada

Focuses on how males attract mates, sing through the dawn chorus, defend territories, and much more

Reveals what singing tells us about mating status, motivations, and emotions

Corrects many misconceptions about warblers

Connects readers to nearly 700 recordings on an accompanying website—more than 50 hours of immersive listening

Features hundreds of sonagrams, graphs, and stunning color photos
books.bio: Donald Kroodsma is a well-known authority on birdsong and professor emeritus of ornithology at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. His many books include The Singing Life of Birds and Listening to a Continent Sing (Princeton). Bruce Byers is a retired biology professor at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, and the coauthor of Biology: Life on Earth .

books.title: The Velocity of Care
books.subtitle: Reimagining the Patient Journey Through American Health Care
books.tagline: A new framework for understanding why patient journeys through American healthcare are circuitous, costly, and lonely—and how to improve them.
books.description:
Every year, millions of Americans endure healthcare odysseys—harrowing journeys in search of clarity and relief from their health problems. The toll is mounting: staggering waste, declining trust, a demoralized workforce, and a growing burden of chronic illness. All are symptoms of a system designed to churn out services rather than guide patients efficiently and humanely from sickness to health.

In The Velocity of Care , Harvard surgeon and former healthcare consultant Rena Xu offers a new framework for diagnosing—and treating—what ails American medicine. “Velocity of care” captures not just speed but direction: it asks whether a patient’s trajectory is advancing from problem to resolution or veering off course.

This missing dimension holds the key to improving care. Xu traces the system’s dysfunction to the relationship problems among four key stakeholders—patients, providers, payors, and places of care—whose competing interests keep trajectories slow, costly, and fragmented. Through vivid stories and incisive analysis, she shows what a system oriented around trajectory improvement would look like and how to achieve it.

The Velocity of Care is essential reading for healthcare professionals, policymakers, and innovators—and for anyone who has struggled to navigate the system and felt the gap between what care is and what it could be.
books.bio: Rena Xu, MD, MBA, is Assistant Professor of Surgery at Harvard Medical School and a surgeon, researcher, and advisor to executive leadership at Boston Children’s Hospital. Previously, she was a management consultant at Boston Consulting Group, focused on healthcare. She has written for the New England Journal of Medicine , The New Yorker , The Atlantic , The Washington Post , and The Yale Review , among other publications.

books.title: To Take Back our Breath
books.subtitle: Maya Women and Art Across Time
books.authors: Victoria I. Lyall and Michelle Rich
books.tagline: A groundbreaking journey through Maya women’s art, agency, and enduring cultural influence
books.description:
Addressing the long-standing absence of Maya women in conventional histories of art, this groundbreaking book highlights the artistic accomplishments of Maya women, as well as their broader influence on Indigenous and non-Indigenous communities in Mexico, Central America, and beyond. Victoria Isabel Lyall and Michelle Rich also interrogate the perceived division between the ancient Maya and their contemporary descendants, highlighting an often-overlooked, yet vibrant, living culture.

Bilingual with English and Spanish text, and richly illustrated with a unique fusion of ancient Maya objects and artworks from contemporary Maya and other Indigenous artists, this book guides readers through nine spaces, examining how Maya women have occupied and transformed them into arenas for intergenerational learning, physical and spiritual nourishment, power, and protest.

The spaces explored in the book are:

• streets/las calles

• plazas/las plazas

• markets/los mercados

• maize fields/las milpas

• patios/los patios

• kitchens/las cocinas

• the natural world/la naturaleza

• the built world/el mundo construido

• bodies/los cuerpos

Complementing Lyall and Rich’s perspective of how each space resonates across time in works of art, profiles of Maya women contribute brief biographies and personal points of view that further underline the significant contributions of Maya women in both ancient times and today.

Published in association with the Denver Art Museum and the Dallas Museum of Art

books.bio: Victoria Isabel Lyall is Frederick and Jan Mayer Curator of Art of the Ancient Americas at the Denver Art Museum. Michelle Rich is Ellen and Harry S. Parker III Associate Curator of Indigenous American Art at the Dallas Museum of Art.

books.title: A Landmark Through Time
books.subtitle: On Classifying Greek Art and Architecture
books.tagline: What representations of a monument across centuries can tell us about how we engage with, study, and understand the past.
books.description:
In a square in the heart of Athens, a cylindrical structure rests on a platform made up of large stone blocks. Semi-columns encircle it, and a slanted roof sits on top, with a plantlike feature at its highest point. Focusing on this well-documented remnant of classical Greece, the so-called Choregic Monument of Lysikrates, Milette Gaifman considers the history of engagement with this ancient landmark, looking at how names, scholarly classifications, and illustrations have shaped our understanding of it from the fourth century BCE to the modern era.

Studying the landmark’s representation through centuries of scholarship and illustrations, she examines how modes of engagement with the past often impose their own baggage, interpretive forces, and inaccuracies. By being aware of their histories, advantages, and limitations, Gaifman argues that we should treat them as helpful tools and flexible guidelines rather than as strict or unmoving criteria. A Landmark Through Time reveals how adapting and expanding traditional frameworks of classification and technologies can open fresh vantage points for appreciating the complexity and ingenuity of ancient Greek art and architecture.

books.title: And Who Will Witness Us?
books.subtitle: A Histofuturist Account of Black Literacies on the Rust Belt
books.tagline: An imaginative exploration of the historical narratives that shape Black life today, showing how the past is never truly left behind, but is always alive in the present, shaping the future.
books.description:
Most people have probably never heard of New Castle, a Rust Belt city in western Pennsylvania. Education scholar S. R. Toliver describes it as “a stop on the road to elsewhere. But as a former resident, New Castle remains the endpoint of my journey, the highway exit I take, the place I go when I say I’m headed home.” Combining an autoethnography of growing up and being educated in New Castle with a remarkable study of Histofuturism, Toliver’s And Who Will Witness Us? reveals the historical erasure of Black people and their literary practices.

First, Toliver turns to the past, presenting a multifaceted portrayal of Black life in New Castle. She draws from personal insights, archival data, and oral histories to uncover historical disinvestment and the violence of anti-Blackness and anti-Indigeneity sown into the soil and soul of a city. At the same time, she highlights how, despite systemic neglect, Black people have used their stories to author themselves into existence, creating counter histories that reflect the richness and depth of Black lives. Toliver explains how these acts of creation, in turn, shape the future, allowing Black people to resist imposed narratives and envision possibilities beyond the limits of traditional ways of thinking, knowing, and doing.

Innovative in both form and style, And Who Will Witness Us? shares how research opens space for Black people to relearn themselves and their communities. It is a reckoning with what it means to call a place, a city, a people, home.

books.title: By Heart or From the Scroll
books.subtitle: Text Quotation and Memory on the Grammatika Vases
books.description:
Grammatika vases, one of the most distinctive varieties of Hellenistic relief pottery, present modern scholars with compelling research opportunities, as they document the reception of ancient Greek literature in the Hellenistic world in various ways. Focusing on the group of grammatika vases that feature citations, By Heart or From the Scroll offers new insights into the archaeological material within its broader literary and historical contexts.

This study is based on a collection of six vases—two Boeotian bowls and four Macedonian fragments—all of which depict scenes inspired by Book 22 of the Odyssey, detailing the slaughter of the suitors by Odysseus. These vases provide a direct glimpse into the transmission of the ancient text within a particularly intriguing—and in some cases well-dated—archaeological context, establishing a reference point for other vases of the same category. The thorough examination of the script used in the citations, coupled with its juxtaposition to the epigraphic and calligraphic literary scripts found on contemporary papyri, reveals a remarkable correspondence and offers a key to understanding this type of pottery, shedding light on the people behind its production and use.

Drawing on both archaeological and epigraphic evidence, and guided by Athenaeus’ testimony regarding Dionysius Thrax and his silver Νεστορίς, this interdisciplinary approach provides a novel interpretation of the literary sources cited on these grammatika vases and a reliable terminus post quem for dating excavation efforts in Macedonia and beyond.
books.bio: Maria Nasioula is a former Fellow and Associate at the Center for Hellenistic Studies at Harvard University and the author of Ἀπὸ στήθους: The Citations on Grammatika Vases .

books.title: Equity Engines
books.subtitle: The Overlooked Colleges Delivering on Higher Education’s Promise
books.tagline: Shares novel insights into American colleges and universities that deliberately support the success of their first-generation, low-income students.
books.description:
In American higher education, universities that prioritize inclusivity and equity over exclusivity and prestige are penalized rather than rewarded, both in terms of status and resources. Consequently, very few colleges and universities both enroll large shares of low-income students and graduate them at high rates. This is terrible news, both for the first-generation, low-income students with big aspirations and for a democratic society that relies on an educated citizenry and a representative government to function.

In Equity Engines, Becca Spindel Bassett shines a light on a small group of colleges that are quietly achieving the improbable. These “equity engines” open their doors widely to low-income students and graduate them at remarkably high rates. Immersing herself in two distinct institutions, a small private liberal arts university and a large regional public university, Bassett offers a window into the unseen mindsets and policies that drive universities toward equitable outcomes. By culturally and structurally centering first-generation, low-income students and challenging the superiority of exclusive, research-oriented cultures, the faculty, staff, and administrators of both institutions achieve extraordinary results.

Combining ethnography with sociological analysis, Equity Engines presents a detailed and nuanced depiction of the people and practices that power equity engines, the pressures that challenge their operation, and how we can transform American higher education to promote a more democratic and equitable society.

books.title: Group 44
books.subtitle: Bob Tullius and the Rise of Professional Sports Car Racing in America
books.authors: Bob Tullius, John Nikas, and Neil Smith
books.tagline: The definitive history of Group 44, one of the most respected and successful racing teams in motorsport.
books.description:
Group 44 Ltd. established an unprecedented standard of professionalism, helping to propel sports car racing into a bold new era. Over the course of more than two decades, the team recorded multiple championships and hundreds of wins in various series, competing with vehicles from American Motors, Audi, Dodge, Jaguar, Lotus, MG, Triumph, and Pontiac. Written with unprecedented access to Group 44’s extensive archives, the book reveals in exacting detail the fascinating account behind this hallowed operation, focusing on the men and machines that left an indelible impression on fans worldwide. Lavishly illustrated with more than 1,400 images, most never previously published, this is an essential volume for racing enthusiasts and aficionados of the pristine green-and-white racers that won with clockwork precision from coast to coast.

Read More about Group 44

Read Less about Group 44

books.title: Hidden Ocean Forests
books.subtitle: An Undersea Journey to Uncover a Fascinating World of Kelp
books.tagline: Stunning underwater photography of the world’s great marine kelp forests and the wildlife they shelter.
books.description:
Kelp forests, which thrive in cold, nutrient-rich waters, are found along the coasts of every continent except Antarctica. These underwater environs are both stunningly beautiful and the key to entire ecosystems, as they provide food, shelter, and breeding grounds for a multiplicity of marine life. Some argue they may even have served as guides for humans over 15,000 years ago—as a continuous corridor of food and resources, along the Pacific coast, from Asia to the Americas.

With transcendent photography and compelling accounts from freedivers and conservationists Faine Loubser and Ross Frylinck, this book offers a glimpse of these ocean forests firsthand. Dive beneath the midnight sun in the Arctic Circle and watch the northern lights dance over the waters of Shetland, Scotland. In New Zealand, swim with playful sea lions off Stewart Island. In South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope, cross paths with dusky dolphins, whales, and sharks. Meet an austral sea wolf in the icy Strait of Magellan and learn from kelp harvesters on remote islands in Japan.

Hidden Ocean Forests documents kelp forests across every continent, showcasing their rich biodiversity and long-lasting impacts on human culture. These remarkable images and enchanting essays reveal the hidden beauty, significance, and fragility of these underwater forests from dives off the coasts of Chile, England, Japan, New Zealand, Norway, Scotland, South Africa, and the United States.

books.title: How to Write Well
books.subtitle: 50 Pointers on Process, Usage, and Style
books.tagline: Stop worshipping Strunk and White. Start writing well, with 50 tips and techniques from language expert Bryan A. Garner.
books.description:
For decades, people looking for a concise guide to English-language writing turned to The Elements of Style by William Strunk Jr. and E. B. White . That slim book has been used by everyone from high school and college students to professionals seeking quick advice on usage, grammar, and form. But The Elements of Style hasn’t been updated in more than a quarter century, and it no longer reflects the way good writers work or what they most need to know, especially in the age of generative AI.

How to Write Well: 50 Pointers on Process, Usage, and Style is the modern, evidence-based alternative. Leading language and writing expert Bryan A. Gamer distills a lifetime of teaching and research into 50 compact pointers for modern writers seeking to produce clear, accurate, and lively prose. You’ll learn how strong writers think, how they turn ideas into blueprints, and how they draft, revise, and tighten with ruthless selectivity. You’ll also encounter lucid guidance on grammar and punctuation that corrects Strunk & White’s famous blunders, including shaky treatment of passive voice and a fixation on trivia over substance.

How to Write Well presents a start-to-finish method: mindset, habits, process, and the concrete techniques that produce clean, forceful writing. Unlike The Elements of Style , this book doesn’t pretend your draft magically appears on the page. It shows you how to generate ideas, structure them, and build a repeatable process for everything you write—from emails and memos to articles, briefs, and books. And while emphasizing the mind and the voice of the writer, it also offers advice on working intelligently with AI while keeping full editorial control.

If you’re serious about writing, Garner’s How to Write Well is the indispensable style book you need now.
