books.title: More Than Friends
books.subtitle: Muslim-Jewish Intimacy in Algerian Music
books.tagline: Explores the Muslim-Jewish relationship through music in Algeria and its diaspora.
books.description: Today, more than six decades after the departure of Jews from Algeria to France at the moment of decolonization, music remains a compelling site for remembering Muslim-Jewish intimacy before the moment of rupture. In this way, music works against dominant discourses of Muslim-Jewish conflict and Jewish outsider status, instead presenting music as a sign of Muslim-Jewish brotherhood and of Jewish rootedness in North Africa. Yet digging deeper into the lived past and its relation to contemporary memory uncovers the fragility of brotherhood as well as competing ways to read Muslim-Jewish intimacy around music, some of which edge into rivalry, hierarchy, and difference. In More than Friends , Jonathan Glasser draws on historical archives and ethnographic research in Algeria and in France to weigh these multiple interpretations of the Muslim-Jewish past, ultimately offering an alternative, more resilient way of imagining what it means to be intimate through music.

books.title: Newspaper Verse
books.subtitle: The Dark Matter of Eighteenth-Century English Poetry
books.tagline: A study of the popular but forgotten poetry published in eighteenth-century English newspapers and their overlooked influence on the canonical work from the period.
books.description: The first book-length study of its kind, Newspaper Verse focuses on poetry published in English-language newspapers during the long eighteenth century, including odes, couplets, news poems, ballads, and elegies by such famous poets as Jonathan Swift, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Alexander Pope, Elizabeth Carter, and Thomas Gray and also verse by lesser-known or anonymous writers. For John O’Brien, these texts constitute something like the dark matter of eighteenth-century letters: the most widely read poetry in the period and yet unincorporated into existing narratives of eighteenth-century English literature. By engaging with these forgotten poems, O’Brien demonstrates how popular media enabled poetry to thrive and recovers their rich influence on the shape of English literary history.

books.title: People of the Machine
books.subtitle: Computers and Human Reason in the Cold War
books.tagline: How Cold War computational experts invested in diplomacy, world peace, and human agency created systems that threatened democratic values.
books.description:
Beginning in the 1950s, international relations experts and United States government officials built novel computer systems designed to make foreign policy knowledge and practice more scientific. Human reason, they feared, might not be enough to guarantee the survival of American democracy in a nuclear-armed world. They didn’t seek to replace humans with machines; they hoped computers would sift information or provide interactive models that analysts could use to make better decisions. But as they struggled to deliver on their ambitious goals, and as the Defense Department became more involved in their projects after the Vietnam War, their commitments to advancing knowledge, policy agency, and peace gave way to very different computing systems, ones in which correlation replaces causality and prediction replaces understanding.

In People of the Machine , Joy Rohde reveals how even the best-intentioned attempts at fostering political engagement and human autonomy evolved into an anti-democratic nightmare. Her political and intellectual history shows how the subtle and corrosive effects of technological change set the template for today’s political and conceptual regimes. Doing so reveals not just the roots of contemporary inequality and disfranchisement but how thoroughly that antihumanism has been baked into our institutions and norms.

books.title: Poetics of the Hold
books.subtitle: Variations on the Slave Ship
books.authors: Fabienne Kanor Translated by Lynn E. Palermo
books.tagline: An essential reflection on the haunting legacy of the transatlantic slave trade from award-winning French filmmaker and writer Fabienne Kanor.
books.description:
A century and a half after the passage of the last known slave ship, the hold—in which captives were imprisoned together under inhuman conditions—still haunts collective memory, particularly that of Afro-descendant artists, thinkers, and writers. With The Poetics of the Hold , scholar, writer, and filmmaker Fabienne Kanor offers a series of meditations on the transatlantic slave trade and on how the experience of the Middle Passage has been represented in modern culture of the United States, Francophone Africa, and the French West Indies.

In this important book, Kanor draws from a multitude of sources—history, literature, art, philosophy, the Négritude tradition, and Caribbean thinkers—to take readers on a journey from colonial archives to public spaces, museums, and other places of commemoration. Throughout, the image of the hold serves as a spectral monument, the traumatic reverberations of which can be felt in both the texts Kanor examines and in her own writing. While archives, logbooks, and sea reports provide information about slave ships, the stories of the slaves themselves too often remain shrouded in silence. This powerful and poetic book seeks to rectify that amnesia and to wrestle with these neglected histories and their afterlives.

books.title: Skyscrapers in Havana
books.subtitle: How the Cuban Revolution Reimagined Modern Architecture
books.tagline: Why Havana attracted the most important architects in the 1950s, and how the Cuban Revolution transformed the uses of these impressive skyscrapers.
books.description:
During the 1950s, Havana’s Vedado district became an epicenter of modern architecture. Architects from around the world—including Mies van der Rohe, Richard Neutra, and Josep Lluis Sert—worked in Cuba and helped make Havana one of the most modern capitals in Latin America. After the Cuban Revolution, the buildings designed during Cuba’s American-influenced hyper-capitalist past had to be reimagined, about what use what use could luxury hotels, private condominiums, and golf clubs could have in a socialist society. Writers and artists from around the world including Simone de Beauvoir, Agnès Varda, Allen Ginsberg, Graham Greene, and Gabriel García Márquez flocked to Havana to witness the first socialist experiment in the Americas and marveled at the modern towers. French philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre wrote about “Skyscrapers in Havana” for his first journalistic piece about his trip. In contrast, modern architects abandoned Cuba after the Revolution: not even those designers who had built projects there set foot in the island again.

Considering Havana’s architecture as part of a larger Cuban modernity, Gallo places built projects in dialogue with film, literature, and other cultural texts, revealing how poets, novelists, filmmakers, and designers theorized the city’s urban fabric. Skyscrapers in Havana features six chapters, each devoted to an iconic modernist structure, as well as five shorter meditations on the architects, including Le Corbusier, who had the opportunity to go to Cuba after the Revolution but decided to stay away.

books.title: Stewards of the Sky
books.subtitle: The Women Who Brought Climate Change Down to Earth
books.tagline: The forgotten history of grassroots climate science, built by women.
books.description:
For over two centuries, scientists have struggled to predict how people will respond to the vagaries of weather and climate. Today, governments, insurance companies, and investment firms continue to forecast what climate change will mean for local communities, setting adaptation goals from the top down. But hidden in the archives is another approach to this problem that is democratic, collaborative, and grows from the bottom up.

In Stewards of the Sky , historian Deborah R. Coen uncovers the stories of women who documented the humble drivers of change that unfold at the scale of everyday life, modeling the stewardship of the atmosphere as an equitably shared resource—a commons. These naturalists revealed how insects and plants work together to survive unusual weather, how air powers the cycle of life and death, and how people with disabilities cope with pollution. Coen spotlights Geneviève Thiroux d’Arconville, Anna Kingsford, Rosa Luxemburg, and Margaret Collins, as well as the contemporary figures Susan Cutter, Diana Liverman, and Maria Lemos, scientists and activists who resisted their colleagues’ efforts to replace traditional forms of collective security with predictive sciences that would make risk profitable. In contrast, Coen’s antiheroines demonstrated the value of humility and respect for the interpersonal and cross-species relationships that make research possible. Their work shows that surviving climate change is not a zero-sum game, that mutual aid is critical, and that antiheroic science can help build alliances that respect different ways of knowing the world.

books.title: Substrate
books.subtitle: The Poetics of Paper and the Textility of Literature
books.tagline: A study of the signifying potential of paper, the foundational material for literary texts in the modern era.
books.description:
For ease of reading, the paper of a printed page must recede far enough into the background to make ink legible. Yet paper—the primary substrate for literary texts—has its own signifying potential, its own poetics. Craig Dworkin shows that looking at the page, rather than through its illusory withdrawal, can unlock interpretive insights that readers would otherwise miss. What often seems incidental can prove to be as semantically important as the words of the text themselves.

Substrate argues that the material affordances of paper in general—its pliability, fibrous weave, and capacity to fold, tear, crumple, and shuffle—variously inform the poetics of William Blake, Stéphane Mallarmé, Jen Bervin, and Susan Howe. For all four of these poets, the qualities of paper serve as models for structuring the language of their poems in innovative ways. Dworkin further shows how each poet in turn engages paper at another level by incorporating it within the thematic ambit of key poems. The full meaning of these poems is thus inextricable from their printing. Substrate is a brilliant inquiry in poetics and the logic of media more generally.

books.title: The Collaborative Editor
books.subtitle: How to Build Trust with Writers Through Queries and Other Communications
books.tagline: Discover the techniques and tools for building a successful editor-writer relationship.
books.description:
Becoming an effective editor involves not only working proficiently with words but also learning to forge successful working relationships with the people responsible for those words. Yet this critical element of the profession is often treated as an afterthought. In this book, long-time editors Christine Steele and Lourdes Venard offer strategies for approaching the editor-writer relationship in a spirit of collaboration and trust.

The Collaborative Editor moves beyond the red pen to explore editing as a creative partnership. It teaches editors how to communicate clearly and confidently, how to listen deeply to the writer, and how to thoughtfully ask questions. By prioritizing empathy and communication, editors can build trust with writers and strip away the adversarial tension that can, at times, characterize the feedback process. With advice based on their own years of experience and drawing from interviews with a wide range of editorial professionals, Steele and Venard begin by establishing what an ideal editor-writer relationship looks like in different settings, whether freelance developmental editing for a publishing house, copyediting in a corporate setting, or other scenarios in journalism, academic publishing, and other fields. They also discuss the elements of effective feedback and how to honor cultural and contextual sensitivity in a writer’s work. Several chapters concern querying, including specific examples and suggestions. The final part of the book covers tools to help editors communicate better with writers—including generative AI—and mental health and well-being practices that support both writers and editors.

Whether you are a beginning editor or a seasoned professional, this book will help you transform your workflow from a transactional service into a true collaboration.
books.series: Chicago Guides to Writing, Editing, and Publishing

books.title: The Deathly Pleasures of Form
books.subtitle: Opera, Mimesis, Agency
books.tagline: Opera offers a rich space in which to think about problems of mimesis—how artworks imitate ideal forms, how humans imitate the things around us, and how words attempt to represent reality.
books.description: In this book, musicologist and cultural historian Sarah Collins shows how the strange, exhilarating, and uniquely self-conscious art form of opera opens itself to such contemporary, theoretical questions. The Deathly Pleasures of Form is especially concerned with the links between linguistic and bodily signification in opera through the genre’s use of figures of partial agency—disembodied voices, enchanted objects, puppets, mechanical devices. The book is structured around four emblematic figures (Faust, Don Juan, Papageno, and Hoffmann) who are paired with four objects of variable animacy (puppet, stone, silhouette, and mirror, respectively). Across these chapters, Collins develops an expanded notion of mimesis that illuminates opera’s material and mechanical investments, its filmic and other adaptations, its explicit negotiation between vocal utterance and bodily gesture, and the epistemological significance of opera’s excesses. Ultimately, Collins claims that opera performs a type of compromised agency that can offer new critical insight into the self-limiting nature of both freedom and representation.

books.title: The Intellectual Earthquake
books.subtitle: How Pragmatism Leveled Philosophy, Caused French Theory, and Reinvented Selfhood
books.tagline: A look at how pragmatism—a quintessentially “American” philosophy—was the vanguard of a cultural revolution that altered the entire world.
books.description: As shaped by William James, John Dewey, Jane Addams, and others, pragmatism is considered the most American of philosophical currents, brashly privileging action, experience, embodiment, contingency, and real-world impact. In The Intellectual Earthquake , James Livingston recaptures pragmatism’s initial scandalous vitality and its worldwide influence. Livingston ambitiously covers more than a century, showing pragmatist roots in countless strains of thought, and connecting seemingly far-flung and disparate thinkers. He also aims to explain how pragmatism has been steadily maligned and misunderstood, and he makes the case for fresh attention to its lineal influence on “French Theory.”

books.title: The Meaning of Weather
books.subtitle: A Media History
books.tagline: A sweeping history of our relationship with weather in art, media, philosophy, religion, and science—and how the climate continually defies demystification.
books.description:
We moderns tend to take the weather for granted. We know it through hourly timetables and radar maps and otherwise make it the subject of predictable and safe conversation. But weather is not safe or predictable and never has been. People have long used all their ingenuity to imagine and portray its shifty ways. As John Durham Peters argues, a closer look at the history of these efforts, from painting and poetry to cartography and close observation, has the potential to disclose something important about what it means to live in the world.

In The Meaning of Weather , John Durham Peters shows how the long history of understanding the weather has seen dreamers and data-crunchers alike craft remarkable visions of the world around us. From Babylonian astronomy to the Event Horizon Telescope, from illuminated manuscripts to television, and more, Peters explores the kaleidoscopic ways people have sought to understand, tame, or manage the weather—and how the climate resists being bridled. In this magisterial telling, Peters reimagines Western culture as a continuing struggle to know ourselves and each other through an ever-changing environment.

books.title: The Properties of Loss
books.subtitle: Riot and Restitution in Civil War New York
books.tagline: A powerful account of the claims made by victims of the 1863 Draft Riots reveals how Americans’ emotional and legal responses to loss informed the development of contemporary capitalism.
books.description: Americans once imagined that property endowed them with dignity along with their rights. But that understanding was lost in the nineteenth century, and as Joanna Cohen argues, property’s broader value went missing from our histories. In The Properties of Loss , Cohen focuses on the aftermath of Manhattan’s infamous Draft Riots in July 1863, where Civil War draft protests fomented anti-Black terrorism that set the city aflame. In the wake of this destruction, nearly 2,000 people filed claims against the city, seeking reparation. But they found that the city chose not to value their property or imagine their losses as they did. Beyond the individual stories of suffering and struggle, these claims serve as a nexus for understanding how the conception of loss, the value of property, and the obligations of restitution changed in the nineteenth century. Charting these changes by focusing closely on emotions, Cohen shows how these changes shaped contemporary capitalism and underpin a surprising array of today’s discriminatory forces.

books.title: The Republic Estranged
books.subtitle: Christians, Muslims, and Jews between Algeria and France, 1870-1919
books.tagline: Examines how the modern French Republic came into being through state efforts to assimilate Christians, Muslims, and Jews across France and colonial Algeria.
books.description:
In The Republic Estranged , Yuval Tal studies three religious communities—Christians, Muslims, and Jews—and their interactions with French settlers in colonial Algeria. While each of these groups wanted to “become French” without abandoning their communal identities, the French system had its own ideas about what kind of assimilation was possible or desirable. It welcomed Christians, excluded Muslims, and enfranchised Jews while insisting that Jews could never become as naturally French as Christians could. The result, Tal shows, was a “republican ethnic common sense” that continues to shape French politics today.

Tal argues we must understand France’s deeply entrenched anti-Muslim rhetoric as part of a larger strategy that selectively privileges Christians over and against Muslim and Jewish minorities. He focuses on a period between 1870 and 1919, in which we see how France’s supposedly universalist project of national assimilation was predicated on the notion that some ethnically and religiously defined communities were more capable of “becoming French” than others. Working with sources in Arabic, French, Spanish, and Italian, including literary, political, and legal texts, this book speaks to readers across French studies, Jewish studies, and Middle East and North African studies, showing the ongoing relevance of this important period in French history.

books.title: The Visibility Bind
books.subtitle: Being Seen, Getting Paid, and Paying the Price of Social Media Success
books.authors: Brooke Erin Duffy Edited by Erin C DeWitt
books.tagline: A revelatory look at the people, platforms, and power struggles shaping work in the creator economy.
books.description:
More than two decades after YouTube first invited scrappy amateurs to “broadcast yourself,” social media content creation has transformed into one of the fastest growing labor markets. Today, some two hundred million people work as platform-dependent content creators, influencers, or streamers. Social media platforms boldly tout the rewards of the digital creator economy: independence, flexibility, and the chance to convert one’s ingenuity into cash. Yet the image of work in this entrepreneurial Promised Land conceals a starker reality—one marked by labor precarity, exploitation, and entrenched structural inequalities.

In this essential work, award-winning communication scholar Brooke Erin Duffy analyzes the paradox of the “visibility bind.” On the one hand, labor devaluation and algorithmic suppression—where unseen forces and so-called “shadowbans” bury worker output—threaten to render creators invisible. On the other, excessive visibility introduces harms of its own, from scrutiny and surveillance to networked harassment. For creators at the margins—among them, creators of color, LGBTQ+ voices, and disability advocates—the bind is especially pronounced, belying the promise of a talent meritocracy.

Drawing on extensive, in-depth interviews and more than a decade of insight, Duffy situates creators’ experiences within the broader landscapes of self-commodification and platform capitalism. But while platforms hold immense power to structure the pathways to success, creators and influencers wield newfound sway in this high-stakes visibility game. They are organizing, building solidarity, and experimenting with new forms of labor consciousness.

Refuting conventional wisdom about creator careers, Duffy illuminates the hidden labor dynamics for a class of workers shaping everything from culture and commerce to civil liberties and geopolitical conflict. The Visibility Bind reveals the price and perils for anyone who “puts themselves out there.”

praise.q: The depth of [Duffy’s] research is evident in her insights. Her investigation reveals the tireless work and immense scrutiny that goes into every post, which are each painstakingly designed to be both ‘on brand’ and ‘authentic.’ . . . Duffy’s exploration of sexism, as well as her probe of the gig economy, makes this an interesting and informative read for anyone—even those who aren’t following Instagram’s foodies and fashionistas.
praise.by: WIRED, Top Tech Books of 2017, on Duffy's "(Not) Getting Paid to Do What You Love"
praise.cred: Top Tech Books of 2017, on Duffy's "(Not) Getting Paid to Do What You Love"

books.title: Unruly Women
books.subtitle: 200 Years of Philosophers, Romantics, and Revolutionaries
books.tagline: A vivid account of the powerful ideas and remarkable lives of eleven women philosophers across two centuries.
books.description:
When you think of modern philosophers, who comes to mind? Likely, they are popular figures such as Kant, Hegel, Marx, and Nietzsche. But what if the history of philosophy we know is missing some of its most vital voices?

As Kristin Gjesdal shows us in Unruly Women , there is an abundance of important thinkers who were famous in their time, helped shape philosophy as we know it, and yet have been pushed into oblivion. She introduces eleven iconic women philosophers, from Germaine de Staël in Paris during the French Revolution to Angela Davis during the Black freedom movement in the U.S.., whose ideas challenged and revolutionized the intellectual orthodoxies of their time. Moving across centuries, traditions, and political contexts, Unruly Women illustrates how the work of these philosophers engaged with questions that remain urgent now: What does freedom imply? How are power and inequality produced and sustained? What roles do gender, race, and class play in shaping our lives? And who gets to define what counts as knowledge, reason, and philosophy?

More than just an act of historical recovery, this book places these forgotten thinkers in conversation with one another, revealing a new history of philosophy—one shaped not only by abstract systems and canonical texts, but also by struggles over justice, emancipation, and political change. The result is a vibrant and accessible account of philosophy as something lived, contested, and deeply connected to the world around us—with unruly ideas that still matter today.

books.title: A World Worth Sharing
books.subtitle: Raymond Williams—Radical, Conservative, Socialist
books.tagline: A rich and illuminating portrait of a leading figure of Britain’s New Left whose ideas about democracy and the influence of mass media speak to us with renewed urgency today
books.description:
Raymond Williams (1921–1988) was an intellectual giant of the decades between World War Two and the end of the Cold War. He was a founding theorist of television and other media who showed how these technologies can have very different effects on our social world depending on who owns them and whose purposes they serve. A socialist with deep strains of both liberalism and conservatism, a fierce critic of capitalism, and an opponent of all forms of arbitrary power, Williams believed in deepening democracy and argued that this was possible only with a deepened sense of community. A World Worth Sharing examines his life and writings, revealing why he is a thinker for our time.

Williams came from a small, working-class village on the Welsh-English border. In novels, historical studies, and theoretical writings, he demonstrates how the experience of rural laborers and industrial workers remains essential to building a more just and humane world. His writings explore the deep and subtle interpenetrations of politics with culture, identity, experience, place, and loyalty. Political theorist and essayist Jedediah Britton-Purdy brings the same subtlety and sympathy to Williams, introducing a new generation to pathbreaking works such as The Country and the City , Culture and Society , Television , and Keywords as well as Williams’s lesser-known novels and their potential for transforming how we think about politics. This book is a critical study of Williams’s call for a democratic future founded on new relationships with each other and the land, one in which reciprocity and mutual appreciation triumph over manipulation and exploitation. It is also a part of the tradition of humane, open-spirited, and democratic radicalism that Williams shaped.

A timely meditation for the age of AI, A World Worth Sharing is a thought-provoking account of a writer and thinker who believed that a better life depends on whether ordinary people can take control of new technology and foster more democratic ways of living together.
books.bio: Jedediah Britton-Purdy is the Raphael Lemkin Distinguished Professor of Law at Duke University. His many books include Two Cheers for Politics , This Land Is Our Land (Princeton); After Nature , and For Common Things .

books.title: Beyond Membership
books.subtitle: A Theory of Modular Citizenship for a Programmable World
books.tagline: A radical theory of citizenship as modular, algorithmically governed rights rather than a fixed status of national membership.
books.description:
Beyond Membership argues that twenty-first-century citizenship is no longer all-or-nothing. It can be pushed and pulled—stretched and warped—by rights. Instead of treating membership as the source of rights, A. Aneesh flips the script. He starts with the enforceable rights people actually hold—the rights to enter, work, reside, claim welfare, or vote—and shows how these bundles now determine how much citizenship one effectively possesses.

The book traces a long arc from kinship-based social reproduction to modern institutions and, ultimately, to the if-this-then-that logic that increasingly governs access to labor markets and social rights. Beneath that arc is a clash between two social orders. One is built around kinship—blood, soil, family, and belonging—the emotional force behind national citizenship. The other is built around function—roles, rules, competence, algorithmic design—where kinship is recoded as nepotism and friendship as cronyism , and steadily discredited by organizational norms. As social reproduction shifts from family and lineage to institutions and rights regimes, citizenship becomes modular: a programmable bundle of rights rather than a fixed status of national membership.

Through detailed cases including Canada’s skilled-worker ranking system, citizenship-by-investment programs that trade capital for passports, and ancestry-based statuses like the Overseas Citizenship of India, Aneesh shows how labor, capital, and ancestry are translated into scores and thresholds that decide who may work, settle, and benefit.
books.bio: A. Aneesh is Executive Director of the Schnitzer School of Global Studies and Languages at the University of Oregon and a professor of global studies and sociology. He is the author of Virtual Migration and Neutral Accent.

books.title: Coded Power
books.subtitle: How to Fight Digital Despotism and Reclaim Our Data
books.tagline: Freeing ourselves from the top-down control of tech oligarchs
books.description:
Coded power is social control—power over other people’s relationships. This can be seen today in the top-down control over data exerted by tech oligarchs—billionaires like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg. DOGE’s takeover of key government institutions early in the second Trump administration was a particularly blatant example of an attempt to exercise coded power by tapping into critical information systems of government. In this book, Co-Pierre Georg and Katharina Pistor call for empowering data producers—that is, all of us who use AI and search engines, or post on social media—rather than those who control proprietary data infrastructures.

Georg, an economist, and Pistor, a legal scholar, explain that coded power emerges when some assert power over the fabric that shapes society. Unchecked, it penetrates deeply into social relationships in order to advance the interests of the coders—the oligarchs—and their clients. Legal coded power goes back centuries. Digital coded power and its effect on our society have become apparent only recently. It is exercised as despotic power imposed by the will of the coders to deny data producers the right to self-determination. Choices about digital technology made in the past, Georg and Pistor argue, were often driven by libertarian ideology rather than technological inevitability. They propose an alternative, decentralized structure, aided by the blockchain and new privacy-enhancing technologies, in which data control is assumed jointly by data creators—and data sharing is determined by creators’ willingness to do so rather than the dictates of digital despots.
books.bio: Co-Pierre Georg is professor of practice in financial technology at the Frankfurt School of Finance and Management and the director of the Frankfurt School Centre for Digital Economics. Katharina Pistor teaches at Columbia Law School and is the codirector of Columbia’s Center for Political Economy. She is the author of The Code of Capital: How the Law Creates Wealth and Inequality (Princeton) and The Law of Capitalism and How to Transform It .

books.title: Collective Stupidity
books.subtitle: When Groupthink Goes Wrong and How to Put It Right
books.tagline: How epidemics of collective stupidity are threatening our world—and how businesses, governments and other organisations can adopt powerful strategies for making better decisions
books.description:
The world is facing epidemics of collective stupidity—and it may be our biggest problem since it prevents us from solving all of our other problems. Every news cycle provides fresh examples of nations and organisations full of smart people with smart technology acting in stupid ways—countries that start wars without serious plans, companies that self-destruct and big groups of people that believe big lies. In Collective Stupidity , Geoff Mulgan provides an engaging new explanation for what’s going wrong and offers a host of practical steps that businesses, governments, nonprofits and organizations of all kinds can take to avoid the pitfalls of bad groupthink.

Collective Stupidity vividly tells stories of this phenomenon—from Australia’s war against emus and China’s battles against sparrows to financial bubbles and conspiracy theories about chemtrails. These aren’t just large-scale versions of individual stupidity. Rather they’re often fueled by benign or rational intentions: our desire to save mental energy, our need to be liked and our hunger for a world that makes sense. But there are concrete steps organisations and whole societies can take to immunize themselves against the worst of collective stupidity. The key is tapping the power of metacognition: methods for thinking better about how we think, including ways to use AI to make us collectively smarter rather than dumber—and ways for countries to learn from their mistakes.

Collective stupidity isn’t inevitable. But it needs to be systematically and deliberately designed against if we are to realise our collective intelligence. This book shows the way.
books.bio: Geoff Mulgan is a professor at University College London and the author of many books, including Big Mind: How Collective Intelligence Can Change Our World (Princeton). He has held senior roles in UK governments, including director of the Strategy Unit. He was CEO of the Young Foundation and of Nesta, the UK’s National Endowment for Science, Technology and the Arts. He has also made TV and radio programs for the BBC.

books.title: Habitats of Asia
books.subtitle: A Field Guide for Birders, Naturalists, and Ecologists
books.authors: Iain Campbell, Charley Hesse, Surya Ramachandran, Dale Forbes
books.tagline: A fully illustrated field guide to all of Asia’s major habitats—packed with invaluable information to help you understand these habitats and their wildlife
books.description:
Whether you’re a birder, naturalist, eco-traveler, or ecologist, knowing the surrounding habitat is essential to getting the most out of your time in the field. This authoritative illustrated guide covers every major habitat found in Asia. It presents an easy-to-use system for exploring and enjoying habitats by combining vivid wildlife assemblages with detailed descriptions of vegetation, geology, and climate. Compact, easy to use, and requiring no scientific background, Habitats of Asia redefines how we experience the landscapes in this spectacular region of the world.

Features engaging, fact-filled descriptions of 113 major habitats

Blends state-of-the-art habitat maps with informative infographics and more than 300 stunning color photos of habitats and their wildlife

The incisive text enables anyone to assess and understand habitats anywhere in Asia—quickly and reliably

Describes iconic and indicator species of birds, mammals, and plants

An ideal travel companion for birders, naturalists, and wildlife enthusiasts

A go-to reference for conservationists within the IUCN framework, ecologists, and policymakers
books.bio: Iain Campbell is a professional nature guide and habitat ecologist whose books include (with Ken Behrens and Keith Barnes) Habitats of Africa (Princeton). Charley Hesse is a professional nature guide whose books include (with Iain Campbell and Phil Gregory) Habitats of Australia, New Guinea, and the Solomons (Princeton). Dale Forbes is a lifelong naturalist and conservationist whose books include (with Iain Campbell and Pete Morris) Habitats of Europe (Princeton). Surya Ramachandran is a professional nature guide and one of India’s most celebrated wildlife photographers.

books.title: Handbook of Learning in Virtual Reality
books.authors: Edited by Jan L. Plass, Richard E. Mayer and Guido Makransky
books.tagline: A landmark reference work on learning and training in immersive virtual reality based on evidence and empirical research.
books.description:
The Handbook of Learning in Virtual Reality is the first comprehensive, evidence-based compendium of research on learning in immersive virtual reality (VR) for academic instruction and professional training. Written by leading researchers from around the globe, this landmark reference work synthesizes the rapidly growing body of the scientific literature on learning with VR, aiming to define and shape this emerging educational technology discipline.

Jan Plass, Richard Mayer, and Guido Makransky establish a solid empirical and theoretical foundation for VR-based learning. They focus on immersive VR—using head-mounted displays like the Meta Quest or HTC Vive—and examine how the subjective feeling of presence impacts learning outcomes.

The book provides foundational overviews, a theoretical framework spanning cognitive, affective, and social processes, and crucial media comparison research (VR versus conventional media). It delves into value-added instructional design features—such as collaboration, generative activities, virtual agents, and haptic input—that boost learning outcomes. Finally, it explores disciplinary-based applications in medicine, science, second language learning, and job training, alongside special topics like accessibility, assessment, and the use of VR with culturally diverse populations.
books.bio:
Jan L. Plass (Editor)

Jan L. Plass is the Paulette Goddard Chair in Digital Media and Learning Sciences and Professor at New York University, the founding director of the CREATE Center for Research and Evaluation of Advanced Technology in Education, and codirects the Games for Learning Institute. He is coauthor, with Slava Kalyuga, of Rethinking Cognitive Load Theory and the lead editor of the Handbook of Game-based Learning (MIT Press).

Richard E. Mayer (Editor)

Richard E. Mayer is Distinguished Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences at the University of California, Santa Barbara. He is the author or coauthor of more than 600 publications and 35 books, including Multimedia Learning , Learning as a Generative Activity , The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning , and Applying the Science of Learning .

Guido Makransky (Editor)

books.title: Heaven's Oblivion
books.tagline: A feverish and gripping novel about obsession, creation, and redemption.
books.description:
After being mauled and disfigured by a lion during the 1966 International Automobile Show in New York City, actress and model Nell Theobald became obsessed with legendary soprano Birgit Nilsson, stalking her from opera house to opera house across the world, before dying mysteriously in 1977.

Forty years later, a young bookseller and music journalist discovers Theobald’s enticingly strange and patchy archive. He grows enamored with the scope of her life, uncovering a woman tormented by her lofty, romantic whims and her need to make art. Who haunted sordid nightclubs and rewrote entire operas by evening. Who was part of the wrong crowd and whose life grew increasingly grim because of it. So what happened to her, really?

As the unnamed narrator struggles to forge a career for himself while attempting to account for Theobald’s life, he grows increasingly desperate to find any semblance of truth in a contemporary New York City complicated by surveillance and infinite layers of mediation.

Heaven’s Oblivion is an operatic noir rendered in sensitive and poetic prose. Its dreamy—and at times searingly comical—tone renders the glamorous clubs and opera houses of the 1970s alongside the experimental art communities present in New York today.

Above all else, it is an exuberant meditation on the struggle to love and create art in a world that doesn’t understand.
books.bio: Chris Molnar is a writer, filmmaker, and editor whose work has appeared in outlets including The Believer , BOMB , and Esquire . He has co-edited anthologies including Unpublishable , Archways 1, and Last Poems by John Farris. His Wild Radio video-poems with B. Kite include Gas Stations at Night and Artifacts of the Moon . He was co-founder of Archway Editions, as well as the Writer’s Block, the first independent bookstore in Las Vegas, and is a founding member of Enigma Editions. He lives in New York City.

books.title: How to Depolarize
books.subtitle: Remaking the World's Democracies in the Twenty-First Century
books.tagline: A new framework for understanding and combating polarization in contemporary democracies
books.description:
Political polarization occurs when a society divides into entrenched, hostile, and persistently antagonistic camps. Can a democracy withstand such pressure? In How to Depolarize , political scientists Jennifer McCoy and Murat Somer call this kind of extreme and tenacious division pernicious polarization and offer both a new way to understand it and methods for countering it. Pernicious polarization, they explain, does not emerge on its own; it is created by political entrepreneurs who deliberately choose divisive strategies that exploit societal anxieties and democratic weaknesses to advance their own agendas. Their opponents then respond in kind. To combat this, McCoy and Somer propose a different kind of politics, equally strategic but constructive rather than pernicious.

Drawing on contemporary and historical examples from around the world, with the United States and Turkey as detailed case studies, McCoy and Somer identify three major societal fault lines that fuel the phenomenon. Issues of national identity and nationalism often result in an “us versus them” outlook; democratic backsliding turns the defense of democracy itself into a political dispute; and economic inequality creates grievances that fuel pernicious polarization both directly and indirectly. McCoy and Somer argue that these fissures can be transformed from sources of division into foundations for renewal. They outline two strategies for depolarization: active depolarization, which works to defuse divisive issues and reactivate shared bonds; and transformative repolarization, which—perhaps counterintuitively—strategically repolarizes society around reconstructive programs including reforms that will eventually foster unity rather than division.
books.bio: Jennifer L. McCoy is the Regent’s Professor Emeritus of Political Science at Georgia State University and nonresident scholar at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. She is the coauthor of International Mediation in Venezuela . Murat Somer is professor of political science and international relations at Özyeğin University Istanbul. He is the author of Return to Point Zero: The Turkish-Kurdish Question and How Politics and Ideas (Re)Make Empires, Nations, and States . McCoy and Somer coedited two special issues on polarization, the later one in The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science , “Polarizing Polities: A Global Threat to Democracy.”

books.title: Outlines of Pyrrhonism
books.tagline: An authoritative new translation of an important work of ancient philosophical skepticism
books.description:
In this volume, Richard Bett, a leading translator of and authority on the ancient Greek skeptic Sextus Empiricus, presents the first new, complete English translation in decades of the philosopher’s best-known work, Outlines of Pyrrhonism , together with an introduction and extensive commentary. In clear, modern English, the translation captures Sextus’s direct and frequently witty style, and the accessible commentary, which draws on the latest scholarship, offers a detailed vision of Sextus’s aims and approach.

Outlines of Pyrrhonism is the only surviving work by Sextus that includes a general account of his variety of skepticism: Pyrrhonian skepticism, claiming inspiration from the philosopher Pyrrho of Elis. This general account appears in Book I of the work, while Books II and III apply Sextus’s method to the main areas of philosophy recognized in later antiquity: logic, physics, and ethics. Bett’s commentary analyzes Sextus’s arguments, explaining their historical context and assessing their philosophical merits, and discusses points of the Greek text and translation where these present difficulties.

The result is an authoritative edition of an essential work of ancient Greek philosophy.
books.bio: Sextus Empiricus, who is thought to have lived around 200 CE, belonged to the Empirical school of medicine. He is the only ancient Greek skeptic of whom complete works survive, and the most important of these is Outlines of Pyrrhonism . Richard Bett is professor of philosophy at Johns Hopkins University, where he is also affiliated with the Department of Classics. His books include Pyrrho, His Antecedents, and His Legacy. He is also the editor of The Cambridge Companion to Ancient Scepticism and the translator and editor of How to Keep an Open Mind: An Ancient Guide to Thinking Like a Skeptic (Princeton). He has now translated all the surviving works of Sextus Empiricus with notes or commentary.

praise.q: This is the best translation of Sextus’s Outlines of Pyrrhonism that has ever been done. I expect that Richard Bett’s edition will become the definitive translation and commentary for generations to come.
praise.by: Chelsea Bowden, Denison University

praise.q: This admirable book offers a systematic, historically sensitive, and philosophically engaged commentary that takes into account the proliferation of new scholarship on the Outlines of Pyrrhonism published over the past few decades.
praise.by: Stefan Sienkiewicz, University of Oxford

books.title: The Arrow of Shame
books.subtitle: How the World Makes Us Feel—and How to Stop Blaming Ourselves
books.tagline: A powerful philosophical meditation on shame, the social emotion that pervades our lives—and isn’t merely in our heads
books.description:
For far too long, we have been led to believe that shame is a feeling we inflict on ourselves. We are told to go easier on ourselves and practice self-compassion. But what happens when self-compassion isn’t enough? Why are we still self-conscious, insecure, or feeling like imposters? The Arrow of Shame gives relief to anyone who has ever blamed themselves for feeling bad.

Philosopher Mariana Alessandri offers a new way of thinking about shame, blending personal stories and real-world examples of shaming with insights from figures such as Jean-Paul Sartre, Gloria Anzaldúa, Erving Goffman, Frantz Fanon, and Simone de Beauvoir. From mild embarrassment to outright self-loathing, shame is the feeling of being involuntarily exposed to judgment. For all of us, but especially for socially stigmatized groups, shame is neither self-caused nor optional. When shame’s arrow pierces us, we often ask, “What’s wrong with me?” when we should be asking, “What’s wrong?” Alessandri helps us to interrogate the shaming practices in society and to realize that, while unavoidable, feeling self-conscious is a perceptive, socially attuned response to a judgmental environment.

This insightful, thought-provoking book offers a new lens through which readers can see how a shaming society encourages us to believe that we are being overly sensitive, that we are making things up, or that our feelings of unworthiness are all in our heads. We can’t avoid shame entirely, but we can stop blaming ourselves.
books.bio: Mariana Alessandri is professor of philosophy at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. She is the author of Night Vision: Seeing Ourselves Through Dark Moods (Princeton). Her writing has appeared in leading media outlets such as The New York Times , Aeon , and New Philosopher .

books.title: The Backsliders
books.subtitle: Why Leaders Undermine Their Own Democracies
books.tagline: Why democracy is under assault across the globe by the leaders entrusted to preserve it
books.description:
Democracies around the world are getting swept up in a wave of democratic erosion. Since the beginning of the twenty-first century, two dozen presidents and prime ministers have attacked their countries’ democratic institutions, violating political norms, aggrandizing their own powers, and often trying to overstay their terms in office.

The Backsliders offers the first general explanation for this wave. Drawing on a wealth of original research, Susan Stokes shows that increasing income inequality, a legacy of late twentieth-century globalization, left some countries especially at risk of backsliding toward autocracy. Left-behind voters were drawn to right-wing ethnonationalist leaders in countries like the United States, India, and Brazil, and to left-wing populist ones in countries like Venezuela, Mexico, and South Africa.

Unlike military leaders who abruptly kill democracies in coups, elected leaders who erode them gradually must maintain some level of public support. They do so by encouraging polarization among citizens and also by trash-talking their democracies: claiming that the institutions they attack are corrupt and incompetent. They tell voters that these institutions should be torn down and replaced by ones under the executive’s control. The Backsliders describes how journalists, judges, NGOs, and opposition leaders can put the brakes on democratic erosion, and how voters can do so through political engagement and the power of the ballot box.
books.bio: Susan C. Stokes is the Blake Distinguished Service Professor of Political Science at the University of Chicago, where she chairs the Chicago Center on Democracy. Her books include Mandates and Democracy: Neoliberalism by Surprise in Latin America and (with Thad Dunning, Marcelo Nazareno, and Valeria Brusco) Brokers, Voters, and Clientelism: The Puzzle of Distributive Politics .

praise.q: A timely and rigorous analysis of arguably the most discussed trend in political science over the last decade: the erosion of democracy, especially among consolidated democracies. . . . Essential.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: This splendid book is a model of well-argued, timely, and accessible scholarship. Stokes draws on an impressive range of methods and evidence to teach us about the economic and institutional roots of democratic backsliding, the ideas that would-be autocrats use to gain support, and the psychological bases of supporters’ responses. Her argument deserves a global audience of academics and activists alike.
praise.by: Nancy Bermeo, University of Oxford

praise.q: The most important book on the most urgent and compelling topic in political science.
praise.by: James A. Robinson, coauthor of Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty
praise.cred: coauthor of Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty

praise.q: A fascinating book that breaks new ground in a crowded field by highlighting both the demand and supply sides of the new authoritarianism (and their mutually reinforcing roles). Notably, Susan Stokes demonstrates how inequality contributes to democratic erosion and how backsliding leaders in turn deepen polarization and sow mistrust in institutions.
praise.by: Dani Rodrik, Harvard University

books.title: The Power of Limits
books.subtitle: The Evolution of the State in China and the West
books.authors: Gary W. Cox, Mark Dincecco, Yuhua Wang
books.tagline: How the West and China each invented distinctive political institutions to empower governments while constraining those in power
books.description:
Every society must empower its rulers so that they can govern in the public interest. At the same time, however, societies must restrain their rulers from pursuing self-serving ends. Many political thinkers, drawing on the historical experience of Western Europe, recommend limiting rulers’ power over taxation and spending to accomplish this. In The Power of Limits , rather than treating “executive constraints” as a uniquely Western innovation, Gary Cox, Mark Dincecco, and Yuhua Wang show that China developed its own institutionalized constraints, limiting the ruler’s patronage power by means of the civil service examination system known as keju . They compare Europe’s limitations on fiscal power, created through local governments and parliaments, to the bureaucratic appointment process in China, which reserved key offices for exam passers, removing them from the ruler’s personal discretion.

Drawing on original datasets documenting city autonomy, parliaments, examinations, ruler survival, taxation, debt, wars, rebellions, and institutions across across premodern Eurasia, the authors show that both systems of institutionalized limits on executive power lengthened rulers’ reigns, helped make sovereign borrowing more credible, and enabled broader groups of elites to acquire durable stakes in the state. But while Europe’s fiscal decentralization preserved political fragmentation, encouraged tax-secured public debt, and eventually enabled heavier taxation, China’s exam-based constraints on bureaucratic appointments helped sustain empire, supported office-secured debt, and contributed to a chronic cycle of light taxation, underfunding, corruption, and recurrent mass rebellion. Different types of limits produce diverse forms of state power. But today, the authors warn, both Western electoral institutions and China’s meritocratic exams are vulnerable to erosion.
books.bio: Gary W. Cox is the William Bennett Munro Professor of Political Science at Stanford University. He is the author of The Efficient Secret, winner of the 2003 George Hallett Award; Making Votes Count , winner of the 2007 George Hallett Award; and Marketing Sovereign Promises , winner of the 2017 William Riker Book Award. Mark Dincecco is professor of political science at the University of Michigan. He is the author of Political Transformations and Public Finances and the coauthor of From Warfare to Wealth , winner of the 2018 William Riker Book Award. Yuhua Wang is the Ford Foundation Professor of Modern China Studies at Harvard University. He is the author of Tying the Autocrat’s Hands and The Rise and Fall of Imperial China (Princeton), winner of the 2023 Gregory Luebbert Book Award.

books.title: The Progress Manifesto
books.subtitle: How Technology and Industry Advance Human Life and Well-Being
books.tagline: A new philosophy of progress: a moral defense of technology in the service of human flourishing, and an ambitious vision for the technological future.
books.description:
The debate over technology and its role in society has reached fever pitch. Skeptics and “doomers” accuse technology of ruining the planet, destroying our health, stealing our jobs, and even threatening human extinction. But a new and growing movement—already influential in Silicon Valley, among prominent academics, and increasingly in both political parties—is promoting technology as the engine of progress and the path to abundance.

The Progress Manifesto is a rallying cry for this movement. It presents a new philosophy of “techno-humanism”: the view that science, technology, and industry are good—not in themselves, but because they promote human flourishing and well-being. In short, it is the idea that material progress leads to human progress. Crawford acknowledges, and even embraces, the problems of progress, but his aim is to point toward solutions. He shows how progress can become not only a practical but a moral ideal, offering us a goal to strive for, a heroic archetype to emulate, and a responsibility to live up to.
books.bio: Jason Crawford is the founder of the Roots of Progress Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to building a culture of progress and restoring a bold, ambitious vision of the future. He is also the host of the Progress Conference, a Founding Fellow at the Cosmos Institute, an advisor to fellows at the Foresight Institute, and a former consultant for Our World in Data. Previously, he spent 18 years as a software engineer, engineering manager, and startup founder.

books.title: The Underwater Eye
books.subtitle: How the Movie Camera Opened the Depths and Unleashed New Realms of Fantasy
books.tagline: A rich history of underwater filmmaking and how it has profoundly influenced the aesthetics of movies and public perception of the oceans
books.description:
In The Underwater Eye , Margaret Cohen tells the fascinating story of how the development of modern diving equipment and movie camera technology has allowed documentary and narrative filmmakers to take human vision into the depths, creating new imagery of the seas and the underwater realm, and expanding the scope of popular imagination. Innovating on the most challenging film set on earth, filmmakers have tapped the emotional power of the underwater environment to forge new visions of horror, tragedy, adventure, beauty, and surrealism, entertaining the public and shaping its perception of ocean reality.

Examining works by filmmakers ranging from J. E. Williamson, inventor of the first undersea film technology in 1914, to Wes Anderson, who filmed the underwater scenes of his 2004 The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou entirely in a pool, The Underwater Eye traces how the radically alien qualities of underwater optics have shaped liquid fantasies for more than a century. Richly illustrated, the book explores documentaries by Jacques Cousteau, Louis Malle, and Hans Hass, art films by Man Ray and Jean Vigo, and popular movies and television shows such as 20,000 Leagues Under the Sea , Creature from the Black Lagoon , Sea Hunt , the Bond films, Jaws , The Abyss , and Titanic . In exploring the cultural impact of underwater filmmaking, the book also asks compelling questions about the role film plays in engaging the public with the remote ocean, a frontline of climate change.
books.bio: Margaret Cohen is the Andrew B. Hammond Professor of French Language, Literature, and Civilization at Stanford University, where she teaches in the Department of English. Her books include the award-winning The Novel and the Sea and The Sentimental Education of the Novel (both Princeton), as well as Profane Illumination: Walter Benjamin and the Paris of Surrealist Revolution . She is also the coeditor of The Aesthetics of the Undersea and general editor of A Cultural History of the Sea . She lives in Stanford, California.

praise.q: A comprehensive, historical examination of underwater films and television shows that reflected the public’s interest in sea fantasies during three periods. . . . Insightful.
praise.by: Choice Reviews

praise.q: Margaret Cohen’s comprehensive research and skilful writing makes this book a fascinating read. . . . Since the early days of underwater exploration and film making where it was exploitation of wrecks as well as recording the unknown wonders of marine life that drove us forward, we now use underwater filming in many other forms such as education, entertainment, science and art. It is an exciting and thrilling environment to be filming in and this book captures all that excitement in both its text and wonderful historic images.
praise.by: Jeff Goodman, Scubaverse

praise.q: Margaret Cohen’s eagerly awaited book juxtaposes three twentieth-century innovations: scuba, underwater film, and modernist artistic experimentalism. Her deft analysis of undersea images uses the experience of immersion, including blurred vision and near-weightlessness, to reframe conventions of gothic narrative, film noir, the Romantic sublime, and heroic epic. Fans of dive movies and scholars of the blue humanities will find much of value in this brilliant and engaging book.
praise.by: Steve Mentz, author of Ocean

praise.q: Most people who have seen the underwater world have seen it, and loved it, in movies. To discover those pioneering underwater productions, the passionate artists that invented the cameras, and the magic of capturing seascapes on film, take a breath and dive into The Underwater Eye . The 'underwater you' will love it.
praise.by: Stephen R. Palumbi, coauthor of The Extreme Life of the Sea
praise.cred: coauthor of The Extreme Life of the Sea

praise.q: Extensively researched, The Underwater Eye deftly assembles previously scattered scenes and disconnected glimpses of underwater filmmaking into a lush, precise, and coherent cultural history. This is an admirable, enticing, and essential volume.
praise.by: Stacy Alaimo, author of Exposed: Environmental Politics and Pleasures in Posthuman Times
praise.cred: author of Exposed: Environmental Politics and Pleasures in Posthuman Times

praise.q: An encyclopedic account of representations of the undersea in film, The Underwater Eye focuses on questions arising from the media that allow this hidden world to be viewed. To what extent is the reality of oceanic nature served or distorted by underwater cameras, lighting, and artificial locations? What would we see if there were no machines to clear the eyes or replenish the lungs of the filmmakers? Cohen offers myriad examples to complicate the answers to these questions in this searching and exciting book.
praise.by: Jonathan Lamb, author of Scurvy: The Disease of Discovery
praise.cred: author of Scurvy: The Disease of Discovery

books.title: The War on Gender
books.subtitle: From the Vatican to the New Global Right
books.tagline: How “anti-genderism” fueled a global right-wing movement
books.description:
In recent years, opposition to “gender ideology” has become a rallying cry for the Right. Politicians throughout the world have invoked the dangers of “gender” to restrict access to abortion, revoke LGBTQ rights, and police education. And yet at the same time, the term“gender” has become standard in everyday speech—a box to check on a passport application or on a form at the doctor’s office. When did the word “gender” become a political controversy? When did the idea of a “gender ideology” first emerge? In The War on Gender , Camille Robcis traces the history of a global movement that she calls “anti-genderism”: the assertion that a “gender ideology,” developed in the halls of academia and foisted on an unwilling public, has become the driving force behind social policy.

Robcis argues that anti-genderism was invented by the Vatican in the mid-1990s in response to demands for reproductive and sexual rights made by feminist activists at conferences sponsored by the United Nations. To counter these claims, Vatican representatives decided to oppose “gender” altogether. The culprits, in their view, were not only the activists at the conferences but the “gender theorists” who had inspired them. During the papacy of John Paul II—who made defense of the heterosexual family the bedrock of his reign—the Vatican propagated the expression “gender ideology” throughout the world. It was embraced by many on the Right, including evangelical Christians, who adopted the rhetoric of anti-genderism to further their own illiberal agendas.
books.bio: Camille Robcis is professor of history and French at Columbia University. She is the author of The Law of Kinship: Anthropology, Psychoanalysis, and the Family in France and Disalienation: Politics, Philosophy, and Radical Psychiatry in Postwar France .

books.title: Tools
books.subtitle: A Human History
books.tagline: An illuminating collection of essays that explores the history of simple tools to reveal how we shape and are shaped by technology. From the former curator of the history of technology at the Smithsonian and a Guggenheim recipient.
books.description:
From the former curator of the history of technology at the Smithsonian and a Guggenheim recipient.

Every tool tells a story. Tools is an engaging collection of essays that explores the history and philosophy of tools and tool use. Each essay focuses on a single tool, wielding it to reveal a larger story about the nature of tools and technology as well as the diverse ways that tools allow us to understand culture and cultural change. As Steven Lubar reveals, seemingly simple workshop tools and household implements can provide insights into innovation and creativity, work and skill, hand and mind, nature and materials, and society and culture.

The book focuses on hand tools from the stone axe to the modern drill, from the broom to the hammer. The author uses their histories to consider big questions about the nature of tools and technology. How do we learn to use tools? How did tools come to define humanity? What shapes the design of tools? How and why do tools change over time? Together, these essays reveal how we shape technology, how we make sense of it, and how it shapes us.

Especially as machines become increasingly challenging to understand and control, it is important for us to understand how we use tools—and how we should build machines we can work with, not machines we work for . This book helps us make that crucial connection.
books.bio: Steven Lubar, George L. Littlefield Professor of American History emeritus at Brown University, writes on museums and the history of technology. A Guggenheim fellowship supported his book Inside the Lost Museum . Before coming to Brown, Lubar was curator of the history of technology at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.

books.title: Against Imperialism
books.subtitle: Imagining a Post-Capitalist World
books.authors: Edited by Sarah E. James and Vera Mey
books.tagline: How art and cultural institutions can resist, critique, and build alternatives to the intersecting crises of racial capitalism, imperialism, neofascism and neoliberal authoritarianism.
books.description:
We are living in a time of global upheaval, genocide, and humanitarian disasters. Driven by big finance and new forms of imperialism, extractive racial capitalism is reaping mass casualties and ecological catastrophes around the world, as the inequalities between nations and the communities within them reach new extremes. Ascendent forms of neofascism, techno-feudalism, and violent systems of oppression have infiltrated our lives, redefining politics, work, leisure, the family, our forms of socialization, cultural production, and consumption. Meanwhile, new forms of censorship, self-censorship, repression, surveillance, and control have proliferated in the last decade—many implemented and escalated since the global pandemic by governments and corporations working in tandem via digital capitalism. Apparently unregulated, these forms have penetrated our social norms, habits, intellectual, public, and pedagogical structures to unprecedented degrees. Moreover, in supposedly democratic states we have witnessed a criminalization of peaceful protest, the normalization of anti-immigration and xenophobic rhetoric and policy, and the dismantling of collective action. Western nations that once defended ideals of liberalism, democracy, justice, and freedom of expression have readily discarded them, as demonstrated by the collective blind eye turned to the Israeli genocide of the Palestinian people in Gaza.

Amid these polycrises, what were once autonomous cultural and educational institutions that fostered discursive critique and freedom of expression have, under the stranglehold of neoliberal privatization, increasingly acquiesced to neoconservative, far right, and neofascist ideologies. Despite the supposed social and political turn in contemporary art and its institutions in the wake of the Occupy and Black Lives Matter movements, the neoliberal public arts museum is arguably less political than it has ever been. This collection of essays addresses these issues, asking what role public arts and other cultural institutions, cultural workers, public intellectuals, arts educators, and practitioners can play—not just in resisting and critiquing right-wing populism and authoritarianism, but in imagining, materializing and mobilizing alternatives to this reactionary political horizon.

Contributors

Ben Burbridge, Tj Demos, Adam Griffiths, The Otolith Group, Sophia Yadong Hao, Deeqa Ismail, Sarah E. James, Yazan Khalili, Alana Lake, Jumana Manna, Stefano Harney & Zun Lee & Fred Moten, Philippe Pirotte, Vera Mey

Copublished by Manchester School of Art.
books.bio:
Sarah E. James (Editor)

Sarah E. James is Professor of Visual Culture at Manchester School of Art, Manchester Metropolitan University. She writes widely about contemporary art, politics, photography, and the visual cultures of the Cold War. She has published two monographs: Common Ground: German Photographic Cultures across the Iron Curtain (2013) and Paper Revolutions: An Invisible Avant-Garde (MIT Press, 2022). Her new book, Art and the Ends of Capitalism: Practising Politics , is forthcoming. She is the founding editor of the series Tomorrow's Art School, c o-published with Sternberg Press and Manchester School of Art.

Vera Mey (Editor)

Vera Mey is Associate Professor of Contemporary Art History and Theory at the Ruskin School of Art, University of Oxford. Along with Philippe Pirotte, she was Co-Artistic Director of the 2024 Busan Biennale, "Seeing in the Dark," and is a founding co-editor of the journal Southeast of Now: Directions in Contemporary and Modern Art in Asia .

books.title: Augmented Human Intelligence
books.subtitle: Empowering Minds in the Age of AI
books.authors: Erik J. Larson and Chee-We Ng
books.tagline: A clear-eyed look at what AI actually is—and why we must focus on AI systems that augment human cognition, rather than mimic it. From a seasoned AI researcher and a VC investor and entrepreneur.
books.description:
From a seasoned AI researcher and a VC investor and entrepreneur.

Augmented Human Intelligence cuts through all the hype and noise around AI by returning to a central, often overlooked question: What is intelligence actually for? Rather than aiming to build autonomous superintelligent agents, AI leaders Erik Larson and Chee-We Ng argue in this book that we should focus on systems that support and extend human judgment, understanding, and decision-making—capacities that the current AI largely ignores.

Most state-of-the-art models rely on statistical induction at scale. They generate text, recognize patterns, and predict outcomes with remarkable speed—but without any grasp of meaning, consequence, or purpose. The authors of this book contend this is not merely a technical limitation, but a conceptual one: intelligence is not pattern-matching alone. It emerges from interaction with the world, guided by goals, feedback, and relevance.

This book aims to clarify the confusion around what AI is and isn’t, across everything from self-driving cars to robotics to conversational systems. In doing so, the authors hope to spur a shift in perspective—toward AI systems that augment human cognitive strengths rather than mimic human beings.

What makes this book unique is its insistence that judgment and understanding aren’t optional extras—they’re central to the very idea of intelligence. By reframing what we mean by thinking, the authors invite readers to imagine a different future for AI: one grounded not in simulation or spectacle, but in support for real human insight.
books.bio:
Erik J. Larson (Author)

Erik J. Larson is a computer scientist, tech entrepreneur, and the author of The Myth of Artificial Intelligence , a widely acclaimed critique of current AI narratives. A Fellow with the Institute for Advanced Studies in Culture (IASC), he has founded two AI companies and contributed to both academic and public debates on the limits and promise of intelligent systems. He has written for The Atlantic , Wired , The Los Angeles Review of Books , Metro Silicon Valley , UnHerd , and other publications.

Chee-We Ng (Author)

Chee-We Ng is the founder and managing partner of Oakseed Ventures, where he seeds transformative startups in AI and cybersecurity. A coauthor of The AI Book , he has been investing in and running AI startups over the past decade.

books.title: Beyond the Plate
books.subtitle: How Restaurants Do Well by Doing Good
books.tagline: Why communities and markets thrive when restaurants invest in their people and the planet
books.description:
Half of all restaurants will fail before their fifth year in operation. With food, rent, and energy costs skyrocketing, restaurant owners struggle daily to keep the lights on. In today’s climate, it can seem like an unattainable luxury to pay higher wages or source sustainable ingredients. Beyond the Plate reveals why it is an imperative.

Katherine Miller presents engaging profiles of Michelin-starred chefs and James Beard award nominees and winners such as Jill Marie Tyler of Rye Bunny in Washington, DC, and Kyle and Katina Connaughton of SingleThread in Sonoma County, who share the secrets of running just, green, and profitable restaurants. By reducing waste, partnering with local farmers, and developing worker-forward business models, they are cutting costs, creating uniquely delicious menus, and providing a top-flight dining experience. These eateries are not just keeping the doors open. They are changing the entire industry and the food system itself.

Miller describes how top restaurant owners and chefs are making a difference by supporting agricultural practices that improve soil health and lower carbon emissions. By paying employees a living wage instead of relying on an antiquated tipping system, they are creating stable incomes for workers and families, broadening healthcare access, and fueling economic vitality and growth.

Drawing lessons from some of the world’s most sustainable and successful restaurants, this inspirational book shows how the rewards of green and just practices go far beyond the plate, benefiting not only restaurateurs and customers but entire communities and the earth that nourishes us all.
books.bio: Katherine Miller was named an industry leader and “Fixer” by Grist magazine and called one of the most innovative women in food and beverage by Fortune and Food & Wine . She led the James Beard Foundation’s Impact programs, including developing the Chef Bootcamp for Policy and Change. She teaches in the Sustainable Food Systems master’s program at the Culinary Institute of America and is the author of At the Table: The Chef’s Guide to Advocacy .

books.title: Horses
books.subtitle: A 4,000-Year Genetic Journey Across the World
books.tagline: From one of today’s leading experts on ancient DNA, a sweeping genetic history that unravels the mystery of where horses were first domesticated
books.description:
Ludovic Orlando garnered world acclaim for helping to rewrite the genomic history of horse domestication. Horses takes you behind the scenes of this ambitious genealogical investigation, revealing how he and an international team of scientists discovered the elusive origins of modern horses. Along the way, he shows how the domestication of the horse changed the trajectory of civilization—with benefits and unforeseen consequences for the animals themselves.

Orlando brought together world-class experts in genomics, archaeology, and the history of peoples, languages, and migrations. Comparing the DNA of ancient horses to the genomes of dozens of modern horse breeds, these researchers reconstructed millennia of equine evolutionary history. They now believe that horses were first domesticated some 4,200 years ago on the steppes of the North Caucasus. Orlando discusses how selective breeding has significantly intensified over the past two centuries, giving rise to faster, stronger horses but also creating a severe decline in genetic diversity that has made horses more prone to genetic diseases. He looks at breeds throughout history and around the world, explaining how they have been bred for particular purposes or environments, from Botai and Przewalski’s horses to the warhorses of the Vikings and Genghis Khan, Arabian horses, thoroughbreds, Himalayan steeds, and mules.

Blending panoramic storytelling with cutting-edge genetic science, Horses chronicles an unbreakable bond that was forged thousands of years ago on the windswept Eurasian Steppe, one that heralded a bold new era in the human drama—that of speed.
books.bio: Ludovic Orlando is a member of the French Academy of Sciences, CNRS Silver Medal–winning research director, and founding director of the Centre for Anthropobiology and Genomics of Toulouse, France. His work has appeared in leading journals, including Nature , Science , and Cell .

praise.q: Orlando, a French expert in ancient DNA, launches into the findings of a global investigation of the relationship between humans and horses that has shaped modern societies. . . . Combing through artifacts and data, the author weaves together centuries of global history, following the beasts across nations as they accompany humans in pursuit of war, trade, food, and pleasure.
praise.by: Kirkus Reviews

praise.q: Orlando's book will interest researchers and scholars in all areas because of his ability to simplify academic research and his innate storytelling ability, combining history with science.
praise.by: Steve Dixon, Library Journal, starred review

praise.q: Orlando is able to convey complex aspects of genetic science so that we are able to follow the straight paths, and the sidetracks and meandering lanes of his research, without difficulty, page after page.
praise.by: David Gascoigne, Travels with Birds

praise.q: This book details with great depth how this remarkable species set about such a revolution.
praise.by: Suzanne C. Miller, Integrative and Comparative Biology

praise.q: Orlando’s brilliance shines. Over the past decade, his sequencing work has overturned so much of what the world thought it knew about horses: domestication, where it happened and how horses evolved afterwards – and even how horse lineages stretched back tens of millions of years. This is all told with vivid detail and captivating storytelling, built on mysteries teased apart through unravelled double helixes. . . . Horses is a thundering read, reminding us that the long, tangled history of humans and horses isn’t just written in bones and genomes, but also in the enduring ways we continue to shape one another.
praise.by: Christa Lesté-Lasserre, New Scientist

praise.q: This is a breathtaking book from the geneticist who decoded the horse’s ancient secrets. It is a modern tale of serendipity, power, and relentless spirit.
praise.by: Christina Warinner, Harvard University

praise.q: Ludovic Orlando is among the most brilliant scientists I have ever worked with. In Horses , he reveals how cutting-edge DNA research is rewriting the story of the four-thousand-year history of human-equine relationships. I warmly recommend his book—a fascinating blend of history, science, and personal narrative.
praise.by: Eske Willerslev, University of Copenhagen and University of Cambridge
praise.cred: University of Copenhagen and University of Cambridge

praise.q: Horses, especially after we learned to ride them, literally changed the course of human history—without them there would be no mega-empires, like Achaemenid Persia. But where and when was the horse domesticated? This wonderful book by Ludovic Orlando, which reads like a detective story, solves this puzzle.
praise.by: Peter Turchin, author of Ultrasociety: How 10,000 Years of War Made Humans the Greatest Cooperators on Earth
praise.cred: author of Ultrasociety: How 10,000 Years of War Made Humans the Greatest Cooperators on Earth

praise.q: Ludovic Orlando weaves together groundbreaking scientific discoveries with rich historical narrative, transforming our understanding of the relationship between humans and horses. This is a wonderful melding of scientific discovery and human history.
praise.by: Beth Shapiro, author of How to Clone a Mammoth
praise.cred: author of How to Clone a Mammoth

praise.q: The origins and subsequent biological and cultural history of most domestic animals remain patchy. With this titanic book, Ludovic Orlando has ensured that what we now know about horses matches the outsized effect they have had on human history over the past four thousand years.
praise.by: Greger Larson, University of Oxford
