books.title: Capitalism in the Colonies
books.subtitle: African Merchants in Lagos, 1851–1931
books.tagline: An account that challenges the conventional views of African merchants under colonialism, examining the emergence and changing fortunes of indigenous entrepreneurs in Lagos, Nigeria
books.description:
In Capitalism in the Colonies , A. G. Hopkins provides the first substantial assessment of the fortunes of African entrepreneurs under colonial rule. Examining the lives and careers of 100 merchants in Lagos, Nigeria, between 1850 and 1931, Hopkins challenges conventional views of the contribution made by indigenous entrepreneurs to the long-run economic development of Nigeria. He argues that African merchants in Lagos not only survived, but were also responsible for key innovations in trade, construction, farming, and finance that are essential for understanding the development of Nigeria’s economy.

The book is based on a large, representative sample and covers a time span that traces mercantile fortunes over two and three generations. Drawing on a wide range of sources, Hopkins shows that indigenous entrepreneurs were far more adventurous than expatriate firms. African merchants in Lagos pioneered motor vehicles, sewing machines, publishing, tanneries, and new types of internal trade. They founded the construction industry that built Lagos into a major port city, moved inland to start the cocoa-farming industry, and developed the finance sector that is still vital to Nigeria’s economy. They also took the lead in changing single-owned businesses into limited liability companies, creating freehold property rights and promoting wage labour. In short, Hopkins argues, they were the capitalists who introduced the institutions of capitalism into Nigeria. The story of African merchants in Nigeria reminds us, he writes, that economic structures have no life of their own until they are animated by the actions of creative individuals.
books.bio: A. G. Hopkins is Emeritus Smuts Professor of Commonwealth History at the University of Cambridge and an Emeritus Fellow of Pembroke College, Cambridge. He is the author of An Economic History of West Africa , American Empire: A Global History (Princeton), Africa, Empire, and World Disorder: Historical Essays, and (with P. J. Cain) British Imperialism, 1688–2016.

praise.q: Capitalism in the Colonies is a masterful history of the emerging merchant class in Lagos, Nigeria, during the advent of British colonial rule. . . . Highly recommended.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: We can now build economic histories of West Africa on a much firmer footing; and for this we have A. G. Hopkins to thank.
praise.by: Reuben Loffman, Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: [A] magisterial study."—Lisa Lyndsay, Journal of Social History

Capitalism in the Colonies is a tremendously rich account of how African merchants in Lagos adapted to and shaped the processes of economic and political change in the region during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. It brings together an astonishing array of primary sources—some rarely or perhaps even never used—to examine the shift to ‘legitimate commerce’ and the process of colonial expansion from the perspective of the African commercial class which made both of these changes possible. A remarkable contribution.
praise.by: Leigh Gardner, London School of Economics

praise.q: This is an exciting, engaging, and highly original account of the development of capitalism in the colonial port city of Lagos, in particular the careers of Lagos merchants and their role in spreading capitalist institutions. The wide chronological scope and large sample of merchants sets this manuscript apart from others in the field.
praise.by: Laura Channing, Durham University

praise.q: Capitalism in the Colonies is not just a work of brilliant scholarship, it’s a time-travelling adventure into the heart of Nigeria’s economic awakening, packed with more intrigue and entrepreneurial spirit than a Lagos street market.
praise.by: Johan Fourie, Stellenbosch University

praise.q: Africa’s population is now close to 1.5 billion, bringing attention to its economy. How does Africa grow today while still under colonial-type constraints? This masterpiece by A. G. Hopkins looks to history to provide a clue. He documents the activities of 116 colonial-era Nigerian entrepreneurs, overcomes the neglect of their skillful agency, and supersedes simplified Eurocentric doctrines with a coherent view of capitalism.
praise.by: Patrick Manning, University of Pittsburgh

praise.q: Capitalism in the Colonies is a richly documented, generously illustrated, and carefully organized insightful study of African business and society in West Africa’s premier port-city from the 1850s to the early 1930s. Woven around three 'shocks' or epochal events in 1851, 1892, and 1914, and illuminated by numerous business biographies, it draws upon massive archival and court records, oral interviews conducted mainly in the 1960s, and contemporary newspapers. This book highlights African agency—innovation, resilience, and adaptation—and provides a magisterial and an innovative (re)interpretation of the business, economic, and social history of Lagos in the vortex of intersecting local, imperial, and global dynamics from the British occupation to the Great Depression.
praise.by: Ayodeji Olukoju, University of Lagos

books.title: Controlling Contagion
books.subtitle: Epidemics and Institutions from the Black Death to Covid
books.tagline: How human institutions—markets, states, communities, religions, guilds and families—have helped both to control and to exacerbate epidemics throughout history
books.description:
How do societies tackle epidemic disease? In Controlling Contagion , Sheilagh Ogilvie answers this question by exploring seven centuries of pandemics, from the Black Death to Covid-19. For most of history, infectious diseases have killed many more people than famine or war, and in 2019 they still caused one death in four. Today, we deal with epidemics more successfully than our ancestors managed plague, smallpox, cholera or influenza. But we use many of the same approaches. Long before scientific medicine, human societies coordinated and innovated in response to biological shocks—sometimes well, sometimes badly.

Ogilvie uses historical epidemics to analyse how human societies deal with “externalities”—situations where my action creates costs or benefits for others beyond those that I myself incur. Social institutions—markets, states, communities, religions, guilds, and families—help us manage the negative externalities of contagion and the positive externalities of social distancing, sanitation, and immunization. Ogilvie shows how each institution enables us to coordinate, innovate and inspire each other to limit contagion. But each institution also has weaknesses that can make things worse. Markets shut down voluntarily during every epidemic in history—but they also brought people together, spreading contagion. States mandated quarantines, sanitation, and immunization—but they also waged war and censored information, exacerbating epidemics. Religions admonished us to avoid infecting our neighbours—but they also preached against science and medical innovations. What decided the outcome, Ogilvie argues, was a temperate state, an adaptable market, and a strong civil society where a diversity of institutions played to their own strengths and checked each other’s flaws.
books.bio: Sheilagh Ogilvie is the Chichele Professor of Economic History at the University of Oxford, a fellow of All Souls College, and director of the Oxford Centre for Economic and Social History. She is the author of The European Guilds: An Economic Analysi s (Princeton), Institutions and European Trade: Merchant Guilds, 1000–1800 , A Bitter Living: Women, Markets, and Social Capital in Early Modern Germany , and State Corporatism and Proto-Industry: the Württemberg Black Forest, 1580–1797 .

praise.q: Ogilvie’s book ranges from the 14th century—the era of the Black Death—to the 21st. . . . [Her] wide-ranging survey throws up some telling points. . . . [And] exposes some cherished fallacies.
praise.by: Virginia Berridge, BBC History Magazine

praise.q: An important book that opens analysis of epidemics across time and space within a new framework of institutional history.
praise.by: Samuel Cohn, Political Quarterly

praise.q: An ambitious study. . . . It is impossible to offer more than a glimpse of Ogilvie’s compass and erudition.
praise.by: Nicholas Brown, Australian Book Review

praise.q: This is the first scholarly work to connect [epidemics] to institutions, markets and how states perform over many centuries. . . . Ogilvie unpacks what history and cross-country comparisons tell us about the ability of societies to respond to epidemics. . . . If there is one lesson from this most impressive book, it is that preparation for and effective responses to epidemics are of critical importance.
praise.by: R. Quentin Grafton, Economic Record

praise.q: This is the book I would have liked to read in March 2020. . . . Ogilvie’s essay is rich and brimming with ideas. . . . For its breadth, documentation, and depth, Sheilagh Ogilvie’s Controlling Contagion is a work you cannot open without learning something. The author deserves her readers’ full gratitude.
praise.by: Alberto Mingardi, Curious Task

praise.q: An impressive study."—David Lorimer, Paradigm Explorer

Sheilagh Ogilvie haswritten another big and important book. It explores a new theme for her: how do societies respond to and tackle epidemics. . . . Controlling Contagion is a heroic work of ingestion that has no obvious equivalent in the literature.
praise.by: Patrick Wallis, Economic History Review

praise.q: Sheilagh Ogilvie has written a definitive book on how people use institutions to respond to infectious diseases. . . . Her argument, theoretical framework, even-handed writing, myriad examples, and organization all make for an incredible resource. Scholars, laymen, and policy makers alike who are interested in public health and epidemics and in the economics and institutions of epidemiology should read Controlling Contagion .
praise.by: Byron B. Carson III, The Review of Austrian Economics

praise.q: A large-scale, timely assessment of human society’s responses to epidemics.
praise.by: George Dehner, American Historical Review

praise.q: This book is groundbreaking in the sociological aspects of epidemics. . . . Essential.
praise.by: Choice

books.title: The Book of Yerba Mate
books.subtitle: A Stimulating History
books.tagline: The untold story of South America’s most interesting beverage
books.description:
Brewed from the dried leaves and tender shoots of an evergreen tree native to South America, yerba mate gives its drinkers the jolt of liquid effervescence many of us get from coffee or tea. In Argentina, southern “gaúcho” Brazil, Paraguay, and Uruguay, mate is the stimulating brew of choice, famously quaffed by the Argentine national football team en route to its 2022 FIFA World Cup victory. In The Book of Yerba Mate , Christine Folch offers a wide-ranging exploration of the world’s third-most popular naturally stimulating beverage. Folch discusses who drinks mate, and why, and whether this earthier caffeinated drink with its promise of a different buzz and a more authentic, spiritual connection to place can find a market niche beyond South America.

Folch traces yerba mate’s odysseys across the globe, from South America to the Middle East and North America . She discovers that mate inspired the world’s first written tango, powered early Jesuit and German nationalist utopias, ignited one of modern history’s most devastating wars, and fueled Catholic conspiracies. And, Folch reports, mate is currently starring in puppet shows put on by Syrian dissidents.

By tracing yerba mate production and consumption as they change over time and place, from precolonial Indigenous beginnings to the present, Folch unravels the processes of commodification and their countervailing forces to show how accidents of botany intersect with political economic systems and personal taste. The stories behind the caffeinated infusions we prefer, she finds, are nothing less than the story of how the modern world is put together.
books.bio: Christine Folch is the Bacca Foundation Associate Professor of Cultural Anthropology at Duke University. She is the author of Hydropolitics: The Itaipu Dam, Sovereignty, and the Engineering of Modern South America (Princeton).

praise.q: A fascinating study that opens a window onto the bigger thematic landscape of colonialism, consumption and market capitalism.
praise.by: Oliver Balch, Times Literary Supplement

praise.q: The research is thorough, the story compelling, and the prose accessible and highly engaging. A clear narrative thread makes the book’s ambitious thematic, chronological, and geographic scope appear effortless, adventurous, and enlightening. . . . Highly recommended
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: This is one of the most original, interesting, and well-written books that I have had the privilege to read in a while. We have plenty of biographies of coffee and tea; this book restores their neglected cousin, yerba mate, to its rightful place. By following the story of mate, this book lets us see Latin America, empire, race, and religion in a new light.
praise.by: Frank Trentmann, author of Empire of Things

praise.q: Yerba mate and its close botanical relatives guayusa and yaupon are among the most widely distributed and readily available psychoactive plants you may have never heard of. With precision and wit, Folch traces their circulation, continual resignification, enduring fascination, and occasional denigration, through space and time, empire and culture. In revealing these plants’ hidden stories, she reveals to us something about our own.
praise.by: Eduardo Kohn, author of How Forests Think

books.title: The Holy Alliance
books.subtitle: Liberalism and the Politics of Federation
books.tagline: A major new account of the post-Napoleonic Holy Alliance and the promise it held for liberals
books.description:
The Holy Alliance is now most familiar as a label for conspiratorial reaction. In this book, Isaac Nakhimovsky reveals the Enlightenment origins of this post-Napoleonic initiative, explaining why it was embraced at first by many contemporary liberals as the birth of a federal Europe and the dawning of a peaceful and prosperous age of global progress. Examining how the Holy Alliance could figure as both an idea of progress and an emblem of reaction, Nakhimovsky offers a novel vantage point on the history of federative alternatives to the nation state. The result is a clearer understanding of the recurring appeal of such alternatives—and the reasons why the politics of federation has also come to be associated with entrenched resistance to liberalism’s emancipatory aims.

Nakhimovsky connects the history of the Holy Alliance with the better-known transatlantic history of eighteenth-century constitutionalism and nineteenth-century efforts to abolish slavery and war. He also shows how the Holy Alliance was integrated into a variety of liberal narratives of progress. From the League of Nations to the Cold War, historical analogies to the Holy Alliance continued to be drawn throughout the twentieth century, and Nakhimovsky maps how some of the fundamental political problems raised by the Holy Alliance have continued to reappear in new forms under new circumstances. Time will tell whether current assessments of contemporary federal systems seem less implausible to future generations than initial liberal expectations of the Holy Alliance do to us today.
books.bio: Isaac Nakhimovsky is professor of history and humanities at Yale University. He is the author of The Closed Commercial State: Perpetual Peace and Commercial Society from Rousseau to Fichte (Princeton).

praise.q: [ The Holy Alliance ] fully inhabits the feverish world of the postwar 1810s and 1820s.
praise.by: James Stafford, London Review of Books

praise.q: Erudite and ambitious. . . . This new study of the Holy Alliance and the strands of discourse that led up to it and followed from it makes a substantial contribution to the histories of political thought.
praise.by: Brian Vick, Journal of Modern History

praise.q: A dazzling, revisionary reconstruction of the Holy Alliance as arguably the earliest attempt to institute a liberal international order thoroughly recognizable to twentieth- and twenty-first-century observers. Nakhimovsky’s astounding account of its global ambition, emancipatory hopes, and eventual failures offers sober political lessons for our own time.
praise.by: Karuna Mantena, Columbia University

praise.q: A hugely impressive achievement: a serious, deeply learned, but also imaginatively important, new book about old politics and the ways it still, in fact, lingers on in the present.
praise.by: Duncan Kelly, University of Cambridge

books.title: Undergraduate Physics
books.subtitle: Four Years in One
books.tagline: A self-contained account of the four core subject areas of an undergraduate physics degree—mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, and statistical mechanics—with more than 150 worked examples
books.description:
Most graduate programs in physics require a preliminary examination on topics covered in undergraduate physics classes. This invaluable text provides a detailed review of the four core subject areas of an undergraduate physics degree—mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, and statistical mechanics—in a coherent and self-contained narrative built around worked example problems. Reader-friendly explanations of each topic are followed by a challenging worked example selected from Princeton University’s famously rigorous graduate preliminary exam in physics. Each problem is accompanied by a detailed solution that demonstrates the key techniques used. Starting with a relatively small set of core ideas, readers will go on to apply them to topics as wide-ranging as explosions, levitating frogs, radioactive decay, and white dwarf stars.

• Can be used as a review of undergraduate topics for graduate students, as a supplemental text for undergraduates, or as a reference for more experienced physicists

• Includes more than 150 problems from Princeton University’s graduate preliminary exam in physics

• Difficulty of problems indicated with distinct iconography for each chapter: apples, resistors, cats, and flames
books.bio: Ross Dempsey is a Pappalardo Fellow in Physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Andrew M. Leifer is an Associate Professor of Physics and Neuroscience at Princeton University.

praise.q: This book is fun to read and engage with. It combines light-hearted banter with hard-core technical topics and worked examples. The selection of material is superb, and reflects well-curated high-level examples. It does a remarkable job of putting together the major topics from a physics undergraduate program, keeping the discussions brief and to the point. It provides a great quick reference even for a seasoned physicist or engineer.
praise.by: Gil Refael, California Institute of Technology

praise.q: This is a valuable collection of exam problems from one of the most excellent physics graduate schools in the world. The dedicated student at any university will derive great benefit from going through this book carefully.
praise.by: A. Zee, author of Top Ten Ideas of Physics
praise.cred: author of Top Ten Ideas of Physics

books.title: American Landlord
books.subtitle: The Dilemma of Profit in a Forever Housing Crisis
books.tagline: A penetrating exploration of the forever crisis that pits landlords against low-income tenants and a road map for change
books.description:
The United States has abdicated its responsibility to provide housing for everyone who needs it, leaving millions of Americans rent-burdened, with only a fortunate few receiving housing assistance. American Landlord shows how this broken system relies on for-profit landlords who are expected to provide decent housing to tenants who do not earn enough money to be profitably housed.

Drawing on in-depth interviews with scores of landlords and property managers in Baltimore, Cleveland, Dallas, and Washington, DC, Philip Garboden and Eva Rosen describe the common strategies these landlords employ to solve this dilemma, from more benign ones like working with tenants on payment plans to more unscrupulous practices like discriminatory screening and targeted eviction. These tactics are not aberrations but the inevitable result of a fundamental dilemma: how to profit off people who cannot afford to pay. We meet the smalltime landlords—mostly ordinary people seeking stability and financial independence—who are drawn into risky investments by popular myths about easy money in real estate. We hear from the corporate landlords who manage tenant relations through automation and algorithmic control. And we learn about the entrepreneurs who specialize in making money from government subsidy programs.

American Landlord demands that we fundamentally reconsider our housing advocacy. Stronger tenant protections and building more housing are both critical, but neither will alone solve the fundamental problem faced by America’s poorest renters. A true solution to the housing crisis requires significant public investment in both people and places.
books.bio: Philip M. E. Garboden is associate professor at the Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice at the University of Chicago. Eva Rosen is professor at the McCourt School of Public Policy at Georgetown University and the author of The Voucher Promise: “Section 8” and the Fate of an American Neighborhood (Princeton).

books.title: Following the Bend
books.subtitle: How to Read a River and Understand Its Nature
books.tagline: An engaging and thought-provoking introduction to river science
books.description:
When we look at a river, either up close or while flying over a river valley, what are we really seeing? Following the Bend takes readers on a majestic journey by water to find answers, along the way shedding light on the key concepts of modern river science, from hydrology and water chemistry to stream and wetland ecology.

In this accessible and uniquely personal book, Ellen Wohl explains how to “read” a river, blending the latest science with her own personal experiences as a geologist and naturalist who has worked on rivers for more than three decades. She charts how water travels through the hydrologic cycle around the globe and downstream to distribute energy, move sediment, and shape river channels, and how living organisms adapt to life in flowing water to create vibrant river ecosystems. Wohl looks at the role of disturbances such as floods and droughts and discusses how geologists interpret the sedimentary records of past river processes. She illustrates how river networks interact with Earth’s surface and considers issues for rivers in the future, such as progressive drying, river restoration, and advocating for the legal personhood of a river to maintain its distinctive spirit, identity, and integrity.

Sharing a new understanding of how rivers function as both physical systems and ecosystems, Following the Bend enables us to observe rivers with fresh eyes and more fully appreciate the beauty, vibrancy, and complexity of our planet’s vital waterways.
books.bio: Ellen Wohl is University Distinguished Professor in the Department of Geosciences at Colorado State University. Her many books include Dead Wood: The Afterlife of Trees , Something Hidden in the Ranges: The Secret Life of Mountain Ecosystems , and Of Rock and Rivers: Seeking a Sense of Place in the American West .

praise.q: An impassioned guide to interpreting rivers. . . . [Wohl's] accessible scientific explanations alternate with lyrical passages that pack an emotional punch.
praise.by: Publishers Weekly

praise.q: Wohl's passion for her subject shines through throughout. . . . A thorough primer on understanding rivers.
praise.by: Genevieve Williams, Library Journal

praise.q: Offers deep insights into river hydrology, geology, and ecology, blending scientific rigor with an engaging narrative voice."—M. E. Lenczewski, Choice
Interspersed with stories of her fieldwork, Following the Bend is a testament to Wohl’s depth of knowledge and public communication thereof.
praise.by: Ted Theisinger, Land & Climate Review

praise.q: A veritable source of wonder for me. Ellen Wohl is a distinguished scientist who has received many awards throughout her illustrious career, yet in this book she presents herself as a story teller, delivering a pleasing combination of history, geography, geology, hydrology and personal recollection. . . . She eschews the use of arcane terminology unless it is critical to the text, but makes sure always to accompany it with an explanation when she does.
praise.by: David Gascoigne, Travels with Birds

praise.q: There is no better guide to rivers than Ellen Wohl. She is as adept at storytelling as she is at science, and Following the Bend is forever surprising, enchanting, personable, and, not least, clarifying. Read this revelatory book and you will find in the path of water an endless universe connecting geology, ecology, human history, and our future in one magnificent, ever-moving flow.
praise.by: Boyce Upholt, author of The Great River: The Making and Unmaking of the Mississippi
praise.cred: author of The Great River: The Making and Unmaking of the Mississippi

praise.q: Ellen Wohl writes beautifully. Following the Bend is a comprehensive but wholly accessible scientific guide, drawn from a life spent thinking about moving water and the ways it shapes the world.
praise.by: David Owen, author of Where the Water Goes
praise.cred: author of Where the Water Goes

praise.q: Almost like a river in miniature, this book moves longitudinally, laterally, and vertically, traversing the intimate world of rivers by blending a lifetime of scientific knowledge with a deep love of riparian landscapes. From the impact of weather and climate to the intricate dance of water, sediment, and life, Following the Bend uncovers the stories carved and etched into every river bend, reminding readers of the essential roles of these waterways.
praise.by: Charlotte Taylor Fryar, author of Potomac Fever: Reflections on the Nation’s River
praise.cred: author of Potomac Fever: Reflections on the Nation’s River

praise.q: If you’d like to take a year’s worth of classes about how rivers function—but you know you never will—this is the book to read! Sit down with Ellen Wohl and learn what we need to understand about the water that flows all around us. From the backyard creek to the Amazon, you'll gain greater appreciation for the essential arteries of the earth.
praise.by: Tim Palmer, author of Seek Higher Ground: The Natural Solution to Our Urgent Flooding Crisis
praise.cred: author of Seek Higher Ground: The Natural Solution to Our Urgent Flooding Crisis

books.title: How to Be Noble
books.subtitle: An Old Irish Guide to Celtic Wisdom
books.tagline: The best of ancient Celtic wisdom from early Ireland, presented together for the first time in modern new translations
books.description:
From an age when warring kings ruled over Ireland and druids still roamed the land, How to Be Noble presents lively new translations of the earliest Irish wisdom literature from the Celtic tradition. For the first time, Philip Freeman has collected these ancient texts from scattered medieval manuscripts and translated them for modern readers. The result is a wonderful collection of pithy sayings that offer timeless wisdom about friends, family, marriage, love, leadership, justice, and finding joy even when life is difficult.

How to Be Noble gathers the best of ancient Celtic wisdom from works that include The Counsels of Cormac , The Testament of Morann, The Sayings of Flann Fína , The Precepts of Cú Chulainn , The Alphabet of Luigne mac Éremóin , The Instruction of Cuscraid , and The Triads of Ireland . Filled with advice for kings and commoners alike, these wry, spiritual, and earthy sayings often connect the nobility of a people’s ruler and their prosperity: “It is through the truth of a ruler that an abundance of fish swim in the streams.” Another saying asserts, “Good fortune is better than treasure.” One observes, “Three sparks that kindle love: a face, a glance, a word.” And another advises, “Don’t be a flea in the ale in a king’s house.”

Complete with an illuminating introduction and the original Old Irish text on facing pages, How to Be Noble is a treasury of memorable sayings that offer fascinating insights into the life and thought of ancient Ireland.
books.bio: King Cormac mac Airt is a legendary figure who is said to have ruled as High King of Ireland from the Hill of Tara in the fourth century CE in the years before St. Patrick. The subject of many tales, he was famed as a wise and generous ruler. Philip Freeman holds the first joint PhD from Harvard University in Celtic languages and classical studies. He is the author of thirty books, including Celtic Spirituality , Celtic Mythology , and a translation of St. Patrick’s letters. He previously held the Fletcher Jones Chair in Humanities at Pepperdine University.

books.title: How to Fish
books.subtitle: An Ancient Guide for Modern Anglers
books.authors: Oppian, James S. Romm, James Prosek
books.tagline: A vivid new translation of an ancient epic about the art—and thrill—of fishing that seems to channel Homer and Melville as it tells the story of a sea adventure for the ages
books.description:
Fishing in the age of Marcus Aurelius could be a heroic endeavor—and not only if you were hunting a whale. How to Fish presents the first English verse translation since the eighteenth century of selections from On Sea Fishing , a little-known Greco-Roman epic poem addressed to an avid fisherman and Stoic philosopher who also happened to be the Emperor of Rome.

The author, Oppian, dramatizes the contest between anglers and their prey in lines that borrow—half-ironically and half-heroically—from the language of warfare found in Homer’s Iliad . Oppian describes many fish species and tells how to catch them. But the longest episode of his poem, a whale hunt—included here in full—displays his epic and tragic techniques at their finest. Unjustly neglected for centuries, this epic fish tale deserves to take its place on the same shelf as other fishing classics such as Walton’s Compleat Angler .

James Romm, a classicist by profession and saltwater fisherman by obsession, provides a lively new translation and an introduction in which he recalls his first encounter with Oppian’s On Sea Fishing as a graduate student and weekend fishing warrior. In addition to the original Greek on facing pages, the volume features illustrations of the poem by acclaimed artist and angler James Prosek, the author of many popular fishing books, including Trout: An Illustrated History.

Recreating the thrill of angling, How to Fish is sure to hook seekers of good fishing and ancient wisdom alike.
books.bio: Oppian was a Greek poet who lived in the mid-second century AD. James S. Romm is the James H. Ottaway Jr. Professor of Classics at Bard College and a saltwater fisherman. His many books include How to Die , How to Keep Your Cool , and How to Live (all Princeton). James Prosek is an acclaimed artist and fisherman whose many books include Trout: An Illustrated History and Ocean Fishes: Paintings of Saltwater Fish .

books.title: No Way on Earth
books.subtitle: How Space Can Help Save and Sustain Our Planet
books.tagline: A bold argument for harnessing space technology to address some of our most daunting challenges here on Earth
books.description:
As a new generation of space missions captures headlines, our gaze is increasingly drawn to worlds far beyond our own. No Way on Earth reveals how the same astonishing technologies applied to space exploration can be used to make life better on Earth, demonstrating how humanity can leverage space and its abundant resources to address planetary-scale issues like climate change, energy security, resource scarcity, and environmental degradation.

Drawing on his decades of experience in the space industry, Les Johnson explains how space-based solar power, lunar and asteroid mining, and in‑space manufacturing can become practical tools for building a more sustainable and prosperous planet. Moving beyond the realm of science fiction, he assesses the technical viability, economic feasibility, and policy implications of these ideas, showing where implementation is possible and where major breakthroughs are still needed. Johnson lays out a practical, step-by-step strategy for creating a resilient, multi-world civilization while prioritizing Earth’s renewal, and calls for public engagement, bipartisan cooperation, entrepreneurial investment, and a multigenerational perspective to make this vision a reality.

At a time when humanity has set its sights on the stars, No Way on Earth asks us to look closer to home, making the persuasive case that investment in space infrastructure is not a luxury but a strategic choice that can lead to a greener and more prosperous future for everyone on the planet.
books.bio: Les Johnson is principal technologist and owner of Infinite Frontiers Consulting and formerly served as chief technology officer at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center. His many nonfiction books include A Traveler’s Guide to the Stars (Princeton) and Graphene: The Superstrong, Superthin, and Superversatile Material That Will Revolutionize the World . His science fiction novels include Mission to Methonē and Saving Proxima .

books.title: The Girl in the Middle
books.subtitle: A Recovered History of the American West
books.tagline: Shortlisted for the Cundill History Prize A haunting image of an unnamed Native child and a recovered story of the American West
books.description:
In 1868, celebrated Civil War photographer Alexander Gardner traveled to Fort Laramie to document the federal government’s treaty negotiations with the Lakota and other tribes of the northern plains. Gardner, known for his iconic portrait of Abraham Lincoln and his visceral pictures of the Confederate dead at Antietam, posed six federal peace commissioners with a young Native girl wrapped in a blanket. The hand-labeled prints carefully name each of the men, but the girl is never identified. As The Girl in the Middle goes in search of her, it draws readers into the entangled lives of the photographer and his subjects.

Martha A. Sandweiss paints a riveting portrait of the turbulent age of Reconstruction and westward expansion. She follows Gardner from his birthplace in Scotland to the American frontier, as his dreams of a utopian future across the Atlantic fall to pieces. She recounts the lives of William S. Harney, a slave-owning Union general who earned the Lakota name “Woman Killer,” and Samuel F. Tappan, an abolitionist who led the investigation into the Sand Creek massacre. And she identifies Sophie Mousseau, the girl in Gardner’s photograph, whose life swerved in unexpected directions as American settlers pushed into Indian Country and the federal government confined Native peoples to reservations.

Spinning a spellbinding historical tale from a single enigmatic image, The Girl in the Middle reveals how the American nation grappled with what kind of country it would be as it expanded westward in the aftermath of the Civil War.
books.bio: Martha A. Sandweiss is professor emerita of history at Princeton University, where she is founding director of the Princeton & Slavery Project. She is the award-winning author of many books, including Passing Strange: A Gilded Age Tale of Love and Deception across the Color Line and Print the Legend: Photography and the American West .

praise.q: [Sandweiss’s] deeply researched book takes its title from an arresting black-and-white photograph of the peace commissioners gathered at Fort Laramie in 1868. . . . Sandweiss is an elegant writer who knows how to craft a satisfying story.
praise.by: Melanie Kirkpatrick, Wall Street Journal

praise.q: Part detective story, part traditional history book, The Girl in the Middle brings to life an often overlooked part of US history. . . . A richly textured view of America both during and in the decades directly after its brutal civil war. . . . A window into the lives of ordinary people at a time and in a place when everyone was on the move and constantly reinventing themselves. It is also a testament to the broader suffering that occurred as the American government repeatedly broke its promises to the continent’s original inhabitants.
praise.by: Brooke Masters, Financial Times

praise.q: Sandweiss’s forensic investigation of a single photograph widens the aperture to depict an astonishingly intertwined frontier society where everyone—soldier, trader, photographer, man, woman, Native, mixed-race, or white—was connected to most everyone else. The result is a fascinating snapshot of this “oddly intimate” world, a bubbling cauldron of people constantly on the move, in contact or in conflict, their lives beset by unremitting public and familial violence.
praise.by: Alix Christie, American Scholar

praise.q: Compelling. . . . A truly revealing image of American empire.
praise.by: Literary Hub

praise.q: Sandweiss. . . shows her extraordinary ability as a historian-detective.
praise.by: David Steinberg, Albuquerque Journal

praise.q: If all books were like The Girl in the Middle , perhaps more undergraduates would become history majors. . . . Highly recommended.
praise.by: Choice

praise.q: Fascinating. . . . this book is a model of historical detective work.
praise.by: Evan C. Rothera, Civil War Monitor

praise.q: A totally absorbing narrative, serving as a model of collective memory and in-depth research that folklorists should appreciate, if not emulate.
praise.by: James I. Deutsch, Western Folklore

praise.q: Riveting. . . . Sandweiss effectively details a previously unknown life and insists that the rest of us could do better.
praise.by: Anne Hyde, Western Historical Quarterly

praise.q: A masterful work of recovery, reconstruction, and research.
praise.by: Elizabeth DeWolfe, Journal of Arizona History

books.title: The Improvers
books.subtitle: The Schuster Siblings and the Making of Modern Britain
books.tagline: A riveting generational saga of a remarkable family that embodied the cultural and intellectual aspirations of late-Victorian Britain
books.description:
From 1870 to 1930, the scientist Arthur Schuster and his siblings, lawyer Ernest, banker Felix, and philanthropist Paula, were among the most prominent figures in Britain. Born German and Jewish, just two generations removed from the Frankfurt ghetto, they built a dazzling network of friends and collaborators that included H. G. Wells, Marie Stopes, Octavia Hill, Chaim Weizmann, Ernest Rutherford, and Lionel de Rothschild and they worked alongside them to change their times. The Improvers is a richly detailed portrait of four extraordinary individuals and the transformational age in which they lived.

Drawing on a newly discovered archive of privately held diaries, letters, and photographs, Dehn Gilmore chronicles the Schuster family’s early struggles to assimilate into British society, their personal and professional triumphs, and their changing fortunes during and after the First World War. She describes their many accomplishments, from advancing women’s rights and building large tracts of public housing, to coining the term “anti-matter,” chasing eclipses around the world, dictating national financial policy, and promoting religious free-thinking. She shows, too, how the Schuster siblings embodied the values and principles of late-Victorian liberal thought.

Beautifully written, The Improvers is an engaging, multifaceted account of a family that rose from humble beginnings to scale the heights of England’s intellectual, political, and economic life, and whose hopes and disappointments mirrored those of the era they helped define.
books.bio: Dehn Gilmore is professor of English at the California Institute of Technology and the author of The Victorian Novel and the Space of Art: Fictional Form on Display . She is the great-great-granddaughter of Arthur Schuster.

books.title: Two, Three, Four, and More
books.subtitle: The Mathematically Special Dimensions
books.tagline: A beautifully illustrated exploration of the remarkable world of mathematics in low dimensions
books.description:
Highly valued results in mathematics are often general: proofs in all dimensions, solutions for all degrees of polynomials. Yet great richness can be found in particular cases. John Stillwell presents a visual panorama of the multitudes that live in dimensions 2, 3, and 4—and a few higher dimensions—through the interplay of geometry, topology, and algebra.

We tend to think of the dimensions 2, 3, and 4 as the dimensions of our physical experience in space and time, but they are also of exceptional mathematical interest. Together with the degrees 2, 3, and 4 of equations, they cover some of the most remarkable mathematical objects and pose problems ranging from easy, to hard, to unsolvable. Each chapter of this engaging book focuses on a dimension or degree, starting at 2 dimensions and ascending to 4 dimensions and then beyond to objects such as the Leech lattice in 24 dimensions. The gradual increase in dimension reveals what is gained and what is lost with a bit more space to work in. Along the way, Stillwell brings the mathematics to life through rich examples, engaging historical context, and vivid anecdotes about the mathematicians who uncovered surprising solutions—or revealed why some problems can’t be solved.

With hundreds of illustrations, Two, Three, Four, and More is an illuminating mathematical tour by one of the discipline’s leading expositors, revealing how these intriguing special cases underpin some of the deepest ideas in mathematics.
books.bio: John Stillwell is emeritus professor of mathematics at the University of San Francisco and an affiliate of the School of Mathematics at Monash University in Melbourne. His many books include The Story of Proof: Logic and the History of Mathematics ; Reverse Mathematics: Proofs from the Inside Out ; and Elements of Mathematics: From Euclid to Gödel (all Princeton).

books.title: Batpedia
books.subtitle: A Brief Compendium of Chiropteran Curiosities
books.tagline: An enchanting, fact-filled treasury for the bat lover in everyone, from A to Z
books.description:
Batpedia is a fun and eclectic collection of lore and learning about these elusive denizens of the night sky. Featuring nearly one hundred alphabetical entries on everything from prehistoric bat fossils to cultural icons like Batman and Dracula, this enticing compendium takes you on an unforgettable journey into the hidden world of these astonishing flying mammals.

Nancy Simmons dispels common myths about bats, explains the traits that make them so special, describes how bats contribute to our ecosystems, and discusses how scientists like herself use the latest technology to study bats. With more than fifteen hundred living species, bats make their livings in a variety of ways. Simmons introduces you to bats from around the world, including charming fruit-eating bats, bats that sip nectar from flowers, fishing bats, carnivorous bats, and yes, even vampire bats. She discusses key traits like flight, echolocation, roosting, and nocturnal habits, and highlights the current threats to bats and steps you can take to help with bat conservation. This entertaining and informative book also describes places where you can visit to safely watch flights of bats emerge to go hunting in the evening.

With captivating drawings by wildlife artist and author Fiona Reid, Batpedia is an engaging and enlightening celebration of these marvelous but misunderstood creatures.

Features a cloth cover with an elaborate foil-stamped design
books.bio: Nancy B. Simmons is curator emerita in the Department of Mammalogy at the American Museum of Natural History, where she continues to lead field expeditions and conduct research on both living and fossil bats. Her books include Bats: A World of Science and Mystery . Fiona Reid is a writer and artist whose books include A Field Guide to Mammals of North America .

books.title: Catpedia
books.subtitle: A Brief Compendium of Feline Curiosities
books.tagline: A captivating treasury of feline fact and fancy—from A to Z
books.description:
Catpedia is a delightful and wide-ranging collection of lore, science, and mischief about an animal that has captivated humans for thousands of years. Featuring dozens of entries on everything from ancient Egyptian cat worship to feline internet celebrities, this irresistible compendium takes you deep into the strange, endearing, and often hilarious world of the domestic cat.

Jonathan Losos dispels common myths about cats, explains the evolutionary quirks that make them such singular companions, and unpacks the science behind behaviors every cat owner has puzzled over. Why do cats knead blankets? What triggers the zoomies? Why does a cat’s belly pouch swing when it runs? Losos answers these and other questions, drawing on veterinary science, evolutionary biology, and feline genetics to explain the anatomy and instincts behind everyday cat behavior. Along the way, he traces the cat’s journey from wild predator to pampered housemate, exploring how millennia of loose domestication shaped both their bodies and their famously independent personalities.

With charming drawings by Kelly Chudler that bring the entries to life, Catpedia is a celebration of the world’s most beloved—and most misunderstood—companion animal.

Features a cloth cover with an elaborate foil-stamped design
books.bio: Jonathan B. Losos is an evolutionary biologist at Washington University in St. Louis and the author of many books, including The Cat’s Meow: How Cats Evolved from the Savanna to Your Sofa . Kelly Chudler is a multidisciplinary artist and musician and the illustrator of books such as Dogpedia and Neuropedia (both Princeton).

books.title: Sensory Gardens
books.subtitle: Designing for Healing, Joy, and Exploration
books.tagline: A hands-on guide to designing sensory gardens, with practical tips for creating outdoor spaces at home and in communities that enrich the senses and heal the mind and body
books.description:
While all gardens offer sensory appeal, intentionally designed sensory gardens balance our senses and support the needs of people with challenges such as depression, anxiety, ADHD and autism, PTSD, mobility concerns, and age-related cognitive issues. Written by an occupational therapist and landscape architect, Sensory Gardens makes these design strategies accessible for everyone, offering scalable solutions for outdoor spaces ranging from balconies and backyards to neighborhoods, public parks, and community gardens.

Amy Wagenfeld and Daniel Winterbottom blend innovative design ideas with digestible information about the eight sensory systems—our five basic senses plus body position and movement, balance, and internal awareness such as hunger, thirst, and heart rate. Attentive to the realities of people’s varied sensory capacities and preferences, Wagenfeld and Winterbottom artfully explain how to create personalized landscapes that comfort, convey meaning, and reconnect us with the earth and ourselves. They provide thirty-five sensory-specific projects along with “Spotlights” that share additional outdoor activities, examples of standout gardens, and stories from people who have experienced sensory enrichment in nature.

Beautifully illustrated, Sensory Gardens empowers gardeners and design professionals to create outdoor spaces that nourish the senses, steady the mind, and promote well-being.
books.bio: Amy Wagenfeld is an occupational therapist and principal of Amy Wagenfeld | Design. She is on faculty in the Department of Landscape Architecture at the University of Washington. Daniel Winterbottom is a practicing landscape architect and professor in the Department of Landscape Architecture at the University of Washington. They have designed, cotaught, and written together for more than a decade, and are the authors of Therapeutic Gardens: Design for Healing Spaces.

books.title: Supplying the Slave Trade
books.subtitle: European Enslavers and African Markets in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic
books.tagline: How European enslavers tried to meet African consumer demand for their trade goods in the eighteenth-century transatlantic slave trade
books.description:
The enormous evil that was the transatlantic slave trade resulted from millions of commercial actions. In Atlantic Africa, European enslavers and African merchants exchanged bundles of goods for small numbers of enslaved people over and over again. To purchase captives, European enslavers needed to meet the tastes and preferences of their African trading partners, which varied over time and across the coast. How did they know what their African customers wanted?

Anne Ruderman’s extensive research into the transatlantic slave trade reveals how enslavers obtained information about consumer demand from the African coast, worked with suppliers to acquire the right trade goods, and then brought those goods to the markets where they were wanted. African consumer demand shaped the transatlantic slave trade, both on the African coast and deep in the European interior, as European enslavers ranged far and wide to get the trade goods their partners desired.

The legacy of race-based slavery continues to define socioeconomic structures, institutions, opportunities, and daily life in modern Europe, Africa, and the Americas. The transatlantic slave trade set this process of racial inequity in motion. And behind the commerce in captives were the trade goods that made it possible.
books.bio: Anne Ruderman is an assistant professor in the Department of Economic History at the London School of Economics and Political Science. She lives in London, UK.

praise.q: This groundbreaking study of market knowledge in the transatlantic slave trade provides a powerful analysis of the mundane everyday acts that make historic transformations possible—and immense human suffering foreseeable.
praise.by: Vincent Brown, author of Tacky’s Revolt: The Story of an Atlantic Slave War
praise.cred: author of Tacky’s Revolt: The Story of an Atlantic Slave War

praise.q: Deeply researched and elegantly written, this sophisticated account offers profound and transformative insights on the material histories that underlie the traffic in slave on the African Atlantic coast. It is a giant step in the history of the slave trade, the Atlantic world, and Europe’s relationship with Africa.
praise.by: Cécile Fromont, author of Images on a Mission in Early Modern Kongo and Angola
praise.cred: author of Images on a Mission in Early Modern Kongo and Angola

books.title: The Quran in the World
books.subtitle: A History of Islam's Sacred Book
books.tagline: The fascinating story of the Quran—how it became the book it is today and how Muslim views of it have evolved over the past 1,400 years
books.description:
The Quran, like most great books, has a history. It went from a largely oral recitation in a region with limited writing and literacy to being the centerpiece of an extraordinary literary and intellectual culture, not only in theology and law but also poetry, prose, and art. In The Quran in the World , Bruce Fudge presents a new history of Islam’s sacred book and how it has been used, shaped, and interpreted from its origin in seventh-century Arabia to today.

The Quran in the World describes how the Quran was put in writing and made into a book, and how Muslim scholars determined how it should be written and recited. It recounts how they developed sophisticated ways of analyzing its language and meanings, how they came to understand it as the “Word of God,” and how Muslims began to see it as an aesthetic miracle, a literary masterpiece no human could have produced. The book also charts Western Europe’s engagement with the Quran, from the first Latin translation in the twelfth century through the Reformation and Enlightenment.

In the modern period, The Quran in the World chronicles Islamic debates about printing and translating the Quran, and its use by Muslim and non-Muslim poets and novelists. The book concludes by tracing how modernity and colonialism challenged traditional understandings of the Quran—and how Muslim thinkers responded.

Vivid and accessible, The Quran in the World is a compelling account of the dramatic, eventful, and colorful history of the sacred book of Islam.
books.bio: Bruce Fudge is professor of Arabic at the University of Geneva. He is the author of Qur’anic Hermeneutics and the translator of A Hundred and One Nights and Sonallah Ibrahim’s The Turban and the Hat .

books.title: Alfred Russel Wallace in Paradise
books.subtitle: The Odyssey of a Victorian Evolutionist in His Own Words
books.authors: Richard Milner, George Beccaloni, Tim Laman
books.tagline: A breathtaking visual narrative of the legendary naturalist’s adventures and pioneering contributions to the life sciences
books.description:
In old age, Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913) became arguably the most famous scientist of his day. He and his senior colleague, Charles Darwin, had independently discovered the theory of evolution by natural selection, which they jointly published in 1858. Yet this genius’s legacy was overshadowed by Darwin’s for more than a century. Alfred Russel Wallace in Paradise paints an unprecedented portrait of the indefatigable explorer and hero of science whose self-effacing modesty contributed to his long obscurity.

Wallace pioneered our understanding of the mechanisms of evolution, humanity’s place in nature, the worldwide distribution of plants and animals, and tribal cultures. Anthropologist Richard Milner scoured Wallace’s journals and papers to recount the naturalist’s voyages to the Amazon and Malay Archipelago and his return to England—entirely in Wallace’s own words—while tracing the origins of his ideas on evolution, biogeography, animal coloration, and sexual selection. Newly illustrated maps, personal letters, and recent photographs of wildlife and tropical ecosystems bring his travels and theories vividly to life.

With sumptuous images by award-winning National Geographic photographer Tim Laman and other artists, Alfred Russel Wallace in Paradise is a visually spectacular account of Wallace’s journeys and his enduring insights into biodiversity and evolution.
books.bio: Richard Milner is an anthropologist and historian of science whose books include Darwin’s Universe: Evolution from A to Z and Charles R. Knight: The Artist Who Saw Through Time . A former senior editor at the American Museum of Natural History’s magazine, he has appeared on Discovery, History, Animal Planet, and NPR, and was profiled by The New York Times . George Beccaloni is an entomologist, evolutionary biologist, and historian of science specializing in Alfred Russel Wallace. He is director of the Wallace Correspondence Project and has authored numerous publications about Wallace and his theory of natural selection. Tim Laman is an acclaimed wildlife photojournalist, ornithologist, and filmmaker.

praise.q: Richard Milner’s Alfred Russel Wallace in Paradise is the most visually stunning treatment of Wallace’s life and thought yet produced!”—James T. Costa, Director, Highlands Biological Station of Western Carolina University, and author of Radical by Nature: The Revolutionary Life of Alfred Russel Wallace

A wonderful photographic essay, lavishly illustrated with stunning, modern images of wildlife and historic scenes that Wallace explored, celebrating the diversity of the natural world and the remarkable insights he brought to it.
praise.by: Janet Browne, Aramont Professor of the History of Science at Harvard University
praise.cred: Aramont Professor of the History of Science at Harvard University

praise.q: Wallace has come to life! His wise words combine with these astounding images to give us a whole new appreciation of his twelve extraordinary years of scientific exploration. A magnificent achievement!”—Andrew Berry, Historian of Science and Wallace Scholar, Lecturer on Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, Harvard University

books.title: Modern Christian Theology
books.subtitle: An Intellectual History
books.tagline: A sweeping history of how Christian theologians have grappled with a rapidly changing modern world
books.description:
From the Enlightenment to the present day, Christian thinkers have labored to understand how ancient doctrines and sacred traditions might speak to a world reshaped by revolution, scientific advancement, political upheaval, and global transformation. Modern Christian Theology traces how theology has responded to—and itself been shaped by—the modern age.

Covering more than two centuries, Thomas Albert Howard charts the development of Protestant and Catholic theology against the backdrop of major historical forces such as the French Revolution, industrialization, nationalism, socialism, historical-critical scholarship, secularization, the ecumenical and missionary movements, two world wars, the Cold War, decolonization, the civil rights movement, modern feminism, and the dramatic worldwide expansion of Christianity. Rarely have both Protestant and Catholic theology been treated together on this scale. Rather than focusing solely on major figures and their texts, Howard situates modern Christian theology within the broader intellectual and institutional contexts in which it unfolded, highlighting the evolving relationship between the church and the modern university.

Beautifully written and panoramic in scope, Modern Christian Theology shows how traditions rooted in the ancient church and monastery have sought to engage modernity’s deepest challenges while adapting to an increasingly pluralistic and interconnected world.
books.bio: Thomas Albert Howard is professor of humanities and history and the Phyllis and Richard Duesenberg Chair in Christian Ethics at Valparaiso University. His books include Broken Altars: Secularist Violence in Modern History ; The Pope and the Professor: Pius IX, Ignaz von Döllinger, and the Quandary of the Modern Age ; and Remembering the Reformation: An Inquiry into the Meanings of Protestantism .

books.title: No Topic Off Limits
books.subtitle: Teaching Polarizing Issues in Higher Education
books.tagline: A practical, evidence-based guide that empowers educators to embrace constructive disagreement as an essential tool for teaching controversial topics
books.description:
Amid political pressure, campus unrest, and growing institutional risk aversion, university educators are retreating from the most contested issues of our time, from race and gender to climate change, religion, sexuality, and political violence. No Topic Off Limits makes the case that teaching controversial subjects is not a choice but a democratic responsibility. Drawing on interviews with more than seventy educators across the globe and anchored in the messy realities of the classroom, this invaluable guide offers a tool kit for teaching polarizing subjects to college students, demonstrating how constructive disagreement can become a source of intellectual growth, creative possibility, and unexpected connection.

The university classroom remains one of the last civic spaces where students can grapple seriously with people whose values, politics, and experiences differ sharply from their own. Daniel Kupfert Heller argues that the retreat from controversy in higher education comes at a dangerous price, leaving students unequipped to engage in the difficult disagreements that democratic life demands. In this book, he shows educators how to create inclusive classrooms where students learn to challenge assumptions, build trust, navigate emotions, and engage meaningfully with diverse perspectives. Rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach, he lays out a set of strategies that educators can adapt to their own contexts, disciplines, and students. Along the way, Heller shares engaging profiles such as a Christian sociologist in Malaysia teaching LGBTQ+ history under laws that criminalize his syllabus, a bioethicist in Tehran inviting students to debate voluntary euthanasia, and literary scholar in Warsaw leading conversations about reproductive ethics in a nation where the topic still tears families apart.

Informed by cognitive psychology, neuroscience, deliberative pedagogy, and trauma-informed teaching, No Topic Off Limits is an essential resource for any educator who believes their students are capable of more—and who wants the tools to prove it.
books.bio: Daniel Kupfert Heller is a senior lecturer and codirector of the Brave Conversations Project at Monash University. He is the author of Jabotinsky’s Children: Polish Jews and the Rise of Right-Wing Zionism (Princeton).

books.title: Reprogram
books.subtitle: How Feminism Can Transform AI
books.tagline: How feminist activists, thinkers, and artists are challenging AI’s status quo and envisioning new and better ways to design and use technology
books.description:
For too long, AI has been the domain of tech bros and their wild fantasies. From gender-based discrimination in the AI workforce to subservient, feminized assistants like Siri and Alexa, the industry and its products are failing women. Reprogram draws on feminism’s immense creative, diagnostic, and imaginative power to chart a better path forward.

Building on a long history of feminists as inventors, creators, and change-makers, Kerry McInerney and Eleanor Drage showcase the work of inspiring activists, thinkers, and technologists who are transforming a broken industry in innovative and unusual ways. Guided by key feminist ideas, McInerney and Drage demonstrate how feminists are rewriting the rules about whose voices and experiences matter in AI and who and what it should be for. From computer scientists who are programming beyond the gender binary to union workers who are collectively standing up to Big Tech’s overreach, this book shares a hopeful vision for AI, one grounded in equality, solidarity, and justice.

Cutting against apathy, fear, and disempowerment, Reprogram explains why changing AI isn’t just necessary but possible, inspiring us to imagine an altogether different future using the knowledge and perspectives that feminism can offer.
books.bio: Kerry McInerney is a Lecturer at the University of Auckland’s School of Computer Science and an Associate Fellow at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence. Eleanor Drage is a Senior Research Fellow at the University of Cambridge, where she is Co-Director of the Narratives and Justice Programme at the Leverhulme Centre. She is the host of The Good Robot Podcast and the author of What If We Got AI Right? McInerney and Drage are the coeditors of The Good Robot and Feminist AI and were the cohosts of The Good Robot Podcast from 2021 to 2025.

books.title: A Register of Wording
books.subtitle: Martine De Maeseneer Architects (MDMA)
books.authors: Martine De Maeseneer and Dirk Van den Brande Edited by Jayne Kelley
books.tagline: Explores the theory behind the work of Brussels-based practice Martine De Maeseneer Architects.
books.description:
Martine De Maeseneer and Dirk Van den Brande, principals of Brussels-based practice Martine De Maeseneer Architects (MDMA), are “not compulsive builders.” From the outset in 1988, they have advanced an architecture self-consciously embedded in text, oscillating between theorization and realization. In their award-winning built and conceptual work, MDMA's interest is in spatial organizations that initiate nonlinear stories and shift identities.

The first of two intended volumes, A Register of Wording assembles the practice’s text-based production to show how writing establishes a fertile—if unstable—ground for design. The book is more than a presentation of words: it unfolds thought expansively, across pages and decades, meandering yet distinctively committed to the search for a wide field of motives and plots for architecture.

It offers previously published essays conjuring the energy of the 1990s and early 2000s alongside unpublished explorations that extend, recast, and complexify earlier lines of thinking. Departing from an early analysis of existing buildings, MDMA’s texts become more autonomous over time, invoking an unexpected array of visual, creative, and philosophical references. Sources are sampled, interrogated, circled around, juxtaposed, and played with to provide a distinctive perspective, without shying away from provocation.

books.title: Black Abstraction in Architecture
books.subtitle: Reviews
books.tagline: Studies the history of abstraction in architecture and posits its subversive potential for contemporary Black creators.
books.description:
In Black Abstraction in Architecture , Sean Canty charts the evolution of architectural abstraction from its roots in Euclidean geometry, through its utilization as a vehicle for colonial expansion, to its contemporary reappropriation by Black cultural practitioners. Canty’s comprehensive historical and critical scrutiny reveals the paradoxical nature of abstraction as both a mechanism of marginalization and a potent instrument for socio-political discourse and renewal. By focusing on the transformative contributions of David Hammons, Amanda Williams, and Theaster Gates, this essay illustrates how these artists and architects employ abstraction to question, reinterpret, and enrich architectural standards, embedding within them a rich tapestry of cultural, political, and societal narratives.

Canty’s approach not only subverts traditional architectural frameworks but also illuminates the potential of abstraction to cultivate a more equitable and introspective architectural conversation. He advocates for a methodology that is at once inventive, inclusive, and sensitive to the intricate interplay of history, identity, and form.

Read More about Black Abstraction in Architecture

Read Less about Black Abstraction in Architecture

praise.q: On the heels of Adrienne Edwards’s influential Art in America essay “Blackness in Abstraction” (2015), Sean Canty—an architect and Harvard professor—turns the question from painting toward architecture. The book focuses on David Hammons, Amanda Williams, and Theaster Gates while arguing for a new methodology.
praise.by: Art in America, "7 Books We're Looking Forward to in January"

books.title: Late Modernism and Other Latenesses
books.subtitle: Architecture, Materials, and Media after Time
books.authors: Edited by Chris Grimley, Michael Kubo, Enrique Ramirez, and Mimi Zeiger
books.tagline: Reflects on the modern impulse for rushed production, expansion, and consumption.
books.description:
Hurry up, we’re late: The early decades of the twenty-first century have demonstrated that we are already behind. Concepts like Moore’s Law, accelerationism, hyperloop, and rapid news cycles push the notion that speed is the answer. Modern-day futurists argue that salvation lies in technology and outer space, while architecture has strived to keep pace with cultural events through the late twentieth century and into the present, even as we face environmental crises and build our lives around the remnants of late modernism.

Late Modernism and Other Latenesses offers an understanding of the contradictory impulses in architecture and culture from the 1960s through the 1980s, a period rich in utopian visions and revolution but also burdened by global expansionism and crisis. Topical essays explore aspects of lateness, referring to concrete buildings and architectural projects, and key texts from the period. The concept of lateness is used not as a backward-looking tool but as one that is simply behind the beat. The book is a reaction and rebuttal to the surging flows of finance, media, and culture that influence architectural production and its aligned disciplines, seeking missing conditions that might redefine architecture's relationship to its cultural moment.

books.title: Maurice Cox
books.subtitle: The Soul of the City
books.authors: Edited by Maurice Cox, Maria Villalobos Hernandez, and Michelangelo Sabatino
books.tagline: The first book on architect Maurice Cox’s dedication to reimagining the American city.
books.description:
Maurice Cox, architect, urban designer, educator, and civic leader, has for more than three decades been working passionately to regenerate American cities through the lens of social justice and design excellence. He does so against considerable odds while achieving remarkable economic and social results. As a visionary leader in cities across America and beyond, Cox has occupied diverse roles ranging from professor and city commissioner to mayor.

This book is the first to present and discuss his multifaced achievements for a diverse audience of academics, community leaders, and professionals. Its seven chapters, focused chronologically on the cities—New York, Florence, Charlottesville, Washington D.C., New Orleans, Detroit, and Chicago—in which he lived and operated, consist of a series of interviews with Cox and collaborators with the stated goal of identifying recurring concepts and strategies, presented against the background of changing discourse and practice of regenerative approaches to American cities.

Combining archival materials, including Cox’s sketchbooks, with period and contemporary photography and artwork, this volume sheds light on the complex process associated with redrawing a city from the ground up. It provides hope and guidance for future generations of city-makers who seek to continue in the approach so fearlessly spearheaded by Maurice Cox.

books.title: Birds of Aotearoa New Zealand
books.subtitle: A Complete ID Guide
books.tagline: A comprehensive, richly detailed photo ID guide to New Zealand’s birds
books.description:
New Zealand is home to spectacular and iconic birdlife, and it is also considered to be the “seabird capital of the world.” Birds of Aotearoa New Zealand is the definitive field guide to New Zealand’s birds, offering an unprecedented level of detail, both on endemic species and on difficult species groups such as shorebirds and seabirds. It draws on the latest information on ID traits to facilitate identification of species and subspecies, breeding, nonbreeding, juvenile, and immature plumages as well as geographic variation and colour morphs. This premier guide features up-to-date distribution maps using data from the New Zealand Bird Atlas and photo contributions from New Zealand’s finest bird photographers.

Covers every species recorded in New Zealand, including birds found in the sub-Antarctic islands and the Ross Sea, as well as taxa not yet recorded but likely to occur in New Zealand

Features around 2,500 stunning photos showing unprecedented detail and variation in plumages and morphology, including exclusive photos of rarely photographed birds and some of the best available images of Southern-Ocean seabirds

In-depth species accounts include information about each species’ morphology, status in New Zealand, habitat, diet, breeding, and conservation status

Provides figures of plumage progression and side-by-side comparisons of difficult species to aid identification

Includes Māori bird names
books.bio: D. Matthias Dehling is a researcher specializing in the community ecology, macroecology, and functional roles of birds. He has worked in a range of ecosystems, from the Amazon rainforest to Antarctica, and he has travelled extensively throughout Aotearoa New Zealand studying the country’s avifauna.

books.title: Enemy Establishments
books.subtitle: How the Hundred-Year War to Control America's Institutions Polarized Its Politics
books.tagline: A major new interpretation of political polarization in America that traces its origins to fundamentally incompatible constitutional visions
books.description:
American politics seem intractably polarized; no-holds-barred political conflict has engulfed not only electoral contests but disputes over courts, universities, expertise, and the administrative state. How did our politics become so gladiatorial? In Enemy Establishments , Calvin TerBeek argues that the conventional wisdom about polarization, centering on political parties, mistakes an outcome for a cause; in fact, parties were among the last major institutions to polarize. TerBeek traces the origins of polarization to the early twentieth century, when the Progressive project remade the Constitution, built the modern administrative state, and embedded new understandings of law, expertise, and governance across an interconnected array of institutions including courts, agencies, universities, and the professions—provoking a fierce conservative response.

Drawing on a wealth of untapped archival materials, TerBeek shows that conservatives targeted these newly reformulated institutions as their collective enemy—what they called the Establishment. They quickly conjured its mirror image, a set of parallel institutions that became a rival Establishment. These two Establishments formed the axes of polarization as competing elites waged protracted institutional warfare long before roll-call votes diverged and party coalitions solidified. TerBeek argues that liberals’ certainty in their own institutional authority is as implicated in our polarized politics as conservatism’s drive to displace it. Anchored in incompatible constitutional visions, each experienced the other’s authority as illegitimate. The century-long struggle that still embroils Americans today is not over what the state should do but what the state fundamentally is.
books.bio: Calvin TerBeek is assistant professor of government at Claremont McKenna College.

books.title: How the Brain Finds Its Way
books.subtitle: A New Theory of Human Navigation
books.tagline: The secrets of human navigation, from Polynesian sailors who navigate without a compass to Inuit trekkers in the Arctic tundra
books.description:
How did humans come to occupy virtually every corner of the earth? How did Polynesian sailors navigate thousands of miles without compasses or sextants? Why does one person get lost two blocks from home while another treks fearlessly through the forest? The secrets of navigation are intimately connected to our survival as a species, but current science is limited in explaining them. In How the Brain Finds Its Way , Arne Ekstrom offers a new theory of human navigation that emphasizes the interaction between brain and behavior. Theories to explain navigation are largely based on lab studies of rats and rely on the metaphor of the map. Yet, Ekstrom points out, much of human navigation predated the invention of maps. He proposes a novel way to think about navigation that focuses on the actions of humans in the wild.

Polynesian and native navigators, whom Ekstrom extensively researched and interviewed for this book, demonstrate a highly developed and intricate ability to detect and act on cues in nature. Human navigation, he shows, can involve a range of different environmental conditions and a number of different strategies. Ekstrom argues that the best way to understand human spatial navigation is through the lens of probability and dynamic feedback. He explores ancient migration; the master navigators of Polynesia, Melanesia, and Micronesia; wilderness wayfinding and the dangers of getting off the trail; the effect of Alzheimer’s disease on the ability to navigate, and the navigational capacities of taxi drivers. Humans, Ekstrom shows, have a unique ability to develop the tools they need to explore and survive in a range of different environments.
books.bio: Arne D. Ekstrom is professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of Arizona, where he directs the Human Spatial Cognition Lab. He is the coauthor of Human Spatial Navigation (Princeton).

books.title: Becoming Métis in Northern Alberta
books.subtitle: Be the first to know
books.tagline: A study of the northern Métis nation in Canada through the lens of ethnogenesis.
books.description:
In recent years, much has been written about the Métis of southern Canada, an Indigenous community that began with those who lived at the Red River and the historic buffalo hunters of the Plains. Whether implicitly or explicitly, these groups have come to define the identity and culture of all Métis in the Northwest. This book challenges the prevailing discourse about “Métis-ness” by considering the circumstances of the northern Métis, many of whom white Canadians thought seemed little different from “Indians,” or First Nations, until government policies made a distinction between Métis and First Nations peoples to deal with them separately and on different terms. In so doing, it draws upon literature related to ethnogenesis, a topic often overlooked by those writing about the development of Métis identities. In addition, Becoming Métis in Northeastern Alberta examines the evolution of legal distinctions between First Nations and Métis—the “dual paradigms” model operative today. It shows how the dominant discourse about “the Métis” has informed legislation and policy vis-à-vis Métis communities, with a special focus on Alberta. It also reviews a series of key pieces of legislation (federal and provincial) and judicial decisions that have had an impact on the situation of northern Métis, notably those in northeastern Alberta.
